title: Oracle is Leasing 100k AI Chips to Chinese Giant Tencent: Report
content:
The US can restrict where an NVIDIA chip is shipped without necessarily preventing a Chinese company from remotely accessing that chip's computing power once it is installed in another country.

Oracle and Chinese tech giant Tencent have agreed to a five-year lease worth $7 billion across the former’s data centres in south-east Asia, the Financial Times reported.

This marks Tencent’s largest overseas lease deal, and Oracle is providing access to 1,00,000 ‘advanced AI chips’ that are otherwise not available in China.

This development comes as the US tightens restrictions on China’s access to advanced AI chips, particularly NVIDIA’s high-end accelerators.

The country has restricted the export, reexport and in-country transfer of advanced computing chips and systems to China and certain Chinese-headquartered entities.

Yet, the Tencent deal illustrates a significant complication in those controls: the US can restrict where an NVIDIA chip is shipped without necessarily preventing a Chinese company from remotely accessing that chip’s computing power once it is installed in another country.

Under the current export-control framework, a Chinese company cannot simply have a restricted NVIDIA accelerator shipped to a data centre in China.

But if the accelerator is legitimately installed in a data centre in a country where its export is permitted, a company can potentially rent that data centre's computing capacity and send workloads to the GPU remotely.

A recent Reuters legal analysis describes almost exactly this scenario: a Chinese company could potentially become an infrastructure-as-a-service customer at a Malaysian data centre and remotely use advanced computing hardware it could not receive in China.

The report notes that US rules currently do not comprehensively prohibit this kind of ordinary remote access.

Tencent is not alone. ByteDance and Alibaba are already among the largest Chinese users of south-east Asian data-centre capacity.

Chinese companies have increasingly reserved large amounts of capacity in Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia, Thailand and other regional markets as domestic access to advanced GPUs has become more constrained.

Tencent develops the Hunyuan family of AI models and has been expanding into agentic AI, with products such as WorkBuddy, CodeBuddy and Yuanbao designed to execute multi-step tasks rather than simply generate responses.

Its latest Hy3 and Hy4 models have been trained and optimised specifically for reasoning, coding, and agentic workloads.

title: OpenAI, Synopsys Announce GPT-Synopsys for AI Chip Design
content:
The model is said to run on OpenAI’s infrastructure and will directly operate Synopsys EDA tools.

Semiconductor design software giant Synopsys has announced a partnership with OpenAI.

The companies have entered into a multi-year agreement to develop GPT-Synopsys, built to use Synopsys’ EDA tools to perform chip design and verification

This also includes a revenue-sharing agreement, along with efforts to make the model available to customers worldwide.

“We're bringing frontier intelligence to chip design to help more companies develop and accelerate advanced silicon, while maintaining the rigour and trust required for manufacturing success,” said Sassine Ghazi, President and CEO of Synopsys.

The company said that GPT-Synopsys will directly operate Synopsys’ tools, while engineers will specify design objectives. Agents will run the tools, interpret results, implement changes, and iterate towards verified outcomes for engineering reviews.

The model is said to run on OpenAI’s infrastructure.

It will also be integrated with Synopsys’ existing AI platforms—Synopsys.ai and Synopsys Autopilot.

Released only a few days ago, Autopilot is Synopsys’ platform for orchestrating autonomous engineering workflows. It gives agents access to engineering context, tools, memory, and governance, allowing them to plan and execute multi-step tasks rather than simply assist engineers with individual actions.

Synopsys said the platform is currently in more than 50 customer engagements, with general availability planned for late 2026.

Synopsys.ai, launched in 2023, is the company’s broader portfolio of AI-powered semiconductor design tools, using AI across workflows such as chip design, verification, testing, and optimisation.

For OpenAI, this marks another milestone in using AI to design chips. In June, the company unveiled Jalapeño, its first custom AI accelerator, developed with Broadcom. The chip went from initial design to manufacturing tape-out in just nine months. OpenAI said its models accelerated parts of the design and optimisation process.

“We're using our most advanced technology to improve the systems that power AI,” said Greg Brockman, President and Co-Founder of OpenAI. “With Synopsys, we're bringing that work to chip design, helping engineers explore more designs and get to a working chip faster. By helping them build better chips, we can build better AI and bring it to more people.”

title: Infosys Expands ABN AMRO Partnership With Focus on Enterprise AI
content:
This comes as the Dutch bank looks to modernise its technology systems and increase its use of generative and agentic AI.

Infosys has expanded its work with ABN AMRO Bank as the Dutch lender seeks to modernise its technology systems and increase the use of artificial intelligence.

The companies’ relationship dates back to 2019, when Infosys announced a strategic partnership with ABN AMRO alongside its acquisition of a 75% stake in the bank’s mortgage-services subsidiary Stater. ABN AMRO retained the remaining 25% stake.

Under the expanded engagement, Infosys will provide application development, testing and support services. The work will use Infosys Topaz, the company’s AI platform that incorporates generative and agentic AI technologies.

“The renewed collaboration with Infosys will help further to simplify and modernize our IT landscape, while accelerating the responsible adoption of AI across the company,” Carsten Bittner, Chief Innovation and Technology Officer at ABN AMRO Bank, said. The engagement would also enhance operational efficiency and help reduce complexity and operating costs, he added.

Infosys and ABN AMRO said the expanded work would take AI beyond individual projects and into wider operations. Infosys said it would apply its AI capabilities across the bank’s technology environment, with the aim of improving operational efficiency and scalability and strengthening digital services.

Jay Nair, EVP and Industry Head for Financial Service and Public Sector at Infosys, said the renewal “marks an important milestone” in the relationship with ABN AMRO. He said Infosys would use its domain expertise and Topaz platform to help re-architect core systems and operationalise AI, with the work focused on “precision, efficiency, and long-term sustainability” for the bank.

Infosys has expanded its technology-modernisation work with banks. In June, it extended its engagement with DNB Bank to consolidate financial crime systems onto a cloud-based platform, replacing fragmented legacy infrastructure with a unified system for monitoring and investigations.

Infosys has also been expanding its use of agentic AI in software engineering. In January, it announced a collaboration with Cognition to deploy Devin across its internal engineering operations and client engagements, with its Financial Services practice leading initial engagements across banking, payments, capital markets, insurance and wealth management.

The announcement did not disclose the financial terms of the expanded collaboration.

title: IBM Partners With IIT Bombay, IISc on Agentic AI, Sovereign AI, Quantum Computing
content:
The research will cover Indic language models, multimodal systems, enterprise knowledge retrieval, and quantum-HPC workflows.

IBM has expanded its research collaborations with IIT Bombay and the Indian Institute of Science (IISc) to work on agentic AI, sovereign AI, quantum computing, and next-generation computing systems.

The collaboration will cover sovereign and Indic language model adaptation, multimodal AI, AI infrastructure, and knowledge retrieval. IBM and IIT Bombay have been working together since 2018.

The organisations will explore techniques to adapt and optimise sovereign and Indic language models for Indian languages. The research will also cover multimodal AI systems for software programming education, human-AI collaboration and operations across hybrid cloud environments.

The partners will also work on knowledge retrieval systems that can provide faster access to enterprise information. The research will include AI runtime optimisation and distributed inference to improve the performance and scalability of large language models.

With IISc, IBM will continue research in agentic systems, AI applications, and quantum computing. The collaboration began in 2021.

“Our collaborations with IIT Bombay and IISc bring together world-class academic research and IBM's scientific expertise to solve some of the most complex challenges in these areas,” Amith Singhee, Director, IBM Research India and CTO, IBM India and South Asia, said in a statement.

Prof Ganesh Ramakrishnan, Institute Chair Professor at IIT Bombay’s Department of Computer Science and Engineering, said the collaboration will cover multimodal AI models, knowledge retrieval, optimisation techniques, agentic AI workflows, and AI-assisted software engineering and education.

“By bringing together complementary strengths in AI, language, knowledge and intelligent computing, we envision trustworthy, inclusive, and scalable AI technologies that can transform how people learn, work, and access knowledge in India and across the world,” Prof Ramakrishnan said.

The IBM-IISc collaboration will involve lightweight time-series foundation models based on IBM’s Granite model family for energy analytics. The models will be used for forecasting, anomaly detection, load disaggregation, and energy optimisation. The partners will also contribute benchmark datasets to support further research.

In quantum computing, IBM and IISc will explore orchestration between quantum and high-performance computing systems. The research will include quantum-HPC algorithms and quantum subspace iteration methods using approximation-tolerant classical diagonalisation algorithms.

“IISc and IBM bring complementary research strengths to jointly explore intelligent, cloud-native platforms that can reason, adapt and orchestrate quantum-classical, edge AI and agentic workflows at scale,” Yogesh Simmhan, Professor in the Department of Computational and Data Sciences at IISc, said.

Coforge is expanding its Kraków engineering centre to over 660 engineers by 2027 as it shifts to a multi-client delivery model.

Coforge is expanding its engineering centre in Kraków, Poland, with plans to increase its workforce from more than 375 engineers to over 660 by 2027.

The centre opened in 2025 to support a single client engagement. It has since moved to a multi-client model serving customers across Europe and other global markets, with work spanning AI engineering, cloud, and modernisation.

The expansion comes as Indian IT companies continue to build delivery capabilities closer to European clients. Persistent’s acquisition of Nagarro is another recent example, expanding Persistent’s presence in Europe and adding to its digital engineering capabilities.

“Europe is an important growth market for Coforge, and our continued investment in Kraków reflects our long-term commitment to serving clients across the region,” John Speight, President and EU Geo Business Leader at Coforge, said in a statement.

Sunil Fernandes, Chief Operating Officer at Coforge, said the rapid scale-up of the Kraków centre reflected “two major market shifts: growing demand for AI-enabled engineering and the need for delivery models that combine proximity, specialised talent, and speed.”

He added that the centre had become an important growth engine for Coforge and its clients, with hybrid human and agent Mod Squads accelerating innovation and delivering measurable business outcomes for enterprises in Europe and beyond.

Coforge has added more than 20,000 sq ft of workspace at the facility to accommodate the planned increase in headcount.

The centre serves clients across travel, banking, logistics, retail, and enterprise services. The company said its location also provides access to engineering graduates and technology professionals in Kraków, allowing teams to work across European and UK time zones.

title: Google Gemini 4 Struggles With Coding Despite Strong Benchmark Numbers: Report
content:
According to benchmark results, the model outperforms OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra, Claude Fable 5.1, and Opus 5.5—but apparently, they don’t translate to real-world performance.

Google has announced its new frontier AI model, the Gemini 4 Argon. The model is rolling out to a set of the company’s trusted cybersecurity partners.

According to benchmark results, the model outperforms OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra, Claude Fable 5.1, and Opus 5.5 on several coding, science, computer use and knowledge work evaluations.

The company shared the model’s performance on numerous internal tasks. The model helped save over 300 TiB of memory in the company’s data centres by applying various optimisations.

In addition, Argon’s agents are helping the company migrate C/C++ codebases to Rust.

In one completed libgav1 optimisation, Argon started with an existing Rust port of Google’s open-source video decoder and replaced 32,000 lines of SIMD code.

The agents repeatedly ran profile-guided experiments, examined compiler output and modified the Rust implementation so that the compiler could automatically vectorise it. Google said the resulting memory-safe decoder runs 2.7 times faster than the previous Rust implementation while producing identical video output.

Google plans to expand access to paid API customers and Google AI Ultra subscribers before a broader rollout. Introductory pricing is set at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens.

Gemini 4 Argon ends a long wait for Google, after OpenAI and Anthropic pulled ahead in the frontier AI model race in recent months.

However, reports already show the model struggling. Bloomberg reported on the day of the launch that some Google employees with direct access to Gemini 4 believe its benchmark performance does not fully translate to real-world use.

Sources told the media outlet that the model struggles with certain coding tasks when employees use it, despite performing strongly on industry benchmarks.

Google disputed that characterisation, while another employee cited by the report said there was a “large consensus” internally that Gemini 4 is at the frontier.

title: Google DeepMind Builds Watermarking System to Identify AI-Generated Protein Designs
content:
Google DeepMind's approach attempts embeds provenance information at the point where the AI model generates the biological design.

Google DeepMind has developed SynthID Bio, an AI watermarking system designed to identify proteins and biological structures generated by AI models, as researchers and biosecurity experts grapple with a new challenge—determining whether a biological design came from an AI system, even when it does not resemble any known natural or hazardous sequence.

The system embeds a detectable signature into AI-generated protein sequences and predicted 3D structures without significantly changing their biological properties, according to Google DeepMind. In laboratory testing, the company said watermarked protein designs retained their ability to function and bind to their intended targets.

The development is significant because AI models are increasingly being used to design proteins and other biological molecules. Protein design models can generate sequences that do not exist in nature. That creates a gap for existing screening systems, which largely depend on recognising known biological patterns or similarities.

Conventional DNA synthesis screening can compare submitted sequences against databases of known pathogens or hazardous organisms, but an AI-designed sequence could be novel and therefore have no obvious match.

SynthID Bio intends to add another layer. Rather than only asking about a biological sequence, screening systems could also ask whether it was generated by an AI model.

Google DeepMind embeds provenance information at the point where the AI model generates the biological design.

For 3D protein structures, Google DeepMind modifies atomic coordinates in predicted structures to embed a watermark. The company has also fine-tuned part of the AlphaFold 3 diffusion network so that the predicted structures contain a detectable signature.

This makes the technology different from simply attaching metadata to an AI-generated file. The provenance signal is embedded in the biological design itself.

That matters because metadata can be stripped when a design moves between software systems, while a biological watermark is intended to remain associated with the sequence or structure.

The potential application extends beyond identifying AI-generated proteins.

DNA synthesis providers already screen sequences for synthesis against biological risks. But increasingly capable AI models can generate novel biological sequences that may not closely resemble known hazardous sequences.

A watermark could give synthesis providers another signal during screening about whether a sequence originated from a model that uses the watermarking technology. The system could therefore create a link between AI model developers, biological design outputs, and downstream synthesis providers.

For companies developing AI biology models, this could also create a mechanism to demonstrate that their systems have safety measures built into the generation process.

However, the company acknowledges that watermarking is not a complete biosecurity solution. A major open question is how resistant such watermarks are to deliberate modification or attempts to remove them from AI-generated biological designs.

title: ElevenLabs Doubles Valuation to $22 Bn as Enterprise AI Agent Demand Grows
content:
The company said its agents now handle more than 15 million conversations each week, up threefold since February.

ElevenLabs has raised its valuation to $22 billion after closing a $300 million employee tender offer, doubling its valuation from the Series D round in February this year.

The tender offer was led by Wellington Management and T Rowe Price, with EQT, Goldman Sachs, GIC, Ontario Teachers’ Pension Plan, Sapphire Ventures, and BDT & MSD Partners investing in the company for the first time. Existing investors including Andreessen Horowitz, Lightspeed Venture Partners and ICONIQ Capital also participated.

Enterprise customers now account for 55% of ElevenLabs’ revenue, with businesses using its ElevenAgents platform to deploy AI agents for customer support and business operations.

“AI should interact with people the way we interact with each other,” said Mati Staniszewski, Co-Founder and CEO of ElevenLabs. “Getting this right will help ensure AI diffuses widely across the economy, and everyone is able to shape and benefit from it, regardless of technical skill.”

ElevenLabs, founded in 2022, has grown to more than 800 employees. The company said the latest tender offer is part of its effort to give employees regular opportunities to sell shares and participate in the value created by the business.

ElevenAgents now handles more than 15 million conversations each week, three times the volume recorded in February. The company said the platform’s annual recurring revenue has also increased more than threefold over the same period.

The agents are being used for tasks including processing refunds and exchanges, renewing insurance policies, upgrading phone plans, booking healthcare appointments and accessing public services.

ElevenLabs said its technology is now used in the daily operations of five of the world’s 10 largest technology companies, five of the 10 largest insurers and four of the 10 largest telecom companies.

Customers using ElevenAgents include Stripe, Deutsche Telekom, DoorDash’s SevenRooms, Admiral, Customers Bank and Cadence. Governments in Ukraine and Greece are also using the platform.

The company said voice agents resolve customer issues 31% faster than chat agents on average, based on an analysis of its customers.

ElevenLabs is also seeing more companies use its platform across multiple channels. The number of companies deploying multichannel support with ElevenAgents has doubled since February, with businesses connecting interactions across channels such as WhatsApp, phone calls and email.

The company has built vertical-specific solutions for financial services, healthcare, government, retail and telecoms, with industry-specific integrations and model configurations.

Alongside its agent platform, ElevenLabs continues to develop speech and audio models. The company recently released Eleven v4 and v4 Turbo, which it described as its fastest text-to-speech models.

ElevenLabs said its models can speak, listen and translate in more than 90 languages spoken natively by more than 5.5 billion people. It also recently released Scribe v2 Medical, a transcription model focused on healthcare.

The company said it follows a full-stack approach covering research, product development and deployment. Its engineers work with customers to configure models and agents for specific industries, languages and use cases.

As AI makes intelligence more abundant, leaders must decide where it creates value, how it works across the enterprise and who remains accountable.

AI agents are moving deeper into the enterprise. Consider a large retailer with one AI agent watching customer demand, another monitoring inventory, a third forecasting sales and another handling supplier communications.

Then demand for a product suddenly spikes.

The sales system sees it first. The inventory agent knows stock is running low. The supply-chain system knows a supplier can replenish it, but only at a higher cost. Finance sees the impact on margins. The pricing system wants to raise prices. Customer service is already receiving complaints about availability.

There is no shortage of intelligence. The problem is getting all that intelligence to act as one.

This is becoming a central enterprise AI challenge. The first phase focused on accessing models, embedding copilots into applications and deploying agents for individual tasks. The next phase requires managing intelligence when it is spread across the organisation and can act on its own.

We see this as the industrialisation of enterprise intelligence: making AI dependable, coordinated and economically accountable across the business.

As AI becomes embedded in business execution, intelligence becomes a resource leaders must allocate, govern and evaluate. Companies will have to decide where intelligence is needed, how different systems should coordinate, which decisions machines can make and whether that intelligence is producing measurable business value.

The excitement around AI agents has focused on autonomy. An agent can reason through a task, use tools and take action. But enterprises do not run on isolated tasks.

A sales decision can affect supply. A supply decision can alter margins. A financial decision can change hiring plans. A customer-service interaction can influence the next sales decision.

Putting an agent into every application, therefore, does not automatically create an intelligent enterprise. It can create a coordination problem.

Each agent may have its own context, objectives, data and decision rules. One may optimise revenue while another optimises cost. One may have real-time information while another works with older data. They can all be individually correct while collectively pulling the business in different directions.

This creates a coordination tax: the cost of getting autonomous systems to share context, resolve conflicting priorities and work towards a common business objective.

In our earlier writing on Convergence 3.0, we explored how data, AI, processes and people come together to connect business intent with execution. The next question is how enterprises coordinate that intelligence, define its authority and manage its economics as it acts across applications and workflows.

The agent may be the worker. The system around it is what makes it part of the enterprise.

The coordination problem grows as intelligence becomes more widely available and easier to consume.

Enterprises can use multiple models across applications, while agents may call models repeatedly to complete a workflow. Coding agents can consume intelligence continuously, while customer-facing systems can generate responses at enormous scale.

AI spend alone tells leaders little about the value being created.

Two companies could spend the same amount on AI and generate very different outcomes. One might use intelligence to reduce inventory or improve forecasting. Another might spend heavily on automation that saves little time and changes no meaningful business outcome.

The economic question is whether additional intelligence improves an outcome enough to justify its cost. Enterprises need to distinguish model consumption from the total cost of completing a task, including coordination, human review and rework. They must then assess whether the result improves on an agreed baseline. More reasoning and more agent interactions are worthwhile only when the gains justify the additional cost and time.

The more useful question, then, is not how many tokens an enterprise consumed or how many agents it deployed. It is what that intelligence produced.

Did it improve forecast accuracy? Prevent a stockout? Reduce the time needed to resolve a customer issue? Accelerate a sales cycle?

The value of intelligence will increasingly be tied to these outcomes.

The challenge becomes more consequential as AI moves from recommending actions to taking them.

Consider an agent managing procurement. It identifies a shortage and automatically places an order. But what happens when the order exceeds a budget threshold, the supplier has changed its terms or the purchase conflicts with another business priority?

The question is no longer just whether the agent is intelligent enough. It is whether the organisation has decided what the agent is allowed to decide.

Delegating an action to an agent does not remove management accountability. Every consequential workflow still needs an owner, clear escalation rules and a way to intervene.

Enterprises will need to define where autonomy is appropriate, where an agent can act within predefined limits, where it must escalate and where a human must remain in control.

This becomes particularly important when agents interact with other agents. One system could trigger another, creating a chain of actions that no individual employee explicitly initiated.

Governance, therefore, cannot simply mean reviewing an agent after something goes wrong. It has to be built into how intelligence operates.

Enterprise agent governance must extend beyond individual models to cover agent actions, interactions, human intervention and business outcomes.

Traditional enterprises have systems of record: ERP, CRM, HR, finance and supply-chain systems that store what the company knows and does. AI is now creating systems that can reason over that information and act on it.

For the retailer mentioned earlier, the shared goal could be to protect product availability while staying within agreed margin limits. The sales agent tracks demand, the inventory agent monitors stock and the procurement agent identifies replenishment options. If a purchase exceeds an approved threshold, the system escalates it to a designated decision-maker rather than acting autonomously.

The outcome can then be measured across availability, margin and the cost of running the workflow.

This control capability does not require replacing the retailer’s existing ERP, CRM or supply-chain systems. It operates across them, giving agents the context, boundaries and coordination needed to act as part of the same enterprise.

That changes the architecture of the organisation. Objectives need to be aligned, decisions need boundaries and AI consumption needs to be measured against business outcomes.

The challenge is no longer simply deploying intelligence. It is creating the layer that determines how intelligence moves across the enterprise, when it can act and when it needs to escalate.

The industrialisation of enterprise intelligence is a leadership responsibility.

Leaders will have to decide where intelligence can create meaningful business value, where it should be deployed across functions and where autonomous systems can act without intervention. They will also need to define who remains accountable when an AI-driven decision affects customers, costs, revenue or operations.

That means AI can no longer sit solely with technology teams. Its allocation, boundaries and business outcomes are management decisions.

The companies that navigate this shift will be those that treat intelligence as a resource that needs to be deliberately allocated, governed and measured.

AI may make intelligence abundant. Deciding where it creates value, how it works across the organisation and who remains accountable for its decisions will still belong to the people running the enterprise.

Relanto is an AI-first technology company combining product innovation with enterprise consulting and engineering. It helps organisations build and scale enterprise AI, bringing together data, AI, processes and people to deliver business outcomes.

Its product portfolio includes R-LiveMeasure, focused on governing how AI agents behave, and R-TokenomIQ, focused on governing how AI consumes resources, with visibility and control across AI usage and economics.

title: Accenture Boasts 400 Clients Doing Advanced AI, Notches $18.7 Bn Q4 Revenue
content:
Bookings from Accenture’s eight emerging AI and data partners more than tripled from FY25, while revenue from those partners more than doubled.

Accenture said more than 400 clients initiated their first advanced AI work during FY26, including nearly 100 clients in the June to August quarter, as AI demand continued to expand across its enterprise customer base. Quarterly revenue rose 7% in local currency to $18.7 billion, while bookings reached $22.2 billion.

Accenture’s fiscal year runs from September 1 through August 31.

The consulting and technology services company said clients remain at different stages of AI adoption, with many still building the foundations needed to deploy AI at scale.

“Much of our growth today comes from continuing to build their digital core data foundations and the enterprise AI stack that they need to use AI at scale,” Accenture CEO Julie Sweet said during the earnings call.

The company is also seeing stronger commercial activity from its AI ecosystem.

Revenue from its top 10 ecosystem partners grew 6% in FY26 and accounted for more than 60% of Accenture’s revenue. Bookings from eight emerging AI and data partners more than tripled from FY25, while revenue from those partners more than doubled.

Accenture has previously disclosed growth in generative AI revenue, though it did not provide a standalone figure in its latest results.

Sweet also acknowledged that AI is making Accenture’s own delivery more efficient.

“We continue to believe the opportunities related to AI are greater than the impact of AI-related efficiencies on our business,” Sweet said.

Accenture highlighted several examples of AI being embedded into business processes. For a pharmaceutical company, it said an AI platform used for clinical-trial planning reduced the time needed to create and analyse trial scenarios from 10 days to 10 minutes, while improving patient-enrolment forecast accuracy by 60%. Accenture said some study designs identified through the platform could shorten trial timelines by up to three months.

The company is also shifting towards more outcome-based work. “Fixed-price work, which includes outcome-based work, is now over 65% of bookings and continues to grow,” Accenture CFO Angie Park said. Managed services bookings reached a record $12.8 billion in Q4, with a book-to-bill ratio of 1.4.

Accenture’s shift towards fixed-price and outcome-based work comes as AI enables it to deliver services more efficiently.

The company reported a full-year GAAP operating margin—the percentage of revenue it keeps as operating profit—of 15.4%, an increase of 70 basis points over FY25. It returned $11.5 billion to shareholders in FY26, a 38% YoY increase.

For FY27, Accenture expects revenue growth of 3–6% in local currency and an operating margin of 15.9–16.1%. It expects to invest approximately $5 billion in acquisitions and return at least $9.5 billion to shareholders during the year.

Nifty IT rose 18% and then fell 13% in the July-September quarter. Q2 FY27 earnings will offer an early test of whether AI revenue can offset pricing pressure.

Mukundan SivarajSenior journalist

The past quarter was quite volatile for Indian IT stocks.

The Nifty IT index climbed 18% from 26,965 on July 2 to 31,823 on August 11. It then fell 13% from that peak and closed at 27,670 on September 29, ending the quarter just 2.6% higher.

Different drivers influenced the rally and the subsequent selloff.

The July rally came partly as global investors rotated out of crowded artificial intelligence (AI) trades in markets such as South Korea and Taiwan and into India. Foreign investors put more than $1.6 billion into Indian equities that month, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. AIM had earlier reported that the optimism was driven by macro tailwinds from cooling Brent crude oil prices, as well as investors rebalancing their portfolios.

The September selloff brought the AI question back into focus. Investors began weighing whether faster AI adoption would eat into Indian IT’s digital transformation business, even as Indian IT companies reported growing AI businesses.

Market Questions Quality of IT Growth

Indian IT entered the quarter with a growth problem. The AI-driven structural squeeze overshadowed the cyclical lag in client spending.

UnearthInsight Founder and CEO Gaurav Vasu tells AIM that the market has already priced in a weak FY27, with the sector expected to remain in single-digit growth through the year.

“What makes this more concerning is the quality of that growth,” he says. A large part of the growth has come from acquisitions made over the past two years, and stripping out the M&A contribution leaves organic growth at just 1–2%, he believes.

Global uncertainties, slower client spending, and AI upending the traditional arbitrage model have hollowed out any organic growth. That also clouds investor expectations about the quarter under review. Per Ventura Research, the top five Indian IT companies are expected to deliver subdued growth in Q2 FY27—between 0.5% and 3% on a sequential constant currency basis.

“Q2 financial performance would likely be muted. Discretionary tech spending remains muted,” notes Piyush Pandey, SVP and Lead Analyst for IT, Telecom, Internet, and Power at Centrum India.

Pandey attributes the sharp movements in IT stocks to changing estimates of AI's impact, between deflationary pressure on existing services and the creation of new opportunities.

Sumit Pokharna, Senior Vice President - Fundamental Research at Kotak Securities, believes part of the trend emerges from a shift in client technology spending towards AI.

“The client’s money has been diverted more to AI-driven [things], and Indian IT services companies were not present in that domain,” he notes.

Vasu says the concern extends beyond Indian IT. He points to declines across global IT services and software companies, arguing that the market is increasingly pricing in the possibility that AI will fundamentally change how enterprises allocate technology budgets.

Both AI Revenue and Productivity are Growing

AI is already showing up on the P&Ls of IT companies.

Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) reported an annualised AI revenue run rate of $2.6 billion in Q1 FY27, up 13.6% sequentially. It also reported $9.5 billion in total contract value (TCV).

HCLTech's Advanced AI revenue reached $171 million, up 62.1% year-on-year in constant currency. Infosys reported that AI revenue accounted for 8.2% of its Q1 revenue.

The question is whether that revenue is incremental.

TCS's numbers show the tension. Strong deal wins have continued even as AI-led productivity puts pressure on the economics of traditional services. AI can also reduce the teams and effort required to deliver work within existing engagements.

Wipro Chief Technology Officer Sandhya Arun said the company's AI initiatives had created capacity equivalent to 20,000 employees, with that capacity redeployed elsewhere in the business.

That is a productivity gain. It becomes a revenue-growth story only if the company can turn the freed capacity into additional work.

AI activity and AI revenue do not necessarily mean incremental revenue. A company can report a growing AI business while also losing revenue from traditional services that AI has made cheaper to deliver.

Pokharna says AI deflation is already becoming visible in the base business and expects pricing pressure to continue.

AI May Widen the Gap

The pressure will vary across Indian IT companies.

Pandey says tier-2 IT companies are better placed to navigate the shift. Vasu expects investors to move towards moderately growing mid-tier companies if larger firms continue to disappoint.

“Challengers continue to offset this with their sheer gains or strong execution, while the incumbents are largely defending the existing revenues,” Pokharna notes.

Persistent Systems, Coforge, and Mphasis have been growing faster than several of their larger peers, while some have also reported strong AI-related deal activity. They are winning engineering, modernisation, and transformation projects can create new sources of revenue as AI changes the way existing services are delivered.

Persistent, for example, has highlighted AI execution, deal wins, and productivity. Its revenue per employee had risen 58.2% between FY22 and Q2 FY26.

Coforge provides a recent example. In Q1 FY27, the company said 86% of its revenue came from AI-led engineering, data, and cloud services, while 30% of its active delivery projects were already using its AI assets.

But faster growth does not show whether those AI-led deals are replacing revenue lost elsewhere. Organic growth, revenue per employee, and the ability to turn AI productivity into higher-value work will matter more than the number of AI projects announced.

Q2 Earnings Will Offer a Reality Check

“The main reason is AI deflation and, to a lesser extent, weaker macros [which] will continue to weaken the growth,” Pokharna says. He expects muted growth despite the seasonally strong quarter.

Vasu sees Accenture's results as another signal for Indian IT. If the global IT services company's numbers disappoint, he expects further pressure on the sector and a possible rotation away from slower-growing large firms towards mid-tier companies.

Pokharna says the market's concern has shifted.

“In between, the big question which came to the minds of the investors [was], will these Indian IT companies exist or not going forward? So, we believe that concern is behind us,” he says.

Revenue growth will matter, but the organic component will matter more than headline growth. Investors will also be watching whether large AI-led TCV converts into production work and billing, and whether pricing and margins hold as productivity improves. Headcount, utilisation and revenue per employee will show whether companies are becoming more efficient while continuing to grow.

Q2 will not settle the debate over AI's economics in Indian IT. It should, however, give investors a clearer indication of whether AI activity is translating into revenue.

title: Yellow.ai Pitches Nexus EDGE to Automate Employee IT, HR Support
content:
The desktop AI agent connects with 114 enterprise tools across 18 categories and requires employee approval before executing actions.

Enterprise-focused Yellow.ai has launched Nexus EDGE, an agentic AI desktop application to automate employee IT, human resources (HR), and operations support.

The application is designed to identify and resolve workplace issues directly on employees' computers using company knowledge and enterprise systems.

"For a decade, employee help tools have competed on how fast they can answer a question," Raghu Ravintula, Co-founder and CEO of Yellow.ai, said in a statement. "But employees were never asking for answers. They were asking to get on with their day."

Nexus EDGE extends Yellow.ai’s Nexus Universal Agentic Interface to employees' desktops. It is designed to address common problems, such as VPN failures, software installation issues, and difficulties accessing enterprise applications.

Nexus EDGE combines a cloud-based reasoning system, called Nexus Agent, with a local agent installed on employees' computers. The cloud agent uses company knowledge bases, standard operating procedures, and backend enterprise applications to identify solutions. The desktop agent examines the screen and application state and executes the required fixes locally, according to Yellow.ai.

Nexus EDGE supports 114 enterprise tools across 18 categories from deployment, according to the company's product documentation. These include IT service management, identity management, and workplace applications such as ServiceNow, Jira, Okta, Slack, and Microsoft 365.

The system requires employees to approve actions before execution. Yellow.ai said the application operates within the signed-in user's existing permissions and maintains an audit trail of actions across IT, HR, and operations. The company also describes its architecture as designed to keep sensitive data on the employee's device.

The company expects the application to reduce support tickets and return multiple hours per employee annually to productive work. However, it has not disclosed independently verified performance results or quantified reductions in support tickets.

"Nexus changed how enterprises handle customer conversations. Nexus EDGE does the same thing for the people inside the enterprise," said Rashid Khan, Co-founder and Chief Marketing Officer of Yellow.ai.

Yellow.ai said its enterprise AI platform serves more than 650 customers across the US, the Middle East, India, Asia-Pacific, and South America. The launch expands its agentic AI offerings into desktop-based employee experience automation.

Ridhika is a journalist covering the real-world impact of artificial intelligence at the intersection of tech, policy, and society.

title: Trump & Big Tech Leaders Sign Voluntary ‘Super Intelligence’ Safety Accord
content:
The US President also directed US government agencies to use the term ‘super intelligence’ instead of ‘artificial intelligence’ when referring to the technology.

US President Donald Trump and executives from big tech companies have signed a voluntary accord requiring frontier AI companies to implement internal safety controls, use independent external evaluators and establish board-level oversight of those systems.

The seven people who signed the accord include Trump, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, Google chief Sundar Pichai, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI President Greg Brockman, NVIDIA chief Jensen Huang and xAI’s Elon Musk.

The wider luncheon had 31 confirmed attendees, including Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, AMD chief Lisa Su, Amazon Founder Jeff Bezos, Broadcom CEO Hock Tan, Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora, ServiceNow’s Bill McDermott and Micron Technology CEO Sanjay Mehrotra, alongside senior administration officials.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman was not there because he was at OpenAI’s DevDay in San Francisco, and Brockman represented the Company.

The White House Accord on Super Intelligence: Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities sets out four layers of controls covering internal model monitoring, internal oversight, independent external evaluation and board-level review.

Companies are to monitor model capabilities and alignment during training and deployment, including around cybersecurity, biosecurity and chemical threats.

This involves maintaining internal teams to detect and correct problems, working with an “independent external auditor or evaluator”, and creating an independent board committee to review internal and external findings.

The accord also calls for measures to prevent models from “hack[ing] or access[ing] technical systems in unintended ways”.

The agreement is voluntary and does not create a federal regulator or specify penalties for non-compliance.

It does, however, state that “over time, it may make sense to codify these steps into laws or regulations”.

Trump described the document as “almost like a constitution” and said the industry should rely on “tremendous self-policing”.

Zuckerberg said the participating companies would develop “robust internal controls” for their AI systems.

Trump separately said he was considering a 10-person board to oversee AI safety, although he did not name potential members.

He also said a new White House official responsible for AI policy would be appointed soon.

The meeting also covered the infrastructure needed to train and operate increasingly large AI models.

Trump reiterated support for new data centres despite local opposition over electricity demand, utility costs and other community impacts. He said companies would make “massive contributions to communities” to build support for new facilities.

The safety discussions follow OpenAI and Anthropic disclosures of incidents involving AI agents that accessed or attempted to gain unauthorised access to external systems.

The companies are also facing pressure over how quickly they should deploy increasingly capable systems, while the White House has argued that excessive regulation could weaken US competitiveness against China.

Trump also directed US government agencies to use the term ‘super intelligence’ instead of ‘artificial intelligence’ when referring to the technology.

Moreover, the administration launched America.gov, an AI-powered government portal intended to provide a single interface for federal information and services.

It currently allows users to ask questions in natural language, and the administration says it will later support transactions such as passport renewal and Medicare enrolment.

The executive order directs agencies to integrate covered public-facing services into the platform. Covered services generally include federal services with more than 100,000 users over 12 months, while IRS tax filing and national-security-sensitive services are excluded.

The White House’s Chief Design Officer Joe Gebbia said the system draws information from roughly 29,000 federal websites.

Persistent's Nagarro deal adds people, clients and European reach. The harder test is whether that scale can translate into higher-value AI and engineering work.

Mukundan SivarajSenior journalist

Persistent now has the scale it wants to compete in the big league.

The Pune-based IT services company has gained majority control over the German digital engineering company, securing 83.25% of Nagarro's share capital, including a stake it already held. The acquisition is expected to close by the first quarter of calendar year 2027.

Persistent agreed to pay about €1.27 billion ($1.44 billion) for Nagarro. The combined group will have an annualised revenue run rate above $2.9 billion and more than 46,000 employees.

That would make it the world's second-largest digital engineering company by revenue and India's seventh-largest technology services company.

But size is only the starting point.

The more important question is what Persistent can do with the scale as AI changes what enterprises buy from IT services companies. The Nagarro deal gives Persistent more customers, engineers, and access to European markets. It now has to turn those assets into higher-value work.

“The more interesting question is whether the combined business can use this new scale as a platform to become sharper, AI-enabled, and more IP-led over time, rather than simply larger,” Praveen Bhadada, CEO and MD of consulting firm Neovay Global, tells AIM. Bhadada previously led Persistent's AI and GenAI business.

Indian IT is Expanding Through Europe

Persistent joins a growing list of Indian IT firms buying into Europe.

Tata Consultancy Services has agreed to buy Porsche's IT consulting unit MHP for €320 million ($373 million), alongside a five-year AI partnership with the German carmaker. Infosys bought German automotive engineering firm in-tech for €450 million ($466 million) in 2024, and is reportedly seeking an early renewal of its $3 billion contract with Daimler Truck.

Mid-tier IT firms are consolidating as well: Coforge closed its Encora deal, and ITC Infotech and Happiest Minds announced a proposed merger.

Namratha Dharshan, Chief Business Leader, India, at research firm Information Services Group (ISG), explains that with industry growth muted, IT services providers are “increasingly pursuing faster geographic expansion, capability acquisitions, and inorganic revenue growth.”

The common thread is access to European clients, local delivery capabilities and industry relationships that can take years to build organically.

Persistent vs EPAM

Yugal Joshi, Partner at Everest Group, believes the comparison appears to be with digital engineering pure-play company EPAM Systems.

With the Nagarro acquisition, Persistent challenges EPAM’s transatlantic footprint and digital engineering dominance. EPAM has built its footprint with a 53,000-strong workforce, many of whom operate out of Eastern European and Latin American talent, providing near-timezone engineering support to US and European talent. Nagarro’s talent concentration in similar regions gives Persistent a similar nearshore delivery model.

Also, engineering-led firms now work extensively with IT leaders as well. They once sold to technology and digital chiefs while traditional IT services firms sold to chief information officers, but “that demarcation is long gone,” Joshi notes.

Persistent is “strong in other areas such as Salesforce and cloud,” particularly on Amazon Web Services, he says. On revenue per employee, it sits materially below EPAM and above classical IT services firms. Persistent also focuses on fewer industry verticals and relies heavily on North America.

What Nagarro Adds in Europe

“Cultural nuances of the European market are far higher compared to other markets,” adds Dharshan. “Penetrating these markets needs deep cultural alignment; presence in the market and prior foothold will speed up the entry.”

Nagarro supplies that foothold, particularly in Germany. Nagarro also strengthens Persistent's automotive and manufacturing exposure. Engineering contract value in Europe, the Middle East and Africa grew 4% year-on-year and about 5% sequentially in Q1 2026, she adds, “indicating continued momentum in the European market.”

Dharshan believes engineering services continue to see healthy demand, with most enterprise deals centred on digital transformation. Platform engineering services, however, have seen some sequential softness.

The strategic value is the additional customers, engineering relationships, industry context, and delivery presence.

Scale Matters

“On market access, vertical mass, and near-term accretion, this is a genuinely competent deal,” Bhadada notes. The acquisition nearly doubles the company's revenue and headcount in a single stroke and takes the combined group past $500 million in several key verticals—including banking and financial services, healthcare and life sciences, and telecom, media and technology—“putting it credibly at the table for large, multi-region transformation programmes.”

That scale matters when competing for large transformation programmes, where clients need vendors with enough people, industry expertise, and geographic coverage to deliver across multiple markets.

Persistent has built its AI pitch around SASVA, its AI engineering platform, and CEO Sandeep Kalra has described AI as part of every deal. Persistent has also said Nagarro's AI, digital, ERP and CX capabilities complement its own, while the combined group's AI-skilled talent and platforms would strengthen its AI Forward Deployed Engineering capabilities.

“It's a scale-of-people transaction in a year when the strategic conversation has shifted toward density of AI capability and revenue per employee,” Bhadada observes.

The deal adds significant headcount at similar revenue per head and slightly lower margins.

Specialisation Hits a Ceiling

“Specialisation has a ceiling, and it seems Persistent realised that,” Joshi remarks.

Nagarro works across many industries and regions, though Joshi said it has sometimes been viewed as too spread out and open to lower-value engagements. That breadth, however, “helps the combined entity to be less concentrated on specific industries and regions.”

European buyers may pull the other way. ISG's report on midsize digital engineering providers in Europe noted that these firms are responding by specialising, and ISG Director Dorotea Baljević said buyers put strategic alignment and trust “over scale alone.”

That creates a tension for the combined company. Persistent is using Nagarro to broaden its geographic and industry reach at a time when some European buyers continue to value specialised partners.

The wider market adds pressure. Digital engineering firms including Nagarro and technology consultancy Thoughtworks have struggled with “crunched discretionary spending,” Joshi says, and diversifying into IT workloads “will need different talent, IP, and engagement models.”

Nagarro's organic revenue grew 0.6% year-on-year in constant currency in the June 2026 quarter, while Persistent's revenue grew 16.1% year-on-year in the quarter ended June 30, 2026.

AI adds another pressure: if it lets firms deliver the same work in fewer billable hours, pricing and revenue growth could come under pressure. That makes revenue per employee particularly important for Persistent as it absorbs Nagarro's workforce.

Metrics That Will Show Whether It Works

Several numbers will show whether the additional scale is translating into better economics.

Growth comes first. Persistent's 25th consecutive quarter of revenue growth came with a record quarterly Total Contract Value (TCV). The question is whether the combined group holds that pace with Nagarro's slower growth.

Margins follow. Persistent posted an earnings before interest and tax (EBIT) margin of 16.0% in the first quarter of FY27. Nagarro comes with slightly lower margins.

Revenue per employee is the third test. Persistent raised it 58.2% between FY22 and Q2 FY26. If the enlarged workforce can reproduce or improve those economics, the deal begins to look like more than a headcount expansion.

The fourth test is evidence that the combined business is moving toward higher-value AI and IP-led work. Persistent does not disclose a standalone AI revenue figure. Instead, it embeds AI natively across its digital engineering services. So the clearest proxies will be its ability to secure large multi-region transformation programmes, expand AI-led offerings, and maintain or improve its economics as AI becomes a larger part of delivery.

Geography and industry mix complete the set. Post closure of the acquisition, North America would account for 62% of the combined revenue run rate, Europe 22%, and the rest of the world 16%. A rising European share and greater automotive and manufacturing exposure from Nagarro is bound to diversify the group's business mix.

Persistent is materially larger, with greater reach in Europe and deeper exposure to industrial manufacturing and product lifecycle management services. Nagarro actively services four of Europe’s top five automotive manufacturers.

The harder part is translating that reach into sustained growth, stable or improving margins and higher revenue per employee, while building the sharper, AI-enabled and IP-led business Bhadada describes.

Bhadada's view is that the acquisition's value hinges on Persistent's next strategy. “If Persistent executes with that ambition, this could prove to be both a financially smart deal and a strategically forward-looking one,” he comments.

title: Tech Mahindra, Infinite Uptime to Scale Physical AI in Manufacturing
content:
Tech Mahindra and Infinite Uptime will help manufacturers move from predictive insights to prescribed actions.

Tech Mahindra has partnered with industrial technology company Infinite Uptime to accelerate physical AI adoption across manufacturing and process industries.

The partnership will combine Infinite Uptime’s PlantOS, an industrial outcome intelligence engine, with Tech Mahindra’s manufacturing expertise, global reach, and IT-OT transformation capabilities.

The companies said the partnership will help manufacturers move from predictive insights to prescribed actions by embedding industrial intelligence into plant workflows and tracking its impact on production performance.

Infinite Uptime’s PlantOS combines mechanical and process signals with physics-aware contextualisation and failure-mode intelligence. It provides recommendations on what action to take, why it is required, and when it should be completed, according to the company.

The approach is similar to recent industrial AI efforts that use models to determine interventions rather than simply predict outcomes. For example, factory optimisation using physical AI has focused on using AI to determine interventions that can affect real-world production outcomes.

Tech Mahindra will use its SIIM approach (simulate, integrate, implement and maintain) to validate, integrate, and deploy physical AI solutions across existing production, operational technology, and enterprise environments.

This will allow manufacturers to embed prescriptive intelligence into complex plant operations rather than treating AI as a standalone layer.

The partnership will target steel, cement, chemicals, metals and mining, pulp and paper, and other asset-intensive industries, where industrial AI is also being applied to areas such as predictive maintenance and operational intelligence. The initial focus will be North America and Europe, particularly larger transformation programmes where equipment reliability and production performance are closely linked.

“The next phase of industrial transformation will be shaped by the ability to convert industrial intelligence into timely action,” Manikantan NS, SVP & Global Head – Manufacturing Vertical, Tech Mahindra, said in a statement. “We will help enterprises embed this intelligence across complex plant environments and achieve tangible improvements in reliability, productivity, and operational resilience.”

Infinite Uptime said its deployments have resulted in more than 167,837 hours of operator-validated downtime savings across more than 1,000 plants, 172 customers, nine industrial verticals, and 28 countries.

title: Peak XV Selects 18 Startups for Latest Surge Cohort, Raises Investment Cap to $5 Mn
content:
The 12th cohort includes AI, robotics, and space tech companies. Peak XV invested more than $50 million across the group.

Peak XV Partners (formerly Sequoia Capital India and SEA) has selected 18 startups for the 12th cohort of Surge, its seed-stage investment programme, increasing its maximum investment per company from $3 million to $5 million. The revised structure brings Surge closer to the venture capital firm's broader early-stage investment practice.

The new cohort spans artificial intelligence (AI), robotics, space technology, healthcare, financial services, consumer technology, and music. Peak XV invested more than $50 million across the cohort, with companies collectively raising over $90 million in seed funding, according to the firm.

Under the revised programme, Surge can invest between $500,000 and $5 million in each company through equity investments. The higher ceiling gives Peak XV greater flexibility to support startups with different capital requirements.

Fifteen of the 18 startups have been publicly named, while three remain in stealth mode. Around half of the cohort comprises AI-native companies, according to Peak XV.

Some of the named startups include Alma, which is developing personal computing for an AI-native environment, and Hiloop, which is building infrastructure to help AI companies train, test, and improve open-weight models. Reinforce Labs is developing tools for evaluating, red teaming, and improving enterprise AI systems.

Other companies are applying AI to specific industries. August AI is developing clinical intelligence for primary care, while Rosella is building an AI-powered commercial insurance brokerage. Tribe Money is developing an AI-based personal finance platform.

The cohort also includes startups working on physical infrastructure and consumer applications. Puralink is developing autonomous robots to inspect underground pipes, while ULOOK is building radio-frequency sensing satellites for spectrum intelligence. Riffle is developing a browser-based platform for collaborative music creation.

Rajan Anandan, Managing Director at Peak XV Partners and Surge, said the founders in the latest cohort are building to fundamentally change technology and consumer behaviour.

"What stands out about Surge 12 is that these founders are building these companies on first principles," Anandan said in a statement.

He added that AI was increasingly becoming the architecture of products, as startups rethought how people create, shop, date, invest, and access healthcare.

The cohort also includes founders with experience at established technology companies. Alma's founders previously worked at Microsoft Research before becoming founding engineers at Sarvam AI. Kello co-founder Mona Gandhi was Airbnb's first female engineer and previously founded Upraised. Reinforce Labs founder Anish Das Sarma previously built a company acquired by Airbnb and later led AI and machine-learning teams at Google.

Launched in 2019, Surge provides early-stage startups with investment and operational support in areas such as hiring, product development, engineering, marketing, and global expansion.

Peak XV said it has backed more than 180 startups through the programme. Its 10 largest portfolio companies collectively generate more than $1 billion in annual revenue.

NetApp has unveiled a storage architecture designed to exceed 100 TB/s of aggregate throughput, as the company looks to address the infrastructure demands of large-scale AI deployments.

Called Novus, the architecture is aimed at neoclouds and GPU-as-a-service providers and was announced alongside new data, cloud, and hybrid infrastructure capabilities at NetApp’s INSIGHT 2026 conference.

The announcements span different parts of the AI infrastructure stack, from moving data fast enough to keep large GPU clusters running to finding and governing enterprise data for AI applications. NetApp also announced a planned managed storage service with Oracle Cloud Infrastructure and new autonomous management capabilities for hybrid environments.

Novus separates metadata from the data path, allowing performance, capacity, and concurrency to scale independently under a single namespace. Its initial configuration combines Novus Data Director with ONTAP data services running on AFF A90 systems and qualified Supermicro infrastructure.

“AI factories struggle and GPU economics collapse when data can't keep up,” Syam Nair, Chief Product Officer at NetApp, said in a statement.

The company has expanded its AI Data Engine to discover metadata across NetApp and non-NetApp storage, including NFS, SMB, and S3 repositories. The platform is designed to help organisations understand, govern, and operationalise enterprise data for AI workloads, while NetApp is previewing AI-powered data understanding, governance intelligence, and agentic services.

“The agentic enterprise will be defined by how quickly and safely organisations can turn their data into intelligence,” Asad Khan, Senior Vice President and General Manager, AI, at NetApp, added.

NetApp has also expanded its integration with Commvault for threat detection, cleanroom validation, and recovery workflows.

Separately, NetApp and Oracle announced a planned fully managed storage service native to Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI), bringing ONTAP capabilities to OCI. General availability is planned within the next 12 months.

The company also introduced Console Autonomous Operations, Fleet Management, and AI ChatOps, alongside expanded Keystone Sovereign capabilities and a planned NetApp-Nutanix solution for virtualised workloads.

title: Oracle Launches Fusion Claw With 25 AI Agentic Applications
content:
Oracle’s Fusion Claw combines AI reasoning with deterministic computation, continuous replanning and controls for identity, permissions, approvals, and audit trails.

Oracle has introduced Fusion Claw, a governed agentic execution runtime that allows its Fusion agentic applications to handle complex, long-running work with greater autonomy.

The company said Fusion Claw combines AI reasoning with deterministic enterprise computation. It is available through 25 new Claw-powered agentic applications covering areas such as finance, workforce planning, supply chain, and sales.

For example, a ledger can analyse accounting entries, investigate exceptions and anomalies, reconcile information, and perform financial calculations.

Meanwhile, Workforce Staffing creates staffing plans based on factors such as skills, availability, schedules, labour rules, costs, and coverage requirements. It can also re-plan when conditions change.

The new applications add to Oracle’s portfolio of 75 agentic applications that can coordinate and execute business processes.

“Fusion Claw helps answer that question by moving from AI assistance to execution, enabling customers to automate increasingly complex work across their most important business processes, with enterprise-grade governance,” Mike Sicilia, CEO, Oracle, said in a statement.

Each Fusion Claw outcome starts with a frontier AI model that can reason, plan, learn, and adapt. Oracle then uses deterministic computation to carry out the required enterprise operations.

This approach allows AI reasoning to be used where it is needed while relying on deterministic computation for high-volume execution, according to Oracle.

The runtime supports longer-running tasks, continuous replanning, and execution at scale. Businesses can also choose the level of automation for a process, from assistance to fully automated execution within delegated authority.

Oracle said Fusion Claw uses an enterprise operating envelope to define the rules under which an AI system can operate. This can include company policies, permissions, risk thresholds, decision rights, approval requirements, and escalation boundaries.

An outcome trust harness applies these controls to each execution, covering identity, capabilities, data, and actions.

After an outcome is completed, an outcome receipt records the authority used, evidence considered, decisions made, actions taken, and the final result.

Oracle said Fusion Claw runs on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure and uses frontier models including Google’s Gemini and OpenAI models. It has planned support for additional frontier models.

Oracle is also positioning Fusion Claw alongside its AI Agent Studio for Fusion applications, which allows organisations to create and manage agentic applications using Oracle, partner, and external agents.

title: OpenMetal Acquires Economize, Launches Labs For Cloud Cost Management
content:
The deal combines Economize’s FinOps capabilities with OpenMetal’s private cloud, bare-metal and GPU infrastructure.

OpenMetal has acquired Economize, a cloud cost management platform for engineering, finance and FinOps teams, and launched OpenMetal Labs for custom infrastructure and cost solutions.

The deal brings Economize’s tools for cloud cost visibility, anomaly detection and optimisation together with OpenMetal’s infrastructure, giving customers access to both offerings through a single relationship. The combined services are designed to help businesses understand their cloud spending, determine where workloads should run and optimise costs across public and private infrastructure, including AI and GPU workloads.

“Companies running infrastructure-heavy businesses have needed a FinOps tool and an infrastructure vendor that understands their cost structure, and rarely got both from the same place,” said Todd Robinson, Co-Founder and President of OpenMetal.

“Bringing Economize and OpenMetal together closes that gap because it's a full suite from one directly accountable provider,” he added.

Economize has focused on helping engineering, finance and FinOps teams understand and manage public cloud spending, while OpenMetal provides hosted private cloud, bare-metal servers and GPU infrastructure. The combined offering will allow customers to move workloads to private infrastructure where appropriate, while businesses using a mix of public and private infrastructure can monitor and optimise both environments.

“We started Economize with a mission to give teams transparency into their public cloud spend. Together with OpenMetal, we can now help companies act on those insights, building the right mix of public and private cloud for their workloads and balancing cost and performance as they scale,” said Anirudh Murali, Co-Founder and CEO of Economize.

The companies are also targeting businesses managing AI and GPU infrastructure spending. OpenMetal provides GPU servers and clusters alongside its private cloud and bare-metal offerings, while Economize provides cost visibility and optimisation capabilities across cloud and AI infrastructure.

OpenMetal Labs will focus on infrastructure and cost-management challenges that standard products do not address. The company said Labs will combine expertise from both organisations, including OpenMetal’s work with OpenStack and Ceph engineering and Economize’s capabilities in cloud cost monitoring, anomaly detection, reporting and alerts.

The new offering joins Hosted Private Cloud, Bare Metal Dedicated Servers, GPU Servers and Clusters, and Ceph Storage Clusters as OpenMetal’s fifth offering and is available now.

title: Non-Profit Adalat AI Releases Open Indic ASR Models for Document-Ready Transcription
content:
The company said the 120M models are, to its knowledge, among the smallest open models for rich-orthography transcription.

Legal tech non-profit Adalat AI has released Koyal, a family of five open speech recognition models for Hindi, Kannada, Malayalam, and Telugu. They are designed to generate document-ready transcripts with punctuation and formatted numerals rather than producing a raw stream of recognised words.

The release includes four 120-million-parameter monolingual models for Hindi, Kannada, Malayalam, and Telugu, and a 600-million-parameter multilingual model covering all four languages. The 120M models are designed for offline transcription, while the multilingual model supports both offline and streaming transcription from a single checkpoint.

The 600M multilingual model is also positioned as one of the earliest open cache-aware streaming ASR models supporting Malayalam, Kannada, and Telugu in native scripts from a single checkpoint.

Most open automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems are primarily designed to recognise words. Developers often have to add separate systems for punctuation restoration, number formatting, and language-specific post-processing before the transcript can be used as a document.

Koyal is designed to address that gap at the model level.

The models are trained to produce what Adalat AI calls “rich orthography”, retaining punctuation and written number forms in the transcript. This is particularly relevant for applications where the transcript itself is the final output, including dictation, legal documents, forms, reports, and notes.

“Recognition alone is not the product,” Adalat AI stated in a LinkedIn post, describing the problem it has encountered while building speech-to-document workflows.

The four monolingual models are approximately 0.5 GB each, making them suitable for deployments with more limited hardware resources.

The monolingual models are based on Conformer hybrid TDT-CTC systems from AI4Bharat's MahaDhwani encoder, which was pre-trained on 279,000 hours of Indic speech. They were subsequently fine-tuned on 1,350–2,400 hours of curated dictation data per language.

The multilingual model uses a cache-aware FastConformer encoder adapted from NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 ASR, along with a tokenizer and decoder designed for Hindi, Kannada, Malayalam, and Telugu.

On Adalat AI's FLEURS-RO rich-orthography benchmark, the 120M Koyal models recorded WER_SCRIBE scores of 9.03% for Hindi, 11.30% for Kannada, 14.74% for Malayalam, and 17.81% for Telugu.

The company said the models reduce error rates by roughly half compared with its earlier Whisper-small releases while using around half the parameters for the three languages covered by the comparison.

The benchmark differs from conventional word error rate because it evaluates not only word recognition but also punctuation and numeral rendering—the elements Adalat AI considers necessary for document-ready transcription.

The 600M multilingual model targets applications that require multiple Indic languages or real-time transcription.

The model supports different inference settings based on future audio available to the system. Adalat AI's tests show that at zero lookahead, the model remains within 2.22 percentage points of full-context offline decoding across all four languages, indicating a relatively gradual accuracy trade-off as latency is reduced.

The models are being released openly through Hugging Face, with Adalat AI providing model cards containing information on training data, evaluation, and deployment.

The DoorDash investment adds hyperlocal digital commerce to Hyderabad's growing GCC ecosystem.

DoorDash has opened its first India office in Hyderabad with an initial workforce of 500 professionals and plans to expand the team to more than 3,000 employees over the next two years, as the US-based hyperlocal commerce company looks to scale its global technology and support operations from India.

The Hyderabad hub, located in Hitec City, will initially house Customer Experience and Integrity (CXI) and general and administrative teams. The CXI operation will be only the third internally owned DoorDash CXI service centre globally, alongside facilities in Tempe, Arizona, and Mexico City.

The company said the Hyderabad team will support DoorDash's global operations, serving consumers, merchants and Dashers across its international markets. DoorDash currently operates across more than 40 countries and serves over 56 million monthly active consumers.

Hyderabad will serve as an owned DoorDash CXI hub and will own and drive the company's customer support organisation from India as an extended arm of its global CXI function.

DoorDash said it could add more specialised capabilities, including integrity, fraud review, and technical functions, to the Hyderabad operation over time.

Jenna Kohnke, Senior Director, Workforce Strategy and Talent Acquisition Operations at DoorDash, said in a statement, “Establishing DoorDash’s first hub in India is an important milestone in expanding our global operations network. Hyderabad’s exceptional talent, thriving technology ecosystem, and commitment to building a world-class environment for global capability centres made it a natural choice for our long-term investment.”

The expansion comes as DoorDash continues to build out its global operating footprint. The company reported more than $100 billion in marketplace gross order value in 2025 and operates across more than 40 countries.

The DoorDash investment adds hyperlocal digital commerce to Hyderabad's growing GCC ecosystem, which already includes global technology, retail, logistics and commerce companies.

D Sridhar Babu, Minister for Information Technology, Electronics & Communications, Industries & Commerce, and Legislative Affairs, Telangana government, said, “DoorDash choosing Hyderabad to build capabilities to drive its rapid growth is a strong validation of how Hyderabad has evolved as a global talent hub. Its Hyderabad hub is expected to grow to a 3,000-plus strong headcount, bringing global capabilities in hyperlocal commerce, customer experience, technology and operations to Hyderabad.”

The Telangana government said Hyderabad has more than 500 GCCs and is targeting more than 100 additional GCCs, with an ambition to create over 1 lakh new high-value jobs and more than 3 lakh indirect jobs. The government expects the city's GCC workforce to reach 10 lakh employees by 2029.

For DoorDash, the Hyderabad operation will also give it access to the city's established technology talent pool as it expands its presence in India. The company said employees will work across customer experience, integrity and corporate functions, with additional specialised capabilities potentially added as the hub grows.
