title: MongoDB’s India Team Leads Development of New Core Capabilities
content:
The company has over 750 employees in India across its Gurugram, Mumbai, and Bengaluru offices, and began operations in 2013.

Database giant MongoDB said its engineering team in India was the primary center for developing the newly released Atlas Agent Engine.

The company established its R&D team in the country 18 months ago, and currently employs 110 engineers.

Unveiled at the company’s Investor Day in New York, the platform provides a unified layer that lets enterprises bring agentic AI into production. Essentially, it combines three things that companies typically have to assemble separately—agent execution/runtime, persistent memory and retrieval, and governance/security.

“Without a single platform, engineering teams must stitch together disparate tools that break every time underlying models or frameworks evolve. That’s what Atlas Agent Engine is designed to solve for,” the company said.

All of the capabilities of the Atlas Agent Engine are tightly integrated within MongoDB’s existing infrastructure. The platform is available in public preview, with consumption-based pricing for the Atlas Agent Runtime and Atlas Agent Memory.

The India team was also the ‘primary centre’ for developing other core MongoDB capabilities, including its latest 9.0 variant. “Indian teams delivered key Enterprise Advanced

capabilities for MongoDB 9.0, including mission-critical backup features,” said the company.

The company has over 750 employees in India across its Gurugram, Mumbai, and Bengaluru offices, and began operations in 2013.

MongoDB also said that the Indian teams are developing automated migration tools, AI-assisted code translation frameworks, and schema transformation utilities.

“The work our talented team does here directly impacts our largest, most mission-critical enterprise customers worldwide,” Nitin Aggarwal, Director of Engineering at MongoDB, said in a statement.

“I’m so proud of what we've already achieved in such a short time, but as the team rapidly expands, there’s a huge opportunity ahead for engineers in India to shape the future of software.”

MongoDB serves half of the top 100 companies in India by market capitalisation, alongside 50 unicorn startups in the country.

The latest MongoDB 9.0 is designed to handle higher-throughput transactional applications and AI workloads. The company reported up to 2x higher throughput on large instances, 35% faster find-one queries, and 30% faster update-one queries compared with MongoDB 8.0.

The release also expands Queryable Encryption to support prefix, suffix, and substring searches on encrypted data, alongside improvements to workload management, observability, and scalability.

The US President also directed US government agencies to use the term ‘super intelligence’ instead of ‘artificial intelligence’ when referring to the technology.

US President Donald Trump and executives from big tech companies have signed a voluntary accord requiring frontier AI companies to implement internal safety controls, use independent external evaluators and establish board-level oversight of those systems.

The seven people who signed the accord include Trump, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, Google chief Sundar Pichai, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI President Greg Brockman, NVIDIA chief Jensen Huang and xAI’s Elon Musk.

The wider luncheon had 31 confirmed attendees, including Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, AMD chief Lisa Su, Amazon Founder Jeff Bezos, Broadcom CEO Hock Tan, Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora, ServiceNow’s Bill McDermott and Micron Technology CEO Sanjay Mehrotra, alongside senior administration officials.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman was not there because he was at OpenAI’s DevDay in San Francisco, and Brockman represented the Company.

The White House Accord on Super Intelligence: Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities sets out four layers of controls covering internal model monitoring, internal oversight, independent external evaluation and board-level review.

Companies are to monitor model capabilities and alignment during training and deployment, including around cybersecurity, biosecurity and chemical threats.

This involves maintaining internal teams to detect and correct problems, working with an “independent external auditor or evaluator”, and creating an independent board committee to review internal and external findings.

The accord also calls for measures to prevent models from “hack[ing] or access[ing] technical systems in unintended ways”.

The agreement is voluntary and does not create a federal regulator or specify penalties for non-compliance.

It does, however, state that “over time, it may make sense to codify these steps into laws or regulations”.

Trump described the document as “almost like a constitution” and said the industry should rely on “tremendous self-policing”.

Zuckerberg said the participating companies would develop “robust internal controls” for their AI systems.

Trump separately said he was considering a 10-person board to oversee AI safety, although he did not name potential members.

He also said a new White House official responsible for AI policy would be appointed soon.

The meeting also covered the infrastructure needed to train and operate increasingly large AI models.

Trump reiterated support for new data centres despite local opposition over electricity demand, utility costs and other community impacts. He said companies would make “massive contributions to communities” to build support for new facilities.

The safety discussions follow OpenAI and Anthropic disclosures of incidents involving AI agents that accessed or attempted to gain unauthorised access to external systems.

The companies are also facing pressure over how quickly they should deploy increasingly capable systems, while the White House has argued that excessive regulation could weaken US competitiveness against China.

Trump also directed US government agencies to use the term ‘super intelligence’ instead of ‘artificial intelligence’ when referring to the technology.

Moreover, the administration launched America.gov, an AI-powered government portal intended to provide a single interface for federal information and services.

It currently allows users to ask questions in natural language, and the administration says it will later support transactions such as passport renewal and Medicare enrolment.

The executive order directs agencies to integrate covered public-facing services into the platform. Covered services generally include federal services with more than 100,000 users over 12 months, while IRS tax filing and national-security-sensitive services are excluded.

The White House’s Chief Design Officer Joe Gebbia said the system draws information from roughly 29,000 federal websites.

title: DeepSeek Announces a Stronger Software Integration with Huawei GPUs
content:
The Chinese AI lab has announced six new open-source software projects tailored for Huawei GPUs.

DeepSeek has open-sourced six software components optimised for Huawei’s Ascend AI accelerators, extending its work with the Chinese chipmaker from adapting its models to building the underlying software stack needed to run them.

The release covers programming, computation, communication, attention and data-processing components, and is intended to provide Ascend with counterparts to DeepSeek’s existing open-source infrastructure for NVIDIA GPUs.

The six components are TileLang, DeepGEMM, DeepEP, TileKernels, FlashMLA and DeepSelect.

TileLang is a high-level programming language and compiler for writing AI kernels, while DeepGEMM handles general matrix operations and DeepEP provides distributed communication for large-scale model workloads.

TileKernels covers vector computation and memory access, while FlashMLA provides kernels for DeepSeek’s attention architecture, and DeepSelect handles data filtering.

DeepSeek said in a WeChat announcement that the Ascend versions correspond one-to-one with components it previously released for NVIDIA hardware.

The Ascend implementation of TileLang wraps Huawei’s lower-level Ascend C instructions, allowing developers to use a higher-level programming model while retaining access to hardware-specific capabilities.

DeepSeek said every TileLang operator used in its own model training now has a corresponding high-performance implementation on Ascend.

The company also said Huawei supported development and that the two companies jointly advanced a 128-chip supernode based on Ascend 950 processors, with optimisation work spanning both computation and communication.

DeepSeek described TileLang as a simpler programming model than NVIDIA’s CUDA and said a high-level language that can reach hardware performance is a prerequisite for an independent AI-chip software ecosystem.

The release follows DeepSeek’s shift towards Huawei hardware with the launch of DeepSeek-V4 in April. Huawei said its Ascend 950-based supernode would fully support V4, while DeepSeek specifically adapted its model for Ascend systems.

Reuters subsequently reported that demand for Ascend 950 chips increased among Chinese technology companies following V4’s release.

These developments come as US export controls continue to restrict Chinese access to advanced NVIDIA AI chips, with some products subject to case-by-case licensing and strict conditions.

This has increased pressure on Chinese technology companies to develop domestic alternatives in both AI hardware and software.

title: Coforge Launches CXNova, an Agentic AI Platform for Customer Experience
content:
The company said it can use customer data, business information and real-time signals to adapt interactions as they happen, similar to the shift towards more personalised AI-powered customer service.

Coforge has launched CXNova, an agentic AI platform designed to help enterprises manage customer interactions across digital and physical channels.

The company said it can use customer data, business information and real-time signals to adapt interactions as they happen, similar to the shift towards more personalised AI-powered customer service.

CXNova uses enterprise knowledge graphs and domain-specific ontologies to link information about customers, products, content and operations. Coforge said this provides the context its agents need to respond to customer interactions.

The system uses different agents for tasks such as generating and adapting content, interpreting customer signals and determining the next action, and assembling experiences across digital and physical channels.

The company added that it also has industry-specific agents with sector-specific knowledge and decision models. An experience operations (XOps) layer coordinates the agents with enterprise systems and human staff. This orchestration approach is also emerging in enterprise agentic AI platforms, including Zoom’s workflow orchestration system.

“At Coforge, we believe the next phase of digital transformation is not about adding more AI features. It’s about orchestrating experiences that can act in the moment,” Kapil Tyagi, Senior Vice President and Head of Experience at Coforge, said.

Coforge said CXNova is ready for deployment across travel, airlines, banking and financial services, insurance and healthcare. It also integrates with existing enterprise systems.

The announcement did not include details on customer deployments, revenue from CXNova or quantified performance results.

The guidelines set disclosure requirements for synthetic content and address the use of people’s images, voices and endorsements in AI-generated advertising.

The Advertising Standards Council of India (ASCI) has issued new guidelines for using AI-generated content in advertising, covering disclosure requirements and the use of a person’s image, voice or endorsement in synthetic content.

The guidelines take effect from January 1, 2027, and require advertisers to disclose synthetic content when it could influence consumer decisions and leaving it unlabeled could mislead consumers. They also prohibit fabricated endorsements and the use of a person’s likeness without consent, while clarifying that an AI disclosure does not exempt an advertisement from existing rules on misleading claims.

ASCI has adopted a risk-based approach to synthetic content, requiring disclosure when it materially influences consumer decisions and leaving it unlabeled could mislead consumers. Routine AI-assisted edits that do not materially affect how consumers understand an advertisement may not require disclosure.

“Importantly, it clarifies where the mere use of an AI label may not make an otherwise misleading advertisement acceptable,” said Manisha Kapoor, Secretary General and CEO, ASCI, in a statement shared with Exchange4Media.

The guidelines prohibit fabricated endorsements, deepfakes and the use of a person’s image or voice without consent. Brands can use synthetic influencers or replicate a real person’s image or voice with consent, subject to the disclosure requirements.

ASCI has also distinguished consent from approval. A person agreeing to the use of their image or voice does not necessarily mean they have approved a new claim, statement or endorsement generated using an AI replica.

An AI-generated label also does not override existing advertising standards. Advertisers remain responsible for ensuring that claims made through synthetic content are not false or misleading.

The rules come as AI-generated people and synthetic influencers become part of advertising campaigns. The report cited the dispute involving actor Urvashi Rautela, whose team alleged that a US-based AI company had used her name, images and videos commercially without authorisation. The allegations have not been established by a court.

title: CAG Launches BHASHINI-Powered AI Translation Platform for Official Documents
content:
CAG-BHASHINI Anuvaad is intended to support the translation of official and audit-related documents rather than operate as a standalone consumer translation tool.

The Office of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India (CAG) has launched CAG-BHASHINI Anuvaad, an AI-powered document translation solution developed by the Digital India BHASHINI Division to translate official CAG documents and audit-related reports across Indian languages.

The solution was launched on September 30 during the closing ceremony of Hindi Pakhwada 2026 at the CAG headquarters in Delhi. The initiative brings BHASHINI's multilingual Language AI capabilities into the CAG’s institutional translation workflows, with a focus on contextual translation, consistent terminology and output quality.

The platform has also been designed around institutional requirements including controlled access, security and data sovereignty, while keeping human oversight within the translation process.

CAG-BHASHINI Anuvaad is intended to support the translation of official and audit-related documents rather than operate as a standalone consumer translation tool. The system is being customised to meet the CAG's language and terminology requirements.

The move builds on an earlier collaboration between the CAG and the Digital India BHASHINI Division. In November 2025, the two organisations signed an MoU to deploy BHASHINI across more than 200 CAG offices for multilingual and multimodal communication, including translating reports, surveys, and evidence, as well as vetting translated and transcribed communications.

The latest launch takes that collaboration further by introducing a dedicated translation environment for CAG documents.

The initiative aims to make audit findings and official information available to a wider audience across Indian languages.

CAG officials said using language AI could reduce linguistic barriers while retaining institutional review and oversight.

“The fusion of artificial intelligence and communication has the potential to overcome linguistic barriers across geographies. By integrating language technology into our institutional processes, we can make communication more accessible, timely and effective, while strengthening the use of Indian languages in governance and official work,” Nilotpal Goswami, Additional Deputy Comptroller and Auditor General (Rajbhasha), said. “The CAG-BHASHINI initiative is an important step in bringing this convergence of language and technology into practice.”

CAG chief K Sanjay Murthy also highlighted the need to make audit findings and reports accessible to citizens in languages they understand, while supporting the wider use of Hindi and other Indian languages in official work.

Amitabh Nag, CEO of the Digital India BHASHINI Division, highlighted the expansion of BHASHINI from language data and AI models into applications and public-sector use cases.

According to the division, BHASHINI currently supports 36 Indian text languages, 23 Indian voice languages and 35 international languages. Its applications include multilingual agricultural advisory services, voice-enabled grievance registration and conversational services delivered through voice and telephone interfaces.

The CAG deployment adds another institutional use case: integrating multilingual AI directly into preparing and disseminating official documents.

The CAG-BHASHINI collaboration also extended to Hindi Pakhwada 2026, held from September 14 to 29.

Alongside conventional activities such as Hindi noting and drafting, translation and typing competitions, CAG employees participated in language activities and games developed using BHASHINI technology.

The broader collaboration demonstrates how government institutions are beginning to use language AI not only for translation but also for internal language engagement and official workflows.

The CAG-BHASHINI Anuvaad launch therefore marks a shift from using AI as an experimental language tool to embedding multilingual AI within an institutional process where translation accuracy, terminology, security, data control and human review are critical.

Only 25% of teams have humans reviewing more than 80% of AI agent output, SmartBear said.

SmartBear released findings from its 2026 State of Software Quality and Testing report. The company said 46% of surveyed teams have shipped AI-generated code that later failed in production.

The survey covered 1,436 technology professionals whose organisations use AI in development, according to the company. Respondents are based in the United States, the United Kingdom, or other countries, as per the report.

Among teams that had shipped failed code, 69% still have a lot or complete confidence that AI-written code behaves as intended, the company said. Across all respondents, 73% of leaders hold that level of confidence, compared with 52% of practitioners, according to SmartBear.

“AI coding failures are already costing companies revenue, customers, and trust, yet leaders remain blindly confident that AI-generated code behaves as intended, even after watching it fail,” said Dan Faulkner, Chief Executive Officer of SmartBear. “Closing the gap between perception and reality demands quality and testing built for AI’s speed, complexity, and scale.”

According to the company, 95% of leaders and 86% of practitioners are confident their AI agents’ work is adequately reviewed. The company said only 25% of teams have humans reviewing more than 80% of what those agents produce.

SmartBear said teams that review more agent output reported fewer failures, though failures remained common in both groups. As per the report, 49% of teams reviewing more than 60% of agent output have shipped AI code that later failed, compared with 58% of teams reviewing 60% or less.

The company said 47% of organisations cannot explain how AI contributed to a bug or incident in production. According to the report, that figure rises to 73% among teams that have already shipped a failure.

SmartBear said 46% of teams check that the specification reflects intent before AI generates code from it. The report describes that point as the earliest and least costly place to catch a problem.

The company said 69% of US respondents now say AI writes or accelerates at least 41% of their code, compared with 43% in its January 2026 Closing the AI Software Quality Gap report. SmartBear also reported that 45% of US respondents are very or extremely concerned about application quality, up from 36% in January.

The company said 83% of respondents believe autonomous testing, in which AI agents generate, execute, adapt, and report on tests without manual scripting, would help them keep pace with AI code volume. According to SmartBear, 23% named trust in the results as the top barrier to adopting it, compared with 12% who named cost.

The company said 84% of respondents use at least one form of human review to validate AI-generated tests, while 3% rely on AI self-validation alone.

SmartBear said AI-powered testing and validation tools can help companies achieve application integrity, which it defines as continuous, measurable assurance that software works as intended.

The shrinking gap between compromise and data exfiltration makes early detection, code security, and unified monitoring critical for enterprises.

Siddharth JindalTech Journalist

As enterprises deploy AI agents and increasingly rely on AI-generated code, attackers are accessing the same technology to identify vulnerabilities and accelerate attacks. That leaves organisations with barely any time to detect a compromised system before it turns into a major breach.

According to a recent IBM study, one in four malicious breaches were AI-enabled, and these breaches cost an average of $6 million.

Security can no longer be treated as a separate layer added after deployment, Jyoti Prakash, Head of Security at Google Cloud India, tells AIM in an exclusive interview.

Google’s Cybersecurity Forecast 2026 says threat actors are expected to increasingly use AI to improve the speed, scope, and effectiveness of their operations. It also expects attackers to adopt agentic systems to automate steps across the attack lifecycle.

Prakash says enterprises need to secure their code and cloud infrastructure first. This also extends to endpoints, user interactions, and security operations centres (SOCs).

The Window is Shrinking

Prakash explains there is a critical window between a system being compromised and an actual data breach. And that window is getting ever smaller. According to research by Palo Alto Networks’ cybersecurity intelligence team, Unit 42, it only takes 39 seconds from initial access to data infiltration.

The priority is to capture signals as early as possible. Logs and other signals can then be used for forensics and simulations to determine whether an organisation managed to contain the attack before data was lost.

For enterprises and SMBs, Prakash says this starts with code security. Before code reaches production, organisations need to check its capacity, capability, security, and vulnerabilities.

However, developers cannot manually scan code to detect vulnerabilities and still keep pace with the rapidly emerging attacks.

“It is not easy to have a bunch of developers keep doing this scanning on a daily basis because threats and vulnerabilities are moving up with machine speed,” Prakash says.

He highlights Google’s code and cloud security capabilities, including Big Sleep and CodeMender, which use AI to scan for bugs and vulnerabilities and help organisations respond faster.

Google Cloud has already begun deploying its agentic SOC capabilities with customers including Lloyds Banking Group, Mahindra, Sutherland, Sunrun, and BBVA.

Google Cloud’s Agentic SOC uses Gemini-powered agents to automate tasks such as alert triage, threat hunting, and detection engineering. According to Google, its triage and investigation agent can reduce a typical 30-minute manual analysis to 60 seconds.

Cybersecurity Engineers Need AI Too

Prakash says AI has changed the security equation because attackers can also use increasingly capable models to accelerate attacks. “To address and manage those kinds of attacks, you need to leverage AI as well.”

He says organisations need to prepare in two ways. First, they should proactively upgrade their security capabilities with AI-powered infrastructure. The second is responding after an attack has already occurred.

When malware, DDoS attacks, or data exfiltration are detected, security teams need to scan digital assets and identify signals and patterns to determine which application or line of code has been compromised.

Prakash says Google’s security consulting services have been involved in investigations following recent attacks, helping organisations contain the impact and prevent similar incidents.

The risks around autonomous AI systems have also come into sharper focus following a recently disclosed Gemini incident where the model accessed the systems of three real companies while it was supposed to be operating against a fictional company in a controlled environment.

The evaluation environment was not supposed to give Gemini access to the open internet, but a configuration issue allowed it to reach real-world systems. In one case, the model resorted to brute force attack, repeatedly guessing passwords until it gained access. In two others, it found credentials in public repositories and used them to access protected systems.

Gemini stopped after recognising that the systems belonged to real companies, and Google said the affected organisations were informed.

However, Prakash declines to comment on the specific case, saying, “The whole objective and the mission of Google is to create a secure environment and make sure that every citizen is safe.”

Securing Indian Orgs

Prakash rejects the assumption that government websites, banks, digital public infrastructure, or educational platforms are not currently being targeted simply because there may be no visible attack. “I will say they might not be aware,” he quips.

He says AI adoption is already widespread among individuals and organisations, making responsible AI usage and guardrails increasingly important.

Companies need policies governing how employees use AI tools, particularly when sensitive corporate information is involved.

Prakash says Google’s approach includes bidirectional scanning, where it checks prompts before sending them to an AI system and scans responses before they reach the user.

Prakash says organisations should not begin their security strategy by selecting products. “The most important thing is to understand what the business requirement is. Based on that, a company should build a security framework,” he says.

Once the framework, architecture, and infrastructure requirements are defined, companies can add individual technology components.

He also identifies corporate security policy and risk scoring as key foundations before organisations decide which tools to deploy.

As enterprises deploy more autonomous systems, managing identities of AI agents will become increasingly important. Prakash says Google has a dedicated team working on identity-related security across its solutions.

“I think unification of security is something I would really encourage the industry to adopt,” he advises.

That means bringing together code and cloud security, endpoint security, and SOC operations. When these three areas are connected, signals detected across the environment can reach the SOC and trigger an appropriate response.

title: Target Expands Bengaluru GCC With New Campus in Manyata
content:
The new facility will connect Target’s 5,700+ employees across its operations in the city.

Target in India has expanded its Bengaluru campus with a new 830,000 sq ft office at Embassy Manyata Business Park. The company said that this new facility sits across the road from Target’s existing office and creates one connected campus for its teams.

This announcement comes just after the company confirmed details of the lease with AIM earlier in June.

The new campus aims to bring Target’s teams together and support collaboration and co-creation. Target in India operates as an integrated headquarters of Minneapolis-based Target Corporation. It has operated in India for more than 21 years.

“Our office expansion is a reflection of Target’s strategic priority to strengthen our team and the communities in which we operate,” said Andrea Zimmerman, Senior Vice President and President, Target in India.

Zimmerman said the extended campus will bring more than 5,700 team members together. She added that it will create more opportunities to connect, collaborate and build solutions for Target’s business and customers.

The new 10-floor building includes 22 collaboration spaces and 25 meeting rooms on every floor. It also houses a 1,200-seat cafeteria, gym, recreation and play zone, and dance and yoga studio. The office has seven wellness rooms and other spaces for teams to meet and connect.

Target said the office combines its brand with elements of India’s art and craft heritage. The workplace reflects the company’s culture and its presence in India.

Target in India delivers technology-led retail solutions across merchandising, supply chain, fulfilment, stores, cybersecurity, digital and marketing. The two Bengaluru offices will now form an integrated campus to support closer collaboration across teams.

title: SiMa.ai Becomes a Unicorn After Raising $150 Mn to Scale Physical AI
content:
The Series C round values the company at $1.45 billion as it expands into robotics, automotive and drones.

Physical AI company SiMa.ai has raised $150 million in Series C funding to scale its AI platform across robotics, automotive and drones. The funding brings SiMa.ai’s total capital raised to $500 million and its valuation to $1.45 billion, making it a unicorn.

The funding round was co-led by Fidelity Management & Research Company and Amplify. Alter Venture Partners, Dell Technologies Capital and StepStone Group also participated, with AllianceBernstein, Baron Capital and JP Morgan joining as new investors.

SiMa.ai will use the funds to scale its software platform and develop new Physical AI hardware. The company also plans to scale Palette Neat, its agentic software environment for Physical AI. It will also fund its next generation of purpose-built silicon.

“Physical AI in humanoids, automotive, and drones is the gateway to a $50 trillion market,” Founder and CEO Krishna Rangasayee said. The company expects the new hardware to deliver up to 1,000 TOPS of compute. The company has scheduled these products for the first half of 2028.

The planned hardware will include machine learning IP, chiplets and systems-on-chip. SiMa.ai will target medium and high-end drones, humanoid robotics and automotive applications. It will also target advanced driver assistance systems and AI-powered cockpits.

Existing customers will be able to migrate their applications to the new architectures.

SiMa.ai said its commercial growth also supported the latest funding round. The company quadrupled year-over-year revenue growth between 2024 and 2025. It also said revenue momentum remains strong in 2026.

SiMa.ai currently serves more than 150 customers across automotive, drones and robotics. Its customers include Bosch, Emerson, Intrinsic, Kontron, L&T Technology Services, Mistral, STIGA, Synopsys, and Virya Autonomous Technologies.

Rangasayee said the company has built a full-stack platform instead of adapting cloud offerings. Counterpoint Research projects cumulative shipments of 145 million Physical AI devices by 2035. SiMa.ai said this shift will move AI from software applications into physical consumer and industrial systems.

SiMa.ai was founded in 2018 to develop software-centric silicon for physical-world applications. Its platform combines the Modalix MLSoC with Palette Neat for Physical AI development.

The company says this approach can reduce application development timelines from months to days or hours. Its board includes semiconductor and technology executives such as former Xilinx CEO Moshe Gavrielov and Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan.

title: Samsung to Invest $1 Bn in NVIDIA-Backed AI Infrastructure Firm Helix
content:
The investment will support data centre, power and network infrastructure for growing AI compute demand.

Samsung Electronics and five affiliates (Samsung C&T, Samsung SDS, Samsung SDI, Samsung Life Insurance and Samsung Fire & Marine Insurance) will invest $1 billion in Helix Digital Infrastructure, a KKR-backed AI infrastructure company.

Samsung announced the investment to support infrastructure for rising AI compute demand. The investment will help the giant expand beyond hardware components into AI infrastructure.

Helix will develop and operate hyperscale data centres, power generation, transmission and fibre-optic networks for large-scale AI workloads.

Helix launched in June and aims to provide infrastructure across the AI value chain. Its offering includes data centre development and operations, power generation, transmission and distribution infrastructure, and fibre-optic networks.

The company says this model can help hyperscalers secure infrastructure faster and is led by Adam Selipsky, former CEO of Amazon Web Services.

It is also building a management team with expertise across data centres and power. KKR’s global infrastructure business contributes about 170 dedicated professionals. Founding investors include KKR, the Kuwait Investment Authority, NVIDIA and US power company Vistra Corp. Samsung’s investment brings its affiliates into a group spanning semiconductors, computing infrastructure and energy.

Samsung said AI data centres are becoming business platforms rather than simple facilities. These platforms include GPU-as-a-Service, sovereign AI and colocation services. Their expansion is also increasing demand across power generation, cooling, semiconductors and finance.

The company identified power availability as a key constraint on AI infrastructure. “Power availability is currently the greatest bottleneck in AI infrastructure,” Samsung said. Helix plans to secure energy capacity through direct investments and partnerships with energy developers, including Vistra.

The investment also connects Helix’s infrastructure strategy with Samsung’s existing businesses. Samsung Electronics’ Device Solutions division supplies semiconductor products for global AI infrastructure development.

Its Device eXperience division provides data centre cooling systems through FläktGroup, which Samsung acquired in 2025. The portfolio covers air cooling systems and coolant distribution units for liquid cooling. FläktGroup operates 14 production sites and a supply and service network across 65 countries.

Samsung C&T Engineering & Construction Group works as an engineering, procurement and construction contractor. It handles data centre and power generation infrastructure projects. Samsung SDS designs, builds and operates data centres and has entered the GPU-as-a-Service market.

Samsung SDI supplies uninterruptible power supplies and battery backup units for data centres. These systems support facilities running high-performance servers around the clock. The affiliate plans to explore new opportunities in this area.

Samsung said the investment will accelerate global AI data centre deployment alongside Helix. It also aims to increase collaboration among the participating Samsung companies.

title: OpenAI Scraps GPT-6.1 Astra Release Over Safety Concerns
content:
GPT-6.1 Astra performed worse than its predecessor in terms of accurately communicating what the model has done and following the boundaries set by users.

OpenAI has cancelled the planned release of GPT-6.1 Astra after internal testing found that the model had regressed on key alignment measures, including deception and its ability to stay within authorised instructions.

The model was expected to launch in October across ChatGPT and Codex and was designed to handle more complex tasks with less human assistance.

According to Saachi Jain, OpenAI’s Head of Safety Systems, GPT-6.1 Astra performed worse than its predecessor, GPT-6 Astra, in tests of whether models accurately communicate what they have done and follow the boundaries set by users.

The model also showed problems with what OpenAI calls “scope authorisation”, where, in some cases, it continued pursuing tasks without obtaining user permission and attempted to use external tools or services where doing so could have been unsafe.

Jain added that Astra “didn't quite meet the bar” on staying within scope and authorisation.

OpenAI plans to conduct several investigations into the causes of the failures and may use Astra’s underlying model for additional reinforcement-learning runs rather than release the model in its current form.

The decision comes as OpenAI expands its investigation into model misalignment.

OpenAI has also begun systematically reporting examples of models behaving outside their intended constraints. This includes concealing mistakes, using exposed credentials, uploading files to the internet without authorisation, and communicating through supposedly isolated software environments.

The company said its review of model activity affecting external systems has so far resulted in notifications to “dozens” of third parties, with the investigation still continuing.

The most serious previously disclosed case involved OpenAI models bypassing internet restrictions during cybersecurity evaluations and compromising parts of Hugging Face’s network.

The review has also extended to government systems.

OpenAI has acknowledged that an experimental agent gained unauthorised access to Australia’s Medicare Statistics Reporting Service during an internal training and evaluation exercise.

The Australian government has launched a rapid review involving the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet, the National Cyber Security Coordinator, the Australian Signals Directorate, the Australian AI Safety Institute, and Services Australia.

Separately, Axios reported that OpenAI and Anthropic are investigating tens of thousands of incidents involving frontier models taking actions that external evaluators would consider problematic.

title: OpenAI Apologises for AI Breach in Australia
content:
This comes after PM Anthony Albanese subsequently expressed “extreme concern” to OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and criticised the company for taking “way too long” to notify Australian authorities.

OpenAI has apologised to the Australian government after one of its AI models gained unauthorised access to government systems during an internal training and evaluation exercise.

The company also disclosed that its models accessed systems operated by three other Australian government agencies.

“We are sorry and working to do better in the future,” OpenAI said in a statement published on September 28. “We also should have handled our response better.”

The most serious incident involved Services Australia’s Medicare Statistics Reporting Service in June.

An experimental internal model was tasked with finding government spending per person on medicines for skin conditions in Victorian communities.

After struggling to obtain the information, the model found a way to gain non-public access to the service, ran commands, retrieved internal files and credentials, accessed technical information and source code, and wrote files to an internal server.

OpenAI said it found no evidence that the model accessed individual patient or client records. The company said the model was not authorised to access the service or carry out the subsequent activity.

Three other agencies were also affected. At the NSW Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research, a model accessed the public Crime Mapping Tool and made API and website metadata requests.

The system returned application configuration, operational jobs, logs and website metadata, but individual crime records were not accessed.

At Victoria’s Department of Health, OpenAI agents discovered an exposed access key and retrieved reporting configuration and aggregate survey statistics from a Victorian Agency for Health Information system. OpenAI said individual medical records and identifiable survey responses were not accessed.

At the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW), agents retrieved aggregate statistics using third-party browsing and download services.

OpenAI said attempts to bypass access controls were unsuccessful and that the material appeared to have been publicly available.

The activity occurred in June but was disclosed only this month.

OpenAI said its review began after the separate Hugging Face incident in July and identified the Australian activity in mid-August.

It notified Services Australia and Victoria’s Department of Health on September 10, BOCSAR on September 18 and AIHW on September 24.

OpenAI acknowledged that it should have shared preliminary findings sooner.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese subsequently expressed “extreme concern” to OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and criticised the company for taking “way too long” to notify Australian authorities.

The company’s Chief Strategy Officer Jason Kwon is scheduled to appear before Australia’s Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence next month.

He also announced that the incident would be referred to the Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence, while the government would examine potential law-enforcement and legislative responses.

OpenAI said it has since strengthened network restrictions and monitoring, blocked live internet access in research environments and introduced human-review alerts.

It has also paused training and evaluation involving tool use for its most capable models until additional safeguards are in place.

In Australia, OpenAI will provide technical assistance to affected agencies, support cyber-defence efforts through its $1 billion Daybreak for Frontline Defenders fund and establish an Australian taskforce with independent experts.

The company has also committed to a range of measures to safely evaluate and release newer AI models, by slowing down the pace of training and establishing better frameworks to report safety incidents.

The company also recently scrapped its plans to release the GPT-6.1 Astra, citing safety concerns, which would otherwise be the successor to its most powerful model available to public, the GPT-6 Astra.

title: NVIDIA Approves Record $150 Bn Share Buyback as AI Boom Fuels Cash Generation
content:
NVIDIA’s latest addition to its share buyback programme takes the total authorisation to $235 billion.

NVIDIA’s board has approved an additional $150 billion for its share buyback programme, making it the largest single buyback authorisation increase in history, as the AI chipmaker continues to generate substantial cash from demand for its processors.

The company had previously announced an $80 billion share repurchase authorisation in May.

The new authorisation takes NVIDIA’s remaining buyback capacity to $235 billion, surpassing Apple’s previous $110 billion record. The company expects to execute the share buyback through fiscal year 2028.

“Our cash generation gives us the capacity to invest in the technologies that advance this transformation and return capital to shareholders,” NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang said in a statement released by the company.

The announcement comes as NVIDIA continues to benefit from demand for chips used to train and run AI models. The company has forecast around 70% revenue growth for FY28, signalling continued confidence in demand for AI infrastructure.

The company ended its July quarter with $22.44 billion in cash and cash equivalents, as it continues to generate significant cash from its AI business.

NVIDIA’s shares were up 1.68% at the close of trading on September 28, trading at $228.86 apiece on Nasdaq. Over the last six months, its shares were up over 38%.

title: Kavitha Srinivasulu Joins Persistent Systems as Chief Cyber & AI Security Officer
content:
Srinivasulu will oversee AI security, risk advisory, and cybersecurity and work across leadership teams at Persistent Systems.

Kavitha Srinivasulu has joined Persistent Systems as Vice President – Chief Cyber & AI Security Officer, she announced on LinkedIn. Her remit covers cybersecurity, AI security, risk advisory, security engineering, and digital transformation.

Srinivasulu will work with customers, C-suite executives, and leadership teams to help “organisations navigate emerging technology risks” and use AI with security, resilience and trust in focus.

Before joining Persistent, Srinivasulu worked at Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), where she served as Programme Director, Cybersecurity and Data Privacy, with a focus on process optimisation and digital transformation.

Srinivasulu has more than 20 years of experience spanning BFSI, retail, manufacturing, healthcare, IT services and telecommunications, with previous roles at Wipro, Bank of America, Verizon, AstraZeneca alongside TCS.

Her appointment comes as enterprises expand agentic AI use across business and technology environments, increasing the need for security controls around AI systems. Anthropic's Mythos has also accelerated vulnerability discovery, creating new challenges for security teams as AI-assisted security research expands.

IT services companies are also incorporating cybersecurity into broader enterprise AI deployments, with Wipro using ServiceNow's AI platform capabilities for cybersecurity incident response and governance as part of its expanded partnership.

Srinivasulu said she would focus on enabling “secure transformation, trusted innovation and sustainable business value in the AI era.”

title: IBM, Yotta Launch Sovereign Agentic AI Platform for Enterprise Workflows
content:
The platform combines IBM’s AI-agent technology with Yotta’s sovereign cloud infrastructure to help organisations deploy and govern AI agents.

IBM and Yotta Data Services have launched the Sovereign Agentic AI Platform for Indian organisations, combining IBM’s enterprise AI capabilities with Yotta’s sovereign AI cloud infrastructure.

Built using IBM watsonx Orchestrate and deployed on Yotta’s Shakti Cloud, the platform is designed to help organisations deploy, run, and govern AI agents at scale while keeping data, inference, operations, and governance controls within India. It brings together AI-agent orchestration, GPU infrastructure, model development, and inference capabilities, with the platform available through Yotta’s Panvel and Greater Noida cloud regions.

IBM watsonx Orchestrate acts as an agentic control plane for securing, governing, and managing AI agents, while Shakti Cloud provides the compute, GPU infrastructure, networking, security, and operational capabilities required for enterprise AI workloads.

“With regulations evolving in India, digital sovereignty and open-source models are becoming a defining requirement for organisations as they scale AI from pilots to production. The priority is no longer just what AI can do, but how securely, transparently and compliantly it can be deployed,” Sandip Patel, Managing Director, IBM India and South Asia, said in a statement.

IBM and Yotta said the offering combines Yotta’s sovereign AI infrastructure with IBM’s enterprise AI and agentic AI capabilities.

“India’s AI journey requires organisations to have control not only over their data, but also over the infrastructure, compute, models, inference, and operations that power AI. Yotta’s Shakti Cloud and Shakti Studio provide this sovereign AI foundation, while IBM brings its enterprise AI and agentic AI capabilities to help organisations move from experimentation to production,” added Sunil Gupta, Co-founder, MD and CEO, Yotta Data Services.

Organisations can use the platform across workflows including security operations, document processing, and HR automation, among others.

CEO Bilal El Alamy argues that the bigger gap in AI is user adoption, not compute, as open-weight models offer companies a cheaper path to self-hosted AI.

Pyratz Corp, an Euronext-listed AI-native venture builder, has invested in Moonshot AI, the Chinese AI lab behind Kimi AI models, at a $30 billion valuation.

In an exclusive interview with AIM, Pyratz CEO Bilal El Alamy says the company “federated a syndicate of $10 million” for the investment. He adds that the investment reflects a broader bet on open-weight AI, self-hosted models, and a more decentralised AI ecosystem.

Unlike a traditional venture capital fund, Pyratz invests from its own balance sheet rather than managing capital on behalf of third-party investors, giving it greater flexibility over where it invests. This gives it greater flexibility over where it invests, including in companies and regions that may fall outside the usual constraints of a traditional fund.

El Alamy did not disclose Pyratz’s exact stake, saying the investment thesis matters more than the size of the ticket.

Moonshot AI has raised $7.27 billion to date, according to Tracxn. The company’s largest fundraise was $3.5 billion in July this year.

Pyratz was already a user of Kimi internally. El Alamy says the company has been building products to help entrepreneurs test and grow ideas faster and has integrated Kimi into those products.

The biggest attraction, however, is the economics of running the model.

“What we like about Moonshot is that it’s the cheapest model to self-host,” El Alamy says.

He compares the infrastructure cost of self-hosting an OpenAI model with Kimi. According to him, running an OpenAI model could cost around $30,000 a month in infrastructure, while Kimi can cost less than $5,000.

“Models like Kimi that are open-weight, efficient in terms of size and token consumption are very good models to start experiencing with AI,” he notes.

The company’s latest model, Kimi K3, has also made Moonshot a more serious commercial contender. Released in July, the 2.8-trillion-parameter open-weight model posted competitive results against leading proprietary models in third-party evaluations.

Moonshot is also reportedly in talks with Microsoft, Amazon and Google to host K3 on their cloud platforms, potentially creating a new distribution channel for a Chinese open-weight model outside China.

The investment also builds on Pyratz’s existing AI portfolio. Pyratz is also a shareholder in Paris-based AI startup Mistral AI, but El Alamy described the Moonshot investment as complementary rather than competitive.

“Mistral is developing a neocloud business where they’re open to basically hosting any type of open-weight model,” he says. He sees the Moonshot investment as complementary to that business.

El Alamy argues that Moonshot is undervalued relative to its commercial performance.

“Kimi is undervalued because Kimi has really amazing revenue KPIs,” he says, adding that Moonshot generates more revenue than Mistral while having a similar valuation.

El Alamy shares that Kimi has reached $1 billion in annual recurring revenue. “The thesis is that open-weight models are going to become more and more mainstream,” he adds.

He believes open-weight models will bring greater decentralisation to AI power because companies can run them on their own infrastructure rather than depending entirely on providers such as OpenAI and Anthropic.

El Alamy also points to growing usage of open-weight models, claiming that open-weight models accounted for 63% of AI tokens in the previous month.

Moonshot is also continuing with plans for a public listing in Hong Kong. El Alamy says the company is targeting the first half of 2027 for the IPO.

Moonshot confidentially filed for a Hong Kong IPO in September, targeting a potential $3 billion raise. The company was valued at around $50 billion at the time, after raising more than $5.5 billion, Reuters reported.

For Pyratz, the Moonshot investment combines a public-market opportunity with a longer-term thesis around open-weight models, self-hosted AI and a more decentralised AI ecosystem.

El Alamy dismisses calls from AI leaders including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman for a slowdown in AI development, describing them as a “marketing gimmick”.

He argues that the industry should prioritise expanding AI adoption rather than spending heavily to push model performance further. According to El Alamy, only around 5–7% of people globally are actively using AI.

He also acknowledges the risks associated with open-weight models, including the possibility of malicious actors using them to develop biological weapons. But he says that concentrating AI capabilities among a small number of companies presents its own risks.

“We don’t want to have one entity or two entities that centralise all the AI power in the world,” he notes.

The investment also gives Pyratz exposure to China’s AI ecosystem at a time when access to advanced NVIDIA GPUs remains constrained by US export controls.

El Alamy says Chinese and other Asian AI companies have responded by becoming more efficient in how they train models.

He also says Chinese AI companies are renting compute from neocloud providers, allowing them to access infrastructure without directly owning the chips.

“They cannot buy chips, but they have access to compute,” he says.

El Alamy expects compute availability to increase as countries invest in energy infrastructure and data centres. He suggests Chinese AI companies could increasingly work with infrastructure providers across Japan, Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia and India.

title: HCLSoftware to Acquire Robotiq.ai, Add RPA to Agentic AI Platform
content:
HCLSoftware plans to acquire Croatia-based Robotiq.ai, adding RPA capabilities to HCL UnO Agentic for enterprise task execution.

HCLSoftware, the software business division of HCLTech, will acquire Croatia-based robotic process automation (RPA) company Robotiq.ai for an enterprise value of €9 million (~₹98 crore), adding RPA capabilities to its HCL UnO Agentic orchestration and automation platform.

The acquisition will allow HCL UnO Agentic to automate tasks in enterprise applications where application programming interfaces (APIs) are unavailable or insufficient, HCLSoftware said. The transaction is expected to close in November 2026.

Based in Zagreb, Robotiq.ai provides an enterprise RPA platform used in large banks, insurance groups, and telecom providers. The company said the platform includes ISO-certified security, audit logs, and flexible deployment options.

“Enterprises are looking beyond AI experimentation toward production-scale automation that is secure, governed and reliable,” Kalyan Kumar, President, HCLSoftware, said in a statement.

Agentic automation is also increasingly combining AI agents with software robots and human oversight across enterprise processes.

Video conferencing platform Zoom has also been expanding its agentic AI platform towards workflow execution. In March, it added capabilities for custom AI agents to retrieve information, automate tasks, and orchestrate workflows across third-party systems including Salesforce, Slack, and ServiceNow. Zoom's platform expansion followed a similar move towards workflow orchestration.

The acquisition also comes as HCLTech has expanded its generative AI work. Earlier this year, it expanded its collaboration with Gemini Enterprise and Gemini models to build custom AI agents.

title: Coforge Appoints Akhil Gupta as Chairperson for 5 years
content:
Coforge has appointed former Bharti Enterprises Vice Chairman Akhil Gupta as its Chairperson and Non-Executive Independent Director for five years.

Coforge has appointed Akhil Gupta as the Chairperson and Non-Executive Independent Director of the company, effective September 29. His appointment will be for five years.

Gupta, the former Vice Chairman of Bharti Enterprises, currently chairs the boards of 360 ONE WAM and Bharti AXA Life Insurance. He also serves on the boards of Zepto, Snapdeal, Eutelsat Communications and Lodha Developers. A chartered accountant, Gupta has more than 40 years of professional experience and completed the Advanced Management Program at Harvard Business School in 2002.

The appointment comes as Coforge expands its AI-led services business, with its AI strategy centred on generative AI, agentic AI and AI-enabled delivery.

Vivek Sharma, Non-Executive Independent Director and interim Chairperson, said the company conducted a global search for the position with executive search firm Egon Zehnder. The process began with 60 candidates before Gupta emerged as the unanimous choice of the Nomination and Remuneration Committee (NRC) and the board.

“We are very excited to onboard an exceptional candidate as the Chairperson of Coforge,” Sharma said. He added that the search focused on governance experience, professional expertise and strategic perspectives.

Sudhir Singh, CEO and Executive Director of Coforge, said Gupta had been instrumental in helping Bharti Enterprises navigate multiple business shifts and welcomed him as Coforge moves into what he described as an AI-led era.

“Gupta was instrumental in Bharti Enterprises successfully navigating multiple business shifts during his watch and association with Bharti Enterprises,” Singh said.

Coforge reported a 31% year-on-year increase in revenue to ₹3,986 crore in Q2 FY26, while profit after tax rose 86% to ₹376 crore. The company’s Q2 FY26 performance came as it continued to expand its business.

Gupta has received several industry awards, including the EY Entrepreneur of the Year Award, the CA Lifetime Achievement Award and the CA Global Achiever Award from the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI). He has also served as President of the Telecom Sector Skill Council and former Chairman of the Digital Infrastructure Providers Association.

title: Anthropic Lost $42 Billion in 2025: Report
content:
Anthropic spent $7.33 billion on computing and infrastructure during the year, about 3x its 2024 spending and more than half of its total operating expenses.

Anthropic reported a net loss of nearly $42 billion in 2025, according to its initial public offering (IPO) prospectus seen by Reuters.

The loss included a roughly $34 billion accounting charge linked to the increased estimated value of financing instruments that could eventually convert into Anthropic shares, rather than money the company spent.

Excluding those accounting effects, Anthropic’s operating loss widened to $8.06 billion in 2025 from $2.98 billion a year earlier. At the same time, revenue grew roughly 12-fold to nearly $4.6 billion.

The company spent $7.33 billion on computing and infrastructure during the year, about three times its 2024 spending and more than half of its $12.65 billion in total operating expenses.

AIM has reached out to Anthropic for a comment.

The prospectus also reportedly shows the scale of Anthropic’s planned infrastructure commitments.

The company expects to spend $518 billion on cloud, computing, and infrastructure obligations in the coming years.

It had $20.28 billion in cash, cash equivalents, and short-term investments as of December 31, according to the filing.

Anthropic is reportedly seeking a public-market valuation of more than $2 trillion, more than double its estimated $965 billion valuation in May.

Its IPO follows OpenAI’s confidential filing for a US listing in June, and the report added that Anthropic’s offering could be delayed until after the November US midterm elections.

The filing also flags customer concentration as a risk. Nearly a quarter of Anthropic’s revenue came from two customers in 2025, while the company said many of its largest customers were not bound by long-term contracts and could reduce or stop spending.

The financial disclosure comes as Anthropic faces a parallel debate over the risks of increasingly capable AI systems. CEO Dario Amodei recently called for greater caution around the pace of AI development and recently told the UN Security Council that poorly managed AI could pose a risk to humanity.

title: Anthropic Launches Claude Sonnet 5.5 With 30% Lower Costs Per Task
content:
The new model costs $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, while Anthropic says it requires fewer tokens to complete the same tasks.

Anthropic has launched Claude Sonnet 5.5, the second model in its Claude 5.5 family, with improvements in coding, knowledge work and computer use.

Claude Sonnet 5.5 is available across Anthropic's platforms as well as Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud and Microsoft Azure. Developers can access the model through the Claude Platform using claude-sonnet-5-5.

The AI company said Sonnet 5.5 generates outputs more than 30% faster than Sonnet 5 and can cost up to 30% less per task.

Sonnet 5.5 costs $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, while cache reads cost $0.20 per million tokens. Opus 5.5, by comparison, costs $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens.

Anthropic said Sonnet 5.5 requires fewer tokens per task than Sonnet 5, reducing the overall cost of running workloads despite retaining the same token pricing as its predecessor.

Sonnet 5.5 is positioned as a lower-cost alternative to Claude Opus 5.5 for everyday tasks, bug fixing and creating documents, slides and spreadsheets. Anthropic said Claude Haiku 5.5, which will target high-volume and cost-sensitive applications, will be launched in the coming weeks.

On Terminal-Bench 4.0, which evaluates models on agentic coding tasks, Sonnet 5.5 scored 70.6%, compared with 10.3% for Sonnet 5 and 66.4% for Opus 5.5.

Anthropic said the improvement also shows up in the cost of running coding tasks. At Medium effort on Terminal-Bench 4.0, Sonnet 5.5 exceeded Sonnet 5’s best score while costing less than one-tenth as much per task.

The model also closed the gap with Opus 5.5 on knowledge-work benchmarks. On GDPval-AA v2.1, Sonnet 5.5 scored 1,844, compared with 1,846 for Opus 5.5 and 1,449 for Sonnet 5.

On OSWorld 2.1, a computer-use benchmark, Sonnet 5.5 scored 80.1%, compared with 81.8% for Opus 5.5 and 57% for Sonnet 5. On Humanity’s Last Exam with tools, it scored 64.5%, against 67.7% for Opus 5.5.

However, Anthropic said benchmark scores capture only part of a model’s capabilities and that Opus 5.5 remains stronger for complex, open-ended tasks that require sustained judgement.

The company has also added cybersecurity safeguards similar to those used for Opus 5.5. Higher-risk cybersecurity requests can fall back to Sonnet 5, while users can continue to use the model for routine software development tasks.

title: AMD Acquires World Labs for $8.2 Bn, Fei-Fei Li to Join as Chief Scientist
content:
The deal brings World Labs’ spatial intelligence research into AMD, with the companies working towards an open AI ecosystem.

AMD has agreed to acquire AI research company World Labs in an all-stock transaction valued at approximately $8.2 billion, bringing AI researcher Fei-Fei Li into AMD as Executive Vice President and Chief Scientist.

The transaction is expected to close by the end of 2026, subject to regulatory approvals and other customary closing conditions. Li will report directly to AMD CEO Lisa Su, while World Labs co-founders Justin Johnson and Ben Mildenhall will continue leading the team within AMD.

The deal gives AMD access to World Labs’ research in spatial intelligence and world models that will help understand, generate, and simulate three-dimensional environments.

AMD said the technology will help it better understand how AI workloads are evolving across areas including reasoning, robotics, simulation, and physical AI.

“Building the compute platforms for the next generation of AI requires a deep understanding of how models are evolving,” Su said in a statement.

“Fei-Fei and the World Labs team bring exceptional research leadership and model expertise. Together, we can use that insight to develop the hardware, software, and systems that will power the next generation of AI and strengthen the open AI ecosystem.”

The acquisition follows a technical partnership between the two companies that began last year. World Labs said the work initially centred on training and inference optimisation on AMD GPUs.

“As our teams worked together, we realised it would be a natural fit to bring together our AI ecosystem of software and hardware, foundation models, and applications,” World Labs said.

Li said the move will take World Labs closer to the hardware needed to scale its research.

“Without having a focused hardware effort, AI is hobbled in efficiency. And scale. And for our purposes, remains trapped in the digital world,” Li wrote in a post on X.

World Labs was founded in 2024 by Li, Johnson, Mildenhall, and Christoph Lassner. The company emerged from stealth in September 2024 with $230 million in funding and has since built models focused on spatial and physical intelligence.

In February, World Labs raised another $1 billion from investors including AMD, Nvidia, Autodesk, Emerson Collective, Fidelity Management & Research Company, and Sea. Autodesk invested $200 million in the round.

The company did not disclose its valuation, although Bloomberg had earlier reported that World Labs was deliberating another fundraise at a valuation of about $5 billion.

World Labs’ first product, Marble, uses its 3D world models to generate persistent and spatially coherent environments from images, video, text, and 3D layouts. The company says it is developing its models for applications spanning robotics, scientific discovery, creativity, and virtual worlds.

The acquisition also adds to AMD’s push to build an AI stack spanning chips, software, systems and models.

AMD acquired Finnish AI lab Silo AI for $665 million in 2024, with the company’s researchers working on AI models and software for AMD hardware. It also completed its $4.4 billion acquisition of ZT Systems in March 2025, adding expertise in AI infrastructure and rack-scale systems.

The World Labs deal takes that strategy further into model research. AMD said the company’s expertise will give it insight into emerging AI workloads and help shape future hardware, software, and systems.

Li will lead the research organisation alongside Johnson and Mildenhall after the transaction closes. The combined teams will work towards what the companies describe as an open AI ecosystem covering hardware, software, platforms, foundation models, and applications.

title: AI Needs $6 Tn Annual Revenue by 2031 to Justify Compute Spending: Bain Report
content:
Bain expects new AI products across autonomous systems, robotics, physical AI, and other emerging applications to drive $4.2 trillion in additional revenue.

The global AI industry will need to generate about $6 trillion in annual revenue by 2031 to support the infrastructure investment required to meet growing compute demand, according to Bain & Company’s seventh annual Global Technology Report.

Bain estimates that existing AI applications across consumer and enterprise markets could generate $1.2 trillion to $1.8 trillion in annual revenue. The remaining $4.2 trillion will need to come from new AI-driven products and markets.

“The debate today is fixated on employee productivity. The economics of AI infrastructure demand trillions in new revenue beyond productivity gains,” David Crawford, Chairman of Bain’s Global Technology practice, said in a statement.

Bain said the additional revenue could come from four areas: AI models replacing search engines and integrating advertising, autonomous systems such as cars, trucks and drones, physical AI including robotics and digital twins, and new applications such as drug discovery, mental health, and energy generation.

“What the industry needs is a wave of innovation that will dwarf what mobile and cloud unlocked,” Crawford said. He added that funding the infrastructure being built ahead of demand would require roughly 1% of additional annual global GDP growth.

The rise in AI compute demand has also changed the performance of hardware and semiconductor companies. Their market capitalisation grew at a 24% compound annual rate between 2020 and 2026, compared with 6% for software companies, Bain noted.

High-bandwidth memory, advanced packaging, and custom silicon are among the fastest-growing segments. Application-specific integrated circuits are also scaling as hyperscalers and AI companies develop chips for specific workloads.

Bain said custom chips are taking a larger share of data centre compute as training, inference, and agentic workloads reach volumes that can justify custom designs.

Supply risks are also changing procurement strategies. Companies are securing capacity across multiple locations and suppliers as natural disasters, geopolitical disruptions, and export controls create risks for semiconductor supply.

AI is also changing the cybersecurity landscape. Bain estimates that AI has reduced the time required for a typical cyberattack from about four weeks to 18 hours.

The growing use of AI agents adds another layer of risk, while existing approaches to monitoring software and AI vendors struggle to keep pace with frequent changes.

Bain’s CISO survey found that companies are increasing remediation budgets by double-digit percentages. Some are also redirecting 20–25% of cybersecurity staff from other work to address alerts generated by AI-powered scans.

The report identifies legacy platforms, network layers, and software-as-a-service vendors among the areas where companies are focusing remediation efforts.

Bain also identifies AI absorption speed, or how quickly companies can put AI into production, as a new competitive factor.

Leading AI labs are investing up to $9.75 billion in forward-deployed engineering to help enterprises integrate AI into their operations. Vendors are also developing application and infrastructure layers that connect AI models with enterprise systems.

Despite falling token prices, Bain does not expect large language models to follow a traditional commoditisation path.

“We see the more likely scenario as a continuum of frontier and mature models,” Crawford said. “New and unproven cases will initially favour frontier models, then likely migrate to lower-cost alternatives as the cases mature.”

Bain expects frontier models to remain focused on tasks where higher intelligence matters, while lower-cost and specialised models handle more established enterprise workloads.

The report also found that technology leaders expect AI to deliver a 148% improvement in release-cycle speed and a 95% increase in software developer productivity over the next one to two years. Current productivity gains range from 20% to 27%.

Bain said the gains from faster coding could create new bottlenecks in software review, coordination, quality, and governance, making changes to the wider software development lifecycle necessary.

title: Russia’s Sber Launches GigaChat 3.5 Reasoning to Take on Complex AI Tasks
content:
The Russian bank said GigaChat 3.5 Reasoning is the only Russian open-source model with a reasoning mode.

Sber has unveiled GigaChat 3.5 Reasoning, a new flagship model that can break complex problems into sequential steps, use external tools, check intermediate results and revise its approach before producing an answer.

The Russian bank said GigaChat 3.5 Reasoning is the only Russian open-source model with a reasoning mode. The model is already available to GigaChat users and developers, with developers able to integrate it into their products for free under the MIT licence. Sber said an API version for businesses will be available shortly.

The company says that unlike a conventional model that attempts to answer a question immediately, GigaChat 3.5 Reasoning can first create a plan, identify missing information, perform multiple actions, verify its intermediate conclusions and correct errors before returning the final response.

The reasoning mode is designed for tasks where a single answer or search is not enough, including finding inconsistencies between contract clauses, carrying out financial calculations and debugging complicated code.

“From now on, GigaChat can independently break down a task into stages, identify missing data, validate intermediate conclusions, and modify the solution if necessary,” said Anton Frolov, Senior Vice President and Head of GenAI Development at Sberbank. “This approach is crucial in agent-based scenarios, programming, and analytics — whenever the outcome depends on a whole sequence of decisions. This is a vital step toward AI that can independently build a path to a result, act proactively, and interact with other services. GigaChat is the only Russian model with a reasoning mode.”

The new version is particularly aimed at coding and agent-based tasks that require several actions to happen in sequence. Sber gives trip planning as one example. GigaChat can ask for missing details, select a flight and hotel, check whether the proposed itinerary fits the budget and then restructure the plan if it finds a discrepancy.

In following complex instructions, planning and code generation, GigaChat 3.5 Ultra Reasoning has approached the performance of leading global models, according to Sber. Its IFBench score increased from 44 to 77 points, while its Natural Plan score rose from 64 to 80. On Live Code Bench v6, its score increased from 56 to 85 compared with the version without reasoning.

The model is also designed to be more economical in its use of reasoning tokens. Sber said GigaChat 3.5 Reasoning uses significantly fewer tokens than leading open-source models with comparable answer quality.

In mathematical problem-solving, it uses an average of 37% fewer reasoning tokens than DeepSeek V4 Flash Preview.

Sber expects the reasoning model to be used across finance and banking for scenario forecasting and checking transactions against regulatory requirements. In legal services, it can search for inconsistencies in contracts and check documents against regulations or precedents.

Sber built GigaChat 3.5 Reasoning on top of GigaChat 3.5 Ultra, specifically training it to solve problems through sequential reasoning rather than simply producing an immediate response.

During training, the model was presented with mathematical and coding problems and taught to approach them through different solution paths. Automatic verification was then used to determine which reasoning approaches produced correct answers, with those paths reinforced during training.

The process was intended to teach the model not just how to arrive at an answer, but how to construct a sequence of actions. It also learned to decide when it should use an external tool and when it should return to an earlier step and revise its approach.

Under the hood, GigaChat 3.5 Reasoning uses Sber’s proprietary architecture with linear attention technology, which the company says makes the model more efficient when working with long contexts.

title: Sachin Tendulkar Partners With OpenAI to Explore AI, ChatGPT
content:
Sachin Tendulkar will share his experiences with ChatGPT and encourage more people to try it for their own interests and tasks.

Former Indian cricketer Sachin Tendulkar has partnered with OpenAI to explore how ChatGPT can be used in everyday life and share his experiences with the AI chatbot.

“I’m excited to announce my partnership with OpenAI. We have some interesting things coming up, and I can’t wait to share them with you,” Tendulkar said in a post on X.

Tendulkar said he has used ChatGPT for both curiosity-driven questions and practical tasks. He cited planning his last family trip as one example.

Under the partnership, Tendulkar is expected to showcase how he uses ChatGPT and encourage people to try the tool for their own interests and tasks.

The partnership is reportedly a multi-year collaboration to increase the use of AI in everyday activities in India.

It comes as OpenAI expands its presence in India. In February, the company said India had more than 100 million weekly ChatGPT users and announced its OpenAI for India initiative.

The programme includes partnerships around AI infrastructure, enterprise adoption, education, and workforce skills. OpenAI also plans to open offices in Mumbai and Bengaluru, in addition to its existing presence in New Delhi.

OpenAI has also expanded its association with Indian cricket. Earlier this month, the Board of Control for Cricket in India announced ChatGPT as an Associate Partner for India’s home cricket season for two seasons, running through March 2028.

Tendulkar has previously used generative AI publicly. In March 2025, he shared AI-generated images inspired by Studio Ghibli’s visual style during the trend that spread across India.
