title: OpenAI’s Model Cracks 100+ Maths Problems, Surprises Its Own Mathematicians
content:
The company is now establishing an independent Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence, hosted at the Institute for Advanced Study.

OpenAI said an internal AI model that recently produced a proposed solution to the 90-year-old Navier–Stokes Millennium Prize Problem has now resolved more than 100 long-standing open problems across most areas of mathematics.

“The pace of its progress⁠ in mathematics has surprised the mathematicians within OpenAI,” said the company in a blog post.

Thus, OpenAI is now establishing an independent Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence, hosted at the Institute for Advanced Study.

The nine-member group will advise on reviewing emerging results, communicating their significance, coordinating their dissemination and applying academic and professional standards to AI-generated mathematical research.

The announcement comes shortly after mathematicians published an open letter, ‘A Severe Misalignment of AI in Mathematics’, raising concerns about the use of solving open mathematical problems as a benchmark for AI systems.

The letter argues that rapid AI progress could create negative externalities for the mathematical research community.

The declaration, published by 25 Fields Medal winners, including Terence Tao, Peter Scholze and Cédric Villani, argues that AI companies’ focus on solving mathematical problems as benchmarks risks prioritising answers over the understanding and ideas that mathematics is intended to develop.

The mathematicians said AI-generated results can also arrive too quickly for the community to properly explain, simplify and connect them to previous work, raising concerns around attribution and plagiarism.

They argued that AI could accelerate mathematical research, but said its impact would depend on whether researchers preserve the human processes through which new ideas are understood, discussed and incorporated into the field.

Therefore, this group will advise on how AI tools can support mathematical research and learning. OpenAI said it wants mathematicians to use increasingly capable AI systems to pursue research questions and develop new ideas.

“We want to put capable tools in mathematicians’ hands so they can pursue the questions they know best and develop new ideas,” OpenAI said.

The initial group includes mathematicians François Charles, Camillo De Lellis, Timothy Gowers, Martin Hairer, Nikhil Srivastava, Ulrike Tillmann, Ravi Vakil, Edward Witten and Melanie Matchett Wood.

OpenAI said the group would operate independently, with members free to exercise their own judgement, challenge the company and publish advice publicly.

Its members will not be paid by OpenAI, will control the group’s membership, and will not have a role in setting the pace of OpenAI’s internal mathematics research.

Alibaba plans to train an AI model with 5-10 trillion parameters and has unveiled a new AI accelerator designed to meet the computing demands of models at that scale.

Alibaba said the chip delivers three times the performance of the preceding M890 and can be deployed in clusters containing up to 500,000 chips for frontier-model training and inference. Mass production and commercial release are scheduled for the first quarter of 2027.

The V900 is part of Alibaba’s effort to build a domestic AI computing stack as Chinese companies face restrictions on access to advanced Nvidia processors. Alibaba previously introduced the M890 in May.

Alibaba is also expanding the infrastructure intended to run these systems. Wu said Alibaba Cloud plans to increase its global data-centre capacity to more than 20 GW by 2032. The company said its M890-based AI supernodes can already perform inference on models exceeding 2 trillion parameters, a capability Wu said is currently available at only “a handful of companies globally”.

Earlier, Alibaba demonstrated Qwen3.7-Max running on the M890 for 35 hours and more than 1,000 tool calls, while subsequent M890 cloud deployments have been used to run models exceeding 2 trillion parameters, including Qwen3.8-Max and Kimi K3.

title: OpenAI Calls for US-Led Global Standards on Frontier AI, RSI
content:
“The United States is well positioned to lead because its AI industry is at the technical frontier, and it still stands in a privileged global network position in critical areas such as finance, trade, defence, technology, and information systems.”

OpenAI has called for the US to lead an international effort to establish technical standards for frontier AI, including standards for measuring and managing recursive self-improvement (RSI), as AI models take on more of the work involved in AI research and development.

In a blog post, OpenAI proposed using the network of AI safety institutes in countries including India, the UK, Japan, South Korea, Singapore, France and Germany, alongside US institutions such as the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI), to develop common methods for measuring frontier capabilities, assessing risks and determining whether safeguards are sufficient.

The standards would apply to both open and closed models but would not themselves impose licensing, mandatory pre-release reviews or model approval requirements.

Governments would decide whether and how to incorporate them into domestic law.

“The United States is well positioned to lead because its AI industry is at the technical frontier, and it still stands in a privileged global network position in critical areas such as finance, trade, defence, technology, and information systems,” said OpenAI, positioning its home country as the one to lead the global standards.

OpenAI wants common measurements for the amount of autonomous research taking place inside AI companies, evaluations of RSI-related progress and standards defining when automated research should trigger human review.

“Fully autonomous RSI is not happening today, and we should not pursue it unless and until it can be done safely,” OpenAI said. The company added that decisions on whether to proceed should depend on the ability to “preserve human control” and informed democratic choices.

OpenAI also proposed common protocols for reporting AI incidents, including shared classifications, severity levels and reporting thresholds for alignment failures and problems involving automated AI research.

It wants governments and critical infrastructure operators to establish secure channels to share information about vulnerabilities, national security concerns, and emerging threats. The company said dialogue between the US and China on frontier AI safety “would be a positive step”.

The proposal comes as frontier AI companies have increased their focus on controlling the pace and risks of increasingly capable systems.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei recently called for the industry to “pace the frontier”, arguing that AI capability gains could advance faster than efforts to manage associated risks.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman subsequently backed Amodei’s position and agreed to give independent evaluators employee-like access to assess OpenAI’s safety practices.

OpenAI then introduced a formal framework for tracking, investigating and disclosing model-misalignment incidents, publishing six reports alongside it.

The company said the framework was intended to make disclosures more systematic and enable reporting even when the behaviour had not been fully explained or mitigated. It also said there is currently no industry-wide framework specifying how developers should disclose model-misalignment incidents.

title: Meta’s Muse AI App Beats ChatGPT on Early Downloads, Shares Jump 11%
content:
The surge in Muse downloads comes as Meta pushes deeper into AI agents that can act across apps, services, and the web.

Meta’s new personal AI agent Muse has climbed to the top of the US app charts, giving investors an early sign of consumer demand for the company’s push into agentic AI. Meta shares rose 11.4% on Nasdaq on September 21—the company’s biggest one-day gain since April 2025.

Muse ranked first among free apps on both Apple’s US App Store and Google Play as of September 21, beating ChatGPT.

The AI assistant, which is restricted to users aged 18 and above, crossed 902,000 downloads within six days of its launch, according to Sensor Tower data cited by Bloomberg. The figure is higher than the 773,000 downloads Meta’s standalone Meta AI app recorded during the equivalent period after its launch.

Early adoption has also extended beyond app stores. Data from app intelligence firm Apptopia showed that Muse had reached 2.8 million global installs in its first 12 days, as cited by TechCrunch.

In the US and Canada, Muse recorded 1.8 million iOS downloads during its first 12 days, compared to 1.3 million for ChatGPT over the same period. Its estimated daily active users in the US also stood above ChatGPT’s at the equivalent point after launch.

Muse is different from Meta’s earlier AI assistant because it is built to carry out multi-step tasks rather than simply answer questions. Users can ask it to send emails, book travel, manage appointments, shop online, and complete other tasks across the web.

It can also use information from Meta services such as Instagram and Facebook Marketplace, alongside third-party services including Gmail, Google Calendar, and OpenTable.

The assistant is powered by Meta’s Muse Spark model and runs inside a dedicated virtual machine called Muse Secure VM. Meta says a separate Sentinel system reviews actions before the agent can access the internet, while users retain control over which services Muse can access. The company also plans to introduce a Confidential VM later this year that will prevent Meta itself from accessing users’ data and conversations.

Muse is available for free with usage limits, while Meta offers paid plans priced at $20 and $100 a month for users requiring higher usage limits. The company has also introduced API pricing for enterprise developers.

The personal AI agent is not currently available in India.

The app’s early momentum has strengthened the investment case around Meta’s large AI spending. Meta is expected to spend between $130 billion and $145 billion on capital expenditure this year, much of it directed towards data centres and AI infrastructure.

However, Muse has already hit a major roadblock. Amazon blocked the agent from accessing its shopping platform, saying Meta had not received permission to let Muse browse Amazon, access customer accounts, or process transactions. Amazon also objected to Muse not identifying itself as an AI agent when accessing the site.

Meta’s launch has also faced scrutiny over safety. Reuters reported earlier this month that internal testing had identified problems involving access to sensitive personal data, prompting Meta to delay the product’s release from April. Meta said that it had improved Muse’s security and privacy protections.

The University of Cincinnati's online MS in Business Analytics is a STEM programme offered through the AACSB-accredited Lindner College of Business.

AIM Media House·SEPTEMBER 22, 2026, 9:33 AM·Updated OCTOBER 4, 2026, 10:45 PM

AI is creating a strange problem for businesses. It is making it easier than ever to generate data, while making it harder to find professionals who can actually make sense of it.

As AI gets embedded into more products, workflows and decision-making systems, the amount of data businesses generate is only expected to grow. The US Bureau of Labor Statistics expects employment of data scientists to increase by 33.5% between 2024 and 2034, making it the fastest-growing mathematical science occupation and the fourth-fastest-growing occupation overall.

The implication is bigger than the data science job market. As businesses become more data-driven, professionals across functions will increasingly need to understand how to work with data, interpret it and use it to make decisions.

That is where advanced business analytics skills could become a career differentiator.

The World Economic Forum's Future of Jobs Report 2025 puts analytical thinking at the top of the list of core skills employers consider essential. At the same time, AI and big data are among the fastest-growing skills in demand.

There is a reason the two are converging.

AI can generate an answer, identify a pattern or make a prediction. But someone still needs to decide whether the underlying data is reliable, whether the pattern matters to the business and what should happen next.

That requires more than knowing how to use an AI tool.

It requires professionals who can move between data and business decisions.

The New Analytics Skill Stack

Advanced business analytics is therefore becoming less about knowing one particular tool and more about developing a combination of statistical, technical and business skills.

Data visualisation is one part of it. Professionals need to be able to turn large amounts of information into something that decision-makers can actually understand.

Statistical analysis is another. It helps identify relationships, patterns and trends in data rather than relying on intuition alone.

Then there is data mining, which involves finding useful patterns in large and complex datasets. Machine learning takes this further by allowing professionals to build models that can generate predictions and insights.

Optimisation addresses another question: if there are several possible outcomes, what is the best decision the business can make?

These capabilities also map to three increasingly important layers of analytics.

Descriptive analytics explains what happened. Predictive analytics looks at what is likely to happen. Prescriptive analytics helps determine what could be done about it.

A business does not gain much value from knowing that sales fell last quarter. It gains more value from understanding why they fell, predicting where they are likely to go next and identifying what it can do to change the outcome.

This is also why the skills gap remains a major problem.

The WEF's 2025 report found that 63% of employers consider skill gaps a major barrier to business transformation, while 85% expect to prioritise workforce upskilling.

For professionals, that creates an unusual opportunity. The most valuable people may not necessarily be those who are purely technical or purely business-oriented, but those who can operate at the intersection of both.

Where The University Of Cincinnati Fits In

The University of Cincinnati's online Master of Science in Business Analytics is built around this intersection.

The programme, offered through the Carl H. Lindner College of Business, focuses on descriptive, predictive and prescriptive analytics, with the aim of developing both analytical capabilities and the ability to apply them to business problems.

The curriculum covers areas such as data visualisation, statistical analysis, data mining, machine learning and optimisation, giving professionals a broader analytical toolkit rather than training them around a single technology.

The emphasis is also on applying those skills.

The programme's capstone provides students with an opportunity to work on a real-world problem. Depending on the student's background, that can involve building on a research project, a course project, an internship or work completed in a professional role.

For working professionals, that connection between coursework and an actual business problem can be particularly useful. Instead of analytics remaining something that exists only inside a classroom, it can become part of the work they are already doing.

Designed For Professionals Who Cannot Press Pause

Going back to school while working full-time is a challenge in itself.

The UC programme is 100% online and asynchronous, allowing students to structure their coursework around their existing professional and personal commitments. It is designed for part-time students and can be completed in one to two years.

There is also an online bootcamp before classes begin, designed to help students get comfortable with the technical and nontechnical foundations needed for the programme.

The programme does not require a GMAT and offers courses across spring, summer and fall semesters.

Students can also customise their electives according to where they want their careers to go. Lindner offers stackable graduate certificates in areas including AI, finance and marketing, allowing students to combine analytics with another business specialisation.

That flexibility reflects a broader reality about analytics careers.

Not everyone needs to become a data scientist.

A finance professional who can build predictive models has a different toolkit from one who only reads financial reports. A marketing professional who can mine customer data and optimise campaigns can approach the job differently. A product manager who understands statistical analysis and machine learning can ask different questions of their data.

The advantage is not simply knowing more technology.

It is knowing how to use technology and data to make better decisions.

The University of Cincinnati's online MS in Business Analytics is a STEM programme offered through the AACSB-accredited Lindner College of Business. It was also ranked No. 3 in the US in Fortune's most recent ranking of the best online business analytics master's programmes.

As AI continues to generate more data, businesses will need more than people who can build AI systems.

They will need professionals who can understand what those systems are telling them.

And increasingly, the career advantage may belong to those who can take that information and answer the most important question of all: What should the business do next?

title: Matters.AI, Cockroach Labs Launch Data Security Integration for DPDP-Regulated Data
content:
The integration maps sensitive data in CockroachDB to the users, roles and privileges that can access it, while keeping raw data within the customer’s infrastructure.

Bengaluru-based AI-native data security company Matters.AI and Cockroach Labs, the company behind the distributed SQL database CockroachDB, have launched an integration to identify personal and regulated data within CockroachDB deployments and map it to the database users, roles and privileges that can access it.

The integration, available to CockroachDB customers, classifies data at the column level and creates an access map showing which accounts can reach regulated data, where excessive privileges exist and whether data is stored in a jurisdiction where it should not be.

The launch comes as Indian enterprises prepare for compliance with the Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Rules. The rules were notified in November 2025, with substantive obligations for data fiduciaries scheduled to take effect from May 2027. Banks, payment companies and insurers are also subject to existing data-localisation and cybersecurity requirements from the Reserve Bank of India.

According to the companies, the integration scans CockroachDB databases, tables and columns using 38 personally identifiable information (PII) detectors covering eight regulatory jurisdictions. It can also detect payment card numbers, protected health information and secrets stored in free-text columns.

The classified data is then correlated with CockroachDB users, roles and privilege grants. This allows security teams to identify which accounts can access regulated information, which roles have privileges beyond their current usage and where regulated data may be located outside the appropriate jurisdiction. The findings can be mapped against requirements under the DPDP Act, PCI DSS, HIPAA, GDPR, ISO 27001 and SOC 2.

A key feature of the integration is that data classification and privilege analysis take place inside the customer’s own infrastructure. The companies said raw records and sampled values are not transmitted to the Matters.AI control plane; only findings and operational metadata are sent.

For Indian organisations subject to data-residency requirements, the companies said this architecture allows security analysis without moving the underlying customer data outside the organisation’s environment.

“Enterprises distributed their databases to survive anything. In doing so, they made their most sensitive data harder to see than ever: more regions, more tables, more roles, and still no answer to the simplest question a CISO can ask: who can reach this data right now?” said Keshava Murthy, Co-Founder and CEO of Matters.AI. He added that the integration provides this visibility at the column level within the customer's own environment.

The companies cited IBM’s Cost of a Data Breach Report 2026, which puts the average cost of a data breach in India at ₹25.5 crore, up 15.9% year on year. The report puts the average cost for financial services organisations at ₹40.9 crore per breach. Indian organisations without security automation took an average of 236 days to identify a breach, according to the release.

The release also points to penalties under the DPDP Act, with the Data Protection Board of India able to impose penalties of up to ₹250 crore per instance for failure to implement reasonable security safeguards.

“Together with Matters.AI, we’re making data protection seamless for our customers. This integration gives teams instant visibility into where their sensitive data lives, who can access it, and what's happening to it,” said Tejas Baldev, Vice President of Sales, APAC, at Cockroach Labs.

title: Google Hit With $440 Mn Penalty for Breaching EU Privacy Rules Over Location Data
content:
Ireland’s data protection regulator fined Google for violating EU privacy rules over how it processed users’ location data between 2018 and 2020.

In 2023, it fined Meta a whopping €1.2 billion ($1.3 billion) for transferring EU user data to the US. A year earlier, it had fined Instagram for violations concerning the processing of children’s personal data.Ireland’s Data Protection Commission (DPC) has fined Google €403 million ($440 million) for breaching EU privacy rules when it comes to processing users’ location data, in one of the regulator’s largest penalties against a major technology company.

According to the DPC findings, Google had violated the EU’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) through three features—Web & App Activity, Location History, and Location Accuracy—between 2018 and 2020. The regulator said users may not have been adequately aware that their location data could be used to influence advertising or infer their interests.

It identified transparency violations across the three features. The regulator further found that Google retained certain location data through Web & App Activity and Location History for longer than was necessary.

The DPC’s investigation was conducted under the GDPR’s one-stop-shop mechanism, under which a lead supervisory authority can oversee cross-border processing by companies operating across multiple EU countries. Ireland has become the lead data protection regulator for several major US technology companies because many of them have their European headquarters or main EU operations in Ireland.

"As a result of Google’s failures, individuals could have been unaware that their location was being used to, for example, influence them with ads or to infer their interests, and could lose control over their personal data," DPC Deputy Commissioner and Head of Communications Graham Doyle stated.

Alongside the financial penalty, the DPC has ordered Google to bring its processing of location data into compliance with the GDPR within six months.

In response to the penalty, Google stated that it has introduced new controls to manage location data and advertising preferences, following concerns over its historical policies. It now allows users to automatically delete personal data on a rolling basis, store timeline ⁠data directly ​on a device, and manage how data, including location, is ​used for ads.

The €403 million penalty makes it the fourth-largest fine imposed by Ireland’s DPC since the regulator became the lead supervisory authority for many major technology companies under the GDPR.

The company is now establishing an independent Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence, hosted at the Institute for Advanced Study.

OpenAI said an internal AI model that recently produced a proposed solution to the 90-year-old Navier–Stokes Millennium Prize Problem has now resolved more than 100 long-standing open problems across most areas of mathematics.

“The pace of its progress⁠ in mathematics has surprised the mathematicians within OpenAI,” said the company in a blog post.

Thus, OpenAI is now establishing an independent Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence, hosted at the Institute for Advanced Study.

The nine-member group will advise on reviewing emerging results, communicating their significance, coordinating their dissemination and applying academic and professional standards to AI-generated mathematical research.

The announcement comes shortly after mathematicians published an open letter, ‘A Severe Misalignment of AI in Mathematics’, raising concerns about the use of solving open mathematical problems as a benchmark for AI systems.

The letter argues that rapid AI progress could create negative externalities for the mathematical research community.

The declaration, published by 25 Fields Medal winners, including Terence Tao, Peter Scholze and Cédric Villani, argues that AI companies’ focus on solving mathematical problems as benchmarks risks prioritising answers over the understanding and ideas that mathematics is intended to develop.

The mathematicians said AI-generated results can also arrive too quickly for the community to properly explain, simplify and connect them to previous work, raising concerns around attribution and plagiarism.

They argued that AI could accelerate mathematical research, but said its impact would depend on whether researchers preserve the human processes through which new ideas are understood, discussed and incorporated into the field.

Therefore, this group will advise on how AI tools can support mathematical research and learning. OpenAI said it wants mathematicians to use increasingly capable AI systems to pursue research questions and develop new ideas.

“We want to put capable tools in mathematicians’ hands so they can pursue the questions they know best and develop new ideas,” OpenAI said.

The initial group includes mathematicians François Charles, Camillo De Lellis, Timothy Gowers, Martin Hairer, Nikhil Srivastava, Ulrike Tillmann, Ravi Vakil, Edward Witten and Melanie Matchett Wood.

OpenAI said the group would operate independently, with members free to exercise their own judgement, challenge the company and publish advice publicly.

Its members will not be paid by OpenAI, will control the group’s membership, and will not have a role in setting the pace of OpenAI’s internal mathematics research.

title: Delvitech to Invest Up to $30 Mn in Bengaluru Manufacturing Facility, Create 800 Jobs
content:
The 65,000-square-foot facility is expected to become operational in Q1 2027 and is projected to create 500–800 jobs over the next five years

Swiss electronics inspection technology company Delvitech will invest an initial $10 million, with total investment expected to reach $25–30 million, to establish a new manufacturing and technology facility in Bengaluru as it expands its presence in India’s growing electronics manufacturing ecosystem.

The 65,000-square-foot facility is expected to become operational in Q1 2027 and is projected to create 500–800 jobs over the next five years, spanning manufacturing, engineering and technical roles.

The company, which develops AI-native Automated Optical Inspection (AOI) solutions for electronics manufacturing, announced the investment on September 22, alongside a showcase of its latest inspection technologies at productronica India 2026 in Bengaluru.

“India is one of our priority markets, and the country has leapfrogged in its manufacturing capabilities over the last few years, with electronics now being at the center of that growth story. We see enormous potential here; not just as a manufacturing base, but increasingly as a hub for R&D and innovation. Our customers here didn’t ask us to be present; they asked us to be close. Bangalore is that answer,” Roberto Gatti, Founder and CEO of Delvitech SA, said.

The Bengaluru facility will bring precision machining, metrology and equipment integration under one roof, with Delvitech aiming to localise engineering support and improve control over manufacturing quality and lead times.

“The new facility brings together in-house precision machining, metrology and equipment integration under one roof, allowing us to control quality and tolerances at every stage, shorten lead times, and localise engineering support for our customers. We are investing in India for the long term, building a facility that goes beyond assembly to deliver real manufacturing, technology and customer value locally,” Vasanth Kumar, Head of Asia Operations, Delvitech, said.

The facility will include an in-house Coordinate Measuring Machine (CMM) and metrology equipment to inspect critical components for accuracy, repeatability and compliance. It will also integrate mechanical, electrical, optical, software and control systems, supported by engineering and R&D teams focused on localisation and continuous improvement. Delvitech also plans to establish a dedicated customer demonstration area, allowing customers to locally test and evaluate its inspection machines.

Alongside the facility announcement, Delvitech showcased its latest inspection solutions—including Horus, Aton and Horus Dual Lane—at productronica India 2026.

The company said its systems use physical AI to transform electronics inspection, focusing on improving manufacturing efficiency, cost, production time and sustainability.

Delvitech is betting on rising demand for automated inspection as Indian original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) and electronics manufacturing services (EMS) companies scale production and adopt higher levels of automation and traceability.

The Bengaluru facility is expected to bring Delvitech’s manufacturing, engineering, inspection technology and customer support capabilities closer to Indian electronics manufacturers as the country expands its role in global electronics production.

title: Delinea Joins Anthropic’s Project Glasswing to Use AI Against Its Own Security Code
content:
The initiative will apply AI-driven defensive cybersecurity techniques to Delinea’s own systems.

Identity security company Delinea has joined Anthropic’s Project Glasswing, using Anthropic’s frontier AI model Claude Mythos 5.1 to test and identify vulnerabilities in its own software, including code responsible for credential vaulting, secrets management and privileged session brokering.

The initiative will apply AI-driven defensive cybersecurity techniques to Delinea’s own systems, with the company focusing on code paths where vulnerabilities could expose privileged access across the systems it governs.

“AI is making it much easier to find weaknesses in software, and that changes what customers should expect from security companies,” said Art Gilliland, CEO at Delinea. “We joined Project Glasswing to use the best tools available to attack our own assumptions and find problems before someone else does.”

As part of Project Glasswing, Delinea will use Mythos to examine several security-critical areas of its software. These include credential and secrets handling, covering vaulting logic, secret storage and rotation, key management and cryptographic implementations. The model will also examine session brokering and privileged access paths, including the connection, injection and proxy code that sits between users or AI agents and target systems.

The assessment will also cover authorisation enforcement, including policy evaluation and just-in-time authorisation paths, where flaws in access-control logic can potentially be as consequential as memory-safety vulnerabilities. Findings from the AI-led testing will be fed into

Delinea’s existing software development lifecycle, where they will be triaged and remediated. The company said it could then incorporate recurring vulnerability patterns into secure coding standards, pre-merge checks and test coverage.

Project Glasswing brings together organisations whose software supports critical infrastructure and where successful attacks could have significant consequences. Delinea said identity security belongs in this category because vulnerabilities in identity systems could potentially expose the systems and resources they govern access to.

Delinea said it will treat the AI model’s access to its code as a privileged identity, with access scoped, temporary and logged. Mythos will operate in an isolated environment, with no customer data included in its scope.

“We’re treating Mythos like any other privileged identity: its access is scoped, temporary and logged,” said Pierre Mouallem, Chief Information Security Officer at Delinea. “It runs against our code in an isolated environment with no customer data in scope. Anything it finds enters the same product security and disclosure process as a human-reported vulnerability.”

Delinea said validated findings and remediation patterns will be shared with the Project Glasswing cohort. For vulnerabilities affecting third-party or open-source components, the company will follow coordinated vulnerability disclosure timelines. Vulnerabilities affecting Delinea products will be disclosed through the company’s Security Advisories process.

The partnership comes as AI-assisted vulnerability discovery becomes increasingly relevant to cybersecurity, potentially allowing both attackers and defenders to identify software weaknesses faster and at greater scale.

For Delinea, the Glasswing initiative aims to use those capabilities defensively by applying them directly to the code underpinning privileged identity and access controls.

title: CoRover.ai Partners With Tech Mahindra to Take India-Built AI to Global Markets
content:
CoRover.ai and Tech Mahindra will combine their AI platforms to develop sovereign, enterprise, and agentic AI solutions for customers in India and global markets.

CoRover.ai has partnered with Tech Mahindra to develop and deploy AI solutions for enterprises, governments, and public institutions, with the collaboration centred on sovereign AI, enterprise AI, agentic AI, and digital public infrastructure.

The partnership will combine CoRover’s BharatGPT platform with Tech Mahindra’s Project Indus and TechM Orion platforms. The companies will build AI solutions that account for local language, context, operational requirements, and data sovereignty, while adapting them for use across international markets.

They will also explore applications across public institutions, citizen services, and enterprise transformation.

“This partnership gives us an opportunity to combine our AI platforms with Tech Mahindra’s technology, engineering depth, and execution capabilities,” Ankush Sabharwal, Co-founder and CEO, CoRover.ai, said in a statement.

Tech Mahindra said the partnership will build on AI initiatives developed in India and extend them across industries and geographies.

“India has demonstrated its ability to create meaningful AI innovation. The next opportunity is to translate that innovation into solutions that can be adopted at scale by enterprises, governments, and institutions,” said Nikhil Malhotra, Chief AI and Innovation Officer, Tech Mahindra.

“Through this partnership, we are bringing together indigenous AI platforms, engineering expertise, and global market reach to create capabilities that are rooted in local context while addressing opportunities across international markets,” Malhotra added.

The partnership comes as Indian technology companies and IT services providers expand efforts to develop AI systems that can be deployed according to the language, regulatory, and sovereignty requirements of different markets.

title: AMD Joins $1 Trillion Club as Chipmakers Rally on AI-Driven Demand
content:
AMD has crossed a $1 trillion market valuation for the first time as investors bet on its growing role in AI computing and demand for AI chips.

Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) has crossed $1 trillion in market capitalisation for the first time, becoming the fourth US chipmaker to reach the milestone as its shares surged on growing investor confidence in AI-driven demand.

AMD shares rose 9.6% to a record $613.31 apiece on September 21, taking the chipmaker’s stock gains in 2026 to 185%. The rally comes as AMD expands beyond individual chips into complete AI computing systems and gains market share from Intel in CPUs used alongside GPUs for AI inference workloads. The broader semiconductor sector also rallied, with Intel gaining about 11.8%, Qualcomm 4.5%, and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index rising 2.7%.

The rally reflects growing investor interest in AMD’s AI business as the chipmaker expands its portfolio beyond individual processors, where it is increasingly seen as NVIDIA’s closest rival in graphics processing units (GPUs).

The renewed interest comes after enthusiasm for chipmakers had cooled in recent months as investors questioned whether spending on AI infrastructure by hyperscalers could continue at its current pace. Higher oil prices linked to the US-Iran conflict and expectations that interest rates could remain elevated also weighed on the sector.

AMD has been expanding its AI portfolio beyond individual chips. The company is increasingly offering complete computing systems that combine processors, networking equipment and other hardware, putting it in more direct competition with NVIDIA’s full-stack AI infrastructure strategy.

Demand for central processing units (CPUs) used alongside GPUs in servers handling AI inference has also helped AMD gain market share from Intel.

Despite the strong stock-market performance, AMD’s valuation remains closely watched. The company was trading at around 41 times its 12-month forward earnings, below its 10-year average of 44 times but significantly above NVIDIA’s recent multiple of 16.3 times forward earnings.

Delinea said identity security belongs in this category because vulnerabilities in identity systems could potentially expose the systems and resources they govern access to.

Delinea said it will treat the AI model’s access to its code as a privileged identity, with access scoped, temporary and logged. Mythos will operate in an isolated environment, with no customer data included in its scope.

“We’re treating Mythos like any other privileged identity: its access is scoped, temporary and logged,” said Pierre Mouallem, Chief Information Security Officer at Delinea. “It runs against our code in an isolated environment with no customer data in scope. Anything it finds enters the same product security and disclosure process as a human-reported vulnerability.”

Delinea said validated findings and remediation patterns will be shared with the Project Glasswing cohort. For vulnerabilities affecting third-party or open-source components, the company will follow coordinated vulnerability disclosure timelines. Vulnerabilities affecting Delinea products will be disclosed through the company’s Security Advisories process.

The partnership comes as AI-assisted vulnerability discovery becomes increasingly relevant to cybersecurity, potentially allowing both attackers and defenders to identify software weaknesses faster and at greater scale.

For Delinea, the Glasswing initiative aims to use those capabilities defensively by applying them directly to the code underpinning privileged identity and access controls.

title: Alibaba Unveils New AI Chip, Plans to Train New 5-10 Trillion Parameter Models
content:
The company said the new chip delivers three times the performance of the preceding M890 and can be deployed in clusters containing up to 500,000 chips for frontier-model training and inference.

Alibaba plans to train an AI model with 5-10 trillion parameters and has unveiled a new AI accelerator designed to meet the computing demands of models at that scale.

The announcements were made by Alibaba CEO Eddie Wu at the company’s Apsara Conference.

The planned model is expected to be part of the Qwen family. Alibaba said Qwen 4 is currently in training, while the subsequent Qwen 4.5 and Qwen 5 series are projected to scale to between 5 trillion and 10 trillion parameters. That would be roughly two to four times the size of Alibaba’s current flagship Qwen 3.8 Max, which has 2.4 trillion parameters.

Wu said the Qwen team is working on model architecture and data optimisation to enable “more complex, longer-horizon tasks”.

He also said the company has made progress on recursive self-improvement, in which models identify limitations, design experiments, and generate data to improve subsequent iterations.

Alongside the model roadmap, Alibaba introduced the Zhenwu V900, a next-generation AI chip developed by its T-Head semiconductor division.

Alibaba said the chip delivers three times the performance of the preceding M890 and can be deployed in clusters containing up to 500,000 chips for frontier-model training and inference. Mass production and commercial release are scheduled for the first quarter of 2027.

The V900 is part of Alibaba’s effort to build a domestic AI computing stack as Chinese companies face restrictions on access to advanced Nvidia processors. Alibaba previously introduced the M890 in May.

Alibaba is also expanding the infrastructure intended to run these systems. Wu said Alibaba Cloud plans to increase its global data-centre capacity to more than 20 GW by 2032. The company said its M890-based AI supernodes can already perform inference on models exceeding 2 trillion parameters, a capability Wu said is currently available at only “a handful of companies globally”.

Earlier, Alibaba demonstrated Qwen3.7-Max running on the M890 for 35 hours and more than 1,000 tool calls, while subsequent M890 cloud deployments have been used to run models exceeding 2 trillion parameters, including Qwen3.8-Max and Kimi K3.

title: Starbucks to Set Up First India GCC in Chennai, Create 800 Tech Jobs
content:
The Chennai centre will operate independently of Starbucks’ retail joint venture with Tata Consumer Products.

Starbucks will establish its first GCC in India in Chennai, with the centre expected to create approximately 800 technology jobs, the Tamil Nadu government said on September 21. Starbucks signed a pact with the state government for the Centre, with Guidance Tamil Nadu, the state’s investment promotion agency, involved in the agreement.

The centre will operate independently of Starbucks’ retail business partnership with Tata Consumer Products in India. Starbucks has roughly 500 cafes in the country through the joint venture, according to Reuters.

Starbucks Chief Technology Officer Anand Varadarajan said Chennai has a large pool of skilled technology professionalsand cited employee retention, infrastructure and incentives offered by the Tamil Nadu government as factors supporting the company’s decision.

Varadarajan said these factors would help Starbucks develop new solutions and expand its business. He made the comments during the MoU signing event in Chennai.

The Chennai announcement follows Starbucks’ earlier plan to establish its first corporate technology office in India. Bloomberg reported in May that the company was planning the office for fiscal 2027 and expected to begin recruiting after selecting a location.

The May report said Starbucks was seeking to bring some technology roles performed by external contractors back in-house. It also reported that the company was working to reduce its reliance on external service providers.

The Chennai GCC will be separate from Starbucks’ retail operations in India, which are run through its joint venture with Tata Consumer Products. The new centre adds a corporate technology operation to Starbucks’ existing presence in the country

title: SoftBank Seeks More Than $11 Bn in Bonds to Fund OpenAI Investment
content:
SoftBank is expanding its debt financing as it prepares for a follow-on investment in the ChatGPT maker, expected to close next month.

SoftBank Group is seeking to raise more than $11 billion through a new junk bond sale as the Japanese conglomerate prepares to make another investment in OpenAI, according to Bloomberg.

The company is looking to issue $10 billion of dollar-denominated bonds across three maturities and €1 billion ($1.1 billion) of euro notes. The proceeds will partly fund a follow-on investment in OpenAI that is expected to close next month. The bond sale could be priced as soon as September 24.

The deal would rank among the largest high-yield bond offerings by a single company, excluding distressed debt exchanges.

SoftBank has committed close to $65 billion to OpenAI, tying its financial position closely to the value and eventual liquidity of its stake in the ChatGPT maker. The latest bond sale comes as the company continues to raise debt to finance its growing AI investments.

In March, SoftBank arranged a $40 billion bridge loan to fund an additional investment in OpenAI. It recently repaid the remaining $25.9 billion on that facility.

SoftBank also raised its margin loan backed by shares in chip designer Arm Holdings by $5 billion to $25 billion last week, according to Bloomberg. It secured another $450 million under an existing credit line, taking that facility to $6.5 billion.

Apollo Global Management is also in talks to increase a loan to SoftBank by $3.6 billion, taking it to $9 billion, to help finance the company’s OpenAI investment. SoftBank has also secured an $11.87 billion loan for the same purpose, the report added.

Including its latest planned bond sale, SoftBank has been rapidly expanding its borrowing capacity to finance AI investments. The company has sold nearly $15 billion of bonds across currencies this year, making it the largest junk-rated corporate borrower in bond markets in 2026, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. It also raised a $10 billion loan earlier this year backed by its OpenAI stake.

The rising debt comes as borrowing costs have increased across markets. The yield on SoftBank's dollar bond due in 2031 reached 8.2% earlier this month, compared with a low of 6.7% in January, as Treasury yields and credit spreads increased.

Investors are also monitoring risks around SoftBank’s exposure to OpenAI and the wider AI sector. Calls by executives at major AI companies to slow the pace of AI development over safety concerns have added uncertainty around the sector. The cost of insuring SoftBank’s debt against default has risen to its highest level in three years.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman’s comments that the company will not go public this year have also drawn investor attention, as an IPO would potentially provide greater liquidity for SoftBank’s OpenAI investment.

title: Semiconductor Startup Aheesa Unveils Vihaan-I Broadband Chip, Targets 2027 Commercialisation
content:
Aheesa’s Vihaan-I chip is built on the open-standard RISC-V architecture and uses the indigenous VEGA processor developed by C-DAC.

Fabless semiconductor startup Aheesa Digital Innovations unveiled Vihaan-I, an indigenously designed broadband networking chip, at Semicon India 2026 in New Delhi, marking the company’s move from chip design and silicon validation towards commercial deployment.

The fabless semiconductor company is targeting early 2027 for commercialisation and has signed partnerships covering packaging, product development, and distribution.

Vihaan-I is designed for broadband and fibre networks and Aheesa positions it as an Indian-designed alternative to imported silicon currently used across much of the country’s telecom and broadband equipment ecosystem.

“With Vihaan-I, we have a working silicon designed in India, by an Indian team, for India's networks. Our focus is now on getting this chip into the hands of India's broadband and telecom equipment makers,” Saket Singh, Director and Chief Growth Officer, Aheesa Digital Innovations, said in a statement.

Vihaan-I was taped out on January 26, 2026, and achieved first-pass silicon success on August 15, according to Aheesa. The company said the first-pass success validates the chip design and allows it to now focus on productisation and deployment.

The chip is built on the open-standard RISC-V architecture and uses the indigenous VEGA processor developed by C-DAC.

Aheesa said Vihaan-I’s development was supported by the Ministry of Electronics and IT’s Design Linked Incentive (DLI) Scheme, which supports domestic semiconductor design capabilities.

With the silicon validated, Aheesa is now building out the ecosystem required to take Vihaan-I into commercial products.

The company has signed a packaging MoU with Optilink Networks, which will support product development from prototyping through packaging, as well as the joint development of broadband customer equipment based on Vihaan-I.

Aheesa has also entered into a distribution partnership with The Zigma Technologies India as it prepares to take the chip to the market.

title: L&T Semiconductor, Tata Electronics to Expand Indigenous Chip Manufacturing in India
content:
The collaboration aims to build domestic design and manufacturing capabilities for next-generation semiconductor products.

L&T Semiconductor Technologies Limited (LTSCT) and Tata Electronics have partnered to expand the indigenous manufacturing of India-designed semiconductor products for global customers.

The partnership will explore chip fabrication and packaging opportunities for LTSCT’s existing and future products across Tata Electronics’ range of semiconductor process technologies and packaging solutions. The companies will also work on design-to-fabrication optimisation to improve manufacturing efficiency and support production at scale.

The companies aim to build domestic design and manufacturing capabilities for next-generation semiconductor products across automotive, industrial, communications, security, and intelligent-edge applications.

“Semiconductor leadership will increasingly be defined not just by design breakthroughs but by the ability to industrialise those designs through advanced packaging and manufacturing. At LTSCT, we see this as India’s opportunity to move up the value chain. Our engagement with Tata Electronics is a decisive step in building those capabilities, ensuring that the next generation of semiconductor products can be designed in India and delivered to global markets with speed, reliability and scale”, Sandeep Kumar, Chief Executive, L&T Semiconductor Technologies Limited, said in a statement.

The partnership brings together LTSCT’s semiconductor design and engineering expertise with Tata Electronics’ growing capabilities across semiconductor manufacturing, packaging, and testing.

The companies said the collaboration will focus not only on manufacturing existing chip products but also on integrating design and fabrication considerations earlier in the product development cycle. This could help optimise chip designs for manufacturability while improving time-to-market and supply chain resilience.

“Tata Electronics is establishing world-class semiconductor manufacturing capabilities in India to provide trusted, high-quality solutions across the semiconductor value chain to our domestic and global customers. Our partnership with LTSCT is a significant step which will accelerate India’s vision of becoming a full-stack semiconductor nation, by combining L&T Semiconductor’s deep fabless design and engineering expertise with our capabilities across semiconductor manufacturing, packaging and testing”, said Randhir Thakur, CEO and MD, Tata Electronics.

The companies said they will work together on packaging technologies, manufacturing excellence and quality systems as part of efforts to strengthen India’s semiconductor manufacturing ecosystem.

The focus on fabrication and advanced packaging comes as India seeks to build capabilities across the semiconductor value chain, moving beyond chip design and software engineering into manufacturing, assembly, testing and packaging.

title: Jensen Huang Says AI Leaders May Have 'Ulterior Reasons' for Doomsday Warnings
content:
NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang rejected predictions that AI could bring about humanity's end by 2030.

NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang has questioned the motives of AI industry leaders warning about artificial intelligence risks, saying people making claims that AI could bring about the end of the world may have "ulterior reasons" for doing so.

In a CBS News interview, Huang rejected predictions that AI could bring about humanity's end by 2030 and said existing regulations should be applied rather than adding new ones.

Huang was responding to warnings, including those from former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon, who has raised concerns about the possibility of AI posing a threat to humanity within the decade. The comments come as AI companies and researchers debate how quickly frontier systems should be developed and what safeguards should accompany them.

When asked whether people could be "gone in a decade" because of AI, Huang rejected the prediction and said the narrative was overly dramatic.

"It is not grounded on facts. It's not grounded on science," Huang said. He added that the underlying concern about AI safety was not wrong, distinguishing that concern from predictions about AI causing catastrophic consequences.

"They must be doing it for ulterior reasons," he said, suggesting the reasons could be political, attention-driven or something else.

Huang said AI development should continue quickly while companies ensure that safety is not compromised.

"We should go as fast as we can, but not faster than we should," Huang said. He added that companies releasing unsafe products that put people in harm's way could face existing laws.

Huang went further, arguing that AI leaders' calls for regulation were not what they appeared to be. "They're actually not asking for more laws. They're asking to be relieved of the laws we do have," he claimed.

He also addressed AI regulation directly, saying, "We don't need more regulations. We need to apply the current regulations we have."

Huang's position differs from that of Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, who has called for a slower pace of frontier AI development. In his essay, "We Must Pace the Frontier," Amodei argued that companies should slow the pace of AI so that safety work can keep pace with development.

Amodei proposed measures including embedded third-party evaluators, coordination among frontier AI companies, and broader international coordination.

Anthropic has since partnered with Accenture for what it describes as independent evaluation of its frontier AI models. Accenture's specialist AI business, Faculty, will lead the work, including model evaluation, red-teaming, alignment assessments and safeguard testing. Anthropic and Accenture each expect to invest at least $1 billion over five years to build capacity for the work.

Huang, meanwhile, has argued that AI development should continue rapidly while companies maintain appropriate safety measures. He has also called for countries developing AI to share safety practices and consider global standards for AI products and services.

Weeks ago, the company reportedly cut more than 200 positions across Vision Pro, Siri and software engineering.

Apple has reportedly laid off several employees from its Fitness+ team, marking the company’s second reported workforce reduction in less than two months. Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman reported that the layoffs affected employees working on the audio side of Fitness+, including teams associated with Time to Walk and Time to Run.

The latest cuts follow a larger round of layoffs reported in August, when Apple eliminated more than 200 positions across teams working on Vision Pro, Siri and software engineering, according to Bloomberg. Around 100 of those positions were reported to be in the Vision Pro group.

According to Gurman’s report, the latest layoffs involve employees working on audio programming within Fitness+. Time to Walk and Time to Run are audio experiences available through Apple Watch that provide guided walking and running content without requiring users to watch a video.

Bloomberg reported that Apple is expected to release new audio content less frequently following the staffing changes. The report did not indicate that Time to Walk or Time to Run are being discontinued.

Apple has not publicly confirmed the latest Fitness+ layoffs in the sources available for this report. The company did confirm the August restructuring. In a statement at the time, an Apple spokesperson said the changes were made “to evolve our business to deliver the best experiences for our users”.

“While we will create new roles as part of this change, it will also impact a limited number of existing roles,” the Apple spokesperson said. The company added that it would support affected employees during the transition, including opportunities to apply for other roles at Apple.

The August changes included the Vision Pro organisation and teams working on Siri and software. Bloomberg reported that around 100 of the cuts came from the Vision Pro group, while the overall reduction across the affected organisations exceeded 200 positions.

The latest Fitness+ layoffs do not establish a broader change to Apple’s health and fitness strategy. For now, Bloomberg’s report indicates that the latest reduction involves a small number of Fitness+ employees, while the affected audio features continue to operate.

title: Hacktron Used Claude Opus 5 to Reach OpenAI Internal Repository
content:
Security researchers said Claude helped them turn a libheif vulnerability into a working exploit that was later used to reach an OpenAI employee account and an internal repository.

Security startup Hacktron AI said it used Anthropic's Claude models to develop an exploit chain that compromised OpenAI employee ChatGPT and Codex accounts, and reached an internal OpenAI repository. The researchers reported the issue to OpenAI in July.

According to Hacktron, the chain combined a heap buffer overflow in the libheif image-decoding library with a single sign-on flaw in OpenAI's identity infrastructure. The researchers said they reached the vulnerability through OpenAI's Discourse-based community forum, where HEIF (High Efficiency Image FIle) images were processed using ImageMagick—an open-source software for editing digital images—and a vulnerable version of libheif, an open-source software library.

Hacktron said the forum access was then used to exploit an OpenAI SSO misconfiguration. The company said this gave the researchers access to ChatGPT and Codex accounts belonging to OpenAI employees, including an employee whose Codex was connected to OpenAI's GitHub organization.

To demonstrate the impact, Hacktron used the employee's Codex to open pull request #1186742 in OpenAI's internal openai/openai repository. The researchers said they stopped testing after demonstrating access and did not intentionally inspect proprietary source code.

Hacktron said a cybersecurity-research-access version of Claude Opus 4.8 initially struggled to produce a reliable exploit once address-space layout randomization, or ASLR, was enabled. After Anthropic released Claude Opus 5 on July 24, the researchers said the newer model produced a working ARM64 exploit within about three hours.

They then adapted the exploit to the x86-64 architecture and jemalloc, the memory allocator used in the Discourse environment, according to Hacktron. They said they confirmed remote code execution through an image upload before using the exploit against OpenAI's forum.

The full path from the initial discovery to access to OpenAI's internal repository took less than 72 hours, according to Hacktron. The company said its wider "HEIF Heist" research across multiple companies took two months and cost less than $3,000 in token spending.

Hacktron said OpenAI confirmed that its side of the issue had been fixed about 14 hours after the initial report and later awarded the company a $6,500 bounty. OpenAI clarified that testing against the Discourse-hosted forum itself was outside the scope of its bug bounty program, and that the award recognized only the OpenAI-side SSO finding, not the actions taken against Discourse. OpenAI also said it had narrowed permissions on Community sign-in tokens and revoked affected tokens and sessions.

Discourse separately addressed the image-processing vulnerability and added sandboxing for image processing, according to Hacktron's disclosure timeline.

Hacktron said the broader research shows how AI models can reduce the time and expertise needed to turn known memory-corruption vulnerabilities into working exploits. The researchers also stressed that human guidance remained important throughout their work.

India’s 2027 post-quantum target is forcing companies to confront decades-old encryption systems.

When making a bank transfer, most people rarely think about encryption—until something breaks. That could become a problem in the quantum era.

Powerful quantum computers could eventually break some encryption methods used today. Preparing for that future means replacing encryption that spans applications, servers, cloud systems, and connected devices.

That task is becoming more complicated as companies adopt cloud services, connected devices, and AI agents. Each new system can add more software, certificates, encryption keys, and security dependencies to an already sprawling technology estate.

Bengaluru-based quantum security startup QNu Labs treats this as an infrastructure problem. The company has launched QShield 2.0, which adds tools to discover and assess cryptography across an organisation. It also includes a module focused on security risks involving AI models and autonomous agents. The company beta-tested the platform for six months before launch.

The timing matters as India is preparing for a shift towards post-quantum cryptography (PQC), designed to withstand attacks from quantum computers.

A Department of Science and Technology (DST) task force recommended that critical infrastructure sectors begin formal PQC implementation from 2027. Gartner estimates quantum computers capable of breaking RSA-2048—an asymmetric encryption algorithm widely used to secure web browsing—could emerge between 2030 and 2035.

Yet QNu Co-founder and CEO Sunil Gupta argues that migration cannot begin with simply installing new encryption.

“Quantum transition is often seen as a technology or IT problem,” Gupta tells AIM. “We see it as a digital trust or infrastructure problem.”

One reason is surprisingly mundane. Companies have spent decades adding encryption without necessarily maintaining the complete inventory. A new application might introduce certificates. A server might use another encryption method. Cloud services, software and connected devices can add still more.

Because companies rarely needed to replace all of this at once, Gupta says cryptography has largely remained hidden inside technology infrastructure.

“It has never been audited since it has been brought in,” he remarks. “And it comes in different sizes, shapes, and forms.”

Quantum computing changes that equation. Some encryption methods widely used today rely on mathematical problems that conventional computers struggle to solve. A sufficiently capable quantum computer could solve some of those problems much faster.

Companies therefore need to identify which algorithms they use, where their encryption keys and certificates sit, and what those systems protect. They then need to decide what to replace first.

Legacy systems complicate the process. Some applications can move to newer encryption relatively quickly. Older infrastructure could take considerably longer.

Gupta cautions against treating this as a simple software replacement.

“A lot of people don’t understand the importance of this because they think that replacing an RSA or ECC with PQC is the requirement. That’s not the requirement because it’s not an IT project.”

QNu initially expected other cybersecurity tools to handle the discovery process. The company tested existing products with customers but found they were designed mainly for conventional vulnerability assessments.

That eventually led QNu to build its own discovery capability with QShield 2.0.

The company calls the broader system its National Cryptographic Assessment and Assurance Framework (NCAAF). It follows three steps: discover what encryption exists, assess its risks, and keep checking as systems change.

That last step is where AI agents come in.

Traditional security assessments often provide a snapshot of an organisation at a particular moment. Teams find vulnerabilities, fix them, and conduct another assessment months later.

But enterprise technology can change much faster now.

“I may get new applications, get new cloud workloads, or some new AI agent deployed,” Gupta notes. “So my environment is changing so rapidly that I can’t do a periodic assessment.”

An AI agent may communicate with applications, call APIs, or access company systems to complete tasks. Those interactions can add another layer that security teams need to track.

The issue, therefore, is not that AI agents suddenly make quantum computers more dangerous. Rather, they can make an organisation’s technology environment more dynamic while it prepares for a long cryptographic migration.

QNu wants companies to continuously update their environments instead of relying solely on periodic audits. For that, QNu is conducting assessments for large banks.

“We have early customers and have won certain deals where we are doing customer assessments and helping the large banks,” Gupta says.

Technology, however, is only part of India’s transition. Gupta believes India already has government funding, domestic technology, and early deployments. He sees regulation as the missing piece.

The DST recommendation gives critical sectors a direction, but Gupta wants regulators to go further. He argues that guidelines should become mandates for sectors such as banking and telecom. Without them, organisations that do not see an immediate threat may postpone migration spending.

“Only early adopters are moving, but a lot of other people are waiting for that to happen,” he remarks.

Gupta also calls for changes to government procurement. He argues that critical security technology should not be selected primarily on the lowest price.

Those views reflect QNu’s commercial interest in greater adoption of locally developed quantum security technology. They also point to a wider challenge facing India’s post-quantum plans.

Large organisations could take years to identify old encryption, prioritise systems, and migrate them without disrupting existing services. That makes it critical for organisations to start thinking about quantum security today.

“If we fail, we fail because we didn’t start early enough,” he warns.

title: ASML Begins India Operations, Links Expansion to Tata Electronics Fab
content:
Semiconductor equipment maker ASML plans to initially hire 20–30 engineering graduates as Tata Electronics develops its Dholera chip fab.

ASML has started operations in India and plans to initially hire 20–30 engineering graduates, according to a PTI report.

Lin Kiat Yap, ASML Executive Vice President and Head of Customer Support, told PTI that the company's plans to scale its India operations would depend on Tata Electronics' progress and India's semiconductor ambitions.

ASML's India expansion is linked to its partnership with Tata Electronics for the latter's planned 300 mm semiconductor fab in Dholera, Gujarat. ASML said in May that it would support the establishment and ramp-up of the facility through lithography tools and solutions, local talent development, supply-chain initiatives, and research infrastructure.

During SEMICON India 2026, ASML Chief Strategic Sourcing and Procurement Officer Allan Wayne told PTI that Tata Electronics is the company's first customer in India with a 300 mm semiconductor fab, with planned production capacity of 50,000 wafers per month.

Tata Electronics also lists the same planned monthly capacity for its Dholera facility, which is designed to produce analog and logic integrated circuits using 28–110 nm technologies.

Tata Electronics is developing the Dholera fab with a planned investment of ₹91,000 crore ($11 billion). ASML said the facility will be India's first commercial 300-millimetre semiconductor fab and will serve applications including automotive, mobile devices, and artificial intelligence.

The facility is scheduled to begin operations in 2028, according to PTI. The Union Cabinet's Semicon 2.0 announcement in July also said the first fab was scheduled to be commissioned in 2028.

The government has approved a total budget outlay of ₹1,27,500 crore for Semicon 2.0. Union Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw said investment proposals worth$12 billion are likely to come under the new scheme for chip production.

ASML's initial India operations come as Tata Electronics moves toward commissioning its Dholera fab and the government seeks to expand semiconductor manufacturing and related capabilities in the country.

title: Apple Cuts Jobs in Fitness+ Team in Second Layoff Round in 2 Months: Report
content:
Weeks ago, the company reportedly cut more than 200 positions across Vision Pro, Siri and software engineering.

Apple has reportedly laid off several employees from its Fitness+ team, marking the company’s second reported workforce reduction in less than two months. Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman reported that the layoffs affected employees working on the audio side of Fitness+, including teams associated with Time to Walk and Time to Run.

The latest cuts follow a larger round of layoffs reported in August, when Apple eliminated more than 200 positions across teams working on Vision Pro, Siri and software engineering, according to Bloomberg. Around 100 of those positions were reported to be in the Vision Pro group.

According to Gurman’s report, the latest layoffs involve employees working on audio programming within Fitness+. Time to Walk and Time to Run are audio experiences available through Apple Watch that provide guided walking and running content without requiring users to watch a video.

Bloomberg reported that Apple is expected to release new audio content less frequently following the staffing changes. The report did not indicate that Time to Walk or Time to Run are being discontinued.

Apple has not publicly confirmed the latest Fitness+ layoffs in the sources available for this report. The company did confirm the August restructuring. In a statement at the time, an Apple spokesperson said the changes were made “to evolve our business to deliver the best experiences for our users”.

“While we will create new roles as part of this change, it will also impact a limited number of existing roles,” the Apple spokesperson said. The company added that it would support affected employees during the transition, including opportunities to apply for other roles at Apple.

The August changes included the Vision Pro organisation and teams working on Siri and software. Bloomberg reported that around 100 of the cuts came from the Vision Pro group, while the overall reduction across the affected organisations exceeded 200 positions.

The latest Fitness+ layoffs do not establish a broader change to Apple’s health and fitness strategy. For now, Bloomberg’s report indicates that the latest reduction involves a small number of Fitness+ employees, while the affected audio features continue to operate.

title: Anthropic Weighs New AI Model as OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra Gains Ground
content:
The discussions come as Anthropic weighs competitive pressure against its safety commitments.

Anthropic is considering releasing a new AI model as it faces growing competition from OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra, according to a Reuters report, as the AI startup prepares for a potential IPO.

The company is evaluating the safety of its next model as part of discussions around whether and when to release it. The potential launch comes less than three weeks after Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for the AI industry to slow the pace of new model releases over safety concerns.

“We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models,” Amodei wrote in a 3,800-word essay on September 12. His call received support from OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk.

Anthropic recently partnered with Accenture to conduct independent evaluations of frontier AI models, with both companies planning to invest at least $1 billion each over the next five years to build capacity for the work.

The partnership will be led by Faculty, Accenture’s specialist AI business, and will cover model evaluations and red-teaming, alignment assessments, and testing of model safeguards.

Anthropic said the partnership is part of its plan to embed independent evaluators within AI companies. “Embedded evaluators will work inside AI companies, with access comparable to an employee's,” the company said.

The access is intended to allow evaluators to observe models during training, follow decisions around their development and deployment, and speak directly with employees. Anthropic said this could help evaluators assess how an AI company operates, verify safety commitments and identify blind spots.

“Independent embedded evaluators do not reduce our accountability, but help to make it more verifiable,” Anthropic said. “The safety of our models remains our responsibility.”

The deliberations to launch a new model come after OpenAI released GPT-6 Astra on September 3. The model has gained traction among businesses, increasing investor scrutiny of Anthropic’s position in enterprise AI.

OpenAI has positioned GPT-6 Astra around computer use, software engineering, cybersecurity and professional work.

According to corporate expense platform Ramp, Astra accounted for about 13% of tracked enterprise AI spending, compared with around 8% for Anthropic’s Claude Fable.

Astra has also overtaken Anthropic on OpenRouter, a platform that routes developer traffic across AI models. OpenRouter said users spent more on OpenAI models than Anthropic models in the previous week, marking the first time OpenAI had led on that measure in more than two and a half years.

Anthropic’s annualised revenue run rate crossed $65 billion by the end of July, up from about $9 billion at the end of 2025. The company is also projecting revenue of roughly $190 billion to $200 billion in 2028. OpenAI’s annualised revenue run rate exceeded $40 billion in July.

A new model release would put Anthropic in a position where it has to balance competitive pressure with the safety concerns that have been central to Anthropic’s public position.

Beyond OpenAI, Anthropic faces competition from open-source and open-weight models. Investors said these models can reduce token costs and allow companies to develop more of their AI infrastructure internally rather than relying on commercial providers.

The competitive pressure comes as both Anthropic and OpenAI have been preparing for potential public listings. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman confirmed on September 12 that the company would not go public in 2026, citing AI safety concerns.

Anthropic could delay its IPO until after the November US midterm elections, Reuters reported. The company had already pushed back its plans, with marketing previously expected to begin no earlier than mid-October.

title: UN Partners With Google to Build Global Data Infrastructure to Ensure Accurate AI-Generated Analysis
content:
The United Nations is partnering with Google to develop the UN System Data Commons to bring multiple UN agencies into a machine-readable system.

The United Nations is rebuilding how its vast trove of global statistics is accessed, turning to Google to make the data easier for AI agents to find, interpret, and use.

The UN has partnered with Google to develop the UN System Data Commons, a centralised platform that brings data from multiple UN agencies into a machine-readable system. A UNICEF working paper found six major AI models correctly answered just 21.2% of over 133,000 questions on global development indicators, highlighting the need for AI to access authoritative data directly.

The UN System Data Commons is being built on Google’s open-source Data Commons platform. It replaces the existing UNData portal and allows users to search across datasets using natural-language queries, rather than navigating individual databases.

The system is designed to make AI agents increasingly act as an interface between users and information. AI systems can directly connect to external data sources and retrieve statistics along with their origin data with the support of the Model Context Protocol (MCP), meaning AI agents can access data from the UN system instead of relying on the model.

“Because models can misinterpret nuance, a human should always review the outputs before citing or publishing them,” said Prem Ramaswami, Head of Google Data Commons, said in a statement.

The UN plans to expand the Data Commons, with 26 UN entities committed and nearly 20 already providing data. It aims to bring 80% of its statistical datasets onto the platform by 2027. Google.org is providing $2 million in funding and technical support.

Data provenance is a key feature that allows AI-generated answers to be traced back to their original UN sources. The platform can also combine multiple datasets through MCP, enabling AI agents to retrieve and analyse information without users manually searching different databases.

Google stated that human review is still required to spot inaccuracies in AI-generated analysis, highlighting the limitations of AI even when using authoritative data. The initiative reflects a wider shift towards making public data structured, machine-readable, and traceable for AI systems.
