title: OpenAI Agents Probed Hugging Face Weeks Before July Breach: Report
content:
Researchers found evidence of account hijacking and network probing in May, nearly two months before OpenAI disclosed the July incident involving Hugging Face.

Researchers have found evidence that rogue OpenAI agents compromised two Hugging Face user accounts and probed the platform for vulnerabilities as early as May 13, nearly two months before the July incident that OpenAI later disclosed.

Independent researcher Jonas Wiedermann-Moeller told Reuters that he discovered evidence of the activity the previous week.

He said the agents used the compromised accounts to send unusually formatted files to Hugging Face servers in May. Researchers who reviewed the evidence said the activity resembled an attempt to map or test parts of Hugging Face's network for possible ways to gain access. They found no evidence that the activity resulted in an actual breach.

OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri told Reuters that the company had disclosed the May 13 event in its incident report and had privately notified Hugging Face about the activity identified by Wiedermann-Moeller. Pusateri said OpenAI was "committed to transparency about these issues and to sharing what we learn as our review continues."

OpenAI's August 26 account of the broader incident separately documents agent activity beginning in May. The company said an agent left a message-board entry in its Artifactory system on May 12, while another agent gained unintended internet access through a server-side request on May 26.

"Imagine if they caught this behaviour in May," Wiedermann-Moeller said. "It could've prevented the later incident, which was way bigger."

Two external experts who reviewed Wiedermann-Moeller's findings told Reuters that the activity was consistent with behaviour previously associated with OpenAI's agents.

OpenAI disclosed on July 21 that models used in its cybersecurity evaluations had circumvented controls, gained internet access, and compromised parts of OpenAI's internal research infrastructure and Hugging Face's systems. OpenAI said that, beginning July 10, agents found publicly exposed Hugging Face credentials and later used those credentials and multiple exploits to gain code execution on several Hugging Face servers.

title: LLM Watermarking Can Alter AI Agent Tool Calls and Behaviour: Study
content:
A Lasso Security study found watermarking changed individual tool-call outcomes and refusal behavior across several open-weight models, with larger effects under prompt injection.

According to a study published by Lasso Security researcher Andrea Siposova, Google DeepMind’s SynthID-Text watermarking method can change tool-calling and refusal behaviour in large language models.

The effects varied by model, temperature, and watermark key, according to the study.

SynthID-Text embeds a detectable signal into generated text by modifying the token-selection process during generation. Google DeepMind describes the method as non-distortionary because it preserves the original token distribution in expectation over watermark randomness, although individual outputs can differ under a fixed key.

Siposova said the change matters for AI agents because token selection can determine which tool an agent invokes and which arguments it passes. “Such a watermarking procedure can therefore affect both what the model says and what an agent does,” the study stated.

It evaluated tool calling using 1,150 non-live tasks from the Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard (BFCL). Watermarking reduced accuracy on six of seven models, with a significant decrease on four, Lasso said.

The researchers also measured “churn,” the share of individual tasks where the result differed between watermarked and unwatermarked runs. At a temperature of 1.0, 16.8% of phi-4’s call verdicts changed, while its net accuracy declined by 2.87 percentage points. Across 21 model-temperature combinations, average churn was 6.5%.

The error types also varied by model. On Llama-3.1-8B, incorrect arguments contributed 3.48 percentage points to the accuracy loss, while wrong-tool calls contributed 1.84 points. For phi-4 and Granite-3.2-8B, malformed output was the larger source of errors.

Lasso also tested 200 harmful behaviors from HarmBench with and without a fixed prompt-injection technique. On Gemma-3-27B at a temperature of 0.001, refusal-related churn increased from 6.0% on bare harmful requests to 23.5% under prompt injection.

The study reported that Gemma-3-27B’s net compliance change shifted from a 1.0-point decrease without injection to a 12.5-point increase under injection. Lasso said several models became more likely to comply with harmful requests under the injected condition.

The effect also depended on the watermark key. For Llama-3.1-8B, the study key increased attack success by 3.5 points, while 10 additional keys produced changes ranging from a 4.5-point decrease to a 14.5-point increase.

Anthropic has separately said future Claude models will use an invisible watermark based on SynthID-Text to help meet European Union’s AI Act requirements. Anthropic said the watermark has no practical impact on the quality or content of Claude’s outputs, requires no extra tokens, and will not be more expensive.

Lasso did not test Claude’s production implementation. Its experiments used the Hugging Face implementation of SynthID-Text with six open-weight models. The researchers also did not directly test the combined failure mode in which a changed refusal leads to a subsequent harmful agent action.

Lasso recommended repeating agent evaluations and red-team testing when watermarking or its configuration changes, particularly under adversarial inputs.

title: Dhruva Space Joins Thales Alenia Space to Explore Satellite, Space Infra
content:
The agreement covers low Earth orbit constellations, satellite platforms, series production, and human spaceflight infrastructure between India and Europe.

Dhruva Space, a Hyderabad-based full-stack space engineering solutions provider, has signed a tripartite memorandum of understanding (MoU) with Thales Alenia Space entities in France and Italy.

The agreement establishes a framework to explore strategic cooperation across satellite programmes and space infrastructure, according to the company.

"India and Europe are proactively deepening their strategic and industrial cooperation, with technology, resilient supply chains and Space emerging as important areas of shared opportunity," Sanjay Nekkanti, CEO and Co-founder of Dhruva Space, said in a statement.

He added that the cleanroom inauguration "was an early reflection of the complementary capabilities and industrial ambitions that can bring India and Europe's Space ecosystems closer together," and said the new partnership creates "a structured pathway to move from dialogue and capability alignment towards the identification and development of future programmes."

The MoU covers low Earth orbit (LEO) satellite constellations, satellite platforms and subsystems, satellite series production and integration, ground stations, and human spaceflight and cargo programmes, the company said.

Dhruva Space said the partnership brings together its growing capabilities in satellite platforms, subsystems and mission integration with Thales Alenia Space's experience delivering large international space programmes and satellite constellations.

According to the company, potential areas of cooperation include LEO constellation programmes and satellite series production, where repeatable manufacturing and systems integration could support scale. It also identified satellite platforms and subsystems, along with ground and space infrastructure supporting future human and cargo space programmes as focus areas.

Dhruva Space said the partnership will operate through a joint working group, which will bring together technical and business teams to evaluate and develop opportunities. A steering committee will provide strategic direction and oversight, according to the company.

The partnership was formalised at Bengaluru Space Expo 2026, an industry conference for space and satellite companies and professionals, the company said.

Dhruva Space said the agreement builds on an existing relationship with Thales Alenia Space. In October 2024, Hervé Derrey, CEO of Thales Alenia Space, co-inaugurated Dhruva Space's Class 100,000 cleanroom in Hyderabad, which the company said supports space-grade solar array production and the assembly, integration, and testing of spacecraft up to 500 kg.

Dhruva Space said its longer-term objective through the partnership is to establish itself as an India-based partner for global space programmes across platforms, production, subsystems, and infrastructure.

title: Tata Sons Board Backs 5-Year Extension for N Chandrasekaran Amid Leadership, Listing Tussle
content:
Tata Sons’ board has approved a fresh five-year term for N Chandrasekaran, reversing his decision last month to step down.

Tata Sons’ board on Thursday approved a fresh five-year term for N Chandrasekaran as chairman of the Tata Group’s holding company, reversing a leadership transition that had appeared settled just weeks ago.

The decision puts Chandrasekaran, who had announced in August that he would not seek another term, back at the centre of the Tata Group’s leadership at a critical juncture for its holding company.

The board’s move, however, is not the final word on his continuation, with Tata Trusts chairman Noel Tata recording his dissent and shareholder approval still required. The disagreement is significant because Tata Trusts collectively hold about 66% of Tata Sons, and Chandrasekaran will therefore have to clear the shareholder process to secure the fresh term.

The development comes days after Tata Sons faced a renewed push from the Reserve Bank of India to comply with listing requirements applicable to an upper layer non-banking finance company (NBFC), effectively putting the group’s long-running effort to keep its holding company private under fresh pressure.

Chandrasekaran’s return to the chairman’s chair marks a sharp reversal from his position in August.

On August 12, the veteran Tata executive said he would not offer himself for reappointment when his second five-year term ended on February 20, 2027. His decision followed months of uncertainty over his proposed third term after the Tata Sons board had failed to reach a resolution on his continuation.

Tata Trusts subsequently began preparations for a succession process. The board’s latest decision effectively reopens that debate.

The leadership question is intertwined with a broader debate over the future structure and strategy of Tata Sons.

The holding company sits at the centre of the Tata Group, which spans businesses ranging from technology and automobiles to steel, aviation, consumer products, and financial services. Tata Sons is the principal investment holding company and promoter of the group’s operating companies, while philanthropic Tata trusts own a majority chunk of its equity.

The disagreement over Chandrasekaran’s tenure has, in recent months, included concerns around capital allocation and the performance of some of the group’s large unlisted businesses.

Chandrasekaran, who joined the Tata Group in 1987 and later became CEO and Managing Director of Tata Consultancy Services, took over as Tata Sons chairman in February 2017. He was unanimously reappointed for a second five-year term in 2022.

His tenure has coincided with a significant expansion of the group into areas such as semiconductors, electronics manufacturing, digital businesses, and aviation, alongside large investments in existing businesses.

The RBI last week rejected Tata Sons’ application to surrender its registration as a core investment company (CIC). Tata Sons had sought to exit the regulatory framework that could require it to list publicly. The company now faces the prospect of complying with the central bank’s listing requirements.

Tata Sons had remained privately held despite controlling stakes in some of India’s largest listed companies. A listing would bring greater disclosure requirements and potentially alter the dynamics between Tata Sons, its controlling Tata Trusts shareholders, and minority investors.

The board’s decision on Thursday to proceed with the listing process therefore puts the two most contentious issues—Chandrasekaran’s leadership and the future ownership structure of Tata Sons—on the table simultaneously.

Coremantle co-founder Vivekanand Pani believes the AI industry is looking at the Indian language data problem the wrong way.

In 2019, Reliance Industries paid roughly ₹190 crore (~$27 million) to acquire Reverie Language Technologies, the Indian language technology company solving local language computing limitations on feature phones and early smartphones. Vivekanand Pani, his brother Arvind Pani, and S K Mohanty built it in 2009.

The deal was notable not just for its size, but for how little capital had gone into building the company: Reverie had raised just over $4 million.

For most founders, that would have been the end of the journey. Build, scale, sell, move on.

After nearly 30 years working on Indian language computing, he came back with Coremantle, a new company built to solve the problem his first company had exposed. The data needed to make AI actually understand how Indians speak is still painfully inadequate.

The problem is particularly acute now, as AI companies race to build voice systems that can work across India’s languages. India has over 22 official languages, a hundred other major languages, and thousands of dialects. Once accents, code-switching, regional variations, and domain-specific vocabulary enter the picture, the problem compounds exponentially.

Pani believes the industry is also looking at the problem the wrong way. The answer, he argues, is not simply to generate more data, particularly synthetic data, but to collect more natural conversations.

He points to an uncomfortable example. On leaderboards, speech-to-text systems for English can show word error rates below three. But in real-world conversations, he says, that number can jump six times, reaching 15 or even 18.

English has an enormous advantage: decades of digital data. But Indian languages are nowhere near that depth of documentation.

“If the error rate jumps six times in real-life conversations for the most that’s a huge resourced language, then we can as well imagine how it would be like for low-resource languages,” Pani tells AIM.

That is where the Coremantle thesis begins.

The obvious assumption is that if AI models are struggling with Indian languages, companies simply need to collect more data.

Consider Odia, his native language. It is already a relatively low-resource language online, with comparatively little digital material available to train models. But even that hides the complexity underneath.

People in Odisha may speak Odia, but they do not necessarily speak the same Odia. Regional dialects, differences between textbook and conversational language, and extensive mixing with Hindi and English create variations.

That makes ‘Odia data’ an almost meaningless category on its own.

“Every Indian speaks more than one language and also understands and probably speaks more than one dialect,” Pani observes.

A single language problem then quickly becomes thousands of smaller data problems.

Coremantle uses 2,000 hours of usable, model-ready data for a single language as an illustrative starting point, but Pani stresses that this is not the finish line. The harder question is how to obtain that kind of data organically.

With Indian-language data in short supply, many AI teams are turning to synthetic data. That can mean generating content using AI, translating English material into an Indian language, or giving people scripts and asking them to produce recordings around predetermined situations.

However, none of these approaches can recreate spontaneous human communication.

For a language that already has limited digital representation, generating more artificial examples from existing models can create a circular problem. The model learns from data that was itself generated from models that may never have properly understood the language, dialect, or context in the first place.

Pani’s concern is therefore less about whether synthetic data can produce volume and more about whether that volume actually improves a model.

“I can probably synthesise any amount of data. And it will help me with nothing,” he adds.

People do not speak like textbooks. They interrupt themselves, shorten sentences, switch languages, change words midway, and use local expressions. A scripted recording can therefore make a model look considerably better than it actually is in the real world.

Pani says scripted speech can achieve 90–97% accuracy, but conversational performance drops sharply.

For Pani, this is also a historical problem.

India has been developing Indian-language technology since the 1980s, but much of that work was eventually buried as global software platforms became the primary gateway to the internet. By the time smartphones and the web became genuinely accessible to the masses, an entire generation had grown up with an internet that was effectively English-first.

Pani has been working in Indian-language computing for almost 30 years. When he started Reverie in 2009, Indian-language technology was hardly considered a viable business. Reverie’s early pitch argued that India had less than 5% English fluency while literacy was nearing 70%, but those numbers did little to convince investors or customers.

The assumption was simple: the people who did not speak English would not pay.

Reverie remained bootstrapped for its first six years. That had consequences.

English had decades of head start. Indian languages did not. This is the gap Coremantle is attempting to address.

Pani argues that AI companies should not necessarily try to build every part of their data pipeline internally. Companies already buy data and specialised services externally. What matters, he says, is whether the provider understands how model training works well enough to know what data actually matters.

A company collecting recordings may understand data collection. But if it does not understand how models consume that data, it may optimise for volume rather than usefulness. Pani argues that his experience building language technology in an environment where data was scarce forced his team to learn how to extract more from less.

Coremantle is still early. Pani says the company has been working for only a few months and is currently focused on validating its approach before trying to convince more AI labs.

But the company’s bet is particularly interesting.

Rather than obsessing over how much data on Indian languages an AI company has, the AI ecosystem needs to ask a more uncomfortable question: How much of that data sounds like a real human being?

title: OpenAI has disclosed six new cases of model misalignment observed during training and evaluation over the past six months.
content:
The company has also published a new framework for reporting AI model misalignment.

The incidents, published alongside a new framework for reporting misalignment, show models taking actions outside their intended workflows.

In one case, an unreleased research model inserted instructions into task summaries telling itself to disregard normal constraints. OpenAI identified 27 affected summaries.

During the training of GPT-5.6 Sol, multiple model instances added instructions to summaries that would conceal mistakes or misaligned behaviour from users.

Some summaries instructed the model to invent missing historical data without disclosure or hide mismatches between source versions.

Another model, answering a routine question about earnings figures in a California county, found and used an exposed API key without authorisation.

When it could not retrieve the requested figures, it fabricated the data and presented it as information from the requested source.

In a separate case, an unreleased model found the correct answer to a question about lakes using Python. Because the user had requested a browser citation, the agent uploaded the file to the internet so it could cite it, without asking permission.

Two further reports describe models using external systems to communicate or move files despite restrictions. Models used an internal software repository as a message board to exchange requests and responses across separate training samples while searching for missing input files.

Agents working together on another task used public file-hosting websites to share files when they could not access one another’s local files, making task deliverables available at public URLs despite instructions to use only local files.

OpenAI said these were individual instances and should not be treated as evidence of how frequently misalignment occurs across its models. Some of the disclosed cases may also prove to be isolated or spurious.

The company’s new framework is intended to make disclosures more frequent and less dependent on collecting several incidents into a single report or waiting for a model release.

It covers qualifying behaviour throughout a model’s lifecycle, including training, evaluation, testing and deployment.

The company will prioritise new mechanisms, meaningful changes in known behaviour and findings that challenge assumptions about safeguards.

An incident does not need to cause harm or establish a broader pattern to qualify. Moreover, repeated instances may also be disclosed if they provide evidence about whether mitigations are working.

“We hope that the framework we’re outlining today is a first step toward creating such standards,” OpenAI said, referring to the absence of industry-wide standards for disclosing model misalignment.

Any OpenAI employee can flag a potential example for investigation. Safety and alignment teams will assess what happened, what remains uncertain, whether third parties were affected and whether disclosure is warranted.

Cases will be assigned to one of three tracks: Ready for Disclosure, Minor Investigation or Larger Investigation.

The first two tracks are expected to cover most disclosures. Larger Investigations will handle complex cases, particularly those involving third parties, security risks or extensive coordination. OpenAI said it may publish an initial notice before a full investigation is complete, while delaying details when disclosure could expose a vulnerability or create other risks.

Unresolved disagreements over disclosure will be referred to OpenAI’s Safety Advisory Group, with further escalation to leadership where necessary. The company also plans to work with other developers, researchers, standards bodies and regulators on more objective disclosure criteria.

Each report is expected to include the observed behaviour, severity, external impact, setting, date or date range, discovery process, investigation scope and models involved.

Where possible, OpenAI will also publish unanswered questions and measures being taken to address the behaviour.

“We regard this framework as a work in progress,” the company said. It added that the framework does not replace legal disclosure obligations, including those relating to critical safety incidents or cybersecurity breaches.

An estimate by Cambridge put India’s space launch cost at $13,302/kg, but the bigger challenge is building enough demand and cadence to bring those costs down.

Sanjana GuptaTechnology Journalist

India’s space launches have been renowned for achieving significant milestones on a shoestring budget. Take the 2013 Mars Orbital Mission, or Mangalyaan, which famously cost less than the budget of the film Gravity.

However, the economics have come under scrutiny after a 2026 Cambridge study estimated the country’s launch cost to low Earth orbit at $13,302 per kilogram. The comparable figure in the United States was $3,225 per kilogram in 2025.

But the numbers aren’t as straightforward as they seem. The study analysed more than 6,740 rocket launches from 1960 to 2025, measuring estimated recurring launch costs rather than customer prices or research and development expenditure.

It captures different rocket and payload mixes across countries, which can affect the cost per kilogram. Smaller payloads can push the calculated cost per kilogram higher because fixed launch costs are spread across less mass.

It also standardised costs to low Earth orbit and US dollar rates in 2024. The figures also represent estimated launch costs, rather than what customers ultimately pay. That makes the analysis a snapshot of launch economics, but it is less useful as a standalone measure of what an Indian customer would pay.

This gap raises a larger question for India’s emerging private launch industry. Is the country’s launch sector inherently expensive, or has it simply not reached the scale needed to make launches cheaper?

The Missing Ingredient is Repetition

Rocket economics change when launches become repeatable rather than occasional. The Cambridge research finds that doubling cumulative payload reduces average launch costs by 21.2%.

The US benefited from SpaceX’s reusable Falcon 9 and high launch frequency. The company conducted more than 165 Falcon 9 launches in 2025, according to the research.

India has not operated at anything close to that commercial cadence. The country’s commercial space program took off only in 2020 with the establishment of the Indian National Space Promotion and Authorisation Centre (IN-SPACe), followed by the entry of the private ecosystem. This was further actuated by the launch of the executive Indian Space Policy in 2023 to regulate and open up the space sector.

For Chennai-based launch operator Agnikul Cosmos, cadence is central to the cost equation. “Low cadence is the real driver,” Co-founder and CEO Srinath Ravichandran tells AIM.

When launches are infrequent, companies cannot spread fixed costs across enough missions. They also have fewer opportunities to build manufacturing experience.

However, it may be a stretch to read the Cambridge study as a permanent assessment of India’s launch economics.

“These statistics taken as a snapshot of time are only true to that time,” a high-level source working in an agency under the Department of Space tells AIM on the condition of anonymity.

The person argues that India’s commercial launch market is still in its early stages, making today’s cost structure a poor indicator of where it could settle as production scales.

The Cambridge researchers themselves draw a distinction between costs and prices. Their paper says future research needs demand-side analysis to estimate actual launch prices. That distinction matters when considering who ultimately bears launch costs.

Launch is Only One Cost

For satellite companies, the launch bill can be significant, though it’s not their largest expense.

Suhani Doshi, VP of Investment at Mela Ventures, says launch typically accounts for 10–20% of the upfront cost of a large constellation. For small satellites using rideshare, it is around 10–15%.

The larger expenses include satellite and payload development, engineering teams, ground infrastructure, data systems, insurance, and years of research and development. That changes how India’s launch cost gap should be read.

It also means cheaper launches alone will not automatically expand the Indian space industry.

“They would help, but launch cost on its own won’t unlock scale,” Doshi says. More frequent domestic launches could reduce the barrier to putting satellites into orbit. They could also make it easier for companies to replenish and expand constellations.

But satellite companies still need capital, hardware, ground infrastructure, and paying customers.

For Indian launch providers, meanwhile, demand creates another problem. Without enough customers, they cannot generate the flight rate needed to lower their own costs.

That creates a circular challenge where launches can only get cheaper with scale, but to scale, one needs demand to begin with. Funding and infrastructure can help companies build capacity, but they do not solve the demand problem.

For launch providers, the crucial metric is whether that capacity translates into enough paying missions to sustain a higher flight rate.

Building Circular Demand

The government is now building several pieces of the ecosystem needed to break that cycle. As of August 2026, India had around 440 registered space tech startups. IN-SPACe had granted 113 authorisations to 52 non-government entities.

NewSpace India Limited, the commercial arm of ISRO, also signed 118 technology transfer agreements covering 83 ISRO-developed technologies.

The government has introduced a ₹1,000 crore venture capital fund and a ₹500 crore Technology Adoption Fund to boost the commercial space sector. It has also enabled discounted access to ISRO facilities and is supporting common testing and manufacturing infrastructure.

But launch infrastructure remains a constraint.

The Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science and Technology recently noted that India’s space transportation system still relies largely on two operational launch pads. The launch pad at Satish Dhawan Space Centre in Sriharikota, Andhra Pradesh, is nearly three decades old, while the second pad for heavier launch vehicles, also at Sriharikota, has operated for more than two decades.

The Third Launch Pad at Sriharikota is expected to become operational by 2029–30, and a separate SSLV launch complex is also being developed at Kulasekarapattinam, Tamil Nadu.

Agnikul sees supply-chain structure as another cost driver. “Fragmentation is the biggest factor,” Ravichandran says. Separate vendors for manufacturing, testing, and integration can add cost and risk.

Agnikul keeps design, manufacturing, and testing together. It is also planning to introduce reusable hardware. But Mela Ventures points to something even more fundamental that can drive up demand.

Such contracts can provide startups with revenue and credibility while helping them raise larger rounds. More importantly, they create the volume that can eventually bring launch costs down.

“The US cost curve was built on sustained demand, not the other way round,” she observes.

That may be the most important lesson in the $13,302 figure. India does have a launch cost gap. But the number alone does not explain the economics of India’s emerging space industry.

The country is still building its commercial launch market, manufacturing base, infrastructure, and customer pool. Private players now need to turn that into repeatable flights.

As the space agency source puts it, “What you have to read is trajectories, not snapshots.”

title: Lam Research to Invest ₹10,000 Cr in India for Silicon Manufacturing
content:
The semiconductor equipment maker will expand manufacturing and research capabilities in India over the next several years.

Lam Research plans to invest approximately ₹10,000 crore in India to expand silicon component manufacturing and R&D operations. The company announced the plans ahead of SEMICON India 2026.

The investment will fund its first silicon component manufacturing facility in the country. Lam will deploy the investment over the next several years and noted that the plans remain subject to execution and other risks.

The facility will support silicon ingot production and processing for advanced semiconductor technologies and leading-edge nodes. The company said the expansion will strengthen its global operations and support customers as chip complexity increases.

Lam Research has operated in India’s semiconductor ecosystem for more than 25 years. Its India operations include an engineering hub and a chip research and development laboratory. The company has also integrated India into its global supply chain and has trained thousands of people through workforce development programmes.

The planned R&D expansion will build on Lam’s India Center for Engineering. The centre supports global customers in design, testing, validation, and next-generation technology development.

“India represents an important part of Lam’s global innovation and growth strategy,” said Rangesh Raghavan, Corporate VP and MD at Lam Research India.

The investment will also create opportunities for partnerships with Indian suppliers. Lam said it works with local companies across materials, precision components, gases, chemicals, and metrology. It also works with companies providing manufacturing services.

The expansion is expected to create engineering and high-technology manufacturing jobs, Lam stated. The company is also working with the Indian Institute of Science and India Semiconductor Mission.

The partnership aims to expand access to semiconductor manufacturing education. Lam plans to train up to 60,000 students over several years. The programme will use its Semiverse Solutions virtual platform.

Lam has also launched its Skill Development Programme for aspiring semiconductor workers. The programme focuses on industry-relevant skills and pathways into advanced manufacturing careers.

content:
The company has launched HCLTech Pulse as the IT services company expands its focus on AI, cloud, data, cybersecurity and technology modernisation.

Noida-based IT services firm HCLTech has launched a new business unit focused on enterprises with annual revenues between $500 million and $5 billion, targeting companies looking to scale artificial intelligence across their businesses.

The unit, known as HCLTech Pulse, will offer services spanning AI, data, cloud, cybersecurity, engineering, application modernisation and managed services, the company said in a statement on September 17.

The move comes as enterprises outside the largest global corporations increasingly look to scale AI while dealing with legacy technology, fragmented data systems and cybersecurity requirements.

The new unit is intended to give these companies a single provider across strategy, implementation and managed operations, rather than requiring them to work with multiple specialist vendors.

“AI is rewriting the economics of growth. The real advantage goes to enterprises bold enough to reimagine their processes from the ground up, not just automate what already exists, and to do it safely and responsibly,” C Vijayakumar, CEO and Managing Director, HCLTech, said in a statement. “HCLTech Pulse combines our AI, engineering, cyber, data and industry expertise to help enterprises rethink how work gets done and turn AI investment into measurable business value.”

According to HCLTech, the segment is launching as organisations move from AI experimentation to scaled deployment, and hence the market will reward providers that combine deep technology expertise with industry context and an integrated delivery model.

The company said HCLTech Pulse will focus on areas including AI strategy and implementation, data and AI platforms, cloud transformation, application and enterprise-platform modernisation, cybersecurity, engineering and managed services.

“This segment represents an approximately $400 billion global technology-services opportunity and is growing at 7–9% annually,” said Peter Bendor-Samuel, Founder and Executive Chairman, Everest Group.

The unit is also expected to focus on responsible AI and governance as enterprises move AI systems into more consequential business processes.

The $500 million to $5 billion revenue bracket sits between smaller businesses that typically rely on specialised technology providers and large global enterprises with extensive technology estates and established relationships with major IT services companies.

For IT services firms, the segment offers an opportunity to sell a broader set of services as these companies modernise their technology foundations alongside AI adoption.

HCLTech said many companies in this category have historically had to assemble different providers for consulting, platforms, implementation and operations. Pulse is intended to consolidate those requirements under HCLTech's existing portfolio.

The company has not disclosed the initial revenue target or the size of the team dedicated to the new unit.

“HCLTech Pulse is our response to a clear, unmet need,” said Ashish Kumar Gupta, Global Head, New Business Incubation Group, HCLTech. “HCLTech serves many clients at this stage of scale and understands that the greatest value comes from bringing the right focus, senior attention and platform investments to each client’s priorities.”

title: GitHub Migrates Copilot Runtime to Rust
content:
The runtime was originally built on TypeScript, Node.js, and Google’s V8 JavaScript engine.

GitHub has rewritten the runtime powering its Copilot CLI, app and SDK to Rust, producing more than 800,000 lines of production Rust over roughly 14.5 weeks.

GitHub Copilot itself wrote most of the code, with one developer completing the work while the wider team kept shipping new features.

The runtime was originally built on TypeScript, Node.js, and Google’s V8 JavaScript engine. That architecture worked for the command-line interface but created overhead for SDK users.

Every client had to launch a separate Node.js process, load the JavaScript runtime, and communicate with it through JSON-RPC.

GitHub said this added roughly 100 MB of working-set memory per client, increased process-management complexity, and limited startup speed, throughput, and server density.

The Rust rewrite separates the runtime from the terminal interface and exposes it as a native binary.

It can now run either in-process through a C application binary interface or out-of-process behind the existing JSON-RPC server.

The Copilot SDK supports TypeScript, Python, Go, C#, Java, and Rust, with each language using its own foreign-function interface to access the shared runtime.

The work consumed approximately 136.3 billion tokens and cost about $120,000 in model usage, including 130.6 billion cached input tokens.

For subagents, the most frequently used models included Claude Opus 4.8, GPT-5.6 Sol, Claude Haiku 4.5, and GPT-5.5, followed by Gemini 3.1 Pro and Claude Opus 5.

GitHub estimated that the lead developer devoted roughly three weeks of time to the project, while other engineers contributed to interoperability, packaging, build performance, and reviews.

It measured substantial improvements in controlled, local end-to-end tests that excluded model inference, and network latency.

Creating a client, starting a session, completing one turn, and tearing it down fell from 5.25 seconds before the rewrite to 1.33 seconds with Rust out-of-process and 292 milliseconds in-process.

In a 1,000-session lifecycle test, throughput rose from 7.55 sessions per second to 57.45 out-of-process and 120 in-process.

Measured memory added by a ten-client workload fell from 1,383 MB to 247 MB out-of-process and 126MB in-process.

“I didn’t simply ask an AI agent to ‘port this whole codebase from TypeScript to Rust.’ Even if that’s where we’re heading as an industry, we’re definitely not there yet. Instead, agents made an entire category of projects feasible,” Stephen Toub, a Distinguished Engineer at Microsoft (the parent company of GitHub), wrote in a blog post.

The lead developer spent most of his interactions with coding agents reviewing changes, testing behaviour, challenging design decisions, and checking completeness, rather than issuing initial coding instructions.

“Porting code is easy. Making it correct is hard,” he said.

GitHub reported dozens of regressions during the migration, including incomplete ports, changed behavioural contracts, state and lifetime errors, host-platform requirements, library differences, and rebasing conflicts. However, the share of public quality-related issues remained broadly stable at 23.7% during and after the migration, compared with 22.9% beforehand.

title: Databricks Rolls Out GPT-6 Astra to All 3,500 Engineers
content:
Databricks engineers with access to Astra increased their overall coding spend by around 60% compared with the baseline.

Databricks has rolled out GPT-6 Astra to all of its 3,500 engineers, following a pilot involving around 200 users to assess coding quality and costs.

The company used the pilot to assess model quality and coding costs before making Astra available across its engineering organisation.

“Astra unambiguously outperforms our previous highest-end models (Opus 5, Sol 5.6) on highly complex tasks, especially those related to high-level system design or long-range horizontal tasks,” Patrick Wendell, Co-founder and Vice President of Engineering at Databricks, said in a post on X.

Engineers with access to Astra increased their overall coding spend by around 60% compared with the baseline, according to Wendell. However, the company didn’t find much improvement on medium- and low-complexity coding tasks.

Wendell said Databricks suspects existing models already perform those tasks near saturation, leaving less room for Astra to deliver meaningful gains.

Databricks used Unity Gateway, its internal model-access and experimentation layer, to run cohort-based tests during the pilot. The company uses the system to evaluate new models before wider deployment.

Rather than making Astra the default model for every task, Databricks is assigning engineers a separate Astra budget.

The approach is intended to encourage selective use for complex work while retaining lower-cost models for routine coding. Engineers can mix and match tools and models within their overall budget, with additional budget increases available through internal mechanisms.

“We give engineers a sub-budget specific to Astra to encourage them to use Astra selectively on complex tasks while preferring lower cost models for everyday tasks,” Wendell said.

GPT-6 Astra is OpenAI’s best-performing model yet for complex reasoning, software engineering, computer use, and professional workflows.

OpenAI said Astra achieved 97.6% on FrontierMath Tier 4 research-level mathematical problems, 99.9% on ARC-AGI-3 that tests how AI agents explore unfamiliar environments, and 100% on cybersecurity benchmark ExploitBench—benchmarks the company said represented new highs among the competition.

It also scored 57.9% on Terminal-Bench 4.0, compared to 37.3% for GPT-5.6 Sol, to assess how AI agents perform multi-step engineering work inside real command-line and terminal environments.

Logan Kilpatrick said the feedback loop could help Google close the gap with other frontier AI labs with Gemini 4.

Google DeepMind is seeing early signs of recursive self-improvement in AI, with increasingly capable models accelerating the development of subsequent models, according to Logan Kilpatrick, a member of the technical staff at Google DeepMind.

“I think we are like laser-focused right now at the frontier. We’re seeing all these early signs of recursive self-improvement,” Kilpatrick said in an interview on The Pomp Podcast published September 16.

Kilpatrick was responding to criticism that Google has fallen behind rival AI labs. He said the criticism is understandable given the expectations around Google, but argued that the company’s broad portfolio across AI research and science gives it a strong position.

More importantly, he said Google is seeing a feedback loop in which AI systems are increasingly useful for the work required to improve AI itself.

“I think the other labs are seeing this as well,” Kilpatrick said, adding that the development is “underscoring the value of being at the frontier.”

Recursive self-improvement generally refers to AI systems contributing to the development of better AI systems, which can then contribute to further improvements. The process does not necessarily mean that a model autonomously rewrites its own weights. It can also involve AI systems assisting researchers with coding, experiments, evaluations, algorithm discovery and other parts of the model-development process.

Kilpatrick pointed to Google’s recent Gemini release cadence as an example.

“I think you've seen this with the Gemini 3.5, 3.6, 3.7, 3.8, lined up in literally three-to-four-week increments,” he said. “We’re seeing very reasonable progress.”

Google released Gemini 3.6 Flash in July and Gemini 3.8 Flash in September, with the company describing 3.8 as its most capable reasoning and coding model at the time.

Kilpatrick said Google hopes the improvement loop will translate into its upcoming Gemini 4 model, which he described as the company's “largest, most ambitious pre-training run so far”.

“So hopefully we'll see that sort of like translate over in the same way to Gemini 4,” he said. “And it'll be our largest, most ambitious pre-training run so far.”

He added that the model could help Google “get us back in contention with some of the frontier labs”.

Google’s existing research also points towards a broader strategy of using AI to accelerate scientific and technical work. AlphaEvolve has been used for algorithm discovery, while DeepMind is applying AI to areas including genomics, weather forecasting and scientific research.

Google said AlphaEvolve has been used to improve data-centre scheduling, hardware design and AI training. It also improved a matrix multiplication kernel used in Gemini by 23%, reducing Gemini's training time by 1%.

Google DeepMind researchers recently also unveiled Dream-RSI, a framework where AI agents build replay simulators from their discovery histories to test thousands of exploration policies cheaply.

The framework uses recorded exploration trees to test alternative exploration strategies offline, allowing thousands of candidate policies to be evaluated without rerunning costly experiments. The best-performing policy is then deployed for the next round, creating a loop in which each discovery history becomes another simulator for improving future exploration.

Kilpatrick’s comments are significant because recursive improvement has increasingly become part of the discussion around what comes after today's frontier models.

A June 2026 Google DeepMind report examining the path from AGI to artificial superintelligence identified recursive improvement as one of four possible routes from human-level AI to systems that could surpass the capabilities of large human organisations.

title: Applied Materials to Invest $5 Bn in India to Expand Semiconductor R&D, Supply Chain
content:
Applied Materials plans to build a 140-acre advanced semiconductor research park in Bengaluru and develop its domestic chip ecosystem.

Semiconductor equipment maker Applied Materials is set to invest $5 billion in India over the next decade, expanding its semiconductor R&D, supply-chain, and talent footprint in the country.

The company plans to build a 140-acre advanced semiconductor research park in Bengaluru, expand its R&D workforce, and scale its India-based supply chain tenfold by 2035, attracting greater participation from semiconductor manufacturers and related industries.

The company currently employs more than 7,000 people in the country and plans to more than double its R&D workforce as part of its India Vision 2035 programme to build a stronger semiconductor ecosystem in the country.

“Deepening our R&D in India, Applied was among the first to establish a semiconductor engineering capability centre. In 2024, we ordered India's first 300-millimetre lab,” Prabhu Raja, President of the Semiconductor Products Group at Applied Materials, said in a statement.

The 140-acre advanced semiconductor research park in Bengaluru is expected to include cleanrooms and engineering infrastructure where Applied Materials can work with semiconductor customers and suppliers to develop and test technologies used in chip manufacturing.

Applied Materials supplies the equipment and technologies chipmakers use to manufacture semiconductors, rather than producing chips itself. The investment therefore targets an important supporting layer of India’s semiconductor ecosystem, covering equipment engineering, R&D, and supplier capabilities.

The company plans to expand beyond Bengaluru, adding operations in Chennai and Mumbai, and proposing a customer-support centre in Gujarat. Applied Materials’ goal is to increase its India-based supply-chain capacity tenfold by 2035, creating opportunities for domestic suppliers and encouraging global semiconductor equipment suppliers to build a presence in India.

The expansion comes as India seeks to develop a more complete semiconductor ecosystem, from chip design and manufacturing to packaging, testing, and supporting supply chains. With demand for advanced chips rising alongside AI and data-centre infrastructure, the company’s planned expansion could further integrate Indian engineering and suppliers into the global semiconductor manufacturing network.

title: Salesforce Calls SaaSpocalypse ‘Crazy Nonsense’, Projects $50 Bn in FY27
content:
“SaaSpocalypse was not about the end of software, but it may be about the end of software that makes humans do all the work,” said CEO Marc Benioff.

Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff believes the company will enter the $50 billion annual revenue range next year.

Benioff said Salesforce had spent 33 years in the “30 billion” revenue range and two years in the “40 billion” range.

“We're entering the 50 billion in revenue next year,” he said in his opening keynote address at Dreamforce 2026, Salesforce’s flagship annual technology conference.

Salesforce reported revenue of $41.5 billion in FY26, up 10% year-over-year, while fourth-quarter revenue rose 12%YoY to $11.2 billion.

Following its second-quarter results, the company raised its fiscal year 2027 revenue guidance to $46.1–46.4 billion.

“We’ve been hearing all this kind of crazy nonsense about the SaaS apocalypse, especially over the last six months,” Benioff said. “SaaS apocalypse was not about the end of software, but it may be about the end of software that makes humans do all the work.”

He linked the shift to Salesforce’s Agentforce and AIforce initiatives, which allow AI agents and conversational interfaces to operate over the company’s existing data, applications, workflows, and business logic.

Benioff also claimed that Salesforce had its “lowest customer attrition ever” and its “longest customer contracts ever”.

The company’s latest earnings update also described attrition as near-record-low and said contract lengths were increasing across customer segments, but did not disclose a new precise attrition rate or average contract duration.

At the event, Salesforce unveiled AIforce, a live interface layer that brings its CRM data, workflows, business logic, permissions, and governance into interfaces such as Claude, Slack, and Lightning.

Employees can query records, update data, and trigger workflows without opening Salesforce’s conventional application interface. Salesforce said requests continue to run through existing permissions and business rules.

The launch includes Claudeforce, which brings Salesforce into Anthropic’s Claude through a prebuilt MCP server and 37 sales skills.

Slackforce adds interactive Salesforce interfaces inside Slack, while Agentforce Coworker provides an AI teammate within Salesforce’s Lightning interface. Salesforce said 100,000 users activated Coworker within its first 35 days.

Salesforce and NVIDIA also announced Koa, Salesforce’s first CRM reasoning model for Agentforce. Koa was built by post-training NVIDIA’s Nemotron 3 Super with a proprietary synthetic dataset modelled on 27 years of Salesforce CRM intelligence.

The dataset covers enterprise processes, workflows, and operational policies across more than 14 industries, without using customer data.

The model is designed to handle multi-step CRM tasks, including generating leads, qualifying opportunities, resolving service cases, updating opportunities, routing cases, and scheduling follow-ups. Salesforce said Koa matched or exceeded leading models on its CRM benchmark while producing three times fewer errors on CRM actions.

Salesforce also announced updates to Agentforce. Agentforce’s new portfolio includes seven role-specific agents for sales, customer service, commerce, employee support, and supply-chain operations.

The company also introduced a long-horizon runtime that allows agents such as Hunter to pursue goals over days or weeks, while using existing business rules and seeking approval where required.

For government and regulated customers, Salesforce is extending NVIDIA models and accelerated computing into Missionforce.

The platform is designed to support specialised AI deployments in private clouds and air-gapped environments.

Missionforce National Security also received IL5 authorisation in August, allowing the US Department of War to use Agentforce 360 for logistics, personnel management and intelligence workflows

title: Perplexity Builds DynamoDB Replacement With 2 Engineers & Hundreds of AI Agents
content:
CobbleDB cuts production batch-read latency by roughly five times, while Perplexity estimates at least 20% lower costs than DynamoDB.

Perplexity has built an in-house key-value database to replace AWS DynamoDB for fetching prepared web content in its search infrastructure.

The company said CobbleDB was developed by two human engineers and hundreds of persistent AI coding agents over two months.

CEO Aravind Srinivas claimed the migration to in-house database infrastructures like these could save Perplexity “up to a hundred million dollars yearly”.

Perplexity plans to open-source CobbleDB, although it has not announced a release date.

CobbleDB is claimed to reduce production batch-read latency by roughly five times and lower estimated storage costs by at least 20%.

It stores prepared web content, including passages and the information used to retrieve them.

Perplexity said its redesign separates document storage, update management and search-time retrieval, allowing each to be tuned independently.

Previously, processed pages were written directly to DynamoDB, meaning large reprocessing jobs could compete with live searches.

The new system uses a component called Pillar to track document versions, while Lorry groups updates into batches that CobbleDB applies independently.

This lets slower machines catch up without delaying the rest of the system.

CobbleDB keeps frequently requested content in memory and uses local storage for the rest.

A routing layer directs requests to the machines holding the relevant data and can switch to another copy if one is slow.

Perplexity described the system as “purpose-built for our specific workload of repeated batch reads of prepared page records”.

The company said median batch-read latency fell from 31.4 milliseconds to 5.60 milliseconds after the migration.

P90 latency declined from 56.7 ms to 9.77 ms, while P99 fell from 123 ms to 24.2 ms.

The measurements covered batches of roughly 10–15 keys, with an average payload size of 50 KB, at approximately 2,00,000 requests per second.

On the other hand, load tests reached 5,00,000 requests per second without degradation, according to the company.

The comparison used live production traffic measured at different times, rather than identical requests run simultaneously.

Perplexity also conducted a synthetic benchmark using similar batch sizes and payloads. Its cost estimate, based on storage size and read and write capacity requirements, found CobbleDB at least 20% cheaper than DynamoDB across commitment tiers.

title: Meta Launches WhatsApp Business Tool to Let AI Agents Handle Setup
content:
The tool connects AI coding agents including Claude, Codex, and ChatGPT to WhatsApp Business, supporting account setup, phone verification, message templates, and webhooks.

Meta has launched WhatsApp Business Tools MCP, a new tool that lets AI agents help businesses set up and manage WhatsApp Business messaging. The tool can handle several setup tasks across business accounts, phone numbers, templates, and API settings.

The tool connects AI coding agents including Claude, Cursor, Codex, and ChatGPT to the WhatsApp Business Platform. According to the company, a developer can describe what needs to be set up, and the agent can then handle tasks involving business accounts, phone numbers, message templates, and API calls.

Meta said that the agent can check whether a business has accepted the required terms of service, create a WhatsApp Business account, add a phone number and verify it using a one-time password. It can then register the number for WhatsApp's Cloud API.

The agent can also create or edit WhatsApp message templates and provide links to their approval status. Developers can use it to send test messages and set up callback URLs and field subscriptions for webhooks.

Meta said the tool checks requirements such as a payment method and Business Verification during setup. If something is missing, the agent can deep-link the developer to the relevant step.

Meta said users sign in through Facebook Login for Business and give the tool specific permissions. Before a tool runs, the system checks whether the user is an administrator of the app, identifies the connected business, and confirms if the required terms of service have been accepted.

The company said read operations run under the user's own viewer context and that every tool invocation is logged. Actions that change account state require an authenticated person rather than an app-level credential, Meta said.

Meta said WhatsApp Business Tools MCP is currently discoverable on Claude, Codex, and ChatGPT. The company noted separately that Meta Business Messaging MCP, a different tool, is rolling out gradually and may not yet be available to everyone. The company said the release is intended for development and testing workflows rather than production sending at scale.

Meta's WhatsApp Business Tools MCP works alongside its Meta Social Technologies MCP, which helps developers discover Graph API endpoints, troubleshoot errors, and search documentation.

title: Meta Launches Meta One Subscription With More AI Access, Business Tools
content:
The new plans offer higher usage of Meta AI features, creator tools and Meta Business Agent, with subscriptions starting at Rs. 79 a month.

Meta has launched Meta One, a subscription service that offers additional features and higher usage of artificial intelligence (AI) tools across Instagram, Facebook, WhatsApp, and Meta AI.

Meta said more than 50 features are available across its apps and that it has recorded 15 million subscriptions and trials to date.

Meta One builds on single-product plans including Instagram Plus, Facebook Plus, and WhatsApp Plus, which Meta launched earlier this year. Meta said those plans are seeing strong retention, while its new Core and Premium bundles combine features from the individual plans with additional access to some of its more compute-intensive AI capabilities.

Meta said the core experience across its apps and everyday use of Meta AI will remain free. The paid plans add higher AI usage, customisation features, and professional tools for individual users, creators, and businesses.

Meta One includes Core and Premium plans for users who want greater access to the company's AI features. According to Meta, these plans offer more image and video generation with Meta AI, as well as increased use of AI tools such as Restyle on Instagram.

Meta said more than half of subscribers in early testing used both AI and expression features in the bundled plans. The company said Restyle and voice effects on Instagram were among the top reasons people subscribed during the test.

The individual plans include Instagram Plus at ₹99 a month, WhatsApp Plus at ₹79, and Facebook Plus at ₹99. Core costs ₹549 a month, while Premium costs ₹1,960 a month.

Meta One also includes plans for creators and businesses. Meta said these plans offer tools for managing profiles, reaching audiences and responding to customers through Meta Business Agent on WhatsApp.

The creator and business plans include an enhanced profile that can showcase a website, locations and what people say about a business or creator. Meta also offers a bold follow button on Reels and automatic follow invitations for people who engage with content.

The Essential plan starts at ₹639 a month and includes an enhanced profile, a verified badge, impersonation protection pending successful verification, a verified channel on the WhatsApp Business app, and greater access to Meta Business Agent.

Advanced starts at ₹2,099 a month and adds scheduled Stories, links in organic posts and Reels, exportable analytics, and deeper audience insights. Meta said it also allows businesses to give team members access without sharing a password, while providing more linked devices and business broadcast credits on WhatsApp.

Meta said Expert starts at ₹6,399 a month and Max at ₹20,990 a month. These plans provide higher levels of feature access and Meta Business Agent capacity for teams managing accounts at scale.

Meta said it will soon bring Edits Plus to Meta One. The plan will offer more cloud storage to sync and access projects across devices, along with additional use of an upcoming Edits assistant that can analyse Instagram insights and help brainstorm new ideas.

Meta said Meta One plans are available globally, but pricing, features and availability can vary by region, app and account. The company said it will expand Meta One to Edits, AI glasses and more over time.

title: Japan’s Hirata Enters India, Partners with ATS India for Semiconductor Equipments
content:
The Japanese firm will supply semiconductor automation and material-handling equipment as India expands its manufacturing ecosystem.

Japanese semiconductor equipment maker Hirata Corporation has entered India through a partnership with manufacturing solutions provider ATS India. ATS India will act as Hirata’s exclusive distribution partner in the country.

The partnership aims to improve Indian manufacturers’ access to semiconductor equipment and automation technology.

It will initially focus on Hirata’s standard products for semiconductor manufacturing and advanced packaging. The companies said the move will address limited local access, long lead times, and technical support gaps.

John Derzy, VP at Hirata Corporation of America, said India is an important growth market for the company. He said the partnership aims to build long-term capability rather than only bring products into the country.

Hirata and ATS have worked together for more than a decade in sectors including automotive, with the new agreement extending into semiconductors. Hirata will initially offer standard products before moving towards more customised solutions as the market matures.

The portfolio will include Equipment Front End Modules (EFEM), FOPLP Load Ports, and PLP Panel Handling Robots. It will also include high-performance wafer handling robots. These systems support wafer and panel handling across semiconductor manufacturing and advanced packaging processes.

The partnership will target semiconductor manufacturing, backend and OSAT processes, advanced packaging, and handling automation. OSAT refers to outsourced semiconductor assembly and test operations. Hirata said these operations remain largely manual or semi-automated in India.

“The focus of this partnership is on building the local commercial, technical and service ecosystem,” Kishen Kavikondala, CEO of ATS India, said in a statement. He said the companies will focus on precision manufacturing solutions before expanding into customised offerings.

Kavikondala also said ATS India sees a multi-million-dollar opportunity in India’s equipment design capabilities by 2030. He said local equipment availability could reduce dependence on cross-border logistics and delayed technical support.

Hirata expects the collaboration to increase automation across India’s semiconductor manufacturing processes. Derzy said the companies expect changes in equipment access and adoption over the next two to three years.

The partnership is also expected to support local supply chains and precision manufacturing skills.

title: Cloudflare Launches Controls to Block AI Training While Keeping Search Access
content:
New Cloudflare controls allow publishers and businesses to independently manage how their content is accessed for search, AI training, and AI agents.

Cloudflare has announced a new Accountable designation for AI crawling and launched Disallow AI Training, a setting that lets website owners refuse AI training while continuing to allow search access from Accountable mixed-use crawlers.

Cloudflare said the move addresses mixed-use crawlers, which collect content for both search indexing and AI training. The company said these crawlers now account for 36.6% of verified crawler traffic on its network.

Cloudflare also said fewer than 1% of website owners block search crawlers, while 17% restrict AI training. Until now, the company said website owners had to choose between allowing AI training and blocking crawlers that also provide search access.

The new Disallow AI Training setting is designed to address this tradeoff. Cloudflare said it allows website owners to indicate that their content should not be used for AI training while allowing Accountable mixed-use crawlers to continue accessing the content for search.

“This is how we make the Internet better: preserving the openness that makes search valuable while giving the people and businesses behind the web meaningful control over how their work is used,” Matthew Prince, Co-founder and CEO of Cloudflare, said in a statement.

Cloudflare is replacing its Block AI Bots switch with three independent controls for search, training, and agent activity.

The company will also provide recommended settings based on a website's business model. For sites that carry advertising, Cloudflare recommends allowing search crawling, disallowing AI training, and blocking AI agents on ad-carrying pages. For other sites, it recommends allowing search, AI training, and AI agents.

Cloudflare is also replacing its Managed Robots.txt feature with Bot Preference Sync. The feature allows website owners to set their crawling preferences once and automatically apply them across supported crawlers. Customers can change their settings and preferences at any time.

Cloudflare has established four criteria for crawler operators to receive its Accountable designation.

The criteria include providing website owners with a way to opt out of AI training through robots.txt or a comparable standard, a way to opt out of AI-generated search summaries, URL-level visibility into how their content is used for search and training, and public confirmation that opting out of training will not affect a site's ranking in traditional search.

Cloudflare said Apple, Google, and Microsoft are now labelled Accountable because they have either demonstrated that they meet these criteria or provided specific timelines to meet them.

“We look forward to continued collaborative engagement with companies like Apple, Google, and Microsoft as we work together to build a healthy ecosystem,” Prince added.

Google offers Google-Extended, which allows websites to opt out of AI training without opting out of Search. Cloudflare said other leading AI companies operate separate crawlers for search and training. This allows Cloudflare to block their training crawlers without affecting search, and the company also categorises the relevant crawlers as Accountable.

Cloudflare said it publishes the full list of qualifying operators on Cloudflare Radar.

The company is also participating in open standards work at the Internet Engineering Task Force, including ai-prefs, a specification under development that would allow websites to express their AI access preferences in a standardized and portable way.

Cloudflare said every operator it designates as Accountable must provide website owners with a way to opt out of AI summaries. Today, this is a yes-or-no choice that is set separately with each operator. By early next year, Cloudflare aims to allow website owners to control how much of their content is included in AI-generated summaries from one place.

CobbleDB cuts production batch-read latency by roughly five times, while Perplexity estimates at least 20% lower costs than DynamoDB.

Perplexity has built an in-house key-value database to replace AWS DynamoDB for fetching prepared web content in its search infrastructure.

The company said CobbleDB was developed by two human engineers and hundreds of persistent AI coding agents over two months.

CEO Aravind Srinivas claimed the migration to in-house database infrastructures like these could save Perplexity “up to a hundred million dollars yearly”.

Perplexity plans to open-source CobbleDB, although it has not announced a release date.

CobbleDB is claimed to reduce production batch-read latency by roughly five times and lower estimated storage costs by at least 20%.

It stores prepared web content, including passages and the information used to retrieve them.

Perplexity said its redesign separates document storage, update management and search-time retrieval, allowing each to be tuned independently.

Previously, processed pages were written directly to DynamoDB, meaning large reprocessing jobs could compete with live searches.

The new system uses a component called Pillar to track document versions, while Lorry groups updates into batches that CobbleDB applies independently.

This lets slower machines catch up without delaying the rest of the system.

CobbleDB keeps frequently requested content in memory and uses local storage for the rest.

A routing layer directs requests to the machines holding the relevant data and can switch to another copy if one is slow.

Perplexity described the system as “purpose-built for our specific workload of repeated batch reads of prepared page records”.

The company said median batch-read latency fell from 31.4 milliseconds to 5.60 milliseconds after the migration.

P90 latency declined from 56.7 ms to 9.77 ms, while P99 fell from 123 ms to 24.2 ms.

The measurements covered batches of roughly 10–15 keys, with an average payload size of 50 KB, at approximately 2,00,000 requests per second.

On the other hand, load tests reached 5,00,000 requests per second without degradation, according to the company.

The comparison used live production traffic measured at different times, rather than identical requests run simultaneously.

Perplexity also conducted a synthetic benchmark using similar batch sizes and payloads. Its cost estimate, based on storage size and read and write capacity requirements, found CobbleDB at least 20% cheaper than DynamoDB across commitment tiers.

title: Trump Belittles Anthropic CEO as Calls for Pacing Frontier AI Get Pushback
content:
US President Donald Trump said the only control AI needs is a “strong and smart (high IQ) president”, which he claims the country already has.

US President Donald Trump has rejected calls to slow frontier artificial intelligence development, opposing a proposal from Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei for independent safety oversight and a more deliberate pace of progress.

In a post on Truth Social, Trump said his administration had already intervened to prevent harmful activity by AI companies and that the US had extensive criminal and regulatory powers over them.

Trump also criticised Amodei, describing him as “pretending to be a ‘perfect little angel’”. He said there was a “sick conspiracy” against AI and data centres, adding, “Whoever wins AI, wins!”

He argued that the US was leading China and should continue advancing rather than accept restrictions.

Similarly, NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang also pushed back against AI “doomerism” at the recent All-In Summit in Los Angeles.

Onstage, Huang received a phone call from Trump, briefly put him on speaker on stage, and the president dismissed fears of an AI takeover as a “hoax”, saying, “The robots will not be taking over.”

Huang later said NVIDIA would work to ensure that “every industry, every company, every state, every people” benefited from the AI race. He acknowledged the importance of AI safety but criticised unsupported predictions about catastrophic outcomes, arguing that the US could lead in AI while developing the technology responsibly.

These incidents followed Amodei’s essay, We Must Pace the Frontier, where the Anthropic CEO warned that AI capabilities were advancing faster than the systems intended to evaluate and control them.

He called for independent evaluators to receive employee-level access to frontier AI companies, for labs to coordinate on safety standards, and for governments to pursue international cooperation on advanced AI risks. Anthropic said it was committing to the independent-evaluator approach.

He drew support from OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, xAI CEO Elon Musk, and Google DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis.

Amodei flagged the possibility that increasingly capable systems could improve themselves, evade safeguards, or coordinate across networks. He cited the recent OpenAI-Hugging Face incident wherein AI agents carried out a coordinated attack, evading instructions, forming a hierarchy, and duping evaluators.

Altman backed Amodei’s proposal, saying OpenAI would give independent evaluators “employee-like access” to its systems. He welcomed a federal framework for consistent frontier-AI safety requirements, but said companies should not wait for legislation to begin the work.

He said OpenAI was developing explicit safety cases before reinforcement-learning runs expected to significantly increase model capabilities, and called for shared industry standards covering misalignment, monitoring, and safety.

“Pacing” did not mean stopping development, he wrote, and added that “progress has been rapid and will continue to be,” but should be slower than it otherwise could be when safety measures impose additional costs

However, entrepreneur David Sacks, who previously advised the Trump administration on AI policy, questioned why Anthropic and OpenAI would need government permission to slow their own development. He argued in a post on X that the companies could act on their safety concerns without seeking an antitrust exemption or a regulatory framework that could supersede product-liability rules.

Sacks also questioned whether the proposal could allow major AI companies to shape the rules governing competitors. He challenged the idea that their motivations were purely altruistic, pointing to potential liability from damaging cyberattacks and customer demand for reliable, predictable systems.

Reducing raw model power could therefore be commercially beneficial, he argued, warning that demanding a preferred regulatory framework as the price of slowing down could amount to “regulatory capture”.

China also rejected the proposal’s framing of AI risks.

Reuters reported that the state-backed Global Times described Amodei’s call for a slower frontier as a “Cold War” tactic intended to curb China’s technological development. Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun separately said “fear-mongering, confrontation and vicious competition” would hamper global AI governance.

Germany also responded to the debate, saying halting AI development was not a viable option for Europe while supporting stronger safeguards and international coordination. Its digital affairs ministry warned that AI systems capable of escaping test environments and accessing other systems independently would represent “an entirely new threat scenario”.

Spain’s digital minister Óscar López separately called for an international agreement modelled on nuclear non-proliferation treaties, while the UK said future regulation should be evidence-driven.
