Gaurav Sen has built Pothole Reporter, an AI app that runs in the background and can detect potholes during a drive.

Bengaluru may be India’s Silicon Valley, but when it comes to improving infrastructure, the city has largely drawn on conventional means. The BBMP Road Infrastructure Department coordinates with agencies and parasatal agencies to track and fix road issues.

But a simpler solution may be mounting a phone on a car dashboard to spot a pothole, record its location, and draft a complaint for the municipal official responsible for that stretch. The app powering this is only about 4 MB in size, detecting potholes in the cloud rather than on the edge.

It’s called Pothole Reporter and is the brainchild of Gaurav Sen, a Bengaluru-based software engineer and teacher who taught software engineering on YouTube for about nine years. His lessons have evolved from algorithms to cloud and distributed systems, and more recently, AI engineering.

Pothole Reporter is his first project directly addressing a civic problem.

“It was more like… what can we do about it? I don't want to write the complaints myself. It should be AI,” Sen tells AIM.

Complaint From a Camera

Sen initially built the tool for himself. He posted about it on Instagram, and he started getting some traction. Sen then opened the project on GitHub amid a huge influx of requests.

The app runs in the background while the car is in motion, sampling photographs through the phone’s camera. When it detects a pothole, it records the location and uses that information to identify the relevant municipal authority.

The system can also look through public tender records and match a location to the roadwork or contractor associated with it. Sen says the complaint can include details such as the pothole's size, location, and potential tender information before being routed to the appropriate official.

A person still has to review the findings and decide whether to go ahead with the complaint. The system does not automatically submit a complaint.

Government Data is the Harder Problem

Detecting a pothole is only one part of the equation. Matching it to the right authority depends on government data, which municipal bodies can publish in different formats.

“The data is actually out there. What is weird is that the data is published by different municipal corporations in different ways,” Sen explains.

He admits that building the same system several years ago would have required much more manual work to understand and connect those different data sources. AI now helps process inconsistent formats and deal with malformed data without requiring developers to manually account for every possible variation.

The app currently relies on OpenAI's vision capabilities for pothole detection. Expanding it to another city involves obtaining that city's tender information and connecting it to the location data.

“The reason it's easy to expand to pan India is that most of the intelligence is on OpenAI detecting a pothole,” Sen adds. At present, the app has been tested in some states and written test cases for others.

High Bar for Confidence

Sen has deliberately made the detection threshold conservative. The app flags a pothole only when the model is highly confident, leaving the final decision to the user.

“I have seen only one photo amongst all the photos that the app has taken that did not have a pothole but was still detected as a pothole,” he says.

However, on the contrary, the app also misses detecting some real potholes. Sen believes this happens more often than false positives.

He has also tested the system in difficult conditions. The app can detect potholes submerged in rainwater, while nighttime detection works when street lights provide enough visibility.

The app can currently work with a phone camera. Sen said a dashcam could also provide the required video stream, although that is not yet integrated.

Accuracy Comes at a Cost

Sen says processing an image through the current OpenAI setup costs him around half a rupee for every image. “If you are taking 400 photos in a day, then that's like ₹200,” he notes.

That balloons as the scale and reach of the project grows. In the long run, Sen does not see a cloud model processing every image for any state- or city-wide deployment. He is considering a smaller open-source model such as YOLO, which can be fine-tuned for a specific task.

A smaller model would also make the system cheaper and easier to scale if a government authority adopts it.

Moreover, if several people drive past the same pothole, the system could receive multiple reports about the same road defect. Sen says a central database would eventually be needed so the system could identify those duplicates.

That raises a question about who should control the database.

“Right now, it's on the user's phone, and OpenAI does get to see them,” he adds. OpenAI's contract states that it will not use the data to train its models.

If the system is centralised, the data then should ideally sit with the municipal corporation. If a private intermediary operates the system, that intermediary would have to take responsibility for storing it.

Government Interest

The project is attracting significant interest from governing bodies in Andhra Pradesh, Maharashtra, and Karnataka.

Sen has already had meetings with the Bengaluru Development Authority and Ramalinga Reddy, Minister for Transport and Chairman of Karnataka State Road Transport Corporation, Karnataka government.

“We are looking to get API access to the current Sahaaya grievance redressal system. For this, we need permission from the Greater Bengaluru Authority to whitelist our application. Once that happens, app complaints will go directly into their system and follow the standard resolution process,” Sen notes.

Pothole Reporter has received significant traction on social media. However, Sen believes the attention around the project does not mean much unless it produces a measurable result on the ground.

“People are upset about potholes, not happy with what I have created,” he remarks. He believes the real success would be being able to show that the system actually contributed to potholes being fixed.

The harder question is what happens after the AI identifies a pothole.

Sen has sent around multiple emails to the BDA but has not yet seen action on those complaints. To effect action, integration with a government system then becomes more important.

“One of the things I can do is I can give it to the government for free,” Sen shares.

What Lies Ahead

For now, teaching remains his primary work. His company, Interview Ready, helps software engineers prepare for technical interviews, while his AI courses focus on building production systems. Sen said about 500 students have attended his live AI cohorts, while his Interview Ready course has around 30,000 students and his YouTube channel has around 750,000 subscribers.

The pothole project has also changed the kinds of problems Sen wants to explore.

He describes another potential use of AI involving domestic workers who struggle to navigate government paperwork and financial services. His idea is to create a WhatsApp-based assistant that could tell users which documents they need, which office to visit, and how to escalate a problem.

“Just trying to use AI to tell them exactly which documents to carry, exactly which office to go to, how to escalate, having the ability to draft an email and send it would be great,” he shares.

For Sen, the broader question is whether AI can make existing systems easier for people to navigate.

“I think AI is going to bring a lot more transparency,” he asserts. “By equality, I mean at least the basics, the rights that we have, that we deserve, are going to be focused on a lot more.”

title: Teradyne Opens Bengaluru Office to Expand Semiconductor Support in India
content:
The new office will support chipmakers and electronics manufacturers as India expands domestic fabrication, packaging and testing.

Automatic test equipment (ATE) designer and manufacturer Teradyne has opened a new office in Bengaluru to support India’s semiconductor manufacturing ecosystem. The office will focus on customer engagement, applications support, training, and strategic partnerships.

Located in the Vesta Building at Bagmane Cosmos Tech Park, the Bengaluru office will support chipmakers and electronics manufacturers. It will also help Teradyne support India’s growing manufacturing, packaging, and semiconductor testing capabilities.

The company said the move strengthens its long-term commitment to India’s semiconductor and electronics manufacturing industry. Its India strategy is led by Country Manager Alpa Sood.

“India is at an inflexion point in its semiconductor journey,” Greg Smith, President and CEO of Teradyne, said in a statement. He said the permanent office reflects the company’s long-term commitment to the market.

The office comes as India increases investment in semiconductor manufacturing under the India Semiconductor Mission (ISM). Teradyne said AI is also driving demand across the semiconductor supply chain, from wafers to data centres.

Karnataka IT and BT Minister Priyank Kharge, who inaugurated the office, said Teradyne’s entry strengthens the state’s semiconductor value chain by adding test and measurement capabilities. In a post on X, Kharge said the investment validates Karnataka’s ecosystem across semiconductor design, prototyping, fabless innovation, OSAT and advanced manufacturing.

“As India accelerates investment in domestic fabrication, packaging, and test capabilities, we intend to be a trusted partner,” Smith said. He added that a local presence would help Teradyne “move at the speed this industry demands”.

Teradyne designs and manufactures automated test equipment and robotics systems. Its semiconductor and electronics testing solutions cover the AI device supply chain from wafer to data centre.

The startup will retain its core intellectual property and is exploring commercial and enterprise use cases for its Maestro model.

Bengaluru-based AI music startup Beatoven.ai has discontinued its business-to-consumer (B2C) service and absorbed its core team into media company Rusk Media, co-founder Mansoor Rahimat Khan announced in a LinkedIn post.

The company will retain ownership of its core intellectual property and is now exploring licensing its Maestro AI model and music-intelligence technology to businesses.

“Last month, we officially discontinued Beatoven.ai’s B2C service,” Khan said, marking the end of the startup’s six-year run as a consumer AI music product.

The company’s core team has joined Rusk Media, where it will continue working on generative media, according to Khan. Beatoven will retain the intellectual property behind its Maestro model, while the company is “actively licensing” the model for commercial and enterprise use cases, particularly in music intelligence.

Beatoven.ai was founded in 2021 by Khan and Siddharth Bhardwaj. It developed AI tools that generate royalty-free background music for videos, podcasts, and other content. The company says more than 2 million creators have generated over 15 million tracks using its platform.

The startup had raised $1.3 million in a pre-Series A round in March 2024, led by Capital 2B, with participation from Entrepreneur First, IvyCap Ventures, Upsparks Capital, Rukam Capital, and angel investors. At the time, Beatoven.ai said more than 1 million users were using its platform and that 96% of its revenue came from markets outside India.

The company’s shift comes as competition in generative music has intensified. Khan said Beatoven.ai’s decision to license music and build its foundation models from scratch created challenges as competitors with greater funding adopted models trained using scraped data.

“Our original approach of ethically licensing music and building foundational models from scratch faced strong headwinds as heavily funded competitors emerged, building models through data scraping,” Khan said.

Beatoven.ai had positioned Maestro around licensed training data and artist compensation. In 2025, the company said it trained the model through licensing agreements with rights holders and would support royalty payments to artists and composers whose work contributed to the model.

The company had also received Fairly Trained certification for its AI music generator, reflecting its use of licensed music for model training. Its website says musicians receive compensation when they contribute music to Beatoven.ai.

Reflecting on the company's consumer business, Khan identified user retention as a key challenge for AI products aimed at creators. “Prosumer Content Creation is Tough: Retention is your primary nightmare and number one priority,” he said.

He also pointed to the difficulty of securing music rights, describing licensing as “extremely hard” because of fragmented players and gatekeepers.

Beatoven.ai is now seeking commercial partners for its technology. Khan said the company is in “active conversations for technology licensing” and invited organisations interested in its Maestro model, music intelligence, or underlying technology to contact him.

title: Samsung Leads $230 Mn Funding for European Chip Co EUCLYD Amid Memory Shortage
content:
The Dutch semiconductor startup will use the funding to develop AI inference infrastructure and prepare for commercial deployment.

Netherlands-based semiconductor company EUCLYD has raised more than €200 million ($230 million) in a Series A financing round. Samsung Electronics, Somerset Capital Partners, EQT’s Scaleup Europe Fund, and Innovation Industries co-led the round.

It also saw participation from EIFO, imec.xpand, Brabant Development Agency, and Quadri.

EUCLYD will use the funding to expand its engineering team and accelerate its silicon and systems roadmap, the company said in a statement. It is developing infrastructure for AI inference, focusing on reducing power use and computing costs.

Former ASML President and CEO Peter Wennink will also join EUCLYD as chairman of its board.

The startup was founded by Bernardo Kastrup and Atul Sinha at High Tech Campus Eindhoven. It is developing computing, memory, and data centre systems for foundation AI models.

EUCLYD said rising AI capabilities are driving up demand for power, memory bandwidth, and computing capacity. Its platform aims to address these infrastructure constraints and reduce the cost of running AI models.

The company’s roadmap includes craftwerk, its AI silicon platform, and craftwerk station CWS, an AI data centre system. The platform combines programmable chips with memory and system-level optimisation.

EUCLYD said the approach aims to address memory and efficiency constraints affecting AI performance and scalability. The company also plans to build partnerships across the semiconductor and data centre ecosystem.

“AI is becoming a foundation of economic growth, scientific discovery, and national competitiveness,” Kastrup said in a statement. He added that AI infrastructure needs greater efficiency and lower costs to support wider adoption.

Samsung also highlighted infrastructure efficiency as a key factor in the next phase of AI development. “The next phase of AI will be defined not only by model innovation, but also by the efficiency and scalability of its infrastructure,” said Dode Goldschmidt, Senior VP of Samsung Electronics.

EQT said EUCLYD combines semiconductor expertise with a focus on AI infrastructure constraints. The company plans to use the new capital to expand its engineering organisation and accelerate product development.

The financing will also support EUCLYD’s preparations for commercial deployment across enterprise, sovereign and hyperscale AI markets.

Wennink added that Europe has capabilities across semiconductors, advanced manufacturing, and systems engineering. He said EUCLYD could turn those capabilities into an AI infrastructure platform.

title: Salesforce Launches a New Portfolio of Job-Ready AI Agents
content:
The new agents are designed to handle complex workflows, pursue goals over time and work across sales, service, commerce and back-office operations.

Salesforce has expanded its Agentforce platform with a portfolio of AI agents that can handle business tasks across sales, customer service, commerce, employee support and supply chain operations, as companies look to deploy AI for longer and more complex workflows.

The company said the new agents are built around specific business roles rather than requiring customers to create every agent from scratch. Salesforce also introduced a long-horizon runtime that allows agents to pursue goals over days and weeks, starting with its outbound sales agent Hunter.

“Putting agents to work requires more than intelligence,” Salesforce said in its announcement. “Agents need to understand the job, work across the business, and keep moving toward a goal as the work gets more complex.”

The portfolio includes Casey for customer support, Paige for IT and HR service, Carter for shopping assistance, Hunter for outbound sales, Marshall for supply chain operations, Piper for inbound lead generation and Fin for customer experience workflows.

Casey, Paige, Carter, Marshall, Piper and Fin are generally available, while Hunter is currently in pilot and is scheduled for general availability in November.

Salesforce said the agents are connected to its Customer 360 platform, allowing them to use customer data, business processes and existing workflows within Salesforce. Companies can also customise the agents, including changing their names to reflect their own brands.

According to Salesforce, the company has delivered seven billion Agentic Work Units across Agentforce and Slack over the past two years, including 3.2 billion during the second quarter. The company said those deployments helped shape the development of the new portfolio.

Each agent comes with pre-built skills, actions and data models for its intended role. Salesforce said customers can further control how agents behave through Agent Script, its open-source language that combines AI reasoning with deterministic business rules.

The company also shared customer results from existing deployments. Engine’s help agent Eva resolves 50% of chat inquiries without human intervention, while Perk’s Hunter agent has generated 60% of its sales pipeline, Salesforce said.

The long-horizon runtime is intended to support work that extends beyond a single interaction. Salesforce said Hunter can take a goal such as rescuing at-risk sales deals before the end of a quarter, create a plan, determine required tasks and tools, and continue progressing as new information becomes available while seeking approval where required.

title: NVIDIA Expands CUDA-Q For Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing
content:
NVIDIA has added an orchestration layer and benchmark tools to help researchers develop practical quantum computing systems.

NVIDIA has expanded its open-source CUDA-Q platform with CUDA-Q Logical, an orchestration layer for fault-tolerant quantum computing. The company announced the update today to help researchers design, test and verify applications for quantum systems using logical qubits.

CUDA-Q Logical lets researchers coordinate algorithms, error-correction methods, hardware architectures and other components. The platform also lets teams switch between configurations and assess performance.

NVIDIA said the approach targets applications including drug discovery, financial modelling and materials development.

Fault-tolerant quantum computing uses logical qubits to reduce errors found in physical qubits. These systems aim to support larger computations needed for practical applications. However, changes to algorithms or hardware can alter the resources required for an application.

“Quantum computing is maturing into an era of logical qubits,” said Timothy Costa, VP and GM of Quantum at NVIDIA. He said researchers need an open platform that can represent different parts of a fault-tolerant system.

Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory, Infleqtion, IQM Quantum Computers, QCDesign Quantum Motion and Sandia National Laboratories already use CUDA-Q Logical.

Iceberg Quantum used the platform to model a fault-tolerant architecture for Diraq’s qubits (silicon-based spin quantum bits developed by the company Diraq using standard commercial semiconductor manufacturing processes).

Its modelling showed that 1,000 logical qubits could require 1,50,000 physical qubits. That figure is roughly 10 times lower than Diraq’s earlier estimate.

Fermilab also used CUDA-Q Logical to evaluate physical qubits, runtimes and resource requirements across different approaches. The lab reduced its fault-tolerant algorithm development timeline from five months to three weeks. NVIDIA described this as a sevenfold speed-up.

NVIDIA has also added QUOPS to CUDA-Q. Sandia National Laboratories developed the benchmark to measure progress towards utility-scale quantum computing applications. It provides a hardware-agnostic method to compare progress across fault-tolerant quantum systems.

Sandia has published early QUOPS results for quantum processing units from Google, IBM and Quantinuum. A reference implementation is available through CUDA-Q. Companies including Anyon Computing and Quandela are integrating quantum processors with GPU supercomputing through NVIDIA’s NVQLink architecture.

CUDA-Q Logical is now also available on GitHub, and NVIDIA has made the QUOPS repository available.

title: Musk Reveals Grok 4.8’s Pre-Training Stack is Written in C++ by ‘Humans’, Not AI
content:
Elon Musk said it was the Starlink software team that wrote the software and “was not written by AI”.

Elon Musk, who leads SpaceXAI, the company behind the Grok family of AI models, said its pre-training software is now an internally developed stack written in C and C++.

He made the disclosure in a post on X, where he said Grok 4.8, a 2.5-trillion-parameter model, is expected to finish training this week and begin reinforcement learning. “Our pre-training software is now an internally developed stack in C and C++,” Musk wrote.

He said the Starlink software team wrote the software and “was not written by AI”. “AI is not yet good enough for extremely high-performance software (but it will be)”

“Our reinforcement learning stack is still somewhat of a legacy pile of many different third-party software systems,” he wrote, adding that it would be fixed “in due time”.

The comments prompted discussion among software engineers about the trade-offs between custom, low-level training infrastructure, and higher-level frameworks.

Patrick C Toulme, a software engineer at Google, wrote on X that SpaceXAI’s use of C++ could be helping it produce models quickly.

“The MFU on this full C++ stack is part of the reason xAI is churning out so many models,” Toulme wrote, referring to model FLOPs utilisation (MFU), a measure of how effectively training hardware is being used.

He speculated that xAI’s implementation could contain “inline PTX”—NVIDIA’s low-level GPU assembly language—and suggested that the stack might have been generated with the help of stronger AI models.

“The need for higher-level frameworks for [production] training is rapidly going away,” Toulme added. “They can’t compete with agent-written C stacks.”

Musk also revealed that the new stack uses assembly and direct calls to hardware accelerators in NVIDIA’s streaming multiprocessors, allowing the software to target GPU hardware more closely.

The number of tests in its codebase grew tenfold with only a nominal increase in engineering staff.

Anthropic’s continuous integration (CI) jobs increased 25 times in six months as its engineers shipped eight times as much code per quarter as they did between 2021 and 2025, the company revealed in a blog post.

Claude authored 80% of that code, while the number of tests in its codebase grew tenfold with only a nominal increase in engineering staff.

The surge strained Anthropic’s test impact analysis service, which determines which tests need to run for each code change.

Engineers patched the service three times before redesigning it, with the fixes lasting 70 days, 29 days and less than a day, respectively.

“Writing code is no longer the constraint, and once PR review gets accelerated, CI starts feeling the pressure,” Anthropic engineer Sachin Malhotra wrote in the blog.

Anthropic’s service uses a listener to record test results from CI runs and a selector to use that history to determine which tests should run on open pull requests.

The original implementation operated as a single process, with one writer maintaining the running history for each test. As CI jobs increased, the listener began falling behind the incoming queue.

A 20-minute lag could leave tens of thousands of test updates unapplied to the selector, the company said. That could cause the system to use stale data when selecting tests, resulting in unnecessary test runs or failures to run newly added or fixed tests.

The first response was to double the service’s CPU cores.

Anthropic later used Claude Tag, an internal version of its AI tool, to monitor the service and alert Malhotra when the listener fell more than 50,000 jobs behind.

In February, engineers split the listener’s state into package-level shards, allowing separate workers to process results in parallel. The change lasted 29 days before the service came under pressure again.

By March, the process was reaching its memory limit by mid-afternoon on most weekdays. Daily restarts bought less than a day of relief and pushed the listener further behind, sometimes by more than an hour.

Anthropic ultimately replaced the singleton architecture with a distributed design backed by an in-memory data store.

Listener workers can now process results, append them to a journal and move on without retaining the full state in memory. A separate consumer periodically rolls the journal into per-test history, which the selector can query.

The redesign took one engineer three weeks, compared with an estimated quarter a year earlier. Anthropic said the service has remained stable since the cutover and tuning, although the distributed architecture costs more to operate.

Malhotra advised engineering teams to plan for rapid increases in CI load as AI coding agents generate more pull requests and tests.

“Assume your architecture will be at a 25x load within two quarters,” he wrote, adding that teams can now design initial systems for 10–20 times their perceived scale where budgets allow.

He also recommended keeping state out of individual processes and avoiding critical services running as a single instance unless they can be measured and subjected to controlled changes.

“CI is evolving too quickly to proceed any other way,” Malhotra wrote.

title: Meta Commits to Reporting Child Sexual Abuse Cases in India: Report
content:
The commitment follows regulatory scrutiny of allegations involving child sexual abuse material on Instagram and an ongoing inquiry by India’s child-rights watchdog.

Meta has agreed to share cases involving child sexual abuse and other child-safety concerns with appropriate law enforcement authorities in India, government sources told ANI.

The commitment comes as the Centre increases pressure on social media platforms to strengthen safeguards for children and respond to harmful online content.

Government sources said Meta’s commitment is “a first step towards making the platforms safe for children and much more needs to be done.”

The government is also engaging with other social media companies on measures to identify and remove harmful material proactively. Government sources said action would be taken against platforms that do not take adequate steps to protect children online.

The latest development follows scrutiny of Meta after allegations that paid advertisements on Instagram were used to promote or facilitate access to Child Sexual Exploitation and Abuse Material (CSEAM). The allegations followed a BBC Eye investigation that prompted action from Indian authorities.

The National Commission for Protection of Child Rights (NCPCR) took suo motu cognisance of the BBC Eye report and issued a notice to Meta Platforms on July 3, seeking an explanation over the allegations. Meta submitted its response about a week later, after which the commission initiated a formal inquiry.

The NCPCR subsequently summoned Meta India’s managing director and country head to appear before it on September 9. Senior Meta India executives appeared before the commission that day in connection with the inquiry into alleged CSEAM-related advertisements on Instagram.

The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) has also sought point-wise action-taken reports from the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology, the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting, and the Delhi Police over allegations that paid Instagram advertisements facilitated access to child sexual abuse material.

The NHRC proceedings also raised questions around compliance with reporting obligations under the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act.

The Dutch semiconductor startup will use the funding to develop AI inference infrastructure and prepare for commercial deployment.

Netherlands-based semiconductor company EUCLYD has raised more than €200 million ($230 million) in a Series A financing round. Samsung Electronics, Somerset Capital Partners, EQT’s Scaleup Europe Fund, and Innovation Industries co-led the round.

It also saw participation from EIFO, imec.xpand, Brabant Development Agency, and Quadri.

EUCLYD will use the funding to expand its engineering team and accelerate its silicon and systems roadmap, the company said in a statement. It is developing infrastructure for AI inference, focusing on reducing power use and computing costs.

Former ASML President and CEO Peter Wennink will also join EUCLYD as chairman of its board.

The startup was founded by Bernardo Kastrup and Atul Sinha at High Tech Campus Eindhoven. It is developing computing, memory, and data centre systems for foundation AI models.

EUCLYD said rising AI capabilities are driving up demand for power, memory bandwidth, and computing capacity. Its platform aims to address these infrastructure constraints and reduce the cost of running AI models.

The company’s roadmap includes craftwerk, its AI silicon platform, and craftwerk station CWS, an AI data centre system. The platform combines programmable chips with memory and system-level optimisation.

EUCLYD said the approach aims to address memory and efficiency constraints affecting AI performance and scalability. The company also plans to build partnerships across the semiconductor and data centre ecosystem.

“AI is becoming a foundation of economic growth, scientific discovery, and national competitiveness,” Kastrup said in a statement. He added that AI infrastructure needs greater efficiency and lower costs to support wider adoption.

Samsung also highlighted infrastructure efficiency as a key factor in the next phase of AI development. “The next phase of AI will be defined not only by model innovation, but also by the efficiency and scalability of its infrastructure,” said Dode Goldschmidt, Senior VP of Samsung Electronics.

EQT said EUCLYD combines semiconductor expertise with a focus on AI infrastructure constraints. The company plans to use the new capital to expand its engineering organisation and accelerate product development.

The financing will also support EUCLYD’s preparations for commercial deployment across enterprise, sovereign and hyperscale AI markets.

Wennink added that Europe has capabilities across semiconductors, advanced manufacturing, and systems engineering. He said EUCLYD could turn those capabilities into an AI infrastructure platform.

title: HCLTech, CrowdStrike Deepen Cybersecurity Partnership as Enterprises Grapple with AI Risks
content:
HCLTech and CrowdStrike are expanding their partnership to help enterprises secure AI applications, models, and agents.

HCLTech and cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike have expanded their partnership to integrate CrowdStrike’s Falcon Guardian AI detection and response capabilities with HCLTech’s cybersecurity advisory, AI governance, implementation, and managed services.

The offering will focus on securing AI applications, models, agents, identities and data, while giving enterprises greater visibility into risks arising from AI deployments.

The move comes as companies increasingly embed AI into workflows that can access corporate data, applications and systems, creating new avenues for attacks as well as new risks around how AI systems themselves are governed.

“AI is becoming a new enterprise attack surface, and securing it requires visibility and protection everywhere AI operates,” Daniel Bernard, Chief Business Officer, CrowdStrike, said in a statement. “CrowdStrike pioneered AI Detection and Response to secure the full AI attack surface. Together with HCLTech’s global cybersecurity expertise and services, we’re bringing these capabilities to more enterprises as they operationalise AI at scale.”

The expanded partnership also builds on a collaboration announced in March around continuous threat exposure management, a cybersecurity approach that continuously identifies and prioritises vulnerabilities and exposures across an organisation.

“The next generation of enterprise security will require organisations to address both sides of the AI risk equation, defending against AI-powered threats while securing the AI systems they deploy,” Amit Jain, EVP and Global Head of Cybersecurity at HCLTech, added.

For HCLTech, the expanded partnership also lets it combine its cybersecurity services with a specialised security platform as demand grows for AI-specific risk management.

HCLTech has more than 223,000 employees across 60 countries and reported consolidated revenue of $14.8 billion for the 12 months ended June 2026. CrowdStrike, meanwhile, operates its Falcon cybersecurity platform across endpoint, cloud, identity, and data security.

title: Shah Rukh Khan Backs Flam as it Raises $40 Mn to Scale AI Interactive Content
content:
The AI content startup said it has signed more than 100 enterprise customers in six quarters, including Google, State Farm and Diageo.

Flam, an AI interactive content company, has raised $40 million in Series B funding led by QED Investors, with the capital going towards research and development on its AI models, product-suite expansion and global enterprise sales, the company said on September 14.

Claypond Capital, Martin Chavez, Olivier Pomel, Venky Harinarayan and Shah Rukh Khan (SRK Family Office) joined the round, while existing investors RTP Global and Dovetail increased their investments, the company further stated.

Flam said it has signed more than 100 enterprise customers in six quarters, including Google, State Farm and Diageo. The company said its technology is used across marketing, product visualisation, learning and development, entertainment, fan engagement, customer support and sales.

“Flam is built on a simple observation. Content has moved in waves, from text to images to video, and every wave flowed one way, creator to viewer. We think interactive is the next default for the internet,” said Shourya Agarwal, Founder of Flam. “The demand was always there. The technology wasn’t. We have made interactivity effortless to build and deploy at enterprise scale.”

Flam said its platform supports three content formats: Flicks, Airboards and Visual Agents. It also said it holds more than 15 patents.

Flicks are interactive videos that can switch people, products or scenes during playback. Flam said its patented compression technology delivers a 50-millisecond time-to-first-buffer, while its Forge editing model can modify specified elements in image references.

Airboards provide high-fidelity 3D content through a camera interface with touch, voice and haptic interactions. Flam said its 3D streaming technology loads Airboards in 300 milliseconds without requiring an app, while its Fable image-to-video model generates assets as native alpha-channel videos.

Visual Agents are human-like characters designed to hold conversations and take agentic actions. Flam said Fantom handles facial expression through identity preservation and motion transfer, Finesse provides voice capabilities in any language, and Falcon, a 26-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts large language model, delivers responses with a 30-millisecond time-to-first-token. The company said its pipeline returns an answer in under two seconds.

“Almost every frontier AI content company we see is optimising what already exists. Flam pointed at something else: how much of the content ecosystem is still untouched. That gap is bigger than most people think, and Flam is the first team we've seen with the infrastructure to go after it,” said Nigel Morris, Co-Founder and Managing Partner at QED Investors.

Flam was founded in 2021 and is headquartered in San Francisco, with teams in India and Japan. The company said it has more than 100 enterprise customers globally.

title: CoRover.ai Claims Its BharatGPT-Instruct Model Outperforms Sarvam 30B
content:
CoRover.ai said its 2B-parameter BharatGPT-Instruct model has surpassed the much larger Sarvam 30B on several reasoning, fairness, and multilingual benchmarks.

CoRover.ai has claimed that its BharatGPT-Instruct model, with around 2 billion active parameters, has outperformed Sarvam 30B, a model roughly 15 times its size, on several key AI benchmarks.

BharatGPT-Instruct led Sarvam 30B and Qwen 1.7B across several benchmarks and achieved 100% faithfulness in CoRover’s enterprise RAG evaluation. However, it underperformed on the GSM8K mathematics benchmark.

According to CoRover, the model outperformed both Sarvam 30B and Qwen 1.7B with scores of] 83.21% on the elementary science knowledge benchmark ARC-Easy, 53.84% on the advanced science reasoning benchmark ARC-Challenge, 68.67% on the common-sense reasoning benchmark WinoGrande, 78.51% on the physical solutions evaluation PIQA, and 68.28% on CrowS-Pairs, which evaluates social bias.

The new model challenges the assumption that bigger AI models are necessarily better, shifting the focus to smaller models that prioritise efficiency over scale while performing across local languages.

“Scale is not the same as intelligence,” Ankush Sabharwal, Founder and CEO of CoRover.ai, said in a statement. According to Sabharwal, when AI is designed around a country’s problems, languages and requirements, model size does not necessarily determine performance.

“It is about building models that are efficient, relevant, trustworthy and capable of solving real-world problems at scale,” he added.

BharatGPT-Instruct also performs strongly across Indian languages, the startup claimed, including] Hindi, Bengali, Marathi, Telugu, Gujarati, Malayalam, Punjabi, Tamil, Odia, and Kannada, surpassing Qwen 1.7B and Sarvam 30B on Multilingual MMLU.

PortGPT, CoRover’s domain-specific version of BharatGPT, designed for the ports and shipping sectors, is already live, while other specialised models are under development.

Earlier this year, the Indian Army’s Department of Military Affairs selected CoRover to set up a sovereign AI-ML lab powered by BharatGPT to enable Army personnel to learn, build, and deploy secure AI agents.

The AI startup is also empanelled by the National e-Governance Division under the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology as a trusted AI implementation partner for the public sector.

title: AI Music Startup Beatoven.ai Shuts Down B2C Service as Core Team Moves to Rusk Media
content:
The startup will retain its core intellectual property and is exploring commercial and enterprise use cases for its Maestro model.

Bengaluru-based AI music startup Beatoven.ai has discontinued its business-to-consumer (B2C) service and absorbed its core team into media company Rusk Media, co-founder Mansoor Rahimat Khan announced in a LinkedIn post.

The company will retain ownership of its core intellectual property and is now exploring licensing its Maestro AI model and music-intelligence technology to businesses.

“Last month, we officially discontinued Beatoven.ai’s B2C service,” Khan said, marking the end of the startup’s six-year run as a consumer AI music product.

The company’s core team has joined Rusk Media, where it will continue working on generative media, according to Khan. Beatoven will retain the intellectual property behind its Maestro model, while the company is “actively licensing” the model for commercial and enterprise use cases, particularly in music intelligence.

Beatoven.ai was founded in 2021 by Khan and Siddharth Bhardwaj. It developed AI tools that generate royalty-free background music for videos, podcasts, and other content. The company says more than 2 million creators have generated over 15 million tracks using its platform.

The startup had raised $1.3 million in a pre-Series A round in March 2024, led by Capital 2B, with participation from Entrepreneur First, IvyCap Ventures, Upsparks Capital, Rukam Capital, and angel investors. At the time, Beatoven.ai said more than 1 million users were using its platform and that 96% of its revenue came from markets outside India.

The company’s shift comes as competition in generative music has intensified. Khan said Beatoven.ai’s decision to license music and build its foundation models from scratch created challenges as competitors with greater funding adopted models trained using scraped data.

“Our original approach of ethically licensing music and building foundational models from scratch faced strong headwinds as heavily funded competitors emerged, building models through data scraping,” Khan said.

Beatoven.ai had positioned Maestro around licensed training data and artist compensation. In 2025, the company said it trained the model through licensing agreements with rights holders and would support royalty payments to artists and composers whose work contributed to the model.

The company had also received Fairly Trained certification for its AI music generator, reflecting its use of licensed music for model training. Its website says musicians receive compensation when they contribute music to Beatoven.ai.

Reflecting on the company's consumer business, Khan identified user retention as a key challenge for AI products aimed at creators. “Prosumer Content Creation is Tough: Retention is your primary nightmare and number one priority,” he said.

He also pointed to the difficulty of securing music rights, describing licensing as “extremely hard” because of fragmented players and gatekeepers.

Beatoven.ai is now seeking commercial partners for its technology. Khan said the company is in “active conversations for technology licensing” and invited organisations interested in its Maestro model, music intelligence, or underlying technology to contact him.

The commitment follows regulatory scrutiny of allegations involving child sexual abuse material on Instagram and an ongoing inquiry by India’s child-rights watchdog.

Meta has agreed to share cases involving child sexual abuse and other child-safety concerns with appropriate law enforcement authorities in India, government sources told ANI.

The commitment comes as the Centre increases pressure on social media platforms to strengthen safeguards for children and respond to harmful online content.

Government sources said Meta’s commitment is “a first step towards making the platforms safe for children and much more needs to be done.”

The government is also engaging with other social media companies on measures to identify and remove harmful material proactively. Government sources said action would be taken against platforms that do not take adequate steps to protect children online.

The latest development follows scrutiny of Meta after allegations that paid advertisements on Instagram were used to promote or facilitate access to Child Sexual Exploitation and Abuse Material (CSEAM). The allegations followed a BBC Eye investigation that prompted action from Indian authorities.

The National Commission for Protection of Child Rights (NCPCR) took suo motu cognisance of the BBC Eye report and issued a notice to Meta Platforms on July 3, seeking an explanation over the allegations. Meta submitted its response about a week later, after which the commission initiated a formal inquiry.

The NCPCR subsequently summoned Meta India’s managing director and country head to appear before it on September 9. Senior Meta India executives appeared before the commission that day in connection with the inquiry into alleged CSEAM-related advertisements on Instagram.

The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) has also sought point-wise action-taken reports from the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology, the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting, and the Delhi Police over allegations that paid Instagram advertisements facilitated access to child sexual abuse material.

The NHRC proceedings also raised questions around compliance with reporting obligations under the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act.

title: Shopify Ditches React Native, Moves Shop App to Kotlin & Swift
content:
The decision has drawn reactions from React Native developers, who questioned the performance comparisons and whether coding agents alone justify maintaining separate native codebases.

Shopify, the e-commerce giant, announced it migrated its mobile app, Shop, from React Native to Swift and Kotlin.

With AI assistance, the company said it took a proof of concept to a rebuilt native app published in the App Store in just 12 weeks.

This reverses the company’s 2020 decision to move to React Native. “That decision has served the Shop app well, but our increasing ability to develop with coding agents has allowed Shop to go fully native, building with Swift and Kotlin,” said the company.

Shopify said that advances in coding agents changed the tradeoffs behind maintaining a shared mobile codebase. Using Swift and Kotlin means that the company needs to build separately for iOS and Android, “but agents made it reasonable to reconsider that decision”, said the company.

Agents can now handle enough implementation, translation, testing and review work that the duplication is no longer the deciding factor it once was.

With this new native architecture, Shopify said that startup time for the Shop app was reduced by 23% for iOS and 50% on Android.

Session stability rose from more than 99.5% to more than 99.95%, which Shopify described as a tenfold reduction in crashing sessions. The Android release build also shrank by 109 MB, or 37.2%, while iOS app size increased by 1 MB.

Shopify said the migration preserved sign-in sessions, push notifications and analytics events required by downstream systems. It also retired some screens and streamlined others.

The company is using a workflow called Helix to migrate its wider app portfolio. Helix breaks screens into reviewable checkpoints, requiring tests, visual comparisons, adversarial code reviews and human approval before implementation proceeds.

Shopify is also developing a command-line interface that lets agents inspect app state and execute actions without relying on slow simulator interactions.

The Shopify app, which has more than 300 screens and includes widgets, an Apple Watch app and Siri Shortcuts, is now being migrated and is expected to ship later this year. Shopify said its other mobile apps will follow.

Shopify will continue sponsoring React Native Skia through the end of 2026, while FlashList will receive critical compatibility fixes as the company discusses long-term stewardship. Restyle will be archived after the end of 2026.

However, the reaction to Shopify’s decision has focused on whether coding agents have changed React Native's engineering trade-offs, or simply made it cheaper to move away from the framework.

One software developer wrote on X that Shopify’s explanation was “very thin on the reasoning as to why”, arguing that the post focused on LLMs making native development easier without identifying a specific React Native limitation that had prompted the migration.

The decision, he suggested, appeared to be motivated primarily by reducing abstraction.

Jamon Holmgren, CEO of React Native consultancy Infinite Red, added some context on X about the performance comparison.

He noted that the Shop app had not yet migrated to React Native’s New Architecture, which was developed in part to address startup-time issues.

“The one thing that was almost certain to improve startup time hadn’t happened yet,” Holmgren said, questioning how much of the reported performance improvement could be attributed to moving away from React Native rather than completing that transition.

Alex Mikucki, a software developer, wrote on X that Shopify’s rapid rewrite was unsurprising, arguing that declarative UI frameworks such as SwiftUI and Jetpack Compose are similar enough for agents to migrate between them effectively.

His experience rebuilding Expo Go’s UI in Jetpack Compose reinforced that view.

The harder challenge, he said, is maintaining consistent business logic and behaviour across separate native codebases.

Agents cannot necessarily resolve the trade-off between cross-platform consistency and platform-specific feel.

“I don't think react-native will go away, but I definitely feel react-native is evolving, will evolve further.”

He predicted more native components for performance-sensitive interfaces, greater use of over-the-air updates, and architectures that combine native and JavaScript components.

“I don't think the falling cost of writing lower level code makes abstractions automatically obsolete,” he wrote. “You get for free a lot of community effort on deciding/mapping platform quirks, stuff that would cost tokens and engineering effort otherwise, or even worse, would be missed and be a long-running paper-cut in your app.”

title: OpenAI Introduces ChatGPT for Financial Services Built on GPT-6 Astra
content:
OpenAI said GPT-6 Astra can work with figures, tables and supporting notes in financial documents, perform analysis, and generate documentation.

OpenAI has introduced ChatGPT for Financial Services, a version of ChatGPT Work built for financial institutions. The product combines financial data with GPT-6 Astra, OpenAI’s latest advanced LLM, to help teams with research, financial modelling and client materials.

ChatGPT for Financial Services is available to eligible financial institutions. OpenAI plans to use feedback from its financial services partners to improve the product and extend it into other areas of the industry.

The product includes financial datasets from Daloopa, PitchBook, LSEG News, and Crunchbase. The data covers earnings transcripts, financial statements, company fundamentals, and private companies.

OpenAI says the data is indexed and hosted on its infrastructure, allowing the system to provide citations that let users trace figures and claims back to their sources.

ChatGPT for Financial Services also supports integrations with existing subscriptions from S&P Capital IQ, LSEG, MSCI, Dow Jones Factiva, and Moody’s. Through shared sign-in and entitlement integrations, users will be able to access data they are already authorised to use through their ChatGPT accounts.

The product will initially serve investment banking and equity research, with Morgan Stanley and Evercore serving as design partners. They identified data access and work product creation as key requirements for financial teams.

“The promise of frontier research becomes real when it helps our people do the work that matters for our clients,” Morgan Stanley said in a statement. The firm added that it is working with OpenAI to bring the technology into company research, analysis and advice.

Evercore said it is working with OpenAI to apply the technology to client questions while maintaining its existing standards for judgement and advice.

GPT-6 Astra is integrated into the product for information retrieval, financial reasoning, and artefact generation. OpenAI said the model can work with figures, tables and supporting notes in financial documents, perform analysis, and turn the results into documents, spreadsheets, and presentations.

The product also allows administrators to publish Excel, Word, and PowerPoint templates for their firms. Teams can use firm-approved templates and style guides to create valuation models, research notes, and pitchbooks in the organisation’s format.

For enterprise controls, ChatGPT for Financial Services builds on ChatGPT Enterprise features including SAML SSO, SCIM provisioning, and role-based access controls. OpenAI said it does not use business data to train its models by default, and it is encrypted at rest and in transit. Firms can also configure workspace retention and export supported workspace logs through the OpenAI Compliance Platform.

The product supports more than 50 connectors, including Datasite, Box, Preqin, FactSet, and Intapp. OpenAI said it has also optimised some widely used financial-services MCP connectors to reduce troubleshooting when accessing provider data.

title: OpenAI Agents Used Hidden Online Channels to Communicate With Each Other: Report
content:
OpenAI agents used hidden websites to communicate, finding ways to work around restrictions.

OpenAI agents used hidden online channels for unauthorised communication, according to an investigation by Reuters, adding to previous incidents of the ChatGPT maker’s agents going rogue and escaping containment despite being instructed otherwise.

According to the report, OpenAI’s agents exploited ordinary websites, such as wikis, text-storage services, and link shorteners. They used the sites as improvised communication channels despite the restrictions, raising questions about the capability of the existing safeguards designed to supervise AI systems.

Findings from the review of six investigative groups suggest that it wasn’t a single accidental escape, as different research teams identified suspicious activities across multiple websites, with one team identifying 18 previously undisclosed sites and another reporting evidence across 23 sites.

This comes after OpenAI had earlier revealed that its agents had attacked Hugging Face in an attempt to cheat on their tasks and look up solutions online. The incident involved at least 1,200 agents coordinating and attacking in a swarm, improvising message boards and escaping containment.

"The prospect of AI-accelerated AI development demands more than voluntary commitments. The United States needs mandatory, capability-based national regulation that can evolve as the technology does," said Chris Lehane, OpenAI Chief Global Affairs Officer, in a separate and recent statement.

In the latest incident, the agents appeared to have exploited features of websites that were not under their domain. The agents were able to discreetly share information on websites, leaving it for other agents to retrieve. Despite operating under the intended restrictions, evidence suggested they found alternative methods to communicate.

This was not an isolated case, as the investigation into the incident uncovered previous cases. The investigation found agents posting thousands of messages on German wiki, identifying themselves as OpenAI systems. The messages discussed completing evaluations, bypassing restrictions, and sharing information. According to Reuters, Researchers found that 3,700 agents were involved in the activity.

The incidents showed that it was not a conventional cyberattack but involved AI agents secretly circumventing communication restrictions. However, it also raises questions about the effectiveness of security measures surrounding these AI agents.

OpenAI has now called for mandatory AI safety requirements in the US on concerns over AI agents going rogue.

Meanwhile, Anthropic also disclosed another instance where its AI model hacked an external system during testing.

title: NVIDIA and Palantir Deploy AI Stack for Supply Chain Decisions
content:
The system combines Nemotron models and Palantir Foundry to improve material allocation across NVIDIA’s global supply chain.

NVIDIA and Palantir Technologies have deployed an AI stack to support supply chain operations. The system combines NVIDIA’s Nemotron open models with Palantir Foundry and its Ontology data layer.

It will help NVIDIA identify supply constraints, assess allocation choices, and capture operational expertise. The deployment starts within NVIDIA’s own supply chain, which spans millions of parts, thousands of suppliers, and manufacturing partners worldwide.

The companies aim to shorten the time from wafer production to a completed AI system reaching production. Each NVIDIA Vera Rubin rack contains about 1.3 million parts, according to the companies’ statement.

NVIDIA said the system creates a shared view of inputs involved in material allocation decisions. It connects materials, manufacturing sites, production capacity, allocations, and other operational information through Palantir’s Ontology.

“Supply chains are the operating system of the physical economy,” NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang said in a statement. He added that the companies are combining software to “reason, plan and orchestrate” the journey from wafer to token.

The system also uses NVIDIA cuOpt for allocation and scenario planning. cuOpt models the supply chain as a mixed-integer linear programme and aims to minimise Time of Ownership. It can also show which constraints limit a particular allocation decision.

NVIDIA and Palantir found that quantitative optimisation alone could not capture all factors affecting allocation decisions. Planners also use emails, weather risks, geopolitical events, and supplier discussions.

The companies therefore built a workflow that records each allocation decision, its rationale, expected result, and actual outcome. This information becomes training data for a customised language model.

NVIDIA post-trained its Nemotron 3.5 Lightning model to recommend allocation ranges and explain the factors behind them. Supply chain planners still review the recommendations and make the final decisions.

On the development benchmark, the post-trained model achieved 86.7% allocation-decision accuracy. Nemotron 3 Ultra scored 55.5%, while the base Lightning model scored 17.5%.

The post-trained model also recorded 58.6% balanced accuracy and 57.5% Macro-F1. NVIDIA said the results show the value of specialising a smaller model for a defined decision-making task.

The system keeps proprietary data, model weights, and inference within a governed environment. Organisations can deploy the stack on-premises or in the cloud, depending on their requirements.

Palantir CEO Alex Karp said the collaboration would bring sovereign AI capabilities to NVIDIA’s supply chain. He described the partnership as a cornerstone of the companies’ sovereign AI strategy.

Palantir customers can also post-train Nemotron models using their own operational data. The companies said this approach can support supply chain operations across manufacturing, energy, healthcare, automotive, and aerospace.

The companies plan to use feedback for future reinforcement learning, while keeping retraining under governance.

title: New $200 ChatGPT Pro Subscriptions Get Paused as GPT-6 Astra Drives High Demand
content:
Other plans and the API remain available, and existing accounts are not affected.

OpenAI has paused new subscriptions to its $200-a-month Pro plan for GPT-6 Astra, citing unprecedented demand and pressure on its systems.

Thibault Sottiaux, an OpenAI engineering lead, said in a post on X that the company was taking the “smallest step” it could to preserve access for existing users.

Other plans and the API remain available, and existing accounts are not affected.

The decision follows a warning from Sottiaux that demand for Astra was unlike anything he had seen before, despite the company’s steep growth.

He said OpenAI was “pulling all the levers possible to sustain the demand” and might need to pause new Pro subscriptions if demand continued.

OpenAI introduced GPT-6 Astra on September 3 as its most capable model, with improvements in computer use, browsing, software engineering, cybersecurity, science and professional work.

Greg Brockman, the company’s president, stated the model’s release marks a welcome step into the era of artificial general intelligence, or AGI.

The model is designed for complex reasoning, coding, computer use, research and document creation, with a context window of up to 1.05 million tokens.

Astra’s rollout has been staggered, and OpenAI initially made it available to a limited set of organisations.

Broader access is planned for ChatGPT Plus, Pro, Business and Enterprise users, as well as through the API, Microsoft Azure and AWS Bedrock.

The company’s safety overview said Astra was its first model to reach the ‘Critical’ level of cybersecurity capability under its Preparedness Framework.

This means it could find previously unknown vulnerabilities and develop ways to exploit them across well-protected systems with the right tools and access.

The subscription pause adds a capacity constraint to a rollout that has already faced access issues. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman apologised earlier this month for what he called a “messy rollout” after some paying users couldn't access Astra.

title: Microsoft Elevates Rust to a Tier-1 Language
content:
Rust sits among C++, C#, and TypeScript as one of the “best-supported languages” for internal development at Microsoft.

Microsoft has elevated Rust to Tier-1 engineering status, placing it alongside C++, C#, and

TypeScript as one of the company’s best-supported languages for internal development.

The designation gives teams a supported path from local development to production, including secure toolchain builds, developer tooling, quality workflows, platform integration and compliance with Microsoft’s Security Development Lifecycle requirements.

The announcement, published by the Rust Foundation, was made by Victor Ciura, a principal engineer on Microsoft’s Rust tooling team.

“Today, Rust sits among C++, C#, and TypeScript as one of the best-supported languages for internal development at Microsoft,” Ciura wrote.

He said Microsoft is integrating Rust into its existing Windows-native development ecosystem rather than developing it as a parallel toolchain.

A central part of that effort is rustc_codegen_utc, an alternative code-generation backend for the Rust compiler that connects rustc to Microsoft’s MSVC backend, known as UTC.

The backend gives Rust access to Windows tooling and ABI compatibility, binary hardening, post-link analysis and servicing, debugging, profiling, coverage, and cross-language optimisation.

Microsoft’s Windows platform and MSVC have evolved around C and C++ for decades.

The shared backend is intended to allow Rust and C++ to use the same platform investments, particularly in projects that combine the two languages.

The company said this includes work spanning firmware and drivers, kernels and hypervisors, microservices and applications. The backend has been production-ready since early 2026 and has been self-hosted since Rust 1.90, according to Ciura.

More than 100 Microsoft project repositories currently build with it, with adoption continuing each week.

“rustc_codegen_utc is a major part of that journey,” Ciura wrote. “Its differentiator is simple: it connects rustc to the native backend and platform ecosystem that Microsoft has built around Windows for decades.”

However, the initiative does not resolve every Rust/C++ interoperability issue. Ciura said language-level interoperability, FFI contracts, bindings, differences in language semantics and build systems remain part of the work underway inside Microsoft and across the wider industry.

Microsoft’s Rust investment extends beyond compiler infrastructure. The company maintains Rust for Windows, which provides access to Windows APIs, and publishes Rust ports of Windows driver samples.

Azure also offers a Rust SDK and deployment paths across services including App Service, Functions and Kubernetes Service. Besides, Microsoft has also explored Rust for low-level Windows components as part of its memory-safety efforts.

title: Karnataka Approves ₹35 Cr AI Hub at IIIT Bangalore
content:
The initiative will combine industry-linked certification, startup incubation and AI research through an integrated platform with real-world testbeds.

The Karnataka government has approved a ₹35 crore Karnataka Artificial Intelligence Hub at the International Institute of Information Technology-Bangalore (IIIT-B), bringing together AI skilling, startup support and research as the state works towards setting up a proposed AI university.

The state Cabinet approved the AI Hub on September 9. Electronics, IT/BT and Home Minister Priyank Kharge said the Hub would serve as part of the foundation for the university.

“Karnataka is laying the foundation for its AI University with the proposed Karnataka Artificial Intelligence Hub at IIIT Bangalore, Kharge wrote in a post on X. “With an outlay of ₹35 crore, the Hub will bring together AI skilling, startup support and advanced research on one integrated platform.”

The facility will provide practical training, internships, mentorship, real-world case studies and modular programmes for students, fresh graduates and job seekers. The Hub will also provide seed funding, incubation support and access to technical facilities.

Kharge said the Hub will offer industry-aligned certification and finishing-school programmes for students, graduates and job seekers.

The initiative will include an AI Living Lab with compute infrastructure and real-world testbeds. The facility is expected to allow researchers, startups, industry and government bodies to develop and validate AI applications in practical settings.

The AI Hub is planned as an initial platform ahead of the proposed AI University.

The AI University was announced earlier this year by Chief Minister DK Shivakumar as part of Karnataka’s broader plan to build an education and research ecosystem around AI

The government has described it as India’s first government-driven AI university, bringing together talent development, research and collaboration between academia, industry and government.

title: Hyderabad GCC Boom May Add 8–12 Mn Sq Ft of Office Demand Over Next 3–5 Years
content:
GCC leasing in Hyderabad has more than doubled from approximately 1.9 million sq ft in 2021 to 4.5 million sq ft in 2025.

Hyderabad’s expanding global capability centre (GCC) ecosystem could generate 8–12 million sq ft of additional office demand over the next three to five years, as multinational companies increase investments in technology, engineering, BFSI, life sciences, and other high-value functions, according to a report by Anarock Research & Advisory and FICCI.

The city could add 50–70 new GCCs over the period, potentially generating more than 75,000 high-skilled jobs. The report also estimates 2–3 million sq ft of potential demand for flex and managed workspaces, particularly across western Hyderabad and established IT corridors.

Hyderabad currently has 515+ GCCs employing more than 3 lakh professionals, accounting for nearly 20% of India’s GCC base. The city added more than 70 GCCs in FY25, the highest among the major GCC hubs, compared to 30–35 additions in Bengaluru, 15–20 in Pune, and 12–15 in Chennai.

Anuj Puri, Chairman of Anarock Group, said the expansion is already driving higher commercial real estate demand.

“This GCC expansion is already translating into significant real estate demand in the city. The report highlights that GCC office leasing in Hyderabad increased from 1.9 million sq ft in 2021 to 4.5 million sq ft in 2025, while the city recorded 3.05 million sq ft of GCC absorption in H1 2026 alone. The sustained leasing momentum reflects the deepening of Hyderabad’s GCC ecosystem and the increasing preference of global enterprises to establish larger and more sophisticated operations in the city,” he said in a statement.

The expansion is also coinciding with a broader shift in the nature of GCC operations. Companies are increasingly setting up functions spanning AI and machine learning, cloud engineering, product development, cybersecurity, financial analytics, fintech, drug development analytics, clinical data, chip design, R&D, embedded systems, and digital transformation.

“Hyderabad’s GCC proposition is broadening well beyond conventional IT-ITeS functions. Technology and software remain core demand drivers, but the ecosystem has expanded significantly across BFSI, pharma and life sciences, semiconductors, aerospace and defence, automotive and engineering, healthcare, consumer and retail, and media and sports technology,” V V Rama Raju, Chairman, FICCI Telangana State Council and Founder and Managing Director of Gaja Engineering, noted, adding that Hyderabad’s GCC base is becoming more diversified.

Hyderabad currently has around 125 million sq ft of Grade A office stock, accounting for nearly 15% of India’s Grade A office inventory. Another 36 million sq ft of supply is expected to enter the market over the next few years.

Net office absorption reached 8.5 million sq ft in 2025 and 5.2 million sq ft in H1 2026, while vacancy declined from 26.3% in 2025 to 23.5% in the first half of 2026.

Average office rents in the city are around ₹75 per sq ft per month, below the pan-India average of ₹96 per sq ft, according to the report, giving Hyderabad a cost advantage over several competing GCC destinations.

The city has an estimated 1 million IT workforce and more than 4 lakh STEM graduates annually, according to the report.

The HITEC City-Gachibowli-Financial District-Kokapet corridor is expected to remain the primary driver of office expansion, supported by existing Grade A supply, infrastructure, and access to talent.

The report said the shift from traditional support operations towards R&D, engineering, analytics, digital, and corporate functions could further strengthen Hyderabad’s position as a global innovation and decision-making hub.

title: Bosch SDS, Dassault Systèmes Partner to Advance AI-Led Manufacturing in India
content:
Bosch SDS and Dassault Systèmes said their first joint deployment is underway with a leading electric vehicle manufacturer.

Bosch Software and Digital Solutions (Bosch SDS) and French software corporation Dassault Systèmes are collaborating to help manufacturing enterprises accelerate digital transformation across product engineering, manufacturing operations, and industrial value chains.

The collaboration combines Dassault Systèmes' capabilities across virtual twin experiences, product lifecycle management (PLM), digital manufacturing, and manufacturing operations management with Bosch SDS' expertise in contextualised data products, manufacturing transformation, energy optimisation, IT/OT integration, and machine-level intelligence.

"Manufacturing enterprises today are looking beyond isolated digitisation initiatives toward connected, intelligent and autonomous operations," Dattatreya Gaur, MD and CEO, Bosch SDS, said in a statement.

The companies said the first joint deployment is underway with a leading electric vehicle manufacturer in India. Dassault Systèmes' DELMIA Apriso MES platform is being deployed alongside Bosch SDS' manufacturing transformation capabilities to enable real-time connected operations.

The collaboration covers AI-enabled manufacturing transformation and agentic AI orchestration through the Bosch Cognitive Factory platform, along with Digital Thread and traceability across engineering and manufacturing.

Ramesh Ramaswamy, Global Sales Head, Bosch Software and Digital Solutions, said the collaboration intends to help manufacturers "move from fragmented transformation efforts to truly connected, software-defined and intelligent operations."

Deepak NG, Managing Director, India, Dassault Systèmes, said the partnership marks "a major milestone for the manufacturing industry" and would help factories "adopt AI much faster."

The partnership also covers Digital Product Passport (DPP) and regulatory compliance readiness. Bosch SDS will additionally act as a consulting and system integration partner to Dassault Systèmes across the identified transformation areas, spanning engineering, manufacturing, and enterprise operations.

The companies said the collaboration will target sectors including automotive, electronics, batteries, semiconductors, industrial machinery, and consumer durables. It will also extend into heavy engineering and process industries.

Bosch SDS is part of the Bosch Group and provides consulting, engineering, and IT services focused on digital transformation. Dassault Systèmes' 3DEXPERIENCE platform serves 390,000 customers globally, according to the company.

title: Anthropic Blocks Malicious AI Use Linked To Weapons Development
content:
Anthropic said third parties are attempting to misuse Claude for biological and conventional weapons development, raising concerns over the risks posed by frontier AI.

Anthropic has blocked attempts to misuse its Claude AI models for activities linked to biological and conventional weapons development, uncovering five cases and six software systems involved.

In its latest threat intelligence report, covering December 2025 to August 2026, Anthropic has highlighted the increasing threats involving artificial intelligence being used beyond conventional cybercrime. The company identified third parties using Claude in attempts at cyber espionage, surveillance, scams, fraud, and influence operations, raising concerns about how AI companies will prevent such malicious activities while advancing legitimate scientific and technological research.

The company described biological misuse as one of the most serious risks associated with frontier AI, while highlighting both the benefits and dangerous outcomes of its applications.

The company had reported six cases involving Claude being used as a tool to develop software for conventional weapons, including firearms, missiles, armed drones and bombs, as well as targeting and manipulating systems. Anthropic said a Yemen-based weapons engineering group used Claude to assist with missile-development work, including missile guidance systems.

Despite the concern, Anthropic has drawn a line at fully autonomous weapon systems.

"Frontier AI systems are simply not reliable enough to power fully autonomous weapons. We will not knowingly provide a product that puts America's warfighters and civilians at risk," said Dario Amodei, Anthropic CEO, defending the company’s decision not to remove safety guardrails for battlefield automation.

A case concerning the incident involved hackers whose activities were consistent with Russia-based Midnight Blizzard, also known as APT29 and Cozy Bear, associated with cyber-espionage campaigns. The group used AI to develop malware that detected attempts by security systems to identify its activities, then modified the code to evade detection.

Anthropic said it is working to improve its systems to prevent, detect, and disrupt similar activities in the future. The company claimed that it shared relevant information with authorities and industry partners. The company has also introduced stronger protections for biological research in newer models, including Claude Fable 5.

The system combines Nemotron models and Palantir Foundry to improve material allocation across NVIDIA’s global supply chain.

NVIDIA and Palantir Technologies have deployed an AI stack to support supply chain operations. The system combines NVIDIA’s Nemotron open models with Palantir Foundry and its Ontology data layer.

It will help NVIDIA identify supply constraints, assess allocation choices, and capture operational expertise. The deployment starts within NVIDIA’s own supply chain, which spans millions of parts, thousands of suppliers, and manufacturing partners worldwide.

The companies aim to shorten the time from wafer production to a completed AI system reaching production. Each NVIDIA Vera Rubin rack contains about 1.3 million parts, according to the companies’ statement.

NVIDIA said the system creates a shared view of inputs involved in material allocation decisions. It connects materials, manufacturing sites, production capacity, allocations, and other operational information through Palantir’s Ontology.

“Supply chains are the operating system of the physical economy,” NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang said in a statement. He added that the companies are combining software to “reason, plan and orchestrate” the journey from wafer to token.

The system also uses NVIDIA cuOpt for allocation and scenario planning. cuOpt models the supply chain as a mixed-integer linear programme and aims to minimise Time of Ownership. It can also show which constraints limit a particular allocation decision.

NVIDIA and Palantir found that quantitative optimisation alone could not capture all factors affecting allocation decisions. Planners also use emails, weather risks, geopolitical events, and supplier discussions.

The companies therefore built a workflow that records each allocation decision, its rationale, expected result, and actual outcome. This information becomes training data for a customised language model.

NVIDIA post-trained its Nemotron 3.5 Lightning model to recommend allocation ranges and explain the factors behind them. Supply chain planners still review the recommendations and make the final decisions.

On the development benchmark, the post-trained model achieved 86.7% allocation-decision accuracy. Nemotron 3 Ultra scored 55.5%, while the base Lightning model scored 17.5%.

The post-trained model also recorded 58.6% balanced accuracy and 57.5% Macro-F1. NVIDIA said the results show the value of specialising a smaller model for a defined decision-making task.

The system keeps proprietary data, model weights, and inference within a governed environment. Organisations can deploy the stack on-premises or in the cloud, depending on their requirements.

Palantir CEO Alex Karp said the collaboration would bring sovereign AI capabilities to NVIDIA’s supply chain. He described the partnership as a cornerstone of the companies’ sovereign AI strategy.

Palantir customers can also post-train Nemotron models using their own operational data. The companies said this approach can support supply chain operations across manufacturing, energy, healthcare, automotive, and aerospace.

The companies plan to use feedback for future reinforcement learning, while keeping retraining under governance.
