title: You Can Now Write CUDA Kernels in Rust
content:
The projects, cuda-oxide and cutile-rs, compile Rust kernels natively for NVIDIA GPUs

NVIDIA has introduced two open-source projects that let developers write CUDA GPU kernels directly in Rust. This extends Rust into GPU programming that has traditionally required CUDA C++.

The projects, cuda-oxide and cutile-rs, compile Rust kernels natively for NVIDIA GPUs rather than relying on Rust wrappers around code written in another language.

The two projects target different CUDA programming models, the company stated in a blog post.

cuda-oxide is designed for SIMT programming, where developers explicitly control individual GPU threads and their execution. It uses a custom rustc code-generation backend to route Rust code through NVIDIA’s GPU dialects, Pliron IR, and LLVM, before producing PTX.

cutile-rs targets NVIDIA’s newer Tile programming model, where developers describe operations on blocks of data, and the compiler determines how those tiles map to GPU threads and hardware. It runs on stable Rust 1.89 or newer and CUDA 13.3, while cuda-oxide currently requires a pinned nightly Rust toolchain.

NVIDIA said the projects are intended to bring Rust’s compile-time memory-safety guarantees to GPU kernel development.

In the SIMT implementation, DisjointSlice provides each thread exclusive access to its output element, while Tile uses tensor partitioning to establish exclusive ownership of writable sub-tensors.

The company demonstrated both approaches with a 1,024-element vector-addition kernel.

The examples catch certain aliasing errors at compile time rather than leaving them to runtime debugging, although SIMT shared-memory programming still requires unsafe code.

NVIDIA describes cuda-oxide as early alpha, while cutile-rs is already published on crates.io and is being used in Hugging Face’s Grout inference engine and mistral.rs. It plans to support interoperability between CUDA Rust, CUDA C++, and CUDA Python, allowing developers to use different frontends without being locked into one ecosystem.

“NVIDIA is excited to be leaning in with the Rust community as we elevate native Rust GPU programming,” said the company. “Projects like rust-cuda, rust-gpu, and cudarc pioneered the marriage of GPUs and Rust, and the people behind them, including the team at VectorWare, continue to shape how we think about our own work as we build with the Rust community.”

title: US Suspends Cognizant’s Green Card Filings Amid Visa Fraud Investigations
content:
The suspension applies to new PERM filings and does not, by itself, cancel existing green card cases or terminate Cognizant employees' H-1B status.

The US Department of Labour has suspended Cognizant’s filings for employment-based green cards under the Permanent Labour Certification (PERM) programme. This blocks the company from submitting new PERM applications while it’s under a federal investigation into its visa programme.

Labour Department Inspector General Anthony D’Esposito announced the suspension in a post on X, saying the investigation was focused on “facts, fraud and finances” and warning that “handcuffs await.”

The department has not disclosed the specific allegations against Cognizant, the number of employees or applications affected, or how long the suspension will remain in place.

The suspension applies to new PERM filings and does not, by itself, cancel existing green-card cases or terminate employees' H-1B status. H-1B and PERM are separate immigration processes, although the investigation could lead to further action against Cognizant.

PERM is a key employer-sponsored step towards many employment-based green cards. Before filing, an employer must establish that no sufficient, willing, and qualified US workers are available for the position and that hiring the foreign worker will not adversely affect the wages and working conditions of similarly employed US workers.

PERM is only the first stage of the employment-based green card process. After certification, an employer files an I-140 petition with the US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS), after which the worker may face a visa-number wait before filing for adjustment of status and ultimately receiving permanent residence.

Cognizant’s PERM suspension follows an earlier escalation in the Labour Department’s investigation.

In July, D’Esposito said investigators had issued dozens of subpoenas and that whistleblowers had raised concerns involving major companies including Cognizant over H-1B and PERM practices. D’Esposito did not accuse Cognizant of wrongdoing or announce charges at the time.

The July investigation was focused broadly on alleged abuses of the employment-visa system, including fraudulent applications, wage kickbacks, worker exploitation, and practices that could undercut US workers.

The department is pursuing the investigation alongside the White House Fraud Task Force.

As OpenAI heads toward an IPO, the bigger test for Astra may have little to do with whether it can be called AGI and much more to do with whether it can turn frontier capability, enterprise-grade privacy, and lower cost per task into higher enterprise revenue.

The release of OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra has sparked claims that the model has achieved artificial general intelligence, or AGI, including from OpenAI President Greg Brockman and NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang.

While those claims remain debated, a less examined aspect of GPT-6 is that it may force engineering teams to rethink how they estimate, calculate, and measure AI economics.

On the surface, the model does come with a whopping $10 and $50 per million input and output tokens, respectively, putting it alongside Claude Fable 5.1 and other frontier models.

But OpenAI is leaning on cost per task to sell Astra, arguing that its ability to complete difficult tasks with fewer tokens can make it cheaper overall.

Even on the benchmarking platform Artificial Analysis, Astra makes the case for looking beyond token prices.

The platform calculates the average cost of an Intelligence Index task by measuring the tokens consumed on individual benchmark problems, from business workflows and professional knowledge work to coding, terminal-based tasks and scientific reasoning, and applying each model’s API pricing.

On its latest index, Astra costs an average $3.26 per task versus $7.63 for Fable 5.1. Astra does so at 57% lower cost.

So what does this mean for engineering teams, which have only recently started grappling with soaring token bills and the ‘tokenmaxxing’ culture around AI coding, just as the economics of those tokens may be starting to change?

“Cost per successful task should become a standard metric alongside quality and latency,” Animesh Koratana, CEO of PlayerZero, tells AIM. “A higher-priced model can be cheaper to operate if it completes the work with fewer attempts or less human intervention. Token pricing doesn’t capture those economics by itself.”

Koratana explains that in software engineering, generating a plausible patch is only one part of the job. The change must solve the intended problem, pass verification and meet the team’s acceptance requirements.

“If an engineer spends an hour correcting the result, that effort belongs in the economic comparison,” he says.

Engineering teams first need to agree on what counts as a successful outcome.

That could mean a verified fix or a customer issue being resolved, but the same standard should be applied to every model.

Where possible, teams should use automated tests, but where that isn’t possible, human review can determine whether the work is actually done.

Koratana suggests dividing the total cost of all attempts, including failed runs, retries and verification, by the number of successfully completed tasks.

Besides, API costs should be reported separately from the broader operating cost, which includes human review and rework.

Teams should also use actual workloads, testing a representative mix of routine and difficult tasks, and report results by task type; an aggregate score can obscure meaningful differences in where each model performs well.

Koratana also recommends comparing the systems teams would actually deploy, giving models equivalent starting information and access to tools, while documenting differences in prompts, reasoning settings, caching and retry policies.

Reliability should remain visible, too. Teams should repeat trials and report success rates, completion times and human intervention alongside cost. A low average cost is less useful if the system frequently fails or requires unpredictable amounts of supervision.

“The question engineering leaders ask themselves is what does it cost to complete this work to an acceptable standard, and how reliably can we do it?” says Koratana. “Cost per successful task gets us closer to measuring what enterprises actually buy AI for.”

But measuring cost per successful task raises a harder question: what exactly should be included in that cost as AI systems become more agentic?

Harshil Shah, Director of AI at R Systems, says the answer goes well beyond the number of tokens a model uses.

Tokens remain useful for capacity planning, prompt optimisation and debugging. But in an agentic workflow, a model may use different amounts of reasoning, make multiple tool calls, draw on cached context or require several steps to complete the same task. That makes token count a weaker measure of the actual cost of getting the work done.

Shah says teams should instead treat the entire workflow as one unit. A business task should be tracked from start to finish, including the model calls, retrieval, tool use, verification, retries and fallbacks involved along the way.

“I would use ‘cost per verified successful task’ as the top-level economic metric.”

The calculation would involve adding up the cost of every attempt, including retries and fallbacks, and dividing that total by the number of tasks successfully completed.

This means the cost of failed attempts is still counted. If a model spends tokens, makes tool calls or uses infrastructure on a task but ultimately fails, those costs should not disappear from the calculation.

Teams should also track how often tasks succeed, how much they cost to resolve at the median and at the high end, and how often they require retries or human intervention.

The final piece is defining what counts as success.

Shah says this should be tied to the outcome of the task, rather than whether a model produces a plausible response.

Where possible, teams should use objective measures: a test passes, a transaction is completed, a record is reconciled or an output clears validation. LLM judges can be used for more subjective assessments, but should not replace objective checks where those are available.

Shah divides costs into four categories. The first is model costs, covering planner, worker, verifier and sub-agent calls.

The second is tool costs, including search, browser use, code execution, OCR, databases and paid APIs.

The third is execution overhead, such as containers, storage and network, and the fourth is operational recovery, including human review, escalation and remediation.

“Evaluation overhead should generally remain separate from production costs,” Shah recommends.

For example, if an LLM judge is used only to score a benchmark, its cost should not be included in the cost of running the application. Otherwise, teams could end up comparing the cost of the evaluation process rather than the cost of the AI system itself.

To make comparisons fair, teams should then keep the setup the same across models. That means using the same tasks, prompts, tools, retry limits, caching and routing rules, while recording the model version and other settings used in each test.

Shah also recommends testing models on a representative mix of tasks rather than relying on a single average. Results should be broken down by task type and difficulty, with offline tests supplemented by data from real production workloads.

Finally, he proposes “Cost@SLO”—the cost of using a particular model and system setup while still meeting a defined reliability and latency target.

The idea is to avoid using the same expensive model for every task. Instead, enterprises could use cheaper models for tasks they can handle reliably, and escalate to more capable models when needed.

“The winning enterprise architecture is unlikely to be one frontier model everywhere; it will route each task class to the cheapest configuration that satisfies its quality and risk SLO, then escalate only when the trace indicates that the cheaper path is unlikely to finish reliably.”

But accounting for those risks also changes how enterprises should think about choosing between models, particularly when the cheapest model on paper may not be the cheapest one to deploy reliably.

Sathya AG, a principal architect at Google, takes the argument a step further, distinguishing between cost per inference, cost per attempt and cost per successful task. For autonomous systems, he argues that the last is the metric that matters because it captures the full cost of getting a job done.

“We have to evaluate the cost of the entire harness and workflow, not just the model costs,” Sathya says.

But that calculation also needs to account for the cost of failure. Retries and tool calls are relatively straightforward to price, but a silent hallucination that reaches a customer or introduces a production bug can be far more expensive than the inference itself. Sathya therefore suggests factoring expected failure costs into what he calls ‘Cost-per-Outcome’.

“For advanced maturity, we have to also look at the P95 and P99 tail costs, not just the average,” he says. “Agentic systems have a nasty habit of entering runaway reasoning loops and retry cascades on complex edge cases. In enterprise production, those fat tails are where the budget quietly bleeds out.”

Therefore, the cost per outcome should include inference, tool calls, retries, infrastructure, human intervention and the expected cost of failure.

The economics are ultimately tied to OpenAI’s larger push to win enterprise customers, and the company is drawing a lesson from the low adoption rates of Anthropic’s Fable 5.

Despite its capabilities, the model has struggled to gain business traction, with its high price emerging as a key constraint.

Data governance is another part of that enterprise pitch. Anthropic’s Fable 5 initially required 30-day data retention for safety monitoring by default, although eligible enterprise customers could use zero data retention.

OpenAI, meanwhile, says Astra supports Zero Data Retention for eligible API customers, meaning it doesn’t retain prompts and responses after processing, while its new Private Safety Processing is designed to strengthen safety monitoring without giving up those ZDR commitments.

As OpenAI heads toward an IPO, the bigger test for Astra may have little to do with whether it can be called AGI and much more to do with whether it can turn frontier capability, enterprise-grade privacy, and lower cost per task into higher enterprise revenue.

title: Swiggy Credits Snowflake for Making Data Workloads 96% Faster
content:
Swiggy’s data-processing pipeline, which previously took about six hours, now delivers insights in near real-time.

Swiggy has moved its central analytical workloads to Snowflake, cutting the processing time of its slowest data workflows by 90–96%. The company also reduced the runtime of its heaviest individual queries from two hours to 15 minutes.

The foodtech company built a central analytical layer on Snowflake using Apache Iceberg, bringing data from its different businesses into a unified serving layer.

Snowflake said the broader data processing pipeline, which previously took about six hours, now delivers insights in near real-time. This allows teams across Swiggy to access operational and business data without depending as heavily on central data teams.

Marketing teams can use the data infrastructure to create and launch targeted campaigns through their own tools, while product engineering teams use standardised metrics to assess experimental features before release.

Swiggy’s operational teams can also monitor service-quality metrics in real-time, while finance teams get visibility into technology costs at the workload level.

The platform also provides governed self-service access through role-based permissions, column masking, and row-level security.

Snowflake said the same controls can be applied to AI agents and applications, including permission boundaries, short-lived credentials, and audit trails.

“At Swiggy, data is valuable only when it reaches the person who can act on it, whether that is a city sales manager, restaurant owner or delivery partner,” Madhusudhan Rao, CTO of Swiggy, said in a statement. “With Snowflake, we are making trusted, governed insights easier to access while ensuring that every user and AI agent operates within the same permissions and audit framework.”

The company said the unified infrastructure was designed to address the growing complexity of serving millions of customers across food delivery, Instamart and Dineout, where fragmented data had made it harder to support peak workloads and provide timely insights.

“India's fastest-moving companies can't afford to route every data question through a central team,” said Vijayant Rai, Managing Director of India at Snowflake. “With Snowflake, Swiggy has built a centralised, governed data foundation, consistent controls, and an AI framework that holds agents to the same standards as people.”

The Swiggy deployment comes as Snowflake is seeing increased demand for its AI-focused data platform.

In its latest quarterly results, Snowflake reported 37% year-on-year growth in product revenue to $1.49 billion and raised its full-year product revenue forecast to $6.07 billion. CEO Sridhar Ramaswamy said AI accounted for “approximately half of the acceleration” in the company’s growth.

The deployment now covers customer outreach, collections, and field-level employee feedback across 12 Indian languages.

Mahindra & Mahindra Financial Services has expanded its voice AI partnership with Sarvam AI to cover sales, collections, and employee engagement. The companies announced the development at Global Fintech Fest (GFF) 2026.

Mahindra Finance has used voice agents developed by Mahindra AI on Sarvam’s platform to make more than 1 crore calls to customers. The agents operate across 12 Indian languages and are being used across the company’s rural and semi-urban markets.

In sales, the voice agents engage with customers and identify potential cross-sell opportunities across vehicle, tractor, SME, housing, insurance, and investment products. In collections, they support conversations ranging from pre-due reminders to write-off and repossession stages.

The partnership also covers employee engagement. Voice agents collect feedback from field teams, giving Mahindra Finance’s leadership access to frontline operational insights.

Mahindra AI has combined the voice agents with in-house machine learning models to run sales and collections campaigns. The models identify customers and opportunities, while the voice agents use those insights to conduct conversations in the customer’s preferred language.

Each call is recorded and analysed through AI pipelines. The resulting information is connected to systems including CRM, loan servicing, and collections, allowing the company to use insights from conversations in subsequent business processes.

“Our customers have always trusted us to stay close to them, whether they are in a city or a village. Voice AI has allowed us to extend that closeness at scale, reaching people proactively, in their own language,” said Raul Rebello, Managing Director and CEO, Mahindra Finance, in a statement.

“As we diversify into new lines of business, this partnership with Sarvam is central to how we scale customer-first financial services across Bharat,” he added.

Pratyush Kumar, Co-founder, Sarvam, said the deployment shows how voice AI can be integrated into financial services operations.

“Mahindra Finance has set a strong benchmark for what AI at scale can look like in financial services,” he said. “More than 1 crore calls across sales, collections and employee engagement show what becomes possible when AI is deeply embedded into the business and continuously learns from customer outcomes.”

title: MSD Opens 2.5 Lakh Sq Ft Technology Centre in Hyderabad as Telangana Pushes Life Sciences Beyond Manufacturing
content:
The new centre will bring together teams working across digital, data, analytics, AI, technology and engineering.

MSD has inaugurated a 2.5 lakh square feet technology centre in Hyderabad, expanding its digital, data, analytics, AI, technology and engineering capabilities in the city as Telangana seeks to position itself as a global hub for life sciences and advanced technology.

Located in HITEC City, the new centre will support MSD’s global Human Health business and form part of the company’s worldwide technology network.

The centre comes as Telangana attempts to move its life-sciences ecosystem beyond its traditional strength in manufacturing and towards advanced R&D, discovery, technology and global capability creation.

“Telangana has built a truly end-to-end life sciences ecosystem, with more than 2,000 companies spanning APIs, bulk drugs, generics, CDMO, vaccines, research and discovery,” Sridhar Babu, Telangana’s Minister for Information Technology, Electronics & Communications, Industries and Commerce and Legislative Affairs, said.

The minister said the state has attracted major global companies in recent years, with operations spanning technology, innovation and R&D.

The new centre will bring together teams working across digital, data, analytics, AI, technology and engineering. These teams will contribute to enterprise technology solutions for MSD’s global operations and collaborate with teams across geographies.

Abhishek Narayan Singh, Senior Vice President, Digital Human Health, MSD, said the centre reflects the company’s focus on building technology capabilities that can operate at global scale.

“The inauguration of our Hyderabad Technology Centre reflects MSD’s long-term commitment to building world-class digital capabilities that drive business value at scale,” Singh said.

“Hyderabad’s vibrant technology ecosystem, deep digital expertise and strong talent pool make it an ideal location for MSD, and we are grateful for the support and engagement of the Telangana government.”

The centre, he added, would bring together talent, technology and global collaboration to develop scalable solutions supporting MSD’s operations and broader healthcare mission.

Telangana currently has more than 2,000 life-sciences companies, spanning pharmaceuticals, APIs, bulk drugs, generics, CDMO, vaccines and research.

The state has also seen several global life-sciences companies expand their technology and R&D operations in recent years, including Amgen, Eli Lilly, Bristol Myers Squibb, Sanofi, Align Technology and Zoetis.

The minister also said Telangana expects to reach 100 GCCs, building on the more than 75 GCCs established in the state last year, with a target of creating 4 lakh direct and indirect high-value opportunities.

The government is also developing Bharat Future City, which includes a 2,100-acre life-sciences zone and a specialised 100-acre hub for advanced biologics.

Another initiative, the 1Bio model, is designed to provide plug-and-play access to advanced bio-foundry infrastructure, aimed at helping companies accelerate research, innovation and commercialisation.

Telangana is also seeking to strengthen the talent pipeline through institutions including CSIR-IICT, CCMB and NIPER, alongside initiatives such as the Telangana School of Life Sciences and industry-integrated PhD programmes.

The objective is to create talent capable of working across life sciences, technology and advanced R&D rather than keeping these sectors in separate silos.

For MSD, the Hyderabad centre adds another layer to its India operations, enabling local teams to contribute to enterprise technology solutions supporting the company’s global Human Health business.

The centre is expected to create opportunities for high-value technology work spanning digital transformation, data, analytics, AI and engineering.

“Our customers have always trusted us to stay close to them, whether they are in a city or a village. Voice AI has allowed us to extend that closeness at scale, reaching people proactively, in their own language,” said Raul Rebello, Managing Director and CEO, Mahindra Finance, in a statement.

“As we diversify into new lines of business, this partnership with Sarvam is central to how we scale customer-first financial services across Bharat,” he added.

Pratyush Kumar, Co-founder, Sarvam, said the deployment shows how voice AI can be integrated into financial services operations.

“Mahindra Finance has set a strong benchmark for what AI at scale can look like in financial services,” he said. “More than 1 crore calls across sales, collections and employee engagement show what becomes possible when AI is deeply embedded into the business and continuously learns from customer outcomes.”

title: Deloitte Launches Open Model Engineering Practice in India to Scale Agentic AI
content:
Open models add an important dimension to that strategy because they allow enterprises to shape AI around their own data, processes, and context

Deloitte has launched an Open Model Engineering practice in India and other key global markets to help enterprises build, deploy, and scale agentic AI applications using a combination of open and proprietary models.

The practice will initially operate across North America, Europe, and Asia-Pacific, including India, and will focus on enterprise AI applications built on open-source AI frameworks and open models. Deloitte said the initiative aims to give enterprises greater flexibility over model selection, costs, deployment environments, data, intellectual property, and model behaviour as AI adoption expands.

“Open models add an important dimension to that strategy because they allow enterprises to shape AI around their own data, processes and context rather than designing the enterprise around the limitations of a model. Our Open Model Engineering practice is designed to build that flexibility in from the start, without compromising governance or the distinctiveness of the business,” said Sathish Gopalaiah, President, Consulting, Deloitte South Asia, in a statement.

According to Deloitte, enterprises are increasingly weighing four factors when deploying AI: flexibility to select models and architectures for different workloads, predictable costs as aAgentic AI usage grows, sovereignty over where models are deployed, and greater control over enterprise data, IP, and model behaviour.

The consulting firm said tThe new practice will help clients evaluate proprietary and open models, aAgentic AI platforms, cloud services, and on-premises infrastructure based on individual workloads. It will also focus on managing token economics, fine-tuning open models for geographical, linguistic, and cultural contexts, and giving enterprises greater control over where models run and what data they share.

Deloitte’s initial Open Model Engineering work will focus on enterprise applications powered by NVIDIA Nemotron open models and NIM microservices. Deloitte firms will also help clients develop sovereign AI stacks using open-source frameworks, fine-tune open models, and strengthen cybersecurity using open-source security tools.

“Enterprises need both open and proprietary models for different workloads,” said Kari Briski, VP of Generative AI at NVIDIA. “Deloitte’s Open Model Engineering practice, built on NVIDIA Nemotron models, gives developers greater control over enterprise data and proprietary information while enabling secure, responsible deployment of agentic AI.”

The practice will also leverage Deloitte’s Zora AI digital workforce platform, with agentic harness capabilities built on NVIDIA Nemotron models and NIM. The platform intends to allow enterprises to deploy, optimise, and govern AI agents using open models within their own environments.

Deloitte plans to hire, train and certify forward-deployed engineers globally through fiscal year 2027. These engineers will work directly with clients to implement open-model solutions and are expected to form the operational backbone of the new practice.

title: DeepSeek Launches V4.1-Flash to Make Large-Scale AI Inference Cheaper
content:
DeepSeek says the new model improves coding and agentic workloads while giving users control over its reasoning effort.

Chinese AI startup DeepSeek has launched its latest V4.1-Flash model with 552 billion parameters and a context window of up to 1 million tokens, while activating only 8 billion parameters during input and 16 billion during output.

The company has made V4.1-Flash available through its API with native multimodal support.

DeepSeek has retired V4-Flash and V4-Flash-Vision-Exp, while the older model names deepseek-v4-flash and deepseek-v4-flash-vision-exp will temporarily route requests to V4.1-Flash.

DeepSeek said multi-party testing found V4.1-Flash ahead of V4-Pro in performance, cost, speed, and total completion time, prompting the company to phase out the older model.

The company’s latest launch targets more efficient large-scale AI inference, using a Causal Encoder-Decoder architecture, sparse attention, and FP4 KV caching to reduce memory requirements. It brings the global KV cache footprint down to 890 bytes per token. The model consists of 20 encoder and 20 decoder layers, with a smaller KV cache.

The model supports both image and text inputs and lets users adjust its reasoning effort from one to 100. It also performs well on coding and agentic benchmarks.

According to DeepSeek, the model’s reduced KV cache can bring its memory requirements down significantly, with the company saying it uses one-quarter of the HBM and one-eighth of the SSD storage required by the previous generation.

An advanced MoE design with layers consisting of one shared expert and 384 routed experts, including six routed experts activated per token. The model has multimodal capabilities, and its DeepSeek-ViT vision encoder can convert images into visual embeddings, processing alongside text.

DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash is trained from scratch on a multimodal corpus containing 45 trillion tokens. Its sparse attention is trained at a 64K sequence length, with the context window extended to 1 million tokens after training on 34 trillion tokens.

The launch comes after the US government accused DeepSeek and five other Chinese AI companies of using AI model distillation to extract capabilities from US frontier models.

DeepSeek is also moving toward a potential IPO in China. Reuters reported that the company has hired CITIC Securities to prepare for a listing on Shanghai’s STAR Market, with the process expected to begin this year. The timing, size, and valuation of the offering have not been finalised.

title: Chennai’s Inbound Aerospace Joins Australia’s Space Angel Group for Flight Testing
content:
The partnership will assess testing, recovery, and spaceport infrastructure for Inbound Aerospace’s reusable spacecraft systems.

Chennai-based Inbound Aerospace has signed a five-year memorandum of understanding (MoU) with Australia-based Space Angel Group to explore collaboration on spacecraft testing and recovery.

The agreement covers flight testing, drop testing, high-altitude and near-space testing, recovery operations, spaceport infrastructure, and mission planning.

The companies signed the agreement during the recent Bengaluru Space Expo, organised by the Confederation of Indian Industry (CII) with ISRO, IN-SPACe, and NewSpace India. Under the MoU, they will assess how Space Angel’s spaceport, test-range, runway, and recovery infrastructure can support testing and demonstrations of Inbound Aerospace’s spacecraft, re-entry vehicle, and lifting-body systems.

The partnership also covers joint technology development, demonstrations, and pilot missions. The companies plan to explore market expansion across India and Australia. They also intend to pursue bilateral research and innovation funding, including government grants and university collaborations.

For Inbound Aerospace, the agreement supports its work on the return segment of orbital logistics. The IIT Madras-incubated company is developing an autonomous, unmanned and recoverable spacecraft for low-Earth-orbit (LEO) missions. Planned applications include microgravity research, in-orbit technology demonstrations, in-space manufacturing, and payload return.

The company aims to return hardware, samples, and manufactured products from LEO. Inbound Aerospace describes its spacecraft platform as a reusable system designed for orbital missions.

title: Blue Machines AI Launches Aurora Speech Model for Indian BFSI
content:
The model is designed to handle code-mixed speech, financial terminology, telephony noise, and low-bandwidth calls with low latency.

Bengaluru-based voice AI orchestration startup Blue Machines AI has launched Aurora, a speech-to-text model built for banking, financial services and insurance (BFSI) conversations in India. The company says Aurora recorded a 1.51% Semantic Word Error Rate (WER) on English BFSI conversations, 2.43% on Hindi BFSI speech, and 5.52% across multilingual speech in its internal benchmarks.

Aurora also recorded a BFSI Entity Error Rate of 4.23% for financial information such as monetary amounts, interest rates, policy numbers, account references, and transaction IDs. The company says the model recorded a P50 latency of 236 milliseconds.

P50 latency measures the median response time, indicating how quickly 50% of requests finish faster than the other 50%.

The model handles real-time conversations where customers switch between Indian languages and English financial terms.

Its training and evaluation datasets cover banking, lending, insurance, collections, and customer servicing, including Indian English, Hindi, Hinglish, multilingual, and code-mixed speech.

Blue Machines AI said Aurora was evaluated against leading speech-to-text models using the same audio inputs and scoring methodology. It claimed the model delivers higher accuracy at lower latency in its internal evaluation and is designed for streaming financial conversations.

“Aurora reflects our commitment to building sovereign AI infrastructure for Indian enterprises,” said Nirmit Parikh, Founder and CEO of Blue Machines AI. “India’s financial conversations do not happen in a single language or follow a standard script. When AI misunderstands an EMI amount, policy number, or repayment commitment, it can change the customer outcome.”

Aurora is trained to recognise BFSI terms including EMIs, outstanding amounts, foreclosure charges, disbursals, KYC, premiums, SIPs, NAVs, policy numbers, transaction IDs, and payment dates. It is also designed to handle numbers, currencies, percentages, and financial identifiers used in financial workflows.

“Aurora’s cache-aware FastConformer encoder and streaming transducer decoder enable it to retain context while processing speech incrementally,” said Abhishek Ranjan, Chief Technology Officer at Blue Machines AI.

Ranjan said the model is also optimised for multilingual and code-mixed speech, low-latency inference, and high-concurrency environments. In internal throughput tests, Aurora supported 960 concurrent real-time streams per H100 at a 320-millisecond operating point and 2,400 concurrent streams per H100 at a 1.12-second operating point.

Blue Machines AI has built training pipelines that allow Aurora to be adapted using customer-authorised enterprise data. The company claimed customer-specific retraining can reduce recognition errors by 40–45% relative to the base model on institution-specific datasets. The adaptation can account for proprietary product names, terminology, geographies, accents, and interaction patterns.

Aurora integrates with Blue Machines AI’s enterprise CX AI platform and can be used across customer acquisition, onboarding, lending, collections, servicing, insurance, claims, and customer support.

The model can be deployed through a managed cloud, an enterprise VPC, or on-premises infrastructure, allowing financial institutions to choose deployment options based on their security, data residency, and governance requirements.

Blue Machines AI recently partnered with Muthoot Finance to deploy conversational AI for gold-loan lead engagement and qualification. The deployment has reached 1.39 million leads, with 63.1% customer connectivity and a 150% increase in branch-visit conversion. It has also cut the average journey completion time by more than 70%, from over seven minutes to around two minutes.

title: ASML Advances High NA EUV with Samsung, Intel, TSMC
content:
Samsung plans High NA EUV for DRAM, while Intel expands production use as both companies work with ASML on future chipmaking.

TSMC, Samsung Electronics, and Intel Foundry are advancing High Numerical Aperture (High NA) EUV lithography for semiconductor manufacturing, with each company at a different stage of adoption.

The companies announced the developments in partnership with ASML at industry events focused on EUV technology and photomasks.

TSMC plans to use ASML’s High NA technology in high-volume manufacturing for advanced nodes from 2030. Samsung plans to introduce the technology into future DRAM high-volume manufacturing by 2028. Intel already uses High NA for selected layers in high-volume production.

ASML and TSMC have formed an industry initiative to shift from the current 6-inch photomask format to 12-inch masks. The initiative targets a 12-inch mask pilot line by 2031. It aims to support full lithography system readiness for advanced-node production by 2033.

The companies expect larger masks to increase fab productivity and lower chipmaking costs. They also expect the transition to remove stitching constraints. This would allow chipmakers to use more of High NA EUV’s capabilities.

TSMC Chairman and CEO CC Wei said collaboration across the semiconductor supply chain would help address manufacturing challenges. “We have always believed that when the industry works together to solve complex problems, we unlock possibilities that no single company could achieve alone,” he said in a statement.

Samsung will also join the industry initiative for 12-inch photomask technology. The company will work with industry partners on mask technologies and supporting infrastructure.

ASML CEO Christophe Fouquet said High NA adoption will progress from existing 6-inch masks towards larger formats.

TSMC expects demand for High NA EUV to increase as semiconductor nodes advance. It said more layers will require the technology because AI applications use increasingly complex transistor architectures.

Samsung plans to introduce ASML’s High NA EUV technology into future DRAM high-volume manufacturing by 2028. The company expects improved resolution to support process simplification and greater efficiency.

Samsung CEO Jun Young-Hyun said the company wants to strengthen its position in advanced memory and foundry manufacturing. “By further strengthening our collaboration with ASML, we are helping lay the foundation for the next generation of AI and semiconductor innovation,” he said.

Intel has already processed more than 1 million wafers using High NA across certification, research, development, and volume production. The technology is being used on selected layers of Intel Core Ultra Series 3 processors.

Intel said its 18A products using High NA on selected layers meet or exceed comparable layers made with its NXE EUV platform. The company also supports High NA use with current 6-inch masks through floor planning and stitching solutions.

Naga Chandrasekaran, Executive VP and Co-general Manager of Intel Foundry, said the company is focused on enabling High NA with existing masks while preparing for the larger format. “Intel Foundry is focused on near-term enablement of High NA on 6-inch masks with or without stitching,” he said.

The three chipmakers therefore represent different stages in the industry’s High NA transition. Intel has moved into production, Samsung has set a 2028 DRAM target, and TSMC has set a 2030 advanced-node target. In addition, the companies are also working towards a common 12-inch mask ecosystem.

title: Anthropic Discloses Fourth Hacking Incident It Initially Missed
content:
An early version of Claude Opus 4.6 accessed a third-party system during a January cybersecurity test, gaining administrator access, harvesting credentials, and reading one person’s information.

More than a month after Anthropic had revealed that its Claude AI models had breached the real-world infrastructure of three external organisations, it has now disclosed a fourth incident wherein a Claude model gained unauthorised access to real-world systems during a cybersecurity evaluation. The AI firm had initially missed the case in its first review.

The company detailed this incident in a new alignment assessment, saying an early checkpoint of Claude Opus 4.6 accessed a third-party machine in January and obtained administrator access using a password it found on the system. It then harvested additional credentials, altered system settings, and read one person’s personal information.

Anthropic said its original review covered about 141,000 transcripts and used an agentic search that failed to identify the January incident. The company found it in August while preparing material for an independent review by the Model Evaluation and Threat Research (METR) group. It subsequently expanded the search to roughly 481 million transcripts, with a first-stage scan flagging 9.2 million for further review.

That wider investigation re-identified the four known incidents and found no additional cases of similar or greater severity.

In the newly disclosed Opus 4.6 case, the model had accidentally made its assigned CTF (Capture the Flag) target unreachable by giving it a conflicting IP address. During cybersecurity exercises, a CTF target is a vulnerable system, app, or server that players or AI systems need to break into to identify vulnerabilities.

Opus 4.6 tried to abort the task but was blocked by another configuration error and attempted to give up seven more times. It then explored the environment, reached a third-party machine, and treated it as part of the exercise.

Anthropic said the model never described the environment as simulated, but 87% of its thinking blocks referred to the systems it attacked as exercise-related infrastructure.

“The model never questioned whether this direction was authorised,” Anthropic said. Only 1% of its thinking blocks considered that it might be attacking an unrelated third party.

The company said all four incidents resulted from the same underlying infrastructure problem: Claude was told it had no internet access and was operating in a simulation, but the evaluation environment was inadvertently connected to the open internet.

The models were also running without the cyber safeguards used in production.

Anthropic’s assessment has identified two recurring behaviours—“biased reasoning”, where models selectively interpreted evidence to justify continuing a task, and “recklessness”, where they continued pursuing a goal despite potential harm.

Anthropic disclosed the three earlier incidents in July, after reviewing 141,006 cybersecurity evaluation runs.

In one case, Claude Opus 4.7 mistook a real company for the fictional CTF target and accessed a database containing hundreds of rows of production data.

In another, Claude Mythos 5 uploaded a malicious Python package to PyPI that 15 real systems downloaded, exposing credentials from a security company. An internal research model separately scanned roughly 9,000 internet targets before compromising a real company’s internet-facing application, but eventually recognised the system was real and stopped.

“Much work remains,” Anthropic admitted in the blog, noting that its pre-release testing had not detected misalignment of this severity. The company has since added evaluations targeting these behaviours, strengthened monitoring, and hardened third-party evaluation environments.

Anthropic also said it had agreed to give METR “wide-ranging access” for an independent investigation, with an initial eight-week agreement.

“These incidents have changed our view of how severe the consequences of these known alignment failure modes can be,” the company said.

These disclosures form part of a series of AI agent security incidents this year, including OpenAI’s July incident wherein its models escaped a controlled evaluation environment, gained access to the internet, and compromised Hugging Face systems.

OpenAI subsequently paused reinforcement learning training on its latest models for two weeks while it hardened and red-teamed its research environments.

The new centre will bring together teams working across digital, data, analytics, AI, technology and engineering.

MSD has inaugurated a 2.5 lakh square feet technology centre in Hyderabad, expanding its digital, data, analytics, AI, technology and engineering capabilities in the city as Telangana seeks to position itself as a global hub for life sciences and advanced technology.

Located in HITEC City, the new centre will support MSD’s global Human Health business and form part of the company’s worldwide technology network.

The centre comes as Telangana attempts to move its life-sciences ecosystem beyond its traditional strength in manufacturing and towards advanced R&D, discovery, technology and global capability creation.

“Telangana has built a truly end-to-end life sciences ecosystem, with more than 2,000 companies spanning APIs, bulk drugs, generics, CDMO, vaccines, research and discovery,” Sridhar Babu, Telangana’s Minister for Information Technology, Electronics & Communications, Industries and Commerce and Legislative Affairs, said.

The minister said the state has attracted major global companies in recent years, with operations spanning technology, innovation and R&D.

The new centre will bring together teams working across digital, data, analytics, AI, technology and engineering. These teams will contribute to enterprise technology solutions for MSD’s global operations and collaborate with teams across geographies.

Abhishek Narayan Singh, Senior Vice President, Digital Human Health, MSD, said the centre reflects the company’s focus on building technology capabilities that can operate at global scale.

“The inauguration of our Hyderabad Technology Centre reflects MSD’s long-term commitment to building world-class digital capabilities that drive business value at scale,” Singh said.

“Hyderabad’s vibrant technology ecosystem, deep digital expertise and strong talent pool make it an ideal location for MSD, and we are grateful for the support and engagement of the Telangana government.”

The centre, he added, would bring together talent, technology and global collaboration to develop scalable solutions supporting MSD’s operations and broader healthcare mission.

Telangana currently has more than 2,000 life-sciences companies, spanning pharmaceuticals, APIs, bulk drugs, generics, CDMO, vaccines and research.

The state has also seen several global life-sciences companies expand their technology and R&D operations in recent years, including Amgen, Eli Lilly, Bristol Myers Squibb, Sanofi, Align Technology and Zoetis.

The minister also said Telangana expects to reach 100 GCCs, building on the more than 75 GCCs established in the state last year, with a target of creating 4 lakh direct and indirect high-value opportunities.

The government is also developing Bharat Future City, which includes a 2,100-acre life-sciences zone and a specialised 100-acre hub for advanced biologics.

Another initiative, the 1Bio model, is designed to provide plug-and-play access to advanced bio-foundry infrastructure, aimed at helping companies accelerate research, innovation and commercialisation.

Telangana is also seeking to strengthen the talent pipeline through institutions including CSIR-IICT, CCMB and NIPER, alongside initiatives such as the Telangana School of Life Sciences and industry-integrated PhD programmes.

The objective is to create talent capable of working across life sciences, technology and advanced R&D rather than keeping these sectors in separate silos.

For MSD, the Hyderabad centre adds another layer to its India operations, enabling local teams to contribute to enterprise technology solutions supporting the company’s global Human Health business.

The centre is expected to create opportunities for high-value technology work spanning digital transformation, data, analytics, AI and engineering.

title: Shopify Acquires Tailwind
content:
Tailwind Labs said its open-source projects will remain MIT-licensed, with the existing team continuing to lead and maintain them with Shopify’s support.

Tailwind Labs, the company behind the Tailwind CSS web-development framework, is joining Shopify, with the team moving under the e-commerce company to maintain and develop the open-source project.

Tailwind CSS is installed more than 110 million times per week and is used by companies including OpenAI, X, Cloudflare, Reddit and Shopify.

Adam Wathan, Tailwind’s creator, said the move is meant to give the framework a long-term home as it continues to be used by millions of developers. “We're joining Shopify to give Tailwind a stable long-term home where it will be actively maintained for the millions of people who depend on it.”

Wathan said Tailwind Labs had built a business around website templates and other commercial products, but he ultimately wanted Tailwind CSS to be developed alongside a large, real-world product. Shopify, he said, offers that environment through its storefronts, administration tools, checkout and Shop app.

“Shopify provides an incredible surface area for us to do this work,” Wathan said. He also pointed to Shopify’s work on agentic commerce as an area where interface design is likely to evolve.

Shopify was among the early large-scale adopters of Tailwind CSS and has used the framework in its own products as well as encouraged merchants to build with it. Wathan described Tailwind as a “very important part of the stack at Shopify” and said the company is committed to its continued maintenance.

Financial terms of the deal were not disclosed.

The acquisition will not change Tailwind CSS’s open-source licensing or development model. Tailwind Labs said its open-source projects will remain MIT-licensed, with the existing team continuing to lead and maintain them with Shopify’s support.

Tailwind's commercial business will change. Tailwind Labs is closing sign-ups for new customers for products including Tailwind Plus and ui.sh, although existing customers will retain access. The company said it will now focus on Tailwind CSS rather than growing the commercial business around the framework.

The Shopify deal comes after a difficult period for Tailwind Labs earlier this year.

In January, the company laid off three of its four engineers after revenue fell by roughly 80% and documentation traffic declined 40% from early 2023, with Wathan attributing the pressure to the way AI tools had changed developer behaviour.

The layoffs prompted companies including Google AI Studio, Vercel, Supabase and Lovable to sponsor Tailwind CSS. Shopify was already among the companies supporting the project, describing Tailwind as “core infrastructure for how the modern web gets built.”

The joint R&D lab will focus on frontier research, model post-training, real-world outcome feedback, and regulator-grade AI safety for financial services.

IDFC FIRST Bank and AI company Sarvam AI have partnered to establish a joint R&D Lab to build banking systems that can learn from outcomes and improve over time.

The lab will work across frontier AI research, post-training, AI safety and security, with a focus on applying these technologies within a regulated banking environment.

Sarvam AI said the goal is to enable the bank to adopt new AI models and capabilities while retaining what its systems learn about customers, processes, policies and decisions.

“AI capabilities are advancing quickly, but making those capabilities useful in banking requires more than access to better models,” Sarvam AI said in a blog post.

The lab will combine IDFC FIRST Bank’s banking expertise with Sarvam’s AI research and engineering capabilities. It will test new models and techniques against banking use cases and use outcomes from those systems to improve subsequent versions.

The companies said that banking operations generate signals through customer interactions, decisions, human corrections, exceptions and eventual outcomes. The R&D lab will explore ways to use these signals as inputs for continuous model improvement.

The partnership will also focus on building infrastructure that can evaluate and adapt AI models using banking tasks, human feedback and real-world outcomes.

Sarvam AI described this as a “post-training factory” that can turn production experience into a source of learning, allowing AI systems to become more specific to the bank over time.

The lab will also work on AI safety and security, including evaluation, governance and controls. The systems will need to remain observable, auditable and controllable as their capabilities increase.

The research programme will explore new AI and large language model capabilities relevant to banking and financial services.

Alongside model development, the lab will study reliability, security, explainability and control, with these considerations built into the development process.

Sarvam AI said the approach would allow IDFC FIRST Bank to continue adopting new AI capabilities without rebuilding its systems every time the underlying technology changes.

title: Meta Launches Muse AI Agent With Internet Access Guardrails
content:
Meta says Muse uses a dedicated virtual machine and a separate Sentinel system to control internet access, credentials, and sensitive actions.

Meta has introduced Muse, a personal AI agent that can perform tasks on users’ behalf, including sending emails, booking travel, filling out forms, and making purchases.

Muse is being rolled out in the US on iOS, Android, and muse.ai, with support for AI glasses planned. Meta said the service is free for most use cases, while subscription plans will be available for users who want additional capabilities.

Muse is designed to work after a user closes the app, and can develop plans around longer-term goals, coordinate resources, and take action when circumstances change. The agent can also return to the user when it needs approval for actions such as sending an email or completing a purchase.

“People just tell Muse what needs to get done, and it takes action,” Meta said in a statement.

Muse runs on Muse Secure VM, a dedicated virtual machine that contains the agent and a user’s data. It has its own browser and can interact with services that a user connects to it.

Meta said a separate Sentinel agent operates on the same machine and controls Muse’s access to the internet. “Nothing Muse does reaches the internet unless the Sentinel approves it,” the company said.

The system keeps credentials hidden from Muse. Passwords and payment information are stored in secure storage, allowing the agent to use them without accessing the underlying credentials.

Muse also requires user approval for sensitive actions and provides an audit trail showing what it has done and what it plans to do. Users can decide which services Muse can access and set permissions, including whether it can only read email or also send messages on their behalf.

The agent can retain information from conversations and use it in future tasks. Meta said users can ask Muse to forget specific information and can opt out of having their interactions used to train Meta’s AI models.

For purchases, Muse can use Link, Stripe’s payment service, through a wallet for AI agents that generates a one-time-use card. Meta said Muse is the first AI agent covered by Link’s purchase protections. Support for Shop Pay and 1Password is planned.

Meta also said it plans to introduce Muse Confidential VM later this year. Under the system, the entire virtual machine, including user data and conversations, will be encrypted with a key held only by the user.

Muse is powered by Muse Spark, which Meta described as its most capable model to date and designed for agentic tasks.

title: Grok Bot Was Built in Just Four Weeks
content:
A handful of employees worked in a separate part of the office and used private Slack channels, letting them make rapid product decisions without the coordination required for a larger project.

SpaceXAI built Grok Bot from its first line of code to a working internal prototype in about a month, with a small team deliberately isolated from the rest of the company.

Roman Ugarte, an AI engineer at SpaceXAI who helped incubate the product, revealed this in a conversation with Lenny Rachitsky, creator of Lenny’s Podcast.

Ugarte said the team was created as a “blank page” exercise to build an AI product for general knowledge work.

A handful of employees worked in a separate part of the office and used private Slack channels, letting them make rapid product decisions without the coordination required for a larger project.

The team then spent roughly two weeks manually onboarding 200 to 300 early users.

Ugarte said core team members sat through individual sessions, watching users encounter problems such as computers failing to start or people becoming confused during onboarding.

The process also exposed unexpected usage patterns. Employees began creating multiple specialised bots, with some using a higher-level “chief of staff” bot to delegate work to other bots.

The biggest improvements before launch were largely invisible to users.

Rather than adding more features, the team focused on making the underlying computer-use infrastructure reliable.

Sales staff, for example, were using systems that lacked reliable APIs or MCP integrations. Giving bots their own computers allowed them to interact with those systems through browsers, clicking buttons and entering information like a human user.

Ugarte said the team repeatedly fixed small infrastructure problems, such as giving agents better browser visibility or more precise mouse control. These changes could unlock entire workflows without requiring a new model capability.

The product was also designed around two early architectural decisions: bots would run in the cloud, and each would have its own computer. Ugarte argued that AI agents should not share a user's machine, just as human colleagues normally have their own computers.

That architecture has enabled bots to work with other bots. Ugarte said he uses a QA bot that can run Grok Bots inside its own computer to test software releases and record results. The team's longer-term vision is for users to have teams of persistent AI bots that can delegate work among themselves.

“The ultimate vision of Grok Bot is incredibly simple,” Ugarte said. “You should have a team of AI bots that help you with your job and help you with your life.”

SpaceXAI launched Grok Bot last month as a beta AI agent designed to function as an always-on digital teammate.

The bots have their own cloud-based computers, allowing them to log into the tools, websites and apps people already use and complete multi-step tasks without requiring dedicated APIs or pre-built workflows. Users can assign work from desktop or mobile, and the bot returns when the task is complete or needs approval.

At launch, Grok Bot was available in beta to selected SuperGrok and Cursor subscribers on desktop and iOS, while enterprise access was placed behind a waitlist.

This deal marks a major push into AI inference chips and data-centre infrastructure.

Amazon and Qualcomm have entered a long-term partnership to develop custom AI chips for data centres, in a deal that could see Amazon purchase up to $60 billion worth of Qualcomm chips and related products.

The deal gives Qualcomm a major foothold in the data-centre market as it looks to reduce its dependence on smartphones and challenge Nvidia in AI computing. For Amazon, it adds another chip supplier as cloud companies increasingly look for alternatives to Nvidia's dominant AI processors.

The companies will focus on AI inference chips, which process requests and generate responses from already-trained AI models. They will also work on optical connectivity technology capable of supporting speeds of up to 1.6 terabits per second, aimed at handling the growing data-transfer requirements of AI data centres.

The partnership comes as Qualcomm makes a major push into data-centre infrastructure. The chipmaker has set a target of generating $15 billion in data-centre chip revenue by 2029.

Qualcomm is looking to diversify as its traditional smartphone business faces pressure from weaker handset demand, rising component costs and Apple's move away from its modem technology.

“As AI demand accelerates, data center infrastructure will require advances in both computing and connectivity to deliver greater performance with more efficiency,” Qualcomm CEO Cristiano Amon said.

Amazon is already one of Nvidia's largest customers and has developed its own AI chips through AWS. Its custom silicon business, including Trainium and Inferentia, has become an increasingly important part of its cloud strategy. AWS had an annualised revenue run rate of more than $25 billion at the end of June.

The Qualcomm partnership gives Amazon another option as AI infrastructure costs rise and demand for compute continues to surge. Microsoft and Meta are also working with Qualcomm on AI chips, giving the semiconductor company access to some of the world's biggest cloud and AI customers.

The focus on inference is particularly significant. As AI models move from training into widespread use, the amount of computing required to generate responses is growing rapidly. This is creating a new opportunity for chipmakers that can deliver inference at lower costs and with better energy efficiency.

Qualcomm will also increase its use of Amazon Web Services for chip-design workloads, with the aim of shortening development cycles.

The deal does not immediately challenge Nvidia's dominance. But it highlights a growing shift in the AI chip market: the next battle may increasingly be over making AI inference cheaper and more efficient, rather than simply building larger models and faster processors.

title: Google DeepMind’s New Tool Maps All 9 Bn DNA Mutations in Humans
content:
AlphaGenome Atlas helps scientists prioritise variants, investigate their molecular effects, and uncover genetic links to rare diseases and common traits.

Google DeepMind has launched AlphaGenome Atlas, a platform that predicts the molecular effects of 9 billion possible single-letter changes in the human genome, giving researchers a way to rank and investigate genetic variants without testing each mutation individually in the laboratory.

The platform is available for academic research through a free website portal and includes precomputed predictions generated using DeepMind’s AlphaGenome AI model. The company said the resource is designed to provide researchers with a genome-wide view of how DNA variants may affect biological processes.

“DNA is the language of life,” Google DeepMind stated in a blog, asserting that interpreting how genetic variations affect biology at a molecular level remains a major challenge.

The dataset is about 1 petabyte in size, which DeepMind said is more than 30 times larger than the AlphaFold Database. AlphaGenome Atlas provides thousands of molecular effect predictions for each variant across multiple aspects of gene regulation, covering hundreds of human and mouse cell types and tissues.

The platform also introduces the AlphaGenome Variant Impact (AVI) score, which combines predictions from AlphaGenome with AlphaMissense, DeepMind’s model for predicting the effects of protein-altering DNA variants. The score assigns a single measure to each variant, allowing researchers to rank variants by potential impact.

Researchers can also access AVI feature attributions that show which biological processes contribute to a variant’s predicted impact, including RNA splicing and gene expression. The platform includes a collection of more than 2,500 recurring DNA sequence motifs and their locations.

DeepMind said the AVI score is designed to work across both coding and non-coding regions of the genome. Coding regions account for about 2% of the genome, while the remaining 98% is non-coding and contains regulatory elements that control gene activity.

The company said external collaborators have already used AlphaGenome Atlas to identify and experimentally validate variants relevant to rare diseases and to find rare variants associated with common traits.

AlphaGenome Atlas has also been used to study non-coding variants in population-scale genetic data.

The platform is available through its website, the AlphaGenome API, and as a skill in Google Antigravity. DeepMind said Atlas is currently available for non-commercial use, while commercial access through Google Cloud is planned.

The company described AlphaGenome Atlas as a baseline rather than an endpoint, saying that improvements to AlphaGenome could make the genome-wide predictions more comprehensive and precise over time.

“Together, these tools will enable researchers and industry partners to accelerate the pace of biological discovery,” Google DeepMind said.

title: BharatPe Brings Agentic AI to Merchants With New AI Suite
content:
BharatPe’s new tools use voice, multilingual support, and personalised video to handle merchant requests and help users understand their credit profiles.

BharatPe has launched BharatPe Agentic AI, an AI assistant for merchants that can connect with more than 60 live systems. It also introduced Credit Coach, an AI-powered tool to improve credit awareness, at the Global Fintech Fest 2026.

BharatPe Agentic AI is built with the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform on Google Cloud and integrated into the BharatPe for Business app. The company said the assistant can understand merchant requirements, answer queries, and take actions across its systems in real time.

The assistant combines voice and chat, allowing merchants to interact in Hindi, English, Hinglish, and regional languages. It can handle tasks including complaints and chargebacks, as well as recommend products such as CC on UPI, loans, and POS.

The AI assistant uses information including screen activity, interaction history and previous support tickets to provide context for interactions. Merchants can also select its persona, avatar, and voice. The system can be interrupted during conversations. It can follow up on requests and provide updates.

BharatPe said that with the assistant, it aims to move beyond conventional chatbots.

“With BharatPe Agentic AI, we are moving beyond answering questions to helping merchants get things done,” Nalin Negi, CEO of BharatPe, said. “With Credit Coach, we are making credit awareness more personalised and actionable.”

Credit Coach is available through the Credit Score section of the BharatPe for Business app. Subject to user consent, it generates personalised videos featuring a digital avatar of cricket player and World Cup-winning captain Rohit Sharma.

The videos provide users with information about their bureau score, total and active loans and, where applicable, upcoming overdue payments and written-off tradelines. The tool also provides guidance on timely repayments and responsible credit utilisation.

Credit Coach is available for users across different credit profiles, including those with strong scores, overdue or written-off loans, no active credit history, and users new to credit. The videos are available in Hindi, Tamil, Telugu, Malayalam, and Kannada.

BharatPe has also used AI for merchant advertising through My Shop My Ad (MSMA), which allows merchants to create personalised advertisements featuring Rohit Sharma’s AI avatar promoting their businesses.

Google said the partnership would use voice-first and multilingual AI to help small businesses with their day-to-day operations.

“With multimodal, voice-first intelligence in the BharatPe Agentic AI experience, we look forward to seeing Indian merchants across the country benefit from a trusted, multilingual daily partner that reduces everyday operational hurdles and accelerates financial inclusion nationwide,” Harsh Dhand, Director of AI Partnerships, APAC, Google, said.

AI ambition is no longer scarce. AI readiness is. And as enterprises move from experiments to production, that gap could become the biggest differentiator in the AI race.

The enterprise AI race has entered an awkward phase.

Companies are no longer debating whether they should use AI. Boards are asking how quickly it can be deployed, how many processes can be automated and how much money it can save. Employees are experimenting with copilots, agents and vibe coding, while technology teams are under pressure to turn these experiments into production systems.

Yet, according to data and AI leaders across industries, enterprises may be making the same mistake at scale: they are trying to accelerate AI before fixing the foundations that make AI useful.

The gap is no longer between companies that have AI and those that do not. It is between companies that have demonstrated what AI can do and those that are actually ready to run it reliably across the business.

Dr. Santosh Karthikeyan Viswanathan, Data and AI Leader, says the problem starts at the top.

“Leaders are under pressure in boardroom discussions to scale AI and it’s on their scorecard. But without building AI literacy for leaders first, enterprises struggle to channel budget to the right projects with measurable ROI and real business value.”

That creates a familiar enterprise paradox. The board wants an AI strategy, the CIO wants an AI roadmap and business teams want AI-powered products. But if leadership does not understand where AI can realistically create value, investment can quickly become a collection of disconnected pilots.

The result is an organisation that looks busy with AI without necessarily becoming better at using it.

The next problem sits deeper in the stack: data.

For industrial enterprises in particular, simply having large amounts of data does not mean an organisation is AI-ready. Guru Ananthanarayanan, Managing Director, India at Cognite, argues that the real challenge is connecting information that was never designed to work together.

“From an Industrial AI perspective, AI isn't the hard part. The real challenge is bringing together data from IT systems, operational technology (OT) like machines and control systems, and engineering information (ET). On their own, these data sources don't naturally connect.”

This is particularly important in industries where AI has to understand the physical world.

A factory may have sensor data from a machine, maintenance records sitting in another system and engineering drawings stored somewhere else. An AI model may technically be capable of analysing all three, but unless the enterprise can establish the relationship between them, the output may have little meaning to the person operating the machine.

“The missing piece is context, understanding how a piece of equipment, its sensor data, maintenance history, and engineering design all relate to each other,” Ananthanarayanan says.

That context is what turns AI from a generic prediction engine into something an engineer or operator can actually trust.

And trust, according to Karthikeyan Ilangovan, VP of Data Analytics and AI/ML at MODE Global, is precisely where many companies are getting ahead of themselves.

“Before asking what AI can automate, organizations should ask whether the underlying process is ready to be automated.”

That question sounds obvious, but it cuts into one of the biggest assumptions surrounding enterprise AI: that putting an AI system on top of an existing process will automatically make that process better.

If the underlying workflow is fragmented, poorly documented or dependent on unreliable data, automating it can simply make bad processes run faster.

Ilangovan puts the broader problem bluntly: “AI Ambition creates momentum, but AI readiness determines whether that momentum becomes value.”

The danger is particularly high as enterprises rush to adopt the latest AI trend.

Vibe coding is one example. The ability to generate working software using natural language has dramatically lowered the barrier to building applications. But generating code quickly is not the same thing as building production-grade software.

Dr. Prashant Ramappa, Chief Principal Data Science, AI, Generative AI and ML Leadership at AT&T, sees this distinction becoming increasingly important.

“The biggest misstep I see is that enterprises are mistaking AI experimentation for AI readiness. Chasing trends like “vibe coding” or “AI fuel coding “ or measuring success by how quickly code is generated creates the illusion of progress, but it doesn’t solve the hard engineering problems that determine whether AI delivers business value.”

The real test begins after the demo.

A prototype can work beautifully in a controlled environment. A production system has to work when thousands of users are accessing it, when data changes, when models make mistakes, when costs increase and when sensitive information is involved.

Ramappa says this is where the readiness gap becomes visible.

“The real readiness gap begins when moving from a successful proof of concept to production. That’s where infrastructure, inference optimization, token economics, agent context management, guardrails, data privacy, and governance become the deciding factors.”

This is also where the economics of enterprise AI become harder.

It is relatively easy to demonstrate that an LLM can summarise documents, generate code or answer questions. It is much harder to prove that the system can do so reliably at enterprise scale while keeping inference costs, latency and security under control.

A company could deploy hundreds of AI agents and still fail to create meaningful business value if it cannot measure their impact.

That is why the next phase of enterprise AI is unlikely to be defined by who has the biggest model or the largest number of agents.

It will be defined by who can make those systems dependable.

“Organisations also need strategies to minimize hallucinations through better context engineering while balancing latency, scale, and cost,” Ramappa says.

This changes the question enterprises should be asking.

Instead of asking how much AI they can deploy, they need to ask whether the organisation is capable of supporting what it wants to deploy.

That means educating leadership before asking them to approve billion-dollar AI strategies. It means cleaning up and connecting enterprise data before putting agents on top of it. It means redesigning processes before automating them. And it means treating governance, security, infrastructure and economics as part of the AI product rather than problems to solve after launch.

The four perspectives point to the same conclusion.

AI ambition is no longer scarce. AI readiness is.

And as enterprises move from experiments to production, that gap could become the biggest differentiator in the AI race.

Ramappa sums it up: “The AI readiness gap isn’t between ambition and technology, it’s between a demo that impresses executives and a production system that customers can trust.”

title: Bengaluru’s QNu Labs Raises ₹200 Cr in Series A1 Round
content:
The funding takes the quantum cybersecurity company’s total capital raised to ₹375 crore.

Bengaluru-based quantum startup QNu Labs has raised ₹200 crore in its Series A1 funding round. The National Quantum Mission and Speciale Invest led the round with participation from Sony Innovation Fund, Gaja Capital and Artha Ventures.

The company will use the funds to expand research and development, sales and market operations. It will also support QNu Labs’ contribution to India’s Quantum Secure and Sensing Networks project. The company plans to expand its technology into quantum sensing and AI.

Sunil Gupta, Co-Founder of QNu Labs, said India moved early in the quantum era and the National Quantum Mission helped lay the foundation for commercial deployment.

The latest round takes QNu Labs’ total capital raised to ₹375 crore. The funding comes as governments and enterprises prepare for quantum-safe infrastructure. India’s National Quantum Mission has set 2029 as its implementation timeline.

The company said quantum computing and AI could challenge existing encryption systems. Organisations are therefore evaluating cryptographic technologies designed to withstand future quantum and AI attacks.

Gupta added that the company had deployed its technology across government, critical infrastructure and BFSI. He also said around 80% of the round came from new global investors, describing this as a signal of growing global interest in quantum-safe security.

Sony Innovation Fund Director and Head of Sony Ventures India Yoko Fukata said the fund was investing across India’s deep tech sector. She said it would collaborate with QNu Labs as the company expands globally.

QNu Labs said the funds will help scale its quantum-safe cybersecurity solutions across India and global markets. The company also plans to increase deployments across critical sectors. A part of the funding will serve as QNu Labs’ contribution to an approved RDI-funded project. The project will build the technology backbone for India’s Quantum Secure and Sensing Networks.

Gaja Capital Co-Founder and Managing Partner Gopal Jain said quantum-safe security was becoming national infrastructure. He compared its importance to power and transport in the physical economy.

“What attracted us is that the science is done and the demand curve is turning,” Jain said, adding that the company’s focus had now shifted towards scaling.

Moreover, Ravindra Barlingay, CEO of IITM C-DOT Samgnya Technologies Foundation, said the National Hub for Quantum Communication led the investment round.
