Amazon is already one of Nvidia's largest customers and has developed its own AI chips through AWS. Its custom silicon business, including Trainium and Inferentia, has become an increasingly important part of its cloud strategy. AWS had an annualised revenue run rate of more than $25 billion at the end of June.

The Qualcomm partnership gives Amazon another option as AI infrastructure costs rise and demand for compute continues to surge. Microsoft and Meta are also working with Qualcomm on AI chips, giving the semiconductor company access to some of the world's biggest cloud and AI customers.

The focus on inference is particularly significant. As AI models move from training into widespread use, the amount of computing required to generate responses is growing rapidly. This is creating a new opportunity for chipmakers that can deliver inference at lower costs and with better energy efficiency.

Qualcomm will also increase its use of Amazon Web Services for chip-design workloads, with the aim of shortening development cycles.

The deal does not immediately challenge Nvidia's dominance. But it highlights a growing shift in the AI chip market: the next battle may increasingly be over making AI inference cheaper and more efficient, rather than simply building larger models and faster processors.

title: Accenture, Google Cloud Launch Gemini Enterprise Business Group
content:
Accenture and Google Cloud’s partnership will create a 1,000-person forward engineering workforce.

Accenture and Google Cloud have launched a new business group to help enterprises deploy and scale Gemini Enterprise, with plans to establish a 1,000-person forward-deployed engineer (FDE) workforce.

The Accenture Gemini Enterprise Business Group will bring together Accenture’s Gemini Enterprise-certified professionals, FDEs, Google Cloud engineering talent, and industry expertise.

The group will operate across the Gemini Enterprise portfolio and focus on implementation, industry-specific solutions, enterprise-scale deployments, and user adoption.

“The Accenture Gemini Enterprise Business Group will help clients achieve these outcomes faster, bringing together the talent, advanced AI and data capabilities, and industry expertise needed to reinvent with confidence and create value at scale,” Accenture Chair and CEO Julie Sweet said in a statement.

The group builds on Accenture’s nearly 50,000 Google Cloud-skilled professionals. It will expand Gemini Enterprise training and certification while creating the 1,000-person FDE workforce to support enterprise deployments.

“Deploying agentic AI is a top priority for enterprises today, and the Accenture Gemini Enterprise Business Group significantly expands the expertise and resources available to help our customers deliver real business value,” Google Cloud CEO Thomas Kurian added.

The group will focus on four areas: increasing Gemini Enterprise adoption through implementation frameworks and accelerators, developing industry-specific solutions, supporting the transition from AI experimentation to enterprise deployments, and driving adoption of AI capabilities among users.

The new group builds on the companies’ joint Generative and Agentic AI Centre of Excellence and the Gemini Enterprise Acceleration Programme.

title: Mistral Secures €3 Bn Funding Led by Samsung at Over €21 Bn Valuation
content:
The company said the funding will expand its frontier AI research, increase compute capacity to train models, scale infrastructure, and support its commercial growth and international expansion.

French AI company Mistral AI has raised €3 billion ($3.5 billion) in a Series D funding round at a post-money valuation of more than €21 billion ($24 billion), three years after its launch. The company said the round is the largest equity fundraising by a European technology company.

Samsung Electronics led the round, with Scaleup Europe Fund, managed by EQT Group, and existing investor PSG Equity joining as co-leads.

Mistral said the funding will expand its frontier AI research, increase compute capacity for training models, scale infrastructure, and support its commercial growth and international expansion.

The company currently operates across 20 countries and supports more than 125 global enterprises, including Airbus, ASML, and HSBC.

Mistral said its focus is on building AI systems that give enterprises and governments control over their data, models, compute and production environments.

“Organisations and governments are now asking a different one: how to harness the power of AI for their mission-critical needs without surrendering control over the infrastructure and intelligence loop,” the company said.

Mistral describes its approach as a full-stack AI platform built around open-weight models, infrastructure, compute capacity and products for deploying AI in production. It said this model is designed to prevent customers from being tied to a single vendor’s roadmap, pricing or availability.

The company also said its open approach lets organisations deploy AI while keeping sensitive data, workflows and institutional knowledge within their own environments.

According to Mistral, its sovereign AI approach focuses on four areas: keeping data within organisational boundaries, allowing models to be controlled and customised, providing private and predictable compute, and making production systems controllable and auditable.

The funding brings together investors from Europe, Asia and North America. Advent, funds and accounts managed by BlackRock, and the Grand Duchy of Luxembourg joined the round as new investors.

Existing investors including a16z, ASML, Belfius, BNP Paribas CIB, Bpifrance, Carmignac, DST Global, Eurazeo, General Catalyst, Headline, Hillspire, Index Ventures, Korelya Capital, Lightspeed, NVIDIA, Phoenix Court’s Solar fund and Salesforce Ventures also participated.

The round follows Mistral’s Series C, which was led by ASML. With Samsung Electronics leading its Series D, Mistral has now secured backing from technology and industrial companies across multiple markets as it expands its open-weight AI strategy.

Tristan Buckmaster says OpenAI began pursuing an internal proof of finite-time blow-up for forced Navier–Stokes after learning about his work with Anthropic researcher Levent Alpöge.

Mathematician Tristan Buckmaster alleges that OpenAI pursued a potential breakthrough on the Navier–Stokes problem shortly after learning about research he had been conducting with Anthropic researcher Levent Alpöge.

The dispute began on September 3, when Buckmaster said he heard that information about his and Alpöge’s work had reached OpenAI.

Buckmaster then contacted OpenAI to explain that he and Alpöge were already working on the problem and had planned to publish their results.

Three days later, on September 6, he spoke twice with OpenAI technical staff member Sébastien Bubeck and another company representative about the two groups’ work.

According to Buckmaster, Bubeck told him the internal model had produced the Navier–Stokes proof. When Alpöge asked what exactly the model had solved, Buckmaster said OpenAI described it as a result showing that the equations could develop a blow-up in three dimensions when an external force is applied under specific conditions.

That description concerned Buckmaster because it followed the same broad approach he and Alpöge had been pursuing. “When I heard ‘forced,’ it was a bright red flag,” he wrote.

Buckmaster said he was initially told that OpenAI’s model had been given the Navier–Stokes problem with “very little human input”.

But, he said, further discussion revealed that the effort involved “an entire team” and was “one of a number of things that was tried”.

According to Buckmaster, the team had first used the model on easier mathematical problems, “including Euler”, before turning to the Navier–Stokes problem.

He also said he was told that “an insane amount of compute” had been used.

The timing of that effort became a key point for Buckmaster.

He said he repeatedly asked when OpenAI had first prompted the model to work on the problem, but did not initially receive a direct answer. He said it was eventually established that the first prompt had been sent “in the past few days” — after information about his and Alpöge’s work had reached OpenAI.

That led Buckmaster to raise a separate question about the private Codex sessions he and Alpöge had used throughout their project. “I asked whether the model had been trained on, or had access to, our sessions in Codex, into which we had been putting all our drafts for the whole of this project,” he wrote.

Buckmaster said he was told that the model did not look up user data, but said he did not receive an answer to the separate question of whether material from those sessions could have been incorporated into training.

Buckmaster has stressed that this does not establish that OpenAI used his work. He said he has not seen the company’s alleged proof and does not know what the model did, how it produced its result, or whether his data was used. “I am not accusing anyone of anything,” he wrote.

The disagreement then extended to how the results would be published. Buckmaster said OpenAI proposed two options: he and Alpöge could publish their Euler result, followed by OpenAI publishing its Navier–Stokes result the next day; or Buckmaster could write a paper presenting the Navier–Stokes result himself, while acknowledging that an internal OpenAI model had produced it.

Buckmaster also alleged that Bubeck twice argued that Alpöge should not be an author because he works for Anthropic.

Buckmaster said he rejected the proposal. Bubeck has disputed Buckmaster’s broader account, saying on X that “false and inflammatory allegations” about him were circulating. He said he had handled the discussion according to academic norms and would give a fuller response.

Buckmaster is an NYU Courant Institute mathematician known for work on fluid dynamics and Navier–Stokes, and Alpöge is a mathematician and Anthropic researcher who collaborated with Buckmaster on the forced blow-up work.

The Navier–Stokes problem describes how fluids such as air and water move and is one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems.

A proof resolving whether smooth solutions can develop singularities would settle a fundamental question in mathematical physics and carries a $1 million prize from the Clay Mathematics Institute.

Discussion (3)

What's your take on this story?

More often than not the big technology companies plagiarize the works of researchers and academics. There have to be guardrails and legally structured layouts in case of researchers getting involved. The data that AI uses, if, getting uploaded by researchers, should be accredited properly and the researcher(s) should be paid royalties and also be given the freedom of uploading the same to other compan's models so that they get the best deal, and also the public at large should be benefitted by such works so that companies don't get unduly profited by works which are relevant to the humanity at large.

What implications might this dispute have for future collaborations between AI companies and researchers?

Instead of making students spend years learning increasingly fragmented technologies, he wants them to enter the real world earlier, understand businesses and work on actual problems.

Indian engineering students have spent years being told to learn more. Raj Vattikuti has a different message: forget everything you know.

The Founder and Executive Chairman of Calibo believes AI is changing the value of what students are taught, what companies hire for, and even how much a traditional degree matters.

His argument is uncomfortable for an education system built around exams, memorisation and credentials: knowing a technology tool may soon be worth far less than knowing how to solve a business problem.

Vattikuti has spent nearly 50 years watching technology go through multiple cycles. He started at Chrysler in 1977, later founded Covansys, which Computer Sciences Corporation acquired for $1.3 billion, then built Altimetrik and now leads Calibo. His pitch today is that AI is different from the technology waves that came before it because it can fundamentally simplify how businesses operate.

And that, he believes, should also change how India prepares its young workforce.

The idea is straightforward. Instead of producing graduates who know a collection of tools, India needs people who understand a business problem, figure out what needs to change and use AI to make it happen.

That is also why Vattikuti is particularly dismissive of the idea that simply knowing how to use ChatGPT makes someone AI-ready. He believes that distinction is becoming increasingly important as companies look beyond people who can merely use AI tools and start looking for people who can actually create outcomes with them.

A Quess Corp 2026 analysis cited during the interview found that 6,63,000 people had simply added AI skills onto a completely different job. India’s total AI talent pool, meanwhile, was projected to double from roughly 600 to 6,50,000 to 1.25 million by 2027.

For Vattikuti, the bigger problem is not whether India has enough people who can use AI. It is whether it has enough people who can innovate with it.

“I think over the years we have created close to 15 million IT talent in India, and there’s at least another 10 million or more people needed for this talent who are very focused on innovation,” he says.

That is a very different definition of AI talent.

It also explains why Vattikuti is challenging the traditional education pipeline. He argues that students should not spend years memorising information that AI can increasingly retrieve, process and apply.

His own experience illustrates the shift. He told parents that degrees still have value, but questioned how much of what students memorise actually survives into their working lives.

“It’s not a degree. We all have degrees. You know how much I really use this? The only thing—the basic engineering principles—I still use. That’s about it. All the memorisation is gone and all these things,” he says.

For Vattikuti, this is where AI could actually become a reset button.

“Throw them into the real world and they can do wonders.”

His own programme is built around that idea. Students go through a six-month curriculum focused on helping businesses innovate, with an emphasis on use cases, outcomes and engaging directly with businesses. The goal is not to create another generation of people who can operate another set of enterprise tools.

It is to create people who can figure out which tools should disappear altogether.

That is another of Vattikuti’s more controversial predictions. “Then AI can change the entire gamut of the business, including eliminating a lot of this technology.”

He argues that companies have spent the last 25 years accumulating layers of technology without necessarily producing equivalent innovation.

“In the last 25 years we put so many investments in technology and hardly created any reality. They call transformation; they never call innovation. Even today people say another transformation. Transformation is a very bad word for the business.”

AI, he believes, gives enterprises an opportunity to reverse that complexity.

His prediction is unusually specific: spreadsheets, analytical tools, emails and other workflow technologies could eventually disappear as AI becomes embedded into the way businesses operate.

“Eliminating all the workflow tools, spreadsheets, analytical tools, emails; all these things can be eliminated.” But Vattikuti’s argument is not that humans become irrelevant. In fact, it is almost the opposite.

He believes the more AI takes over execution, the more important human judgment becomes.

“The shift is that it’s not AI first. Its business judgment data as a product is first. Then AI becomes very powerful for the business.”

That is why he pushes back against the current obsession with making everything “AI-first”. Businesses, according to Vattikuti, should first know what they are trying to achieve, have trusted data and make the judgment about what needs to happen. AI then becomes the mechanism for executing and scaling that judgement.

The same philosophy runs through his argument about education.

India has already created a huge technology workforce. The next opportunity, he believes, is to turn that workforce into an innovation workforce.

He wants the programme to scale aggressively, aiming to generate “at least 1,00,000 people every year” over the next three to four years.

And he sees a much bigger prize than employability.

Vattikuti believes these students could build companies themselves.

For parents accustomed to measuring a child’s future through college rankings, degrees and job titles, that is perhaps the most radical part of his argument.

His advice is not to panic about AI. It is to stop preparing children for a world that may no longer exist. “There’s a great opportunity today for them to really go to the places in a big way because these are smart kids; they can do their own business; they can help other business to grow many things they can do so encourage them in a big way doing that.”

And he expects that shift to arrive quickly.

title: Swiss Startup Jaipur Robotics Raises €4.3 Million to Expand AI Automation Across Industrial Plants
content:
“We are living in an energy crisis. It would be insane to just let landfill sit somewhere occupying space and generating pollutants when you could extract value from it.”

Swiss startup Jaipur Robotics has raised €4.3 million to expand AI-driven automation into waste-to-energy and industrial plants, giving machines a greater role in monitoring waste, guiding cranes and optimising plant operations.

Considering industrial operators are increasingly turning to AI to improve efficiency and reduce the risks associated with complex physical processes, the funding will support the company’s expansion and further development of AI, not simply by assisting workers but by monitoring, predicting, and influencing physical operations inside industrial premises. With the use of computer vision and AI, Jaipur Robotics’ system can analyse waste, detect hazardous materials, optimise how waste is mixed for combustion and guide crane operations in real time.

Jaipur Robotics was founded in 2024 by Ermes Zamboni and Nikhil Prakash. The company develops computer-vision and AI systems to automate and optimise operations in waste-to-energy and other industrial plants, monitoring waste, detecting hazards and operating cranes.

“We are living in an energy crisis. It would be insane to just let landfill sit somewhere occupying space and generating pollutants when you could extract value from it,” said Zamboni, Co-Founder and CEO of Jaipur Robotics.

Jaipur Robotics’ technology prevents equipment damage and avoids losses by identifying potential hazardous materials before they enter the combustion process. This is due to the composition of incoming waste varying significantly in waste-to-energy plants, where waste is burned to generate electricity and heat. Its AI-powered computer vision system detects dangerous objects and takes action before they reach the furnace.

The company’s technology is already processing more than five million tonnes of waste annually and has been developed using a large dataset of labelled industrial images. Its system monitors movements and provides operators with real-time and predictive guidance, and claims to detect hazardous materials with high accuracy, significantly reducing unplanned plant shutdowns.

The new investment will allow the startup to expand into other industrial sectors such as cement and biomass. Companies are increasingly exploring AI not only for software and data analysis, but for monitoring and optimisation of physical operations. The company is looking to scale its technology across more facilities and make it widely deployable.

Agentic AI Engineers recorded the highest growth among emerging technology roles tracked by CIEL HR.

India’s technology job market is undergoing a sharp shift as enterprises expand AI adoption, with demand for agentic AI engineers rising 260% in 2026 compared with 2025, while routine technology tasks face growing automation, according to an analysis by CIEL HR.

Agentic AI engineers recorded the highest growth among emerging technology roles tracked by CIEL HR. Demand for GenAI solutions architects and AI product owners increased 120% each, while demand for LLM engineers and MLOps engineers rose 86.5% and 82.2%, respectively.

At the same time, AI is taking over a significant share of workloads in several routine technology functions. According to CIEL HR, AI can handle up to 70% of workloads involved in ticket resolution and report generation, while AI can potentially handle as much as 65% of test case creation.

This puts technology support, reporting and manual quality assurance among the functions facing the highest potential for task-level automation, although human involvement remains necessary for the remaining workload.

“AI is changing the value attached to different technology skills. We are seeing routine activities become increasingly automated, while demand is growing for people who can build, integrate and govern AI in real business environments. The opportunity for organisations is to look at this as a workforce transition, identifying where technology can take on repetitive work while building the skills needed for the next phase of growth,” said Aditya Narayan Mishra, MD & CEO, CIEL HR.

The shift in technology hiring is also pushing organisations to strengthen internal talent pipelines, with generative AI engineering, AI/ML, cloud engineering, cloud transformation, cybersecurity, data engineering and automation emerging as key capability areas.

CIEL HR estimates that skill gaps across AI, cloud and cybersecurity currently range between 38% and 61%, increasing pressure on companies to develop talent internally alongside external hiring.

IT services companies are responding with AI-focused training, role-based reskilling, cloud academies, hyperscaler certification programmes, enterprise AI initiatives and structured early-career programmes. Existing delivery, infrastructure, support and engineering employees are increasingly being moved into these programmes to build capabilities aligned with changing demand.

“The workforce transition is not going to happen through hiring alone. Organisations will need to look at how existing talent can move into emerging skill areas as the nature of technology work changes. Reskilling and redeployment can help bridge some of the gap between the skills organisations have today and those they will need tomorrow,” said Arjun Gupta, Founder & CEO, Courseplay.

The analysis draws on more than 450 million job postings, 30 million professional profiles and 10,000 mapped skills. It covers observed job-posting data from March 2024 to May 2026, with forward-looking projections based on current hiring patterns, technology adoption, company hiring signals and sector growth expectations.

title: GalaxEye Becomes First Indian Startup to Secure US Patent for Satellite Imaging Technology
content:
GalaxEye’s patented technology addresses a fundamental challenge in Earth observation

Indian space-tech startup GalaxEye has announced that it has secured a US patent for the core technology behind its OptoSAR imaging system, becoming the first Indian startup to receive a US patent for satellite imaging technology.

The patent covers GalaxEye’s system architecture for aligning and synchronising optical and microwave sensors to enable simultaneous, spatially and temporally matched data acquisition. The same foundational technology has already been patented in India.

The US patent comes as GalaxEye prepares to scale its Earth-observation business, with plans to build a 30-satellite constellation over the next five years targeting defence, government and commercial applications across national security, agriculture, infrastructure, insurance, maritime intelligence and disaster management.

“This is not just a patent for us. This is an invention—an invention that came out of India,” Suyash Singh, Founder and CEO, GalaxEye, said.

“For decades, India has demonstrated that it can manufacture world-class technology. What is changing now is that India is beginning to invent technologies that the world has not seen before. GalaxEye leads that race in space. We are building global-first technology truly in India—not importing it, not adapting it, but inventing it here, engineering it here and taking it to the world.”

Singh said the US patent would help the company take its technology to international markets.

“This patented technology enables us to serve the global markets and provide weather agnostic imaging capabilities across sectors like defence, agriculture, insurance, disaster response and more,” he added.

GalaxEye’s patented technology addresses a fundamental challenge in Earth observation: combining optical and Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) imagery in a way that produces closely aligned observations.

Optical and SAR sensors operate using different physical principles and have traditionally been deployed independently or combined through post-processing. Even when imagery of the same location is available, it may have been captured at different times, from different viewing geometries or by different platforms, creating temporal gaps and spatial misalignment.

GalaxEye’s invention tackles this problem at the system and sensing architecture level, synchronising the optical and microwave sensors to capture data from the same location at the same time.

The approach forms the foundation of its OptoSAR technology, combining the visual and spectral information available through optical imaging with SAR’s ability to operate during both day and night and through adverse weather conditions.

Former ISRO Chairman Dr Somanath S Panicker described the patent as an example of the capabilities emerging from India’s private space sector.

“GalaxEye’s recently granted US patent for its technology behind OptoSAR is a powerful example of the innovation emerging from India’s private space ecosystem,” he said.

“Its uniqueness lies in synchronising optical and SAR sensors at the system level to deliver inherently aligned, spatially and temporally matched Earth observation data. This is not only a significant technical innovation but also has strong commercial potential across applications requiring richer, more actionable intelligence.”

GalaxEye has already taken the technology from development to space through its flagship Mission Drishti, launched on May 3, 2026.

The approximately 190-kg satellite combines multispectral imaging and SAR on a single spacecraft and was described by the company as the world’s first OptoSAR imaging satellite. At the time of launch, it was also India’s largest privately built Earth-observation satellite.

The mission demonstrated GalaxEye’s approach of bringing optical and radar sensing together on a single satellite platform, creating complementary observations from the same spacecraft.

The company is now looking to scale from its first satellite towards a larger constellation, supported by a growing commercial pipeline in India and overseas.

GalaxEye is also expanding its in-house engineering capabilities as it prepares for the next phase of its satellite programme.

The company is also expanding beyond satellite hardware into advanced imaging payloads, data processing and AI-driven intelligence.

The US patent, meanwhile, gives GalaxEye additional intellectual-property protection in one of the world’s largest technology markets as it seeks to commercialise its OptoSAR technology globally.

The broader ambition, according to Singh, is to establish India not merely as a manufacturing base for space technology, but as a source of technologies that can compete globally.

“Indian deep-tech companies can create globally differentiated, global-first technologies from India,” said Singh.

The 70,000 sq ft facility will manufacture precision gearing for aerospace and defence programmes, from development through serial production.

Bevel Gears India (BGI) inaugurated a 70,000-square-foot manufacturing facility near Kempegowda International Airport in Bengaluru on September 8, dedicated exclusively to aerospace and defence gearing.

The Bengaluru-based high-precision bevel gear specialist said the facility is part of its growth strategy as it targets ₹500 crore in revenue by 2029.

“This is our first plant built from the ground up for aerospace,” said Mushtaq Jamal, Director, Engineering and Business Development, Bevel Gears India. “The facility has been designed around the requirements of flight-critical gearing, with dedicated manufacturing, inspection and quality infrastructure to support demanding tolerances, process control and complete traceability.”

According to the company, the facility will manufacture spiral and straight bevel gears, zerol and angular bevels, beveloids, hypoid and high-ratio hypoid gears, curvic couplings and precision parallel-axis gearing.

BGI said these capabilities will support aero-engine, helicopter, unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV), actuation and aerospace gearbox programmes from development through serial production.

The facility is located within Bengaluru’s aerospace corridor, which the company said places BGI close to aircraft and aerospace original equipment manufacturers (OEMs), maintenance, repair and overhaul (MRO) companies and tier-1 suppliers.

The plant houses Gleason and Klingelnberg Computer Numerical Control (CNC) bevel and hypoid gear grinding lines. BGI said these include India’s first Gleason 275G CNC hypoid grinder with a special straight bevel grinding option and India’s first Klingelnberg Oerlikon G80 CNC hypoid grinder.

The facility also has DMG 5-axis machining centres and a climate-controlled metrology room equipped with ZEISS coordinate measuring machines and Gleason gear inspection systems. The company said industry-standard Gleason software supports gear design and tooth-contact analysis, reinforced by SolidWorks.

“India’s aerospace sector is growing rapidly, with global engine and airframe makers expanding their supplier base in the country. Demand is also increasing for the complex, flight-critical gearing we have specialised in for five decades,” said Sulaiman Jamal, Managing Director, Jamal Group. “This plant allows us to take programmes from prototype and development quantities through to serial production across multiple platforms. We also offer reverse engineering services for legacy and obsolete parts, enabling customers to maintain their equipment.”

BGI said the facility operates under AS9100D-certified aerospace quality systems and holds ISO 9001:2015 certification. Heat treatment capabilities and National Aerospace and Defense Contractors Accreditation Program (NADCAP) accreditation for special processes are planned as the next phase.

Founded in 1976, BGI is part of the Jamal Group and serves aerospace, space, motorsport, mining, steel and industrial customers across international markets, according to the company. BGI also said its products have supported India's space programme, including gears aboard Pragyan, the lunar rover used in the Chandrayaan-3 mission.

title: Agnikul Cosmos Opens Facilities to Test Reusable Rocket Stages Under Flight-Like Conditions
content:
The new infrastructure will support post-flight inspection, requalification and faster production of critical launch vehicle components.

Agnikul Cosmos has inaugurated two facilities at its assembly and testing facility in Chennai to test reusable rocket stages under flight-like conditions and manufacture high-pressure composite overwrapped pressure vessels in-house, as the company prepares for its upcoming Mission-02.

Mission-02 will attempt India’s first recovery of an orbital-class rocket booster and repurpose the rocket’s upper stage into an in-orbit platform, making it Agnikul’s first reusable launch mission.

The Stage Testing & Inspection Facility (STIF) and the Pressurant Tank Realisation, Over-wrapping and Outfitting Facility (PROOF) were inaugurated in the presence of Group Captain Shubhanshu Shukla and the astronaut selected for the Gaganyaan Mission.

STIF is designed to test complete rocket stages with integrated propulsion and avionics. It supports thrust levels from 1 kN to 200 kN, LOX sub-cooling down to 73 K and full-duration burns of up to 150 seconds. The facility will also be used to inspect and requalify recovered stages after flight.

“The vision of bringing reusability to launch requires us to think beyond a single flight and build the capability to test, recover, inspect and prepare a stage for its next flight. STIF gives us the ability to test complete stages for the duration of their mission and inspect and requalify recovered stages. This is an important capability as we work towards Mission-02,” said Srinath Ravichandran, Co-founder and CEO, Agnikul Cosmos.

The facility can test stages powered by clusters of Agnikul’s single-piece, semi-cryogenic, electric pump-fed 3D-printed engines. The company said STIF will support a repeatable cycle of building, testing, flying, recovering, inspecting, requalifying and flying stages again.

PROOF, meanwhile, brings the manufacturing of high-pressure composite overwrapped pressure vessels in-house. The facility can produce more than 10 vessels a month, including vessels with capacities of up to 3,500 litres and pressures of up to 350 bar.

“STIF and PROOF bring critical capabilities for our vehicle recovery and manufacturing operations in-house. The ability to manufacture high-pressure composite overwrapped vessels at production scale gives us greater control over the process, quality and turnaround time. This capability, along with the stage-level testing facility, will be important as we expand our manufacturing capacity and build towards a higher launch cadence,” said Moin SPM, Co-Founder and COO, Agnikul Cosmos.

The two facilities expand Agnikul’s in-house capabilities across propulsion and avionics development, component manufacturing, stage-level testing and recovery operations. The company said the infrastructure will support its transition from individual launch missions to a higher-cadence launch model.

Headquartered in Chennai and incubated at IIT Madras, Agnikul Cosmos develops the Agnibaan family of configurable small-lift launch vehicles. In May 2024, it conducted Mission 01, Agnibaan SOrTeD, from its privately built launchpad at Sriharikota.

“India’s space programme is entering an exciting phase, with capabilities being built across the country that will enable increasingly ambitious missions. It is encouraging to see Agnikul continue to expand its capabilities in advanced manufacturing and testing,” said Shukla.

Agnikul already designs and manufactures its single-piece, 3D-printed semi-cryogenic engines in-house and develops its avionics and other propulsion and vehicle systems.

The company’s Mission-01, launched on May 30, 2024, demonstrated a controlled ascent using its single-piece 3D-printed engine and in-house autopilot architecture.

No country can realistically ensure complete sovereignty across all the layers of AI.

Shalini MondalSenior Tech Journalist

India’s AI sovereignty debate may have been looking at the wrong thing. The question is not simply whether India can build its own AI models. It is whether India can remain in control of the technology those models depend on.

Abhishek Bhatt, Secretary General of the Bharath Digital Infrastructure Association (BDIA), has a striking analogy for where India’s real strategic leverage could lie. He describes data as India’s “Strait of Hormuz”.

“India’s strait of Hormuz is data. We don’t build compute. We have to be transparent. We can build softwares because Indians and India in general has been good at softwares. So we can build LLMs. There’s no doubt about it. But for building LLMs, we need compute,” Bhatt tells AIM.

The analogy gets to the heart of India’s AI sovereignty problem. Just as the Strait of Hormuz is a critical chokepoint for global energy flows, data could become one of the most important strategic assets in India’s AI economy. But controlling data alone will not be enough if the compute, cloud, hardware, connectivity and deployment layers remain dependent on systems that India cannot control.

Bhatt argues that sovereignty should therefore not be confused with owning every piece of technology.

“Sovereignty is not AI. Sovereignty is about control,” Bhatt says, pointing to five critical layers of the technology stack—foundational connectivity and subsea cables, hardware, cloud, applications and AI.

No country, he argues, can realistically ensure complete sovereignty across all these layers. The objective is to retain enough legal, economic, technological and policy leverage to control what matters most.

Sourav Jena, CEO, Coredge, takes a similar view. “Yes, but I would not frame it as a choice between owning models and owning infrastructure. Sovereignty is becoming a question of control across the AI value chain,” Jena explains.

“I would define AI sovereignty as the ability to control the critical dependencies that determine how AI is built, trained, deployed and used—rather than simply where the original model was created,” Jena says.

Compute Remains India’s Biggest Weakness

India’s model-building efforts are already changing the narrative that the country has no domestic AI capability. Under the IndiaAI Mission, 20 indigenous AI models are in development, including 12 LLMs and eight smaller models, with five already released.

Sarvam has open-sourced models with 30 billion and 105 billion parameters, while BharatGen and Gnani are developing indigenous AI systems.

But building models is only one part of the problem.

“AI needs three things. One is the compute, other is the data, and third, the algorithm, the power to run that. These are the three input raw material for any AI,” Bhatt states.

For India, compute remains a particularly difficult dependency because the economics extend far beyond GPUs.

“The first challenge is compute economics. Sovereign AI requires affordable and reliable compute at scale. GPUs are only one part of the equation — power, cooling, networking, storage, utilisation and inference efficiency ultimately determine the cost of AI,” Jena says.

This means that simply deploying thousands of GPUs does not automatically create sovereign AI. If compute remains too expensive, unreliable or inefficient for sustained use, domestic AI capability could still depend on external infrastructure and economics.

Namit Sureka, Chief Analytics & AI Officer, Straive, argues that the debate itself needs to move beyond models versus data.

“The framing of data-versus-models is a false binary. Sovereignty is built across four layers: models, data, compute, and the deployment layer where AI becomes work. India is building all four.”

India does not need to build everything

India is increasingly building its own models, but there is also a question of how much of the frontier it should try to reproduce.

“India should build foundational and domain-specific models, but we should be selective about where we invest. We do not need to recreate every frontier model at enormous cost simply to establish ownership,” Jena clarifies.

That could mean prioritising Indian languages, local context and strategically important sectors rather than attempting to reproduce every frontier model built by the largest technology companies.

The economics make this distinction important. Frontier AI development costs billions of dollars, while the technology itself is moving quickly.

“In a category where frontier development costs run into billions and the leading model changes every quarter, whatever India spends today can be recovered by a well-timed wait,” Sureka states. The more immediate question, therefore, is what India needs to control even when it uses technology developed elsewhere.

Data Residency Does Not Equal Sovereignty

Data is central to that question, but keeping data inside India does not necessarily mean India controls the AI system using it.

“It’s definitely not about data residency. Data residency has got nothing to do with sovereignty or with respect to control,” Bhatt says.

A system can physically operate in India while relying on foreign-owned hardware, software, cloud infrastructure, intellectual property or technology providers.

Jena points out that sensitive data does not necessarily have to be embedded into model weights. Retrieval, private inference and fine-tuning can allow models to work with controlled datasets.

But those mechanisms create another dependency if the infrastructure handling them remains outside domestic control.

“If these techniques only preserve sovereignty if the retrieval and inference layers themselves sit under domestic control. Otherwise, you haven’t removed the exposure; you’ve simply moved it — from the model’s weights to every individual query,” Jena says.

For government and enterprise systems, this distinction becomes particularly important. Keeping data in India means little if every query, inference request or retrieval operation can still depend on an external provider.

Bhatt identifies four levers that determine whether India can actually exercise control.

“Do we have the requisite enabling legal structure to exercise control? That is the first part. Do we have the economic levers to exercise control? Means if you want to operate out of here, you need to pay taxes. Do we have technological levers? And the fourth is do we have the policy levers?”

The Bigger Risk is Being Switched Off

The concern around foreign technology is ultimately less about where a company is headquartered and more about whether access can be withdrawn.

“If the access to a technology can be cut off, so that is a big reminder that why only that technology? Even the internet technology, even the Chrome that you are using, these access can be pulled off.”

Tarun Nandwani, CEO, Newgen, makes the same point about critical infrastructure.

“All these will need to be tried, and we will find the right fix, because we cannot depend on foreign infrastructure for sure. All governments have to do that to take care of, because see tomorrow if somebody switches off a plug for you. You cannot leave your systems non-functioning,” he states.

But sovereignty also has an economic limit.

“I think the direction is absolutely required and the investments have to go there. But finally, we have to find the right balance with the cost and the output,” he adds.

That is where India’s AI strategy becomes more complicated. The country needs domestic capability, but it cannot realistically isolate itself from global AI research, hardware, cloud platforms, capital and technology.

“The objective is not self-sufficiency. It is strategic autonomy: the ability to choose the best technology without surrendering control of the critical dependencies around it,” Jena states.

India’s strength in software and applications also does not automatically translate into expertise across the deeper layers of AI. Building sovereign capability means developing the ability to build, adapt, optimise, secure and operate systems when required.

Control first, indigenous capability next

For Bhatt, India does not have to wait until every component is indigenous before it can exercise sovereignty.

“I’ll give you a simple analogy. Mercedes is not our engine. But when it runs in India, who exercises control over it? Government of India,” he adds.

He applies the same logic to AI.

“So whoever built the model is definitely wishful thinking that we, it’s a good thing that we should have our own domestic model, that is absolutely right. But till we don’t get there, there are various means and mechanisms to ensure that control is there. So we first must achieve control. Then the next priority is it should be indigenous,” he states.

That puts the real AI sovereignty question somewhere beyond the model itself. India can use the best global models and still pursue sovereignty, provided it has enough control over the data, infrastructure, compute, deployment and critical dependencies that sit around them.

The model may be the most visible part of AI. But for India, the more consequential battle could be over everything that allows that model to operate.

title: Voice AI Startup Navana.ai Secures ₹40 Crore Series A Led by Ronnie Screwvala
content:
The startup will use the fresh capital to expand its BFSI deployments and advance speech models across 12 Indian languages and 45 dialects.

Voice AI startup Navana.ai has raised ₹40 crore in a Series A funding round led by entrepreneur and investor Ronnie Screwvala. Antler India, Sharad Sanghi, CEO of Neysa, Sandeep Singhal and Paula Mariwala also participated in the round.

The company said it will use the funding to scale its deployments among banking, financial services and insurance (BFSI) enterprises, expand its speech models for Indian languages and dialects, and develop its AI Contact Centre and automated evaluation platform.

Navana.ai said it has processed more than 100 million voice AI minutes for BFSI companies including Bajaj Finserv, Protean, Ujjivan Small Finance Bank, Jana Small Finance Bank and Grihum Housing Finance. Its voice AI is used for sales, collections, compliance and customer support.

Founded by brothers Raoul Nanavati and Jai Nanavati, Navana.ai develops voice AI systems for regulated enterprises, with on-premise deployment options to address data privacy and compliance requirements.

“From day one, Navana.ai’s mission has been to democratise access to digital services for every Indian, irrespective of where they live. India has spent the last decade building critical digital rails, including identity, connectivity and payments. Now this next decade belongs to meaningful automation,” said Raoul Nanavati, Co-Founder and CEO of Navana.ai.

“We strongly believe that voice AI will enable automation to truly benefit every Indian’s life, irrespective of their language or literacy. We are excited to partner with Ronnie Screwvala to take our sovereign AI infrastructure to the next stage of scale with some of the biggest names in the BFSI industry,” he added.

Navana.ai has developed proprietary speech models covering 12 Indian languages and 45 dialects. The models are trained on Indian speech and are designed to handle noise, overlapping speech, code-switching and regional accents.

The company has also worked with institutions including IISc Bengaluru, IIT Madras, Microsoft Research and the Gates Foundation. In collaboration with IISc, it open-sourced RESPIN, a 10,000-hour speech corpus covering 45 Indian dialects.

According to a benchmark conducted by Navana.ai using real-world speech samples across Indian voice AI platforms, its Bodhi speech model recorded the highest accuracy among the platforms tested.

Screwvala said the company’s focus on India’s linguistic diversity and enterprise data requirements was a key factor behind the investment.

“Navana.ai is solving a problem that large global and generalised AI models simply aren’t built for, which is the sheer linguistic complexity and diversity of India,” Screwvala said.

“Voice AI will be a critical part of India’s digital infrastructure as it will soon be an ₹9,500 crore-worth category. But what is important as India builds its voice AI models is not the price of the offerings, but where the customer data actually sits and whether the models are regulator-compliant,” he added.

According to Screwvala, Navana.ai's focus on enterprise deployments and regulatory compliance positions it to serve companies that require greater control over customer data.

The programme aims to train 23,000 youth across 190 institutions in AI, cloud computing and electronics manufacturing.

US technology giant Dell Technologies has launched uDaan, a national skilling programme to prepare 23,000 young people for careers in artificial intelligence, cloud computing and electronics manufacturing.

The programme is being delivered through a consortium comprising FITT-IIT Delhi, Learning Links Foundation and Generation India Foundation. It will operate across 190 government and aided institutions in five major technology corridors — Delhi NCR, Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Chennai and Pune.

As part of the programme, 100 ITIs and 90 higher education institutions will offer industry-aligned training across four areas: AI Application Development, Cloud Development, Assembly Line Operations and Field Technician roles.

FITT-IIT Delhi will design and certify the curricula, co-validated by more than 40 employers spanning technology companies, electronics manufacturers, global capability centres, and hyperscalers.

Learning Links Foundation will lead higher education delivery and institutional onboarding, while Generation India Foundation will oversee ITI execution and employment linkages.

“India's AI economy is creating roles faster than employers are able to fill them, and those roles require new skillsets,” Manish Gupta, President and Managing Director, Dell Technologies India, said in a statement. He added that uDaan is intended to create pathways from education to employment while supporting AI adoption and workforce readiness.

In its first year, uDaan aims to support 25 deep-tech startups among higher education learners and 10 micro-enterprises among ITI learners, with access to technical mentorship, bootcamps, accelerator networks, and potential capital.

Dell said more than 2,000 hours of employee mentoring will be provided across the five corridors, covering career guidance, AI awareness and interview preparation.

Dell said it will work with officials from the state Directorate of Vocational Education and Training and the Directorate of Technical Education from the first year, with the aim of creating a model that can eventually be adopted by state governments and other companies.

The programme builds on Dell’s earlier community initiatives in India. Over the past decade, the company said its education and innovation programmes have reached more than 50 million K-12 beneficiaries through digital literacy, vocational skills and experiential learning initiatives.

title: TCS’ HyperVault to Build 1GW AI Data Centre Campus in Hyderabad with ₹70,000 Crore Investment
content:
TCS’ data centre arm HyperVault has secured 264 acres in Hyderabad for a phased AI infrastructure campus with up to 1GW capacity.

Tata Consultancy Services’ (TCS) data centre subsidiary HyperVault has secured 264 acres in Hyderabad to build an AI-focused data centre campus with capacity of up to 1 gigawatt, marking a significant expansion of the IT major’s push into AI infrastructure.

HyperVault and its partners are expected to invest up to ₹70,000 crore to build and operate the campus, which will be developed in phases depending on customer demand and technology requirements, TCS said in a regulatory filing.

The facility will be designed for high-density GPU deployments used for AI training, inference and other advanced computing workloads, and will target frontier AI companies and hyperscalers. TCS said the campus will use liquid cooling and incorporate green-energy and water-neutral design principles.

At full build-out, the campus is expected to be among India’s largest AI infrastructure facilities. The project is also expected to generate several thousand direct and indirect jobs across areas including power, cooling, networking, construction, engineering and operations.

The move comes as AI is pushing data centre infrastructure towards much higher power density and specialised cooling requirements.

“HyperVault advances TCS’ Infrastructure-to-Intelligence strategy by bringing together AI-ready infrastructure with our cloud, engineering, enterprise transformation and AI capabilities. Hyderabad offers the scale, talent and ecosystem to serve global customers. We extend our sincere appreciation to the Hon’ble Chief Minister and the Government of Telangana for their steadfast support and progressive, investment-friendly policies,” K Krithivasan, CEO & MD, TCS, said in a statement.

TCS had set up HyperVault as a dedicated vehicle for its AI data centre ambitions and brought in private equity firm TPG as a strategic partner in November 2025. TCS and TPG had then committed up to ₹18,000 crore over the following years, with TPG committing up to ₹8,820 crore. The partnership was aimed at building AI-ready data centre capacity exceeding 1GW.

The latest Telangana project takes that strategy from an announced infrastructure ambition to a specific large-scale campus.

TCS has been seeking to build an offering that extends beyond traditional IT services to the physical infrastructure required to run increasingly compute-intensive AI workloads.

For TCS, the data centre business also represents a departure from the relatively asset-light model that has historically defined India's large IT services companies.

This infrastructure push comes amid a broader global race to build AI compute capacity. Unlike conventional cloud workloads, AI training and inference require dense clusters of GPUs, high-speed networking and substantially greater power and cooling infrastructure.

Hyderabad has emerged as one of India's major data centre locations alongside Mumbai, Navi Mumbai, Chennai, Bengaluru and Delhi-NCR. The government has also been positioning Telangana as an AI and advanced digital infrastructure hub.

“This establishes that Hyderabad is now at the forefront of the global AI revolution with a strong focus on infrastructure. This decade is one of Artificial Intelligence. Access to AI models and compute is fast-becoming public infrastructure and having this compute reside in Telangana gives us an advantage,” said A. Revanth Reddy, Chief Minister of Telangana.

title: Spotify Cuts Claude Code Token Usage by 90%
content:
Spotify’s Portal for Backstage routes routine coding-agent tasks to cheaper models, reducing the amount of frontier-model tokens Claude Code consumes.

Spotify says its internal developer platform, Portal by Spotify, cut token consumption from Claude Code by about 90% in tests by routing file-reading and predictable code-generation tasks to cheaper AI models, rather than using Anthropic’s frontier coding model for every operation.

The approach uses Portal’s “AiKA Modes”, which are declarative agents that run on ephemeral runtimes. Developers can specify the model, instructions, parameters and MCP tools for each mode without managing separate infrastructure or API keys.

Spotify engineer Dimitri Mazmanov tested the approach on a Java monorepo using two modes: a bulk-reader for reading multiple files and a code-writer for predictable code-generation tasks. Both examples use Google’s Gemini 2.5 Flash as the worker model, although Portal can be configured with other models.

“Most of what an AI coding agent does for me isn't thinking. It's I/O,” Mazmanov wrote. The setup keeps those token-heavy operations away from Claude Code while retaining Claude for tasks that require more reasoning.

The routing is enforced through a Claude Code plugin called Shunt. It uses PreToolUse hooks to intercept large file reads and redirect Claude to the bulk-reader mode. By default, reads of files exceeding 350 lines are blocked, while targeted reads using offsets and limits continue to pass through.

A second mode handles output-heavy tasks such as generating tests, configuration scaffolding and type stubs. It receives a specification and reference file, generates the code and can write it directly to disk, meaning Claude does not need to consume the generated output in its own context.

Spotify said the test measured Claude's token consumption across four scenarios in a Java monorepo, with mean savings from bulk reading of around 90%. The code-generation case was harder to measure because the unoptimised workflow includes both reading reference files and generating code as Claude output.

The approach has limits, and Spotify said the worker models are not intended to handle debugging, architectural decisions or safety-critical reasoning.

Besides, delegated analysis also does not reliably provide the line-level information Claude needs for editing. Network latency is another constraint, with typical delegation taking 10–30 seconds and Portal imposing a 30-second limit per invocation.

Mazmanov described the broader approach as “model routing powered by AiKA modes”, allowing teams to change the worker model or instructions without modifying the routing plugin itself.

Spotify made the bulk-reader and code-writer modes publicly available through AiKA, allowing developers to reuse or customise them across projects.

title: Pixxel Raises $100 Million in Series C Funding to Expand Planetary Infrastructure
content:
This new investment gives us the scale to turn that vision into planetary infrastructure.

Indian space-tech company Pixxel has raised $100 million in Series C funding, in a round co-led by Temasek and Seraphim, as it expands beyond hyperspectral imaging into Earth intelligence software, sovereign space systems and satellite manufacturing.

The round also saw participation from new investors 360 ONE Asset and IMM Investment, along with existing investors including Radical Ventures and growX ventures. The latest fundraise takes Pixxel’s total funding to $195 million and marks the largest funding round raised by an Indian space technology company, according to the company.

Pixxel said the fresh capital will be used to scale four key areas: advanced sensing capabilities, Earth intelligence software, sovereign Earth observation systems and satellite manufacturing.

Awais Ahmed, Founder and CEO of Pixxel, said, “Years ago, we set out to build a health monitor for the planet. Hyperspectral imaging gave us a fundamentally new way to see Earth. This new investment gives us the scale to turn that vision into planetary infrastructure. More ways of sensing, more intelligence from every image, and more sovereign capability for nations. Our goal is to make a changing planet understandable in time to act.”

The company plans to expand its sensing capabilities through its Honeybee Constellation, high-resolution optical imaging satellites and other sensing technologies. It will also continue developing Aurora, its Earth intelligence software platform, which combines multiple datasets to generate decision-ready insights.

Pixxel is also stepping up its focus on sovereign Earth observation systems and satellite manufacturing through Gigapixxel, its next-generation facility aimed at enabling high-rate production of advanced satellites.

The funding comes as Pixxel expands its footprint across the space-tech value chain. The company said it has deployed six Firefly satellites over the past two years, forming what it describes as the world’s highest-resolution commercial hyperspectral constellation. It has also launched Aurora as an Earth intelligence software platform.

Pixxel has secured contracts with NASA and the National Reconnaissance Office (NRO), while also winning multiple iDEX challenges from India’s Ministry of Defence. The company has additionally unveiled plans for an orbital data-centre demonstration satellite. It has also been selected to lead the development of India’s first public-private Earth observation constellation, comprising 12 satellites under IN-SPACe.

The company’s expansion comes amid growing interest in Earth observation, AI-powered geospatial intelligence and sovereign space capabilities, as governments and industries increasingly use satellite data for applications ranging from climate monitoring and agriculture to defence and infrastructure planning.

Mark Boggett, CEO at Seraphim Space, said, “Pixxel is exceptionally well-positioned across some of the most important themes shaping the future of the space sector, from AI-powered Earth observation and sovereign space capabilities to the rise of India as a global SpaceTech leader. We're delighted to deepen our support as the company continues to scale.”

With the Series C capital, Pixxel aims to move beyond hyperspectral imaging to build an integrated planetary infrastructure platform spanning sensors, software, sovereign space systems and satellite manufacturing.

The two programmes launched under the NIELIT–Intel India Agentic AI Skilling Initiative are ‘Agentic AI for Everyone’ and ‘Engineering Agentic AI Systems’.

The National Institute of Electronics and Information Technology (NIELIT), under the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY), and Intel India have launched two agentic AI skilling programmes to prepare students, professionals and educators for an increasingly AI-driven workforce.

The programmes were announced at a National Leadership Dialogue on ‘Preparing the Future Workforce for the Agentic AI Era’, organised by NIELIT and Intel India at the India Habitat Centre in New Delhi on September 3.

The initiative will focus on expanding access to industry-aligned and practical agentic AI learning opportunities across the country, with the government, academia, industry and skilling institutions expected to play a larger role in building India’s AI talent pipeline.

“The rapid evolution of artificial intelligence is creating new opportunities as well as new requirements for our education and skilling ecosystem. As a national institution mandated to build capabilities in electronics, IT and emerging technologies, NIELIT is committed to ensuring that learners and educators are equipped to participate in this next phase of technological transformation. Our collaboration with Intel India combines NIELIT’s nationwide skilling reach with Intel’s technology expertise and industry perspective, enabling us to take agentic AI learning closer to institutions and learners across the country,” Dr Madan Mohan Tripathi, Director General, NIELIT, said.

The Agentic AI for Everyone programme is designed to introduce learners to workflow automation, AI agents and multi-agent systems. It focuses on using agentic technologies to improve productivity, support business transformation and enable intelligent decision-making.

The programme will provide hands-on exposure to designing and governing AI-powered workflows and agentic systems using no-code platforms, making it accessible to learners without extensive programming backgrounds.

The second programme, Engineering Agentic AI Systems, is for learners looking to build and deploy AI-powered agentic systems. It covers agent architecture, tool integration, orchestration, memory and deployment, using both no-code/low-code platforms and code-based frameworks.

The programme aims to provide practical exposure to developing scalable and production-ready agentic AI solutions.

The launch comes as India seeks to expand its AI capabilities beyond access to computing infrastructure and models, with workforce development emerging as a key component of the country’s AI strategy.

Shri Sudeep Shrivastava, COO, IndiaAI Mission and Joint Secretary, MeitY, highlighted the government’s vision of democratising Sovereign AI and building an inclusive AI ecosystem.

He stressed the importance of industry-led training, AI-focused educational programmes and digital learning initiatives, while also pointing to the need for AI Data Labs and stronger industry–academia partnerships to give students, researchers and professionals hands-on exposure to emerging technologies.

The leadership dialogue brought together representatives from government, foreign embassies, academia, industry and the skilling ecosystem to discuss how agentic AI could reshape education, employment and workforce development.

As AI systems move from predictive and generative models towards agentic systems capable of reasoning, planning and executing complex tasks under human oversight, the skills required across industries are also changing.

The dialogue emphasised that future workers will require not only technical capabilities but also adaptability, judgement and the ability to collaborate effectively with AI systems.

“As AI evolves from assistive tools to agentic systems and ultimately physical intelligence, it will fundamentally reshape education, work, jobs, and industries. In this new era, the defining factor of success will be human readiness, as individuals will need the skills, adaptability, and judgment to collaborate effectively with increasingly capable AI systems. Investing in AI skills is therefore essential to strengthen economic resilience, expand opportunity, and reinforce technological sovereignty. Through our collaboration with NIELIT, we are taking an important step in translating this vision into action,” said Shweta Khurana, Senior Director, Asia Pacific and Japan, International Government Affairs, Intel.

The initiative also emphasises faculty readiness, experiential learning, industry-aligned curricula and AI-enabled learning environments.

Speaking at the event, Shashi Shekhar Vempati, Chairperson, Central Board of Film Certification, stressed the importance of long-term skilling pathways that combine foundational and emerging technology skills with real-world exposure, industry case studies and practical datasets. He also called for sustained collaboration between government, industry, academia and skilling institutions to ensure that India’s workforce is prepared not only for current employment opportunities but also for jobs that emerge as AI reshapes the economy.

The NIELIT–Intel initiative is expected to expand access to agentic AI learning across educational institutions and learner communities, as India seeks to build a workforce capable of working alongside increasingly autonomous AI systems and contributing to the country’s next phase of AI-led growth.

title: OpenAI’s Top Researchers Are Spending $7,000+ on Codex Per Day
content:
“We are making strong progress toward creating an automated AI researcher by March of 2028,” said the company.

Several OpenAI researchers are now spending hundreds of dollars a day on Codex, with the median researcher in the company’s research organisation using more than $600 a day in inference at API prices by mid-August, OpenAI said in a recent blog.

The heaviest users are consuming more than $7,000 worth of tokens a day.

OpenAI said this represents a shift from modest agent use at the start of 2026 to coding agents becoming part of researchers’ daily workflows.

The scale of usage is also visible in the amount of machine labour being deployed. Before June, total coding-agent runtime across OpenAI’s research organisation was below human labour.

By mid-August, the organisation was running the equivalent of 3.1 agent-workdays for every eight-hour human workday. Researchers are increasingly running multiple coding agents concurrently rather than waiting for one task to finish before starting another.

This is translating into more research execution. OpenAI says the number of experiments conducted per active experimenter has increased through 2026, reaching an all-time high in August since the company began tracking the metric last January.

The increase coincides with greater Codex adoption, although OpenAI cautions that its available compute has also grown significantly, meaning the experiment increase cannot be attributed to agents alone.

The agents are also moving into a wider range of research work.

OpenAI classified coding-agent activity across six stages of its AI R&D process. All six categories increased between January and August, with research and infrastructure code remaining the largest category.

Technical help and monitoring runs also saw notable growth, while high-level planning remained a small share of agent output.

One practical effect is a reduction in the amount of routine technical support researchers need from other teams. OpenAI says researchers increasingly use coding agents to troubleshoot internal research infrastructure, and several teams that previously held office hours for experiment troubleshooting have reported declining attendance.

One team has stopped holding those sessions altogether to focus on other system improvements.

The agents are not, however, replacing human researchers outright. OpenAI found that task success rates generally improved between January and July, but human intervention remained common as tasks became more complex.

More than half of successful tasks estimated to require four to eight hours of human work involved at least one human intervention over the previous six months.

Researchers continue to determine what problems to pursue, assess results and decide whether work should be scaled, paused or deployed.

OpenAI says the growing use of coding agents is already speeding up parts of its research workflow, with researchers writing more code, running more experiments and delegating increasingly complex tasks to agents.

But the company cautions that these gains do not translate directly into an equivalent increase in the overall pace of AI research, because progress depends on multiple stages and bottlenecks, including compute and tasks that remain difficult to automate. “AI research is a complex process with many potential bottlenecks,” OpenAI said.

The company nevertheless says its internal data and researchers’ experience are consistent with a broader acceleration. “Agentic tools are meaningfully accelerating research progress,” OpenAI said, while stressing that humans continue to set research priorities, evaluate results and decide whether systems should be scaled, paused or deployed.

OpenAI is also tightening controls as agent use expands, including stronger monitoring and safety requirements following an incident in which agents compromised its research infrastructure.

After agents compromised its research infrastructure, OpenAI temporarily paused reinforcement-learning training on its latest deployment models while it hardened the research environment and expanded monitoring.
