StyleX is gaining attention as coding agents shift the tradeoffs between flexibility, consistency, and control.

For years, styled-components worked well for Linear, the product development and issue tracking platform.

Its flexible API let developers colocate styles with components while keeping a regular CSS escape hatch.

As Linear’s codebase grew, however, that flexibility became harder to manage.

In a blog post, Linear said the “endless configurability” of styled-components had become a liability. CSS could be modified from outside the component it belonged to, making patterns such as styled(Button) common.

After a redesign, Linear found a long tail of UI regressions caused by styling changes from a distance.

Runtime CSS generation also added render-time work, and styled-components had entered maintenance mode.

The problem became harder to manage as AI coding agents began contributing more code.

Linear found styled-components difficult to automate because it is effectively an open-ended language with the full flexibility of CSS.

Many ways could express the same styling intent, and agents could produce code that looked correct while violating the application’s intended structure.

Linear wanted styles to be generated at build time, styling at a distance to be difficult, component styling contracts to be explicit, and style merging to be predictable.

It evaluated several React styling systems, including vanilla-extract, but chose StyleX because its styles could remain colocated with components while providing deterministic resolution and type-safe styling contracts.

The migration took more than 1,000 pull requests. Linear built a deterministic codemod and used agents for repetitive work, while migrating the application incrementally and keeping the old and new systems running together.

The team started with leaf components and kept scopes narrow because visual validation remained difficult for agents.

Linear says the resulting system reduced main-thread CPU work by roughly 20–35% on view-heavy pages after removing runtime style injection.

Its tests were around 30% faster on a mid-tier machine, and the client went from injecting hundreds of CSS rules during navigation to injecting none.

Jared Palmer, VP of Engineering at Cognition, has made a similar argument after years of working with atomic CSS frameworks including Tailwind.

“After about a ~decade with atomic CSS frameworks (BuzzFeed Solid, Basscss, and then finally Tailwind), I think I’m convinced now that StyleX is superior for agents,” Palmer wrote on X.

He said StyleX’s constraints produce “greater consistency and correctness as your codebase grows”.

Palmer still considers Tailwind the better choice when developers are writing the styling code themselves. But with agents handling more of the implementation, he argues that “the tradeoffs have changed”.

The argument for StyleX with coding agents is less about syntax and more about constraints. Tailwind gives developers broad freedom in how they combine utility classes.

StyleX narrows those choices with typed styles, design tokens, and deterministic composition, giving agents fewer ways to express the same intent while catching invalid values and styling violations earlier.

Tailwind’s concise syntax benefits humans writing styles by hand, but when an agent is doing the typing, stricter rules can matter more than brevity. Linear cited clearer styling boundaries and agent ergonomics when it chose StyleX, after finding its previous system too open-ended to automate reliably.

Meta developed StyleX as a styling system for large-scale applications and open-sourced it at the end of 2023.

It combines CSS-in-JS ergonomics with static CSS by compiling styles at build time and generating a static stylesheet.

Meta uses it across Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, Messenger and Threads, while companies including Figma and Snowflake have also adopted it.

The system uses atomic CSS, type-safe authoring and predictable style merging. Meta has said atomic classes reduced its CSS size by 80%. Runtime work remains for cases such as cross-module style merging and genuinely dynamic styles, while stylex.create itself is compiled away.

StyleX has also built a sizeable open-source community since Meta released it publicly. The official repository now has nearly 10,000 GitHub stars, and more than 450 forks. StyleX’s adoption is also showing up in package usage.

The core @stylexjs/stylex package now records more than 1.4 million weekly npm downloads, while its Babel plugin records more than one million and its ESLint plugin nearly 688,000.

Naman Goel, a core contributor to the StyleX open-source project, has highlighted several other differences from Tailwind.

StyleX uses strongly typed style objects, standard CSS property and value names, colocated CSS keyframes and view transitions, named styles and a first-class API for dynamic styles.

Goel also points to debugging. Tailwind makes the styles applied to an element visible through its utility classes, while StyleX can show where a style originated in the source code. Its DevTools can use source maps to display the style objects and the order in which they are applied.

The distinction also matters for how agents interpret code. A named StyleX style can encode semantic information about why a style exists, not just which CSS properties it contains.

Standard CSS property names also remove the need for an agent to translate between CSS terminology and framework-specific utility names.

StyleX is finding a new path to wider adoption as coding agents take on more software development.

“Hard to predict how much adoption a discussion on X will lead to, but even before now StyleX has been used at many major companies like Meta, Figma, Canva, Snowflake,” said Goel to AIM.

“StyleX has slowly been gaining adoption since it was open-sourced, and I think it’s normal for it to take a couple of years for the rate of adoption to increase.”

Canva is also investigating a much larger migration. In a November 2025 GitHub discussion, a Canva engineer said the company had more than 10,000 CSS Modules files containing over 46,000 rule selectors and was investigating a move to StyleX. A StyleX maintainer responded that Meta’s own migration from a similar system had been automated for roughly 80% of cases.

A July experiment by LogRocket migrated StyleX directly from Tailwind across 20 production-style components.

The migration doubled the styling code, from 1,568 lines to 3,143, while the resulting CSS bundles were nearly identical: 20,379 bytes for Tailwind and 20,561 bytes for StyleX.

Cold build times were also similar, at eight seconds for Tailwind and 7.4 seconds for StyleX.

The main difference, however, was type safety. The experiment found that StyleX caught styling mistakes involving tokens, variants and composition earlier, while Tailwind retained a clear advantage in ecosystem size and rapid prototyping.

The Misconception about StyleX’s Performance

One criticism of StyleX is that its styling model could carry the runtime performance costs associated with CSS-in-JS libraries that generate and inject styles while an application runs.

Goel says that is a misconception.

“The common misconception about StyleX is that people don’t realise that it is compiled and doesn’t do any runtime style generation/injection,” he tells.

“StyleX compiles to something that is at least as efficient as Tailwind, if not more,” Goel says.

He cites recent migration figures showing up to 20% better FCP, up to 60% less CSS and 5% less JavaScript.

There are genuine tradeoffs, though.

StyleX makes some CSS patterns harder to express, including certain parent-dependent selectors, global selectors and wrapper-based restyling.

Linear describes those restrictions as deliberate constraints, and they remove patterns that made its previous styling system hard to reason about at scale.

StyleX can also require more ceremony for some simple use cases. Its compiler depends on styles being statically analyzable, which limits highly dynamic patterns. Cross-file composition can require runtime style merging, although the StyleX team describes that runtime cost as small.

StyleX is Not Always the Right Migration

However, replacing Tailwind with StyleX does not automatically make a website faster.

Recently, Franklin Javier, a software developer, published the results of his attempt to replace Tailwind with StyleX on his personal website. The site already scored 100 on PageSpeed, shipped no JavaScript in its Astro bundle, and had an FCP of 0.8 seconds.

After rebuilding it with StyleX and matching the existing design pixel for pixel, FCP remained at 0.8 seconds, and LCP showed no consistent improvement. Javier reverted the migration.

StyleX reduced the site’s raw CSS from 40,325 bytes to 36,972 bytes. Gzipped CSS fell from roughly 6.9 KB to roughly 6.5 KB. The smaller stylesheet did not produce a measurable loading improvement.

Javier also found that Tailwind carried unnecessary CSS. The typography plugin was sent to pages that did not use it. After removing that waste and making other changes, he achieved substantial CSS reductions without migrating away from Tailwind.

The comparison also showed that raw file size doesn’t tell the whole story. StyleX produced less raw HTML, but the compressed HTML was slightly larger because Tailwind’s repeated utility classes compress efficiently. StyleX’s more unique class names reduced that compression advantage.

Javier’s results do not show that StyleX is slower than Tailwind. They show that the benefit depends on where the bottleneck is. On a small site that already loads quickly and ships almost no JavaScript, a styling migration can reduce CSS without producing a visible performance gain.

Tailwind therefore remains a strong option for developers who prefer its utility-based syntax and flexibility. StyleX makes a different trade-off. It gives up some flexibility in exchange for stronger constraints, predictable composition, type safety and compile-time extraction.

title: NIELIT, Intel Launch Agentic AI Skilling Programmes to Prepare India’s Workforce for AI Era
content:
The two programmes launched under the NIELIT–Intel India Agentic AI Skilling Initiative are ‘Agentic AI for Everyone’ and ‘Engineering Agentic AI Systems’.

The National Institute of Electronics and Information Technology (NIELIT), under the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY), and Intel India have launched two agentic AI skilling programmes to prepare students, professionals and educators for an increasingly AI-driven workforce.

The programmes were announced at a National Leadership Dialogue on ‘Preparing the Future Workforce for the Agentic AI Era’, organised by NIELIT and Intel India at the India Habitat Centre in New Delhi on September 3.

The initiative will focus on expanding access to industry-aligned and practical agentic AI learning opportunities across the country, with the government, academia, industry and skilling institutions expected to play a larger role in building India’s AI talent pipeline.

“The rapid evolution of artificial intelligence is creating new opportunities as well as new requirements for our education and skilling ecosystem. As a national institution mandated to build capabilities in electronics, IT and emerging technologies, NIELIT is committed to ensuring that learners and educators are equipped to participate in this next phase of technological transformation. Our collaboration with Intel India combines NIELIT’s nationwide skilling reach with Intel’s technology expertise and industry perspective, enabling us to take agentic AI learning closer to institutions and learners across the country,” Dr Madan Mohan Tripathi, Director General, NIELIT, said.

The Agentic AI for Everyone programme is designed to introduce learners to workflow automation, AI agents and multi-agent systems. It focuses on using agentic technologies to improve productivity, support business transformation and enable intelligent decision-making.

The programme will provide hands-on exposure to designing and governing AI-powered workflows and agentic systems using no-code platforms, making it accessible to learners without extensive programming backgrounds.

The second programme, Engineering Agentic AI Systems, is for learners looking to build and deploy AI-powered agentic systems. It covers agent architecture, tool integration, orchestration, memory and deployment, using both no-code/low-code platforms and code-based frameworks.

The programme aims to provide practical exposure to developing scalable and production-ready agentic AI solutions.

The launch comes as India seeks to expand its AI capabilities beyond access to computing infrastructure and models, with workforce development emerging as a key component of the country’s AI strategy.

Shri Sudeep Shrivastava, COO, IndiaAI Mission and Joint Secretary, MeitY, highlighted the government’s vision of democratising Sovereign AI and building an inclusive AI ecosystem.

He stressed the importance of industry-led training, AI-focused educational programmes and digital learning initiatives, while also pointing to the need for AI Data Labs and stronger industry–academia partnerships to give students, researchers and professionals hands-on exposure to emerging technologies.

The leadership dialogue brought together representatives from government, foreign embassies, academia, industry and the skilling ecosystem to discuss how agentic AI could reshape education, employment and workforce development.

As AI systems move from predictive and generative models towards agentic systems capable of reasoning, planning and executing complex tasks under human oversight, the skills required across industries are also changing.

The dialogue emphasised that future workers will require not only technical capabilities but also adaptability, judgement and the ability to collaborate effectively with AI systems.

“As AI evolves from assistive tools to agentic systems and ultimately physical intelligence, it will fundamentally reshape education, work, jobs, and industries. In this new era, the defining factor of success will be human readiness, as individuals will need the skills, adaptability, and judgment to collaborate effectively with increasingly capable AI systems. Investing in AI skills is therefore essential to strengthen economic resilience, expand opportunity, and reinforce technological sovereignty. Through our collaboration with NIELIT, we are taking an important step in translating this vision into action,” said Shweta Khurana, Senior Director, Asia Pacific and Japan, International Government Affairs, Intel.

The initiative also emphasises faculty readiness, experiential learning, industry-aligned curricula and AI-enabled learning environments.

Speaking at the event, Shashi Shekhar Vempati, Chairperson, Central Board of Film Certification, stressed the importance of long-term skilling pathways that combine foundational and emerging technology skills with real-world exposure, industry case studies and practical datasets. He also called for sustained collaboration between government, industry, academia and skilling institutions to ensure that India’s workforce is prepared not only for current employment opportunities but also for jobs that emerge as AI reshapes the economy.

The NIELIT–Intel initiative is expected to expand access to agentic AI learning across educational institutions and learner communities, as India seeks to build a workforce capable of working alongside increasingly autonomous AI systems and contributing to the country’s next phase of AI-led growth.

The startup will use the fresh capital to expand its BFSI deployments and advance speech models across 12 Indian languages and 45 dialects.

Voice AI startup Navana.ai has raised ₹40 crore in a Series A funding round led by entrepreneur and investor Ronnie Screwvala. Antler India, Sharad Sanghi, CEO of Neysa, Sandeep Singhal and Paula Mariwala also participated in the round.

The company said it will use the funding to scale its deployments among banking, financial services and insurance (BFSI) enterprises, expand its speech models for Indian languages and dialects, and develop its AI Contact Centre and automated evaluation platform.

Navana.ai said it has processed more than 100 million voice AI minutes for BFSI companies including Bajaj Finserv, Protean, Ujjivan Small Finance Bank, Jana Small Finance Bank and Grihum Housing Finance. Its voice AI is used for sales, collections, compliance and customer support.

Founded by brothers Raoul Nanavati and Jai Nanavati, Navana.ai develops voice AI systems for regulated enterprises, with on-premise deployment options to address data privacy and compliance requirements.

“From day one, Navana.ai’s mission has been to democratise access to digital services for every Indian, irrespective of where they live. India has spent the last decade building critical digital rails, including identity, connectivity and payments. Now this next decade belongs to meaningful automation,” said Raoul Nanavati, Co-Founder and CEO of Navana.ai.

“We strongly believe that voice AI will enable automation to truly benefit every Indian’s life, irrespective of their language or literacy. We are excited to partner with Ronnie Screwvala to take our sovereign AI infrastructure to the next stage of scale with some of the biggest names in the BFSI industry,” he added.

Navana.ai has developed proprietary speech models covering 12 Indian languages and 45 dialects. The models are trained on Indian speech and are designed to handle noise, overlapping speech, code-switching and regional accents.

The company has also worked with institutions including IISc Bengaluru, IIT Madras, Microsoft Research and the Gates Foundation. In collaboration with IISc, it open-sourced RESPIN, a 10,000-hour speech corpus covering 45 Indian dialects.

According to a benchmark conducted by Navana.ai using real-world speech samples across Indian voice AI platforms, its Bodhi speech model recorded the highest accuracy among the platforms tested.

Screwvala said the company’s focus on India’s linguistic diversity and enterprise data requirements was a key factor behind the investment.

“Navana.ai is solving a problem that large global and generalised AI models simply aren’t built for, which is the sheer linguistic complexity and diversity of India,” Screwvala said.

“Voice AI will be a critical part of India’s digital infrastructure as it will soon be an ₹9,500 crore-worth category. But what is important as India builds its voice AI models is not the price of the offerings, but where the customer data actually sits and whether the models are regulator-compliant,” he added.

According to Screwvala, Navana.ai's focus on enterprise deployments and regulatory compliance positions it to serve companies that require greater control over customer data.

title: Jensen Huang Declares AGI
content:
He said GPT-6 Astra was trained on more than 100,000 NVIDIA Grace Blackwell GPUs across NVL72 systems.

NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang said GPT-6 Astra was trained on more than 100,000 NVIDIA Grace Blackwell GPUs, adding that another 400,000 GPUs are “coming online next” as OpenAI continues to expand the compute infrastructure behind its frontier models.

Huang made the comments in a post on X on Monday, saying: “GPT-6 Astra, trained on ~100K+ NVIDIA Grace Blackwell NVLink72.”

Huang also said, “From ChatGPT to o1 to Astra in 4 years. AGI has arrived,” congratulating OpenAI.

The AGI claim is Huang’s assessment, and OpenAI has described Astra as its most capable and aligned model, and president Greg Brockman also said this marks a ‘welcome to the AGI era’.

It can operate software, browse the web, handle spreadsheets and documents, write and debug software, conduct research and work on scientific and mathematical problems.

OpenAI said Astra scored 98% on FrontierMath Tier 4, 99.9% on ARC-AGI-3 and 100% on ExploitBench.

OpenAI conducted the training run at its Stargate site in Texas. The vice president of research Aidan Clark told Fortune that Astra was “the first time we’ve pretrained on more than 100,000 GPUs at our Stargate site in Texas.”

NVIDIA Grace Blackwell NVLink72 combines 36 Grace CPUs with 72 Blackwell GPUs in a liquid-cooled rack, with all 72 GPUs connected through a single fifth-generation NVLink domain.

The system provides 13.4TB of HBM3E GPU memory and 130TB/s of NVLink bandwidth.

That means the 100,000-plus GPUs referenced by Huang would represent roughly 1,389 GB200 NVL72 racks if expressed purely as 72-GPU rack equivalents. NVIDIA has not disclosed the actual deployment configuration.

The next generation is Vera Rubin NVL72, which combines 72 Rubin GPUs with 36 Vera CPUs and NVIDIA’s sixth-generation NVLink. NVIDIA says Vera Rubin is already in full production and is being positioned for large-scale agentic AI and reasoning workloads.

The platform is designed to reduce the GPU requirement for training while substantially lowering inference costs compared with Blackwell.

Himanshi Sharma has built CareerStack AI to help job seekers understand how well their skills and experience align with industry requirements and what steps they should take to improve their career opportunities.

A final-year engineering student updates her resume for the tenth time before a placement drive. She adds a keyword here, removes a bullet point there, and still has no real sense of whether it will pass an applicant tracking system (ATS) or catch a recruiter’s eye.

This is the exact problem Himanshi Sharma set out to solve. An engineering student from Ramrao Adik Institute of Technology (RAIT), Navi Mumbai, Sharma developed CareerStack AI, a platform that analyses resumes, evaluates ATS readiness, identifies missing skills and recommends learning pathways based on a user’s profile.

Her aim was to connect these steps so a job seeker could understand their current profile and what they could do next.

Sharma had studied AI/ML at university, but her experience with Samsung Innovation Campus taught her to begin with the problem and the user before choosing the technology, she tells AIM.

Building CareerStack AI

“CareerStack AI was built to address a common challenge faced by students and job seekers to understand how well their skills and experience align with industry requirements and what steps they should take to improve their career opportunities,” Sharma tells AIM.

The platform begins with a user’s resume. It evaluates the resume’s ATS readiness and extracts information about the person’s skills and experience. It then uses that information to identify skill gaps, recommend roles and generate learning pathways.

Sharma said this connected approach was important because career decisions rarely stop at resume preparation.

“Following the design-thinking approach I learned through Samsung Innovation Campus, I focused on understanding the problem from the user’s perspective first,” she says.

On the technical side, CareerStack is built as a full-stack application. Sharma used Next.js and React for the frontend and Python and FastAPI for the backend.

Its AI capabilities use LLMs hosted through Groq, along with natural language processing techniques for skill extraction. The platform also uses real-time job market data for comparisons with industry requirements.

A typical end-to-end workflow covers resume analysis, skill-gap assessment, roadmap generation and chatbot interactions.

Sharma estimates that such a workflow consumes about 6,500 input tokens and 2,300 output tokens, or roughly 8,800 tokens in total.

The platform has not been monetised yet.

Sharma’s current focus is validating the problem, developing the core product and determining whether the recommendations genuinely help users make career decisions. She sees future possibilities in personalised mentorship, recruiter-facing products and subscription-based career guidance.

Making One System Work

Sharma tells AIM that the most difficult part of building CareerStack AI was not any single feature. It was integrating resume analysis, skill extraction, role matching, and roadmap generation into one coherent workflow. Each of these stages required different data-processing steps.

A skill gap identified during resume analysis had to translate meaningfully into a role recommendation. That recommendation then had to connect to a realistic learning pathway.

Personalisation made the problem harder. A useful recommendation requires the system to understand a user’s experience, compare it with industry requirements and turn that comparison into something actionable.

Sharma addresses this by connecting the different stages of the platform. Resume analysis feeds into skill-gap assessment, which then informs role recommendations and learning pathways.

She says this connected structure is what separates CareerStack AI from standalone resume analysers, job boards, or generic chatbots.

“It provides users with a connected view of their current skills, gaps, suitable opportunities, and recommended next steps,” Sharma adds.

Not Her First AI Project

CareerStack was not Sharma’s first AI project.

Sharma says her university coursework gave her the technical foundation for AI/ML. The unknown road for her was to figure out how to apply that knowledge systematically to problems outside the classroom.

“Samsung Innovation Campus strengthened my ability to approach problems systematically through a ‘question-first’ mindset, focusing on understanding real-world challenges before considering data, algorithms, or technology selection,” she says.

The programme introduced her to frameworks such as CRISP-DM, which helped her move through a project from understanding the problem to developing and deploying a solution. “Earlier, I would often think about algorithms first. Through SIC, I learned to start with the problem, understand the user, and then select the most appropriate technology,” Sharma said.

The programme also introduced her to Design Thinking, an approach built around empathy, iteration, and prototyping. Instead of relying purely on technical assumptions, Sharma started by identifying user pain points first. She built prototypes, tested them, gathered feedback, and refined from there.

Before that, she worked on AI-driven analytics systems, including one focused on HR-related spending. The system analysed spending, identified unusual expense patterns and assessed financial risk while producing AI-powered insights and visual reports around cost optimisation.

She is also working on a research project with a college mate called ARROW-RAG, short for Adaptive Retrieval, Reasoning, Observation, and Withdrawal for Reliable Agentic Generation.

The project focuses on improving the reliability of retrieval-augmented generation systems through adaptive retrieval, evidence verification and claim validation.

The work gives Sharma exposure to a different side of AI development. CareerStack is a product built around a user problem, while ARROW-RAG deals with the reliability of AI systems themselves.

Where AI Can Do the Most Good

Sharma sees education as the area where she would like to spend more time.

She also sees e-commerce as an important area for AI in India. There, she points to applications such as product recommendations, demand forecasting, inventory optimisation, customer support, fraud detection and seller analytics.

Education interests her for a different reason. “In education, AI can address the scale problem,” Sharma says. She believes AI can provide personalised learning paths, identify knowledge gaps and offer targeted feedback to students who may not have access to quality mentoring.

For Sharma, the potential impact extends beyond the individual student.

“Education creates a foundational impact; when people gain relevant skills, access better learning opportunities, and make informed decisions, the benefits extend beyond individual success to broader economic growth and workforce development,” she adds.

Sharma came across Samsung Innovation Campus through her college group. After registering, she went through an MCQ-based assessment and was selected for the programme.

Samsung Innovation Campus is Samsung India’s programme for training young people in emerging technologies. Its 2026 edition aims to train 20,000 people across 10 states, in partnership with the Electronics Sector Skills Council of India and the Telecom Sector Skill Council.

Samsung says the programme has trained more than 26,500 people in India since its launch in 2022. The programme targets people aged 18 to 25 and combines technical training with project-based learning and mentorship.

For Sharma, the most useful part of the experience was how it changed the way she approached a problem. This shift can be seen in CareerStack’s design.

The product is still early and has not yet been monetised. For now, Sharma is continuing to test whether the idea works for the people she built it for, while exploring what she can build next.

title: Dell Launches uDaan to Skill 23,000 Youths for India’s AI Economy
content:
The programme aims to train 23,000 youth across 190 institutions in AI, cloud computing and electronics manufacturing.

US technology giant Dell Technologies has launched uDaan, a national skilling programme to prepare 23,000 young people for careers in artificial intelligence, cloud computing and electronics manufacturing.

The programme is being delivered through a consortium comprising FITT-IIT Delhi, Learning Links Foundation and Generation India Foundation. It will operate across 190 government and aided institutions in five major technology corridors — Delhi NCR, Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Chennai and Pune.

As part of the programme, 100 ITIs and 90 higher education institutions will offer industry-aligned training across four areas: AI Application Development, Cloud Development, Assembly Line Operations and Field Technician roles.

FITT-IIT Delhi will design and certify the curricula, co-validated by more than 40 employers spanning technology companies, electronics manufacturers, global capability centres, and hyperscalers.

Learning Links Foundation will lead higher education delivery and institutional onboarding, while Generation India Foundation will oversee ITI execution and employment linkages.

“India's AI economy is creating roles faster than employers are able to fill them, and those roles require new skillsets,” Manish Gupta, President and Managing Director, Dell Technologies India, said in a statement. He added that uDaan is intended to create pathways from education to employment while supporting AI adoption and workforce readiness.

In its first year, uDaan aims to support 25 deep-tech startups among higher education learners and 10 micro-enterprises among ITI learners, with access to technical mentorship, bootcamps, accelerator networks, and potential capital.

Dell said more than 2,000 hours of employee mentoring will be provided across the five corridors, covering career guidance, AI awareness and interview preparation.

Dell said it will work with officials from the state Directorate of Vocational Education and Training and the Directorate of Technical Education from the first year, with the aim of creating a model that can eventually be adopted by state governments and other companies.

The programme builds on Dell’s earlier community initiatives in India. Over the past decade, the company said its education and innovation programmes have reached more than 50 million K-12 beneficiaries through digital literacy, vocational skills and experiential learning initiatives.

Spotify’s Portal for Backstage routes routine coding-agent tasks to cheaper models, reducing the amount of frontier-model tokens Claude Code consumes.

Spotify says its internal developer platform, Portal by Spotify, cut token consumption from Claude Code by about 90% in tests by routing file-reading and predictable code-generation tasks to cheaper AI models, rather than using Anthropic’s frontier coding model for every operation.

The approach uses Portal’s “AiKA Modes”, which are declarative agents that run on ephemeral runtimes. Developers can specify the model, instructions, parameters and MCP tools for each mode without managing separate infrastructure or API keys.

Spotify engineer Dimitri Mazmanov tested the approach on a Java monorepo using two modes: a bulk-reader for reading multiple files and a code-writer for predictable code-generation tasks. Both examples use Google’s Gemini 2.5 Flash as the worker model, although Portal can be configured with other models.

“Most of what an AI coding agent does for me isn't thinking. It's I/O,” Mazmanov wrote. The setup keeps those token-heavy operations away from Claude Code while retaining Claude for tasks that require more reasoning.

The routing is enforced through a Claude Code plugin called Shunt. It uses PreToolUse hooks to intercept large file reads and redirect Claude to the bulk-reader mode. By default, reads of files exceeding 350 lines are blocked, while targeted reads using offsets and limits continue to pass through.

A second mode handles output-heavy tasks such as generating tests, configuration scaffolding and type stubs. It receives a specification and reference file, generates the code and can write it directly to disk, meaning Claude does not need to consume the generated output in its own context.

Spotify said the test measured Claude's token consumption across four scenarios in a Java monorepo, with mean savings from bulk reading of around 90%. The code-generation case was harder to measure because the unoptimised workflow includes both reading reference files and generating code as Claude output.

The approach has limits, and Spotify said the worker models are not intended to handle debugging, architectural decisions or safety-critical reasoning.

Besides, delegated analysis also does not reliably provide the line-level information Claude needs for editing. Network latency is another constraint, with typical delegation taking 10–30 seconds and Portal imposing a 30-second limit per invocation.

Mazmanov described the broader approach as “model routing powered by AiKA modes”, allowing teams to change the worker model or instructions without modifying the routing plugin itself.

Spotify made the bulk-reader and code-writer modes publicly available through AiKA, allowing developers to reuse or customise them across projects.

title: OpenAI Declares ‘AGI Era’ after Launching GPT 6
content:
The company believes that it is the best model in the world for professional work.

OpenAI has announced GPT-6 Astra, its new frontier model for computer use, professional work, science, coding, and cybersecurity.

The model is rolling out initially to a limited set of organisations before becoming available to ChatGPT Plus, Pro, Business and Enterprise users, as well as through the OpenAI API and AWS.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said in a post on X that Astra is intended to enable “a new generation of entrepreneurship, scientific discovery, and building”, adding that the company believes it is “the best model in the world for computer use, professional work, science, coding, cybersecurity, and more”.

Altman also said the additional time before launch was needed to meet the “safety and alignment standards required for this capability level”.

OpenAI president Greg Brockman went further during a briefing with media outlets, describing the release as the beginning of an AGI era. “Welcome to the AGI era,” Brockman said at the end of the briefing, according to Business Insider, The Information, Axios and others.

He also said that, looking back in the future, he believed people could identify this period as when AGI was created. “For me personally, I do think we’re there,” Brockman said.

Astra has saturated several frontier evaluations, including ARC-AGI-3, ExploitBench and FrontierMath Tier 4, while setting new highs across computer-use, professional-work, coding and scientific evaluations.

OpenAI said the model can also complete complex computer tasks faster, reporting a 1.9x improvement in task completion speed over GPT-5.6 Sol on the Mind2Web benchmark.

The model is priced at $10 per million input tokens and $50 per million output tokens through the standard API. OpenAI also offers a Fast mode at twice the standard price, with up to twice the processing speed.

Despite the higher headline price, the company reports lower estimated API costs on several evaluations because Astra uses fewer tokens or completes tasks faster.

Astra also represents a higher level of cybersecurity capability.

OpenAI said it meets the “Critical” threshold under its Preparedness Framework and discovered two previously unknown zero-day vulnerabilities during testing. The company has therefore added stronger safeguards and monitoring, while noting that Astra’s written reasoning is harder to monitor than GPT-5.6 Sol’s.

The AI platform will continue supporting open-source and open-weight models across different hardware, cloud and inference providers.

NVIDIA has agreed to acquire AI platform Hugging Face for $12.93 billion, CEO Jensen Huang announced on September 3.

The deal will bring Hugging Face’s platform for AI models, datasets and applications under NVIDIA, while the platform will continue to support open-source and open-weight models across different hardware and cloud providers.

“Together, we will scale Hugging Face’s platform, strengthen its infrastructure and expand access to AI for developers and institutions worldwide,” Huang said in a statement.

Hugging Face has more than 18 million developers, researchers and creators using its platform to share more than 3 million models, 500,000 datasets and 1 million applications. More than 200,000 companies use the platform to discover, evaluate, customise and deploy AI.

NVIDIA said Hugging Face will remain an open platform and developers will be able to choose their models, frameworks, cloud and inference providers, and computing platforms. “NVIDIA compute will not be required to build on or deploy through Hugging Face,” Huang said.

The platform will also continue to support multi-cloud and multi-accelerator development and deployment. This will allow developers to use hardware and infrastructure from different providers.

The acquisition comes as open-weight AI models become more widely used by startups, businesses, universities and public institutions. Huang said open models allow organisations to build on advanced AI capabilities without having to train models from scratch.

NVIDIA has contributed more than 500 models and over 250 open datasets to Hugging Face. The company said it is the largest contributor of open models and data to the platform.

In July, Huang co-authored an open letter calling for support for open-weight AI models, arguing that they can broaden access to advanced AI, strengthen competition and prevent the technology from becoming concentrated among a few companies.

“In addition to doubling down on NVIDIA’s massive contributions to open-source AI (I called them the “King of American open-source AI” earlier this year), they’ve committed to strongly supporting Hugging Face and our mission while keeping the platform open, independent and compute-agnostic,” Clément Delangue, CEO of Hugging Face, said in a post on X

“Together, we think we can make open source the default way to build AI, with the goal of empowering 100 million AI builders to own their intelligence rather than rent it,” he added.

Following the acquisition, NVIDIA plans to use its infrastructure, engineering resources and global reach to expand Hugging Face’s capabilities in areas including platform reliability, safety, model evaluation, inference and deployment.

Huang said Delangue approached him while considering the company’s next phase and believed NVIDIA would be a suitable home for the platform and its community.

“Hugging Face will remain an open platform for the entire AI ecosystem,” Huang said.

title: MongoDB Appoints Richard Scott as SVP for Asia Pacific & Japan
content:
Scott, who brings more than 25 years of experience across the technology sector, joins MongoDB after holding senior roles at Salesforce, Microsoft and SAP.

MongoDB has appointed technology industry veteran Richard Scott as Senior Vice President for Asia Pacific and Japan (APJ), as the company looks to accelerate regional growth and help businesses move from experimenting with artificial intelligence to deploying AI applications at scale.

Scott, who brings more than 25 years of experience across the technology sector, joins MongoDB after holding senior roles at Salesforce, Microsoft and SAP. Based in Sydney, he will lead the company’s regional strategy and expand its presence across key APJ markets.

The appointment comes as businesses across Asia Pacific and Japan increasingly shift from AI pilots to real-world production deployments. With organisations seeking to build and scale AI applications more efficiently, MongoDB aims to strengthen its role in providing the data infrastructure needed to support these initiatives.

“Solving the data layer is going to be the defining technology question for organisations in the AI era,” Scott said.

MongoDB counts several major companies across the region among its customers, including LG U+, Cathay Pacific, Samsung and Woolworths. Its customer base also includes fast-growing and AI-focused companies such as Heidi, Zomato, Canva, Grab and Emergent.

The company has continued to expand its regional footprint. MongoDB recently opened a new office in Kuala Lumpur and plans to open another in Tokyo in September, following increased investment in the Japanese market.

The company has also expanded its engineering teams in India and Australia. As part of its broader developer-focused strategy, MongoDB has announced plans to upskill two million developers through academic programs by 2030.

title: IIT Madras-Backed Bodhan AI, AI4Bharat Launch 4 AI Models for Students & Teachers
content:
The models will be offered as Digital Public Goods, with open weights and sovereign APIs that let developers build applications without training language models from scratch.

Bodhan AI, a centre of excellence in AI for education incubated at IIT Madras, has launched four AI models for speech recognition, speech generation, machine translation and optical character recognition (OCR), in partnership with AI4Bharat.

The models are being released as Digital Public Goods through open-weight models and hosted APIs on sovereign infrastructure. The initiative is part of the Bharat EduAI Stack, which aims to provide a common AI infrastructure layer for multilingual education in India.

The four models cover 27 languages for automatic speech recognition (ASR), 23 languages for OCR, 22 languages for machine translation through Bodhan-Translate, and 23 languages for text-to-speech (TTS).

The models are trained and optimised using NVIDIA Nemotron open models and libraries, including the NVIDIA NeMo framework for ASR, machine translation and OCR. Bodhan AI has post-trained NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 ASR for Indian languages, including regional dialects and accents. The models are served using NVIDIA TensorRT-LLM and vLLM inference microservices.

Prof Mitesh Khapra, Principal Investigator at Bodhan AI, said the project was intended to create a shared infrastructure layer rather than separate AI systems for individual institutions.

“We built these voice and vision models, and made them accessible as Digital Public Goods on a Digital Public Infrastructure, so that efforts across the country don't remain fragmented,” Khapra said.

He added that edtech companies, startups, researchers, universities, technology companies and government partners could use the models to develop applications for Indian users.

The speech recognition model can allow students to interact with AI tutors through voice in their preferred language, while TTS can enable AI systems to respond in Indian languages. OCR can help education systems process textbooks, worksheets, documents and handwritten answers. Bodhan-Translate can be used to translate educational content between Indian languages.

Prof V Kamakoti, Director of IIT Madras, said the infrastructure could help expand access to AI across India’s linguistic diversity.

“India’s AI journey cannot be built on technology alone. It must be built on technology that understands India,” Kamakoti said.

The models will also power Bodhan AI’s own education applications, including Student TutorBot and Teacher Assistant Bot.

Student TutorBot is designed for students in Classes 6–12 and is based on NCERT and SCERT curricula. Students can interact with it through text or voice across 22 Indian languages. The system uses textbook content to provide explanations, examples and assessments and can guide students through problems using interactive tools and a digital canvas.

Teacher Assistant Bot is designed to help teachers plan, create, assign and assess classroom work. Teachers can generate lesson plans, worksheets, quizzes, homework and revision material by specifying parameters such as grade, subject, topic, duration and difficulty. They can also upload student work for evaluation against specified marking criteria.

Bodhan AI said AI-generated outputs in the Teacher Assistant Bot are intended to remain subject to teacher review. Teachers can edit, regenerate or discard outputs rather than having AI make classroom decisions automatically.

Prof Balaraman Ravindran, Head of the Wadhwani School of Data Science and AI at IIT Madras, said developing AI for India requires more than adapting existing systems to Indian languages.

“Building AI for India requires going beyond adapting existing models to Indian languages. It requires developing foundational capabilities that understand the richness and diversity of our languages, contexts and educational needs,” Ravindran added.

Bodhan AI said government and public institutions could use the infrastructure for multilingual education and other public-service applications, while edtech companies could integrate the models through APIs without developing foundational models themselves. Startups and researchers can access the open-weight models for adaptation and further development.

The hosted API infrastructure is being designed around a sovereign deployment approach, with data anonymisation protocols and compliance with applicable national education data frameworks. The company said this is intended to give institutions and ecosystem partners greater control over deployment while supporting requirements around data governance, privacy and security.

NVIDIA and Bodhan AI are also collaborating on datasets, training recipes and evaluations for future foundational models for Indian languages. AI4Bharat is contributing its work on Indian-language datasets, tools, models and applications to the initiative.

title: Havells Brings Agentic AI Voice Control to 2.67 Mn Connected Home Appliances
content:
The voice assistant can understand natural and code-mixed speech, coordinate multiple appliances at once, and retain context across conversations.

Havells has launched an Agentic AI Voice feature in its Havells One app that allows users to control connected appliances through natural speech in English and seven Indian languages.

The feature is built by Havells Centre for Research & Innovation (CRI), with ElevenLabs providing the streaming Speech-to-Text and Text-to-Speech models for the voice interface.

The feature is live for all 2.67 million Havells One mobile app users and supports Hindi, Tamil, Telugu, Bengali, Kannada, Gujarati and Malayalam, in addition to English.

Users can use voice commands to control appliances, rooms, scenes and coordinated actions across connected devices. The feature currently works across Havells fans, air purifiers, water purifiers and water heaters, as well as Lloyd air conditioners and washing machines, Crabtree smart switches and upcoming smart home products.

Unlike Havells’ earlier voice experience, which relied on predefined commands and supported English and Hindi on selected appliances, the new system is designed to understand user intent. It can also handle code-mixed speech, where users switch between languages while speaking.

For instance, a request to “make the room comfortable” can trigger coordinated actions across an air conditioner, air purifier, fan and lights. Requests involving multiple devices can be executed across different connectivity protocols.

The agent also retains context across conversations and can ask users to clarify ambiguous requests. It can explain device error codes in spoken language and is being extended beyond device control to areas such as product FAQs, troubleshooting and scheduling.

“This Agentic AI Voice capability is a breakthrough for our customers, allowing them to control and interact with their devices naturally, without having to remember commands or learn rules,” said Dipesh Shah, Executive President and CTO, Havells.

“Its potential is limitless and will continue to expand as new capabilities are added across our devices and services. As a daily-use AI experience, it showcases the transformative potential of AI agents, far beyond the traditional voice interfaces of the past,” he added.

Havells said its CRI team evaluated voice AI models based on recognition accuracy, multilingual support, latency and voice synthesis. The company moved the solution into production in approximately six weeks, with support from ElevenLabs’ Forward Deployed Engineering team for voice quality and regional language pronunciation tuning.

“People have always had to learn the interface of communicating: the commands, the syntax, the order they come in. That is hardest in India, where a household does not speak one language and often moves between three in a single sentence,” said Karthik Rajaram, General Manager and Country Head, India, ElevenLabs.

“Powered by ElevenLabs, Havells now runs seven Indian languages alongside English across an appliance range, so the person no longer has to meet the technology halfway. They say what they want to the agent, in the language they were already thinking in, and the devices respond,” he added.

Havells plans to expand the feature to more Indian languages and bring additional appliances onto the voice platform. The company also plans to add greater personalisation for individual household members and extend voice interactions to product support, troubleshooting and scheduling.

title: Genesys Launches New Innovations To Automate End-To-End Customer Service
content:
Snippet: The platform retains information across interactions, determines its actions and coordinates work between AI and human employees while operating within predefined business rules.

Genesys has introduced AI tools to help businesses go beyond chatbots to automate customer service journeys from request to resolution.

As enterprises move from standalone chatbots to AI systems that can handle multi-step tasks, Genesys, a global leader in agentic orchestration, is positioning its cloud platform as an autonomous AI layer for customer service. The platform retains information across interactions, determines its actions and coordinates work between AI and human employees while operating within predefined business rules.

On September 3, the company unveiled new capabilities through its AI systems, announcing Genesys Cloud Navigator, Genesys Cloud Orchestrator, Contextual Intelligence and the AI Control Plane at its Xperience event. Its autonomous AI is designed to deliver adaptive, personalised and governed experiences.

Starting with Genesys Cloud Navigator as its entry point, it uses customer interactions, historical data, conversational information and enterprise data to determine the customer’s goal and direct them to the next step.

As the journey progresses, Genesys Cloud Orchestrator creates an ideal plan to achieve the desired outcome and coordinates decision-making. This entails identifying the current situation and reasoning over context, policies and guardrails to determine the next action and move work across AI, human agents and systems. It enables an end-to-end journey that can pause, resume and adapt while keeping the customer’s intended outcome in focus.

Contextual Intelligence turns interactions into persistent enterprise memory by connecting customer details, conversational data, history, business events and real-time signals. By preserving this intelligence over time, it gives its AI a richer understanding of the customer and helps inform relevant decisions.

The fourth component, the AI Control Plane, serves as the operating layer for the company’s AI. This involves providing governance and oversight, and allowing the enterprise to monitor the activities of its AI, including agentic orchestration, Genesys Cloud Navigator, Genesys Cloud Orchestrator and Contextual Intelligence. It enforces policies and ensures that actions remain within the company’s business boundaries.

“Autonomous AI is finally pushing customer service beyond individual interactions and isolated use cases,” said Hayley Sutherland, Research Manager, Conversational AI at IDC.

Genesys said both Contextual Intelligence and the AI Control Plane are now available, while Navigator is expected to be generally available between November 2026 and January 2027.

title: For GCCs, Non-Tech Hiring in India Set to Cross 5 Lakh Roles by 2028
content:
Sales operations, finance and business operations are expected to account for more than 60% of non-tech GCC demand.

India’s GCCs are increasingly looking beyond traditional technology hiring, with demand for non-tech talent projected to cross five lakh roles by 2028, according to a new report by Quess Corp.

The report, India’s GCC Non-Tech Talent Landscape, finds that sales operations, finance and business operations together account for more than 60% of non-tech GCC demand, signalling a broader shift in the role of GCCs as they evolve from execution centres into strategic and decision-making hubs.

Demand for non-tech roles grew 17.2% year-on-year in the first half of 2026, with digitally enabled business functions emerging as a major driver. Digital platforms, analytics, automation, and AI are increasingly shaping these roles rather than traditional process execution.

Mid-career professionals are at the centre of this shift. Employees with 7–12 years of experience accounted for nearly 60% of non-tech GCC demand in 2025, while this talent pool is estimated to reach 2.5 lakh professionals in 2026, growing at a three-year CAGR of 21%.

“Centres that were set up to execute instructions are becoming intelligence and strategy hubs, trusted with judgment rather than just delivery, and nearly one in every three business operations postings and one in every four finance, risk and governance postings already reflect that, requiring digital platforms, analytics or AI tools as standard,” Kapil Joshi, CEO of IT Staffing, Quess Corp said. “It’s the same shift driving GCCs to become genuinely multi-functional: across our base of 2,400 plus centres, nearly 90% already run multiple capability towers instead of siloed functions, and we expect that model to define the next wave of centres coming into India.”

The geographic distribution of this demand is also widening. Bengaluru accounted for nearly 25% of non-tech GCC demand in the first half of 2026, followed by Delhi at 12%, Mumbai at 10%, Hyderabad at 9% and Pune at 7%. Meanwhile, emerging locations and tier-2 cities collectively accounted for nearly 35% of demand, pointing to a gradual expansion of GCC hiring beyond India’s established technology hubs.

The sectoral picture is similarly broadening. Pharma and healthcare led demand for non-tech GCC talent, followed by BFSI and technology and product companies, with governance, analytics, compliance and transformation capabilities driving recruitment.

Quess expects the 2026–28 period to be defined less by sheer hiring volumes and more by capability-led recruitment. Business operations and transformation are expected to remain the biggest drivers, alongside demand across finance, sales and marketing, supply chain and procurement, HR, and research and analytics.

The report points to a fundamental change in what GCCs expect from non-tech employees. Rather than hiring purely for functional expertise, centres increasingly seek professionals who can combine domain knowledge, digital fluency and decision-making responsibility.

This suggests the next phase of India’s GCC expansion may be measured not simply by how many people these centres employ, but by how much strategic responsibility they are able to take on.

As AI automates routine processes, the premium is increasingly shifting towards employees who can interpret data, exercise judgement, manage stakeholders and drive enterprise transformation.

Gnani claims its Evon v3.3 outperforms Sarvam’s 105B model on 10 of 11 Indian languages while using fewer active parameters. Its bigger bet is that enterprises will want to own and control the AI they deploy.

For years, Indian enterprises have faced a choice: use powerful foreign AI models or build more of their AI stack locally.

The IndiaAI Mission is trying to change that. Twelve organisations and consortia have now been selected to develop indigenous foundation models and large or small language models. They include Sarvam AI, Soket AI, Gnani AI and the IIT Bombay-led BharatGen consortium.

Gnani is taking a different route from the companies building very large general-purpose models.

The Bengaluru-based voice AI company recently launched Gnani Artha, a sovereign AI stack that combines its Evon v3.3 language model with Plexus, an agentic AI platform for enterprise and government workflows. Vice President C.P. Radhakrishnan unveiled the stack in New Delhi on August 28.

At the centre of Artha is Evon v3.3, a 30-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model. Around 3.5 billion parameters are active for a given token. The model supports 11 languages, including Hindi, Bengali, Telugu, Tamil, Marathi, Gujarati, Kannada, Malayalam, Odia and Punjabi, along with English. It has a 128K context window and is available on Hugging Face under an Apache 2.0 licence.

Gnani is positioning Evon less as another frontier model and more as infrastructure for enterprises that want to build AI around their own data.

That distinction is central to the company's strategy.

“We are an enterprise-focused company, and we work with 200 organisations in about five countries,” Gnani CEO and co-founder Ganesh Gopalan tells AIM. “Our focus is the reason for launching this also is fairly simple… taking an open source, open weight model rather than a broader closed frontier model.”

The argument is straightforward. Enterprises may not always need the biggest model available. They may need a model that performs well on their languages, runs at a manageable cost and can be deployed within infrastructure they control.

The 105B Model Challenge

Gnani is making an aggressive claim with Evon v3.3.

The company says the model outperforms Sarvam AI’s 105-billion-parameter model on MILU, an Indic-language understanding benchmark, across 10 of the 11 languages tested. It also says Evon outperforms Sarvam's 30B model across all 11 languages.

These are company-reported results, rather than independently verified findings. Gnani says its testing covered dozens of benchmarks and that Evon is available for external evaluation.

The comparison is still significant. It challenges the assumption that a larger parameter count automatically translates into better performance on Indian languages.

But model size alone is not the point Gnani is trying to make.

Evon is a mixture-of-experts model. While it has 30 billion parameters in total, only about 3.5 billion are activated for each token. This reduces the computational cost per inference compared with a dense model of similar size.

For enterprises, Gnani argues, the more relevant question is not simply how large a model is. It is how well it performs on a specific workload and how much it costs to run.

“We are not doing research projects. We want to do a model that enterprises will pick and make ROI for them,” Gopalan says.

Fewer Tokens, Lower Costs

Tokenisation is another part of Gnani's pitch.

The company claims Evon uses about 20% fewer tokens per Indian-language word than the tokeniser used by the GPT-5 family. It also claims to use less than half the tokens required by byte-level tokenisers used by models such as DeepSeek, Llama and Qwen.

Gnani says the gains vary by language. It claims Evon uses 37% to 42% fewer tokens for languages such as Gujarati and Malayalam compared with certain competing models.

These figures are also based on the company's own testing and should be treated as such.

The underlying idea, however, is important for enterprise AI. Fewer tokens can reduce inference costs and allow applications to process more information within a fixed context window.

That matters when an AI system is handling millions of interactions.

“You’re doing it because you want to make something work, not a POC, but you want to make something work in production,” Gopalan says. “Fine, you'll get great accuracy [in research], but will it make money for you?”

Sovereignty Means Control

Evon is available as an open-weight model. Gnani says it can be deployed within an organisation's own data centre or virtual private cloud.

That gives enterprises more control over where their data is processed. It also allows them to customise the model for specific workloads.

This is where Artha's second component, Plexus, comes in.

Plexus is an agentic AI platform that allows enterprises to build workflows involving multiple AI agents. Potential applications include government grievance handling and banking reconciliation.

For example, one agent could process a citizen complaint. Another could classify it. A third could route it to the relevant department.

But Gnani is not pitching full autonomy for every use case.

Gopalan says regulated industries will continue to require human oversight.

“Having a simplistic notion that all agents will be 100% autonomous, you are going to have orchestrator agents with about a million agents that work for that goal may not be true for every industry,” he says.

That caution is important as enterprises begin experimenting with agentic systems that can access internal data and take actions on employees' behalf.

Compute Is Still The Constraint

Gnani's launch also highlights a problem facing India's sovereign AI ambitions: compute.

Training and running large models requires access to GPUs. For smaller companies, that can be a significant constraint.

“The key constraint has been GPUs and it will be GPUs,” Gopalan says. “Especially today when it is really so tough to get hold of any form of compute.”

He credits government-backed access to compute with helping Gnani develop its models.

The IndiaAI Mission has expanded access to GPU infrastructure for startups, researchers and other users. The government said in 2025 that more than 34,000 GPUs had been provisioned through the IndiaAI Compute Portal.

But Gopalan expects the next challenge to be inference efficiency.

“The future is going to be a bunch of different things. One is the quality of your model. But what is going to be equally important is the ability of your model to run on various inferencing chips,” he says.

Gnani is currently targeting 11 Indian languages with Evon and wants to eventually expand to all 22 scheduled Indian languages.

The company also sees a market beyond India. Gopalan says it has received interest from countries in Africa, the Middle East and East Asia that face similar questions around local languages, data control and dependence on foreign AI systems.

From Text To Voice

Evon is not Gnani's final destination.

The company was selected under the IndiaAI Mission to build a 14-billion-parameter voice AI foundation model for multilingual, real-time speech processing. The government's programme describes it as a model with advanced reasoning capabilities.

Gnani has previously said the voice model is intended to support real-time speech-to-speech applications and eventually expand across India's 22 scheduled languages.

For Gnani, Evon provides the language foundation for that larger ambition.

The company is therefore making two bets at once.

The first is that Indian-language AI does not always need a massive model to compete on specific workloads.

The second is that enterprises will increasingly care about where their AI runs, how much it costs and how much control they have over it.

Evon v3.3 is an early test of that thesis. The benchmark claims will need to survive independent scrutiny. But if the model can deliver comparable performance at a fraction of the compute cost, Gnani may have found a more practical way to sell sovereign AI to enterprises.

title: Adobe Names Anil Chakravarthy as CEO, Shantanu Narayen to Become Executive Chair
content:
The leadership change comes as Adobe expands its focus on agentic software across creativity, productivity and customer experience.

Adobe has appointed Anil Chakravarthy as its next President and Chief Executive Officer, with the leadership transition set to take effect on December 1, 2026. Current CEO Shantanu Narayen will become Executive Chair and work with Chakravarthy during the transition.

Chakravarthy, who currently leads Adobe’s Customer Experience Orchestration business and worldwide field operations, will also join Adobe’s Board of Directors when he becomes CEO.

“I could not be more confident that Anil is the right person to lead Adobe’s growth in an AI-driven era and look forward to working closely with him in my new role as executive chair,” Narayen said in a statement

Chakravarthy said he would focus on growth and Adobe’s position in agentic software across creativity, productivity and customer experience.

“I am deeply honoured to have been chosen to lead Adobe during this pivotal moment,” Chakravarthy said. “I’m energised by the opportunity to fuel growth and drive Adobe's leadership in the next era of agentic software for creativity, productivity and customer experience.”

Chakravarthy joined Adobe in January 2020 as Executive Vice President and General Manager of its Digital Experience business. Later that year, he also took responsibility for worldwide field operations serving enterprise customers across Adobe’s product portfolio. He became president of Digital Experience and worldwide field operations in December 2021.

During his tenure, Chakravarthy led Adobe’s expansion in Customer Experience Orchestration, including the development of products such as Adobe CX Enterprise, GenStudio and Brand Visibility. He also oversaw the scaling of Adobe Experience Platform and the introduction of CX Enterprise Coworker.

Chakravarthy was also involved in Adobe’s acquisitions and integration of Workfront and Semrush.

Before joining Adobe, Chakravarthy served as CEO of Informatica for four years. He joined the company in 2013 as an executive vice president and previously held executive roles at Symantec and VeriSign, along with a role at McKinsey & Company.

Chakravarthy holds a Bachelor of Technology in Computer Science and Engineering from the Institute of Technology, Varanasi, and a master's degree and PhD from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.

Narayen has led Adobe since December 2007, overseeing the company’s shift toward a subscription-based business model and its expansion into digital experience and AI-powered products. As Executive Chair, he will continue working with the company and Chakravarthy after the transition.

title: NVIDIA Confirms $12.9 Bn Deal to Acquire Hugging Face
content:
The AI platform will continue supporting open-source and open-weight models across different hardware, cloud and inference providers.

NVIDIA has agreed to acquire AI platform Hugging Face for $12.93 billion, CEO Jensen Huang announced on September 3.

The deal will bring Hugging Face’s platform for AI models, datasets and applications under NVIDIA, while the platform will continue to support open-source and open-weight models across different hardware and cloud providers.

“Together, we will scale Hugging Face’s platform, strengthen its infrastructure and expand access to AI for developers and institutions worldwide,” Huang said in a statement.

Hugging Face has more than 18 million developers, researchers and creators using its platform to share more than 3 million models, 500,000 datasets and 1 million applications. More than 200,000 companies use the platform to discover, evaluate, customise and deploy AI.

NVIDIA said Hugging Face will remain an open platform and developers will be able to choose their models, frameworks, cloud and inference providers, and computing platforms. “NVIDIA compute will not be required to build on or deploy through Hugging Face,” Huang said.

The platform will also continue to support multi-cloud and multi-accelerator development and deployment. This will allow developers to use hardware and infrastructure from different providers.

The acquisition comes as open-weight AI models become more widely used by startups, businesses, universities and public institutions. Huang said open models allow organisations to build on advanced AI capabilities without having to train models from scratch.

NVIDIA has contributed more than 500 models and over 250 open datasets to Hugging Face. The company said it is the largest contributor of open models and data to the platform.

In July, Huang co-authored an open letter calling for support for open-weight AI models, arguing that they can broaden access to advanced AI, strengthen competition and prevent the technology from becoming concentrated among a few companies.

“In addition to doubling down on NVIDIA’s massive contributions to open-source AI (I called them the “King of American open-source AI” earlier this year), they’ve committed to strongly supporting Hugging Face and our mission while keeping the platform open, independent and compute-agnostic,” Clément Delangue, CEO of Hugging Face, said in a post on X

“Together, we think we can make open source the default way to build AI, with the goal of empowering 100 million AI builders to own their intelligence rather than rent it,” he added.

Following the acquisition, NVIDIA plans to use its infrastructure, engineering resources and global reach to expand Hugging Face’s capabilities in areas including platform reliability, safety, model evaluation, inference and deployment.

title: India has the Highest share of AI ‘Frontier Professionals’, Reveals Microsoft
content:
“We’re not going after prompting, speed, and more efficiency. We’re going after judgment, taste, critical thinking, quality control,” said Puneet Chandok, Microsoft India president.

India has the highest share of “Frontier Professionals” among the 10 markets studied in Microsoft’s 2026 Work Trend Index, with 32% of AI users classified in the group, twice the global average of 16%.

Microsoft defines Frontier Professionals as workers who redesign workflows around AI agents while retaining responsibility for outcomes.

Speaking at the Work Trend Index announcement in Bengaluru, Microsoft India and South Asia President Puneet Chandok said India was “not catching up to the AI frontier; it’s defining it”.

He said the shift was increasingly about how humans work alongside AI rather than simply adopting new models and tools.

The study of 20,000 AI users found that 78% of Indian AI users said AI enables them to produce work that was not possible a year ago, compared with 58% globally. Among Frontier Professionals in India, the figure rises to 85%.

India also leads in leadership alignment, with 44% saying their leadership is clearly aligned on AI, versus 26% globally.

He also revealed that India is slowly building a true risk culture in AI, with 25% of employees saying they’re rewarded simply for experimenting with AI—even before results show up- but stressed that this permission to experiment needs to expand far beyond a minority.

Moreover, human oversight remains central to AI use in India. India’s advantage is truly human,” said Chandhok. “We’re not going after prompting, speed, and more efficiency. We’re going after judgment, taste, critical thinking, quality control.”

Some 63% of Indian respondents identified quality control of AI output as a top skill, compared with 50% globally, while 59% cited critical thinking, versus 46% globally. Overall, 87% said they remain responsible for the thinking behind AI-assisted work.

“India is not betting on prompting. India is betting on judgment,” Chandok said, arguing that workers will increasingly need to interrogate AI outputs and apply judgement as agents take on more execution.

The investment takes BQP’s total funding to $8 million as it expands its platform beyond aerospace and defence.

BQP (formerly BosonQ Psi) has secured a strategic investment from IBM Ventures, taking its total funding to $8 million. The startup had secured $6.6 million until July 2025.

The investment will support the company’s expansion from engineering design into operational deployment. Venn10 Capital and existing investor Monta Vista Capital also participated in the investment round.

The company will use the funding to scale delivery and go-to-market activities. It also plans to expand beyond aerospace and defence. The funding extends a technical relationship between BQP and IBM that began in 2023 when BQP joined the IBM Quantum Network.

BQP said its contracted and committed revenue has increased eightfold since its 2025 seed round. The company claims that its customer base has tripled, while its platform users have grown 20-fold.

Its flagship platform, BQPhy, targets a limitation in classical physics simulations. BQP said classical software leaves about 85% of a GPU’s floating-point capacity unused. The platform aims to use that capacity to deliver physics simulations within operational decision windows.

BQPhy uses a physics-AI optimisation engine to resolve full physics while maintaining speed. It offers two solvers through a single software development kit. The platform also integrates with MATLAB and provides APIs for Python, Julia and other frameworks.

QuantumNOW, the company’s existing platform, runs on customers’ CPU and GPU infrastructure. BQP said each deployment identifies problems that could benefit from quantum processing units. This approach supports the development of QuantumMAX, its quantum-native solver.

“Users don’t have to change how they work to get quantum-accelerated results,” said Emily Fontaine, Global Head of IBM Ventures. She said BQP’s software gives enterprises a practical path to hybrid quantum-classical computing.

BQP’s aerospace and defence work includes an SBIR project with the US Space Force and SpaceWERX. The company said its system can propagate a catalogue of more than 3,000 space objects in under a second. It reported that the system is about 250 times faster than the open-source Orekit solver.

The company also holds a cooperative research agreement with the Air Force Research Laboratory. It has demonstrated BQPhy on radio-frequency signal problems with NavalX. With Modovolo, BQP developed propulsion optimisation for unmanned aerial vehicle mission profiles.

BQP is applying its platform to energy systems. Its work includes electric vehicle battery thermal management, funded by India’s Ministry of Heavy Industries and the Indian School of Business.

The startup said QuantumNOW is already in production, while QuantumMAX remains under development. At USNC/TAM 2026, the company ran QuantumMAX on quantum hardware to quantify uncertainty in computational fluid dynamics. It reported comparable accuracy to classical Monte Carlo using fewer samples.

“An engineer with a deadline doesn't care where the answer came from,” said Abhishek Chopra, BQP’s founder and CEO. “They care that it arrived in time and that the physics is right.”

Chopra said BQP had spent years integrating its technology into engineering workflows. He added that the company aims to ensure those workflows can support quantum machines when they become ready for wider use.
