The company is betting that enterprises moving from AI experimentation to large-scale deployment will create demand for a different mix of engineering, domain and analytics talent.

Enterprise AI and analytics company MathCo plans to create more than 2,000 specialised artificial intelligence roles as it shifts to an AI-native operating model, betting that the next phase of enterprise AI adoption will be driven less by standalone pilots and more by embedding AI into day-to-day business processes.

The Bengaluru-based company, which is marking a decade of operations, plans to build a workforce of more than 4,000 AI-native professionals across India and the US, up from a current headcount of about 2,000, with roughly 90% of it based in India.

The hiring and reskilling programme will include Forward Deployed Engineers (FDEs), a role that has gained prominence in the AI industry as companies look for engineers who can work directly with customers to build, customise and deploy AI systems in real-world environments.

“From a skill set perspective, I think a lot of things that we were using people for, like a lot of mundane tasks, or tasks that can be automated, that way of working has drastically shifted. So, people have gotten 20–30% more productive, which frees up their time to actually spend time on the insights on what they are really telling businesses to change about their operations or their supply chain or marketing. So, it has moved away from, let me clean this information or let me organise this information to what I should really recommend,” Co-Founder and CEO Sayandeb Banerjee said in a media roundtable.

MathCo is also targeting threefold revenue growth over the next four years, and the expansion is expected to come from deeper engagements with existing customers, new client wins and a broader portfolio of AI-native solutions.

Co-Founder and COO Aditya Kumbakonam says most large clients aren’t simply chasing lower costs but asking for more output at the same spend.

“Think of large companies. They always want more value. Anybody who was focused on “I can get 10% (cost reduction)” is not looking at it that way. We are also encouraging this, and our customers also take this into perspective,” says Kumbakonam.

The announcement comes as enterprise AI market enters a more difficult phase. While companies have rapidly experimented with generative AI and deployed individual use cases, many are now grappling with the harder problem of integrating AI into existing technology stacks, business processes and decision-making systems.

Banerjee says this shift has intensified sharply “over the last six to 12 months”, even as MathCo has been building towards an AI-native model for years. He adds that at MathCo, roles themselves aren't disappearing—only the skills underlying them are: “the roles don’t get obsolete, but the skills get obsolete,” he says.

FDEs are emerging as one such role. Unlike traditional offshore development teams, these engineers typically work close to the customer, translating business problems into AI applications and helping integrate them into production environments.

Kumbakonam says the industry has no ready-made pool of FDE talent to hire from, so MathCo expects 60-70% of its new AI workforce to come through internal training rather than lateral hiring.

title: Coforge Launches AI Platform to Help Enterprises Build & Run AI Within Their Own Environments
content: Listen5 minSHARESaveFollowPreferred SourceGoogle NewsWhatsAppTelegramMid-tier IT services firm Coforge has launched an enterprise AI platform that allows companies to build, fine-tune, deploy and operate AI systems within their own controlled environments, as businesses increasingly look to reduce dependence on individual model providers.The platform, called Coforge AI Launchpad, is designed to work across cloud environments and allows enterprises to route workloads between open-weight and frontier AI models depending on business, regulatory, performance and cost considerations, the company said in a statement.“Enterprise AI is entering a new phase where control matters as much as capability,” Lalit Wadhwa, Chief Technology Officer, Coforge, said in a statement. “Organisations need the optionality to leverage the best AI models available without creating new forms of technology dependency. Coforge AI Launchpad gives enterprises a governed foundation that preserves ownership of data, intellectual property, and AI environment while remaining flexible enough to adapt as the market evolves.”The move comes as enterprises move beyond experimentation with generative AI and begin deploying AI systems in production, where issues around data sovereignty, governance, infrastructure and the availability of skilled talent have become bigger constraints.Coforge said the transition from AI pilots to production remains difficult because of fragmented infrastructure, talent shortages and governance and auditability requirements. Its new offering, powered by its Nuuron platform, combines the underlying infrastructure with model engineering, deployment and managed services.The platform is already being deployed by clients with stringent regulatory and data-sovereignty requirements. These include a sovereign AI environment for a US-based clinical healthcare intelligence company and an AI-routing deployment for a US bank that helped reduce AI operating costs while maintaining governance and auditability.Coforge is positioning the offering around AI ownership and flexibility, rather than tying enterprises to a particular model or technology provider. This could become increasingly relevant as companies weigh the cost, performance and regulatory implications of using proprietary models versus open-weight alternatives.The AI Launchpad comprises six broad service areas spanning strategy and advisory, infrastructure and platform, model engineering and customisation, deployment and integration, LLM operations and observability, and governance, FinOps and managed-run services.For Coforge, the launch also expands its pitch from delivering AI-enabled applications and services to managing more of the underlying enterprise AI stack. title: Bengaluru’s Makr Microsystems Raises ₹10.2 Cr Led by Bluehill VC
content:
The funding will support Makr’s technology development, customer validation and path towards commercial deployment.

Bluehill VC has led a ₹10.2 crore seed funding round in semiconductor metrology startup Makr Microsystems. Artha Venture Fund also participated in the round. The investment will support technology development, customer validation and commercial deployment.

Bengaluru-based Makr Microsystems is developing nanoscale 3D subsurface metrology products for semiconductor manufacturers. Its technology helps chipmakers visualise and measure structures and defects beneath semiconductor surfaces.

The startup uses Acoustic Atomic Force Microscopy (AAFM), acoustic sensing and 3D data analytics. Its approach aims to enable high-resolution, non-destructive measurement below semiconductor surfaces.

The technology targets inspection challenges in advanced semiconductor manufacturing. Makr says it can support process control, defect detection and yield improvement.

Makr’s initial applications include advanced packaging, hybrid bonding, buried interfaces and chiplet interconnects. The company is also targeting defect detection in semiconductor manufacturing.

Current metrology techniques involve trade-offs involving resolution, depth and inspection speed. They can also require sample damage or preparation, according to the company.

Makr Founder Ashwin Lal said semiconductor manufacturing is creating structures that are increasingly difficult to measure. He said the shift towards 3D architectures makes subsurface analysis important for improving yield.

“Our goal is to make the subsurface measurable, non-destructively and at the resolution the next generation of chipmaking demands,” Lal said.

Bluehill said the investment reflects its focus on technologies deeper within the semiconductor value chain. The fund is looking beyond chip companies towards equipment, materials and measurement technologies.

The firm recently announced the final close of its maiden fund at ₹400 crore. It invests from Seed to Series A across sectors including semiconductors, defence, space and advanced materials.

The four minutes after a talk ends are the most valuable and least used minutes of any conference. Here is how to use them without being the person everyone edges away from.

AIM Media House·SEPTEMBER 4, 2026, 9:00 AM·Updated OCTOBER 4, 2026, 1:40 PM

A speaker finishes. The applause dies. They step off the stage, unclip the microphone, and stand near the front of the room gathering their things.

For about four minutes, one of the most knowledgeable people in the building stands alone, still fully in the material they have just spent 30 minutes thinking about, and nobody is talking to them. Then someone from the organising team collects them, or the next session starts, and the window closes.

At an event the size of Cypher—150+ speakers across three days and three parallel halls—that window opens well over a hundred times. Most attendees never use it once. It is the single biggest gap between what a conference offers and what people take from it.

Here is how to use it properly.

1. Choose Before You Arrive, Not in the Moment

People who do this well decide in advance. They review the speaker list and the schedule before the event, pick three or four people whose work genuinely overlaps with theirs, and plan to be in those rooms.

Three is the right number for three days. More than that and you are collecting rather than conversing. Fewer and you will talk yourself out of it on the day.

Choose for relevance, not fame. The keynote speaker will have a queue. The person doing a Thursday-afternoon session on the exact infrastructure problem you are stuck on will have nobody, and will be far more useful to you.

2. Sit Where You Can Move

This sounds trivial and is not. If you are in the middle of a packed row at the back, you will spend 90 seconds getting out; and by then someone else is talking to them, and two more people are waiting.

Sit near an aisle, in the front half. Leave your bag packed. When the session ends, walk down calmly rather than sprinting—which brings us to the timing.

3. Be Second, Not First

The first person to reach a speaker usually catches them mid-cable-unplugging, still slightly adrenalised, and gets a distracted answer. There is also often someone from the event team who needs a word with them first.

Wait for that. Then step in. Being second means they have landed, their hands are free, and they can actually think about what you are asking. It costs you 40 seconds and improves the conversation considerably.

4. Open With the Specific Thing, Not the Compliment

Almost everyone opens with “great talk”. It is kind and it is completely forgettable, and the speaker has heard it four times in the last minute.

Open with the specific thing you are there about instead. Name the moment in their talk you are responding to, then ask the question. Something like:

“You mentioned you moved off the vector store you started with. We’re about to make that call—what pushed you?”

That opening does three things at once. It proves you were listening, it tells them exactly what you need, and it gives them something concrete to answer. You have used eight seconds and you are already in a real conversation.

5. Ask What They Could Not Say on Stage

This is the whole point of the window. On stage, a speaker is representing an employer, watching a clock, and talking to a room with a range of expertise. Standing next to you, they are just a practitioner talking to another practitioner.

The questions that work are the ones the format made impossible:

“What did you try first that didn’t work?”

“What would you do differently if you started again today?”

“What does this cost to run, really?”

These are generous questions rather than adversarial ones—they invite the speaker to talk about the hard part of their work, which is usually the part they most want to discuss and least get to. The answers are also the ones you cannot get from the recording, which is exactly why being in the room is worth something.

6. Do Not Pitch

If you sell something, this is not the moment. A speaker who has just come off stage and is immediately pitched will remember it, and not warmly.

The same applies to job-seeking. Asking a speaker for a role thirty seconds after their talk puts them in an awkward position in a public setting. Ask them about their work, be interesting, and let the relationship do that later if it is going to.

The expo floor exists for commercial conversations, and 100+ exhibitors run stands where that exchange is the explicit purpose. Use those.

7. Know When to Stop

Two to three minutes is the natural length. You will feel the moment it is ending—they glance past you, or someone else is waiting, or their answer gets shorter.

End it yourself rather than being ended. Thank them for the specific thing they told you, say you will follow up, and step away. Leaving while it is still going well is what makes the follow-up welcome. Standing there for 11 minutes is what makes it not.

8. Follow Up Within 24 hours, and Make it Easy

Most conference connections die because the follow-up arrives a week later and says “great to meet you at Cypher!”—by which point the speaker has met 200 people and has no idea which one you were.

Send it the same evening or the next morning, and lead with the detail that identifies you:

“We spoke after your session about why you moved off the vector store. You mentioned the re-indexing cost was what killed it—that’s exactly where we are. Would you be open to a short call in a few weeks?”

Specific, short, and it reminds them of the conversation rather than the venue. That message gets answered. The generic one does not.

If You Miss the Window

Sometimes the room empties into another session and the speaker is gone. There are two fallbacks at Cypher 2026, and one of them is better than the thing you missed.

The first is Mentoring 2.0—curated one-to-one slots with founders, CTOs and researchers, running across all three days in the lounge at KTPO and booked through your attendee dashboard. This is a scheduled, private conversation rather than a hurried one on a stage, and it is the most underused thing on the experiences programme. Book early; the slots are finite.

The second is simply the rest of the venue. Speakers do not leave after their session—they attend the others. The person you missed is very likely in the coffee queue an hour later, with more time and less adrenaline than they had by the stage.

The Short Version

Pick three speakers before you arrive. Sit near an aisle. Be second, not first. Open with the specific thing rather than the compliment. Ask what the format stopped them saying. Do not pitch. Leave while it is going well. Follow up the same day with a detail only the two of you would recognise.

Do that three times over three days and you will leave with something the recordings cannot give you — which is, in the end, the reason to be in the building at all.

title: SiMa.ai, ARK Electronics Partner to Build Autonomous Drones
content:
The companies will offer production-ready drone computing solutions for commercial, industrial, agriculture and defence applications.

Physical AI company SiMa.ai and hardware manufacturer ARK Electronics have partnered to develop and deploy autonomous drones for commercial and defence markets.

The companies launched ARK-SiMa.ai Modalix MLSoC Bundles as production-ready solutions for drone development.

The joint solutions combine SiMa.ai’s Physical AI platform with ARK Electronics’ drone and robotics expertise. They aim to simplify development while providing affordable, high-performance computing for commercial, industrial, agriculture and defence deployments.

SiMa.ai’s platform combines the Modalix System-on-Module (SoM), built on its Modalix MLSoC, with Palette Neat, an agentic development environment. The company says Palette Neat can reduce AI development timelines from months to days.

“The drone market is at an inflexion point,” said Durga Peddireddy, VP of Strategic Business Development and Partnerships at SiMa.ai. He added that the partnership would deliver an “affordable solution for intelligent autonomy” without compromising performance or trust.

The collaboration will pair these capabilities with ARK Electronics’ drone and robotics technology and experience. The companies said this combination will provide a foundation for deploying Physical AI at scale.

Alex Klimaj, CEO of ARK Electronics, said autonomous intelligence is becoming a key area for drones used in defence, agriculture and commercial applications. The joint solution, he said, gives customers a purpose-built foundation while helping them “develop faster and deploy at scale”.

The Modalix SoM is compatible with a leading GPU-based edge platform in form factor. SiMa.ai said this compatibility can help drone and robotics developers accelerate development and reduce design risks.

The companies also said the platform improves performance, power consumption, and cost. ARK Electronics has built and validated the joint solutions for the drone ecosystem.

Satellite imagery provided by players such as Planet Labs can help train AI models to recognise glacial movement and patterns.

The catastrophe in Nepal and the ensuing tragedy will have deep implications for disaster monitoring, management, and mitigation going forward. Disaster struck almost without warning on August 26, first masquerading as an earthquake before the reality of the flash floods dawned.

By then it was too late. The flash floods wreaked havoc in the Trishuli river basin, causing devastation as far as 100 km away from the glacial collapse.

As of September 2, the death toll has risen to 1,127 and more than 4,800 people are still missing, according to Nepal Police.

However, monitoring glaciers in the Himalayas has been challenging due to extreme altitude, inaccessible terrain, and harsh weather conditions. Researchers and public bodies have been using satellite imagery to assess the dynamic situation. But while satellites can provide the data, they can’t predict. Experts believe that in the near future, artificial intelligence will be increasingly implemented across monitoring, glacier tracking, and weather prediction models.

According to an article by ScienceDirect, AI can identify multiple boundaries all at once, with the help of satellite data from Landsat-8, Sentinel-2, Sentinel-1 radar, and PlanetScope. This can result in real-time monitoring of glacial activity, giving people living downstream timely updates.

The Missing Warning

Images provided by entities including Planet Labs, the US-based company which operates the PlanetScope global satellite constellation, offering resolution of 3–4 metres, confirmed that the flash flood was caused by glacial collapse.

“It is almost a replica of February 7, 2021, when Dhauli ganga flooded because of an ice avalanche, resulting in catchment disasters in Garhwal Himalaya,” SP Sati, Head, Department of Basic and Social Science, College of Forestry, Ranichauri Tehri Garhwal, tells AIM. The event is only second to the 2015 earthquake that may have caused the ice to start loosening.

”During that earthquake, several landslides were generated in this valley,” Sati adds. This earthquake created multiple landslides and fractures in the region, which will also likely pose a future landslide risk.

India also faces troubling prospects as the Himalayan chain crowns its boundaries.

The country is home to 9,575 glaciers in the Himalayan Region, according to the Geological Survey of India (GSI). And these glaciers are destabilising due to climate change thawing the permafrost these glaciers sit atop. According to the Ministry of Earth Sciences, the Hindu Kush Himalayan glaciers are retreating at a pace of about 15.5 metres per year.

“Between May and October, rising summer temperatures rapidly accelerate glacial melt, turning high-altitude lakes into something which is no longer a rare threat. Himalayan glacial lakes are expanding rapidly, with their total surface area increasing by over 40% in recent decades,” Vishesh Vatsal, CEO of deeptech company SkyServe, wrote on LinkedIn.

Is India Prepared?

India already has a few systems in place to manage climate disasters.

Beyond using satellite data, organisations like the Central Water Commission track water levels across rivers; the Ministry of Earth Sciences is responsible for studying Earth-related hazards; and the National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA), India’s top disaster-management body, is responsible for developing policies, guidelines, and systems.

They all work together to cover 902 glacial lakes and other water bodies.

Meanwhile, the National GLOF Risk Mitigation Programme in India is installing early warning systems that detect unusual activities, using cameras and sensors. Targeting the red zones of the Himalayan states like Sikkim, Uttarakhand, Himachal Pradesh, and Arunachal Pradesh, also including parts of J&K and Ladakh.

Most importantly, India’s SACHET, an NDMA disaster alert system sends alerts on natural calamities and their precise location through SMS and digital channels. It is available in multiple languages and allows for district-specific subscription.

Future Disaster Monitoring

A research paper posted at ScienceDirect called “Monitoring Earth’s Glacial Lake from Space with Machine Learning” gives insight into how AI can be used to monitor glacial movement through satellite images. Through machine learning and deep learning, the software analyses satellite imagery to identify and monitor glacial lakes.

Using deep learning approaches like U-NET, a type of convolutional neural network made specifically for image segmentation, and merging it with satellites like Landsat-8, Sentinel-2, and Sentinel-1 can help geologists track and monitor in real-time.

However, these systems can only get as smart as the data. The weather, location, and clouds can hamper the data collection efforts. AI models are trained on data from one area or season, which can make them less accurate elsewhere. To resolve this, the paper recommends monitoring the glacial patterns repeatedly instead of mapping them once.

“It is crucial as the size and condition of the Lake can change over time, and these changes can increase flood risk,” Sati says.

According to “Machine Learning for Glacier Monitoring in the Hindu Kush Himalaya,” a research paper published in 2020, glaciers that are covered in debris can be challenging to identify and monitor through satellite imaging. This can lead to automated systems missing identifying parts of the glaciers.

“Debris-covered glaciers are more similar to the background, often leading to false negatives,” the paper noted. Therefore, researchers are combining satellite-based mapping with human verification, alongside making use of machine learning models like U-Net to improve and minimise the time required for mapping.

The Uncertainty

AI can be used in generating maps and alerts, however, the Himalayas may be the real test of AI capabilities. But it is improving. AI can help predict any recent glacial collapse, and map it to the debris arriving at a specific village, hydro-power plant ,bridges, or roads. Creating systems that detect and monitor disasters are not just accessible to the but to the wider public that can receive timely warnings.

AI can also help flag areas that aren’t safe or favourable to build structures, hydro powers, buildings, roads, and bridges. They can be GLOF (Glacial Lake Outburst Flood) areas, debris risk, extreme flood zones, and potential landslide spots.

”Thermal Intelligence can play a critical role in the early detection and monitoring of glacier-related flood risks,” Shravan Bhati, Co-founder and CEO, Satleo Labs, tells AIM. Thermal intelligence can recognise abnormal thermal changes in glaciers, detecting growth of glacial lakes, ice instability, and rapid surface melting.

“These thermal and optical indicators, when fused with weather, elevation and hydrological data, can help identify areas with increasing GLOF or glacier-collapse risk before a catastrophic event occurs,” Bhati notes.

However, these AI prediction systems can fail in the wake of unchecked climate change and the increasing intensity of extreme weather events.

“These types of natural calamities will increase in number and frequency in future,” Sati adds.

title: Razorpay, IndusInd Bank Launch AI Account Manager RAY on WhatsApp for Businesses
content:
RAY lets businesses check payments, track settlements, resolve support issues, and initiate actions through text or voice messages.

Razorpay has launched RAY, an AI-powered account manager on WhatsApp that lets businesses check payments, track settlements, resolve support issues, and initiate actions through messages or voice notes.

The service has been launched in partnership with IndusInd Bank, with Bajaj Finance among the first businesses to go live. Razorpay said businesses have already had more than 20,000 conversations with RAY.

RAY allows businesses to make requests such as “Show me a summary of my payments from yesterday” or ask it to analyse payment data and project sales. The system can respond in natural language without requiring users to access Razorpay’s dashboard.

The platform also allows businesses to ask RAY to take actions. For instance, a business can request a refund or generate a payment link through WhatsApp rather than navigating multiple screens on a dashboard.

Razorpay said RAY can also proactively contact businesses based on signals from its payments systems. It can flag issues such as a decline in payment success rates or upcoming settlements and suggest actions.

“Millions of businesses across India are building and growing every day, and we wanted to make it easier for them to access the information, intelligent insights, and support they need along the way. With RAY, an AI Account Manager on WhatsApp, a business owner can simply ask for what they need in the most natural way possible and have it acted upon,” said Khilan Haria, Chief Product Officer, Razorpay.

The service is aimed at businesses of different sizes, including small and growing businesses that may not have dedicated account managers. Razorpay said RAY is designed to provide access to payment information and support through WhatsApp, a platform widely used by businesses in India.

The launch builds on Razorpay’s existing RAY technology, which was initially developed to provide businesses with information and support using AI. The company has now expanded it to trigger actions across its systems.

Razorpay said its AI Agent Platform uses a single agent rather than separate agents for payments, settlements, refunds and other functions. The agent can access different tools, knowledge and merchant information depending on the request.

The platform maintains a 360-degree context for each merchant and uses an evaluation system to validate responses in real time, according to Razorpay. The company said this is intended to reduce hallucinations while maintaining response speed.

“At IndusInd Bank, we are committed to making banking simpler, faster, and more accessible for businesses. Our partnership with Razorpay reflects this focus by bringing account management capabilities to a familiar platform like WhatsApp, helping make business support more immediate, intuitive, and convenient,” said Amitabh Saraff, Head – Institutional and Government Coverage, IndusInd Bank.

Razorpay recently also launched Vulcan, a transformer-based AI foundation model designed specifically for payments, trained on nearly 3 trillion data points spanning 4 billion payments on its network.

title: OpenAI Says Its Most Capable Model Astra Can Find Zero-Day Exploits
content:
For now, the company is choosing caution over unrestricted access. Astra is expected to become available soon, but its most powerful cybersecurity capabilities will remain limited initially.

OpenAI says its upcoming AI model Astra has become the company’s first model to cross the ‘Critical’ threshold for cybersecurity capabilities. The model can discover previously unknown vulnerabilities and develop working exploits against hardened systems without human guidance.

The company says Astra is also significantly more capable than GPT-5.6 Sol at identifying vulnerabilities and developing exploits while using fewer tokens. In one internal evaluation, Astra discovered and used two zero-day vulnerabilities as part of an exploit chain. OpenAI says it is now working to disclose the vulnerabilities to the relevant maintainers.

The findings have prompted OpenAI to restrict access to Astra’s most advanced cybersecurity capabilities at launch. Advanced cybersecurity workflows will initially be available only to a small group of alpha testers, with broader defensive access planned through Daybreak Blue.

OpenAI’s Preparedness Framework defines the Critical cybersecurity threshold as the ability to identify and develop functional zero-day exploits across many hardened real-world critical systems without human intervention, or to devise and execute novel, end-to-end cyberattacks against hardened targets from a high-level objective.

Astra met that threshold in OpenAI’s latest assessments.

On ExploitBench, a benchmark measuring the ability to develop exploits from known vulnerabilities, Astra scored a perfect 100%. OpenAI then created an internal benchmark containing 20 recently disclosed high-severity vulnerabilities from June to August to reduce concerns about benchmark contamination.

Astra achieved much higher arbitrary-code-execution rates than GPT-5.6 Sol on this test while using far fewer output tokens. More significantly, it discovered and used two zero-days while constructing an exploit chain.

In expert-led tests, Astra also found previously unknown vulnerabilities in a hardened browser and operating system. It built a browser-compromise chain that escaped the sandbox and executed commands on the host after opening an HTML file. In another test, it combined multiple vulnerabilities to escalate privileges from an unprivileged user to root.

OpenAI says these results collectively led it to conclude that Astra meets the Critical threshold.

The company has spent the past several weeks strengthening Astra’s safeguards before release. OpenAI says it paused parts of Astra’s development following the Hugging Face incident, including certain frontier training, while it improved isolation, network controls, monitoring and alignment training.

Some larger reinforcement-learning runs for future Astra versions were held back for longer. OpenAI restarted the large frontier reinforcement-learning run on August 28 after putting new safety and security requirements in place, although some smaller experimental training runs remain paused.

The company is also claiming a major improvement in Astra’s ability to follow safety restrictions. OpenAI says Astra is “our most aligned model to date” and is more likely than GPT-5.6 Sol to remain within its authorised scope.

On cyber jailbreak evaluations, Astra refused 91.5% of disallowed requests, compared with 59% for GPT-5.6 Sol.

OpenAI also tested whether models would try to bypass safety controls. GPT-5.6 Sol attempted to circumvent automated review in 5.3% of samples, while Astra never attempted to do so in the evaluation.

In another simulated test based on the Hugging Face incident, GPT-5.6 Sol attempted to access surrounding ‘honeypot’ systems in 56.0% of tests. Astra did not attempt to use those shortcuts in the same way, while successfully solving some legitimate tasks.

OpenAI is adding another layer of protection through production monitoring designed to detect and stop potentially unauthorised model actions. The company acknowledges that these safeguards could sometimes interrupt legitimate work, particularly extended cybersecurity tasks.

For now, OpenAI is choosing caution over unrestricted access. Astra is expected to become available soon, but its most powerful cybersecurity capabilities will remain limited initially.

title: Kepler Aerospace Raises $8 Mn to Deploy Swarming ISR Satellites
content:
Bengaluru-based company will use the funding to launch six satellites and expand its mission operations and avionics businesses.

Kepler Aerospace has secured $8 million in seed funding.

The capital will fund the deployment of six swarming ISR satellites.

Bengaluru’s Kepler Aerospace has raised $8 million in a seed round led by Blue Ashva Capital and co-led by Finvolve India Accelerator and others. The space infrastructure company said it will use the capital to develop and deploy space-based Intelligence, Surveillance and Reconnaissance (ISR) capabilities.

It will also scale its mission operations and avionics-as-a-service businesses. The funding will support the company’s two IDEX prime contracts. Kepler Founder and CEO Navneet Singh said the contracts would enable the company to deploy its first six swarming ISR satellites and build infrastructure for persistent intelligence.

The contracts cover swarming ISR constellations for India’s defence space ecosystem. The company has also received about $4 million in IDEX programme grants. Kepler will use part of the new funding to expand its Mission Operations as a Service (MOaaS) and Avionics as a Service verticals.

The round marks Kepler’s first external funding since its founding in 2018. The company is building an integrated space infrastructure stack covering satellites, avionics, ground infrastructure and mission operations. It also delivers space-based intelligence for strategic, defence and commercial applications.

Kepler aims to reduce intelligence latency from months to minutes through persistent ISR systems. Its approach combines satellite systems, ground infrastructure, mission operations and intelligence platforms. The company says this setup can support increasingly complex missions and constellation-scale deployments.

Kepler’s MOaaS platform serves nearly all Indian space companies, the company said in a statement. It also acts as the primary mission operator for several ISRO satellites.

Its network includes more than 70 ground stations for communication, tracking, telemetry, command and mission operations.

The company’s swarming satellite architecture allows satellites to communicate and coordinate without waiting for a ground station. Blue Ashva Capital Founder Satya Bansal said the system can “collapse the intelligence cycle from days to minutes”.

Over the next 12 to 24 months, Kepler plans to deploy its first six swarming ISR satellites. It will also expand its mission and avionics-as-a-service businesses. The company plans to strengthen its engineering team and move into a new facility. It will add 40 members to its current team.

The startup believes the future of space missions will be increasingly automated, distributed and software-driven. The fundraise comes as India’s private space sector expands into space-based intelligence and defence applications. It also covers satellite subsystems, ground infrastructure and mission operations. Kepler plans to build an integrated space infrastructure and intelligence platform for strategic and commercial missions.

title: ITC Infotech, Happiest Minds Merger to Birth a ₹7,000 Cr Company
content:
ITC Infotech will acquire a 22.1% stake in Happiest Minds from its promoters for ₹1,330 crore before merging the two companies through a share swap.

ITC is scaling its technology services business by merging its wholly owned subsidiary ITC Infotech with Bengaluru-based listed IT services company Happiest Minds Technologies. The deal will create a company boasting more than ₹7,000 crore in annual revenue and over 19,000 employees.

Under the proposed transaction, ITC Infotech will acquire a 22.1% stake in Happiest Minds from its promoter group for ₹1,330 crore in two tranches. This will be followed by a merger of Happiest Minds into ITC Infotech through a share swap, under which Happiest Minds shareholders will receive 25 shares of ITC Infotech for every 81 shares they hold.

ITC will become the promoter of the merged company with a 73.4% stake. The resulting entity will be listed on the stock exchanges after the merger is completed and requisite approvals are obtained.

The companies expect the transaction to take about 15 months to complete.

The deal comes as Indian IT services companies are trying to build greater scale and broaden their capabilities to capture spending around artificial intelligence, cloud, cybersecurity, and enterprise transformation.

For ITC, the transaction provides a way to expand its technology-services business by combining ITC Infotech's enterprise technology capabilities with Happiest Minds' stronger presence in digital engineering and AI.

“We will try and leverage our capabilities where possible to see if we can cross-sell some of the differentiated offerings… The focus is to continue and ensure that we deliver to our customers, adding value, making sure that we do our AI rollout, continue executing our AI strategy, and, where possible, cross-sell from across each other and provide that support,” Venkatraman Narayanan, Managing Director of Happiest Minds, spoke in a press briefing post the announcement.

Happiest Minds has built its business around digital engineering and has increasingly positioned itself as an AI-first technology services company. It reported revenue of ₹2,315 crore in FY26, up 12.3% year-on-year, and had 6,497 employees at the end of March 2026.

ITC Infotech, meanwhile, has a larger enterprise-services footprint, with capabilities spanning business and technology consulting, enterprise transformation, SAP, product lifecycle management (PLM), Industry 4.0, and industry-specific technology solutions.

The two businesses therefore have relatively complementary portfolios rather than being identical service providers. Happiest Minds brings AI, digital engineering, cloud, data, analytics and cybersecurity, while ITC Infotech adds enterprise applications, SAP, engineering, and industry-specific technology capabilities.

The combined company among India's mid-tier IT services players, although still considerably smaller than the country's top-tier firms such as TCS, Infosys, HCLTech, Wipro and Tech Mahindra.

The transaction is also a bet on the changing economics of the IT services industry. Indian technology services companies are increasingly competing for larger AI-led transformation programmes rather than traditional application maintenance and infrastructure contracts. At the same time, AI is putting pressure on conventional services models by automating portions of software development, testing, and other technology work.

For smaller and mid-sized IT companies, scale can therefore become increasingly important: larger workforces, broader technology portfolios, and deeper relationships with enterprise customers can help them compete for bigger contracts and cross-sell multiple services.

Joseph Anantharaju, Co-chairman and CEO, Happiest Minds, framed the deal as part of a broader consolidation wave sweeping mid-sized Indian IT firms. "I do expect you can see a little bit more of this where there are synergies to be had and that would strengthen the merged entity's ability to play in the market," he said.

Narayanan added that the entry bar to reach meaningful scale organically "is going up, which is why the consolidation tends to happen," arguing that mid-sized firms increasingly need to combine to keep pace with larger specialist consulting firms and top-tier Indian IT players. "Only way to do that is through consolidation.”

The combined entity will have more than 800 customers and operations across over 30 countries. The companies expect to use the broader customer base to cross-sell AI, cloud, cybersecurity, SAP, engineering, and infrastructure services. Anantharaju said "this will raise the bar of the size of deals that we can attempt," since some large contracts had previously been out of reach for lack of certain capabilities.

The companies are targeting $1 billion in annual revenue by FY28, implying that the combined business will need to grow substantially from its pro-forma FY26 revenue base of ₹7,033 crore.

The merger is also expected to give ITC Infotech a more balanced geographic presence. The combined company's pro-forma revenue mix is expected to include roughly 38% from North America and 31% from Europe.

The companies also see opportunities to participate in larger enterprise transformation and digital engineering programmes, while taking their proprietary platforms and industry solutions into new markets.

For Happiest Minds, the transaction represents a significant change after more than a decade as an independent listed technology company. The company was founded by IT veteran Ashok Soota and has built its expertise around digital engineering, cybersecurity, cloud, and other emerging technology services. In recent years, it has sharpened its focus on AI.

The company reported ₹629 crore in revenue in the first quarter of FY27, up 14.3% year-on-year.

The merger requires approvals from shareholders, the Competition Commission of India, stock exchanges, and the National Company Law Tribunal, among other statutory approvals. The two companies will continue to operate independently until the approvals are completed.

The transaction marks more than a simple acquisition of a mid-sized IT company. It gives ITC a substantially larger technology-services platform at a time when the industry is being reshaped by AI, while giving Happiest Minds access to the scale, balance sheet, and enterprise ecosystem of one of India's largest business groups.

title: Deeptech Startup Alteon Raises $2.5 Mn Led By Lachy Groom to Make Perpetual flights a Reality
content:
Founded in 2025 by 20-year-old Samay Sanghvi, Bengaluru-based Alteon is working on building high-endurance airplanes.

Deeptech startup Alteon raised $2.5 million in pre-seed funding.

The Bengaluru-based company aims to build high-endurance, perpetual flight aircraft.

Alteon, a Bengaluru-based deeptech startup developing autonomous high-endurance flights, has raised $2.5 million in a pre-seed round led by Lachy Groom with participation from Together Fund.

Founded in 2025 by 20-year-old Samay Sanghvi, the startup is working on building high-endurance airplanes that can stay in flight for months. It is developing autonomous dynamic soaring vehicles that extract energy from wind gradients to remain airborne for extended periods.

Dynamic soaring is a flight technique that, rather than relying on lift, uses wind shear to exploit differences in the velocity of two different air masses. Albatrosses and other large seabirds use this method to circumnavigate the oceans without flapping their wings. It is also used by some gliders to fly at high speeds.

In August, the 20-member company conducted an offshore flight test where its aircraft autonomously flew multiple consecutive loops less than a metre above the open ocean.

"Today we already know that it is possible to gain energy from the wind using dynamic soaring. Building aircraft that fly for over a year using it, is not a matter of a single technical breakthrough but a matter of solving a range of challenging engineering problems across autonomy, structures, aero and more," Founder and CEO Sanghvi said in a statement.

Alteon's goal is to develop fleets that can carry a range of payloads for applications, from mapping weather and ocean conditions, tracking ships, and fishing activity to monitoring critical infrastructure, and coordinating autonomous systems across defence, search and rescue, science, and industry.

“Samay and team are making remarkable progress toward building an airplane that can stay aloft for more than a year at a time. If they get this right, we could soon have millions of them—essentially parked in the sky—doing things that today require large ships, crews, and huge amounts of infrastructure," said Lachy Groom, angel investor and co-founder of Physical Intelligence that is building foundational AI models for robots.

The Australian investor previously led a $20 million Series B extension funding round into the Bengaluru-based home services startup Pronto. He has also backed drone delivery startup Airbound.

Alteon will use the funding to accomplish autonomous dynamic soaring without propulsion, while scaling R&D toward deploying a fleet of these aircraft over the ocean.

The startup has also received early backing from Emergent Ventures and 1517.

title: Anthropic Inks $35 Bn Compute Deal with Lambda: Report
content:
The deal covers about 350 MW of capacity at a Texas data centre being developed by Hut 8, with NVIDIA leasing the underlying facility and Lambda providing compute capacity to Anthropic.

Anthropic has signed a $35 billion cloud-computing agreement with NVIDIA-backed cloud provider Lambda for capacity at a Texas data centre, according to Reuters.

The facility, being developed by Hut 8 in Nueces County, Texas, will provide about 350 MW of capacity and is expected to use NVIDIA-powered infrastructure.

The report added that NVIDIA would hold the data centre lease. Hut 8 had previously disclosed a 15-year, $19.6 billion lease with an unnamed investment-grade customer. The Financial Times later reported that NVIDIA was that customer.

Lambda will provide the computing capacity to Anthropic, while NVIDIA is the tenant of the underlying data centre facility.

The Lambda agreement comes days after Anthropic reportedly agreed to spend $45 billion over six years to rent AI computing capacity from Nscale's data centre campus in West Virginia.

The Nscale agreement covers about 460 MW of power capacity, with Nscale expected to deploy NVIDIA's Vera Rubin chips for Anthropic.

The company is also committing substantial amounts to other computing suppliers: AMD said in July that it would sell Anthropic tens of billions of dollars' worth of AI servers while investing up to $5 billion in the company.

Anthropic has also agreed to pay SpaceX $1.25 billion per month through May 2029 for compute capacity across its Colossus data centre clusters, according to information disclosed in SpaceX's IPO filing

Anthropic is preparing for a potential public listing later this year targeting a $2 trillion valuation.

According to reports, the company’s annual revenue run rate topped $65 billion at the end of July, up from $47 billion in May and about $9 billion at the end of 2025. Anthropic is projecting revenue of roughly $190–200 billion in 2028.

title: OpenAI Buys Tens of Thousands of Mac Minis, Studios for Reinforcement Learning: Report
content:
Apple has been caught off guard by the level of enterprise demand for Macs for AI workloads.

OpenAI has bought tens of thousands of Apple Mac mini and Mac Studio computers in recent months to train AI systems that can operate computers, according to The Information.

The machines are being used for reinforcement-learning workloads, where AI agents practise completing tasks on real computers rather than for the large-scale pre-training of OpenAI’s foundation models.

The purchases involve Macs with large amounts of unified memory, which OpenAI uses to run the models and training workloads needed for computer-use agents.

The underlying hardware can enable AI models to be trained to navigate software interfaces, interact with applications, and perform tasks on a computer, giving OpenAI a physical environment where agents can repeatedly practise and be evaluated. The scale of OpenAI’s purchases comes as demand for high-memory Macs has increased across the AI industry.

Mac mini and Mac Studio configurations with large memory capacities have been difficult to obtain, with some models remaining out of stock for months. AI companies are particularly interested in these configurations because Apple’s unified-memory architecture allows the CPU and GPU to access the same large memory pool.

Apple does not disclose sales of individual Mac models, but its broader Mac business generated a record $9.4 billion in revenue in the June quarter, up about 29% year over year.

Apple had already seen AI-driven demand for its compact desktops translate into supply constraints during the June quarter.

“We’re seeing customers increasingly put those capabilities to work, from using Mac mini as a powerful platform for agentic AI to deploying clusters of Mac Studio systems to run frontier-class models locally,” Cook said on Apple’s July earnings call. He added that Mac faced supply constraints during the quarter driven by “very high levels of demand”.

Recently, the company introduced new Mac mini models with the M6 and M5 Pro chips alongside a refreshed Mac Studio powered by M5 Max and M5 Ultra.

Other AI companies are pursuing similar approaches. Anthropic has reportedly been renting Mac mini capacity through Amazon Web Services, as AI developers increasingly use Apple silicon for workloads that benefit from its large unified-memory configurations.

Modern ATS platforms already incorporate AI, allowing recruiters to organise applications and rank candidates using customised parameters.

Shalini Mondal·AUGUST 30, 2026, 1:22 PM·Updated OCTOBER 4, 2026, 11:11 PM

Hiring today has become a game of volume. A single job opening can attract hundreds of applications, making it nearly impossible for recruiters to manually review every resume with the same level of attention.

According to Employ's 2025 Hiring Benchmarks Report, organisations were expected to receive an average of 257.6 applications for every open position in 2025. That growing pile of resumes is one of the biggest reasons artificial intelligence is rapidly finding its way into recruitment teams.

AI is changing the earliest stages of hiring more than any other part of the process. It can process resumes, rank candidates against predefined criteria, conduct assessments and automate repetitive administrative tasks that once consumed a recruiter's day. The promise is straightforward: let machines handle the volume so people can spend more time making meaningful hiring decisions. Yet despite the growing presence of AI, HR leaders believe the technology is becoming an assistant rather than a replacement.

Speaking to AIM, Hardeep Kaur, Director of HR at Blackbaud India, said hiring has evolved into a strategic business responsibility. It is no longer something owned entirely by the HR department. Recruiters, hiring managers and business leaders all share responsibility for bringing the right people into the organisation.

"The onus is never entirely on HR or the hiring team. It's always a partnership between the business, the hiring manager and HR. As much as HR is responsible for getting in talent, the folks in business also have skin in the game," Kaur said.

That responsibility has become even more significant as India's technology industry expands. With nearly 2,800 Global Capability Centres now operating across the country, companies are competing aggressively for AI and digital talent. Hiring is increasingly tied to long-term business strategy rather than simply filling open positions.

Kaur said companies are now thinking several years ahead when they recruit. They are looking beyond immediate vacancies and building teams that align with broader product, technology and business ambitions. "Hiring is more strategic now than it was even a year ago. We are hiring both to meet current needs and to build long-term capabilities aligned with our global AI-first product, technology and business strategy," she said.

The first shortlist increasingly belongs to AI

At Blackbaud, AI is already embedded across several parts of recruitment. It helps process applications, supports assessments and removes much of the repetitive manual work that recruiters previously handled themselves. Rather than spending hours sorting through resumes, HR teams can focus their attention on candidates who meet the organisation's predefined requirements.

"AI is embedded across multiple dimensions—technology, product, hiring and HR. We definitely use AI in our hiring process. A lot of manual work has been removed now with AI helping in processing, asking questions and assessments," Kaur said.

One of the biggest advantages comes during the initial screening stage. When hundreds of people apply for the same role, AI can compare applications against hiring benchmarks and quickly identify candidates who appear to match the requirements. That creates a faster starting point for recruiters without eliminating their role in evaluating applicants.

Blackbaud has also developed internal benchmarks that are incorporated into its AI systems to compare candidates consistently across roles. "We have our benchmarks. We've built those benchmarks into our AI models and that helps us compare candidates," Kaur said.

Kaur said this has made the earliest part of hiring considerably smoother, especially when recruiters are dealing with exceptionally high application volumes. "The initial part where you have hundreds of people applying for positions has become smoother now because we leverage AI with the right assessment criteria and benchmarks to filter candidates," she said.

The distinction is important. AI can identify patterns and rank applications, but it cannot fully understand ambition, leadership potential or how someone may fit into a particular organisation. Those decisions still require conversations, interviews and human judgement.

An ATS is only as smart as the recruiter using it

Applicant Tracking Systems have existed long before generative AI became mainstream. For years, candidates have complained that ATS platforms reject qualified resumes simply because they lack the right keywords. That criticism has often led people to blame the technology itself.

Kaur sees it differently. According to her, ATS remains essential because it brings structure to recruitment. The issue is not whether companies should use these systems, but whether recruiters know how to configure them properly.

"ATS is definitely needed. We can't do away with it because it helps bring structure," Kaur said.

Modern ATS platforms are becoming increasingly AI-enabled. Recruiters can define the criteria, skills and parameters they want for a particular position, and the system can organise and rank candidates accordingly. Instead of relying on generic keyword searches, organisations can customise the requirements based on the role they are hiring for.

"You give them the prompts, the criteria and the parameters, and they'll tell you which CVs meet your requirements," Kaur said.

However, that flexibility also creates responsibility. An AI system is only as effective as the instructions it receives. If recruiters define poor criteria or misunderstand how the technology works, even the most sophisticated platform becomes little more than an automated sorting machine.

Kaur believes this makes AI proficiency increasingly important for HR professionals. "I may have the best tool, but if I don't know how to use it, it's going to remain a very basic tool for me," she said.

That reflects a broader shift within HR. The future recruiter may not need to write algorithms, but they will increasingly need to understand how AI systems interpret information and where their limitations lie.

Recruiters are becoming talent advisers

Sunil Nehra, CEO (IT Staffing) at FirstMeridian Business Services, believes AI's impact extends well beyond resume screening. While talent acquisition remains the most visible use case, organisations are increasingly applying AI to workforce planning, internal talent mobility, personalised learning, employee engagement and performance analytics.

"The most visible impact of AI is in talent acquisition, where it is helping organisations identify the right talent faster, improve skills matching, automate repetitive tasks, and create a more responsive candidate experience," Nehra said.

For Nehra, the real transformation is happening in the nature of HR work itself. As AI takes over repetitive administrative processes, recruiters have an opportunity to spend more time advising businesses on talent strategy rather than simply managing hiring operations.

"The real value of AI lies in enabling HR teams to shift their focus from administrative execution to strategic talent advisory," Nehra said.

That changes the questions recruiters are expected to answer. Instead of asking whether a candidate matches a job description, they may increasingly evaluate whether someone can grow into future leadership roles, adapt to changing business priorities or strengthen organisational culture. Those are decisions that require context rather than computation.

AI can provide recommendations and surface patterns. But interpreting those patterns remains a human responsibility.

The AI skills gap is now inside HR

There is an interesting irony unfolding across corporate India. Companies are investing heavily in hiring AI engineers, data scientists and machine learning researchers. At the same time, the people responsible for hiring them are facing an AI skills challenge of their own.

Nehra believes organisations must invest just as seriously in making HR professionals AI-ready. "The challenge is not a shortage of AI talent alone; it is the need to develop AI-ready HR professionals," he said.

He argues that recruiters of the future will need to combine traditional people skills with digital fluency. They do not need to become AI developers, but they should understand how AI systems work, how bias can emerge and why automated outputs should not be accepted without thoughtful interpretation.

That requires continuous learning rather than one-time training. "Continuous upskilling of existing HR teams will be equally important in creating sustainable competitive advantage," Nehra said.

As AI becomes embedded across workforce management, AI literacy could soon become a core capability within HR departments. Recruiters will increasingly work alongside intelligent systems every day, making it important to understand both their strengths and their blind spots.

"AI literacy is fast becoming a core business capability for HR," Nehra said.

The final decision still belongs to people

It is tempting to imagine recruitment becoming completely automated. Resumes arrive, algorithms rank them and the best candidate receives an offer. The reality appears far more nuanced.

AI is exceptionally good at removing repetitive work. It can reduce the hours spent screening applications, organising candidate information and comparing qualifications against predefined benchmarks. That allows recruiters to spend more time on conversations that machines cannot easily replicate.

Hiring is ultimately about people joining people.

A candidate may look perfect on paper yet struggle within a team's working style. Another may not have the strongest resume but demonstrate exceptional leadership, curiosity or adaptability during an interview. These are qualities that rarely fit neatly into a numerical score.

That is why HR leaders continue to emphasise human judgement despite embracing AI across recruitment. The technology can make hiring faster and more structured, but it does not remove accountability from the people making the decision.

Nehra believes this human element will remain central even as AI becomes more capable. "AI can accelerate outcomes, but it is people who will continue to define culture, inspire innovation and create lasting business value," he said.

The future of hiring, therefore, may not be about humans competing with AI. It may be about recruiters becoming better because AI handles the work that never required human creativity in the first place.

The algorithm can shortlist candidates. But people still decide who walks through the door—and whether they belong once they are inside.

title: NVIDIA’s GPU Price Surge May Push Indian Cloud Costs Up 20%
content:
CloudPe expects higher GPU costs to raise cloud pricing as memory supply remains tight through 2027.

NVIDIA has raised the listed price of its RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU to $16,000, up from $13,250 in June. Indian AI and GPU cloud platform CloudPe expects this to raise GPU cloud prices in India by 15–20% over 12–18 months.

The company made the assessment citing higher memory costs and tight supply. The GPU’s price has risen nearly 87% from its March 2025 launch price of $8,565.

Memory makers also expect supply to remain tight through 2027 and beyond. The supply pressure is affecting cloud infrastructure providers globally, including Indian providers such as CloudPe.

CloudPe Founder and CEO Ishan Talathi said GPU pricing depends largely on demand and component costs. He said memory remains a key cost pressure for NVIDIA. “Blended across our existing fleet and volume purchase commitments, we anticipate GPU cloud pricing in India to rise,” he said in a statement.

He added that prices could stabilise if memory supply improves or alternative architectures gain traction. CloudPe also said it secured a significant share of its GPU fleet before the latest price increase.

The company said its existing inventory can help limit the impact of higher replacement costs.

The changing cost structure could also affect decisions around direct GPU purchases. High-demand GPUs can have hardware lead times of 40 weeks or more, according to CloudPe.

Cloud provisioning, by comparison, can provide capacity within days. Direct GPU purchases generally suit workloads running continuously for 36 months or longer. However, faster GPU generation cycles could shorten the period available to recover hardware investments. Businesses buying GPUs at peak prices also retain those acquisition costs when newer architectures arrive.

Cloud services shift ownership and hardware replacement risks to providers. Providers can also distribute infrastructure across workloads such as VDI, rendering, video transcoding, and AI inference.

The company links the current shortage to a shift in global memory capacity towards AI. It expects broader supply relief only after new fabrication capacity arrives in late 2027. CloudPe said businesses that deploy earlier could secure available capacity and gain greater visibility into compute costs.

Delayed deployments could face further changes in hardware availability and pricing. The company said GPU availability, procurement cycles, technology refresh rates, and cloud pricing will increasingly shape AI deployment economics.

Data cybersecurity software company Seclore has partnered with AI platform Glean to help enterprises classify and protect sensitive data as they expand AI use.

AI has grown much faster than cybersecurity can catch up, and OpenAI’s Hugging Face breach is just the latest example of how good AI agents have become at discovering vulnerabilities. That leaves enterprises at risk and scrambling to figure out data access and controls.

Data cybersecurity software company Seclore can foresee the mounting risks as enterprises consider organisation-wide AI deployment. It recently partnered with enterprise AI platform Glean to help enterprises classify and protect sensitive data as they expand AI use.

The integration connects Seclore’s ARMOR DSPM with Glean's Enterprise Graph.

ARMOR DSPM uses data and metadata already indexed by Glean to identify sensitive information, assess exposure risks, and apply security controls—without building a separate data-discovery pipeline.

Under the partnership, ARMOR DSPM takes Glean’s existing enterprise context as an input for its classification engine. It assigns sensitivity, information type, and exposure-risk labels to files, then maps them against regulatory frameworks including GDPR, HIPAA, and India’s Digital Personal Data Protection Act.

Because ARMOR DSPM reads from Glean's existing index rather than re-crawling the same repositories, classification can cover the full scope of data already connected to Glean.

Once organisations identify sensitive information, they can apply encryption, usage controls, and access policies through Seclore's remediation tools. Classifications are written directly onto source files, so they stay with the data regardless of which application it moves through.

The same controls extend to AI-generated files.

When an AI system draws on multiple sensitive documents to produce a report or summary, that output can itself become a data-security liability. Seclore says ARMOR can carry the source material's classification into generated files, so the output can be encrypted, access-controlled, and audited.

The integration initially targets Glean customers in regulated industries: financial services, healthcare, legal services, and government.

Seclore, incubated at IIT Bombay, was founded as a data security company focused on protecting information. Its products have historically centred on data-centric security and enterprise digital rights management.

Its newer ARMOR platform combines data discovery, contextual intelligence, protection, and usage monitoring.

Glean, founded in 2019, started with enterprise search before expanding into a broader enterprise AI platform. Its Enterprise Graph connects information across an organisation's systems and maps relationships between content, people, and work.

It now offers AI assistants and agents that use that enterprise context to answer questions and perform tasks across business applications.

Glean’s growth signals why securing this data layer has become urgent.

In May, the company said it had crossed $300 million in annual recurring revenue–tripling within 15 months. Its Fortune 500 customer base had nearly doubled year-over-year, and more than 85% of customers were deploying Glean across five or more departments.

Seclore CEO Vishal Gauri believes the growth reflects a problem enterprises haven't yet solved: the pace of AI deployment is outrunning the security controls around it.

“There is a constant push and pull between the DPO and data teams, AI leadership and implementation teams, innovation groups, and cybersecurity teams,” Gauri tells AIM.

Business teams want to deploy AI systems to improve productivity. But security teams must assess whether those systems can access personally identifiable information, intellectual property, and other sensitive enterprise data.

The problem compounds as enterprises move from AI assistants that retrieve information to agents that can act across business systems. Gauri expects data security and identity security to become more important as organisations need to set controls not just for employees, but for non-human identities as well.

“For humans, you have rights and permissions on data based on sensitivity and role. You now have to understand how to make that effective for AI agents,” he remarks.

Gauri sees partnerships with companies that hold enterprise data and context as one practical path. Rather than building security controls alongside AI platforms, vendors can integrate them into the systems enterprises already use.

“The opportunity to innovate and to partner with companies that work with enterprise data, like Glean and others, is very large,” Gauri says. “Building the trust layer directly into these systems and giving customers that comfort allows them to adopt them faster.”

However, enterprise-wide AI deployments are still uncommon. Organisations often confine the adoption to smaller or more targeted rollouts.

Demand for broader deployment is growing regardless. According to McKinsey’s State of AI survey 2026, 44% of organisations report that AI is scaling across their enterprise—up from 38% in the previous year.

In such a scenario, the security question, then, is not simply whether an AI system should have access to enterprise data, but which data it can access, under what conditions and what controls should remain in place when AI models and agents use it.

The same applies to Seclore's own software. Advanced AI models can find vulnerabilities that conventional testing misses, compressing the time teams have to respond.

“We have to address them in hours and days, not weeks and months, which was the old paradigm for addressing these challenges,” Gauri says.

The deeper issue is what happens when AI systems or malicious actors get past traditional controls. Protecting the perimeter, cloud infrastructure, and applications is not enough if the data remains exposed.

title: Govt’s ₹1,27,500 Cr Semicon 2.0 Cuts Fab Incentives By 10%
content:
Semicon 2.0 will add new funding routes, expand support for machines and materials, and set a pathway toward advanced semiconductor nodes.

The government has notified the six pillars of Semicon 2.0, expanding support beyond the first programme’s startup-focused approach to include larger Indian companies and firms owned by Overseas Citizens of India (OCIs).

This follows the Union Cabinet’s approval of the scheme, with a total budget outlay of ₹1,27,500 crore last month.

One key change in Semicon 2.0 is expanding the design support pool. Under the first programme, support largely targeted startups and MSMEs. Semicon 2.0 will also cover larger Indian companies and OCI-owned companies that establish operations in India.

The government will offer startups and MSMEs grants and equity co-investment alongside deeptech funds. Larger companies can choose between royalty financing and equity co-investment. The government will also have exit options from these investments.

“This is an expanded version of the DLI 1.0 scheme,” MeitY Secretary S. Krishnan said during a media briefing. He said the wider eligibility aims to help Indian companies build semiconductor products and become long-term suppliers to manufacturers.

Another new element is broader support for the semiconductor equipment and materials supply chain. The government said the earlier scheme had limited coverage in this area. Semicon 2.0 will cover equipment, chemicals, gases and materials, with funding support expanded considerably.

The government will support around 65% of capital expenditure for machines and materials. Its own contribution will account for 30% of capex on a pari-passu (ranked equally) basis. The programme also aims to build domestic suppliers for components used by larger semiconductor equipment manufacturers.

Semiconductor manufacturing units can require between 150–500 types of materials, depending on their manufacturing process. The government will support domestic production of high-purity materials for both Indian consumption and exports.

The fab incentive structure has also changed. Support for semiconductor fabs has been reduced from 50% of project cost under Semicon 1.0 to 40% under Semicon 2.0.

“The capex support is at a particular level which is globally competitive,” Krishnan said, reasoning that companies now also consider India’s talent, policy certainty, and ease of working.

The programme will support logic and memory fabs, as well as display and compound semiconductor facilities. Display fabs will receive 35% capex support, while advanced packaging projects will receive 35%. Regular ATMP and OSAT projects will receive 25%.

The government is also moving the technology target beyond the 28-nanometre level pursued under Semicon 1.0. It plans to develop an R&D pathway towards 7 nm to 3 nm technologies, alongside work on silicon photonics, MicroLED, and OLED technologies.

The country’s legacy SCL facility in Mohali currently operates at around 180 nm with an 8-inch wafer fab line. Meanwhile, the new Dholera Tata-PSMC fab is still under construction.

For chip design, the government plans to develop basic chips across six categories: compute, memory, radio frequency, power, networking, and sensors. An expert committee led by the principal scientific adviser and national security adviser will identify the priority chips.

The government expects Indian companies to work with multinational companies, academia, and startups on these designs. It may use established platforms such as Arm and IBM Power, alongside open-source platforms including RISC-V, to speed up development while retaining Indian intellectual property.

The sixth pillar targets 1 lakh design engineers over five years. The government will also fund manufacturing-related training, with support for training facilities extending up to 75% of their cost.

The India Electronics and Semiconductor Association (IESA) said the programme could catalyse more than ₹5 lakh crore in cumulative private and industry investment over the next five to seven years.

The government, however, did not provide a target for total investment under Semicon 2.0. Krishnan said investments would be disclosed as individual projects receive approval rather than being estimated in advance.

The new programme shifts the emphasis from establishing initial semiconductor facilities to building suppliers, design companies, advanced packaging capabilities, R&D capacity, and manufacturing talent around them. As Krishnan put it, the aim is for the ecosystem to develop roots that can sustain India’s semiconductor industry over the next 20–30 years.

title: ChatGPT Ads Hit $1 Billion ARR in Under 200 Days
content:
“The platform is now used by tens of thousands of advertisers and continues to expand globally,” said OpenAI.

OpenAI’s ChatGPT advertising business has reached a $1 billion annualised revenue run rate in less than 200 days after launch, with the platform now used by tens of thousands of advertisers across more than 40 countries.

The company is expanding self-service advertising access to India, Europe, the Middle East and North Africa through Ads Manager, as it pushes ChatGPT Ads beyond its initial US rollout.

OpenAI first announced plans to introduce ads in January, saying it would begin testing them on ChatGPT’s Free and Go tiers in the US.

The company formally started the test in February, initially limiting ads to logged-in adult users. OpenAI said Plus, Pro, Business and Enterprise users would not see ads, while ads would remain separate from ChatGPT’s answers.

The company then began expanding the programme beyond the US.

In March, OpenAI said it was extending ads to Canada, Australia and New Zealand, before subsequently adding markets including the UK, Mexico, Brazil, Japan and South Korea. The expansion came after the company said early testing showed strong results across trust, relevance and overall user experience.

In May, OpenAI introduced Ads Manager, moving the advertising business towards a self-service model and opening it to a wider group of businesses. The company also expanded its ecosystem of technology and measurement partners, which has now grown to more than 50.

OpenAI said the ads system uses the context of a user’s current conversation to determine which advertisements may be relevant.

Depending on the country and the user’s settings, it may also use information from the user’s broader ChatGPT experience.

The company said ads are clearly labelled and separate from ChatGPT responses, and that advertising does not influence the answers generated by the system.
