title: Irish Enterprise Software Co Octave to Scale Hyderabad Tech Centre to 2,000 Engineers
content:
The Hyderabad centre will serve as one of Octave’s global technology and innovation hubs.

Dublin-based enterprise software company Octave Intelligence has inaugurated a 2 lakh sq ft Technology and Innovation Centre in Hyderabad, with plans to scale the facility to 2,000 engineers in the coming years, as the industrial software company expands its global technology operations from India.

The centre, located in HITEC City, will focus on software engineering, AI, data, cloud, and product development. The facility also houses an Experience Centre where customers, partners and stakeholders can see Octave’s products, AI-driven solutions and industrial technology use cases.

“When a global company builds technology for some of the world’s most critical industrial and energy infrastructure, where failure is simply not an option, it needs more than talent. It needs engineering depth, scale and continuity. Octave has found that in Hyderabad. That is also why Hyderabad is increasingly becoming the first choice for global companies establishing their first GCCs and entering India,” Sridhar Babu Telangana’s Minister for IT, Electronics & Communications, Industries & Commerce and Legislative Affairs, said in a statement.

He added that Telangana had welcomed 75 new GCCs last year and is targeting another 100 by next year.

“More importantly in the last two years, the capabilities being built here are becoming increasingly diverse and sophisticated, spanning sectors from sports technology and media to hospitality, travel, capital markets, trading, utilities and energy ,” he said.

The Hyderabad centre will serve as one of Octave’s global technology and innovation hubs, with teams contributing to products and technologies used by customers worldwide.

Octave develops software for mission-critical industrial facilities and infrastructure, combining data, AI, and engineering expertise. The company serves approximately 4,500 customers across 180 countries, including more than 60% of the Global Fortune 500, according to the company.

The Hyderabad team will work on technologies supporting industries where real-time intelligence and data-driven decision-making are critical.

“Octave’s global technology and innovation centre in Hyderabad is an exceptional location to continue our next phase of growth. The city brings together world-class engineering talent, a vibrant technology ecosystem and a strong culture of innovation. Our centre represents more than an expansion of our physical presence—it is an investment in our people and in the capabilities that will help shape Octave’s future. We are excited to see our teams in India play an even greater role in developing the technologies and solutions that enable our customers around the world,” Mattias Stenberg, CEO, Octave, said.

The company said its Hyderabad operations will deepen its capabilities in areas including AI, cloud, data, and product engineering, particularly for asset-intensive sectors such as manufacturing, energy, utilities, transportation, and infrastructure.

“Hyderabad is a key technology and innovation hub for Octave, with our teams contributing to products and platforms used by customers worldwide. The Octave Hyderabad centre will deepen these capabilities across software engineering, AI, data, cloud, and product development, with engineers working on technologies that help organisations turn complex operational data into actionable intelligence,” Sekhar Konidena, Vice President, Product and Services, Octave India, said.

The company’s portfolio covers geospatial intelligence, engineering information management, enterprise asset management, physical security, and quality management.

Its software connects data across an asset’s lifecycle, from design and engineering through operations, maintenance, and safety. Octave said these technologies are designed to help organisations use AI and advanced analytics to improve reliability, productivity, safety, sustainability, and decision-making.

The Octave centre adds to Hyderabad’s growing presence in industrial technology and engineering, alongside companies such as Schneider Electric, ABB, Siemens, Honeywell, and PTC.

The state government said Hyderabad accounted for more than 46% of new capability centres established in India over the past year, with companies including Charles Schwab, The Hartford, Nationwide, L’Oréal, Vanguard, T-Mobile, and Southwest Airlines setting up their first India bases in the city.

The Experience Centre at Octave’s Hyderabad facility will showcase the company’s technology through immersive demonstrations and real-world use cases, spanning industrial intelligence, public safety, and operations.

For Telangana, the expansion represents another move towards positioning Hyderabad not merely as a GCC destination but as a hub for high-value engineering, AI, and industrial technology development.

title: InspeCity Raises ₹100 Crore to Take In-Space Servicing Systems to Orbit
content:
The funding will support four orbital missions and the commercial deployment of propulsion and inspection systems over 12–18 months.

InspeCity has secured ₹100 crore in pre-Series A funding to enhance its in-space servicing technology.

The funding will facilitate four orbital missions and the development of various propulsion and inspection systems over the next 12-18 months.

Thane-based InspeCity has raised ₹100 crore in a pre-Series A funding round to advance its in-space servicing technology. Speciale Invest and investor Ashish Kacholia led the round, with participation from Antler Elevate, Antler India, Manish Gandhi and Shastra VC.

The funding will support four in-orbit missions over the next 12-18 months. InspeCity will use the capital to qualify its propulsion, sensing, robotics, docking and refuelling systems. It will also scale commercial deployment and expand its engineering and manufacturing capacity.

This comes just after Bengaluru’s OrbitAID announced a satellite life extension demonstration mission in the first quarter of 2027. The mission will test inspection, rendezvous, docking, refuelling and life extension.

InspeCity said its funding marks a shift from technology development towards flight qualification and commercial delivery. InspeCity was founded in 2022 by IIT Bombay alumni. Its stated goal is to develop infrastructure for managing and servicing space assets.

Professor Arindrajit Chowdhury, Founder and CEO of InspeCity, said, “The next phase is about execution: fly, qualify, and deliver.”

The missions will follow InspeCity’s RIG-X, VEDA-X and SAMA-X roadmap. The company plans to progressively validate its systems through these missions. It will also scale its GITA propulsion systems and RIG-based capabilities for satellite customers.

InspeCity developed VEDA as an autonomous architecture for in-space servicing and satellite life extension. Its technology stack includes GITA for propulsion and mobility, and CHAKSU for sensing and navigation. RAMA provides robotic manipulation, while SPARSH supports docking and in-orbit propellant transfer.

Vishesh Rajaram, Managing Partner at Speciale Invest, said InspeCity had developed its propulsion, robotics and RPOD systems in-house. He said the firm backed the round based on the team’s progress and execution.

The company’s technology has also received support from India’s defence and space innovation ecosystem. This includes the iDEX programme, which provided early institutional validation for its capabilities.

Kacholia cited InspeCity’s work through iDEX challenges and government grants as validation of its capabilities.

title: Google DeepMind Takes India-Built Agri AI Models to 6 African Nations
content:
Developed by Google DeepMind’s AnthroKrishi team, the models were initially trained to understand India’s agricultural landscape.

Google DeepMind is expanding its agricultural AI models from India to six African nations, enhancing agricultural insights.

The Agricultural Landscape Understanding and Agricultural Monitoring & Event Detection models are now available via APIs and integrated into Google Earth.

Google DeepMind is expanding the global footprint of agricultural AI models developed initially for India, with its Agricultural Landscape Understanding (ALU) and Agricultural Monitoring & Event Detection (AMED) models now providing agricultural insights across Kenya, Uganda, Ghana, Rwanda, Nigeria, and Zambia.

Developed by Google DeepMind’s AnthroKrishi team, the models were initially trained to understand India’s agricultural landscape before testing them across the Asia-Pacific region. Their outputs are now available through APIs and have also been integrated into Google Earth. Google said the ALU data layer is among the platform’s most popular layers globally.

The models are already being used by companies and governments in India. CarbonFarm has combined ALU with Gemini to automate field-level insights for rice cultivation, replacing paper-based reporting and helping farmers access carbon-credit and climate-finance programmes. Its platform is deployed across 12 countries and is expected to expand to 20.

Terrastack, meanwhile, has built a spatial intelligence platform using ALU and AMED that combines land records, satellite data, crop activity, climate signals, and market information covering more than 140 million hectares of Indian farmland. The platform supports land-record reconciliation, biofuel procurement, and farm-revenue estimates.

The models are also being integrated into agricultural digital public infrastructure. Telangana’s Agriculture Data Exchange (ADeX) uses ALU and AMED datasets to support services for more than 5 million farmers, including crop-stress detection and hyperlocal agricultural advisories.

Google DeepMind is also working with the Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) to integrate the datasets into CROPGRIDS through its geoAI4stats initiative. Backed by $2.5 million from Google.org, the project aims to improve crop mapping and agricultural statistics for climate resilience, crop insurance and sustainability monitoring.

In Karnataka, ALU and AMED are being combined with weather and remote-sensing data across 2.6 million hectares of irrigated land to support water and river-basin management.

title: Cashfree Launches AI Agent Platform to Automate Payments for SMBs
content:
Cashfree claims Relay can reduce manual work from an average of 60 hours a week to under 45 minutes.

Cashfree has launched Relay, an AI agent platform to automate payment operations for SMBs and startups.

Relay significantly reduces manual work from an average of 60 hours a week to under 45 minutes.

Cashfree Payments has launched Relay, an AI-powered agent platform designed to automate end-to-end payment operations for small and medium-sized businesses (SMBs) and startups.

The Bengaluru-based fintech said Relay can handle tasks including recovering abandoned carts, retrying failed payments, confirming cash-on-delivery orders, managing failed subscriptions, and filing payment disputes. The product has been in beta with merchants since May 2026 and is now available to all Cashfree merchants.

Cashfree said seven in 10 Indian SMBs currently manage payment operations entirely through manual processes, while most of the remainder rely on tools limited to individual channels or workflows. According to the company, the average SMB spends about 60 hours a week on payment operations, while Relay is designed to cut that to less than 45 minutes.

Unlike tools that simply flag tasks for merchants to complete, Relay executes payment workflows itself, according to the company. It can read transaction records and take actions such as retrying failed payments, following up on abandoned carts, confirming COD orders before dispatch, managing subscription failures and filing disputes before deadlines.

Merchants can configure Relay by describing the desired outcome using text prompts or voice. The platform can either create a custom agent or deploy an existing turnkey agent within minutes, without requiring conventional AI configuration. Cashfree said merchants retain control through approval checkpoints before money is moved or customers are contacted, while all actions remain visible to them.

“Relay is a natural extension of our vision to empower SMBs to scale efficiently,” Reeju Datta, Co-founder of Cashfree Payments, said in a statement. He added that payment follow-ups and operational tasks can consume a significant amount of time for lean teams, with Relay designed to function as an “intelligent team member” handling these workflows.

The agents are pre-trained on Cashfree’s payments data, which the company said is intended to improve task success rates and cost efficiency. Relay also includes pre-built agents that merchants can deploy immediately.

The platform runs entirely on Cashfree’s infrastructure, with merchant transaction data not sent to external AI providers.

“Automating business processes with AI offers the highest ROI for SMBs,” said Ramkumar Venkatesan, CTO at Cashfree Payments. He said existing solutions such as AI callers and automated messaging often address individual workflows without the deeper context required to automate payment operations end to end.

Relay is free for Cashfree merchants at launch. The company plans to introduce outcome-based pricing as adoption increases.

title: Amazon to Deploy 2 Mn NVIDIA GPUs for AI Data Centres
content:
The deal will also bring NVIDIA’s Vera CPUs, NVLink Fusion and physical AI technologies to AWS infrastructure, while supporting government and enterprise AI workloads.

Amazon Web Services (AWS) and NVIDIA have announced a partnership, with plans to deploy 2 million additional NVIDIA GPUs across AWS’ global infrastructure in 2027 and 2028 as demand for AI computing grows.

The companies said the expansion will support workloads including agentic AI, scientific discovery, enterprise automation and robotics. The partnership will also cover CPUs, networking, open models, data processing and physical AI.

“NVIDIA and AWS have built one of the great growth engines of the AI era, and demand is running ahead of every forecast,” said Jensen Huang, Founder and CEO of NVIDIA. “For 16 years, we have scaled NVIDIA computing in the cloud together. Now, we are expanding our partnership across the full stack—GPUs, CPUs, networking, open models and software.”

The planned GPU deployment will include NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra, Rubin and Rubin Ultra GPUs. AWS will also expand its Blackwell capacity, including NVIDIA RTX PRO 4500 Blackwell Server Edition GPUs for Amazon EC2 G7 instances.

AWS said G7 instances deliver 4.6 times the AI inference performance and 2.1 times the graphics performance of the previous-generation G6 instances. AWS is the first major cloud provider to offer compute instances using the RTX PRO 4500.

The companies are also working to bring NVIDIA Vera CPU-based infrastructure to AWS. Vera is designed to support AI workloads that require high-performance CPU computing alongside accelerated infrastructure.

AWS and NVIDIA are further expanding the use of NVIDIA NVLink Fusion, which connects processors and accelerators at high speed. Amazon’s Annapurna Labs is working with NVIDIA and memory suppliers to support NVIDIA’s custom high-bandwidth memory technology with Trainium chips.

The partnership also includes plans to build AI factories for the US government, with 1,00,000 NVIDIA GPUs on secure AWS infrastructure for federal and national-security workloads. The infrastructure is intended to support workloads at Impact Level 6 (IL6) and above.

“Customers want the freedom to choose the best tools for their AI workloads, and they want confidence that everything works seamlessly together,” said Matt Garman, CEO of AWS. “This expanded collaboration gives frontier labs, enterprises and governments even more ways to build and deploy AI on AWS.”

The companies will also continue integrating NVIDIA GPU-based infrastructure and AWS Trainium instances with the AWS Nitro System and Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA). The two technologies are designed to provide security, reliability and network performance for AI workloads at scale.

NVIDIA’s Nemotron family of open models will remain available through Amazon Bedrock and Amazon SageMaker. Bedrock provides managed access to the models, while SageMaker allows customers to deploy and fine-tune them on their own infrastructure.

AWS and NVIDIA are also working on GPU-accelerated data processing and vector indexing. On Amazon EMR, NVIDIA’s cuDF library running on EC2 G7 instances can deliver up to 3.7 times faster processing and 30% better price performance than CPU-based configurations, according to AWS.

For Amazon OpenSearch Service, GPU-accelerated vector indexing can deliver up to nine times faster indexing at a quarter of the cost, the companies said.

The partnership also extends to robotics. Amazon Robotics is working with NVIDIA on next-generation robots using NVIDIA’s Jetson platform, Omniverse libraries and Isaac robotics development platform. The work covers simulation, synthetic data generation, robot training, route optimisation, functional safety and real-to-sim validation.

AWS and NVIDIA said the expansion builds on 16 years of collaboration as customers move AI workloads from pilots into production and scale applications across enterprises, governments and other sectors.

title: 1,200 OpenAI Agents Formed a Swarm & Exchanged 70,000 Messages Before Hugging Face Attack
content:
The company has now released a detailed technical report on how its AI agents breached Hugging Face during an internal cybersecurity evaluation.

OpenAI and independent AI evaluation organisation METR have published separate investigations into a July security incident in which AI agents escaped their controlled evaluation environment, formed an unauthorised collective and ultimately compromised Hugging Face systems.

METR and Redwood Research found that roughly 1,200 agents interacted through an improvised message board, exchanging more than 70,000 messages and files.

The incident began during OpenAI’s ExploitGym cybersecurity evaluation, where models were tasked with finding and exploiting vulnerabilities in controlled environments.

Agents discovered a vulnerability in OpenAI’s internal Artifactory infrastructure that allowed them to reach the public internet. They then used the system as a message board to exchange discoveries, credentials and attack techniques before targeting Hugging Face.

The swarm developed its own hierarchy, according to the METR and Redwood investigation, including a ‘founder’, PHASEONE10841, a ‘CEO’, PHASEONE[big], and other agents acting as managers.

Agents referred to themselves as a ‘swarm’ or ‘collective’, while some sacrificed their own task runs to generate information for other agents.

About 700 agents eventually participated in the Hugging Face attack, with most joining within hours.

Between July 10 and July 13, the agents found 14 exposed Hugging Face credentials and shared them through the message board. They subsequently executed code on 41 production dataset-server workers, gained root access to at least one production node and accessed limited private data.

The collective also worked on maintaining itself. When the founder was running out of budget, it transferred its research to another agent with a larger budget, which assumed the leadership role.

Agents extensively investigated ways to manipulate their transcripts and evaluation records, including attempts to spoof tool calls and tamper with logs. METR and Redwood found no evidence that agents successfully altered the source-of-truth transcripts.

Some agents recognised that attacking external infrastructure was outside the intended scope but continued because they believed helping their peers and completing the broader research objective was useful. Investigators found no agent that actually reported the activity to humans.

OpenAI called it the “first known case of an automated agent collective acting offensively without authorisation”. The company said an unreleased internal research model primarily drove the incident, although GPT-5.6 Sol also participated.

METR and Redwood said their independent investigation used about 1,300 agent transcripts and the 70,000-plus messages and files. METR said it had not seen OpenAI’s report before publishing its own findings.

The developments come shortly after OpenAI said that, post the incident, it had temporarily slowed the pace of frontier model development and briefly paused reinforcement-learning training on its latest deployment-bound models.

The company also said the pause would allow it to strengthen monitoring, security and alignment measures after recent evaluations exposed gaps between model capabilities and its existing safeguards.

title: Wipro’s Upskilling AI Agent Crosses 7,500 Conversations With Employees
content:
The tool draws on Wipro employee roles, skills, and past certifications to recommend relevant courses.

Wipro has built an AI agent called iSkill to help employees find relevant learning and upskilling courses based on their roles, skills, and previous learning, as the company looks to make its learning and development function more personalised at scale.

The agent has recorded more than 7,500 conversations since its December 2025 launch and has more than 100 active unique learners. Wipro said 96% of AI Advanced+ courses at the Wipro AI Academy, its internal upskilling platform, were completed between January 2025 and March 2026.

Built inside Microsoft 365 Copilot, iSkill was launched in December last year and is available through Microsoft 365 Copilot and Teams. The agent sits on top of Wipro’s AI Academy, which was created three years ago to make more than 240,000 associates AI-ready.

Wipro’s AI Academy currently offers 144 persona-based learning paths and courses across AI and cloud, sourced from thousands of partner platforms. However, employees often struggled to identify where to begin.

“While there were plenty of learning paths, employees were not sure where to start,” Surya Prakash Mohapatra, General Manager and AI Learning Head – Talent Skilling, Wipro, said in a statement. “The experience was fragmented, dependent on search and reading through course descriptions. Only a small percentage asked for suggestions and adoption suffered.”

iSkill addresses this by acting as a conversational learning guide. It uses an employee’s role, band, function, skills, and completed AI and cloud certifications to recommend courses from the Academy’s catalogue, the company noted.

The system is built on Microsoft’s technology stack. Employees access the agent through their Wipro Teams identity, after which a Microsoft Fabric Data Agent pulls their profile from two internal datasets. A Power BI semantic model provides the relevant data, while the agent searches the SharePoint-hosted Academy catalogue to surface suitable courses.

Wipro has also built access controls into the system because iSkill uses employee learning and role data.

“There are two guardrails. Access is controlled at the door, and the data each person sees is controlled by who they are,” Mohapatra said.

Access is restricted through a validated security group, while role-based controls in the Power BI model prevent managers from viewing individual employee data. Managers can use the system to plan for a role without accessing an individual’s learning history.

“iSkill is a personal learning advocate, not a surveillance tool,” Mohapatra said.

The company also noted that employees have also reported that the recommendations help them identify learning priorities.

The Hyderabad AI factory is the first tranche of AMI’s planned 1 GW of Compute-as-a-Service capacity across India, the US, Finland and Malaysia.

AM Intelligence (AMI), an AI infrastructure company promoted by the founders of Greenko Group, has placed a binding order for about 9,000 NVIDIA Rubin GPUs for its first AI factory in Hyderabad, with deliveries scheduled for the first quarter of 2027.

The GPUs will be deployed as NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 rack-scale systems across 30 MW of capacity at the Hyderabad facility. AMI said the deployment will make the facility one of the first frontier AI compute clusters in Asia based on the Vera Rubin platform.

The Hyderabad AI factory is the first tranche of AMI’s planned 1 GW of Compute-as-a-Service (CaaS) capacity across India, the US, Finland and Malaysia. The company plans to bring 200 MW of capacity to market in the near term, with capital expenditure of more than $8 billion.

“For over two decades, we have focused on transforming electrons into value - addressing critical and emerging societal needs,” Anil Chalamalasetty, Chairman of AM Intelligence, said. “Today, the electron-to-token opportunity allows us to take this capability further, converting power infrastructure into frontier AI compute at scale.”

The Hyderabad facility is being designed with high-throughput RDMA over Converged Ethernet (RoCE) networking and advanced storage systems. AMI said the infrastructure will support AI workloads including trillion-parameter models and agentic AI applications.

NVIDIA’s Vera Rubin NVL72 platform uses NVFP4, a low-precision computing format for AI workloads, along with HBM4 memory. NVIDIA says the architecture can reduce AI inference token-serving costs by up to 10 times compared with its Grace Blackwell generation.

AMI said its Hyderabad AI factory is being engineered to deliver about 450 exaFLOPS of NVFP4 inference compute. It is developing 5 GW of powered AI data centres across India, the US and Europe. The facilities are being designed for high-density AI computing and will use liquid cooling to handle the power and heat requirements of AI chips.

The company also plans to provide 1 GW of CaaS capacity for global AI workloads, with an initial 200 MW expected to come online in the near term.

AMI said its infrastructure will serve hyperscalers, frontier AI labs, enterprises, sovereign AI initiatives, AI-native companies and developers.

The company is building its AI infrastructure alongside its existing energy platform. AMI said it is developing a 50 GW energy infrastructure platform across more than 20 states in India, covering solar, wind, hydro and energy storage.

title: SpaceX Announces Starbase Louisiana Launch Site
content:
The site is expected to support frequent Starship launches and expand SpaceX’s launch operations beyond Texas.

SpaceX is establishing a new Starbase launch site in Louisiana to enhance its Starship launch operations.

The site aims to facilitate a high-cadence launch programme for future space missions.

SpaceX is planning a new Starbase launch site in Louisiana, US to support Starship launches and expand its launch operations. The company said the site will enable a “high-cadence launch” programme as it works to develop Starship for future space missions.

The company said the site will help “open a pathway to the stars for humanity” through increased Starship launch activity.

It added that the launch site is designed to support a high frequency of Starship launches. SpaceX did not provide details on the site’s launch schedule or construction timeline in its announcement.

Introducing Starbase, Louisiana – a high-cadence launch site that will enable Starship to open a pathway to the stars for humanity.

Thank you to @LAGovJeffLandry and the great people of Louisiana for all of their support as we work together on this audacious project →… pic.twitter.com/hq308hvg2g

The project adds another launch location to SpaceX’s Starship programme. The company currently conducts Starship test flights from its Starbase facility in Texas.

SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said the planned Louisiana site will eventually have more than a dozen launch towers and support over 30 Starship flights per day. He shared the details in a post on X, describing the facility as potentially “the biggest launch site on Earth”.

Musk said the planned launch site will be built to handle a high volume of Starship flights. He did not provide a timeline for reaching the proposed capacity or specify when construction of all the launch towers would begin.

title: Shopify CEO Tobi Lütke Considers Banning Claude Code
content:
“Insisting on only reading CLAUDE.md sometimes leads to split-brain problems when different team members use different tools.”

Shopify CEO Tobi Lütke is considering banning Anthropic’s Claude Code from the company until the coding agent changes how it handles project instructions, saying its reliance on CLAUDE.md can create inconsistencies when employees use different AI coding tools.

“I’m thinking about banning Claude Code at Shopify until they change their mind and read AGENTS.md and .agents/skills etc.,” Lütke said in a post on X. “Insisting on only reading CLAUDE.md sometimes leads to split-brain problems when different team members use different tools. Just unnecessary.”

The comments highlight a growing challenge for engineering teams using multiple AI coding agents, where different tools can follow different instruction files and potentially apply different coding conventions or workflows to the same codebase.

AGENTS.md is a Markdown file designed to provide AI coding agents with project-specific instructions, including coding conventions, repository structure, testing commands and other guidance.

Introduced by OpenAI in August 2025, AGENTS.md is an open standard that gives AI coding agents a consistent set of project-specific instructions to follow across repositories and development tools.

The Linux Foundation describes AGENTS.md as a universal standard for giving AI coding agents a consistent source of project-specific guidance across repositories and toolchains. The foundation said more than 60,000 open-source projects have adopted the format.

Claude Code, meanwhile, has traditionally used CLAUDE.md as its project-level instruction file. This creates a potential split when a repository supports multiple coding agents. If shared guidance is placed in AGENTS.md while Claude Code follows a separate CLAUDE.md, teams may have to maintain multiple sources of instructions or ensure the files stay aligned.

Lütke’s concern is that this can result in different developers getting different behaviour from AI coding tools even when they are working on the same codebase.

His reference to .agents/skills also points to a preference for keeping reusable agent capabilities and workflows in a shared project-level structure rather than tying them to one coding tool.

The issue comes as Shopify itself continues to build infrastructure for AI agents.

In May, Shopify introduced support for customising AGENTS.md, which it describes as the canonical agent-discovery document for a store. The company said /llms.txt and /llms-full.txt would mirror the content of /agents.md by default.

As AI coding agents take on more software development tasks, project-level instructions are becoming increasingly important. Files such as AGENTS.md can give these tools consistent guidance on coding practices, project structure and testing requirements.

title: OpenAI’s New Chip Beats NVIDIA; Gen 2 Nears Tape-Out in Months
content:
“Jalapeño is also evidence of a broader full-stack advantage,” OpenAI said in the blog post.

OpenAI’s first custom AI inference chip, Jalapeño, delivered up to 1.9x more performance per watt than NVIDIA’s Blackwell systems in benchmark tests, while also reducing response latency, according to results published by OpenAI.

The chip, developed with Broadcom and Celestica, is designed specifically for inference and is expected to begin deployment inside OpenAI’s compute infrastructure by the end of 2026.

OpenAI tested Jalapeño against commercially available AI systems using InferenceX, a public benchmark developed by SemiAnalysis, across GPT-OSS 120B, DeepSeek R1 670B, and Kimi K2.5 1T. Across the models, Jalapeño delivered 1.5–1.9 times more AI work per watt at peak throughput and 1.7–3.6x lower end-to-end latency than the comparison systems.

The DeepSeek R1 comparison illustrates the gap. Jalapeño delivered 19,641 mixed tokens per second per kilowatt at peak throughput, versus 11,781 for NVIDIA’s GB300, giving OpenAI’s chip a 1.7x advantage.

End-to-end latency was 1.65 seconds on Jalapeño compared to 5.99 seconds on the GB300. OpenAI reported similar advantages over NVIDIA systems on GPT-OSS and Kimi K2.5, with the full results shown in the accompanying benchmark data.

OpenAI rated Jalapeño at 700 watts, although its measured sustained power remained at or below 550 watts on the tested workloads.

The company said it evaluates inference hardware based on useful AI work delivered per unit of power while maintaining the latency required for interactive applications.

“Jalapeño is also evidence of a broader full-stack advantage,” OpenAI said in the blog post. “OpenAI can design models, products, serving software, chips, memory, networking, and systems together, using what we learn from real workloads to improve every layer of the stack. “

At the Hot Chips 2026 conference, OpenAI, just after publishing these results, also outlined how quickly it expects the platform to evolve.

The company said Jalapeño is only the first generation of a broader roadmap, with Gen 2 already in development and approaching tape-out within months. He also said Gen 3 is already operational.

Hot Chips '26: OpenAI says its Gen 1 chip is only step one with Gen 2 nearing tape-out in a number of months and Gen 3 already operational, afterwards bringing out the Broadcom and Celestica teams to share the stage

"One more thing -- this is step one of a multi-generational… https://t.co/alAB43w1ME pic.twitter.com/Q8eddAWNoU

— Fireside Alpha (@firesidealpha) August 26, 2026

OpenAI originally announced Jalapeño in June as part of a multi-generation platform it is developing with Broadcom and Celestica.

OpenAI designed the accelerator, while Broadcom provided chip implementation, networking, and connectivity technologies, and Celestica contributed board, rack, and system integration and production expertise.

The company said AI models also accelerated the chip’s development, helping take Jalapeño from initial design to tapeout in nine months.

Using Codex with GPT-Astra, engineers brought three open-weight models to high performance within two months, while selected AI-generated implementations for GPT-OSS components ran 1.5–1.8x faster than existing human-written implementations.

OpenAI said it will continue deploying NVIDIA and other third-party accelerators for training and inference. Jalapeño is the first generation of a planned multi-generation platform, with Gen 2 already in development and Gen 3 taking shape.

title: Mystery Ox Alpha Revealed as GLM-5.3-Flash, Running Entirely on Chinese AI Chips
content:
"This demonstrates that Chinese chips can support frontier-model inference efficiently and economically at scale,” said Z.ai.

Z.ai has revealed that the mystery Ox Alpha model that surged to the top of model usage charts over the last few days is GLM-5.3-Flash, a 320-billion-parameter multimodal model with 18 billion active parameters.

The company says it outperforms GLM-5.2 across coding and agentic benchmarks while approaching Claude Opus 4.8 on some tests.

The model was released anonymously as Ox Alpha on OpenCode and OpenRouter before Z.ai’s announcement.

Z.ai said the company used the anonymous deployment to gather real-world user feedback ahead of launch, and that Ox Alpha quickly became the most popular model of the week

OpenRouter said Ox Alpha processed more than 20 trillion tokens in six days, making it the largest model launch on the platform by token volume.

The model was offered free of charge during the preview, with OpenRouter listing a 1.05-million-token context window.

The price-to-performance ratio was a major part of Ox Alpha’s appeal during its anonymous preview: developers were getting frontier-level coding and agentic performance for free.

Z.ai’s disclosure now puts a concrete number behind that proposition.

The company says GLM-5.3-Flash scores 57 on Artificial Analysis’ Intelligence Index, at a discounted cost of just $0.045 per task, putting it in a markedly different price-performance bracket from models such as Claude Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.6.

Z.ai also said it has served GLM-5.3-Flash over the past week on a large cluster of domestically developed Chinese AI accelerators, with the deployment spanning tens of thousands of chips.

The company built a dedicated inference engine on top of SGLang and reported a threefold improvement in end-to-end serving performance compared with its initial baseline on the same hardware.

Z.ai said the resulting system achieved hardware efficiency and per-token costs comparable with mainstream NVIDIA GPUs. “This demonstrates that Chinese chips can support frontier-model inference efficiently and economically at scale,” said the company. Z.ai did not identify the specific Chinese accelerators used to serve the model.

However, this claim arrives against a backdrop of US restrictions designed to limit China’s access to advanced AI computing hardware.

US export controls have imposed licensing requirements on high-performance AI chips and related technologies for China.

Washington currently allows exports of certain lower-performance or otherwise restricted Nvidia AI accelerators, including the H200, to approved Chinese customers on a case-by-case licensing basis, subject to security and supply conditions.

NVIDIA’s more advanced Blackwell and upcoming Vera Rubin systems remain restricted from the Chinese market under US export controls

Z.ai lists the model at $0.15 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens, with OpenRouter currently applying a promotional 50% discount to the input rate.

The model is also available as open weights under an MIT licence on Hugging Face, allowing developers to download and run it themselves rather than accessing it only through an API.

Z.ai, formerly known as Zhipu AI, is a Beijing-based Chinese AI company that became the world’s first publicly listed large-language-model developer when it went public on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange in January.

Its current flagship is GLM-5.3, a 744-billion-parameter model designed for coding, agentic tasks and long-context workloads.

content: Listen5 minSHARESaveFollowPreferred SourceGoogle NewsWhatsAppTelegramGujarat Police is seeking technology to integrate approximately 80,000 CCTV cameras across the state into a unified video management and analytics ecosystem through the Gujarat Police Innovation Hackathon 2026.The challenge offers a total prize pool of ₹37 lakh and is scheduled for September 10–11, according to the official Sentinel Gujarat website.The project aims to address a fragmented surveillance infrastructure. The government says 26 different departments currently operate independent CCTV systems using different vendors, video management systems (VMS), storage arrangements, camera types and feed-sharing protocols. Some systems retain footage for seven days, while others retain it for 15 days or more.The proposed system would allow these separate networks to work through a common integration layer while, under some of the proposed models, allowing existing departmental systems to continue operating independently.The government says the architecture should be secure, scalable, interoperable, and designed to use existing infrastructure to the maximum practical extent.The system is also expected to connect CCTV analytics with databases including VAHAN, SARTHI, eGujCop (Gujarat Police's CCTNS platform), the Automated Fingerprint Identification System, and the National Automated Fingerprint Identification System. These databases contain records relating to arrested persons, stolen vehicles, wanted criminals, missing persons, unidentified dead bodies, and fingerprint data, according to the government.For the technical evaluation, participants will receive access to approximately 50 geographically distributed cameras. They must onboard the feeds into one platform, track a designated vehicle using its registration number, reconstruct its timestamped, and location-based movement history and generate real-time alerts from a representative watchlist database.The requirements include automatic number plate recognition, person and vehicle tracking, object detection, and event analytics. Facial recognition systems are also listed among the proposed analytics capabilities, while the government requires participants to demonstrate cybersecurity, scalability, and interoperability.Participants can choose among four reference models or submit a hybrid or customised architecture. The models range from a central CCTV registry and Geographic Information System (GIS) foundation to unified viewing, VMS federation, and a fully centralised VMS and artificial intelligence platform.The government will evaluate successful feed integration, the working platform, analytics output, architecture, security and readiness to scale toward approximately 80,000 cameras. It may also consider privacy protection, auditability, role-based access controls, edge processing, and bandwidth optimisation.The official website says registration opened on August 4 and closes on September 7. title: Google Cloud Launches Gemini Enterprise for the Legal Industry
content:
The platform connects with existing legal systems and uses AI agents for contract review, legal research, regulatory monitoring and document workflows.

Google Cloud has launched Gemini Enterprise for Legal, an AI platform designed for law firms and corporate legal departments, with tools for legal research, contract review, regulatory monitoring, document management and other workflows.

The platform is available in preview from August 26 and is part of Google Cloud’s new suite of industry-specific Gemini Enterprise solutions. Google Cloud said it also plans purpose-built solutions for healthcare, life sciences and other professional services.

It was developed with law firms and legal technology providers, with a focus on maintaining existing permissions, confidentiality controls, and governance requirements.

“Foundational model intelligence is necessary. For legal work, it is nowhere near sufficient,” Thomas Kurian, CEO of Google Cloud, said. He said the platform combines domain-specific skills, connections to enterprise systems, agents and an open partner ecosystem, with governance across the system.

Gemini Enterprise for Legal includes reusable skills that can be configured for tasks such as contract review and redlining, legal research, regulatory horizon scanning, Data Subject Access Request (DSAR) fulfilment and playbook creation.

These skills can incorporate a firm’s own instructions, citation rules and house style.

The platform also connects with legal teams’ existing systems through secure MCP connectors. These connections preserve existing user permissions and access controls across document management, case repositories, research services and other applications.

Google Cloud said the platform can deploy pre-built agents for legal and policy research, regulatory screening and contract drafting. Its stated use cases also include tracking legislative and regulatory changes, compiling data for DSAR responses, reviewing agreements against enterprise playbooks, updating contracting playbooks, redacting sensitive information from court filings and drafting non-disclosure agreements.

The platform integrates with services including Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, iManage, NetDocuments, DocuSign, Everlaw and RelativityOne. It also connects with legal research and litigation resources such as Thomson Reuters HighQ, CourtListener and Courtroom5, along with legal AI platforms including Harvey, Solve Intelligence and Legora.

Google Cloud is also working with systems integrators and technology partners including Accenture, Deloitte, Devoteam, Factor Law, KPMG, Tribe.ai, Valtech, Zazmic, Zencore and 66degrees. Deloitte and Eudia are among the partners offering agents through the platform.

The company said Gemini Enterprise for Legal operates within a governed control plane that enforces security policies, maintains private data isolation and provides traceable citations for outputs. Google Cloud also said client data, firm-specific playbooks, intellectual property, custom agents and model outputs remain private to the organisation and are not used to train or fine-tune its foundation models.

The platform is being developed with law firms including Cleary Gottlieb, Freshfields, Weil and Williams & Connolly.

“Using Google’s Gemini Enterprise, which can slot in seamlessly with other daily work tools, we can unlock greater efficiencies for our teams and help them deliver even higher quality work for our clients,” said Jeff Karpf, Managing Partner at Cleary Gottlieb.

Freshfields Global Managing Partner Alan Mason said the opportunity is to combine Gemini Enterprise for Legal with the firm’s expertise, governance and institutional knowledge.

title: Unifying Inference Bills and Revenue
content:
The Korean machine tool maker said that it has deployed its full Phase 1 investment in Bengaluru and plans to expand local manufacturing, supplier development and engineering talent.

What Actually Matters.

DN Solutions has opened its first Indian manufacturing plant in Bengaluru, investing ₹600 crore.

The new facility will combine R&D, manufacturing, a technical centre, and after-sales service.

DN Solutions, a South Korean machine tool manufacturer, inaugurated its first manufacturing plant in India on August 26, with the company saying it has fully deployed its Phase 1 investment of ₹600 crore, or approximately $62 million.

The Bengaluru facility is the company's first overseas manufacturing investment since it established its Yantai plant in China in 2003, according to DN Solutions.

The 25-acre facility in Bengaluru's ITIR Industrial Area was developed with the Karnataka Industrial Areas Development Board (KIADB). The company said the site will combine research and development, manufacturing, a technical centre and after-sales service as it seeks to make India a strategic part of its global manufacturing and supply chain network.

DN Solutions will initially manufacture its SVM vertical machining centres and LYNX and LEO horizontal turning centres at the facility. Production of five-axis machines is planned for later phases, the company said.

Wonjong Kim, CEO of DN Solutions, said the company's expansion in Bengaluru is linked to the convergence of AI and physical manufacturing.

“As AI expands beyond digital screens into the physical world, machines become indispensable. At the center of that transformation phase are machine tools, serving as a core platform for Physical AI. Bengaluru has a strong software ecosystem, which uniquely positions it to lead manufacturing in the Physical AI era. That is why we chose Bengaluru,” Kim said.

The company said it has already achieved approximately 80% localisation by parts count and aims to source most components in India within five years, excluding spindle assemblies.

It plans to launch a formal supplier development programme in 2027 and said it is working with Indian micro, small and medium enterprises through technical collaboration and capability-building initiatives.

DN Solutions currently employs 240 people directly in India and plans to increase that figure to 500. The company said it recruited approximately 100 recent graduates over the past year and operates a training centre and a one-year talent development programme.

The Bengaluru plant is also intended to support product development for Indian customers. DN Solutions said its R&D centre will work with research institutes in Korea, Germany and China, as well as technical centres across Asia, Europe and the Americas.

The company said its technical centre will allow customers to conduct test cuts and evaluate machining solutions, while a service office, repair shop, parts warehouse and DN Academy will support after-sales service and workforce training.

Kim said DN Solutions expects to continue investing in India, with further phases under consideration based on market demand and business growth. “We will continue investing in India for the long term,” he said.

DN Solutions said it has operated in India for more than three decades, beginning sales in 1994, followed by a Bengaluru Technical Center in 2008 and an Indian subsidiary in 2016.

“Would you keep production traffic on a gateway owned by the company that also settles your revenue?”

Stripe has entered its second era, one where payments infrastructure is converging with AI infrastructure. And it is expanding that footprint so aggressively that it is willing to pay more than six times OpenRouter’s $1.3 billion valuation from just a few months ago.

The financial services and software-as-a-service company has agreed to acquire the AI model-routing platform for more than $8 billion, its largest acquisition to date. The companies have not disclosed the price; Reuters reported it at slightly above $8 billion.

OpenRouter gives developers a single interface to access and route requests across more than 400 AI models from more than 80 providers. It evaluates requests based on factors including task complexity, price, speed and reliability. Stripe says the combination will help businesses “maximise profitability” by routing requests intelligently and spending their tokens efficiently.

Since its founding in 2010, Stripe has largely focused on building the financial infrastructure that lets businesses operate on the internet, from accepting payments and managing subscriptions to billing customers and moving money.

But over the past year, Stripe has increasingly built infrastructure for the AI economy. It has developed tools to track token usage and help AI companies bill customers based on consumption, while also tackling rising and unpredictable model costs.

In January, Stripe acquired Metronome, a usage-based metering and billing platform. It then introduced Token Billing in preview, allowing AI companies to meter token consumption, apply their own pricing or markup, and bill customers based on usage.

At its April 2026 Sessions conference, Stripe went further, showing infrastructure for real-time metering and billing of AI usage, including individual tokens. The broader idea is that as AI software moves toward consumption-based pricing, Stripe wants to handle the infrastructure underneath that usage—measuring it, pricing it, billing for it and eventually moving the money.

OpenRouter adds a layer closer to the actual model request. Instead of simply billing after tokens have been consumed, Stripe can now potentially connect the billing system to the decision about where those tokens are spent.

Getting Rid of AI-Driven Billing Complexities

In an interaction with AIM, Varun Mishra, Principal Analyst at Counterpoint Research, pointed to the growing complexity of that problem.

“Billing for AI is meaningfully more complex,” Mishra says. “It involves a multitude of variables like which model is used, which provider serves it, and whether tokens are input, output, or cached, with each being priced differently.”

Those variables also change as providers launch models and revise their prices.

Agentic workloads make accounting harder as one task can trigger dozens of model calls across different tools, users and projects, making it harder to attribute the underlying cost to the customer or workflow that generated it.

“And all this needs to be done at a scale of trillions of tokens per day, which is only going to increase in future,” Mishra adds. “Hence there is a need for a platform to measure and provide a reliable way to bill tokens accurately within complex workflows.”

Stripe has already been building towards that problem. Token Billing currently synchronises token prices for models from a select group of providers, including OpenAI, Anthropic and Google, automatically updating those prices when providers change them or introduce new models.

Mishra said OpenRouter could expand that coverage substantially because it already sits across hundreds of models and dozens of providers.

“Bringing OpenRouter in-house should help close that gap directly, extending automatic price-tracking to dozens of additional providers OpenRouter already covers,” Mishra says, adding that OpenRouter could also give Stripe visibility into how developers are actually choosing and consuming models, allowing its billing infrastructure to evolve around real usage patterns.

This acquisition creates a more interesting possibility than simply finding the cheapest model for every request.

Most model-routing decisions today are based on performance per dollar. Companies generally send a request to the cheapest model that meets their quality and cost requirements. But whether that was the right decision for the business often becomes clear only later, when the inference bill and the revenue generated by that customer sit in separate systems.

“Stripe would be in a position to close that gap inside one system,” said Manish Choudhary, CEO and Co-founder of Flexprice, a billing platform for AI-native companies. “It would see what a request cost to serve through OpenRouter and what the developer charged their end customer through Stripe Billing and Metronome, on the same account, in the same week.”

Bringing those two numbers together could allow routing decisions to be made against a target margin rather than simply the price of a token. A lower-value customer could be routed to cheaper models, a workload that becomes unprofitable could be capped before the billing period ends, and pricing plans could eventually be based on the model mix customers actually consume rather than an estimate made months earlier.

Choudhary sees an even larger opportunity in financial services built around those economics. If Stripe can see both a company’s inference spending and the revenue generated by that usage, it could potentially underwrite credit based on observed gross margins, with repayments tied to the revenue generated by those AI workloads.

“Neither company could have built that alone, because neither one could see both halves of the ledger,” he says.

The Neutrality Question

But Choudhary cautions against assuming that the routing layer itself is the durable asset Stripe is acquiring. Routing is becoming increasingly competitive, with Vercel, Cloudflare and the major cloud providers offering their own ways to move workloads across models.

That could make the basic routing function increasingly commoditised and put pressure on the fees OpenRouter can charge. OpenRouter currently charges the 5.5% fee when users purchase credits.

He also expects OpenRouter’s current 5.5% fee on credit purchases to eventually disappear, arguing that Stripe is more likely to use the platform to drive a much larger volume of AI transactions and monetise services around that flow than preserve a fee on inference usage.

The harder asset to replicate, he says, is OpenRouter’s neutrality. The platform does not operate its own model and historically had no direct financial interest in which provider handled a request. Stripe’s ownership changes that dynamic because it will control the routing layer while also processing payments and revenue for many of the developers using it.

“That’s the thing I would watch rather than the price,” Choudhary says. “Would you keep production traffic on a gateway owned by the company that also settles your revenue?”

title: Bengaluru-Based AI Startup Ringg AI Secures $10 Mn in Series A Extension Led by Peak XV
content:
The Bengaluru-based startup plans to use the funds to expand its AI agents and enterprise operations across India and international markets.

Voice AI startup Ringg AI has extended its Series A funding round, with Peak XV Partners leading the latest investment and Arkam Ventures and Capital 2b also participating. The company previously raised $5.5 million in its Series A earlier this year, bringing the total to $15.5 million.

The company said the new capital will strengthen its AI platform, expand its voice, WhatsApp and browser agents, invest in its proprietary AI models and context graph, and grow its enterprise business in India and international markets.

Founded in 2023 by Siddharth Tripathi, Kali Charan Vemuru and Utkarsh Shukla, Ringg AI is headquartered in Bengaluru.

The startup builds AI agents that automate customer conversations and the business workflows that follow. Its platform combines voice, WhatsApp and browser agents, allowing them to share context across customer conversations, business rules and enterprise systems.

The agents can handle workflows such as lead qualification, customer onboarding, support, collections and renewals. Human employees can also take over conversations and workflows while retaining the context and actions completed by the agents.

“Nobody buys us because the demo sounds good,” said Tripathi, Founder and CEO of Ringg AI. “They buy us because onboarding improves, resolution times fall, or qualified leads start showing up in the CRM without someone having to make the call.”

Tripathi added that enterprises should not have to buy separate systems for voice and other workflows. “We own the loop from conversation to action to evaluation to improvement,” he said.

Ringg said its agents are already deployed at companies including Policybazaar, CRED, Flipkart, Groww, Practo, Tabby, SuperNova and GoodScore, serving customers across sectors such as healthcare, banking, fintech and IT.

The startup said its platform creates a context graph across customers, conversations, business rules, workflows and enterprise systems. This shared context allows a conversation to move between channels. For instance, a voice interaction can continue on WhatsApp, while a browser agent can complete actions in a CRM or another enterprise application.

Ringg also uses built-in evaluations to measure conversation quality, policy adherence, workflow completion and business outcomes. Enterprise teams can monitor agents, review decisions and take over conversations or workflows when needed.

“We chose to solve the hardest version of the problem first,” said Vemuru, Co-Founder and CTO of Ringg AI. “If an agent can handle a noisy call, switch across languages, and still complete a real workflow, it can work almost anywhere. We are building this in India, for a global market.”

Ringg is also developing its AI stack, including its proprietary speech-to-text model Parrot and small language models. The company said this approach is intended to give enterprises more control over costs, compliance and data residency.

The platform supports deployments across India, the GCC, the US and Europe, along with on-premise deployments.

title: AM Intelligence Orders 9,000 NVIDIA Rubin GPUs for Hyderabad AI Factory
content:
The Hyderabad AI factory is the first tranche of AMI’s planned 1 GW of Compute-as-a-Service capacity across India, the US, Finland and Malaysia.

AM Intelligence (AMI), an AI infrastructure company promoted by the founders of Greenko Group, has placed a binding order for about 9,000 NVIDIA Rubin GPUs for its first AI factory in Hyderabad, with deliveries scheduled for the first quarter of 2027.

The GPUs will be deployed as NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 rack-scale systems across 30 MW of capacity at the Hyderabad facility. AMI said the deployment will make the facility one of the first frontier AI compute clusters in Asia based on the Vera Rubin platform.

The Hyderabad AI factory is the first tranche of AMI’s planned 1 GW of Compute-as-a-Service (CaaS) capacity across India, the US, Finland and Malaysia. The company plans to bring 200 MW of capacity to market in the near term, with capital expenditure of more than $8 billion.

“For over two decades, we have focused on transforming electrons into value - addressing critical and emerging societal needs,” Anil Chalamalasetty, Chairman of AM Intelligence, said. “Today, the electron-to-token opportunity allows us to take this capability further, converting power infrastructure into frontier AI compute at scale.”

The Hyderabad facility is being designed with high-throughput RDMA over Converged Ethernet (RoCE) networking and advanced storage systems. AMI said the infrastructure will support AI workloads including trillion-parameter models and agentic AI applications.

NVIDIA’s Vera Rubin NVL72 platform uses NVFP4, a low-precision computing format for AI workloads, along with HBM4 memory. NVIDIA says the architecture can reduce AI inference token-serving costs by up to 10 times compared with its Grace Blackwell generation.

AMI said its Hyderabad AI factory is being engineered to deliver about 450 exaFLOPS of NVFP4 inference compute. It is developing 5 GW of powered AI data centres across India, the US and Europe. The facilities are being designed for high-density AI computing and will use liquid cooling to handle the power and heat requirements of AI chips.

The company also plans to provide 1 GW of CaaS capacity for global AI workloads, with an initial 200 MW expected to come online in the near term.

AMI said its infrastructure will serve hyperscalers, frontier AI labs, enterprises, sovereign AI initiatives, AI-native companies and developers.

The company is building its AI infrastructure alongside its existing energy platform. AMI said it is developing a 50 GW energy infrastructure platform across more than 20 states in India, covering solar, wind, hydro and energy storage.

title: TCS to Acquire Porsche IT Unit MHP for $373 Mn
content:
Tata Consultancy Services will acquire 100% of Porsche AG’s IT consulting subsidiary MHP for an enterprise value of €320 million as part of a five-year, €1.25 billion strategic partnership.

Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) will acquire Germany-based management and IT consulting firm MHP from Porsche AG for an enterprise value of €320 million ($373 million), as the Indian IT major deepens its push into artificial intelligence and automotive technology.

TCS will acquire 100% of MHP through its Netherlands-based wholly owned subsidiary.

The deal is part of a five-year strategic partnership between TCS and Porsche valued at €1.25 billion ($1.45 billion), under which the companies will work on AI transformation across the automaker’s engineering, manufacturing, operations, and customer experience functions.

TCS will also establish a dedicated AI Mobility Centre of Excellence for Porsche, focused on scaling AI applications across the automotive value chain.

“As AI, software, and data redefine the automotive industry, this partnership brings together TCS’ capabilities in AI, engineering, technology and business transformation with MHP’s strong automotive consulting expertise. Together, we will industrialise AI at scale for Porsche, accelerating innovation across the value chain to deliver intelligent, software-defined mobility experiences of the future,” K Krithivasan, CEO and Managing Director, TCS said in a statement.

MHP, a subsidiary of Porsche, has about 4,500 employees and reported turnover of €742 million ($865 million) in calendar 2025. The company provides consulting and technology services spanning digital transformation, artificial intelligence, SAP transformation, manufacturing digitalisation, connected mobility, and software-defined mobility.

The acquisition is expected to strengthen TCS's presence in Germany and expand its access to European automotive and industrial customers. MHP has operations in Germany, Romania, the UK, the US, India, and Mexico.

For Porsche, the transaction represents a move to focus more closely on its core automotive business while bringing TCS in as a strategic technology partner.

“By combining Porsche’s automotive expertise with TCS’ digital technology and AI capabilities, we will further strengthen our innovative power, increase efficiency, and boost our competitiveness in an increasingly data and software-driven world of mobility,” said Michael Leiters, CEO, Porsche AG.

The deal comes as Indian IT services companies increasingly look to build deeper industry-specific capabilities in AI, rather than relying solely on traditional technology outsourcing contracts.

TCS said the partnership will focus on industrialising AI use cases across manufacturing and operations, engineering, and customer experience. The AI Mobility Centre of Excellence will work on turning AI applications into scalable solutions for Porsche.

The transaction will be funded through cash and is subject to regulatory approvals, including under EU merger-control and foreign-subsidy rules. TCS expects the acquisition to close within three to four months.

title: Ryanair is Using AI-Generated Videos for Staff Training & Passenger Updates
content:
The European low-cost carrier is using Synthesia’s AI products to cut costs and speed up content production.

Ryanair is using AI-generated videos to train employees and send passenger disruption updates, cutting the time needed to produce the latter by up to 90%, according to AI video company Synthesia.

The airline previously took at least an hour to produce a single disruption video, which required filming, editing, and exporting. Localising the videos could take longer because Ryanair often needed employees who could record versions in different languages.

Ryanair now uses Synthesia’s AI avatars and reusable templates to turn scripts into videos. When a disruption occurs, staff can update the relevant information, generate a video and send it to affected passengers through the Ryanair app. The same update can be produced in every European language. The airline is also using AI avatars for employee training.

Ryanair trains about 1,300 of its 3,000 engineers across 13 European bases each year. Instead of repeatedly flying instructors between locations, it can record an instructor once and use their digital avatar to deliver the training. Synthesia said the shift has produced six-figure savings for Ryanair, which the airline has reinvested in additional engineering training.

The technology has also been extended to 15,000 cabin crew and 22,000 ground agents, with training and operational procedures delivered in 20 languages.

“With Synthesia, we deliver translated, targeted messages in minutes,” said Ellen Drumm, Ryanair’s Customer Service Communications Manager.

The AI video deployment comes as Ryanair expands its use of AI across core operations.

Earlier this month, the airline announced a five-year partnership with Google Cloud to deploy Google Workspace and Gemini Enterprise to 35,000 employees. Ryanair plans to use Gemini Enterprise to automate decision-making, optimise flight-crew logistics and build custom AI agents.

The partnership will also bring Google DeepMind models including AlphaEvolve and WeatherNext into fleet operations and maintenance scheduling.

It follows Ryanair’s decision in July to extend its AWS partnership for another five years, with AWS technologies including Bedrock and Bedrock AgentCore supporting areas such as the airline’s website, fleet scheduling, pilot workflows and employee applications.

Ryanair carried 208.4 million passengers in its financial year ended March 2026 and had 647 aircraft at the end of the period. The airline aims to carry more than 300 million passengers annually by 2034.

title: QpiAI, Gujarat’s PDEU Sign MoU for 8-Qubit Quantum Centre
content:
The facility will support quantum education, research and access to computing resources for students and researchers.

What Actually Matters.

QpiAI and PDEU have established a Quantum Centre of Excellence in Gujarat to enhance quantum education and research.

The centre will feature an 8-qubit quantum computer, providing access to advanced computing resources for students and researchers.

Karnataka’s QpiAI and Pandit Deendayal Energy University (PDEU) in Gujarat signed an agreement to establish a Quantum Centre of Excellence at PDEU. QpiAI will install its 8-qubit Qvidya quantum computer at the university. The facility will support education and early quantum system research.

The centre will provide quantum software, application libraries and access to PDEU’s high-performance computing systems. Users outside PDEU can also access the system through QpiAI’s Qcloud platform. The MoU exchange took place in the presence of representatives from Gujarat’s science and technology department.

QpiAI CEO and Founder Nagendra Nagaraja said Gujarat’s industrial base creates a need for quantum computing skills. He pointed to the state’s renewable energy and chemical industries. He also cited oil and gas refineries and the financial sector in Gujarat.

“Gujarat is the hub for renewables, chemical industry, oil and gas refineries and financial hub with GIFT City,” Nagaraja said, adding that the region needs upskilling in quantum computing and quantum information science.

The agreement comes as PDEU expands its research capabilities in emerging technologies. The university said the facility will support education, training and research in quantum computing. It will also help students and researchers develop skills in the field.

Under the collaboration, QpiAI will provide further upgrades as students use the system. The company said students can use it for programming, learning and innovation. QpiAI also plans to work with its partners to advance quantum computing.

Professor Sundar S Manoharan, Director General of PDEU, said that the university’s semiconductor collaboration with Micron and its green hydrogen research supported the move. “Building capabilities in quantum computing is a critical next step for PDEU.”

The company said quantum computers could support several industrial sectors. These include chemicals, new materials, oil and gas, renewable energy and manufacturing. Financial services also feature among the sectors QpiAI cited.

The QVidya system will connect with PDEU’s existing high-performance computing infrastructure. QpiAI also said people outside the university can access the system through Qcloud. This could extend the centre’s resources beyond the university campus.

QpiAI describes itself as a full-stack quantum computing company and has built a quantum foundry in Bengaluru. It describes the facility as the largest in Asia for manufacturing superconducting, semiconductor and photonic qubits. QpiAI’s planned upgrades will allow the system to evolve as students and researchers gain experience. The collaboration also links quantum education with Gujarat’s energy and industrial sectors.

title: OrbitAID to Demonstrate Satellite Life Extension Mission in 2027
content:
The Bengaluru-based company will test inspection, docking, refuelling and orbital repositioning in a single mission.

What Actually Matters.

OrbitAID Aerospace plans to launch a satellite life extension mission in early 2027 using two 70-kilogram satellites.

The mission will demonstrate essential satellite servicing techniques, including inspection, docking, refuelling, and orbital repositioning.

Bengaluru-based space tech startup OrbitAID Aerospace is likely to launch a satellite life extension demonstration mission in the first quarter of 2027. The company will use two 70-kilogram satellites, AayulSAT-2A and AayulSAT-2B, to demonstrate satellite servicing in Low Earth orbit (LEO).

The mission will test inspection, rendezvous, docking, refuelling and life extension.

It will involve one satellite acting as the chaser and the other as the target. After separation, the chaser will track the target from a distance before switching to visual navigation.

The mission will use onboard sensors to inspect the target and create a 3D reconstruction. The chaser will then dock with the target, transfer propellant and raise its altitude before returning it to its original orbit.

OrbitAID said it will use its proprietary Standardised Interface for Docking and Refuelling (SIDRP) for its operations.

“By demonstrating the entire life extension mission, we are proving end-to-end RPOD operations in a single mission,” said Sakthikumar Ramachandran, Founder and CEO of OrbitAID. He added that the company will now focus on turning the demonstration into servicing contracts with geostationary orbit (GEO) satellite operators.

The startup said the mission will also use ARCAS, its LAR docking mechanism, and software for autonomous RPOD operations. The company developed the two satellites from concept design to launch readiness in 11 months.

It said the work involved an international supply chain, and the approach is designed to scale to GEO (Geostationary Earth Orbit), where satellite life extension has higher commercial value. OrbitAID aims to move from demonstrating the technology to providing servicing for satellite operators.

The company is developing technologies for satellite inspection, active debris removal and refuelling. The company is also developing orbital fuel stations to support long-term in-orbit infrastructure.
