content:
The company is expanding beyond AI code reviews with tools that prioritise changes, explain large pull requests and monitor software for security risks.

AI code review company CodeRabbit has raised $143 million in a Series C round at a $1.5 billion valuation, less than a year after its Series B.

The round was co-led by Atomico and Smash Capital, with participation from BMW i Ventures, Datadog, Hirtle Callaghan, SineWave Ventures and existing investors including CRV, Scale Venture Partners and Engineering Capital.

CodeRabbit said it will use the funding for international expansion, research, infrastructure and product development. The company also plans to invest more than $10 million over the next 12 months to keep its AI code review and agent capabilities free for open-source projects and maintainers.

The funding comes as coding agents generate more code and pull requests, creating a new problem for engineering teams: deciding which changes need human attention and whether AI-generated changes are safe to ship.

“The new bottleneck is judgement,” CodeRabbit said in its announcement.

Alongside the funding, CodeRabbit has introduced a product category called Agentic Change Management. It extends the company’s AI code review system into a platform for validating, prioritising, explaining and monitoring software changes created by both humans and AI agents.

The platform includes three new capabilities: CodeRabbit Triage, CodeRabbit Change Stack and CodeRabbit Security.

Triage scores incoming pull requests based on factors such as value, urgency, risk, dependencies and readiness. It can route higher-risk changes to human reviewers while moving lower-risk changes into automated workflows.

Change Stack is designed to help developers understand large AI-generated pull requests without requiring a line-by-line review. It organises changes into semantic layers and shows their purpose, dependencies, affected systems and risks.

CodeRabbit Security extends the company’s code analysis to software already running in production. It examines relationships across files, services, data flows, authorisation boundaries and trust boundaries to identify security and business-logic risks.

“A diff shows what changed. Change Stack shows what it means,” the company said.

CodeRabbit argues that AI coding agents are reversing the traditional software development sequence. Instead of teams deciding what to build before investing significant engineering time, agents can turn product requirements, support tickets and security findings into code changes and pull requests.

The company cited data showing that GitHub is on pace for 14 times more commits this year, while autonomous agents account for 35% of pull requests among companies in the 90th percentile of coding-agent adoption.

That is shifting the pull request from a record of completed engineering work into a place where teams decide whether AI-generated work should be shipped.

“The PR is set to become the auditable planning and decision point where the team determines what to ship,” CodeRabbit said.

CodeRabbit’s expansion comes as the market for AI coding tools grows. The company now conducts more than two million code reviews a week and has more than 17,000 customers, including NVIDIA, BMW, JFrog, Trivago, Adyen and Indeed.

The company said its revenue grew more than fivefold over the past year. It also said its platform is used across more than 1,50,000 open-source projects.

CodeRabbit previously raised a $60 million Series B round in September last year.

The company has also expanded beyond pull-request reviews. In April, it launched CodeRabbit Agent for Slack, extending its code context engine into team conversations and the wider software development lifecycle. At the time, CodeRabbit said it served more than 15,000 teams and ran more than two million code reviews each week.

The company now plans to expand further into Europe and Asia, including Japan. Atomico partner Luca Eisenstecken is also joining CodeRabbit’s board.

CodeRabbit’s broader pitch is that AI can increase the amount of software produced, but human oversight still needs to keep pace. “People remain responsible for intent, architecture, product judgement, acceptable risk, and the consequences of what ultimately ships,” the company said.

content:
SpaceXAI has launched Grok Bot in early beta. It is an AI agent designed to operate inside users’ apps and websites and complete multi-step tasks without requiring users to supervise every action.

The bot can run on persistent cloud computers, retain context between tasks, and return to users when an approval is needed.

Each bot runs on a persistent cloud virtual machine with its own browser, filesystem, and terminal. It can use connected tools and computer-use capabilities to operate software even when a service does not provide a dedicated API. This allows it to perform tasks directly in applications rather than simply producing instructions or drafts.

Users can create multiple bots for different jobs, such as managing an inbox, researching sales prospects, handling expenses, or reproducing software bugs. The bot can work in parallel and pass context between one another, allowing one agent to hand off part of a task to another.

Grok Bot can also learn workflows from demonstrations.

A user can make a bot follow a multi-step process once, after which it can save the workflow as a routine and repeat it on demand or on a schedule. Bots retain their memory, files, browser sessions, and preferences, allowing work to continue across separate tasks.

SpaceXAI said Bots are designed to complete work end-to-end and only return when human input is required. Its examples include researching prospective customers, scoring accounts, drafting outreach messages, and leaving the final communications for the user to approve.

Grok Bot is available today in early beta to SuperGrok Heavy, Cursor Ultra, and Cursor Premium Teams subscribers on desktop and iOS. Enterprise customers can currently join a waitlist for access.

Grok Bot’s integration with Cursor is a result of SpaceX agreeing in June to acquire AI coding startup in an all-stock transaction valued at about $60 billion. Before the acquisition, Cursor and SpaceXAI jointly trained Grok 4.5.

Cursor said the model was trained using trillions of tokens from Cursor data capturing developer-agent interactions and was designed for long-running work beyond software engineering.

content:
Bengaluru-based startup Sarvam AI is deploying its Indus AI workspace across the Maharashtra government, with around 2,500 officials expected to use the platform in their daily work.

The deployment will allow officials across state departments to research policies and precedents, draft notes and replies, translate and summarise government documents, analyse data and convert scanned records into searchable text.

Indus will support workflows across 22 Indian languages, including Marathi.

The deployment is part of a broader partnership between Sarvam and the Maharashtra government that will also cover voice agents for citizen outreach and speech technologies for public services.

According to Sarvam, officials will be able to use Indus for tasks that form part of routine administrative work, including researching government policies, preparing first drafts and analysing long documents.

The platform can also be used to process scanned records and make them searchable, which could help departments work with legacy documents that are not available in digital formats.

Sarvam says the system will run on infrastructure located entirely in India, with government data remaining within the country.

The company has positioned Indus as part of its broader sovereign AI strategy. When Indus was introduced in February, Sarvam said, “True AI sovereignty means building the full stack of technology from the ground up.”

Indus is powered by Sarvam’s 105B sovereign model. The company opened the platform to users in limited beta in February, describing it as an interface for its Indian-language AI models.

The Indus deployment follows Maharashtra’s broader push to integrate AI into government operations.

In March, Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis announced letters of intent with OpenAI and Sarvam AI, alongside MoUs with IIT Bombay and BharatGen, as part of the state’s plan to strengthen its AI capabilities.

The state has since created an Electronics, Information Technology and Artificial Intelligence Department. The department was constituted through a government notification dated April 21, 2026, and is responsible for AI policy, digital governance, data governance, cybersecurity and digital infrastructure.

Maharashtra has also published its AI Policy 2026, signalling a broader effort to incorporate AI into public administration and build an AI ecosystem in the state.

The government has separately announced plans for an advanced State Data Centre in Nagpur to secure the state’s data and applications.

The Maharashtra deployment gives Sarvam another government use case for its full-stack AI platform. The company was selected by the central government in 2025 to build a sovereign large language model under the IndiaAI Mission, with the model to be built and deployed in India.

Sarvam has since expanded beyond foundation models into products covering AI assistants, speech, translation and document processing.

The company raised $234 million in the first close of its $300 million Series B in June at a post-money valuation of $1.5 billion. HCLTech led the round with a $150 million investment, while Bessemer Venture Partners and existing investors Khosla Ventures and Peak XV Partners also participated.

Following that, it also secured $75 million from investors including NVIDIA, Glade Brook, Gaja Capital, IndiGo Ventures, and several individual investors.

Sarvam said the funding would support research into its next models and expand its compute capacity and deployments across enterprises, developers and government.

The Maharashtra rollout puts that strategy into practice at the administrative level, with thousands of officials using an Indian AI system for day-to-day government work rather than limiting deployment to a standalone pilot.

Samsung India will train 20,000 young people in artificial intelligence across 10 states under the 2026 edition of its Samsung Innovation Campus (SIC) programme.

The programme will be conducted in partnership with the Electronics Sector Skills Council of India (ESSCI) and Telecom Sector Skill Council (TSSC).

The fourth edition of SIC in India will provide AI training to people aged 18 to 25, including hands-on learning, projects, mentorship and exposure to real-world applications.

The programme aims to build technical and career-ready skills as demand for AI talent grows across industries.

Samsung said SIC has trained more than 26,500 young people in India since its launch in 2022. Women accounted for 48% of participants in 2025, according to the company.

“AI represents one of the greatest opportunities of our time, and India is uniquely positioned to lead this transformation through the strength of its young talent. Realising that opportunity will require sustained investment in developing the right skills, encouraging innovation and making AI education more accessible to every aspiring learner, regardless of where they come from,” said JB Park, President and CEO, Samsung Southwest Asia.

“Through SIC, we are investing in the next generation of AI talent, helping young Indians build the knowledge, confidence and practical experience needed to contribute to India’s innovation journey.”

The 2026 programme will also focus on problem-solving, critical thinking and collaboration alongside technical AI skills.

Samsung said participants will work on practical AI solutions as part of the training. The company is also running Samsung Solve for Tomorrow, focused on young innovators and entrepreneurs, and Samsung DOST, which provides training for sales and technical service roles.

The initiative builds on Samsung’s earlier skilling efforts in India. In April, the company certified 1,000 students in Maharashtra in AI and coding through Samsung Innovation Campus, with the programme also incorporating soft-skills and career-readiness training.

ESSCI, established in 2012, works with industry, academia and government bodies including MeitY, the Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship and the National Skill Development Corporation. The council says it has trained, upskilled or reskilled more than 2.5 million people across India for roles in electronics system design and manufacturing.

On the other hand, TSSC focuses on building the workforce for India’s telecom and digital-infrastructure industry, covering roles across 5G, broadband, optical fibre, IoT and related technologies.

In June, Ericsson and TSSC launched a nationwide initiative to train 10,000 ITI students in 5G and emerging telecom technologies.

The programme will establish 10 Ericsson ITI Labs across a network of 100 ITIs and provide a 60-hour curriculum covering 5G networks, wireless infrastructure, fibre-to-the-home systems and telecom operations.

content:
Samsung Electronics has cut a semiconductor verification task that was expected to take more than a month to just two days using Anthropic’s Claude, according to South Korean media outlet Chosun Biz.

Its System LSI division used Claude to build a verification environment for a customer-specific SoC involving 64 interconnected data paths.

The work was complicated by delays in receiving some standard design data, including the RTL (register transfer level) for a DRAM controller, as well as the use of third-party IP.

According to the report, Samsung fed Claude the available SoC design information, internal chip communication specifications, and verification IP from electronic design automation vendors. Claude then identified the required verification IP, connected the components, created a virtual verification environment, and generated test scenarios.

For the missing DRAM controller, it used virtual verification blocks to examine core data paths and identify errors before the actual RTL became available.

Samsung found no manual errors during the environment-building process and assessed the overall workflow as roughly 15 times faster.

The effect was also visible in work that would normally require engineers to spend weeks learning unfamiliar specifications.

The report added that a second-year Samsung engineer used Claude Code to develop and verify virtual USB keyboard and mouse models in one day. The work would have normally taken about a month, including learning USB communication standards and developing separate models. Claude helped interpret the requirements, propose an implementation, and modify the resulting code.

Samsung has been expanding this use of AI beyond Claude Code. The company initially opened Claude Code to software developers last May before extending it to specialised semiconductor development.

It has also brought in external generative AI tools including ChatGPT and Gemini as part of its broader “Great AI Transformation” programme, which covers areas from R&D and production to marketing and support.

However, the report flagged instances where Claude changed an error message instead of fixing the underlying issue, restored unrelated completed work when asked to roll back one function, and attempted to modify RTL when instructed only to analyse verification results.

Samsung is therefore keeping engineers responsible for defining the scope of AI tasks and re-verifying the output.

content:
Quantum computing company Quantinuum and Oracle have signed a multi-year partnership to bring quantum computing to Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI), with Quantinuum’s Helios quantum computer set to be deployed at a US-based OCI AI data centre.

The deployment will allow OCI customers to access Helios through a planned OCI quantum service alongside Oracle’s high-performance computing (HPC) and GPU infrastructure.

The companies will explore hybrid workloads that combine quantum computing with AI and classical computing for applications including drug discovery, materials science, financial modelling, and optimisation.

“We believe the next phase of enterprise computing will be shaped by bringing quantum, AI, and high-performance computing together,” said Rajeeb Hazra, President and CEO of Quantinuum. “Deploying Helios inside OCI allows Quantinuum and Oracle to create a unique deeply integrated environment for hybrid workloads, explore enterprise use cases with customers, and accelerate commercial adoption.”

Helios, which Quantinuum launched commercially in November 2025, is a 98-physical-qubit trapped-ion quantum computer. The system has been used in demonstrations involving 48 logical qubits and has an average two-qubit gate fidelity of 99.921%, according to the company.

The planned OCI quantum service will give customers access to quantum computing without having to procure or operate dedicated quantum hardware. Oracle said the service is expected to integrate Quantinuum’s development stack with open-source hybrid programming frameworks.

“By bringing Quantinuum’s Helios to Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, we want to give developers a practical and secure way to explore how quantum computing could complement their existing AI and HPC workloads on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure while improving compute efficiency and energy use,” added Mahesh Thiagarajan, Executive Vice President of Oracle Cloud Infrastructure.

Helios will integrate with OCI compute, networking, storage, identity, and data services under the same governance and access controls used by customers, the companies said.

Oracle plans to preview the OCI quantum service in the coming months. The service is expected to allow developers to move from quantum simulation to execution on physical quantum hardware while combining quantum processors with classical compute resources.

Quantinuum also said a single Helios system has an estimated power draw of less than 1% of the power draw reported for leading supercomputers, positioning quantum computing as a lower-power resource for suitable hybrid workloads.

The companies expect the partnership to support enterprise customers as well as AI labs, universities, and research institutions. The initial use cases will span areas where organisations face computationally intensive problems that can be combined with classical HPC and AI workloads.

“As quantum computing moves closer to enterprise adoption, simplifying how organisations access and integrate quantum resources has become just as important as advancing the hardware itself,” said Heather West, Global Quantum Research Lead at IDC. “Deploying quantum systems within private cloud environments enables organisations to integrate quantum computing into existing AI and HPC workflows through familiar cloud infrastructure and development tools.”

content:
Brad Lightcap, one of OpenAI’s longest-serving senior executives, is leaving the company after eight years to start a new venture.

Lightcap announced his departure in a post on X, saying he would be “moving on from OpenAI to start something new”. He did not disclose details about the venture, but said he had spent the past few months thinking about “the next horizon” and the issues that could affect the AI industry’s next phase.

“I believe there are a few important new things the world will need to get right as we enter this next period,” Lightcap wrote. He said he would share more about those plans soon.

Lightcap will remain at OpenAI for the next few weeks. “I am not going far and hope to continue to support you all however I can,” he wrote.

His departure comes months after OpenAI moved him out of the Chief Operating Officer role as part of a broader leadership reshuffle.

OpenAI had expanded Lightcap’s COO remit in March 2025 to cover global deployment, business strategy, partnerships and infrastructure. Altman said at the time that Lightcap would oversee the company’s business and day-to-day operations.

Lightcap joined OpenAI in 2018 after being introduced to Altman, Greg Brockman and Ilya Sutskever. In his farewell message, he recalled seeing an early pitch deck arguing that AI models could improve predictably with scale.

“If you had told me then that we’d be where we are today, I wouldn't have believed you,” he wrote.

During his tenure, Lightcap said he helped build early versions of OpenAI’s finance, legal, people, corporate security, go-to-market and government relations, and partnerships teams.

He also played a role in expanding the company’s commercial operations as OpenAI moved from a research organisation into a company serving consumers and enterprises.

OpenAI appointed Lightcap as COO in 2022. His role also extended to major commercial partnerships and acquisitions.

Altman thanked Lightcap for his contribution, saying the two had first discussed OpenAI when the idea “sounded totally crazy”.

“Since then, you have taken on any function and challenge OpenAI has needed; we would not be where we are without you,” Altman wrote. “Excited to work together on what's next.”

Lightcap’s exit adds to a series of senior leadership changes at OpenAI as the company prepares for its next stage of growth.

Fidji Simo, who had served as CEO of Applications and later CEO of AGI deployment, stepped down from her full-time role in July and moved to a part-time advisory position. Kate Rouch, OpenAI’s Chief Marketing Officer, also left the company after announcing in April that she would step down to focus on her recovery.

Srinivas Narayanan, who led engineering for OpenAI’s B2B applications, left in April after three years at the company. Kevin Weil, OpenAI’s Chief Product Officer, and Bill Peebles, a research scientist associated with Sora, also departed around the same period.

content:
AI software coding platform Lovable has raised $400 million in a Series C round at a $13.3 billion valuation as it expands from helping users build applications to supporting businesses with software, workflows and operations.

The round was led by Menlo Ventures and co-led by the Scaleup Europe Fund, managed by EQT.

Balderton Capital, Carmignac, Kaszek Ventures, LTS Growth, Tencent, World Innovation Lab and Regent also participated. Existing investors including Accel, Antler, CapitalG, DST Global, Evantic Capital, HubSpot Ventures and Salesforce Ventures returned for the round.

“Lovable has become the place where founders create million-dollar businesses, business leaders spin up new product lines, and people inside companies rewire workflows and build tools that fit their exact needs, typically at a fraction of what software used to cost,” said CEO Anton Osika in a LinkedIn post.

Lovable said users have created more than 60 million projects since its launch in November 2024. Applications built on the platform now receive more than 900 million visits each month. The company said its tools reached employees at nearly two-thirds of Fortune 500 companies, up from half within its first year.

The company is also seeing users build businesses rather than simply prototype software. According to Lovable, nearly eight in 10 users are building a business or side project they hope to monetise, while more than one-third are already generating revenue from those projects.

Lovable has added payment functionality, SEO and AI-search tools, integrations with Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, Salesforce, Stripe and ElevenLabs, as well as automated security scanning and governance features. It has also received AIUC-1 certification, which it describes as a security standard for AI agents.

The company is positioning the platform as a way for employees who understand a business problem to build the software needed to address it without relying entirely on engineering teams.

“Instead of adding another tool to our marketing stack, our teams can quickly create whatever they need to solve problems,” said Veronika Zatulovskaya, VP of Marketing at Handshake.

At Checkr, Lovable says teams have built internal tools and used the platform to improve operational workflows. Its operations team used Lovable to address a QA workflow issue and increased the number of reports it could process by 10 times, according to Luca Bonmassar, CTO of Checkr.

Lovable plans to use the new funding to expand its product, infrastructure and team. It expects to grow to roughly 450 employees this year, with hiring focused on machine learning, product, infrastructure and security. The company will retain Stockholm as its centre while expanding in London, Boston, San Francisco and New York.

The company also plans to make its platform more proactive. Rather than waiting for users to issue instructions, Lovable wants its system to understand what users are trying to achieve, identify tasks that need attention and increasingly carry out work itself.

It wants to use data from the products built on its platform to improve how its system evaluates successful outcomes and try to understand not only if software works, but whether it generates revenue, improves workflows or helps businesses grow.

The platform will continue using multiple AI models rather than relying on a single model. Lovable said it will match different parts of a task with the model best suited to handle them and will continue post-training open-source models.

Menlo Ventures partner Matt Murphy said Lovable is targeting people who have the knowledge and ideas to build products but have historically been constrained by technical skills.

“From the very start, Lovable was built for the billions of people with the creativity and knowledge to make something, but who had always been blocked by technical ability,” Murphy said.

The latest funding round gives Lovable more capital to compete in a growing market around AI-assisted software development while pushing the company further into business operations and software creation.

title: What Actually Matters.
content:
Indian semiconductor startups raised $61.9 million in H1 2026, nearing the total raised in all of 2025.

Funding came through only seven rounds in H1 2026, indicating larger investments in more developed startups.

Indian semiconductor startups raised $61.9 million in the first half of 2026, already reaching 81% of the $76.6 million raised in the entirety of 2025, according to the Indian Semiconductor Startup Landscape 2026 report by Speciale Invest and Startup Policy Forum (SPF).

The funding came through just seven rounds in H1 2026, compared to 13 rounds in 2025 and 16 in 2024. The decline in deal count alongside the rise in capital deployed indicates that investors are concentrating larger cheques in semiconductor startups that have progressed further in product development and commercialisation.

Since 2022, Indian semiconductor startups have raised approximately $206 million across 51 funding rounds. Funding increased sharply from $1.5 million in 2022 to $76.6 million in 2025, a roughly 51-fold increase.

Government-backed programmes are also helping startups reach milestones that can attract private capital. Of the 24 chip-design projects supported under the Design Linked Incentive (DLI) programme, 14 have subsequently raised institutional venture capital, collectively securing $100.8 million across their first and second rounds. Six of these companies have already raised follow-on rounds worth a combined $53.6 million.

Four companies—C2i Semiconductors, NetraSemi, Morphing Machines, and Mindgrove Technologies—account for approximately 56% of the private capital raised by DLI-backed companies. The report says public funding for design, tooling, and tape-outs is helping startups cross expensive technical milestones before attracting institutional investors.

The funding is also moving into larger rounds. Seven recent Series A rounds highlighted in the report account for $73.7 million, or roughly one-third of all semiconductor startup capital raised in India since 2022. Some companies have progressed from seed to Series A within seven to 22 months.

Vishesh Rajaram, Managing Partner at Speciale Invest, said the next test for India's semiconductor ecosystem is whether the current momentum can take companies beyond design and validation into scaled products, repeat customers, and globally relevant businesses.

The startup landscape is also expanding beyond chip design into photonics, power and compound semiconductors, fab tooling and metrology, AI data-centre silicon, AI-led semiconductor design workflows, and analog AI inference.

The report identifies equipment and materials, design IP and EDA, and analog and RF as major areas of opportunity over the coming decade. It also expects India Semiconductor Mission 2.0 to potentially expand opportunities in fab-adjacent tooling, compound semiconductors, advanced packaging, RISC-V IP and AI-assisted EDA and verification tooling.

Strategic investors are playing a growing role, with companies including Zoho and TDK Ventures anchoring funding rounds.

i-Hub Gujarat's TattvaX Acceleration Programme supports 30 startups in defence, drone, and space technology.

The programme offers mentorship and investor access to early-stage deeptech startups.

Government-backed startup incubator Gujarat Student Startup and Innovation Hub (i-Hub Gujarat) has extended support to 30 startups working in defence, drone, and space technology through the second cohort of its TattvaX Acceleration Programme, in partnership with deeptech community network SanchiConnect.

TattvaX Acceleration Programme supports early-stage deeptech startups in India's defence, drone and space sectors, supporting them with mentorship and investor access.

i-Hub Gujarat said the programme is designed for founders who have strong technical capabilities but need structured support to build investable, scalable companies.

"Our vision with TattvaX transcends standard acceleration; we are building a robust support system that empowers deeptech founders to solve hard, strategically important problems,” Hiranmay Mahanta, CEO of i-Hub Gujarat, said in a statement.

"By actively promoting indigenous technology adoption within the SME ecosystem, we are not just nurturing individual startups, we are cultivating resilient local markets that provide the essential testing ground for home-grown innovation to scale and compete globally," he added.

According to i-Hub Gujarat, the partnership with SanchiConnect is expanding beyond TattvaX. The two organisations are launching sector-specific accelerators aligned with state priorities, with active programmes already underway in the drone and aerospace sectors, the company said.

The accelerator programe includes innovation showcases that connect startups with investors and stakeholders such as state police departments, municipal corporations, and regional public sector undertakings (PSUs). i-Hub Gujarat said this is intended to create pipelines that move indigenous technology from research labs to large-scale deployment.

SanchiConnect said its approach centres on building focused micro-ecosystems by partnering with state governments, industry associations, and incubation centres. This model gives startups a structured way to engage with industry buyers, investors, and policymakers to develop solutions that can be deployed at scale.

Sunil K Shekhawat, Co-founder and CEO of SanchiConnect, said the focus has been on connecting research and development with private capital and the SME sector.

"Our primary focus has been to bridge the gap between cutting-edge R&D, private capital, and the SME ecosystem. By ensuring our founders are ready with the fundamentals- story, numbers, and market insight, we are actively generating local demand for indigenous technology, turning the SME sector into a launchpad for the startups that will define India's self-reliant future," he said.

i-Hub Gujarat said the program's Demo Day brought together 30 startups over two days with more than 20 investors and corporate leaders in attendance.

Google and Lightspeed are hosting a one-day AI workshop for India's consumer tech and fintech startups on September 23.

The programme aims to transition AI projects from experimentation to real-world deployment, focusing on practical implementation.

Google for Startups and Lightspeed are set to host a full-day AI workshop for India’s venture-backed startups, bringing founders and technology leaders together to build AI applications using Google’s Gemini and Vertex AI platforms.

The Google for Startups Sprint, powered by Lightspeed, will take place on September 23 at Google’s office in Gurugram. The programme is aimed at Seed to Series B startups in the consumer technology and fintech sectors, with a focus on moving AI projects from experimentation to deployment.

Unlike a conventional startup conference, the programme is designed around live implementation. Participating founders and CTOs will work with Google’s AI and engineering teams on architecture, infrastructure and agentic AI use cases, while Lightspeed will focus on the business and economic considerations involved in scaling AI products.

The Google-led track will cover areas including cloud infrastructure, high-traffic scalability and real-time fraud detection. Participants will also work with Google’s templates and engineering resources to explore how Gemini and Vertex AI can be integrated into existing products and workflows.

The programme will also focus on AI agents. Startups will have the opportunity to build applications such as commerce agents for hyperlocal transactions and financial agents for automated KYC and credit assessment.

For fintech startups, the sessions are expected to address use cases around fraud detection, digital lending and credit workflows. Consumer technology companies, meanwhile, will explore applications spanning commerce, customer experiences and personalised interactions.

Lightspeed’s role will centre on the economics of deploying AI at scale. The venture capital firm will examine areas such as customer acquisition costs, margins, repeat usage and sustainable growth—issues that become increasingly important as startups move AI applications into production and absorb higher computing and infrastructure costs.

The programme comes as Indian startups increasingly shift their AI strategies from experimentation towards deployment. Rather than simply adding generative AI features to existing products, startups are exploring AI agents that can execute multi-step tasks across customer service, commerce, finance and operations.

The Sprint is therefore positioned around three areas: AI architecture, venture economics and execution. The organisers say participants should leave with an AI architecture and strategy that can be taken beyond a workshop environment.

The programme is open to founders and CTOs from Seed to Series B companies in consumer tech and fintech with the technical capabilities required to work with APIs and advanced AI architectures. Each startup can send a maximum of two CXOs, with both required to register individually using their official business email addresses.

Discovered Materials, a materials science startup using AI agents to identify new materials for semiconductor applications, has raised $9 million in a seed round led by Lightspeed India Partners.

The round also saw participation from Peak XV Partners and angel investors including Paul Graham, Gokul Rajaram, and Thariq Shihipar. The startup emerged from Y Combinator and was founded by Advaith Sridhar and Akash Ramdas.

The company is targeting one of the growing challenges in AI infrastructure: heat. As AI workloads become more computationally intensive, chips generate increasing amounts of heat, driving demand for electricity-intensive cooling systems in data centres.

Discovered Materials is building an AI-powered software pipeline designed to accelerate the search for materials that could make chips more thermally efficient. The system uses Anthropic models through a custom framework to generate potential material candidates, which are then evaluated using physics models developed by the company to simulate and validate their properties.

In a post on X, Sridhar said the system can generate thousands of material candidates a day, compared with the roughly 20 guesses a day that co-founder Ramdas was able to explore during his doctoral research at Stanford.

The startup has also released examples of hundreds of newly identified materials and a Material Discovery Bench designed to evaluate how advanced AI models perform on materials-discovery problems.

Discovered Materials is entering a competitive field that includes companies such as MatNex, SandboxAQ, and CuspAI, which are also applying AI to materials discovery. However, the startup is focusing specifically on materials that could address thermal challenges in semiconductor manufacturing.

“A material is only useful in the real world if all of them converge at once,” Hemant Mohapatra, Partner at Lightspeed, which led the round, told TechCrunch, describing the process as “playing whack-a-mole with atomic structures.”

The company claims to have already identified several materials that match properties of existing materials used by major chipmakers, although it has not disclosed details of those candidates.

Discovered Materials plans to pursue patents covering potential uses of its materials in GPUs or the processes required to manufacture chips using them. Sridhar expects the company to have new materials that are ready for patenting within the next year.

title: Hang Ten Systems CTO Believes AI Cannot Replace Some Indian IT Assets
content:
The company has launched a dedicated private equity business unit as PE firms increasingly look to technology and AI to improve portfolio-company performance, margins and valuations.

Mid-tier IT services firm Coforge has launched a dedicated business unit focused on the private equity (PE) sector, seeking to tap growing demand from PE firms for technology-led operational improvements across their portfolio companies.

The move comes as private equity investors face changing market conditions, tougher valuations and longer holding periods, increasing the pressure to improve operating performance and create value within portfolio companies, the company said in a regulatory filing.

The new unit will draw on Coforge’s experience of integrating and turning around businesses it has acquired, including NIIT Technologies, Incessant Technologies, SLK Global, Cigniti Technologies and Encora. The company said the unit will use these acquisition and integration playbooks to help PE firms improve operational performance and scale growth.

“Our acquisition integration playbook has allowed us to leverage technology to create enterprise value at scale over the last decade. Consequently, this new business unit is aligned with our DNA as a company,” Preeti Singh, Executive Vice President and Head of North America, Coforge, said in a statement.

She added that private equity firms are moving from exploring AI opportunities to embedding AI-driven value creation into their investment strategies, and executing AI initiatives at scale across the portfolio is becoming a strategic differentiator that requires a repeatable, scalable model tied to measurable business outcomes.

The business will be powered by Coforge Nuuron, the company’s AI operating system and enterprise autonomy platform, and will combine technology, data, governance and execution capabilities.

The offering is positioned as a broader proposition than traditional deal advisory or standalone technology services.

The launch also gives Coforge another avenue to monetise its experience with private equity-owned businesses. The company has worked with PE firms for more than a decade, according to Singh, and has built a track record around integrating acquisitions and improving growth and margins across acquired entities.

AI is forcing India's IT services industry to rethink the people-based billing model that has powered its growth for three decades.

What Actually Matters.

India's IT services industry must adapt its billing model as AI alters the connection between team size and software output.

The shift from large teams to smaller, outcome-focused teams is deemed structural, not cyclical, according to Hang Ten Systems' CTO.

The billing model that has powered India's IT services industry for three decades, charging clients by the number of people staffed on a project, is running out of road as AI collapses the link between team size and software output, believes Navin Budhiraja, Chief Technology Officer of AI-native enterprise services firm Hang Ten Systems.

In an interview with AIM, Budhiraja says the shift is structural, not cyclical, and will force even the largest services providers to move away from large, multi-year implementation teams toward smaller teams delivering outcomes in weeks or months.

"The model that is based on the number of people that I needed to create software—I think that is going to be difficult to continue," he says. "The business model has to evolve, where it's no longer about large teams and multi-year projects. It has to be small teams delivering outcomes in a matter of months."

Barely three months old, Hang Ten Systems, founded by former Infosys CEO Vishal Sikka, has positioned itself as an "AI-native" enterprise services provider, focused on building, modernising, and running enterprise software for large clients using large language models paired with an in-house agentic delivery platform, rather than the large offshore implementation teams that have defined Indian IT services for decades.

The Palo Alto-based company has raised roughly $32 million, led by Mayfield with strategic investment from Aramco Ventures and participation from angel investors. It counts German healthcare firm Fresenius and Siemens Energy among its early clients.

Its work already spans SAP migrations, finance and HR transformation, and software engineering—segments long dominated by tier-1 IT majors such as TCS, Infosys and Wipro.

Separate Conversations

According to Budhiraja, people routinely conflate the pace of AI-driven change in how software gets built with its effect on jobs. "I think of these as two separate things."

First, the act of writing software has been decoupled from the size of the team writing it. "Something that may have taken a team of 10 people to do can be done by one or two people," he says.

That is exactly why the per-head billing model cannot hold. Budhiraja believes businesses built on multi-year, large-team contracts have to give way to short engagements built around outcomes, delivered by much smaller teams.

However, regarding jobs, Budhiraja pushes back on the idea that roles are simply disappearing. "It's not that the job changes. It is still a software job, but the task that you do as part of that may evolve," he notes.

The developer's role, in his view, is shifting from writing code to exercising judgement, understanding domain context, and reviewing what AI produces—the kind of work he believes AI will not replicate at the level of someone embedded in a business.

More Software, Not Less Demand

On whether AI will shrink the market, Budhiraja invokes the Jevons paradox, the idea that falling costs per unit can expand overall demand, to argue that cheaper, faster software production will make custom software economically viable for companies that previously couldn't justify the expense.

He describes this as an opportunity to deliver "bespoke SaaS"—tailor-made enterprise software at something closer to the economics of commercial, off-the-shelf platforms.

That, he says, also opens a large opportunity to modernise decades-old legacy systems that companies have long been reluctant to touch because rebuilding them was too expensive or risky.

Forward Deployed Engineers

On the growing trend of ‘forward-deployed engineers’, a model popularised by Palantir and now being explored by both OpenAI's deployment arm and Anthropic, alongside Indian IT majors, Budhiraja expects it to coexist with, not replace, offshore and nearshore delivery.

Early-stage, ambiguous problems benefit from engineers sitting with the customer, he says, while more mature, better-understood workstreams can move to distributed teams. "It's going to be a clear mix," he notes.

On enterprises' anxiety over AI compute costs, Budhiraja says the fixation on token pricing misses the point that not every problem needs a frontier model. Hang Ten Systems, he says, deliberately routes work to smaller, open-weight models where cost, data privacy, or sovereignty concerns make sense, reserving frontier models for harder problems.

He also pushes back on the narrative that enterprise AI pilots are broadly failing to reach production, framing it instead as an expectations mismatch.

"It's not just about the model—it's about the ability to get the right data to the model, the ability to build the right guardrails," he notes. Much of the "rest of the stack" like data pipelines, governance, security, applications hasn't kept pace with how fast the underlying models improved, he says, and enterprises often signed up expecting gains the tooling around the model wasn't yet built to deliver.

On what large Indian IT services company should be doing today, Budhiraja points to three shifts: blending forward-deployed and distributed delivery models, moving sales conversations away from multi-year contracts toward shorter, outcome-based engagements, and leaning on the deep client trust and domain expertise that established players have built over decades—an asset he said AI cannot replicate.

title: N Chandrasekaran to Step Down as Tata Sons Chairman, Won’t Seek Reappointment
content:
N Chandrasekaran will step down as Tata Sons chairman in February 2027, ending months of uncertainty over his succession.

N Chandrasekaran, Chairman of Tata Sons, has decided not to seek reappointment when his current term concludes on February 20, 2027, ending months of uncertainty over the leadership of India's largest business conglomerate.

The announcement comes just days ahead of Tata Sons' annual general meeting and marks his early exit after a proposed five-year extension of his tenure failed to secure unanimous board approval earlier this year.

In a letter addressed to the board, Chandrasekaran reflected on completing 40 years of his professional career with the Tata Group, calling it an "immensely satisfying opportunity" to have contributed to the institution.

He described leading Tata Sons over the past decade as "a great honour and a profound responsibility."

“Sir Dorabji Tata Trust and Sir Ratan Tata Trust had unanimously resolved and recommended the extension of my next term for a period of five years, which was recorded and recommended by the Tata Sons Nomination and Remuneration Committee and the Board. Subsequently, the resolution was tabled in the Tata Sons Board on Feb 24, 2026. However, the proposal was not carried through because one of the Board Members did not support it, and in the absence of unanimous support, I chose to defer the decision,” Chandrasekaran said in his letter.

Citing these circumstances, Chandrasekaran said he had informed the Tata Sons Board that he would not offer himself for reappointment when his term ends, and had urged the board to move swiftly on succession planning "to ensure a proper transition."

The development brings to a head a succession question that has been simmering within Tata Sons' boardroom for much of 2026. While Tata Trusts had reportedly thrown their weight behind a second extension for Chandrasekaran, Chairman Noel Tata had reportedly opposed the move, and Chandrasekaran failed to secure unanimous board consent in February.

The AGM, scheduled for August 18, was originally expected to also take up his reappointment as a director of the company. With Chandrasekaran now confirming he will not continue beyond February 2027, the board faces the task of identifying a successor to helm one of India's most influential business houses.

Popularly known as "Chandra" within Tata circles, Chandrasekaran joined Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) in 1987 and rose through the ranks over nearly three decades, eventually becoming its Chief Executive Officer and Managing Director in 2009. Under his leadership, TCS grew into India's most valuable listed company and cemented its position as a global IT services bellwether.

He was named Chairman of Tata Sons in January 2017, taking formal charge in February that year, succeeding an interim stint by Ratan Tata following the acrimonious ouster of Cyrus Mistry in October 2016. Chandrasekaran was reappointed for a second term in February 2022.

India is rapidly expanding AI and future-skills training, but PMKVY 4.0 has stopped tracking placements, leaving a widening gap between training and outcomes.

What Actually Matters.

India is expanding AI and future-skills training under PMKVY 4.0, focusing on emerging technologies.

The government has stopped tracking placements, leading to a gap between skill training and employment outcomes.

India’s skilling machine is getting bigger, faster, and more technologically ambitious. At the same time, it’s getting harder to track skilling outcomes.

A fresh Lok Sabha reply from the Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship (MSDE) shows that the government is expanding AI, machine learning, robotics, cloud computing, data analytics, cybersecurity, and other emerging technologies through the fourth phase of the Pradhan Mantri Kaushal Vikas Yojana (PMKVY). The government says it has also developed 170 National Skills Qualification Framework (NSQF)-compliant courses, including 32 future-skills courses, through the Craftsman Training Scheme.

Yet, what is a more troubling revelation, the Ministry also admitted that it was no longer monitoring placements under PMKVY 4.0. The government reasoned that since PMKVY 4.0, operational since FY2022-23, is focused on enabling trainees to choose different career paths, it is not tracking placements.

The result is a peculiar asymmetry. India is operating on the fast lane to certify students with new-age skills, while turning a blind eye to whether those skills translate into employment.

From millions of certificates to AI learners

The scale of the earlier PMKVY programme is substantial. Between 2015 and 2022, the first three phases had an outlay of around ₹14,450 crore, with 1.11 crore candidates certified from a utilisation of ₹9,261 crore. The government now says 24.38 lakh candidates were placed under the Short-Term Training (STT) component.

However, the CAG's audit presented a more complicated picture. It flagged that only 23.18 lakh candidates, or 41% of those trained under the STT component, were placed.

The audit also found that training did not consistently align with job-role-specific or state-level skill gaps. Placement verification itself was problematic. In Kerala, the CAG found incorrect placement documents submitted by training partners that led to the recovery of ₹22.33 lakh.

The report also identified weak controls around beneficiary identities and bank details. Almost 94.53% of candidate records examined had blank bank account details, while thousands of bank accounts were associated with multiple beneficiaries. The audit also found apparently invalid account numbers and other unreliable entries.

That history makes the decision not to monitor placements under PMKVY 4.0 particularly significant.

As Sumesh Nair, Co-founder of upskilling platform Board Infinity, puts it, AI-skilling programmes should be measured through a “verified employment-and-performance scorecard”, rather than course completions or certificates. He tells AIM that this should include employment or self-employment at six and 12 months, job retention, wage progression, employer satisfaction, industry projects or apprenticeships, and independent competency assessments.

“For AI roles especially, the meaningful test is whether graduates can apply skills in real workflows with limited remedial training, rather than whether they have completed a course,” he stresses.

AI-Skilling Boom is Highly Uneven

The data submitted in the Lok Sabha offers a detailed picture of how PMKVY 4.0's AI and emerging-technology training is spreading across states.

Roughly 5.4 lakh candidates were trained in future-forward skills between FY2023-24 and June 2026. The programme recorded around 19,500 such trainees in 2023-24 before surging to more than 4.48 lakh in 2024-25. The figure then falls sharply to around 45,000 in 2025-26, with 2026-27 standing at roughly 31,000 by June 2026.

The state-wise distribution has been dropping.

Uttar Pradesh reported more than 1.03 lakh AI/emerging-tech trainees across the period, including 88,868 in 2024-25. Rajasthan recorded 84,144, while Madhya Pradesh reported around 67,064. Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Punjab, and Bihar follow at considerably lower levels.

The number of candidates trained dropped dramatically in the following year. Tamil Nadu trained 7,086 candidates in 2025–26, followed by Uttar Pradesh at 6,672, Madhya Pradesh at 5,260, Karnataka at 4,259, and Punjab at 3,356.

The government does not explain in the parliamentary answer why reported PMKVY 4.0 AI/emerging-tech training fell by roughly 90% in 2025-26. More importantly, there is no corresponding state-wise placement picture for these trainees.

Learning Itself is Changing

The industry is seeing a different evolution when it comes to not just only the kinds of skills that are in demand, but also how one obtains them.

Shronit Ladhani, Founder of AI-led learning platform LearnTube by CareerNinja, says learning is moving “from the degree to the course to the task.” Learners increasingly want AI training that solves an immediate workplace problem rather than a generic qualification.

“The fastest-growing course isn't ‘learn AI’. It's AI plus the job you already have. Marketers running campaigns with AI, analysts automating their reporting, HR teams screening with it,” he highlights.

Ladhani also believes that the “demand frontier has already moved past prompts to agentic AI.”

Apurv Mehra, Co-founder and CEO of edtech startup Disha AI, sees a similar shift. Generative AI fundamentals, prompt engineering, and hands-on familiarity with tools such as ChatGPT, Claude, Midjourney, and NotebookLM are seeing strong demand. Learners, however, are primarily interested in practical workplace applications.

That creates a challenge for a government system traditionally built around courses, certifications, and training numbers.

“Certifications are losing their signal value. Degrees are headed the same way,” Mehra says. Increasingly, what matters is proof of work—whether someone can build something, solve a real problem, and think from first principles.

“The market is already moving this way; employers are asking ‘show me what you've built’ far more than ‘show me what you've passed,” he adds.

AI Literacy is Not AI Employability

The distinction becomes even more important as India attempts to move millions of people into an AI-enabled economy.

Nair says companies can find candidates with basic exposure to AI tools, but struggle to find people who can work with data, assess AI outputs, understand business applications, follow responsible-AI and security practices, and deliver practical projects.

“AI literacy is not the same as AI employability,” he says. “Industry should be a co-owner of quality, not simply the recipient of trained candidates.”

The government has recognised the need for industry alignment, establishing institutions such as Sector Skill Councils to study skills gap, District Skill Committees to identify local employment opportunities, and the SANKALP programme, which supported a national skill-gap study by NCAER. It also points to partnerships with IBM, Cisco, Microsoft, and AWS.

But the CAG's findings show why the existence of skill-gap studies does not necessarily guarantee effective training. Earlier PMKVY phases suffered from weak micro-level skill-gap mapping and training that did not consistently correspond with available demand data.

The issue, therefore, is less about the number of reports, partnerships or courses and more about whether those inputs improve the quality and durability of employment.

“The real skills story of this decade is getting that same rigour into the other 90%. That's the gap we're building for,” Ladhani adds.

The Risk of the Certificate Economy

Alisha Butala, Policy Analyst and Researcher, argues that India's deeper problem is not simply a shortage of AI-ready talent. It is that the education and skilling system is designed to respond to innovation rather than produce it.

“AI is the latest example,” she says.

An AI-ready India cannot simply mean training people to use technology developed elsewhere. India is racing to make students AI-ready while the technology frontier is already moving towards quantum computing and other advanced technologies.

That concern echoes Niranjanaradhya's criticism of the broader skilling architecture, as reported by AIM in November 2025. The programme head of universalisation of education at the National Law School of India, Bengaluru, argued that without a clear vision of the target group, the purpose of training, and the opportunities available after training, programmes inevitably create a gap between spending and outcomes.

The government is now proposing PM-SETU, a ₹60,000 crore programme to upgrade 1,000 government ITIs, with industry-led governance, work exposure, career guidance, and placement support.

PMKVY 4.0 has also introduced future-skill roles, and the wider Skill India ecosystem now covers AI, robotics, cybersecurity, cloud computing, IoT, and data analytics.

The direction is clearly changing. The government is moving from conventional vocational training towards a workforce shaped around emerging technologies. But the central weakness identified in the earlier programme remains relevant: training numbers are not employment numbers.

As Nair puts it, funding and evaluation should follow sustained employment, productivity, and real-world skill application, with live projects and post-certification tracking acting as early warning systems when a skill begins losing market value.

xAI’s Co-founder Igor Babuschkin’s startup River AI has raised $1.1 billion across its Series Seed and Series A rounds, with General Catalyst and AMP PBC leading the funding. NVIDIA and AMD Ventures also invested, alongside Y Combinator and Temasek.

The company said the funding will support its efforts to give developers and enterprises tools to train, fine-tune and own AI models using their own data.

River is building an API that lets companies run reinforcement learning and LoRA fine-tuning on open-weight models without managing the underlying infrastructure.

The company said enterprises can complete reinforcement learning runs in 15 to 20 minutes, while its platform handles weight transfers, sampling-training consistency and elastic compute.

The API charges based on tokens used for training and inference, rather than requiring customers to pay for unused GPU capacity. River said this can reduce costs by two to four times compared with closed-source alternatives.

“The way AI is built today is not how it will be built in the future. AI should be open, freely available, and affordable,” said Babuschkin, co-founder and CEO of River AI.

“It should feel like it is working for the person using it, not the lab that trained it. We started River to allow people and companies to own their intelligence.”

River said its longer-term goal is to build personal AI that learns from individual users and can be controlled by them. The company plans to work across training infrastructure, personalised AI products, continual learning and hardware for running AI closer to users.

The company was founded by a team with experience at xAI and Tesla. Babuschkin previously worked on generative modelling and reinforcement learning at Google DeepMind and led large-scale training efforts at OpenAI before joining xAI.

General Catalyst CEO Hemant Taneja said River’s focus on open-weight models could support US AI development.

“American leadership in AI urgently requires leadership in open-weight models, while maintaining a lead in closed frontier models,” Taneja said. “The core philosophy of putting ownership of intelligence in the hands of the people using it will prove to be on the right side of history for the open-weight ecosystem.”

Marc Bhargava, Managing Director at General Catalyst, said River addresses the gap between AI capabilities and how companies currently use the technology.

“There is a gap between what AI can do and what most companies actually experience,” Bhargava said. “Until now, companies have lacked a cost-efficient way to train, tune, and own custom AI models.”

Babuschkin has worked across several of the major AI labs. Before founding River, he co-founded xAI with Elon Musk, where he worked on infrastructure, model training, multimodal systems and products. He has also held roles at OpenAI and Google DeepMind.

River AI was publicly launched by Babuschkin in June this year with the River API as its first product.

TCS and Google Cloud have opened a Gemini Experience Center in Mexico to promote AI adoption among enterprises.

The centre features over 3,000 AI agents designed to integrate with customer environments and support various use cases.

TCS and Google Cloud have launched a new Gemini Experience Center in Mexico City to help enterprises accelerate AI adoption and move from experimentation to implementing AI solutions.

The centre is TCS’ ninth Gemini Experience Center globally and its second in Latin America, following the launch of its first Latin American centre in São Paulo, Brazil, in 2025. The new facility is located at TCS’ Mexico City office and aims to help organisations develop AI solutions focused on innovation, productivity, and data-driven decision-making.

The centre is equipped with more than 3,000 industry- and context-aware AI agents built by TCS using Gemini Enterprise, according to the company. These agents are designed to integrate with customer environments and support use cases such as intelligent process assessment, fraud investigation for financial institutions, automated insurance claims processing, and generative AI-powered data acceleration.

“As AI reshapes how organisations compete and create value, unlocking its full potential depends on giving businesses the right environment to adopt and apply AI with confidence,” said Javier Carrique, Head of Partners and Alliances for Latin America at Google Cloud, in a statement.

TCS will combine its consulting, engineering and innovation capabilities with Google Cloud’s technology ecosystem at the centre. The companies said the facility will help organisations bridge the gap between AI experimentation and implementation while reducing the time required to achieve business outcomes.

The centre will support the development of industry-specific AI solutions across financial services, retail and consumer goods, manufacturing, healthcare and life sciences, and energy and utilities.

“The Gemini Experience Center, launched by TCS, brings advanced AI capabilities closer to enterprises in Mexico, helping them turn ideas into practical, scalable solutions,” said Marcelo Wurmann, CEO of TCS Latin America. “Together with Google Cloud, we are creating a space for organisations to explore how technology can transform their operations and add greater value.”

The launch is part of TCS’ broader strategy to expand its global network of innovation centres and support responsible AI adoption. TCS has operated in Mexico since 2003 and currently serves more than 260 clients through a workforce of more than 12,000 associates across Mexico City, Guadalajara, Querétaro, and Monterrey.

Piyush Goyal emphasised the need for an AI-enabled Government e-Marketplace to enhance public procurement efficiency.

The platform has achieved significant scale, facilitating over ₹20 lakh crore in procurement since its launch in 2016.

Union Minister of Commerce and Industry Piyush Goyal has called for a new, user-friendly, and artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled Government e-Marketplace (GeM) as the platform marks its 10th anniversary. Goyal said the platform would make public procurement more efficient, cost-effective, transparent, and competitive with AI.

"What truly defines GeM is not only the scale we have achieved, but the spirit with which we continue to improve, listening, refining and remaining responsive to the needs of those who use the platform," GeM CEO Mihir Kumar said at the event.

GeM, India's government procurement platform, was launched on August 9, 2016, under the Ministry of Commerce and Industry. The platform now has more than 25 lakh sellers and over 1.37 lakh buyer organisations and has facilitated cumulative procurement of more than ₹20 lakh crore through over 3.78 crore orders, according to the ministry.

Addressing the gathering, Goyal outlined five priorities for GeM's next decade. These included deeper use of AI for price intelligence, price sanity, and marketplace integrity, alongside last-mile access through GeM's Suvidha Kendras, integration of states, public enterprises, panchayats and cooperatives, credit and sustainability initiatives, and university outreach.

Goyal said the new platform would help buyers and sellers make more intelligent use of the procurement process and the latest technologies.

The AI push builds on technology GeM has already deployed. In May 2025, GeM launched GeMAI, which it described as India's first generative-AI-powered chatbot in the public sector. The system supports voice and text interactions in 10 Indian languages and was introduced to improve user support on the procurement platform. It enables users to search, navigate, and complete transactions on GeM.

Earlier this year, GeM collaborated with BHASHINI, an AI-powered language translation and technology platform launched by the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology. It aims to promote multilingual access, multilingual governance, and multilingual service delivery across GeM's digital platforms, enabling stakeholders to access information and services in their preferred languages.

title: What Actually Matters.
content:
Pathway's BDH-CQ model achieves a 29.5% score on the ARC-AGI-1 benchmark while being significantly more cost-efficient than larger models.

The model operates at an inference cost of $0.0007 per task, making it approximately 11 times cheaper than GPT 5.6 Luna.

Pathway’s 150-million-parameter reasoning model BDH-CQ has scored 29.5% on the public ARC-AGI-1 benchmark at a reported inference cost of $0.0007 per task, positioning the model as a significantly more cost-efficient alternative to larger reasoning models.

According to Pathway, BDH-CQ achieved a 29.5% pass@2 score on the ARC-AGI-1 public evaluation set at a computed inference cost of $0.0007 per task. The company said the model runs approximately 11 times cheaper per task than GPT 5.6 Luna (Low), which scored 34.2% on the same benchmark. Pathway described the difference as a trade-off between a modest accuracy gap and a substantial reduction in inference cost.

The company has reached a $500 million valuation, following additional funding, taking total seed funding to $30 million, and appointed Adam Kurzrok, former Google DeepMind Gemini product lead, as the CPO.

ARC-AGI-1 is designed to test whether an AI system can identify an underlying rule from a small number of examples and apply that rule to a new input. The benchmark is often used to evaluate reasoning capabilities that require models to generalise beyond patterns seen during training.

Pathway attributes BDH-CQ’s cost advantage to its architecture. While many transformer-based reasoning models generate intermediate chains of text as part of their reasoning process, BDH-CQ performs its reasoning in a recurrent latent state without producing an intermediate text trace.

The company said this allows the model to refine solutions internally rather than generating and processing additional reasoning tokens, reducing both compute requirements and latency.

“Today’s AI pays a steep token cost for reasoning, but that cost is imposed by architecture, not by any law of intelligence. Currently, every reasoning step consumes context, adds latency, and burns compute,” said Zuzanna Stamirowska, CEO and Co-Founder of Pathway.

“We show that a different architecture changes the game and opens up a whole new space in terms of how much intelligence per dollar. A 150M-parameter model, built on Pathway’s BDH architecture, reasons recurrently in latent space and sets a new state of the art in cost efficiency on ARC-AGI-1.”

The results were independently evaluated by Łukasz Kaiser, co-author of the 2017 ‘Attention Is All You Need’ paper that introduced the Transformer architecture. Kaiser said the results point to architecture as an important factor in advancing AI reasoning, rather than relying solely on increasing model size.

“I’ve followed Pathway closely and replicated their ARC-AGI-1 results myself. Pathway shows that model architecture, not just scale, can drive the next leap in AI reasoning,” Kaiser said.

The results were also reproduced by Richard Zhong, an NYU researcher focused on model evaluation and benchmark robustness.

Pathway said the scores and comparison costs were drawn from the ARC Prize Foundation’s public leaderboard, which compares benchmark performance with cost per task. The leaderboard data used by the company was based on submissions available as of July.

Pathway’s cost figure was calculated using measured hardware time, while the costs of comparison models reported on the leaderboard may reflect API pricing for general-purpose models.

The company plans to scale the BDH architecture and test it on more demanding reasoning benchmarks, including mathematical reasoning, ARC-AGI-2 and ARC-AGI-3. It also plans to develop a latent-reasoning large language model based on the architecture.

Pathway said early experiments indicate that Transformer-like scaling laws continue to apply during pretraining at scales ranging from 1 billion to 600 billion parameters while retaining the latent reasoning capabilities demonstrated by BDH-CQ.

The company expects the approach could eventually be applied to workloads that require models to reason continuously as information and constraints change, including cybersecurity incident response and real-time industrial operations.

NVIDIA has partnered with Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR to create financing platforms that could mobilise more than $500 billion in third-party capital for AI infrastructure.

The partnerships are intended to help NVIDIA customers finance large-scale compute deployments, including AI factories, data centres and other infrastructure built around NVIDIA’s accelerated computing platform.

The platforms will provide financing for AI factories serving AI labs, enterprises and cloud providers. The financial institutions will independently assess projects based on customer demand, utilisation, cash flow and the residual value of the infrastructure.

The company has signed memorandums of understanding with the six financial institutions.

NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang said the initiative brings a new financing model to AI infrastructure. “We have moved from an era in which companies bought chips and built data centres project by project to one in which AI factories can be financed as productive infrastructure,” he wrote in a blog on X.

Huang said NVIDIA’s AI factory model goes beyond GPUs, combining accelerated computing, networking, systems software, AI frameworks and the CUDA ecosystem.

The company argues that this infrastructure can serve multiple customers and workloads, allowing capacity to be redeployed as demand changes.

NVIDIA also cites the continued use of older hardware as evidence that its compute infrastructure retains economic value. The company said its A100 GPU, launched in 2020, remains in commercial use for AI training, fine-tuning, inference and high-performance computing.

“In AI, compute is revenue,” Huang said, arguing that the growing use of AI applications will drive demand for the infrastructure needed to run them.

NVIDIA also cited rising GPU rental prices. One-year H100 rental pricing increased from about $1.70 per GPU-hour in October 2025 to about $2.35 per GPU-hour in March, while cross-provider on-demand median pricing rose from roughly $2 to $2.70 between October 2025 and June 2026.

The financing model also addresses concerns over whether NVIDIA’s role could create a circular financing structure in which the company indirectly funds demand for its own GPUs. Huang said the initiative is intended to bring independent institutional capital into AI infrastructure, with investors making their own decisions on projects.

In some cases, NVIDIA may provide residual-value support of up to 25% of an opportunity. Huang said this support would be assessed on a project-by-project basis and would be “limited, residual-value based and designed to complement—not replace—independent underwriting.”

The financing platforms will therefore place the risk assessment with the participating financial institutions, while NVIDIA supplies the underlying AI factory platform.

Huang said the model depends on AI infrastructure being used to generate economic output rather than simply adding data centre capacity.

NVIDIA expects the model to connect demand from frontier AI labs, AI-native startups, enterprises, cloud providers and governments with institutional capital looking for long-lived infrastructure assets.

Huang described the broader thesis as a cycle in which more compute produces better AI, better AI drives usage, and increased usage creates demand for more compute.

title: NVIDIA targets model costs with Switchyard
content:
NVIDIA has released Nemotron 3.5 Lightning, a 30-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model, alongside NeMo Switchyard, an open-source model routing library for agentic AI applications.

The two releases target systems where multiple AI models handle different parts of a workflow. Nemotron 3.5 Lightning is intended for specialised, high-volume tasks, while Switchyard routes requests to different models based on factors such as quality, latency and cost.

NVIDIA said Nemotron 3.5 Lightning can deliver up to four times faster output and 30% faster agentic task completion than other models in its class.

The model is available through Hugging Face, ModelScope, OpenRouter and NVIDIA's build.nvidia.com platform. NeMo Switchyard is available on GitHub.

The company said the model is built for “high-volume tasks powering always-on agents” and can be customised using NVIDIA NeMo with an organisation’s own data, tools and workflows.

NVIDIA sees the model working alongside larger reasoning models rather than replacing them. “A frontier reasoning model such as Nemotron 3 Ultra or GPT-5.6 may plan and orchestrate a workflow, while smaller specialised models like Nemotron 3.5 Lightning can perform targeted tasks such as code review, tool use, security alert monitoring and answering billing questions,” the company said.

The model is being customised for use cases including cybersecurity, legal services, code review, science, finance and healthcare. NVIDIA cited work by CrowdStrike, Harvey with Trajectory, CodeRabbit with Baseten, Lila Sciences and Fastino Labs.

Nemotron 3.5 Lightning can also run locally on NVIDIA RTX PCs, DGX Spark, DGX Station and Jetson devices, as well as on RTX PRO workstations, data centres and cloud infrastructure.

NVIDIA is also releasing the Nemotron-RL-Agentic-Terminal-Pivot dataset, which was used to post-train the model for coding-agent capabilities.

NeMo Switchyard addresses another problem in multi-model AI systems: deciding which model should handle each request.

Instead of sending every task to a single model, Switchyard can route requests to different models according to an application's requirements. Developers can modify the routing algorithms to prioritise quality, latency or cost.

“Some models are better for coding, some for reasoning, some for lightweight tasks and some are optimised to run locally for greater privacy and efficiency,” NVIDIA said.

The company said internal benchmarks showed Switchyard maintaining frontier-level accuracy while reducing task-completion costs to nearly one-third of using Opus 4.8 alone.

Early partner tests have produced further cost and latency reductions. LangChain reported a 74% reduction in cost across 145 multi-turn Deep Agents tasks by sending only 7% of calls to a frontier model, with a 6% accuracy trade-off.

Cognition integrated Switchyard into Devin Desktop for NVIDIA’s internal use and reported a 28% reduction in mean cost compared with routing all requests to a single frontier model.

Switchyard is also being integrated with tools and platforms including Kong AI Gateway, LiteLLM, Hermes and Devin Desktop.
