Lightstorm has secured a ₹2,500 crore debt facility from IndusInd Bank to build out its fibre network connecting India’s AI infrastructure with data centre hubs in Singapore and Malaysia.

The 10-year facility is fully underwritten and will fund the expansion of Lightstorm’s India network across the southern corridor, along with international connectivity through the I-2SEA subsea cable system.

The company said its ‘AI Superhighway’ will connect AI infrastructure across India and extend to Southeast Asia, as hyperscalers expand data centre and GPU capacity in the region.

“India is building the compute infrastructure of the AI era, and the network connecting that compute needs to be built to the same standard: purpose-built, performance-guaranteed, and designed to scale,” said Scott McGibbony, Group CFO at Lightstorm.

The network is being built with deep-trenched fibre to support low-latency and deterministic connectivity for AI workloads. Lightstorm said the network will provide a direct route between Indian AI infrastructure and hyperscale hubs in Singapore and Malaysia.

Lightstorm currently operates more than 30,000 km of terrestrial fibre and 21,000 km of subsea fibre, connecting more than 100 data centres globally. The company said the new investment will increase its network capacity in India and extend its reach across Southeast Asia.

“The AI Superhighway we are creating spans the length and breadth of India and reaches internationally into Southeast Asia, giving hyperscalers and enterprises a single, high-performance connectivity layer from the subcontinent to the region’s major AI hubs,” McGibbony said.

Niraj Shah, Head of Corporate & Institutional Banking, Gems & Jewellery at IndusInd Bank, said the bank’s financing will support connectivity infrastructure as India increases investments in AI, cloud computing and hyperscale data centres.

“Lightstorm’s vision of creating a high-capacity, low-latency network connecting India's key AI corridors with the rest of the world aligns strongly with the next phase of the region's digital growth,” Shah said.

Lightstorm said its network serves hyperscalers operating in India and is also used by enterprises and AI infrastructure providers. Its connectivity services are delivered through its Polarin network-as-a-service platform, which provides on-demand provisioning and monitoring of network performance.

ideaForge now has drones taking off every two minutes for customer missions, highlighting its operational efficiency.

The company reported a revenue of ₹68.6 crore and a positive EBITDA, despite a net loss for the quarter.

Drone tech company ideaForge announced that it now has drones taking off every two minutes on average to carry out customer missions. It reported this along with the company’s recent revenue numbers. The drone maker said it has crossed one million customer flights across different terrains and operating conditions, while executing more than 20% of its opening FY27 order book.

The Mumbai-based company announced its audited results for the quarter ended June 30. It reported revenue of ₹68.6 crore and EBITDA of ₹4.3 crore, while posting a net loss of ₹2.6 crore.

It said global supply chain disruptions and component shortages continued to affect deliveries, but it remains on track to complete its opening FY27 order book by the third quarter.

During the quarter, ideaForge also secured DGCA Type Certification for its Q6V2 GEO UAV. It raised ₹500 crore through a qualified institutional placement and received a Letter of Intent from the government for financial assistance of up to ₹151 crore under the Research, Development and Innovation Scheme. The funding will support the development of its YETI middle-mile logistics platform.

Commenting on the results, Co-Founder and CEO Ankit Mehta said the company entered FY27 with an order book of more than ₹300 crore and is working towards fulfilling deliveries in line with customer timelines.

“We have made good progress in our development efforts of combat drone capabilities such as air-launched effects and fuel-hybrid long-endurance capability for ZOLT. We are also actively developing long-range strike platforms, loitering munitions, and other capabilities through in-house and collaborative developments,” Mehta said.

He said higher procurement limits for field commanders under DFPDS 2026 could accelerate procurement activity in the third and fourth quarters. He also pointed to public reports of nearly ₹20,000 crore in fast-track defence procurement opportunities, with one already at the request-for-proposal stage.

content:
IBM and Together AI have signed a multi-year $240 million agreement to deploy a large cluster of NVIDIA HGX B300 systems on IBM Cloud, with the infrastructure expected to be available in the first quarter of 2027.

Together AI will use the cluster to provide inference for open-source AI models. The deployment will be the first dedicated large-scale inference cluster on IBM Cloud using NVIDIA HGX B300 systems and NVIDIA Spectrum-X Ethernet networking.

The companies said the infrastructure will help Together AI increase inference capacity while reducing the cost of serving AI models to enterprise customers.

“Enterprises want the performance of the best frontier models without the closed-model price tag, and that only works if the infrastructure underneath is fast and reliable at scale,” said Vipul Ved Prakash, CEO of Together AI.

“Working alongside IBM with NVIDIA gives us that foundation. This cluster lets us bring production-grade inference to more companies, faster, and it's a big step in our push to make open-source AI the obvious choice for enterprises,” he added.

Together AI said its inference business now processes 400 trillion tokens a month. The company raised $800 million in a Series C round at an $8.3 billion valuation, with the funding going towards its AI Native Cloud.

Its platform covers inference, model training, fine-tuning and agentic workflows. The company has positioned open-source models as an alternative to closed AI systems, with developers able to build applications using modular model and infrastructure stacks.

Together AI selected IBM and NVIDIA based on their infrastructure roadmaps and ability to provide GPU capacity at the pace required for its expansion. The companies also pointed to the cost of serving tokens as a key consideration.

The cluster will use NVIDIA HGX B300 systems connected through NVIDIA Spectrum-X Ethernet networking. NVIDIA said its B300 platform can deliver 30 times more AI factory output than prior generations.

IBM said the infrastructure will also give Together AI a path into the enterprise market by combining its inference platform with IBM Cloud infrastructure.

“Enterprises are in a race to adopt agentic AI at scale to drive real business outcomes,” said Alan Peacock, General Manager of IBM Cloud. “IBM and NVIDIA are delivering scalable, economical, enterprise-grade AI infrastructure that can help Together AI accelerate innovation for the next generation of AI infrastructure.”

The deal also expands an existing collaboration between IBM and NVIDIA. The companies have been working across GPU-native data analytics, unstructured data extraction, on-premises and cloud infrastructure, and consulting services.

Dion Harris, Senior Director of HPC and AI Infrastructure Solutions at NVIDIA, said the infrastructure would help enterprises deploy open-source AI for real-time services.

“AI factories are becoming essential enterprise infrastructure—like electricity and telecommunications—turning compute and data into intelligence,” Harris said.

Cloud-based ERP provider Acumatica has opened a new global capability centre (GCC) in Hyderabad, starting with more than 30 employees, as the company expands its engineering footprint in India to drive product development and serve customers globally.

Located in Nanakramguda, the Hyderabad centre will initially focus on engineering and is expected to grow its workforce in the coming months. Acumatica said the GCC could eventually expand into additional functions as the company increases its presence in the region.

“We have created the core of our growth engine in India with an initial seed, and we look forward to it becoming a mature tree and a major contributor to the success of Acumatica customers and Acumatica itself,” said Miten Mehta, Chief Engineering Officer of Acumatica.

“India’s deep engineering talent pool, thriving technology ecosystem, and growing reputation as a destination for global innovation centres make Hyderabad the ideal home for this next chapter of how we deliver value to small and mid-sized businesses,” Mehta stated.

The new GCC is being positioned as an engineering centre of excellence that will develop products and capabilities for Acumatica’s customers worldwide. The company said the centre will form part of its globally distributed engineering organisation and support its longer-term product innovation and growth strategy.

Acumatica currently operates across the US, Canada, Serbia and Sri Lanka. The Hyderabad GCC adds India to this global engineering network, with the company looking to build a larger local team over time.

The company is actively hiring engineering talent for the Hyderabad centre. While the GCC currently has more than 30 employees, Acumatica said additional employees will join in the coming months.

The centre will initially focus on engineering, while its mandate could expand into other disciplines as the operation matures.

Acumatica has established the Hyderabad GCC in partnership with Summit Consulting Services, an ANSR company that specialises in helping companies build and scale GCCs.

title: Pathway Claims 11x Lower AI Reasoning Costs With 150M-Parameter Model
content:
The invitation marks a new step in US-India cooperation on lunar exploration and deep space missions.

What Actually Matters.

NASA has invited ISRO to join its Moon Base programme, enhancing US-India cooperation in space exploration.

The announcement was made during the ninth US-India Civil Space Joint Working Group meeting in Bengaluru.

NASA has invited the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) to join its Moon Base programme, expanding cooperation between the United States and India on deep space exploration.

The announcement came during the ninth US-India Civil Space Joint Working Group meeting, co-chaired by the US Department of State and NASA in Bengaluru, where both sides advanced the TRUST initiative, a bilateral partnership between the two countries.

NASA has invited @ISRO to join its Moon Base program, deepening the U.S.-India deep space partnership! The news came as @StateDept and @NASA co-chaired the 9th Civil Space Joint Working Group in Bengaluru, advancing the 🇺🇸-🇮🇳 TRUST initiative. https://t.co/qLbhitmHCO

— Ambassador Sergio Gor (@USAmbIndia) August 11, 2026

The invitation signals a broader role for India in NASA’s long-term plans to establish a sustained human presence on the Moon. While NASA has not disclosed ISRO’s specific role, the Moon Base programme aims to build infrastructure near the Moon’s South Pole. It plans to accomplish this through a phased series of robotic and crewed missions, supported by international and commercial partners.

Notably, India made history in 2023 after becoming the first country to successfully land a spacecraft, Chandrayaan-3, near the lunar south pole.

According to NASA, the Moon Base will serve as humanity’s first lunar outpost where astronauts will live, work, and conduct scientific research near the lunar South Pole.

The programme will support long-term exploration, unlock scientific discoveries, and prepare future missions deeper into the solar system. NASA plans to develop the outpost in phases.

The first phase, running until 2029, will focus on robotic missions to study the lunar environment, test technologies, and identify locations for future infrastructure. Later phases will establish power systems, communications, cargo transport, and habitats before enabling astronauts to live and work on the Moon for extended periods.

NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman described the effort as a gradual learning process. “Every mission, crewed and uncrewed, will be a learning opportunity as we return to the lunar surface, build the infrastructure to stay, and master the skills required to live and operate in one of the most demanding and dangerous environments imaginable,” he said.

NASA said the Moon Base strategy relies on commercial participation and international collaboration. It expects governments, private companies, and global partners to contribute across different stages of development, from early technology demonstrations to long-term surface operations.

The invitation also builds on broader efforts to strengthen US-India commercial space ties.

In February, the two countries held the inaugural US-India Space Business Forum and Trade Mission in Bengaluru, bringing together officials and executives from 14 American space companies. The forum focused on improving market access, government procurement, regulatory cooperation, and industry partnerships, while advancing the priorities of the US-India Commercial Space Sub-Working Group.

The company has reached a $500 million valuation, following additional funding, taking total seed funding to $30 million

What Actually Matters.

Pathway's BDH-CQ model achieves a 29.5% score on the ARC-AGI-1 benchmark while being significantly more cost-efficient than larger models.

The model operates at an inference cost of $0.0007 per task, making it approximately 11 times cheaper than GPT 5.6 Luna.

Pathway’s 150-million-parameter reasoning model BDH-CQ has scored 29.5% on the public ARC-AGI-1 benchmark at a reported inference cost of $0.0007 per task, positioning the model as a significantly more cost-efficient alternative to larger reasoning models.

According to Pathway, BDH-CQ achieved a 29.5% pass@2 score on the ARC-AGI-1 public evaluation set at a computed inference cost of $0.0007 per task. The company said the model runs approximately 11 times cheaper per task than GPT 5.6 Luna (Low), which scored 34.2% on the same benchmark. Pathway described the difference as a trade-off between a modest accuracy gap and a substantial reduction in inference cost.

The company has reached a $500 million valuation, following additional funding, taking total seed funding to $30 million, and appointed Adam Kurzrok, former Google DeepMind Gemini product lead, as the CPO.

ARC-AGI-1 is designed to test whether an AI system can identify an underlying rule from a small number of examples and apply that rule to a new input. The benchmark is often used to evaluate reasoning capabilities that require models to generalise beyond patterns seen during training.

Pathway attributes BDH-CQ’s cost advantage to its architecture. While many transformer-based reasoning models generate intermediate chains of text as part of their reasoning process, BDH-CQ performs its reasoning in a recurrent latent state without producing an intermediate text trace.

The company said this allows the model to refine solutions internally rather than generating and processing additional reasoning tokens, reducing both compute requirements and latency.

“Today’s AI pays a steep token cost for reasoning, but that cost is imposed by architecture, not by any law of intelligence. Currently, every reasoning step consumes context, adds latency, and burns compute,” said Zuzanna Stamirowska, CEO and Co-Founder of Pathway.

“We show that a different architecture changes the game and opens up a whole new space in terms of how much intelligence per dollar. A 150M-parameter model, built on Pathway’s BDH architecture, reasons recurrently in latent space and sets a new state of the art in cost efficiency on ARC-AGI-1.”

The results were independently evaluated by Łukasz Kaiser, co-author of the 2017 ‘Attention Is All You Need’ paper that introduced the Transformer architecture. Kaiser said the results point to architecture as an important factor in advancing AI reasoning, rather than relying solely on increasing model size.

“I’ve followed Pathway closely and replicated their ARC-AGI-1 results myself. Pathway shows that model architecture, not just scale, can drive the next leap in AI reasoning,” Kaiser said.

The results were also reproduced by Richard Zhong, an NYU researcher focused on model evaluation and benchmark robustness.

Pathway said the scores and comparison costs were drawn from the ARC Prize Foundation’s public leaderboard, which compares benchmark performance with cost per task. The leaderboard data used by the company was based on submissions available as of July.

Pathway’s cost figure was calculated using measured hardware time, while the costs of comparison models reported on the leaderboard may reflect API pricing for general-purpose models.

The company plans to scale the BDH architecture and test it on more demanding reasoning benchmarks, including mathematical reasoning, ARC-AGI-2 and ARC-AGI-3. It also plans to develop a latent-reasoning large language model based on the architecture.

Pathway said early experiments indicate that Transformer-like scaling laws continue to apply during pretraining at scales ranging from 1 billion to 600 billion parameters while retaining the latent reasoning capabilities demonstrated by BDH-CQ.

The company expects the approach could eventually be applied to workloads that require models to reason continuously as information and constraints change, including cybersecurity incident response and real-time industrial operations.

title: OpenAI Launches GPT-5.6-Cyber Through Daybreak for Advanced Security Research
content:
OpenAI says the model has already helped identify vulnerabilities across Chrome’s V8 engine, databases, mobile operating systems, and kernels.

OpenAI has expanded its Daybreak cybersecurity programme with two access tiers and introduced GPT-5.6-Cyber, a model trained for tasks including zero-day discovery, exploit development, and security testing.

The company said Daybreak Blue will give approved defenders access to GPT-5.6 Sol with safeguards for authorised security work, while Daybreak Red will provide access to purpose-trained cybersecurity models. GPT-5.6-Cyber will be available through Daybreak Red.

“Threat actors will increasingly use AI to conduct cyberattacks at unprecedented speed and scale, including in fully autonomous ways,” OpenAI said. The company added that defenders have a “narrowing window” to prepare for these capabilities.

GPT-5.6-Cyber is built on GPT-5.6 Sol and trained for specialised cybersecurity tasks, including finding zero-day vulnerabilities and developing exploit chains. OpenAI said the model also reduces refusals for certain higher-risk, dual-use cybersecurity tasks.

In an internal evaluation called Advanced Cybersecurity Completion Rate, OpenAI tested how often models responded to requests involving exploit-chain development, authentication bypass, privilege escalation, and other advanced cybersecurity scenarios. GPT-5.6-Cyber completed 95% of these requests, compared with 1.5% for GPT-5.6 Sol and 2% for GPT-5.6 Sol with Daybreak Blue access. GPT-5.5-Cyber recorded a 57.3% completion rate.

OpenAI said Daybreak Blue is intended for vulnerability discovery, secure code review, malware analysis, incident response, patch validation, and security assessments. Daybreak Red is intended for authorised vulnerability research, exploit validation, and security testing.

The company also said GPT-5.6-Cyber performed better than GPT-5.6 Sol and GPT-5.5-Cyber on ExploitGym2, an evaluation that tests whether AI agents can turn known vulnerabilities into working exploits in controlled environments.

OpenAI said it used GPT-5.6-Cyber to investigate V8, the JavaScript engine used by Chrome, and found two previously unknown vulnerabilities that could be chained to corrupt memory and escape the V8 heap sandbox.

The researchers validated the findings and reported them to Google through coordinated vulnerability disclosure. Google subsequently fixed the vulnerability, which OpenAI said was assigned CVE-2026-15903.

OpenAI also said GPT-5.6-Cyber helped identify at least five vulnerabilities in a mobile operating system, three critical vulnerabilities in a database, and more than 400 vulnerabilities that could lead to privilege escalation in an operating system kernel.

The company said GPT-5.6-Cyber was assessed as reaching the High threshold under its Preparedness Framework, but not the Critical threshold for cybersecurity capability.

Daybreak Blue and Daybreak Red are available to approved individuals and organisations conducting authorised cybersecurity work. OpenAI said access will be controlled through identity verification, account security, monitoring, approved-use restrictions, and legal attestations.

OpenAI is also requiring individual Daybreak accounts to use hardware security keys from September 1. The company said it is working on additional monitoring measures and is encouraging customers using Codex to use auto-review mode for actions requiring elevated permissions.

OpenAI recommends Daybreak Blue as the starting point for most defenders, while organisations involved in advanced vulnerability research, exploit development, or red teaming can request Daybreak Red access.

title: Workato Opens Hyderabad AI Collaboration Hub for Enterprise AI Development
content:
The new facility will bring customers, partners, and engineers together to build and deploy AI solutions.

What Actually Matters.

Workato has launched an AI Collaboration Hub in Hyderabad to facilitate enterprise AI development.

The hub aims to streamline co-development of AI solutions between customers, partners, and engineers.

Cloud-based integration and automation platform Workato has opened AI Collaboration Hub in Hyderabad to help customers and partners co-develop and deploy enterprise AI solutions. The company announced that Hyderabad will be home to its third such hub, after San Francisco and Singapore.

The facility is located at Aurobindo Orbit in HITEC City and is designed to bring customers, global system integrator partners, and Workato engineers together to build production-ready agentic AI workflows.

The hub houses an Enterprise AI Collaboration Centre where customers, partners, and developers can jointly design, test, and deploy AI solutions on their own enterprise systems. Workato said the initiative aims to shorten the time between AI development and production deployment by enabling teams to work directly with its engineers.

The launch comes as many enterprises struggle to move AI projects beyond the pilot stage. Workato cited McKinsey & Company, which found that nearly 80% of organisations report no tangible business impact from generative AI. The company said the challenge lies in integrating AI with legacy enterprise systems, regulated data, and multi-cloud infrastructure while maintaining governance.

Workato said it chose Hyderabad because of India’s growing role in enterprise AI engineering. The company pointed to the Stanford 2026 AI Index Report, which found that India is the world’s second-largest contributor to GitHub AI activity. Workato has expanded its India operations to more than 200 employees across Hyderabad, Bengaluru, and Chennai since entering the country in 2022.

“I grew up in Hyderabad, so opening this hub is personal, but why it matters to our customers is anything but sentimental,” said Vijay Tella, CEO and Co-founder of Workato. “The hard part of enterprise AI was never the model; it's making AI work within real companies, with their enterprise systems, data, and compliance realities."

He said that the hub would allow customers and partners to “build production-grade AI with us, in the same room, and walk out with something tangible.”

Persistent Systems said the collaboration hub would help organisations jointly design and accelerate production-ready AI solutions. Sameer Dixit, Corporate VP, Data, Integration and AI at Persistent Systems, said enterprise AI adoption requires integration, orchestration, and governance alongside AI models.

Tech Mahindra also backed the initiative. Gopikrishnan Konnanath, Global Head of Digital Enterprise Applications, said the hub would help customers move from ideas to deployed agentic workflows more quickly by allowing architects and Workato engineers to build solutions together in real customer environments.

content:
Vertiv is expanding its data centre training programme to Maharashtra, aiming to train 1,500 engineering students by 2026.

The initiative is backed by IIT Madras and focuses on practical industry exposure alongside classroom learning.

Digital infrastructure player Vertiv is expanding its IIT Madras-backed data centre training programme into Maharashtra, with plans to provide free training to 1,500 engineering students in 2026 as demand grows for professionals who can operate and manage data centres.

The programme, supported by Vertiv through its corporate social responsibility (CSR) initiative, is being expanded through a collaboration between the IIT Madras Pravartak Technologies Foundation and Ratan Tata Maharashtra State Skills University (RTMSSU). The two institutions signed a Memorandum of Understanding on July 10 during the “Start-up Frontier 1.0” exhibition and conference in Mumbai.

The programme will use RTMSSU’s network of pre-incubation centres across 60 colleges in Maharashtra. Participants will receive online training and certificates, along with opportunities for internships and mentoring to prepare them for careers in data centre operations and digital infrastructure management.

Vertiv said the training will draw on its expertise in areas such as power, cooling, and IT infrastructure. The company is also working with IIT Bombay, IIT Madras Pravartak Technologies Foundation, and IIT (BHU) on initiatives designed to give engineering students practical exposure to data centre operations and infrastructure.

“Through this initiative, we provide engineering students with practical knowledge, industry exposure and the skills needed to contribute to India's evolving digital infrastructure ecosystem,” AS Prasad, Vice President of Product Management and Engineering, Vertiv India, said in a statement.

The Maharashtra expansion builds on a programme launched by Vertiv and the IIT Madras Pravartak Technologies Foundation in 2025 to strengthen the talent pool for India’s growing digital infrastructure sector.

The initiative comes as the growth of AI is driving demand for more data centres and the people needed to run them. Data centres provide the computing infrastructure required to support AI services and other digital applications.

MJ Shankar Raman, CEO, IIT Madras Pravartak Technologies Foundation, said the expansion aims to address the shortage of skilled professionals needed to support this growth.

“This rapid growth has created an urgent need for skilled specialists who can operate and maintain these essential facilities. Through this programme, we are dedicated to building a workforce that supports India’s AI ambitions with the technical talent required to sustain them,” he said.

The programme will focus not only on classroom learning but also on giving students exposure to industry practices through internships and mentoring. The partners said the aim is to create a larger pool of engineering graduates equipped to work in data centre operations and digital infrastructure as India’s digital economy expands.

Skyroot Aerospace has signed a multi-launch agreement with HEX20 for three dedicated missions starting in late 2027.

The Vikram launch vehicles will support Earth observation and payload demonstration missions.

Hyderabad-based Skyroot Aerospace has signed a multi-launch agreement with Kerala’s space tech company HEX20 to launch the latter’s Earth observation constellation and in-orbit payload demonstration missions.

The agreement includes three dedicated launches aboard Skyroot’s Vikram launch vehicles, with the first mission scheduled for the fourth quarter of 2027.

The agreement was signed in Hyderabad by Naga Bharath Daka, Co-founder and COO of Skyroot Aerospace, and MB Aravind, Co-Founder and COO of HEX20. Under the deal, the Vikram missions will also offer rideshare opportunities for third-party spacecraft alongside HEX20’s satellites.

The announcement comes weeks after Skyroot’s Vikram-1 became India’s first privately developed orbital-class rocket to reach orbit on its maiden flight in July 2026. The company said the mission established flight heritage for all major subsystems and supports its plans to increase launch frequency to 12 missions annually.

It added that the HEX20 agreement accounts for three slots in its near-term launch manifest.

“Enabling innovators like HEX20 with reliable and responsive access to space is what the Vikram series is built for, and we look forward to supporting their ambitions for years to come,” said Daka.

Skyroot said Vikram-1 can deploy small satellites weighing up to 350 kg into low Earth orbit. The company develops its launch vehicle structures and propulsion systems in-house and is expanding its launch operations to meet demand for dedicated small satellite launches.

Amal Chandran, CEO of HEX20, said the partnership reflects the growing maturity of India’s private space ecosystem. “Our partnership with Skyroot brings complementary capabilities together, allowing us to create stronger pathways to orbit and enable more ambitious missions for customers in India and around the world.”

NetApp has acquired JetStream Software to enhance its disaster recovery and cloud migration capabilities for VMware environments.

The integration will enable protection of VMware workloads on various storage platforms, including recovery options on Azure NetApp Files.

Data infrastructure company NetApp has acquired JetStream Software, a provider of VMware disaster recovery and migration technology, as it expands its data protection and cloud migration capabilities for enterprise customers.

The company did not disclose the financial terms of the acquisition

The acquisition will allow NetApp to protect VMware environments running on different storage platforms and recover them on NetApp storage offerings, including Azure NetApp Files. Financial terms of the deal were not disclosed.

“Data has become the foundation for business growth, AI innovation, and operational continuity,” said George Kurian, CEO of NetApp. “As customers look to unlock greater value from their data while strengthening protection against disruption, bringing JetStream into NetApp expands our ability to help keep their data secure, available, and ready for what comes next.”

JetStream’s technology will complement NetApp’s SnapMirror replication technology. SnapMirror will continue to be the preferred replication solution for NetApp environments, while JetStream will extend protection to VMware workloads running on third-party storage.

The acquisition comes as enterprises evaluate cloud migration while continuing to run critical applications on VMware. NetApp said disaster recovery can serve as an initial step in moving workloads to the cloud, with production workloads migrating as cloud strategies develop.

“Customers want to move to the cloud on their schedule, not their infrastructure’s schedule,” said Pravjit Tiwana, Senior Vice President and General Manager of Cloud Storage and Services at NetApp. “JetStream helps customers start with disaster recovery and seamlessly evolve to production in the cloud.”

Tom Critser, Co-Founder and CEO of JetStream Software, said joining NetApp would allow the company to bring its technology to more organisations.

“Joining NetApp allows us to bring our technology to more organisations worldwide and deliver even greater value by combining our expertise with NetApp’s industry-leading data services and cloud storage portfolio,” Critser said.

NetApp said the combined portfolio will support application protection, cloud migration and infrastructure modernisation while allowing customers to transition workloads at their own pace.

The company also said the acquisition is expected to expand its cloud offerings within hyperscalers as enterprises look to move VMware workloads from existing infrastructure to cloud environments.

title: What Actually Matters.
content:
Meta is releasing the Muse Glimmer model, which features 30 billion parameters and can operate on consumer hardware.

The Muse Spark 1.2 model will also have an open-weight version available soon.

Meta is releasing the weights for Muse Glimmer, a 30-billion-parameter dense model that can run on a laptop or a single consumer GPU, while preparing to open source a version of Muse Spark 1.2, one of its leading foundation models, in the coming weeks.

Muse Glimmer is being released under the Apache 2.0 licence, with its weights available through Hugging Face. Meta says the model is intended for local agents, function calling, coding and LLM-as-a-judge workloads without requiring a cloud connection.

For Muse Glimmer, integrations with llama.cpp, MLX and ExecuTorch are expected in the coming days. Meta also plans support through Ollama, LM Studio and Unsloth, alongside deployment options including vLLM and SGLang.

Meta said it is working with AMD, Arm, Dell, Intel and NVIDIA to optimise the model across different hardware platforms.

“Running models locally enables you to use AI anywhere, anytime, with or without an internet connection,” Meta said in its announcement.

Muse Glimmer can handle multi-step agent workflows, including tool use, failure recovery, multimodal inputs and long-context tasks. It supports text and image inputs through a dedicated perception encoder and can work with agent orchestration frameworks such as OpenClaw.

Meta said Muse Glimmer was trained using outputs from its larger Muse Spark model. The training process used logit distillation during pre-training, followed by mid-training on longer-context and agent-focused data.

For post-training, Meta combined supervised fine-tuning with on-policy distillation and reinforcement learning across reasoning, coding and agentic tasks.

The company said the approach was intended to transfer capabilities from a larger model into a model that can run within the memory limits of consumer hardware.

“At full precision, a 30-billion parameter model would require over 55 GB of memory,” Meta said.

Meta uses quantisation to bring the model down to under 20 GB at roughly 4-bit precision. This allows the model, its KV cache, perception encoder and speculative decoding system to operate within a 24 GB or 32 GB memory envelope.

Muse Glimmer supports tool calling, multi-step reasoning and failure recovery. Meta said the model can diagnose failed tool calls and retry rather than stopping the workflow.

It was evaluated on benchmarks including DeepSearchQA, MCP-Atlas, τ-Bench and SWE-Bench. Meta compared its performance with Gemma 4 31B and Qwen3.6 27B, saying Muse Glimmer performs strongly across several benchmarks for models in its size category.

The model also supports different reasoning strengths, allowing developers to trade off response quality and speed. It was trained on data covering more than 100 languages.

Meta is also using speculative decoding to reduce generation latency. Muse Glimmer comes with a lightweight drafter based on DFlash, which proposes blocks of tokens for the main model to verify in parallel.

“An agent that takes minutes to reply or plan its next step breaks the flow of real work,” Meta said.

The company tested its K-Quant-17GB version with a quantised DFlash drafter on Apple’s M4 Max and M5 Max Macs, as well as NVIDIA’s RTX 5090. Meta said the combination is intended to support real-time interaction while keeping processing on the device.

GalaxEye has acquired StarOps to enhance its satellite engineering capabilities and expand its technology offerings.

The acquisition brings in StarOps' engineering team and proprietary spacecraft technologies, supporting integrated space technology development.

Bengaluru-based GalaxEye has acquired spacecraft engineering company StarOps (formerly part of TeamIndus) to strengthen its satellite engineering capabilities and expand its end-to-end space technology stack.

The acquisition brings StarOps’ engineering team, satellite platforms, and proprietary spacecraft technologies under GalaxEye’s umbrella.

“From day one, our vision has been to build a company that develops and owns the technologies defining the future of space,” said Suyash Singh, Co-founder and CEO of GalaxEye, in a statement.

The acquisition aims to help GalaxEye build a fully integrated space technology company by combining spacecraft platforms, satellite subsystems, and Earth observation payloads. StarOps, incorporated in 2022, will contribute engineering expertise spanning mission design, propulsion, avionics, flight computing, guidance and navigation, structures, electrical systems, and ground operations.

Several members of the StarOps team previously worked at TeamIndus on its lunar lander and rover programme. GalaxEye said their experience across the full mission lifecycle will strengthen its capabilities throughout the satellite value chain.

The acquisition also adds qualified satellite bus platforms across the 50 kg, 150 kg, and 250 kg classes, along with testing infrastructure, engineering tools, and proprietary subsystem technologies.

StarOps said more than 66% of its satellite systems are indigenised, reducing dependence on global supply chains while enabling faster development and lower mission costs.

Nirmal Suraj Gadde, Co-founder and Missions Lead at StarOps, said the company has focused on building indigenous satellite systems and manufacturing capabilities for India’s commercial space sector. He added that the team will now contribute its experience to GalaxEye’s plans to develop and deploy a constellation of OptoSAR satellites.

GalaxEye said the acquisition aligns with its long-term strategy of developing indigenous technologies across the satellite value chain. The company expects the integration to accelerate product development, deepen vertical integration, and strengthen its ability to deliver complete space missions from concept to operations.

DePuy Synthes is establishing a global capability centre in Bengaluru focused on innovation and technology.

The centre aims to employ around 500 professionals within the next 18–24 months.

DePuy Synthes, the orthopaedics business of Johnson & Johnson MedTech, plans to establish a global capability centre (GCC) in Bengaluru that will serve as a global hub for innovation, engineering, technology and enterprise services.

The company expects to build a team of approximately 500 professionals at the centre over the next 18–24 months, with recruitment and initial operational activities set to begin in August.

The new GCC will bring together technology, data and business capabilities to support clinical innovation and operational excellence for patients, surgeons and healthcare partners globally. The centre will house capabilities including software development, data and AI, enterprise applications, technology services and cybersecurity, among other functions.

“India is one of the fastest-growing markets in the world for orthopaedic care, and this investment deepens our long-term commitment to patients, surgeons, and colleagues here,” said Namal Nawana, Worldwide President, DePuy Synthes.

The company said the centre will be established in phases, with recruitment forming part of the initial operational activities. While the initial workforce is expected to comprise around 500 professionals, DePuy Synthes said the centre will have room to expand as it matures.

The GCC will be led by Nicholas Parrotta, Chief Information Officer at DePuy Synthes. He will be supported by technology and local leadership as the company plans and establishes the centre and its future operations.

Dr Jai Ganesh, Chief Technology Officer at DePuy Synthes, will oversee technology engineering, architecture, infrastructure, cybersecurity engineering and digital platforms for the company. Nagaraj Bhat, GCC Leader at DePuy Synthes, will support the establishment of local operations and the centre’s leadership team.

The Bengaluru centre is expected to serve as a global engine for innovation and engineering, bringing together technology and business capabilities that can support DePuy Synthes’ operations across markets.

The company’s decision comes as India continues to expand its role as a hub for global engineering, technology, data and AI operations. For DePuy Synthes, the new centre is expected to provide access to India’s technology talent while supporting the company’s broader innovation and digital capabilities

The facility will support up to 30 high-performance computing workloads simultaneously and will be used for AI research, industry projects, and skilling programmes

What Actually Matters.

IBM and MAHE have established an AI lab in Bengaluru to enhance access to high-performance computing.

The facility will support multiple AI research areas including machine learning and natural language processing.

IBM and Manipal Academy of Higher Education (MAHE) have launched an artificial intelligence research and computing lab at MAHE’s Bengaluru campus, adding to a growing pool of industry-backed infrastructure aimed at giving students and researchers access to high-performance computing.

The IBM-MIT AI Lab, also called MAHE Intelligence GPU (MIG), will house a GPU-enabled high-performance computing (HPC) facility capable of supporting up to 30 computing workloads simultaneously, according to the companies.

The facility will be used for research across machine learning, deep learning, generative AI, computer vision, natural language processing, cybersecurity, healthcare, and data analytics.

“MIG is primarily a collaboration between industry and academia, looking at how this next-gen technology, or the requirement for compute power, can actually be leveraged by students,” Iven Jose, Director, MIT Bengaluru, told AIM.

According to Jose, the MIG lab is built around eight NVIDIA H200 GPU stacks. The facility will be used for research across machine learning, deep learning, generative AI, computer vision, natural language processing, cybersecurity, healthcare, and data analytics.

The launch comes as access to AI compute has emerged as a key bottleneck for researchers, startups, and educational institutions seeking to build and train AI systems.

The Centre's infrastructure is expected to be used not only by MAHE students and faculty but also as part of programmes aimed at institutions beyond the campus.

Under the partnership, IBM and MIT Bengaluru will also run an AI learning initiative through IBM SkillsBuild, the company's free technology education programme. It will include workshops, bootcamps, hands-on AI and machine learning training, digital credentials and mentorship.

The programme is intended to reach students from tier-2 and tier-3 institutions.

IBM and MAHE intend to make the Bengaluru lab an industry-academia platform. It will support industry-sponsored projects, interdisciplinary research, faculty development, student innovation, hackathons, internships, startup incubation, and joint technology development.

“India stands at a pivotal moment in its AI journey,” IBM India and South Asia Managing Director Sandip Patel said in a statement, adding that stronger collaboration between talent, research, advanced computing and industry would be needed to build India's AI ecosystem.

Priyank Kharge, Cabinet Minister for Home, IT & BT, e-Governance, Government of Karnataka, said the collaboration would strengthen the state's AI ecosystem by providing students and researchers access to advanced infrastructure and hands-on learning.

"By providing access to advanced AI infrastructure, hands-on learning, and resources, the lab will empower students and researchers to accelerate innovation and develop AI-driven solutions that address societal challenges and contribute to inclusive growth," said Kharge.

Beyond Sarla Aviation, Siemens has also worked with Skyroot Aerospace, helping the startup build its engineering stack

What Actually Matters.

Sarla Aviation significantly reduced its aircraft build time from ten days to three using digital engineering.

The startup leveraged Siemens’ Xcelerator software to enhance innovation while managing costs effectively.

When Bengaluru-based urban air mobility startup Sarla Aviation set out to build its electric vertical take-off and landing (eVTOL) aircraft, it faced a challenge common to most deeptech startups: how do you innovate at the pace of a startup without the budgets of aerospace giants?

The answer, according to the startup, lay in digital engineering.

Using Siemens’ Xcelerator portfolio of software, Sarla says it was able to dramatically cut development time, reduce costs, and accelerate learning cycles while building its next-generation air taxi platform.

Siemens Xcelerator is an open digital business platform that brings together software, hardware, and services from Siemens and its certified partners in a single marketplace. It allows businesses to quickly access and deploy technologies that help streamline operations, accelerate innovation, and solve industrial challenges.

By adopting Siemens’ integrated digital thread, the company is connecting product design, simulation and lifecycle management in a unified environment to improve engineering efficiency, streamline certification readiness, and support faster product development.

Sarla Aviation has tapped into Siemens solutions, including Designcenter for mechanical design and CAD framework, Simcenter for engineering simulation and 3D modelling, Capital for electrical engineering, Polarion for application lifecycle management, and Teamcenter for product lifecycle management and data unification. The startup says these software products have helped reduce design iterations through early-stage simulation, enhancing collaboration across engineering teams and strengthening the traceability, verification, and validation processes required for certification.

"The fundamental shift here is economics of innovation," observes Rakesh Gaonkar, Co-founder and CTO of Sarla Aviation, in a conversation with AIM on the sidelines of Siemens’ Realize LIVE Asia-Pacific 2026.

"Being a startup, we don't have a billion dollars to spend like other companies. We have to make sure we do it at a certain cost."

The startup plans to launch electric air taxi services in Bengaluru by 2028.

Sarla and other Indian startups are turning to digital twins, AI-powered engineering, and simulation tools to speed up product development.

From Virtual Prototypes to Flying Aircraft

Before building physical prototypes, Sarla relied heavily on virtual engineering tools.

"Money is scarce," Gaonkar says. "So what we did is we did a lot of virtual prototyping from an architecture point of view, from space allocation, from aerodynamic lofting and others."

Using Siemens' simulation tools, Sarla could evaluate aircraft performance long before constructing hardware. "We got lift-to-drag ratios around 13, which is quite good for an eVTOL," Gaonkar adds.

The next challenge was determining whether the aircraft could actually be manufactured and withstand real-world stresses. Traditionally, aerospace companies build multiple prototypes, test them extensively, and learn through failures. Startups, however, rarely have that luxury.

"Usually, conventional companies build a couple of airframes, and they drop them, and then they learn and iterate. But we don't have that kind of money. We have to get it right in the first instance," Gaonkar states.

According to Gaonkar, Siemens' simulation technologies enabled Sarla to move much closer to real-world performance before committing resources. "Simulation tools these days are 90% closer to what reality could be," he states.

The company then used Siemens NX and Simcenter platforms to bridge the gap between design and manufacturing. "Simcenter NX is something that glued it together in terms of design for manufacturing."

More importantly, the software helped create a collaborative engineering environment where teams could work simultaneously instead of sequentially.

"What kept everything glued together under one umbrella was Simcenter," he explains. "It helped us streamline our company, our specialists, their flow of information, the release of data, and the different iterations that we have."

The results, according to Sarla, were significant. "We were able to get the weight down by close to 80%," he states.

The company also reduced manufacturing timelines substantially. "We got that time down by 70%—from 10 days to three days," Gaonkar shares. "In fact, we are even pushing to do it in one day itself."

Cost savings were equally dramatic, with expenditure dropping by 74%.

"All this together means that we are learning faster—3x faster,” he states. "And that's game-changing."

Siemens Bets Big on India's Startup Ecosystem

Sarla Aviation is not an isolated case.

Mathew Thomas, CEO and MD, Siemens Digital Industries Software India, highlights that startups across electric vehicles, aerospace, defence, and advanced manufacturing are increasingly adopting digital engineering technologies at much earlier stages.

"To answer your question on demand—it’s massive," he notes.

According to him, startups no longer view engineering software as a luxury.

"Today, startups see technology as a differentiator," Thomas mentions. "They are adopting technology much earlier because they understand it gives them a competitive advantage."

The company structures its offerings to allow startups to begin with smaller deployments and expand as they grow.

While Siemens declined to share the exact number of startups using its platforms, the executive notes that the company adds hundreds of new startups across industries.

Another example is Skyroot Aerospace, a pioneering space tech company that recently put Vikram-1 into orbit, making it the first private Indian player to do so. Siemens has worked with Skyroot since its early years, helping the startup build its engineering stack.

"They started with Product Lifecycle Management, then moved to Designcenter and Simcenter," Thomas reveals. "We've been working with them for years and have grown with them as they scaled."

He also sees startups as critical to India's ambitions in strategic sectors. From electric aircraft and space rockets to next-generation manufacturing, Siemens believes startups will increasingly drive India's innovation economy—and faster, thanks to digital engineering tools, that will enable them to compete with far larger rivals.

Solinas Integrity has raised $5.5 million to enhance its AI-powered robotics for water and sanitation infrastructure.

The funding will support manufacturing, product development, and expansion into global markets, including the Middle East and Southeast Asia.

Chennai-based deep-tech startup Solinas Integrity has raised $5.5 million in a Series A1 funding round co-led by Mela Ventures and Hero Enterprise Family Office, as the company looks to expand its AI-powered robotics platform for underground water and sanitation infrastructure in India and overseas.

The round also saw participation from Luthra Group, along with follow-on investments from existing backers SVL-SME Fund (managed by SBI Ventures Limited), Rainmatter Capital, and 8X Ventures Fund I.

The fresh capital will be used to expand manufacturing capacity, strengthen product development and software infrastructure, support working capital needs, and scale government and enterprise contracts. The IIT Madras-incubated startup also plans to deepen its presence in the Middle East and Southeast Asia while expanding into adjacent sectors such as oil and gas and defence.

Founded in 2018 by Divanshu Kumar and Moinak Banerjee, Solinas develops robotics and AI solutions for inspecting, cleaning, and managing underground water and wastewater infrastructure. Its portfolio includes Endobot, a robotic pipeline inspection system capable of navigating pipes as small as 90 mm; Homosep, a mechanised sewer and septic tank cleaning robot; and Swasth AI, a software platform that converts inspection data into GIS-based asset maps and predictive infrastructure intelligence.

The company says its solutions have been deployed across more than 30 cities in 15 Indian states and are also being used by Dubai Municipality.

“Solinas has come this far by proving that the technology and the model work, city after city, contract after contract, at a sizable scale,” said Divanshu Kumar, Co-Founder and CEO of Solinas. He added that the company aims to build India’s largest technology company focused on underground asset management while expanding into high-stakes sectors such as defence and oil and gas.

The startup is addressing longstanding challenges in India’s water infrastructure. According to the company, the country loses an estimated 38% of treated water before it reaches consumers, with losses exceeding 60% in some cities. Globally, non-revenue water accounts for nearly $39 billion in annual losses. The company also highlighted the continued risks faced by sanitation workers despite the ban on manual scavenging, positioning mechanised inspection and cleaning as a safer alternative.

Krishnakumar Natarajan, Managing Partner at Mela Ventures, said the firm had tracked Solinas for four years and believes its vertically integrated robotics platform addresses a critical gap in underground infrastructure management. “Current methods of maintaining India's water infrastructure are manual, hazardous, time-consuming, and costly. Solinas is changing that through a robotics platform that maps underground infrastructure, diagnoses issues, and delivers end-to-end solutions,” he said.

The company said government initiatives such as AMRUT, Jal Jeevan Mission and NAMASTE schemes are accelerating demand for technology-driven inspection and sanitation systems, creating a growing market for mechanised and AI-enabled infrastructure management.

With the new funding, Solinas plans to broaden its technology portfolio across the water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) sector while developing new products for industrial and defence applications.

OpenAI's first consumer hardware product is a doughnut-shaped smart speaker, expected to launch in 2027.

The device will be battery-powered, screen-free, and designed for voice interactions, similar to ChatGPT's Advanced Voice Mode.

OpenAI’s first consumer hardware product will reportedly be a portable, doughnut-shaped smart speaker priced between $300 and $400, marking the company’s first step into dedicated AI devices following its acquisition of Jony Ive's startup io.

According to a Bloomberg report citing people familiar with the matter, the battery-powered device is expected to launch in 2027 and is designed as an “AI-first computer” that users can carry around the home.

The device is said to be roughly the size of a hockey puck and will not include a display. Instead, it will rely on voice interactions similar to ChatGPT’s Advanced Voice Mode, paired with more capable conversational models designed to make interactions feel more human.

Bloomberg reported that the hardware will include speaker grills, microphones, cameras, and environmental sensors, allowing it to perceive its surroundings and personalise responses over time. Lights will indicate when it is listening, while mechanical moving parts are intended to make the device appear more expressive during conversations.

The product has been designed in collaboration with Jony Ive’s LoveFrom studio and is expected to use premium materials, including metal construction.

OpenAI reportedly sees the speaker as the first product in a broader hardware family that could eventually reduce users' reliance on smartphones. The company apparently opted for a smart speaker first because always-on wearable devices such as smart glasses continue to face privacy concerns.

The development comes as OpenAI and Apple remain locked in an escalating trade secrets dispute over OpenAI’s consumer hardware programme. Apple alleges that former employees transferred confidential hardware knowledge to accelerate OpenAI’s device development and has sought a preliminary injunction and expedited discovery. OpenAI has rejected the allegations, arguing its hardware is “entirely new and different” and has asked the court to dismiss the lawsuit, describing Apple’s claims as baseless.

OpenAI formally entered consumer hardware last May when it agreed to acquire Jony Ive’s AI hardware startup io in a deal valued at approximately $6.5 billion, bringing the startup’s engineering team into OpenAI while Ive assumed broader design responsibilities across the company's hardware efforts.

The company completed the merger last July and has since positioned hardware as a long-term strategic initiative alongside its AI models.

HCLTech has been named an Advanced Partner in the OpenAI Partner Network, strengthening its collaboration with OpenAI as enterprises increase deployments of generative AI and agentic AI systems.

The designation places HCLTech among the global systems integrators selected by OpenAI to build, sell, and deploy AI solutions using the company's models and products.

The OpenAI Partner Network brings together consulting and technology partners to help enterprises adopt OpenAI's models and move AI projects into production.

As an OpenAI Advanced Partner, HCLTech said it will use its industry-specific AI offerings to help customers adopt GPT-5.6 and ChatGPT Work across business functions. HCLTech also said its AI Force platform is integrated with OpenAI models to help enterprises improve productivity, automate service delivery, and increase returns on AI investments.

“We’re pleased to welcome HCLTech as an OpenAI Advanced Partner. The HCLTech team brings practical enterprise AI delivery experience across strategy, implementation and adoption,” said Colleen Kapase, Vice President of Strategic Global Partnerships and Ecosystems at OpenAI, in a statement.

“Through the OpenAI Partner Network, HCLTech can help more enterprises move from AI pilots to measurable business impact,” Kapase added.

Raghu Kidambi, Corporate Vice President, AI Partnerships at HCLTech, said the recognition reflects the companies' collaboration on enterprise AI deployments.

“Together, we are helping clients transition into new agentic operating models across value streams by building, deploying and scaling industrialised enterprise AI operating systems and control towers to unlock measurable business value with AI,” Kidambi said.

HCLTech also plans to expand its OpenAI Agentic Transformation Studio, which combines AI governance, agentic engineering, AgentOps, and optimisation capabilities to help enterprises build and manage AI systems across business functions and industry workflows.

KühlTherm has introduced Made-in-India liquid cooling systems tailored for AI data centres in response to rising demand for computing infrastructure.

The new systems include Rear Door Heat Exchangers and Cooling Distribution Units, which enhance efficiency by managing heat and coolant flow.

KühlTherm, a startup based in Ahmedabad that builds precision liquid cooling hardware and software for AI data centres, has launched Made-in-India Rear Door Heat Exchangers (RDHx) and Cooling Distribution Units (CDUs), alongside an integrated liquid cooling validation laboratory, as India sees rising demand for high-density computing infrastructure.

The RDHx captures heat directly from the rear of a server rack before it enters the facility, while the CDU manages coolant flow, temperature and pressure. Both systems will be integrated with KühlTherm’s proprietary AI-powered thermal intelligence platform, NexusFlow OS.

NexusFlow OS combines thermal and power intelligence to provide visibility, predictive optimisation and autonomous orchestration across a data centre’s liquid cooling infrastructure. The company said its new Ahmedabad laboratory will enable products to be tested under real-world conditions before deployment.

“The new RDHx and CDU are a part of our goal to help our customers confidently adopt next-generation cooling technologies, while strengthening India's position in the global thermal management ecosystem,” said Shailesh Bishnoi, Founder and CEO, KühlTherm. He added that as AI, high-performance computing and data-centre infrastructure evolve, demand for efficient and reliable liquid cooling solutions is expected to grow.

KühlTherm currently has 300MW of manufacturing capacity and is targeting 2GW by 2027. The company designs and manufactures its complete thermal loop for AI data centres in India, from chip to chiller.

The company said its systems are being engineered for Indian data-centre conditions, including local climate, grid fluctuations and infrastructure requirements, with the aim of improving deployment speed, serviceability and cost efficiency.

The launch follows KühlTherm’s $1.1 million seed funding round led by Arkam Ventures to scale its liquid cooling solutions for AI data centres, hyperscale infrastructure and other high-density computing environments.

As AI and GPU-led workloads increase compute density, data-centre operators are increasingly looking for cooling systems that can support higher performance, uptime and energy efficiency. KühlTherm’s portfolio includes Direct-to-Chip cooling, RDHx, immersion cooling systems, CDUs and NexusFlow OS.

ByteDance is developing an AI model with up to 10 trillion parameters, positioning it among the world's largest foundation models.

The model is anticipated to be three times larger than China's current largest released model, Kimi K3.

ByteDance is training an artificial intelligence model with up to 10 trillion parameters, according to a Financial Times report citing people familiar with the matter.

If completed, it would rank among the world’s largest foundation models.

The TikTok parent is in the early stages of pre-training the model. That phase is expected to take three to six months before fine-tuning begins. The final parameter count has not yet been decided, the report said.

At the reported scale, the model would be about three times larger than Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3, currently China’s largest released model.

Industry estimates cited by the Financial Times suggest Anthropic’s flagship Mythos 5 contains around eight trillion parameters, though the company has not disclosed official figures.

The report said several Chinese AI labs are building models comparable in size to Anthropic’s Fable 5. ByteDance is reportedly pursuing the largest model among them.

The effort is being led by ByteDance’s Seed AI team, which has around 2,000 researchers, infrastructure engineers, data specialists and translators across China and overseas. The group is headed by former Google DeepMind scientist Wu Yonghui.

Unlike Alibaba, Moonshot and DeepSeek, ByteDance has largely kept its frontier models closed. Its latest 10 trillion-parameter effort suggests the company is prioritising frontier capabilities over open-weight releases.

The report also adds that ByteDance has avoided using model distillation to accelerate development.

Founder Zhang Yiming has instead pushed the company to build models independently, arguing that this is the only path to “world-leading model capabilities”.

In its AI portfolio, ByteDance already offers the Doubao chatbot, China’s most widely used AI assistant with 324 million monthly active users, and the Seedance video generation model.

It has also expanded its Volcano Engine cloud platform for enterprise AI services while developing its own Seed family of foundation models and investing in custom AI chips.

The latest push comes as Chinese AI companies continue to lead the open-weight model ecosystem.

Over the past month, Moonshot AI released its 2.8 trillion-parameter Kimi K3 model, while Alibaba unveiled Qwen3.8-Max, a 2.4 trillion-parameter flagship that it plans to release under an open-weight licence.

Both companies claim performance approaching leading proprietary models from Anthropic and OpenAI, while making their weights available to developers.

Microsoft has launched its fourth cloud region in India, located in Hyderabad, to meet growing AI and cloud service demand.

The new cloud region features three Availability Zones, enhancing Microsoft's local infrastructure capabilities.

Microsoft has launched its fourth cloud region in India with the general availability of the India South Central region in Hyderabad, expanding its local cloud infrastructure as enterprise demand for AI and cloud services continues to grow. The new region comprises three Availability Zones and enables customers to run eligible Microsoft Cloud services and workloads from Hyderabad.

With the launch, Microsoft now operates cloud regions in Pune, Chennai, Mumbai, and Hyderabad. The company said the expansion builds on its previously announced investments of $3 billion in January 2025 and $17.5 billion in December 2025, taking its total commitment to $20.5 billion.

“The Microsoft India South Central datacenter region is a critical part of…$20.5 billion investment commitment to India’s cloud and AI future,” said Puneet Chandok, President, Microsoft India and South Asia, in a statement.

Microsoft said the Hyderabad region has already seen early demand from customers including Adani Group, Bajaj Finserv, HDFC Bank, and PB Pay. It is using the new region to support business continuity, expand cloud capacity for mission-critical applications, and provide infrastructure for AI workloads.

The launch comes as Microsoft reports strong growth in its cloud business in India. The company said Azure has registered double-digit growth over the last two years, topping $100 billion in annual recurring revenue for the first time.

It added that more than 90% of NIFTY 100 companies use Microsoft 365 Copilot, while Infosys, TCS, Wipro, and LTIMindtree have together signed up for more than 400,000 Copilot seats. Globally, Microsoft 365 Copilot has crossed 30 million paid seats.

Microsoft said the India South Central region uses air-cooled chillers that consume zero water for cooling. The company added that it matched 100% of its global annual electricity consumption with renewable energy in February 2026 and has agreements supporting more than 1 GW of renewable energy projects in India, of which over 630 MW are already operational.

The company also said it remains committed to training 20 million Indians in AI skills by 2030. Since January 2025, it has trained 5.6 million people, with more than 125,000 accessing jobs or entrepreneurial opportunities through these initiatives.

According to IDC, India's public cloud services market is projected to reach $45.7 billion by 2030, growing at a compound annual rate of 22.2%, while AI spending is expected to grow at nearly twice that pace.

Meta has launched Muse Code, a terminal-based coding agent powered by the new Muse Spark 1.2 model.

Muse Code is designed for debugging and supports long-running software engineering workflows across large code repositories.

Meta has launched Muse Code, a terminal-based coding agent powered by its new Muse Spark 1.2 model, adding tools for software engineering workflows and long-running development tasks to its AI coding portfolio.

The company said Muse Code, currently available in beta for macOS and Linux, can plan code changes, write code, validate results and coordinate multiple persistent subagents to work across large code repositories.

Muse Spark 1.2, the underlying model, is available through Muse Code and the Meta Model API.

“We’re excited to release Muse Code (beta), a terminal coding agent powered by Muse Spark 1.2, our newest model,” Meta said in a blog post. “This marks our next step towards the frontier, with larger and much more capable models on the way.”

Muse Code runs on a local event log that records every model call, tool execution, approval and code edit, allowing sessions to resume after interruptions. Rather than creating new agents for each task, it relies on persistent background agents that remain active throughout a session to gather information and execute steps with less user intervention.

The coding agent also includes built-in commands such as /plan, which converts a request into an approval-based execution plan, /grill, which tests the plan before execution, and /goal, which works towards completing a specified objective.

Alongside the agent, Meta introduced Muse Spark 1.2, a coding-focused update to Muse Spark 1.1. The company said the model improves code generation, debugging, codebase understanding and end-to-end software development workflows after increasing training compute for coding tasks and expanding the diversity of training environments.

Meta said Muse Spark 1.2 was co-trained with Muse Code using rejection-sampled harness trajectories, optimisations for planning, context compaction and subagent coordination, along with integration of Muse Code’s toolset to improve compatibility between the model and the coding agent.

The company said the model was trained on long-horizon coding tasks, including whole-repository code generation, large software projects and automated research. It uses planning, goal conditioning and context compaction to maintain progress across extended development sessions.

Meta also said it used Muse Spark 1.1 to generate coding environments and instruction-following templates that were then used to train Muse Spark 1.2. The earlier model evaluated candidate solutions to create a larger training dataset, a process the company described as a self-improvement loop.

As part of its evaluation, Meta tested Muse Spark 1.2 on GPU kernel optimisation tasks involving more than 1,000 tool calls over as long as 24 hours. The company said the model wrote, compiled, profiled and iteratively improved NVIDIA Hopper GPU kernels, delivering performance gains over a baseline implementation without relying on third-party kernel libraries.

The centre is expected to scale to 1,600 employees within the next two years, enhancing global operations across various sectors.

JLL Business Services (JBS) inaugurated a 1,20,000 sq ft global capability centre (GCC) in Hyderabad, its second hub in India after Gurugram. Telangana IT and Industries Minister Sridhar Babu inaugurated the facility, which is located in the Prestige Sky Tech building in the city’s Financial District.

JBS said the centre will expand to 1,600 employees over the next two years and support its global operations across finance, HR, analytics, technology, project management and business process optimisation.

Matthew Rees, Chief Shared Service Centre Officer at JBS, said Hyderabad was a strategic choice for the company’s expansion.

“By establishing our GCC in one of India’s deepest talent markets, we are integrating exceptional people with standardised processes and AI-enabled workflows. This powers our commitments under the global strategy and strengthens the services we deliver to clients worldwide,” he said.

The company added that the new facility incorporates accessibility features, hybrid workspaces and wellness amenities. It said the centre is designed to support future growth while strengthening service delivery for global clients.

Speaking at the inauguration, Babu said Telangana had attracted nearly 150 GCCs over the past 20 months, creating more than 1.5 lakh technology jobs.

“At a time when AI, automation and global restructuring are reshaping the technology industry, our GCC strategy is designed to future-proof employment by creating the jobs of tomorrow,” he said. “Hyderabad continues to demonstrate that innovation-led GCCs are a powerful engine for investment, resilience and high-value job creation.”

According to JBS, the Hyderabad centre will function as its integrated capability centre, providing analytics, technology-enabled solutions and advisory services across multiple business functions. The company said JBS operates in six countries and employs more than 6,500 people globally.

Dheeraj Popli, Head of Global Service Centre for India at JBS, said Hyderabad’s talent pipeline, innovation ecosystem and sector diversity supported the company’s decision. The city also has its Accelerate 2030 strategy supporting such innovations.

The announcement comes as the city strengthens its position as a GCC destination, with gross leasing rising 10.5% year-on-year to 6.27 million sq ft in the first half of 2026 from 5.68 million sq ft a year earlier.

“Our office facility here is a strategic investment in a city redefining what global operations can achieve, providing JLL with the calibre of talent needed to deliver the sophisticated analytics and strategic advisory services that power our competitive advantage globally,” he said.

JBS said Hyderabad accounted for 16% of India’s GCC leasing activity between 2024 and mid-2026. GCCs also represented 42% of the city’s overall office leasing activity during the period. Financial services and insurance firms contributed 34.5% of GCC activity, followed by technology companies at 23.2%, healthcare and biotech firms at 17%, and engineering R&D operations at 12.1%.

title: What Actually Matters.
content:
Jeff Dean and Sanjay Ghemawat have left Google to establish Discovery Loop, focused on automating scientific and engineering research.

The startup aims to use frontier AI models to streamline experimental workflows in machine learning, science, and engineering.

Jeff Dean, Google’s former Chief Scientist, and former Google Senior Fellow Sanjay Ghemawat have left the company to launch Discovery Loop. The public benefit corporation will build AI systems to automate scientific and engineering research.

They are joined by Oriol Vinyals, formerly Chief Scientist at Google DeepMind, and Quoc Le, an ex-Google Fellow.

Alphabet has joined the company as a founding investor alongside venture capital firms Radical Ventures, Khosla Ventures, Lightspeed Venture Partners, Kleiner Perkins, and Doerr Capital.

The startup’s mission is to “automate machine learning, science, and engineering to accelerate discoveries and progress.”

Its first area of work will be machine learning research and engineering, where it plans to build AI systems capable of proposing experiments, running them, analysing results, and iterating with minimal human intervention.

“Our general approach is to automate the experimental loop,” Dean wrote in a post on X. “We'll initially focus on ML research and engineering, but believe the approach can help with important subproblems in nearly every one of the 14 NAE Grand Challenge problems.”

According to the founders, today’s scientific process depends on sequential experimentation, wherein researchers propose an idea, conduct an experiment, analyse the outcome, and repeat the cycle. Discovery Loop aims to automate that workflow using frontier AI models and large-scale computing infrastructure.

“By utilising frontier AI models and large-scale computational infrastructure, our systems will be able to rapidly propose, run, and learn from evaluations,” the company said in a blog post. “This approach allows for the parallel execution of thousands of experiments, drastically compressing iteration time.”

The founders said they will first use the platform internally to improve machine learning research.

The company is now looking for office space and hiring its founding team while beginning work on its infrastructure, AI models, and research systems.

Discovery Loop has been incorporated as a public benefit corporation, a structure that allows companies to pursue public-interest goals alongside shareholder returns. OpenAI’s commercial arm also operated as a public benefit corporation.

The founders said their long-term objective is to accelerate progress across science and engineering by automating experimental workflows beyond machine learning.

Dean is stepping down after nearly 27 years at Google, where he helped build the company’s distributed computing infrastructure and co-founded the Google Brain project in 2011.

Ghemawat was one of Google’s earliest engineers and co-created foundational technologies including Google File System, MapReduce, and Bigtable. Their departure is part of a wider reshuffle of Google’s AI leadership under Demis Hassabis and Koray Kavukcuoglu.
