title: What Actually Matters.
content:
Google has appointed Demis Hassabis as Chair of Google DeepMind and Chief Scientist of Alphabet to focus on AGI and long-term research.

Koray Kavukcuoglu has been promoted to Senior Vice President of Google DeepMind, overseeing the development of Gemini models and AI research.

Google has reshuffled its AI leadership, appointing Demis Hassabis as Chair of Google DeepMind and Chief Scientist of Alphabet while promoting Koray Kavukcuoglu to Senior Vice President of Google DeepMind, as the company pushes to accelerate its AI roadmap.

The changes, announced by Google and Alphabet CEO Sundar Pichai, shift Hassabis away from day-to-day operational responsibilities at Google DeepMind so he can focus on the company's long-term work on artificial general intelligence (AGI) and scientific research. Hassabis will continue leading Isomorphic Labs and advise Google DeepMind’s research and model teams.

“We have to accelerate all this work and stay focused on the AI frontier,” Pichai said in a message to employees. “At the same time, there’s never been a more important moment to shape the future of AGI and science.”

Kavukcuoglu, who has spent 13 years at DeepMind and currently serves as its Chief Technology Officer and Chief AI Architect, will report directly to Pichai. He will oversee Gemini model development, frontier AI research, the Gemini app and the company’s developer teams.

Pichai said the leadership changes come as Google’s AI products continue to expand. He said Gemini models are seeing growing demand from developers and enterprises, the Gemini app has crossed 950 million monthly users, and Gemma open models have surpassed 900 million downloads. He also pointed to recent advances in Gemini Robotics and upcoming model releases.

Google also announced that Jeff Dean, Chief Scientist at Google DeepMind and Google Research, will leave the company after 27 years. Along with Google Senior Fellow Sanjay Ghemawat, Dean is launching Discovery Loop, an independent public benefit corporation that develops AI systems for machine learning, scientific discovery and engineering research. Google said it will remain a founding investor, provide cloud infrastructure and collaborate on research into machine learning systems and related infrastructure advances.

Explaining the transition, Hassabis said he wants to dedicate more time to shaping the future of AGI.

“I’ve been working towards AGI my whole life, and now, like many of you, I feel it is close at hand,” he said. “It’s critical that we collectively get the next steps right to ensure this all goes well for humanity.”

Hassabis said Kavukcuoglu would continue leading Google’s AI model efforts alongside the existing executive team.

“The Gemini models are in good hands with Koray and the leads, as they have been for a while, and I’m excited about the great progress we're making with our new models including Gemini 4,” he said.

In his new role, Hassabis said he will work with Pichai on strategic AGI initiatives while spending more time at Isomorphic Labs, Alphabet’s AI drug discovery company.

“As you’ve heard me say many times, I’ve always believed the No.1 application of AI should be to improve human health,” Hassabis said. “It’s time for AI to prove its unequivocal value to the world, and what better way to demonstrate that than to help finally cure diseases like cancer.”

Pichai said the leadership changes are intended to maintain Google’s momentum across its AI research, infrastructure and products as competition in frontier AI continues to intensify.

title: Karnataka Eyes Anthropic Partnership to Bring AI Into Public Services
content:
The discussions included plans for an AI University, Claude certification programmes and hosting government data within Karnataka.

What Actually Matters.

Karnataka is exploring a partnership with Anthropic to integrate AI into various sectors including governance and healthcare.

Discussions included establishing an AI University and Claude certification programmes to enhance skill development.

Karnataka is in talks with Anthropic to build a long-term partnership focused on deploying AI across governance, higher education, healthcare, scientific research and the state’s startup ecosystem, Chief Minister D K Shivakumar said after meeting the company’s leadership on August 6.

The discussions covered the use of AI in public services, cybersecurity, data privacy, data sovereignty and skill development, with the government proposing that public-sector data be hosted within Karnataka.

“Artificial Intelligence presents one of the greatest opportunities to transform governance, empower citizens and accelerate economic growth. Karnataka is committed to leading this transformation with a clear vision that places people, trust and innovation at its core," Shivakumar said in a LinkedIn post.

He said he met Michael Sellitto, Anthropic’s Head of International Policy, and the company's leadership team to discuss a long-term partnership with the Karnataka government.

According to Shivakumar, the state’s approach is “Government First”, with AI being used to improve public services through secure and transparent systems.

“We discussed strengthening AI-driven governance while ensuring responsible deployment, robust cybersecurity, data privacy and data sovereignty, with government data securely hosted within Karnataka,” he said.

The talks also included plans for a proposed AI University, large-scale AI skilling under the NIPUNA programme, Claude certification programmes, collaboration with the Indian Institute of Science (IISc), and support for more than 20,000 startups in Karnataka, particularly those working in deep technology.

Shivakumar said the government sees AI being applied in areas including healthcare, scientific research, tax administration and examination security.

“Karnataka has consistently led India's technology journey. We are now laying the foundation to become the global hub for responsible artificial intelligence by bringing together government, academia, industry and startups to build solutions that are innovative, trusted and designed for public good,” he said.

Shivakumar added that he looked forward to converting the discussions into a partnership that delivers measurable outcomes for the state’s citizens.

Anthropic recently announced that it will make its Claude family of AI models available with in-country inference in India through Amazon Bedrock in the coming weeks, allowing requests to be processed on servers located within the country.

The company said the move is aimed at organisations in regulated sectors that require greater control over where customer data is processed.

title: KDEM & GoodWorks Target ₹5,000 Crore GCC Investments, 50 New Centres in Karnataka
content:
The collaboration also places significant emphasis on workforce development.

What Actually Matters.

Karnataka aims to enhance its position in India's global capability centre landscape through a partnership with GoodWorks Group.

The collaboration targets attracting significant investments and establishing 50 new GCCs in the state.

Karnataka is looking to deepen its dominance in India’s global capability centre (GCC) landscape, with the Karnataka Digital Economy Mission (KDEM) and Bengaluru-based GoodWorks Group signing a strategic partnership aimed at attracting ₹5,000 crore in new investments and facilitating the establishment of 50 new GCCs in the state.

The two organisations signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) on August 6 to jointly drive investment promotion, international outreach, policy support, talent development and ecosystem-building initiatives focused on global enterprises looking to establish or expand operations in Karnataka.

According to an economic impact assessment conducted by GoodWorks Group, the initiative aims to bring over ₹5,000 crore in investment commitments, generate more than 62,500 direct and indirect jobs, create ₹2,250 crore in annual salaries, and drive the absorption of 1.25 million square feet of commercial real estate over the coming years.

The partnership will combine KDEM’s investment promotion and ecosystem-building efforts with GoodWorks Group’s enterprise network and Sansovi GCC-as-a-Service platform, which supports global companies in setting up and scaling operations in India.

As part of the collaboration, the two organisations will engage global investors, organise sector-focused roundtables, facilitate international business delegations, publish GCC-focused industry research, support policy implementation and strengthen industry-academia collaborations. The outreach effort will target key markets including North America, Europe, Japan, South Korea and the Middle East.

The initiative will also support the creation of specialised ecosystem programmes, including virtual centres of excellence for strategic sectors, to foster collaboration among government, academia, industry and global enterprises.

“Our partnership with GoodWorks Group brings together complementary strengths to further enhance Karnataka’s value proposition for global enterprises and accelerate the next phase of GCC-led growth for the state,” Sanjeev Gupta, CEO of KDEM, mentioned.

GoodWorks Group said the partnership is intended to strengthen Karnataka’s position as the preferred destination for high-value global capability centres across sectors such as artificial intelligence, engineering, financial services, manufacturing, healthcare and semiconductors.

“India’s GCC opportunity is entering its most exciting phase, and Karnataka has the potential to lead that transformation globally,” said Vishwas Mudagal, Co-Founder, GoodWorks Group. The collaboration also places significant emphasis on workforce development. According to GoodWorks, the initiative could create over 12,500 direct high-skilled jobs and another 50,000 indirect jobs across supporting industries.

Karnataka currently hosts more than 1,100 GCCs, accounting for around 40% of India's GCC base, and generates over $22 billion in economic output from the sector. The state government has been actively pursuing policies and partnerships aimed at maintaining its leadership position amid growing competition from states such as Telangana, Tamil Nadu, Maharashtra and Andhra Pradesh.

title: Schreiber Foods Taps Ascendion to Deploy Agentic AI Across Global Business
content:
The partnership will introduce AI agents to automate technology workflows, improve food safety monitoring and modernise ERP systems across its global network.

What Actually Matters.

Schreiber Foods has partnered with Ascendion to implement agentic AI across its global operations.

The AI initiative aims to automate workflows, enhance food safety monitoring, and modernise ERP systems.

Schreiber Foods has signed a multi-year partnership with Ascendion to deploy agentic AI across its global operations and software development, as the food manufacturer looks to automate technology workflows, improve operational efficiency and support future growth.

The partnership will see Ascendion deploy its proprietary AAVA agentic AI platform across Schreiber’s global capability centres, which support more than 10,000 employee-partners and operations spanning over 40 locations across five continents.

The companies said AI agents will be used to improve decision-making in food safety and quality, modernise enterprise resource planning (ERP) systems, strengthen collaboration across regions and automate repetitive technology tasks.

“To fuel Schreiber’s next era of rapid growth, we are taking a bold, transformational leap forward in how we operate and serve our customers,” said Trevor Farrell, President of Schreiber Foods.

“By leaning into next-generation, agentic AI with Ascendion, we are reinforcing the very foundation of what our customers rely on us for: world-class quality, safety, and service. This technology will empower our employee-partners, accelerate our innovation, and allow us to deliver even greater impact at scale.”

Schreiber supplies food and beverage products to retailers, restaurants, distributors and food manufacturers in more than 95 countries.

According to the companies, AI agents will help surface food safety and quality signals faster, support ERP modernisation and provide regional teams with a unified way to collaborate. Over time, repetitive technology work will increasingly be handled by AI agents, allowing engineers and analysts to focus on work requiring human judgement.

Ascendion said it will use its Engineering to the Power of AI methodology to balance work between people and AI while maintaining security, privacy, compliance and governance requirements.

“Schreiber Foods’ mission is one of the most consequential out there. We are honoured to deploy technology that helps Schreiber bring food to people all over the world,” said Karthik Krishnamurthy, chief executive officer of Ascendion.

“Schreiber leaders recognise the impact that can be unlocked by AI-native operations across their global network. It’s a vision built on a foundation of success, and we're thrilled to bring the full power of AI to this partnership.”

Sri Kantamneni, executive vice president and chief information and digital officer at Schreiber Foods, said the collaboration would equip the company’s capability centres with AI-native tools while reducing manual processes.

“AI is a significant driver of transformation, but its real strength lies in how it empowers our people,” Kantamneni said. “By giving our employee-partners better, smarter tools to work with, we enable them to focus less on manual processes and more on driving customer success and accelerating our growth.”

Dharam Gurbani, Chief Growth Officer at Ascendion, said the partnership would focus on measurable business outcomes across Schreiber’s capability centres in the United States, Mexico, India, Spain and Poland.

“We’re accountable for outcomes, not effort,” Gurbani said. “What changes for Schreiber Foods’ plants, customers, and consumers is the only scorecard that matters.”

title: What Actually Matters.
content:
224 Ventures is launched by Yann LeCun, Oriol Vinyals, and Shaun Johnson with a focus on early-stage AI startups.

The firm has $100 million in assets and plans to invest between $1 million and $5 million per startup.

Yann LeCun, Meta’s former Chief AI Scientist, and Oriol Vinyals, Gemini Co-lead at Google DeepMind, have joined entrepreneur and co-founder of AIX Ventures Shaun Johnson to launch 224 Ventures, a venture capital firm which will invest in early-stage AI startups.

The firm starts with $100 million in assets under management and will invest exclusively in AI-native companies.

The launch comes as venture capital firms continue to increase investments in AI startups, particularly those building foundation models, AI infrastructure, robotics and enterprise AI applications.

According to Johnson, the firm has already started investing in companies across AI applications, robotics, infrastructure and core intelligence. It plans to write $1 million to $5 million cheques and participate alongside lead investors rather than lead funding rounds itself.

Johnson said all three partners would be involved in sourcing, evaluating and voting on every investment.

“We’ve already begun backing technical founders across applications, robotics, infrastructure, and core intelligence—writing $1–5M checks as a collaborative investor, partnering alongside lead investors to back companies advancing the frontier of AI,” Johnson wrote in a post on X.

The firm said it intends to source startups from research and engineering communities where frontier AI work is taking place, arguing that many technical founders emerge from these networks before entering traditional venture pipelines.

Johnson also outlined the firm’s limited partner base, saying it consists of AI operators including frontier researchers, engineering and product leaders, chief AI and data officers, sales and marketing executives, and CEOs.

He said the network spans major AI hubs including the San Francisco Bay Area, New York, Paris, Toronto, London and Tel Aviv.

According to Johnson, this network is expected to help portfolio companies find customers, design partners, employees, mentors and future investors.

The launch of 224 Ventures follows LeCun’s own push into AI entrepreneurship. He recently launched Advanced Machine Intelligence (AMI), a Paris-based AI startup focused on developing world models that learn from real-world data rather than relying primarily on large language models.

In March, AMI raised $1.03 billion in seed funding at a $3.5 billion pre-money valuation, making it one of the largest seed financings for an AI startup.

“My main gigs are still with AMI - Advanced Machine Intelligence and the NYU Courant Institute School of Mathematics, Computing, and Data Science. But 224 Ventures connects us deeply with the AI startup scene through our network of founders and amazing LPs,” he added.

title: What Actually Matters.
content:
SpaceX aims for $100 billion annual recurring revenue, leveraging advancements in AI, Starlink, and Starship.

The company reported significant revenue growth, nearly doubling to $7.8 billion in the second quarter.

SpaceX reported a strong second quarter, with revenue nearly doubling year-on-year to $7.8 billion, as growth across Starlink, launch services, and AI infrastructure helped narrow losses.

The company posted a net loss of $541 million for the quarter ended June 30, compared with a loss of $1.0 billion a year earlier. Adjusted EBITDA rose 191% to $3.5 billion from $1.2 billion.

The company ended the quarter with $100 billion in cash, cash equivalents, and marketable securities, along with a backlog of $47.5 billion.

Speaking during the earnings call, CEO Elon Musk outlined an aggressive roadmap spanning reusable rockets, satellite internet, and AI, arguing that all three businesses are reaching inflection points.

The space business reported revenue of $962 million, up 29% from the same period last year, helped by a higher number of customer launches.

During the quarter, SpaceX completed Starship V3’s first suborbital mission and successfully carried out Flight 13, which deployed 20 production V3 satellites and demonstrated an in-space Raptor engine relight.

“We’re making great progress developing a fully and rapidly reusable reliable rocket with Starship. We're connecting millions more people globally across 170 markets with fast, reliable Starlink internet. We’re building AI compute capacity at scale faster than anyone else,” Musk said.

Musk said SpaceX completed two successful flights of its Starship V3 vehicle over the past 90 days, with Flight 13 validating capabilities required for orbital missions and booster recovery. Flight 14 will carry the first V3 Starlink satellites to operational orbit.

He described Starship as the company’s most significant long-term project, claiming it could increase payload capacity from roughly 2,500 tonnes annually with Falcon rockets to more than 1 million tonnes per year, with a long-term ambition of reaching 10 million tonnes.

Musk said Flight 13 performed better than expected and that SpaceX now considers the heat shield challenge largely solved.

“I would say that we do not see any technical obstacles at this point to achieving full and rapid reusability,” he said. The company expects to attempt catching the ship on the next flight, subject to regulatory approval, and aims to reach at least one Starship launch per day eventually.

Starlink, SpaceX’s connectivity business, remained the company's largest revenue contributor, generating $4.29 billion, up 66% from a year earlier. Operating income for the segment increased 79% to $1.66 billion as Starlink subscribers doubled to 12 million.

Enterprise and government revenue more than doubled YoY, supported by agreements with airlines and telecom operators, while Starshield secured more than $6 billion in multi-year US government contracts.

President and COO Gwynne Shotwell said Starlink added more than 1.7 million net subscribers during the quarter, its strongest customer addition to date, while maintaining average revenue per user at $66 per month.

The network now operates in 167 markets with around 10,200 satellites in orbit, including 9,600 broadband satellites delivering roughly 800 TB per second of downlink capacity.

Musk argued investors underestimate Starlink’s long-term potential. The V3 satellites are about 10 times more capable than V2 satellites, and the company expects to launch roughly 10 times as many, increasing overall network bandwidth by around 100 times.

AI emerged as the fastest-growing business during the quarter, climbing to $2.6 billion, up 247% year-on-year, helped by new cloud computing agreements and higher Grok and X subscription revenue.

The company also turned positive on adjusted EBITDA for the AI segment while expanding compute capacity to 1.4 GW, up from 1 GW in the previous quarter. The company signed cloud services agreements worth $14.1 billion in contracted sales, contributing $1.6 billion in AI infrastructure revenue during the quarter.

SpaceX also announced that it was acquiring AI coding startup Cursor for $60 billion, with the transaction expected to close in the third quarter of 2026.

Following the quarter, it released Grok 4.5, which it described as its “largest and smartest model yet,” built for coding, agentic tasks and knowledge work. During the earnings call, Musk said Grok 4.6 is expected next week, followed by Grok 4.7 within weeks, while Grok 5 will launch before year-end.

The company has also standardised future AI infrastructure around NVIDIA’s Vera Rubin architecture.

CFO Bret Johnsen said SpaceX expects compute capacity to exceed 2 GW by year-end, while Musk later suggested total installed power and cooling infrastructure could approach 15 GW by the end of 2027 as the company prepares for further GPU deployments.

SpaceX spent $18.4 billion in capital expenditure during the quarter, including $15.8 billion on AI infrastructure. It also completed its IPO, raising $85.7 billion, followed by a $25 billion investment-grade bond offering, ending the quarter with $100 billion in cash and marketable securities and a $47.5 billion backlog.

The company expects to reach a $100 billion annualised revenue run rate by the end of the year, driven primarily by cloud computing services, Starlink expansion, and AI products.

“We’ve already contracted an additional $6.7 billion of cloud services revenue over a six-month period,” Johnsen said, adding that the company remains on track for “$100 billion of ARR... by the end of this year.”

Musk went further, saying internal projections have also accelerated.

“Our internal projections for reaching $1 trillion in revenue... have moved up from 2031 to 2030. There’s a non-zero chance of that being in 2029,” he said.

title: What Actually Matters.
content:
Sarvam has launched the Circle programme to enhance AI adoption across enterprises and public institutions in India.

The programme aims to transition AI projects from pilot stages to full production by integrating Sarvam's AI models with partner capabilities.

Sarvam AI has launched Sarvam Circle, a partner programme that brings together cloud providers, system integrators, consulting firms, original equipment manufacturers (OEMs), enterprise software companies, and investors to expand the deployment of its AI models across enterprises and public institutions in India.

The company said the programme will help organisations move AI projects from pilot stages to production by combining Sarvam's AI models with partners’ infrastructure, consulting, engineering, and enterprise software capabilities.

“Today, we are announcing Sarvam Circle, our partnership programme for the firms that hold the reach, resources, and trust to reach every institution in India," the company said in a blog post. “Together we will co-create industry solutions on Sarvam's stack, pursue opportunities jointly, and work side by side with our forward-deployed engineering teams to scale pilots into production.”

The announcement comes as Sarvam expands beyond foundation models into enterprise AI products spanning conversational agents, document intelligence, content transformation, coding and work agents. The company said its AI stack is already operating at scale, handling more than 2 million voice conversations daily, digitising 35 million pages, and processing around 10 million API calls a day across public and private sector deployments.

As part of the programme, Sarvam has partnered with Amazon Web Services (AWS) to make its AI models available through AWS Marketplace.

“Our partnership with Sarvam represents a shared commitment to India's AI mission. With Sarvam’s AI models available on AWS Marketplace, businesses can discover, access, and procure them with ease,” said Sandeep Dutta, President, AWS India and South Asia.

In the consulting segment, Sarvam is working with consulting firm YCP India, which will help enterprises incorporate AI into business operations and strategy.

“Our role is to bring Sarvam’s models to where they matter most, translating them into sector strategy and boardroom decisions across enterprise and public institutions in the region,” said Abhisek Mukherjee, Managing Partner and Head of Management Services Division, YCP India.

For enterprise implementation, Sarvam has partnered with HCLTech and tech firm Thoughtworks to integrate its AI platform into customers' existing systems and workflows.

“HCLTech and Sarvam have a shared vision to bring sovereign AI solutions to private and public sector enterprises and government entities in India and beyond by bringing together HCLTech's full-stack AI offerings and Sarvam's models,” said Sandeep Kumar Saxena, Chief Growth Officer – Growth Markets 2, HCLTech.

The company has also onboarded IBM and HP as OEM partners. IBM said the collaboration would combine its Sovereign Core offering with Sarvam's AI models to help governments and regulated industries deploy AI while maintaining governance and compliance.

HP said it would integrate Sarvam's AI capabilities with its PC portfolio to enable on-device AI deployments across enterprises, classrooms, and government offices.

In enterprise software, Sarvam has partnered with MoEngage to integrate its voice AI capabilities into customer engagement workflows. Sanjay Kupae, Global Head of Partnerships at MoEngage, said the partnership would combine MoEngage's customer engagement platform with Sarvam's voice AI to personalise marketing messages and improve customer engagement.

Sarvam said the programme will help scale enterprise AI adoption by combining its AI stack with partners that provide infrastructure, consulting, implementation, and software used by organisations across sectors.

title: What Actually Matters.
content:
NVIDIA has commercialised its Alpamayo 2 Super autonomous driving model under an open licence for broader use by automakers and suppliers.

The Alpamayo model family has surpassed 500,000 downloads, highlighting its popularity among developers.

NVIDIA has commercialised its Alpamayo 2 Super autonomous driving model under an open licence, allowing automakers, robotaxi operators, and suppliers to build, fine-tune, and deploy the model without seeking additional permissions.

The company said that the Alpamayo family has surpassed 500,000 downloads on Hugging Face.

It released Alpamayo 2 Super under the Linux Foundation's OpenMDW-1.1 licence, which permits fine-tuning, derivative models, and commercial redistribution. NVIDIA is also extending the same licence across the entire Alpamayo model family, which had previously been available primarily for research and development.

“Earlier Alpamayo releases were initially introduced for R&D. The OpenMDW license is now being applied across the entire Alpamayo model family so developers can deploy any of the models commercially without requiring additional permissions,” NVIDIA said in a statement.

The company said the move provides autonomous vehicle developers with greater control over their data, infrastructure, and deployment strategies while reducing the cost of developing production-ready systems.

Alpamayo 2 Super is built on NVIDIA Cosmos 3 Super Reasoner and post-trained using reinforcement learning. According to NVIDIA, the model is intended to handle complex driving scenarios by combining perception, reasoning, and planning within a single foundation model.

For each driving scenario, the model generates five outputs: a planned driving trajectory, a chain-of-causation explanation for its decision, a high-level driving action such as yielding or changing lanes, reasoning-based labels for training data, and visual question-answering responses linked to specific regions in camera images.

“Developers can tie what the model observed to the action it selected, making decisions easier to understand, critique, and validate,” the company said.

NVIDIA said the reasoning traces integrate with its Halos safety validation workflows and support AI safety processes aligned with ISO/PAS 8800 requirements.

The company also positioned Alpamayo 2 Super as part of a cloud-to-car development workflow. It said the model can generate reasoning traces, synthetic training data, and teacher outputs in cloud environments, while smaller Alpamayo models can be distilled and optimised for real-time inference inside production vehicles.

“For AV programmes, that means frontier-scale reasoning in the cloud and efficient, specialised models in the vehicle—a more sustainable way to scale safe autonomy into commercial fleets,” NVIDIA said.

In NVIDIA’s benchmark testing, Alpamayo 2 Super ranked first on the LingoQA autonomous driving reasoning benchmark among nearly 40 evaluated models. Using the company’s Lingo-Judge metric, it outperformed Qwen2.5-VL 72B by 17 points, Gemini 2.5 Pro by 15.1 points and GPT-4o by 23.2 points.

The company said Alpamayo 2 Super has three times the scale of its 10-billion-parameter Alpamayo 1 and Alpamayo 1.5 models, enabling better reasoning across rare driving situations involving multiple road users. The model also processes inputs from front, side, and rear cameras to generate a 360-degree understanding of the driving environment.

Alongside Alpamayo 2 Super, NVIDIA highlighted its broader autonomous driving software stack, including AlpaSim for closed-loop simulation, AlpaGym for reinforcement learning, Physical AI Open Datasets, and open training recipes with an autolabelling pipeline.

content:
IBM has launched a FutureNow Centre in Visakhapatnam to enhance global consulting and accelerate AI-driven digital transformation projects.

The centre will focus on various domains including AI, hybrid cloud, cybersecurity, and user experience services.

IBM has expanded its footprint in India with the launch of a new IBM Consulting FutureNow Centre in Visakhapatnam, aimed at supporting global consulting delivery and accelerating AI-driven digital transformation projects for clients worldwide.

The new centre will provide consulting and technology services across key domains including artificial intelligence (AI), hybrid cloud, software engineering, cybersecurity, data and analytics, and enterprise transformation. It will also serve as a hub for AI-first cloud transformation, platform engineering, service integration, quality engineering, and user experience services.

The launch comes as Andhra Pradesh seeks to position Visakhapatnam as a major destination for technology investments, AI innovation, and digital services.

“IBM’s FutureNow Centre is a strong endorsement of Visakhapatnam’s emergence as a global hub for artificial intelligence, digital services and technology-led innovation. Our vision is not merely to attract technology investments, but to build a complete ecosystem that creates high-quality employment, develops future-ready talent and enables young people from Andhra Pradesh to participate in the global digital economy,” said Nara Lokesh, Andhra Pradesh Minister of IT, Electronics and HRD.

IBM said the FutureNow Centre reflects its strategy of expanding innovation and delivery capabilities in emerging technology hubs across India. The company noted that Visakhapatnam’s growing digital talent pool, strong academic institutions, and evolving technology ecosystem make it a strategic location for supporting global client engagements while creating opportunities for local professionals.

“At IBM, we are committed to helping build the capabilities that enable our clients to accelerate AI adoption and other emerging technologies that create lasting value. The IBM Consulting FutureNow Centre in Visakhapatnam reflects this commitment, while reinforcing India’s role as a global destination for innovation and technology delivery,” said Sandip Patel, Managing Director, IBM India and South Asia.

The company said the centre will play a key role in helping enterprises accelerate AI adoption and digital transformation initiatives while strengthening IBM’s consulting delivery network.

“Vizag offers a compelling combination of emerging digital talent, strong academic institutions and a growing technology ecosystem, making it an important location for supporting client transformation journeys. Through the IBM Future Now Centre, we are bringing together technology expertise and local talent to help clients accelerate AI and digital transformation while creating meaningful opportunities for the region's next generation of technology professionals,” said Usha Srikanth, Managing Partner, IBM Consulting FutureNow Centre, India.

With the addition of Visakhapatnam, IBM Consulting now operates FutureNow Centres across 15 locations in India, including Ahmedabad, Bengaluru, Bhubaneswar, Chennai, Coimbatore, Gurugram, Hyderabad, Kochi, Kolkata, Lucknow, Mumbai, Mysore, Noida, Pune, and Visakhapatnam.

The latest investment also aligns with Andhra Pradesh’s broader push to attract global technology firms and build a strong AI and digital services ecosystem in the state.

title: Advertise with Us
content:
AMD reported a record second-quarter revenue of $11.5 billion, up 50% year-over-year (YoY), as data centre revenue more than doubled to $6.7 billion on strong demand for EPYC server processors and Instinct AI accelerators.

The data centre business accounted for 58% of total revenue, up from 42% a year earlier.

The company also guided for approximately $13 billion in third-quarter revenue, representing 41% YoY growth.

Its quarterly profit rose 163% YoY to a record $2.3 billion.

AMD materially raised its long-term outlook as it sees AI infrastructure demand expanding faster than previously expected.

CEO Lisa Su said the company now expects revenue growth to be substantially above the long-term target of more than 35% outlined at its Financial Analyst Day.

The company also forecast that its data centre business will more than double in 2027, supported by server CPU growth of more than 70% and a faster ramp in AI accelerators.

AMD also increased its view of the AI infrastructure opportunity, estimating the data centre AI accelerator market will grow to approximately $1.4 trillion by 2030.

Su said “agentic AI is creating a new growth vector for server CPUs”, prompting AMD to raise its estimate for the server CPU market to $220 billion by 2030 as AI workloads increasingly require more CPU infrastructure alongside accelerators.

The company said cloud and enterprise server CPU sales each grew more than 70% during the quarter, marking its fifth consecutive quarter of record server CPU revenue.

Unveiled at AMD’s Advancing AI 2026 event last month, the sixth-generation EPYC Venice processors were positioned by the company as outperforming Intel Xeon, NVIDIA’s Vera and rival Arm-based CPUs across AI and data centre workloads.

Su added that customer demand for Venice processors is stronger than for any previous EPYC generation, while adoption continues to expand across hyperscalers including AWS, Microsoft, Google Cloud and Oracle.

On the AI infrastructure side, AMD said its Helios rack-scale platform is now in production, with initial shipments scheduled to begin later this quarter before ramping through the fourth quarter and into 2027.

Helios integrates sixth-generation EPYC Venice CPUs, Instinct MI455X GPUs and AMD Pensando networking into a rack-scale AI system designed for frontier AI training and inference.

Su said customer demand for Helios is running ahead of AMD’s initial forecasts, referring specifically to expected deployment volumes.

The company also said supply constraints that affected server CPUs during the first half are easing as additional wafer, packaging and substrate capacity comes online to support future growth.

The momentum builds on AMD’s recent announcement that Anthropic will deploy up to 2 gigawatts of Instinct MI450 GPUs in Helios from 2027, following similar large-scale AI infrastructure commitments from OpenAI, Meta, Microsoft and Oracle.

Despite the strong earnings beat and an upbeat long-term outlook, AMD shares fell nearly 8% in after-hours trading.

content:
Tamil Nadu is enhancing its Artificial Intelligence Mission to include quantum technology and various creative industries.

A budget allocation of ₹398 crore aims to strengthen the state's IT sector, which significantly contributes to exports and employment.

The Tamil Nadu Artificial Intelligence Mission is to be strengthened to cover AI, quantum technology, and animation, visual effects, gaming, comics and extended reality, with applications targeted at health, agriculture, education and citizen services.

State Finance Minister N Marie Wilson announced that ₹398 crore has been allocated to the Artificial Intelligence, Information Technology and Digital Services Department. The government noted that the state’s IT sector generates exports of more than ₹2.5 lakh crore annually and employs over 20 lakh people, directly and indirectly.

The revised budget estimates for total expenditure stand at ₹4,05,802 crore, up from ₹3,93,272 crore in the Interim Budget.

A flagship proposal is ‘Arivagam’, a dedicated AI and innovation city, planned to include an AI university, an international skill development centre, a semiconductor hardware testing lab and innovation incubators for AI and deep-tech firms. At this stage, only a feasibility study has been funded, at a cost of ₹5 crore.

AI also features in governance plans: an AI-enabled planning approval system called SPEED is to be introduced for construction permissions, a quality assurance audit board ‘backed by AI’ is proposed to monitor government file flows, and the Namma Arasu WhatsApp chatbot is to be expanded from 76 to 275 public services.

The government said the state aims to grow its gross state domestic product to a $1.5 trillion economy by 2036. Since taking office, it has signed seven memoranda of understanding worth ₹35,062 crore, which it says could generate 14,790 direct and indirect jobs.

A new Tamil Nadu Industrial Policy is to be released, alongside a Tamil Nadu Industrial Capability Directory, a digital platform listing the state’s manufacturing and supply capabilities for prospective investors.

The government also plans to introduce ‘Guidance 3.0’, an AI-poweredinvestment service system intended to bring clearances and approvals for companies onto a single platform, alongside an upgraded Tamil Nadu Single Window Portal 3.0

Other investment-related announcements include a Non-Resident Tamil Investment Facilitation Desk to channel diaspora investment, new State Industries Promotion Corporation of Tamil Nadu (SIPCOT) industrial parks in industrially backward districts at an estimated ₹3,200 crore over five years, and the declaration of Thoothukudi and Tirunelveli as a Space Industrial Investment Zone, linked to the spaceport at Kulasekarapattinam. About ₹4,414 crore has been allocated to the Industries, Investment Promotion and Commerce Department.

On skilling, the government announced the Vetri Skill Training Scheme, intended to provide industry-aligned training to 12 lakh college students and one lakh unemployed youth this year, with internships for 20,000 young people in a first phase, backed by ₹150 crore.

A new AI Industry Development Programme was also announced, under which an expert committee will design AI curricula for higher education, in partnership with institutions including IIT Madras, with a stated aim of training five lakh youth across engineering colleges, polytechnics and Industrial Training Institutes (ITIs) by 2031.

More specifically, a new artificial intelligence and machine learning trade is to be introduced in 50 government ITIs over five years, at an estimated cost of ₹10 crore, which the government says could benefit around 24,000 students.

The TN SPARK school programme on AI, robotics and digital tools is to be expanded from 5,000 to 7,600 government schools. About ₹2,022 crore has been allocated to the Labour Welfare and Skill Development Department.

title: IG Defence Eyes Global Drone Exports Amid Gulf Tensions
content:
The drone company plans to export its indigenous long-range attack drone after securing government approvals.

What Actually Matters.

IG Defence plans to export its indigenous KAL long-range attack drone amidst increasing demand in the Gulf region.

KAL is India's first indigenous long-range one-way attack drone, designed for deep-penetration missions against strategic targets.

IG Defence (previously IG Drones) has positioned its indigenous KAL long-range one-way attack drone for global export as demand for autonomous strike systems grows amid changing defence priorities in the Gulf. The company said exports will remain subject to Indian government approvals and regulatory clearances.

KAL is the company’s, and what they claim to be India’s first, indigenous 1,000-km-class long-range one-way attack drone. IG Defence said it developed the platform for deep-penetration missions against high-value strategic targets.

The company expects growing demand from Gulf countries and other strategic regions investing in autonomous strike capabilities.

“The future battlefield will increasingly be defined by autonomous, long-range precision strike capabilities,” said Bodhisattwa Sanghapriya, Founder and CEO of IG Defence. He added that KAL marks an important step in India’s self-reliance in advanced defence technologies and demonstrates the country’s ability to develop indigenous systems.

KAL belongs to the emerging class of Shahed-136-type long-range one-way attack drones. Such systems have changed modern warfare by combining extended range, precision strike capability, operational simplicity and lower costs.

IG Defence identified Russia’s Geran-2 and the United States’ LUCAS as comparable platforms. The drone has an operational range of up to 1,000 km, an endurance of seven to eight hours and can carry a 50 kg payload.

Sanghapriya said India is well placed to become “a trusted partner for reliable, affordable, and mission-ready unmanned platforms”, subject to government approvals and export controls. The platform also enables armed forces to engage strategic targets from extended stand-off distances while maintaining operational flexibility and cost efficiency.

The company said long-range one-way attack drones have become a key defence technology because they can deliver strategic effects at a lower cost than conventional missile systems. It added that governments worldwide are increasing investments in autonomous precision strike platforms to support deep-penetration operations and strengthen deterrence.

KAL supports India’s ambition to become a trusted supplier of indigenous defence technologies to friendly foreign nations. The company added that the platform aligns with the Atmanirbhar Bharat initiative and India’s goal of expanding its defence manufacturing and export capabilities.

The company also said it has developed defence technologies across interceptor drones, FPV combat drones, autonomous UAVs, counter-UAS systems, AI-enabled swarm technologies, electronic warfare solutions, tactical robotics and logistics drones.

title: India’s Simple Energy Deepens Siemens Partnership to Speed Up EV Engineering
content:
The move comes as Indian EV manufacturers increasingly invest in digital engineering infrastructure to support larger product portfolios

What Actually Matters.

Simple Energy is enhancing its partnership with Siemens to utilise advanced digital engineering tools for electric vehicle development.

The adoption of Siemens' cloud-based software suite aims to streamline vehicle complexity and reduce time-to-market.

India's electric vehicle ecosystem is deepening its use of digital engineering tools, with Bengaluru-based electric two-wheeler manufacturer Simple Energy expanding its adoption of Siemens' cloud-based software suite to accelerate vehicle development, manage growing product complexity, and shorten time-to-market.

Siemens Digital Industries Software announced that Simple Energy has expanded its use of solutions from the Siemens Xcelerator portfolio, including Teamcenter X for product lifecycle management (PLM) and Designcenter X for advanced vehicle engineering. The company is also leveraging Teamcenter X's advanced product configurator capabilities to manage complex vehicle variants and enterprise-level bills of materials (BOMs).

The move comes as Indian EV manufacturers increasingly invest in digital engineering infrastructure to support larger product portfolios, faster innovation cycles, and more sophisticated vehicle architectures.

Simple Energy said the expanded deployment will help its engineering teams manage complex assemblies, advanced surface design, electrical routing, and multiple vehicle configurations through a unified cloud-based environment.

"As our products scale in complexity, we're strengthening the systems behind how we build them. With Teamcenter X and Designcenter X, we're able to manage complex variants and large assemblies with greater speed and control—enabling us to accelerate development without compromising agility," said Kiran Poojary, chief technology officer at Simple Energy.

The company initially adopted Teamcenter X to create a centralised product data management backbone and improve collaboration across engineering teams. As its EV programmes matured, it expanded the platform to support enterprise BOM management and variant configuration through a "150 percent BOM" approach, which allows all possible components, options, and variants within a product family to be managed through a single master configuration.

Simple Energy has also replaced its legacy 3D computer-aided design (CAD) platform with Siemens' Designcenter X, which integrates with Teamcenter X and supports advanced vehicle engineering functions including large assembly management and 3D electrical routing.

Siemens said the deployment highlights how cloud-based engineering platforms are increasingly being used by emerging EV manufacturers to scale product development while maintaining flexibility and cost efficiency.

"Simple Energy's expansion of its Siemens software footprint demonstrates how customers can scale their digital foundation as product complexity increases," said Matthew Thomas, vice president and managing director for India, Siemens Digital Industries Software.

"Through close collaboration, we are supporting Simple Energy with a fully integrated vehicle engineering and lifecycle management digital thread that helps accelerate innovation and support its growth targets," he added.

The expanded adoption also allows Simple Energy to scale software usage through Siemens' value-based licensing model as the company grows its electric vehicle portfolio.

title: Wipro Teams Up With Rubrik to Offer AI-Driven Cyber Resilience Service
content:
The new managed offering, Enterprise Resilience as a Service, combines Wipro’s consulting capabilities with Rubrik’s cyber recovery platform to help enterprises continuously assess, automate and recover from cyber disruptions as AI adoption accelerates.

What Actually Matters.

Wipro has partnered with Rubrik to launch Enterprise Resilience as a Service, enhancing cyber recovery capabilities for enterprises.

The service combines Wipro’s consulting strengths with Rubrik’s technology to automate recovery and assess resilience continuously.

IT giant Wipro has announced a partnership with cybersecurity firm Rubrik to launch Enterprise Resilience as a Service (ERaaS), a managed cyber resilience offering aimed at helping enterprises strengthen recovery capabilities as artificial intelligence increases the complexity of IT environments.

The new service combines Wipro’s consulting and managed services capabilities with Rubrik’s cyber recovery platform to provide continuous resilience assessment, automated recovery workflows and AI-assisted recovery decisions, moving beyond traditional backup and disaster recovery models.

According to a statement, the consulting-led, outcome-driven ERaaS is designed to help enterprises prevent, withstand, and rapidly recover from cyber and operational disruptions.

The launch comes as enterprises face growing cyber risks while scaling AI deployments across business operations.

According to Wipro, the AI capabilities will be delivered through its WINGS platform, part of the company’s Wipro Intelligence suite of AI-powered platforms and services.

“Together with Rubrik’s Zero Trust recovery capabilities, ERaaS will identify critical systems, map impact tolerances, and quickly establish recovery priorities,” Satish Yadavalli, Global Business Head of Cloud, Infrastructure, and Security Services, Wipro, said in a statement. “Leveraging our consulting capabilities, we will work closely with clients to translate these insights into resilience-by-design architectures, governance frameworks, and recovery playbooks.”

Rubrik’s platform will provide capabilities including immutable data protection, identification of clean recovery points, rollback of AI-driven changes, threat-aware recovery and protection of enterprise identity systems, according to the companies.

“Together with Wipro, we are helping customers operationalise cyber recovery as a core part of a broader enterprise resilience strategy,” said Alok Agrawal, Chief Solutions Officer, Rubrik. “Moments of disruption are inevitable, which is why this joint offering is critical for safe, confident, agile recovery.”

The announcement expands Wipro’s portfolio of AI-enabled infrastructure and cybersecurity services at a time when IT services firms are increasingly positioning cyber resilience as a strategic business capability alongside cloud and AI transformation initiatives.

content:
Yotta Data Services has introduced a ₹10,000 free credits programme for its AI development platform, Shakti Studio.

The programme offers complimentary GPU access for developers, startups, enterprises, and researchers to build AI applications.

Yotta Data Services has launched a ₹10,000 Free Credits Programme for Shakti Studio, its end-to-end AI development and inferencing platform.

The programme gives developers, startups, enterprises, researchers, and global capability centres (GCCs) complimentary access to build, fine-tune, and deploy AI models on serverless GPU infrastructure.

The credits apply against Shakti Studio's standard pay-as-you-go rates.

They cover the platform's full stack, including serverless H100 and L40S GPUs billed per minute and scaling to zero when idle, OpenAI-compatible AI Endpoints billed per token, full fine-tuning and LoRA adapters on proprietary data, deployment of externally fine-tuned checkpoints, and a Developer Portal for API key generation and console access.

Shakti Studio offers access to more than 25 open-source models spanning large language models, speech-to-text, text-to-speech, image generation, and OCR, alongside the option to deploy custom models on serverless GPUs.

The platform is hosted entirely across Yotta's own Indian data centres, providing in-country inferencing, low latency and data residency.

Billing is in Indian rupees, and Shakti Studio does not add extra invocation or platform service fees on top of compute pricing.

The announcement comes as Yotta aims to diversify its client base. In an earlier interview with AIM, CEO Sunil Gupta told AIM that more than 75% of Yotta’s existing 10,000 GPU capacity was contracted by overseas customers. “The US customers are using this GPU cluster to serve their respective US and European markets—nothing to do with India,” he added.

The programme intends to benefit Indian AI startups prototyping without locking capital into reserved infrastructure, GCCs building for global parent organisations while keeping data within India, enterprises in regulated sectors fine-tuning proprietary models on domestic infrastructure, and researchers and independent developers seeking on-demand access to enterprise-grade compute.

content:
Razorpay has appointed four senior engineering leaders from Microsoft, Salesforce, CRED and Divyam.ai as it expands its AI capabilities and prepares its financial infrastructure for agentic commerce.

The appointments include Sudhir Reddy, former CTO and Co-Founder of Divyam.ai, who joins as the company’s senior-most individual contributor to lead AI and data architecture.

The company has also hired Abhishek Agarwal, formerly Principal Group Engineering Manager at Microsoft; Bhavya Shivaprakash, formerly Senior Director at Salesforce; and Anuj Mathur, formerly Senior Director at CRED.

The hires come as Razorpay increases investments in AI across payments, banking, fraud prevention, reconciliation, merchant operations and developer platforms. The company said it is building systems that can increasingly make financial decisions rather than only process transactions.

“The next decade of financial infrastructure will be built very differently from the last,” said Shashank Kumar, CTO and Co-Founder of Razorpay. “We believe software won’t just help businesses operate—it will increasingly reason, decide, and act on their behalf. That requires a fundamentally different engineering organisation, one that combines AI expertise, large-scale engineering experience, and a strong product mindset.”

He added that the new leaders’ experience building technology platforms at scale would help accelerate Razorpay’s plans to build AI-native financial infrastructure for businesses globally.

The expansion builds on the company’s engineering reorganisation that began in September 2025, when Praburam Rambadran joined as Senior Vice President of Engineering.

Since then, Razorpay said it has launched products including Agentic Payments, Agent Studio, Agentic Dashboard and Onboarding, Connected Banking Agents, and internal AI developer tools.

Rambadran said the company prioritised engineering experience in deploying AI systems in production.

“Getting AI into production at financial scale is a hard, unglamorous problem. It’s about data quality, system reliability, and judgment under real constraints, not just model capability,” he said. “Sudhir, Abhishek, Bhavya and Anuj have each done this before, at scale, at Divyam.ai, Microsoft, Salesforce and CRED. Adding them to the team lets us move faster on the engineering work that agentic commerce is going to demand.”

Reddy, who has nearly two decades of experience building AI platforms and enterprise systems, previously held leadership roles at Flipkart, Yahoo and Symantec.

“I’ve always believed AI earns its place not by being clever, but by being trustworthy—and nowhere is that tested more than in financial systems, where every decision carries real consequences for real businesses,” Reddy said. “I’m looking forward to building the data and AI architecture this next chapter of Razorpay needs.”

According to the company, the engineering leadership team will build AI capabilities across payments, banking, risk, data and developer platforms as Razorpay develops systems that can support financial decision-making alongside transaction processing.

Enterprise software company Palantir reported record second-quarter 2026 results, with revenue rising 93% year-over-year to $1.935 billion, as CEO Alex Karp described the quarter as ‘otherworldly’ and pointed to accelerating demand for sovereign AI.

Its US commercial revenue grew 149% YoY to $764 million, while US government revenue increased 90% YoY to $809 million. Also, adjusted free cash flow reached $1.22 billion, representing a 63% margin.

The company raised its full-year revenue guidance to $8.15–8.16 billion. It also increased its US commercial revenue outlook to more than $3.42 billion.

Palantir has argued that enterprise AI is entering a new phase where customer-specific evaluation and sovereign model deployment matter more than frontier benchmark rankings.

CTO Shyam Sankar said during the earnings call that public AI benchmarks are no longer reliable indicators of enterprise performance, citing Palantir’s experience integrating NVIDIA’s open-weight Nemotron Ultra into its Artificial Intelligence Platform (AIP). The companies partnered in June to enable sovereign AI deployments and enterprise fine-tuning using Nemotron models.

“We’re excited for a new era, not one of benchmaxing, but of benchmaking. The assumption that the frontier is actually the best performing is just not borne out in practice,” said Sankar.

He revealed that within 24 hours of bringing Nemotron Ultra into Palantir’s AI stack, they found five production tasks where a standard Nemotron Ultra model without post-training beat frontier models.

“This underscores that a handful of common benchmarks can be gamed,” added Sankar.

Palantir also claimed its deployment approach is outperforming frontier AI providers during enterprise implementations.

Sankar described a competitive evaluation where Palantir’s Forward Deployed Engineers (FDEs) competed directly against a frontier AI lab on an enterprise automation project. He said the frontier AI lab selected a ticketing automation use case for the evaluation but failed to produce a meaningful solution.

Palantir instead built agent swarms for the customer's clients that generated marketing, packaging, and pricing recommendations to improve revenue and utilisation, resulting in a $10 million annual contract value deal.

Ryan Taylor, Palantir’s Chief Revenue Officer and Chief Legal Officer, argued that enterprises relying on rented frontier models are paying rising inference costs while allowing their proprietary operational knowledge to improve these third-party foundation models.

“Enterprises that are not using Palantir are seeing their token meters spinning endlessly just to get slop without any correlation to value. This token model may be working for the labs, but it is not working for anyone else,” he said.

Taylor used the argument to position Palantir's ‘AI sovereignty’ strategy as an alternative, which enables customers to retain control over their data, business logic, actions, and security.

Dabur India has partnered with Accenture to accelerate AI adoption across its operations as part of a multi-year digital transformation initiative to improve decision-making, business agility, and long-term profitability.

The collaboration will focus on building a unified data foundation and embedding AI into core business processes across functions including finance, procurement, marketing, sales, and supply chain management.

As part of the initiative, Accenture will help Dabur create a centralised data lake by integrating internal, external, structured, and unstructured datasets. The company will also deploy control towers and digital dashboards to provide real-time visibility into key performance indicators, enabling faster responses to changing market conditions.

The project will leverage advanced analytics and AI to identify revenue growth opportunities, optimise costs, improve demand forecasting, and enhance end-to-end operational visibility. Dabur also plans to roll out generative AI-powered conversational assistants that will allow employees to access insights and query enterprise data more efficiently.

“By building a digital brain on strong data foundations and advanced AI, we are embedding intelligence across the enterprise. Our collaboration with Accenture will help us sense demand more accurately, respond with greater agility and deliver sharper insights with stronger governance,” Manas Mehra, Global Chief Information Officer, Dabur India, said in a statement.

The initiative builds on Dabur’s earlier investments in cloud infrastructure and digital core modernisation. The company said the collaboration will prioritise outcome-based use cases focused on value realisation, spend optimisation, and EBITDA margin expansion.

Accenture will also support Dabur in redesigning talent strategies, operating models, and governance frameworks to sustain AI adoption at scale.

“FMCG companies are navigating increasing complexity, from diversified portfolios to fast-changing consumer expectations,” said Ankur Chaudhary, Managing Director and Lead for Products Group, India Business, Accenture.

“Dabur’s AI-led reinvention is both timely and strategic. By strengthening its data foundation and embedding AI into core processes, Dabur can make faster decisions, improve demand sensing and build more resilient operations, creating a stronger platform for purpose-led, profitable growth,” he added.

The partnership extends Dabur’s ongoing digital transformation journey with Accenture and reflects a broader trend among Indian FMCG companies adopting AI to improve operational efficiency, demand planning, and business resilience.

Kily, an enterprise AI startup, has secured ₹30 crore in funding led by Sorin Investments.

The company develops autonomous AI agents to automate commerce operations for brands across various platforms.

Early-stage venture capital firm Sorin Investments has led a ₹30 crore ($3.1 million) funding round in enterprise AI startup Kily, which builds autonomous AI agents for consumer brands operating across e-commerce and quick commerce platforms. The round also saw participation from Razorpay and Wyser Capital.

Founded in 2025 by Sankalp Mehrotra, Anurag Singh, and Sharad Chitlangia, Kily develops agentic AI systems that automate commerce operations for brands by managing pricing, advertising, inventory, and marketplace decisions across platforms such as Amazon, Flipkart, Blinkit, Zepto, and Swiggy Instamart.

The Bengaluru-based company said its AI agents continuously analyse marketplace signals alongside a brand's business context to execute workflows aimed at improving growth, profitability, and operational efficiency.

The startup has already partnered with consumer brands including ITC, as enterprises increasingly look to adopt AI systems capable of autonomous execution rather than merely providing recommendations.

Kily plans to use the fresh capital to strengthen its product capabilities, expand its go-to-market efforts, and accelerate adoption among large consumer brands across India.

Commenting on the investment, Subeer Monga, Partner at Sorin Investments, said enterprise software is shifting from systems that assist human decision-making to those that can execute decisions autonomously. He added that Kily's founders, with experience at companies including Flipkart, Affle, and Amazon, are building an AI-native execution layer that could define a new category of enterprise software for digital commerce.

Kily co-founder and CEO Sankalp Mehrotra said brands and online sellers now need to make thousands of marketplace decisions every day, making autonomous commerce management increasingly important. He added that the company aims to help brands execute faster, make better decisions, and scale profitably.

Cisco and IIT Delhi have launched a Technology Hub to enhance AI and cybersecurity in India.

The initiative aims to advance research, innovation, and talent development in the Indo-Pacific region.

Cisco and the Indian Institute of Technology Delhi (IIT Delhi) have launched the Cisco Technology Hub on AI and Cybersecurity, a collaborative initiative to advance research, build skills and strengthen the AI and cybersecurity ecosystem in the country.

The technology hub aims to boost AI and cybersecurity research, innovation, and talent development in the Indo-Pacific region.

Powered by Cisco's Country Digital Acceleration Programme, this three-year collaboration involves working with government policymakers to strengthen digital frameworks and security standards while co-creating solutions to real-world challenges for a more resilient digital ecosystem.

The hub focuses on three areas: research, talent, and ecosystem engagement.

On research, it will support fundamental and applied work in AI and cybersecurity, backed by grants and fellowships for PhD and MTech students, a chair of excellence, and joint projects with Cisco's global research teams, while also enabling IIT Delhi scholars to publish white papers that inform government policy and regulatory frameworks.

On workforce skills, it aims to continue education programmes developed with Cisco Networking Academy for industry professionals and government, alongside short training courses for government entities and public sector undertakings on emerging technologies and cybersecurity risks.

On thought leadership, it aims to facilitate dialogue across industry, academia and government, including security workshops, research forums and an annual Security and Trust Summit.

"This collaboration builds on the Institute's commitment to enable knowledge exchange and co-creation with industry partners. Through this initiative, we aim to foster innovation, develop future-ready talent, and contribute to strengthening India's digital ecosystem," Prof Jayant Jain, Dean, Corporate Relations, IIT Delhi, said in a statement.

Prof Ashwini K Agrawal, Dean (R&D), IIT Delhi, noted that the collaboration strengthens IIT Delhi's research in AI and cybersecurity and supports India's digital future.

Daisy Chittilapilly, President, Cisco India & South Asia, added, "Our partnership with IIT Delhi brings together research and technology expertise to advance frontier AI research, develop secure solutions for real-world challenges in AI and cybersecurity, while building a pipeline of next-generation talent that will shape India's digital future."

Earlier, Cisco partnered with IT services company LTM to offer a managed Secure Service Edge to help enterprises adopt zero trust security frameworks while managing access to applications, data, and AI models.

content:
Research lab AI4Bharat at IIT Madras and media edtech platform Josh Talks AI have launched Voice of India, an independent multimodal AI evaluation platform that will benchmark AI systems against real-world Indian languages, accents, dialects, and deployment environments.

The platform targets governments, enterprises, researchers, and AI developers to independently assess how AI models perform in India rather than relying only on vendor-reported benchmarks or evaluation standards developed for Western markets.

The platform features a suite of benchmarks, including a finance-focused benchmark for evaluating AI systems across banking workflows. Over time, it plans to expand evaluations across voice AI, large language models (LLMs), OCR and document processing, safety and cultural assessment, and Indian legal reasoning.

For enterprises and government agencies deploying AI, the platform introduces a three-stage evaluation process comprising constituent model evaluation, end-to-end deployment testing under real operating conditions, and periodic post-deployment audits. The framework aims to measure how AI systems perform in production environments rather than only in controlled benchmark settings.

“Evaluation determines what gets built. With AI systems becoming more deeply integrated into society, rigorous evaluation becomes as important as model development itself,” said Prof Mitesh Khapra of AI4Bharat at IIT Madras in a statement.

He added that Voice of India aims to provide “scientifically robust evaluation frameworks that reflect India's linguistic diversity,” and said India has an opportunity “not just to build AI for the world, but to help define how the world measures it.”

The platform will benchmark technologies including automatic speech recognition (ASR), text-to-speech (TTS), end-to-end voice agents, and speech translation across sectors such as finance, agriculture, healthcare, and government services. It will also evaluate LLMs on text reasoning, instruction following in Indian languages, retrieval-grounded search, long-document processing, and translation involving code-mixed languages.

Additional evaluation areas include OCR accuracy for Indic scripts and multilingual documents, safety and bias assessment across Indian languages, and legal reasoning involving statutes, contracts, and case law.

Supriya Paul, Co-founder of Josh Talks AI, said trust in AI will depend on how well systems understand the people they serve rather than only on their intelligence.

“India has a once-in-a-generation opportunity to contribute something unique to global AI, not necessarily the biggest models, but the evaluation infrastructure that makes AI trustworthy for the world,” she said.

Shobhit Banga, Co-founder of Josh Talks AI, said the focus of the next phase of AI development should shift towards measuring real-world performance.

“The next frontier in AI isn't building larger models. It’s building better ways to measure whether they actually work,” Banga said. "The Voice of India AI Evaluation Platform aims to bridge that gap by creating independent, transparent evaluation infrastructure that helps AI builders understand where models succeed, where they fail, and why.”

Activate, an early-stage AI venture fund, has announced an investment in Bengaluru-based AI startup Sarvam as part of the company’s ongoing Series B funding round, adding another investor to a round that is targeting $300 million.

The investment comes after Sarvam raised $234 million in the first close of its Series B round at a $1.5 billion post-money valuation in June. HCLTech led the first close with a $150 million investment, alongside Bessemer Venture Partners, while existing investors Khosla Ventures and Peak XV Partners also participated. Sarvam said it intends to raise a total of $300 million in the round.

Announcing the investment on X, Activate said it views AI as one of the largest technology shifts and believes India has an opportunity to play a leading role in the sector. The firm said that achieving that goal would require companies building foundational AI technology, research, and products tailored to India’s needs.

“Realising that vision requires ambitious founders building foundational technology, world-class research, and products designed for India’s unique needs. Sarvam has consistently demonstrated that ambition,” Activate said.

The firm added that it is partnering with Sarvam Co-founders Pratyush Kumar and Vivek Raghavan as they continue building the company.

Sarvam has not disclosed the size of Activate’s investment or whether the latest capital forms part of the remaining money yet to be raised in the Series B round.

Sarvam is set to raise $75 million from investors including NVIDIA, Glade Brook, Gaja Capital, IndiGo Ventures, and several individual investors, according to regulatory filings with the Registrar of Companies (RoC), as reported by ET.

The funding is expected to support Sarvam’s work across AI infrastructure, model research, and enterprise deployments. The company previously said the proceeds would be used to train its next frontier model for agentic AI, coding, and cybersecurity applications, while expanding access to compute infrastructure.

The company recently hosted Epoch, its frontier AI conference in Bengaluru, where it revealed that it is working on a trillion-parameter model expected to launch within the next six months.

Sarvam also hired Devendra Singh Chaplot, a former researcher at xAI, Thinking Machines Lab and Mistral AI, as an advisor to accelerate work on its frontier AI models.

Founded in 2023, Sarvam develops foundation models, speech AI, document intelligence, and enterprise AI products. Earlier this year, the company released its Sarvam 30B and Sarvam 105B models trained in India.

It says its conversational AI platform handles more than two million interactions a day, its inference platform processes over 10 million API calls daily, and its speech models transcribe more than 5,00,000 hours of audio every month.

title: Anthropic Launches In-Country Claude Inference in India With Amazon Bedrock
content:
Anthropic also announced new enterprise partnerships, expanded its Bengaluru team, and unveiled initiatives spanning cybersecurity, research, and Indian language AI.

Anthropic will make its Claude family of AI models available with in-country inference in India through Amazon Bedrock in the coming weeks, allowing requests to be processed on servers located within the country.

The company said the move is aimed at organisations in regulated sectors that require greater control over where customer data is processed.

The announcement comes as Anthropic expands its operations in India following the opening of its Bengaluru office earlier this year. Alongside the infrastructure update, the company disclosed new enterprise deployments, startup partnerships, cybersecurity initiatives, and efforts to improve Claude's performance in Indian languages.

“Bringing Claude inference to India is a turning point for enterprise AI in this country,” said Irina Ghose, Managing Director of Anthropic India, on LinkedIn. “India’s banks, insurers, telecoms, public and government agencies steward the data of a billion people. When that data can stay in India, AI moves from pilots into the systems that matter most."

Sandeep Dutta, President of AWS India and South Asia, said the availability of Claude through Amazon Bedrock's India endpoint would allow organisations to deploy frontier AI on infrastructure already used for critical workloads. “Institutions from banks to government agencies are ready to harness frontier AI at scale,” he said.

Anthropic said enterprises including Axis Bank, NPCI, IndusInd Bank, and Godrej Industries are using Claude across engineering, knowledge management, and internal operations. It also highlighted adoption by technology services firms such as TCS, Infosys, Cognizant, L&T, and LTTS for software development, client delivery, and workforce training.

The company also outlined deployments across consumer internet firms and startups. Swiggy has integrated Claude with its MCP capabilities, while Instamart now allows customers to browse more than 40,000 products using natural language prompts. Other companies, including Invideo, Rocket, Atlan, Cred, Zamp.ai, and Freshworks, are using Claude for software development, data management, and enterprise workflows.

Anthropic said India recorded some of the highest registrations in its Claude Partner Network after the network's launch in March. This week, the company is conducting its first Claude Certification for Partners programme in Bengaluru, with plans to certify up to 5,000 people.

The company also highlighted research and public-sector projects built on Claude. These include work at the Indian Institute of Science on venom research, PopVax’s drug discovery platform, astrophysics research at the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research, legal tech initiatives by Agami and Civis, and Digital Green's FarmerChat platform. Anthropic said in-country inference would enable additional deployments involving sensitive personal data.

On cybersecurity, Anthropic said the Data Security Council of India is developing a Claude-powered AI testing sandbox for its members, while MOSIP and OpenG2P are using the model to strengthen the security of open-source digital infrastructure.

The company also affirmed that it is working to improve Claude’s performance across Indian languages as part of its commitments announced at the New Delhi Frontier AI Impact Commitments. Anthropic said that through its partnership with Bengaluru-based ethical AI data platform Karya, it has already evaluated Claude across seven Indian languages in agriculture-related use cases, and the work will be expanded to additional domains and languages.
