Google is expanding Gemini Spark, its AI agent that can complete tasks in the background, to Google AI Pro subscribers in India over the next few weeks. The service, powered by Gemini 3.6 Flash, is available to Google AI Ultra and Pro subscribers and integrates with Google Workspace applications including Gmail, Docs and Sheets.

Unlike a traditional AI assistant that responds to prompts, Gemini Spark is built to carry out ongoing tasks on a user’s behalf. It runs on Google’s cloud infrastructure and continues working even when a user’s device is offline or locked.

Google said that Spark can “work quietly in the background” and connect with Workspace applications “with zero setup required”.

It further added that Spark automates recurring digital tasks while keeping users in control.

Users can decide whether to enable the service and which applications it can access. The company said Spark asks for confirmation before carrying out high-impact actions such as sending emails or making purchases.

“Spark always operates under your direction,” Google said. “You choose whether to turn it on and what apps it connects to, and it is designed to ask you first before performing high-stakes actions like spending money or sending emails.”

Google also shared examples of how the agent can be used. Travellers can instruct Spark to automatically add flight and hotel booking confirmations from Gmail to a Google Sheet and populate their calendar with local events during a trip.

Users can also schedule weekly searches for local activities and monitor sports court availability based on weather conditions.

For businesses, Spark can scan customer enquiries and prepare draft replies. It can also analyse a user’s previous emails to create a personalised writing style that is applied to future email drafts.

Google said Gemini Spark is part of its broader push towards AI agents that can complete tasks on a user's behalf instead of just answering questions.

Freshworks has appointed Ryan Manning as its Chief Product and Technology Officer (CPTO), effective August 10, as the software company brings its product and technology organisations under a single leadership structure.

Manning will report to CEO Dennis Woodside and succeed Srini Raghavan, who is leaving the company to pursue an entrepreneurial venture. Murali Swaminathan will continue as Chief Technology Officer and report to Manning.

The appointment comes as Freshworks expands its presence among mid-market and enterprise customers. In his new role, Manning will lead the company's product and technology strategy across its AI, IT, and customer experience portfolios, overseeing the global product roadmap and engineering organisation.

“Ryan has the unique ability to quickly turn what customers need into products that win in the market," said Dennis Woodside, CEO of Freshworks, in a statement. “As AI changes how quickly and how deeply our customers can put new capability to work, we’re excited to bring product and engineering back together under a single organisation so we can move with more speed and less friction.”

Manning joins Freshworks after holding leadership roles at startups and enterprise software companies. He helped build and scale ServiceNow around the time of its IPO and co-founded FreeAgent CRM, now Servis.ai. Most recently, he served as Chief Product Officer at BMC Helix, where he led product strategy during the company’s transformation, including its focus on ServiceOps and agentic AI.

“AI is changing what businesses should expect from service software," Manning said. "Having built service management products across startups and global software businesses, I believe Freshworks is uniquely positioned to lead the shift, combining powerful capability with rapid impact in a way the market needs right now.”

Manning holds a bachelor’s degree in accounting and finance from San Diego State University, where he also serves on the board of the university’s Computer Science programme. He will be based at Freshworks’ headquarters in San Mateo, California.

Freshworks said the leadership change is intended to align product development and engineering under a single executive as AI reshapes enterprise software development and deployment.

title: What Actually Matters.
content:
Cognizant's revenue rose by 4.5% in Q2, supported by its focus on AI-driven strategies.

A 6% decline in quarterly bookings indicates a slowdown in AI-led deal activity.

Cognizant Technology Solutions posted a 4.5% year-on-year rise in revenue for the June quarter, even as the IT services major leaned harder into its ‘AI builder’ strategy, striking new deals around Anthropic's Claude, Google's Gemini, and OpenAI's GPT-5.5 while flagging a sharp slowdown in fresh bookings.

The Nasdaq-listed company, which counts India as its largest talent base, reported revenue of $5.48 billion for the quarter ended June 30, 2026, up from $5.24 billion a year earlier.

Growth in constant currency terms was 4.1%, decelerating from the 7.2% pace clocked in the same quarter last year, which can be considered as a sign that the initial AI-led deal momentum is beginning to normalise.

Cognizant’s quarterly bookings fell 6% year-on-year, even though trailing twelve-month bookings rose 5% to $29.1 billion, translating into a book-to-bill ratio of roughly 1.3x.

The company signed seven large deals (contracts worth $100 million or more) during the quarter.

“Our organic revenue growth momentum continued in the second quarter and was at the high end of our expectations,” Chief Executive Officer Ravi Kumar S said in a statement.

"As organisations shift from AI experimentation to enterprise-scale execution, we believe the market opportunity ahead is larger than ever," he said, adding that the company was helping clients "close the AI velocity gap" by combining industry expertise with engineering and data modernisation capabilities.

Financial Services, Cognizant's largest and most mature vertical, was the standout performer with 12% year-on-year growth (11.7% in constant currency). Health Sciences grew a modest 1.4%, Products and Resources rose 1.2%, and Communications, Media and Technology grew 1.5%.

North America, which accounts for more than 75% of revenue, grew 5.5%, while Europe grew a slower 2.5% and Rest of World contracted 1.2%.

Margins Hold Up Despite Restructuring Costs

Cognizant’s operating margin came in at 15.9%, up 30 basis points year-on-year, while adjusted operating margin expanded 40 basis points to 16.0%.

The quarter absorbed $84 million in restructuring charges under Project Leap, the company's ongoing efficiency programme, which were largely offset by an $81 million one-time benefit from the reversal of a legacy India Provident Fund liability following recent labour law changes.

Cognizant's AI narrative extended well beyond internal tooling in the quarter. The company is now working with travel technology firm Travelport to embed Claude into software development workflows spanning airlines, hotels, and travel agencies.

Separately, Cognizant has also become one of a small number of Global Premier Partners in Anthropic's Claude Partner Network, and is training what it calls a "Frontier Certified" workforce.

The company also expanded ties with Google Cloud around Gemini Enterprise, and said it would apply OpenAI's GPT-5.5 within its cybersecurity practice as part of the "OpenAI Daybreak Cyber Partner Program," aimed at speeding up the process of finding and fixing security vulnerabilities.

The company repurchased 22.5 million shares for $1,153 million during the quarter, including through a previously announced $500 million accelerated buyback programme, leaving $2.3 billion still authorised for future repurchases. In July, it also declared a quarterly dividend of $0.33 per share.

During the quarter, Cognizant also closed its $634 million acquisition of Astreya, an AI-focused IT managed services provider, funding part of the deal through a $1 billion drawdown on its revolving credit facility.

Total headcount stood at 356,700 as of June 30, down 900 sequentially but up 12,900 from a year earlier. Voluntary attrition in technology services rose to 13.0% on a trailing-12-month basis, up from 12.3% in the previous quarter.

Cognizant revised its full-year 2026 constant-currency revenue growth guidance to a range of 4.0–5.5%, while keeping its adjusted operating margin guidance unchanged at 16.0–16.2%.

For the September quarter, the company guided for revenue of $5.60–5.68 billion, implying year-on-year growth of 3.4–4.9%.

Andrew Ng, Co-Founder and Chairman of Coursera, has launched a new AI education startup, LearnVector, with a $100 million investment from Coursera to develop AI-driven personalised learning experiences.

The companies also plan to work together on course development and distribution, with LearnVector collaborating with both Coursera and Udemy.

Announcing the venture on X, Ng said online education had expanded access to learning over the past 15 years, but the learning process itself had remained largely unchanged.

“With advances in AI, we can now build a custom learning guide for each person. We will turn learning from one-to-many to one-to-one,” he wrote.

LearnVector is focused on building AI learning guides that adapt to each learner’s progress rather than functioning as conventional chatbots. Ng argued that effective AI learning requires structured guidance instead of simply answering questions.

“Research shows that chatbots without guardrails harm learning. They help complete tasks and enable students to do better on homework. But cognitive offloading to a chatbot results in them being less skilled. And, you cannot always trust what a chatbot tells you,” he said.

Instead, he said LearnVector would “plan a path with you, adapt to how you learn, and patiently stay with you until you've mastered new skills”.

According to Reuters, Coursera’s investment gives it roughly a one-third stake in LearnVector, implying a valuation of about $300 million. The startup plans to launch its first courses in early 2027 and will initially target corporations, governments and higher education institutions.

It will use AI foundation models from multiple third-party providers to deliver personalised courses that evolve as learners progress.

Ng said the company is being built around the idea that AI will reshape work by changing the skills people need rather than replacing them entirely.

He added that trust remains central to online education, saying learners need “material that is accurate, relevant, and worth the effort you put into it”. Ng said LearnVector plans to work with Coursera to combine AI-driven instruction with the platform’s library of learning content.

Safe Superintelligence Inc (SSI), the AI startup founded by former OpenAI Chief Scientist Ilya Sutskever, has partnered with NVIDIA. The collaboration entails an equity investment and access to the chipmaker’s next-generation Vera Rubin systems, giving the startup a tenfold increase in computing capacity.

The companies did not disclose the financial terms of the deal. However, Reuters reported that NVIDIA is investing about $5 billion in SSI.

SSI said the investment and access to NVIDIA’s Vera Rubin platform will substantially increase its compute. The companies will also work together on advancing NVIDIA’s current and future computing platforms, with SSI contributing insights from its AI research.

The partnership marks one of the first major public announcements from SSI since the company was founded in 2024 by Sutskever, Daniel Gross, and Daniel Levy. The startup has largely operated in stealth, developing ‘safe superintelligence’ rather than releasing commercial AI products.

According to NVIDIA, the company decided to partner with SSI after obtaining what it described as rare access to the startup’s closely guarded research. SSI has spent the past two years pursuing a new research direction in developing a robustly aligned artificial intelligence.

“Ilya has pioneered fundamental breakthroughs at the foundation of modern AI, beginning with AlexNet,” NVIDIA Founder and CEO Jensen Huang said in a statement. "We are excited to see what new breakthroughs SSI will discover powered by our Vera Rubin platform.”

Sutskever said the startup had reached a stage where it was ready to expand its research efforts.

“We have research that is worthy of scaling up, and having access to a big NVIDIA computer will let us do so,” he said. “We're incredibly proud to be partnering with Jensen and the NVIDIA team, and we are confident that our big bet on the Vera Rubin platform will take us to the next level.”

The partnership adds SSI to a growing list of AI companies securing large-scale infrastructure commitments from NVIDIA as demand for compute continues to rise.

Last year, OpenAI partnered with the AI chipmaker to deploy chips in 10 GW of AI data centres, backed by over $100 billion in progressive investment. More recently, SK Group and NVIDIA announced plans for a $500+ billion partnership to establish AI infrastructure, featuring a 2 GW NVIDIA Vera Rubin DSX AI Factory built by SK Telecom.

SSI last raised $2 billion at a $32 billion valuation, backed by investors including Greenoaks, Lightspeed Venture Partners, and Andreessen Horowitz. The NVIDIA investment deepens the relationship between the AI chipmaker and one of Silicon Valley’s most closely watched AI research startups.

content:
Microsoft has introduced MAI-Cyber-1-Flash, its first AI model built for cybersecurity, alongside updates to MDASH, its multi-agent vulnerability identification and remediation platform.

The company said the new model enables MDASH to deliver “world-class performance at 50% of the cost” of its previous offering while outperforming rival AI systems on a cybersecurity benchmark.

According to Microsoft, the combination of MAI-Cyber-1-Flash and GPT-5.4 achieved a score of 95.95% on CyberGym, a benchmark that evaluates how AI systems identify vulnerabilities across large codebases. The company said this was about 12 percentage points higher than Anthropic’s Mythos model.

Microsoft said MAI-Cyber-1-Flash was built to handle up to 90% of vulnerability detection tasks, allowing MDASH to reserve larger models, including GPT-5.4, for more complex cases. The company said this multi-model approach cuts costs by 50% compared with its earlier MDASH configuration, which relied on GPT-5.4, GPT-5.4 mini and GPT-5.3 Codex.

The company also announced Perception, a new agentic security system within MDASH. Microsoft said Perception uses teams of AI agents to monitor, patch and remediate vulnerabilities continuously, and will expand to additional security workflows using MAI-Cyber-1-Flash.

Microsoft attributed the model’s performance to three factors: the model itself, security data collected over years of operating its platforms, and MDASH's orchestration layer.

The company said the compact model was derived from its MAI-Thinking-1 family and trained on security-focused data. It also said its security operations generate more than 100 trillion security signals daily across identity, endpoint, cloud and network environments, while MDASH coordinates more than 100 specialised AI agents for vulnerability detection and remediation.

“Three things matter today: Model. Data. Harness,” the company said. “We have jointly optimised our world-class models, our unmatched historic data, and our expert-tuned harness to ensure that our customers have a uniquely powerful security offering.”

Microsoft said MAI-Cyber-1-Flash was evaluated by its AI Red Team, tested through automated and expert-led adversarial exercises, and independently assessed by a third party before release. Through MDASH, customers will also have access to role-based access controls, tenant isolation, encryption, audit logs and sandboxed execution environments without internet access.

The company said its long-term goal is to improve cyber models through reinforcement learning based on real-world security operations.

content:
Cursor has launched Cursor Start, a new subscription plan exclusively for developers in India, priced at ₹649 per month inclusive of tax, as the AI coding platform deepens its presence in one of its fastest-growing markets.

The plan includes access to Grok 4.5, Cursor’s flagship coding model, Composer, higher agent request limits than the Free tier, always-on cloud agents and UPI payments.

The company said its user base in India has tripled over the past year to more than three million developers, making the country its third-largest market globally.

It also said India has more power users than any other region, with developers generating more agent requests per user than anywhere else.

“For a long time, our users in India have asked us for two things: pricing that reflects the local market, and the ability to pay with UPI,” the company said.

Cursor Start sits between the company’s Free and Pro subscriptions. It includes Grok 4.5, Composer, higher agent request limits, always-on cloud agents, iOS support, and integrations with plugins, MCP servers, hooks and skills.

The subscription is billed in Indian rupees and supports payments via UPI, credit cards and debit cards.

“Cursor Start sits between our two other individual plans, Free and Pro,” said the company. Cursor said the Free plan is designed for first-time users, offering Composer access and a limited number of local agent requests each month without requiring payment.

The Pro plan targets heavier users, adding access to models from multiple AI providers alongside Cursor's own models, as well as features including Bugbot, Auto mode, Automations, the Cursor SDK and the ability to purchase additional usage beyond included limits. The Pro plan is priced at $20 per month.

According to the company, Start is intended for everyday development workloads, while Pro is aimed at developers requiring broader model access and advanced automation capabilities.

Cursor is also expanding its developer outreach in India. The company announced community events in Hyderabad on July 30 and Bengaluru on August 1, saying it plans to learn from Indian developers before considering similar localised plans in other markets.

content:
Cognizant has expanded its strategic partnership with artificial intelligence startup Anthropic, becoming one of a select group of Global Premier Partners in the Claude Partner Network, as the Nasdaq-listed IT services company steps up efforts to commercialise generative AI across enterprise clients.

The expanded alliance will see Cognizant embed Anthropic’s Claude family of AI models into its proprietary engineering and IT operations platforms, while scaling a workforce certified on frontier AI models as enterprises move beyond proof-of-concept projects to production deployments.

According to the companies, the expanded partnership addresses the gap between model capability and companies’ ability to drive business results. Closing that gap extends beyond model capability. It takes the domain context, engineering depth and delivery scale to embed AI into the systems enterprises already run on.

The partnership builds on an agreement signed in late 2025 and comes as global IT services companies race to differentiate themselves through alliances with leading AI model providers including Anthropic, OpenAI and Google.

“AI capability is rising faster than enterprises can absorb it, and that gap is the defining problem of this moment,” Ravi Kumar S, CEO, Cognizant, said in a statement. “Our role is to be the bridge. We bring the industry context, the engineering scale and the trust frameworks that use Claude to deliver production outcomes inside the most demanding enterprise environments.”

As part of the partnership, Cognizant will integrate Claude into platforms including Flowsource, Neuro AI Engineering and Neuro IT Ops under what it described as a model-agnostic AI strategy. The company said Flowsource now incorporates Claude Code into its software development workflow to automate coding and validation against engineering standards.

Cognizant also said it has already deployed Claude-powered solutions across several industries. These include an AI-based customer experience portal for a global manufacturer, an agentic contract intelligence platform for a biopharmaceutical company that reduced contract review time by up to 40%, and a risk navigation tool for insurers that cut manual research time from hours to about a minute, saving underwriters roughly eight hours a week.

The company said more than 30,000 employees have completed Claude training so far. Under its recently announced Frontier workforce model, Cognizant plans to prepare 5,000 Frontier Certified Engineers and 10,000 Frontier Business Operators as part of a broader certification pipeline covering 40,000 professionals. Over time, the company expects Claude training to extend across its workforce of more than 3,50,000 employees.

“Deepening our partnership with Cognizant will help more companies harness AI’s growing capability and deploy it in real, practical ways for their businesses. From manufacturing to the life sciences, Cognizant is bringing Claude into the everyday work of some of the world's most demanding industries—the kinds of contexts where AI can demonstrate its greatest value for humanity,” said Daniela Amodei, Co-Founder and President of Anthropic.

title: AI at the Core
content:
Mid-tier IT services firm Coforge reported a 63% year-on-year jump in consolidated net profit for the June quarter, driven by growth in its AI-led engineering business and the integration of its recently acquired US firm Encora.

Consolidated net profit for the quarter stood at ₹518.6 crore ($54 million), compared with ₹317.4 crore a year earlier.

However, on a sequential basis, the net profit dropped 15.3%, primarily due to multiple one-offs incurred by the company during the quarter. These include acquisition and integration costs of ₹61.3 crore related to Encora, ₹5 crore of legal costs related to a cyber litigation matter, and provisions against customer receivables of ₹10.8 crore. These were partly offset by forex gains of ₹22.1 crore, arising from the devaluation of the Bolivian currency.

These led to Coforge incurring net exceptional costs of ₹55 crore during the quarter.

Revenue from operations totalled ₹5,527.7 crore ($577 million), up 49% year-on-year in rupee terms and 33% in dollar terms.

EBITDA rose 74% year-on-year to ₹1,123.3 crore ($117 million), with EBITDA margin expanding 285 basis points to 20.3%.

Basic earnings per share rose 67.3% to ₹12.34. The board also declared an interim dividend of ₹4 per equity share and gave in-principle approval to set up an entity in China as part of the company's expansion plans,

Coforge said AI-led engineering, data, and cloud services together accounted for 86% of its revenue in the quarter. AI-led Engineering alone made up 50.4% of revenue by service line, up from 45.9% in the year-ago quarter.

“The confluence of our next twelve-month signed order book of $2.23 billion, an exceptionally strong large deal pipeline and differentiated capabilities with 86% of our revenues coming from AI-led engineering, data and cloud services has set us up to be the industry growth leader for the third year running,” Sudhir Singh, Chief Executive Officer and Executive Director, Coforge, said in a statement.

During the quarter, the company launched Coforge Nuuron, described as an AI operating system meant to help enterprises industrialise AI-driven outcomes across the business by orchestrating knowledge, decision intelligence, AI agents, and execution systems into a unified autonomous operating model.

It also unveiled the NEXA Agentic AI Platform, built for the insurance industry, and Aeronova.AI, an AI-enabled framework to help airlines transition from legacy PNR-based systems to order-led retailing.

Fresh order intake for the quarter stood at $691 million in total contract value, up from $648 million in the preceding quarter.

The executable order book for the next 12 months rose to $2.23 billion, up 27% sequentially.

The company signed four large deals during the quarter across North America, Europe, and Latin America.

Coforge said its acquisition of Encora, a digital engineering services firm, was now fully operationally integrated. Two months of Encora's contribution added $100.7 million to the topline following the deal's completion on April 23.

“With the Encora acquisition completely operationally integrated and with strong demand, record visibility, and a rapidly expanding pipeline of AI-led opportunities, FY27 is shaping up to be an exceptional performance year for the firm,” said Singh.

The company reported a next-12-month order book increase of 27% quarter-on-quarter, and said its top five clients contributed 18.0% of quarterly revenue while its top 10 clients contributed 26.1%.

Total headcount stood at 46,228 at the end of the quarter.

Coforge’s shares were up 9.48% on the NSE at 12:30 pm on July 28, trading at ₹1,672.7 apiece.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said the company has never supported banning open-weight AI models, as Washington debates potential restrictions on Chinese open-weight models

In a blog post, Amodei said reports suggesting that some US officials were considering banning Chinese open-weight models had led to claims that Anthropic supported such measures to protect its commercial interests.

“Anthropic has never advocated for a ban on open-weights models,” he wrote. “Open-weights models that don't have dangerous capabilities are a public good.”

The statement comes as more than 50 technology companies and organisations, including NVIDIA, Microsoft, Meta, IBM, Dell Technologies and Hugging Face, signed an open letter opposing restrictions on open-weight AI models and arguing that they are important for innovation, competition and national security.

Instead of restricting open-weight models, Amodei outlined three policy measures that he believes would better address national security risks.

To begin with, he called for tighter controls on exports of advanced AI chips and chipmaking equipment to China, along with stronger enforcement against smuggling. According to Amodei, China’s limited domestic semiconductor manufacturing capacity means access to advanced US chips remains a key factor in training frontier AI models.

He also urged governments to target what he described as “industrial-scale distillation operations”. Distillation is a training technique that allows smaller models to learn from larger ones while requiring far less compute than training from scratch.

“Distillation is a much more compute-efficient process than training models from scratch,” Amodei wrote. “It allows China to build much better models than its number of chips would ordinarily enable.”

He argued that policies should focus on deterring state-backed distillation efforts rather than banning open-weight models. “A blanket ban on open-weight models is neither the correct remedy nor something we have called for,” he said.

Lastly, Amodei proposed mandatory safety testing for all sufficiently capable AI models, regardless of whether they are open or closed. He said testing should evaluate cyber, biological and alignment risks before deployment.

“The best way to address threat #2 is to just directly test models for cyber, biological, and alignment risks before release,” he wrote, adding that the approach should apply equally to open and closed models while exempting less capable models from startups and academia.

Amodei also addressed arguments made in the industry-backed open letter. While agreeing that open-weight models broaden access to AI and strengthen competition in some areas, he disputed claims that they inherently improve security.

“I don't agree with the letter’s assertions that open-weight models necessarily make it easier to develop safeguards or that broad access to capabilities necessarily helps defenders more than attackers,” he wrote. “It seems at least as likely to me that the opposite will be true.”

He warned that advances in biology could create an attacker advantage if capable AI models make it easier to develop dangerous pathogens while defensive measures continue to take years to deploy.

Summarising Anthropic’s position, Amodei said the company’s focus remains on “keeping powerful chips out of authoritarian hands, stopping industrial-scale distillation, and requiring safety testing of all sufficiently capable models, open and closed,” rather than banning open-weight AI models.

Wipro has expanded its partnership with data and artificial intelligence (AI) platform provider Databricks and launched a self-contained business practice to help enterprises modernise their data infrastructure and deploy AI applications at scale.

The new Databricks-focused practice will develop industry-specific AI solutions by combining Databricks' data and AI platform with Wipro's own AI offerings and delivery capabilities.

The initiative, according to a stock exchange filing, is intended to help customers move from fragmented data environments and experimental AI projects to enterprise-wide AI deployments.

As part of the collaboration, Wipro will integrate Databricks' capabilities in agentic AI, data modernisation, analytics, and application development with its Wipro Intelligence suite and agent-native delivery platform WEGA to modernise legacy systems and build AI-ready data architectures.

“Our long-standing collaboration with Databricks reflects a shared commitment to help enterprises move from AI experimentation to measurable value,” Kanwar Singh, Managing Partner - Technology Services, Wipro, said in a statement. “The business practice will bring together platform specialists, consulting expertise, and industry teams to co-create solutions that accelerate data transformation and enterprise-wide AI adoption.”

The company did not disclose the financial terms of the partnership.

The partnership will initially focus on developing AI-led offerings across wealth management, manufacturing planning, telecom sales and marketing, energy asset management, and finance transformation.

“This global practice with Wipro will enable enterprises to build trusted data foundations and deploy production-ready AI at scale, turning data intelligence into real, measurable business impact,” said Kori O’Brien, Senior Vice President, Partnerships, Databricks.

The announcement comes as Indian IT services firms deepen alliances with hyperscalers and AI platform providers to capture growing enterprise demand for agentic AI and data modernisation projects.

NVIDIA is in discussions to provide a roughly $250 billion financial guarantee that would help OpenAI lease a planned 10-gigawatt AI data centre campus in southern Ohio in the US, according to a Wall Street Journal report.

The proposed arrangement would support debt financing for the project, which is being developed by SoftBank (SB) Energy, and could ultimately cost more than $500 billion once NVIDIA's AI chips are included.

The guarantee would act as a credit backstop, allowing lenders to offer better financing terms even though OpenAI does not have an investment-grade credit rating. It would cover the lease and construction financing, but not the NVIDIA GPUs that will power the facility.

NVIDIA is also separately discussing financing for OpenAI’s chip purchases, which could total $350 billion, according to the report.

If completed, the Ohio campus would become the largest AI data centre project announced so far.

The first phase is expected to deliver around 800 MW of capacity by 2028, with the rest of the campus being built over the following years. The report said OpenAI has been in advanced talks to lease the site for several weeks, while Anthropic, Microsoft, and Google have also shown interest.

The project is also tied to a broader US-Japan infrastructure initiative. Under a recent trade agreement, Japan committed $33 billion to fund a natural gas power project on federal land in Ohio that will supply electricity to the campus. Building the campus on federal land is expected to reduce permitting delays and local opposition that have slowed other large AI data centre projects across the US.

For OpenAI, the lease would mark its first dedicated data centre tenancy, reducing its reliance on cloud providers such as Microsoft, Amazon, and Oracle.

The company recently raised its projected spending on computing infrastructure to around $750 billion through 2030, up from an earlier estimate of roughly $600 billion. NVIDIA, meanwhile, is looking to secure long-term demand for its AI chips while expanding into infrastructure financing as AI data centre projects continue to grow in scale.

The latest project builds on the Stargate AI infrastructure initiative announced by OpenAI, SoftBank, MGX, and Oracle last year to develop AI computing capacity across the US. Arm, Microsoft, and NVIDIA were listed as technology partners for this project.

Since its launch, OpenAI has expanded Stargate beyond its flagship campus in Abilene, Texas, adding new sites with Oracle and SoftBank while increasing its projected computing spend to around $750 billion through 2030.

Earlier this year, OpenAI and SoftBank also invested $1 billion in data centre and power infrastructure venture SB Energy, with OpenAI signing an initial 1.2 GW data centre lease to support future Stargate deployments.

LTM, the technology services company formerly known as LTIMindtree, has partnered with US-based artificial intelligence startup Cognition to integrate its AI software engineering agent Devin into the company's cybersecurity platform, making it the latest Indian IT firm to commercialise autonomous AI agents for enterprise clients.

The partnership will initially focus on banks and financial institutions, where the companies said they will use Devin through LTM's BlueVerse RightLogic platform, an AI-led cybersecurity assessment and risk assurance framework, to identify, prioritise, and remediate cybersecurity vulnerabilities across applications, AI systems, and software supply chains.

Under the partnership, BlueVerse RightLogic will ingest vulnerability data from enterprises' existing security tools, prioritise issues based on business criticality and regulatory exposure, and assign high-confidence fixes to Devin for automated remediation. Human engineers will continue to review fixes before deployment and handle more complex cases, according to the companies.

“The financial services sector is under constant pressure to strengthen security while accelerating AI adoption. Through BlueVerse RightLogic and Devin, we are helping clients reduce vulnerability backlogs, automate remediation, and improve cyber resilience across financial services, empowering them to innovate faster without compromising security,” Harsh Naidu, Chief Business Officer – Banking & Financial Services, LTM, said in a statement.

LTM and Cognition said the platform is designed to increase the proportion of Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) that can be remediated from around 60% to 80%, although they did not disclose customer deployments or financial terms of the partnership.

As part of the partnership, LTM and Cognition will jointly offer five AI-led services spanning autonomous security remediation, legacy application modernisation, software development lifecycle (SDLC) automation, technology and business transformation, and database and ETL migration to modern data platforms such as Databricks and Snowflake. The offerings are aimed at helping enterprises automate software engineering, modernise legacy systems, and accelerate AI adoption.

LTM also said it has already trained a large pool of engineers on Devin through workshops, enabling deployment teams to work with the AI agent without an extended onboarding period.

"Security has become a volume problem that no human team can staff its way out of. Devin lets security teams move from reporting issues to resolving them, and LTM brings the expertise and customer relationships to deliver that outcome at enterprise scale," said Gardner Johnson, Global Head of Partnerships, Cognition.

The announcement comes as IT services companies increasingly look to move beyond AI-assisted coding tools towards autonomous AI agents capable of executing software engineering tasks with limited human intervention. Firms including TCS, Infosys, Wipro, and HCLTech have been investing in agentic AI offerings as enterprises seek measurable productivity gains from generative AI deployments.

Infosys has been fined €175,000 ($200,000) by French labour authorities after its employee working time recording system was found to be non-compliant with local legal requirements for certain categories of employees.

The penalty was imposed by DRIEETS Île-de-France, the regional authority responsible for labour, employment. and economic affairs in the Paris region, according to a stock exchange filing.

The French authority concluded that Infosys' working time recording system "did not fully comply with French legal requirements," citing shortcomings in its reliability, auditability, and monitoring capabilities for certain employee categories.

The Bengaluru-headquartered IT services company said the order would have no material impact on its financials, operations, or other business activities.

Infosys also explained the delay in disclosing the development, saying it was "in the process of checking the veracity and determining further steps" after receiving the communication from the French authority.

The company reported a 12.2% year-on-year rise in consolidated net profit to ₹7,769 crore for the June quarter (Q1 FY27), even as it trimmed the upper end of its full-year revenue growth guidance. Revenue from operations came in at ₹48,211 crore, up 14% YoY and only 3.9% quarter-on-quarter.

In 2013, Infosys received a penalty over allegations of systemic visa fraud and misuse of B-1 business visitor visas. It paid a record $34 million civil settlement.

Oracle has secured a 10-year Indefinite Delivery/Indefinite Quantity (IDIQ) contract under the US Department of War’s (DoW) Enterprise Software Initiative (ESI), with a base value of $3.31 billion for the first five years and a potential total value of $6.99 billion if all option years are exercised.

The contract establishes a central procurement framework that allows authorised DoW organisations and contractors to purchase Oracle’s commercial software, cloud services, SaaS applications, support, and professional services through task and delivery orders. The ESI vehicle is intended to reduce procurement time and standardise technology acquisition across the department.

The DoW employs more than 3.4 million civilian and military personnel across multiple agencies and branches, making technology procurement a complex process.

Under the new agreement, Oracle said DoW organisations will be able to procure commercial products and services through a common contracting framework while retaining flexibility through order-specific pricing, deliverables, and performance criteria.

“For the Department of War, the challenge is not just finding the right technology; it's doing so quickly, compliantly, and at scale, without getting bogged down by complex procurement processes,” said Kim Lynch, Executive Vice President, Government Intelligence and Defence, Oracle.

“ESI is designed to address those challenges by creating a more standardised and efficient path to Oracle cloud and AI technology tuned to support mission-critical scenarios,” Lynch added.

Oracle said the department, which has been its customer since the 1990s, will transition to the ESI contract vehicle during the summer of 2026. As part of the transition, the company will provide dedicated programme operations and a standardised intake process to route requests and coordinate engagements across Oracle teams.

The company said the ESI contract covers Oracle’s on-premises software, software support, SaaS applications, and professional services. Individual task and delivery orders placed under the contract will define pricing and performance requirements based on operational needs.

Oracle expects the DoW to expand its use of standardised procurement vehicles such as ESI as it adopts commercial technology for future mission requirements.

Karnataka aims to establish itself as India's deep tech and AI hub over the next decade.

The Innoverse Foundation will support deep tech startups with mentorship and market access.

Karnataka has announced a series of initiatives aimed at cementing its position as India’s deep tech and AI hub, with state IT and BT Minister Priyank Kharge declaring the next decade as Karnataka's “deep tech decade”.

Speaking ahead of the 29th edition of the Bengaluru Tech Summit (BTS) 2026, Kharge outlined a roadmap that spans AI, deep tech, startup funding, innovation infrastructure and international collaborations.

“Karnataka should and will lead India and the world in AI,” Kharge said, adding that the state would focus on building a robust deep tech ecosystem over the next 10 years.

Among the key announcements was the launch of the Innoverse Foundation, a new government-backed initiative designed to mentor revenue-generating deep tech startups and help them scale into globally competitive companies. The foundation will provide market access, capital connections and mentorship, while also opening applications for its Deep Tech Enabler Programme.

The state also reinforced its support for startups through the Elevate and Elevate NxT programmes. A total of 33 deep tech startups were selected under Elevate NxT 2026, with the government distributing nearly ₹33 crore in grants. Each startup will receive between ₹85 lakh and ₹1 crore to support research and product development. Notably, 12 of the 33 selected startups are women-led, highlighting increasing diversity in India’s deep tech ecosystem.

Kharge also announced plans for the Museum of Innovation, Startup & Technology (MIST), describing it as India’s first museum dedicated to showcasing the country’s innovation and startup journey.

In a move to help startups commercialise solutions built on public data, the minister said the government would act as an early customer for companies developing products using government datasets. The initiative is expected to give startups a reference client while accelerating the adoption of AI-driven public services.

The announcements come as Karnataka prepares to host Bengaluru Tech Summit 2026, scheduled for November 17-19 at the Bangalore International Exhibition Centre under the theme ‘AI & Beyond’. The summit is expected to attract more than 1,800 exhibitors, 25,000 delegates and over 60,000 visitors from 75 countries.

The government also revealed two major international collaborations for this year’s summit. The India edition of ChangeNOW, the global sustainability and impact platform, will be co-located with BTS 2026. In addition, embedded world India, organised in partnership with NürnbergMesse India, will make its debut, bringing a dedicated conference and exhibition focused on electronics and semiconductors.

The Indian government has directed GitHub to remove repositories hosting Bitchat, the Bluetooth-based messaging application developed by Twitter Co-Founder Jack Dorsey, citing concerns that the app could be used to bypass internet shutdowns, evade lawful interception and facilitate unlawful activities during the ongoing Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) protests in Delhi.

The order, dated July 23, was issued under Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology Act, 2000, read with Rule 3(1)(d) of the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021. It instructs GitHub to remove access to the identified URLs within three hours of receiving the notice.

According to the order, GitHub has been asked to disable access to three repositories: permissionlesstech/bitchat, permissionlesstech/bitchat-android, and permissionlesstech/bitchat-android/releases.

The Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C) said it identified Bitchat as “a communication platform capable of establishing decentralised peer-to-peer messaging over Bluetooth mesh networks without relying on mobile networks, internet connectivity, or centralised servers.”

According to the notice, the government believes the platform “can be misused to evade lawful surveillance, facilitate anonymous coordination, and circumvent lawful restrictions imposed by competent authorities during situations involving public disorder, riots, terrorism, organised crime, or internet shutdowns.”

The directive reportedly asks GitHub to act against the repositories hosting the application’s source code.

Dorsey published the alleged government notice on X, saying, “The government of india does not like technologies like Bitchat and wants it taken down.”

Bitchat is a decentralised messaging application that operates over Bluetooth mesh networks rather than the internet. Because messages are relayed directly between nearby devices, the app continues to function even when mobile data or Wi-Fi services are unavailable.

The architecture also means there are no central servers that authorities can access for user records or message logs, making communications significantly harder to monitor.

According to the notice, the absence of a centralised service provider limits the ability of law enforcement agencies to obtain subscriber information, communication records, or timely assistance during investigations.

The notice cites alleged violations of Sections 43, 84B and 84C of the Information Technology Act, 2000, as well as Sections 61 read with 196 and 197 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. It classifies the repositories as containing information prohibited under the law.

The order also reminds intermediaries that failure to comply with takedown directions issued under Section 79(3)(b) and the IT Rules, 2021, could result in the loss of safe harbour protections available under Section 79(1) of the Information Technology Act and expose them to legal liability under applicable laws.

The move comes after authorities suspended mobile internet services in parts of Delhi during the ongoing CJP protests. According to the reported government notice, officials believe protesters were using Bluetooth-based messaging applications such as Bitchat to remain connected despite the internet restrictions.

title: Global Technology Centre in Bhubaneswar
content:
After TCS, now HCLTech is also embarking on a sovereign AI infrastructure push with plans to establish its first AI data centre at the upcoming Odisha Sovereign AI Park in partnership with foundational AI startup Sarvam AI and the Odisha government.

The project will involve a planned capital outlay of ₹14,257 crore, including financial assistance from the state government.

HCLTech said the facility will combine its full-stack AI capabilities with Sarvam's foundation models to develop sector-specific AI applications for public and private sector organisations while supporting the government’s data sovereignty requirements.

The companies said the data centre will also support multilingual AI services and expand India's local AI developer ecosystem.

“HCLTech has been a flagbearer of India's technology industry. In line with the Digital India and Atmanirbhar Bharat vision of Hon'ble Prime Minister Narendra Modi, we strive to be an enabler of India's sovereign AI ecosystem with differentiated offerings across the value chain through focused investments and partnerships,” Roshni Nadar Malhotra, Chairperson of HCLTech, said in a statement.

C Vijayakumar, CEO and Managing Director of HCLTech, said the project marks an important step in the company's full-stack AI strategy.

“This is an important milestone in our full-stack AI play and will enable us to serve the large demand for sovereign AI solutions and unlock the scale of our strategic partnership with Sarvam. Odisha offers a progressive policy environment backed by infrastructure, and we look forward to working with them in collaboration with Sarvam,” he said.

Pratyush Kumar, Co-founder of Sarvam, said the project will bring together compute infrastructure, Indian AI models, and enterprise applications.

“The Odisha Sovereign AI Park will connect high-performance compute with Indian models and real-world applications. Together with HCLTech, we are excited to bring Sarvam's full-stack AI capabilities to enterprises and public systems at scale,” Kumar said.

The announcement comes weeks after HCLTech said it would enter the full-stack AI market.

HCLTech has also signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) with the Odisha government to establish a global technology centre in Bhubaneswar, expanding its footprint in eastern India as it continues to invest in AI-led digital services.

The facility, which is expected to begin operations by 2028, will employ 5,000 people. It will work alongside HCLTech’s proposed AI Data Centre in the upcoming Odisha Sovereign AI Park, announced earlier this month.

According to the company, the new centre will develop and deliver AI-led digital solutions for global enterprises. HCLTech said the investment will generate direct and indirect employment while strengthening Odisha's technology talent pipeline through collaborations with educational institutions and the state government.

HCLTech currently employs more than 170,000 people in India across campuses and technology centres in Noida, Bengaluru, Chennai, Hyderabad, Pune, Lucknow, Nagpur, Madurai, Vijayawada, and GIFT City.

Genpact has launched Banking Analyst Suite, a new enterprise platform that applies agentic AI to regulated banking operations, with its first module focused on anti-money laundering (AML) alert investigations.

The first module, Genpact Transaction Monitoring Analyst, aims to help banks complete routine AML alert investigations faster while maintaining human oversight and audit trails. According to Genpact, analysts remain responsible for final decisions and the system does not take regulated actions without human approval.

The module is based on Genpact’s experience managing financial crime operations for financial institutions, including reviewing millions of AML alerts each year.

It uses multiple AI agents to perform different stages of an investigation, including analysing customer behaviour, reviewing transactions, validating customer profiles, checking previous alerts, and recommending the next course of action.

Unlike systems that only prioritise or score alerts, Genpact said the platform completes the first-level investigation workflow and produces a recommendation supported by documented reasoning and an audit trail for analysts to review.

According to the company, the platform can reduce handling time for in-scope AML investigations by up to 80% and lower total cost of ownership by up to 40%. The system intends to improve consistency in investigations by documenting the rationale behind every recommendation.

“What sets Genpact Transaction Monitoring Analyst apart is the operating expertise behind the AI,” Satish Acharya, Service Line Leader, Financial Crime and Risk Management at Genpact, said in a statement.

“We have run financial crime programmes for some of the world's largest financial institutions, and we have built that knowledge into how these AI agents investigate. This solution helps analysts shift time from repetitive alert work to the higher-risk cases where human judgment matters most,” he added.

Genpact plans to expand Banking Analyst Suite beyond transaction monitoring to other regulated banking functions, including customer due diligence, sanctions screening, fraud investigations, customer service, and other risk management workflows.

The suite is also designed to support governance, data isolation, information security, and system integration requirements for regulated environments.

The company added that Banking Analyst Suite will run natively alongside its riskCanvas financial crime platform for customers already using the software.

Australia and New Zealand-based financial services company AMP Limited is among the first organisations to deploy Genpact’s Transaction Monitoring Analyst.

Fractal Analytics reported a significant year-on-year net profit increase, driven by rising enterprise spending on AI initiatives.

Despite a strong year-on-year performance, net profit declined 37% sequentially, leading to a drop in share value.

Pure-play AI company Fractal Analytics reported a 97.8% year-on-year jump in net profit for the first quarter of FY27, as rising enterprise spending on AI-led transformation programmes helped revenue cross ₹900 crore and boosted operating margins.

The Mumbai-headquartered company posted consolidated operating revenue of ₹912.5 crore for the quarter ended June 30, up 20% from a year earlier. Net profit rose to ₹74.2 crore, while adjusted EBITDA grew 35% year-on-year. However, on a sequential basis, the profit after tax declined 37%.

Gross margin improved by 29 basis points to 46%, and adjusted EBITDA margin expanded by 189 basis points to 17%.

Commenting on the results, Srikanth Velamakanni, Co-founder, Group CEO and Executive Vice-Chairman of Fractal, said enterprises are increasingly committing larger budgets to AI initiatives.

"Enterprises are putting real transformation budgets behind AI now, and we're seeing it directly in the size of the deals coming to us. Telecom, Media and Technology (TMT) was the drag on our headline growth this quarter. Excluding TMT, our business grew 35% year on year, which is a better read on the underlying demand we're seeing," he said in a statement.

Healthcare and Life Sciences emerged as the fastest-growing business segment, with revenue rising 69% year-on-year to become Fractal's second-largest vertical. BFSI grew 36%, while Consumer Packaged Goods and Retail (CPGR), the company's largest business, expanded 19%. Revenue from the TMT segment, however, declined 22% during the quarter.

He added, "As data sovereignty becomes a bigger priority for governments and enterprises, and as open-weight models keep improving, clients need a partner who can work across models and infrastructure. We have invested heavily in our people, our research, and our own intellectual property to be that partner.”

Geographically, the Americas remained Fractal's largest market, accounting for 67.4% of revenue, followed by Europe at 21.4%, and Asia-Pacific and other regions at 11.2%. Revenue from the Americas and Europe grew 24% and 25%, respectively, while APAC and other markets recorded modest growth.

Fractal debuted on the Indian stock exchanges in February 2026 after raising about ₹2,834 crore through its IPO. The company said the quarter reflected sustained demand for enterprise AI solutions despite weakness in the TMT vertical, with improving margins underpinning stronger profit growth than revenue growth.

The company’s shares plunged on July 24, trading 5.94% lower at ₹810 apiece at 12:25 pm on the NSE.

The Delhi High Court on July 24 dismissed Asian News International’s (ANI) application seeking an interim injunction against OpenAI in its copyright infringement lawsuit over ChatGPT, holding that the news agency had failed to establish a prima facie case for interim relief.

Justice Amit Bansal, while pronouncing the order, ruled that the court has territorial jurisdiction to hear the matter but declined to restrain OpenAI from using ANI’s content at this stage.

“I am of the prima facie view that OpenAI’s act of storing ANI’s original works… falls under Section 52(1)(a) of the Copyright Act and therefore does not amount to infringement under Section 5,” the judge said.

The court also held that ChatGPT’s responses do not constitute copyright infringement under Section 51 of the Copyright Act because the outputs generated by OpenAI are not substantially similar to ANI’s original works.

The court found no evidence that ChatGPT had memorised and reproduced ANI’s content. “ANI has failed to satisfy this court that any memorisation regurgitation of ANI’s work has happened from responses generated by ChatGPT,” Bansal said.

A detailed copy of the order is awaited.

The case, in which summons were issued in November 2024, is the first copyright lawsuit against ChatGPT in India. ANI has alleged that OpenAI commercially exploited its original news content by using it to train ChatGPT without permission.

It also claimed that the chatbot could reproduce its reports verbatim and sometimes attributed fabricated statements to the news agency through AI “hallucinations”, harming its reputation and potentially spreading misinformation.

OpenAI contested the maintainability of the suit before Indian courts, arguing that its AI models were trained outside India and that its servers are located in the United States. The company also argued that its training process is transformative, that factual news cannot be protected by copyright, and that publishers can opt out of web crawling through a blocklist if they do not want their content used.

title: What Actually Matters.
content:
Databricks and Microsoft have renewed their partnership, extending it into the 2030s.

Databricks will enhance its operations by utilising Azure Databricks and upgrading to Azure Cobalt 200 for improved performance.

Databricks and Microsoft have extended their strategic partnership, taking the agreement, which began nearly a decade ago, into the 2030s.

Under the arrangement, Databricks will increase its use of Azure Databricks to run its core business operations and build its lakehouse. The company will also expand its use of Azure Cobalt, Microsoft's Arm-based infrastructure, moving from Cobalt 100 to Cobalt 200, which Microsoft claims improves performance by up to 50% and includes memory encryption by default.

Microsoft, in turn, will continue to integrate the Databricks Data and AI Platform across its product range, bringing tools such as Genie, Databricks' AI co-worker, into customer workflows across Microsoft 365, Teams, Copilot, Power BI, Power Platform, Microsoft Purview, and Microsoft Foundry.

Ali Ghodsi, Co-founder and CEO of Databricks, said that the partnership is now at its strongest. "For nearly a decade, Databricks and Microsoft have helped enterprises innovate with data and AI," he said in a statement.

He added that Genie and Unity AI Gateway are now built into Microsoft's products, letting customers unify their data and ground AI systems in business knowledge, while managing costs and governance as they scale their use of agents and models.

Judson Althoff, chief executive of Microsoft's commercial business, added that the companies are working to connect data, AI, and business context so that firms can make decisions faster and measure the results. He noted that Databricks' expanded use of Azure Databricks and Cobalt-based infrastructure should give customers more performance, efficiency and scale for demanding workloads, along with confidence in a platform already used at enterprise scale.

According to the companies, customers including Banco Bradesco, the Cincinnati Reds, Electrolux, SMBC, and Unilever already run workloads on Azure Databricks.

Databricks says more than 20,000 organisations, including AT&T, Bayer, BMW Group, HSBC, and T-Mobile, use its Data and AI Platform, which includes Genie, Lakebase, Agent Bricks, Lakeflow, Lakehouse, and Unity Catalog.

title: AMD Extends CPU, GPU and Rack-Scale Roadmap Through 2030
content:
AMD announced the Instinct MI400 GPU family, the Helios rack-scale AI platform, the 6th Gen EPYC 9006 processors, at its Advancing AI 2026 event.

The Instinct MI400 series includes the MI455X for frontier AI workloads and the MI430X for sovereign AI and high-performance computing. The GPUs feature HBM4 memory and are designed for large-scale training and inference, offering a substantial performance improvement over their predecessors.

The company also introduced the 6th Gen “Venice” EPYC 9006 processor family, positioning it as CPUs designed for the emerging era of agentic AI. AMD claims the processors offer better performance than competing CPU offerings from NVIDIA, Intel and Arm.

AMD now expects the global server CPU market to grow by more than 50% to over $200 billion by 2030, up from roughly $25 billion today.

Su also confirmed that these server processors have entered full production, describing customer demand as the strongest AMD has ever seen for an EPYC launch.

She added that all major server OEMs and leading cloud providers are expected to begin deploying Venice-based systems in the fourth quarter.

AMD has designed the sixth-generation EPYC Venice family for three distinct classes of workloads rather than a single universal configuration.

The portfolio spans general-purpose CPU servers for enterprise and cloud computing, GPU host-node servers that orchestrate large-scale AI clusters, and CPU servers optimised for AI agent sandbox environments.

According to AMD, EPYC is the only server CPU portfolio purpose-built to address all three workload categories.

AMD officially introduced Helios, its rack-scale AI platform that combines Instinct MI455X GPUs, 6th Gen EPYC processors, Pensando networking and ROCm software into a unified system designed to scale from individual racks to gigawatt-scale AI clusters.

Helios has entered production, and the company states it offers 15% more compute and 50% more memory than NVIDIA’s Vera Rubin NVL72 rack-scale solution.

Several of the announcements build on products AMD had previously outlined. The company first disclosed its MI400 roadmap and previewed the Helios architecture during Advancing AI 2025.

AMD said its Helios rack-scale AI platform has been adopted by several leading AI labs and cloud providers, including OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, Microsoft, Oracle, HUMAIN, TensorWave, Vultr and Cirrascale.

The company added that Helios systems will be available through OEMs such as Bull, HPE, Lenovo and Supermicro, alongside manufacturing partners Sanmina and Wiwynn.

AMD also announced a partnership with Cerebras to combine the latter's Wafer-Scale Engine with Helios rack-scale infrastructure, aiming to improve the performance and economics of low-latency AI inference deployments.

Recently, Anthropic announced it will deploy up to 2 gigawatts of AMD’s Instinct MI450 Series GPUs through Helios rack-scale systems. AMD has committed to make an equity investment of up to $5 billion in Anthropic.

The first gigawatt of deployments is scheduled to begin in the first half of 2027. The announcement expands Anthropic’s use of AMD hardware, building on its existing deployment of AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs.

Anthropic said it will deploy AMD Helios systems powered by Instinct MI455X GPUs, EPYC Venice CPUs, Pensando networking and ROCm software to support training and inference for its Claude family of models.

AMD also extended its product roadmap through the end of the decade, outlining plans for annual updates across its EPYC server CPUs, Instinct GPUs, networking portfolio and rack-scale AI systems.

On the CPU side, the company said its “Zen 7”-based EPYC processors, codenamed “Florence,” “Ferrara” and “Fidenza,” are scheduled to arrive in 2028, followed by the “Zen 8”-based “Ravenna” family in 2030. AMD said the upcoming chips will continue to focus on improving server density, performance, performance per dollar and energy efficiency.

For AI accelerators, AMD confirmed that the Instinct MI500 Series will launch in 2027, followed by the MI600 Series in 2028, both featuring next-generation compute, memory and interconnect technologies.

Together, the roadmap signals AMD's intent to maintain an annual release cadence across its AI and data centre portfolio through 2030.

title: Margins Under Pressure
content:
Mid-tier IT services firm Mphasis reported a nearly 11% year-on-year rise in consolidated net profit to ₹489.5 crore for the June quarter, as the company continued to bet on artificial intelligence-led deals even as margins came under pressure.

The net profit, however, declined sequentially from ₹509.6 crore reported in the March quarter.

Revenue from operations for the quarter stood at ₹4,384 crore, up 17.5% from ₹3,732.5 crore a year earlier and 3.3% higher sequentially.

In constant currency terms, revenue growth was more muted at 8.3% YoY and 2.1% sequentially, while in US dollar terms the company grew 7.7% YoY and 1.8% QoQ.

Earnings per share for the quarter were ₹25.6, up from ₹23.2 a year ago but down from ₹26.7 in the preceding quarter.

The Bengaluru-headquartered company said new deal wins, measured in Total Contract Value (TCV), stood at $461 million for the quarter, of which 63% were classified as AI-led—the company's clearest disclosure yet on how much of its incremental business is being driven by AI-related work.

"We are pleased with the momentum as we enter the financial year, and the early market acceptance of Mphasis Tria, which has elevated us to a platform-led AI partner for enterprise clients," Nitin Rakesh, CEO and Managing Director of Mphasis, said in a statement.

"Q1 FY27 was a strong start, with revenue growth of 2.1% sequentially in constant currency, with strong pipeline and TCV wins. We expect further acceleration in sequential growth in Q2 FY27," he added.

Gross margin for the quarter fell 140 basis points sequentially and 200 bps year-on-year to 26.9%, signifying that the IT firm is left with less cash to back new products. Operating margin declined 60 bps QoQ and 50 bps YoY to 14.8%, while net margin slipped 80 bps QoQ and 60 bps YoY to 11.2%, even as the topline expanded, pointing to rising costs even as the company scales its AI offerings.

Total expenses for the quarter rose to ₹3,784.5 crore from ₹3,203.3 crore a year earlier, with employee benefit costs, the largest expense line, at ₹2,408.7 crore.

Banking and Financial Services remained the largest vertical, contributing revenue of ₹2,354.8 crore for the quarter, followed by technology, media, and telecom at ₹812.4 crore, and insurance at ₹665.9 crore. The logistics and transportation segment saw a decline YoY.

Among the deals disclosed for the quarter, Mphasis said a tier-1 US telecom company picked the firm for AI-driven cost reduction and automation initiatives, while a top-tier investment bank engaged it for crypto, tokenisation, and multicurrency capability work.

The company completed two inorganic additions during the quarter—the acquisition of Theory and Practice Business Intelligence, a Canada-based decision-intelligence platform maker, and OKIN Process Inc's business process outsourcing unit.

In a subsequent event, Mphasis said it had signed a definitive agreement on July 1 to acquire a customer contract from IT staffing and recruitment firm Red Oak Tech for a consideration of up to $28 million, including $15 million in contingent payments. The deal had not closed as of the date the board approved the results.

Mphasis’ shares remained relatively stagnant post the results, trading at ₹2,235 apiece on the NSE at 12:10 pm on July 24.

content:
Travis Kalanick’s industrial AI startup Atoms has raised $1.7 billion in equity financing led by Andreessen Horowitz (a16z). a16z’s co-founder Ben Horowitz will be joining the company’s board.

As part of the transaction, Kalanick said Atoms has consolidated its various businesses, including CloudKitchens, under a single Atoms equity structure, marking the next phase of the company he publicly launched earlier this year after operating largely in stealth.

Kalanick described the investment as “unfinished business,” referring to his long-standing relationship with Andreessen Horowitz.

In a post on X announcing the financing, he said, “Fuel to complete the bits-to-atoms story arc we started at Uber, continued at CloudKitchens and will now finish at Atoms.”

In March, Kalanick launched Atoms by consolidating CloudKitchens, his ghost-kitchen and food logistics business, and City Storage Systems, the industrial real estate company that acquires and redevelops properties for logistics and food production, under a single corporate structure.

He said the business had spent roughly eight years operating in stealth before unveiling its industrial robotics strategy.

At launch, Kalanick said Atoms would prioritise specialised industrial robots over humanoids, arguing that purpose-built systems are better suited for sectors such as mining, transport and food production than general-purpose robotic platforms.

The company previously said it is exploring technologies spanning autonomous mining equipment, food production infrastructure and transportation robotics as part of its broader vision to digitise physical industries through AI-driven automation.

The former Uber CEO said the funding follows strong investor interest after Atoms emerged from years of “ninja-level stealth.”

He reiterated the company’s ambition to digitise industrial sectors through what it calls Industrial AI, combining software, sensors, robotics and AI to automate large-scale physical operations.

Kalanick argues that Atoms extends a strategy that began with Uber’s transportation network and later CloudKitchens’ food infrastructure.

“Uber was first. Network for the physical world,” he wrote. “CloudKitchens was next. A food computer with a focus on CPU and Storage.” Atoms, he said, is intended to become an OEM building “atoms-based computers” for industries including manufacturing, mining, construction, transport and food production.

When Atoms emerged from stealth in March, Kalanick positioned the company around specialised industrial robots rather than humanoid systems.

The company said it would focus on robotics platforms for food, mining and transportation, arguing that task-specific machines offer a clearer path to commercial deployment than general-purpose humanoid robots.

Kalanick also described transportation as the “network” layer of the physical economy and manufacturing as its “CPU,” framing Atoms as software for large industrial systems rather than standalone robots.

Alongside Andreessen Horowitz, Atoms listed Bain Capital, Uber, Fifth Wall, Chemistry, A*, K5 Global, Abstract, SV Angel and Alpha Square Group as equity investors, while Bank of America, Goldman Sachs, Wells Fargo, JPMorgan and Barclays were named as debt partners.

title: Advertise with Us
content:
ServiceNow has invested $40 million in Indian banking software company BUSINESSNEXT as part of its Series C funding round, valuing the company at $700 million.

The companies said the investment will be used to expand autonomous banking capabilities and private AI deployments for banks and financial institutions.

The partnership combines BUSINESSNEXT’s banking-focused customer relationship management (CRM), lending, and AI capabilities with ServiceNow’s Financial Services Operations (FSO) platform, which manages middle and back-office workflows such as case management, complaints handling and AI-driven operations.

The companies said the joint offering is intended to create a unified operating platform for financial services institutions by connecting customer-facing operations with enterprise workflows. The collaboration will initially focus on accelerating adoption across the Asia-Pacific region.

“Autonomous banking is not a vision we are chasing—it is a category we have been building for years,” said Nishant Singh, CEO of BUSINESSNEXT. “Today, as AI has matured, this investment will further accelerate our efforts to deliver private AI solutions, meeting the unique needs of banking and financial services, helping ensure the highest level of security while meeting all regulatory governance frameworks and sovereignty aspects.”

Kulmeet Bawa, Group Vice President and Managing Director for India and SAARC at ServiceNow, said India’s financial services sector is moving from digital transformation to AI-led operations.

“ServiceNow’s investment in BUSINESSNEXT is a direct bet on that transformation, bringing together deep banking intelligence and enterprise-grade AI orchestration to help Indian banks and insurers move faster, serve customers better, and operate with far greater efficiency,” Bawa said.

According to the companies, BUSINESSNEXT manages customer acquisition, engagement and real-time customer intelligence, while ServiceNow’s FSO platform orchestrates operational workflows across the middle and back office.

The integration will also incorporate ServiceNow’s AI Control Tower to coordinate AI workflows across financial services organisations.

Singh said the partnership connects customer intelligence with enterprise execution in real time.

“With deep banking intelligence and AI-led customer engagement capabilities, financial institutions can now operate with greater speed, intelligence, and coordination across all customer and operational touchpoints,” he said.

BUSINESSNEXT said its platform is deployed across more than 75,000 branches and serves over one billion end customers globally through banks and financial institutions. The company said it supports more than one million users across customer engagement, lending and financial services operations.

title: Advertise with Us
content:
ServiceNow has revealed its AI platform ServiceNow AI has crossed $1 billion in annual contract value (ACV) during the June quarter, indicating the rapid monetisation of enterprise AI as the workflow software company posted stronger-than-expected second-quarter results and raised its full-year revenue outlook.

ServiceNow AI is the enterprise-wide AI platform embedded directly into the core ServiceNow infrastructure, rather than being a separate, standalone business entity.

The US-based enterprise software company reported subscription revenue of $3.88 billion, up 24.5% year-on-year, while total revenue rose 24% to $3.99 billion in the quarter ended June 30.

Current remaining performance obligations (cRPO), contract revenue that will be recognised as revenue in the next 12 months, climbed 21% to $13.2 billion, while total remaining performance obligations reached $29 billion, also up 21% from a year earlier.

The company attributed much of the momentum to accelerating enterprise adoption of AI, particularly agentic AI applications.

“With our AI Control Tower as the market standard, agentic deployments of ServiceNow AI increased ninefold in just nine months. Our $29 billion in remaining performance obligations is fueled by longer customer commitments and skyrocketing demand from our partner ecosystem. We are who we said we were: a defining company that is only just getting started,” ServiceNow Chairman and CEO Bill McDermott said in a statement.

During the quarter, ServiceNow expanded its AI portfolio with the launch of Otto, a unified AI interface combining Now Assist and Moveworks capabilities, alongside new AI governance and measurement features under AI Control Tower.

It also introduced AI specialists for IT, customer service, employee workflows and security, while making its Build Agent generally available across developer tools including Cursor, Claude Code, Windsurf and GitHub Copilot.

The company also unveiled Action Fabric, enabling third-party AI models to securely execute workflows through the ServiceNow platform, with Anthropic becoming its first design partner. It further strengthened AI partnerships with NVIDIA, Microsoft, AWS and Accenture during the quarter.

Notably, its collaboration with Accenture includes a forward-deployed engineering programme aimed at helping enterprises scale AI deployments from pilots to production.

Reflecting confidence in AI-led demand, ServiceNow raised its full-year 2026 subscription revenue guidance to $15.76 billion-$15.78 billion, representing about 22.5% reported growth. The company said stronger-than-expected AI-driven contract wins, along with robust US federal demand, supported the upgrade.

ServiceNow said it closed 123 transactions worth more than $1 million in net new ACV during the quarter, up nearly 40% year-on-year, and ended June with 658 customers generating over $5 million in ACV, reflecting continued expansion among large enterprises.

Earlier this year, at its Financial Analyst Day, the company outlined long-term goals of generating more than $30 billion in subscription revenue by 2030, with 30% of ACV expected to come from AI.
