title: Guidance Trimmed
content:
Infosys said artificial intelligence work now accounts for 8.2% of its revenue, as India's second-largest IT services company reported a 12.2% year-on-year rise in consolidated net profit to ₹7,769 crore for the June quarter (Q1 FY27), even as it trimmed the upper end of its full-year revenue growth guidance.

However, the net profit slid 9.3% sequentially.

Revenue from operations came in at ₹48,211 crore, up 14% YoY and only 3.9% quarter-on-quarter.

In dollar terms, the revenue was $5.082 billion, up 2.4% YoY and 1% QoQ.

Infosys’ operating margin was 21.1%, an improvement of 30 basis points YoYr and 10 basis points sequentially.

The company said large deal wins totalled $3.6 billion for the quarter, with 61% of that being net-new business, a signal of AI-linked engagements converting into fresh mandates rather than just renewals.

“We saw strong acceleration in our AI work with AI revenues at 8.2%. This is growing at double digits quarter-on-quarter for the last several quarters. With this momentum, we see long-term relevance of our services for our clients, which are all driven through AI,” Salil Parekh, CEO of Infosys, said in a press briefing.

Infosys narrowed its FY27 constant-currency revenue growth guidance to 1.5–3.0%, down from the 1.5–3.5% range it had given at its Q4 FY26 results in April, effectively a cut to the top end of the band. Operating margin guidance was retained at 20–22%.

“The upper end of the guidance was really based on whether the macro (factors) were improving. We now see the macro may improve, but not at the level that we were thinking initially, and so that's how we really constructed the guidance,” Parekh added.

The company also had a one-time revenue impact of a client decision during the quarter.

In a separate, significant announcement alongside the results, Infosys said its board has appointed Ashiss Kumar Dash, a three-decade Infosys veteran currently heading a diverse portfolio of industry verticals, as CEO Designate with immediate effect.

Dash is set to take over as Chief Executive Officer and Managing Director from April 1, 2027, succeeding Salil Parekh, whose second term concludes after more than nine years leading the company.

Infosys affirmed that large deal wins were powered by Infosys Topaz, its AI-first set of services, solutions, and platforms. Like other IT majors, it plans to position forward deployed engineers into clients’ AI workflows as AI giants like OpenAI and Anthropic threaten to eat into the IT enterprise services revenue.

“We are building a team of frontier engineers to support client work. Our plan is to have 6,000 frontier engineers over the next few years. We built a platform, Topaz Fabric, that enables our clients to get the benefits of AI while keeping the sovereignty of their own data within their company,” said Parekh.

Infosys has signed several AI-linked collaborations during the quarter.

This includes a renewed, expanded engagement with Mercedes-Benz Group AG to move its hybrid cloud and data-centre operations to an AI-led operating model, a tie-up with OpenAI to help enterprises move Codex—OpenAI's coding agent platform—from pilot use into large-scale deployment, spanning legacy code modernisation, code review automation, and vulnerability detection.

It has also collaborated with the US-based software delivery platform Harness for enterprise transformation and modernisation programs.

Geographically, North America continues to dominate the topline, with 56.35% of revenue coming from the region. Curiously, contribution from India slid to 2.46% in Q1 FY27 from 2.88% in the comparable quarter a year ago.

The quarter also saw contribution from Europe increasing by a percentage point.

Total headcount stood at 328,062 as of June 30, a marginal sequential decline of 532 employees but up 4,274 from a year earlier. Employee benefit expenses continued to be the major incurring costs, up 10.7% YoY to ₹25,287 crore.

Voluntary attrition ticked up to 13.0% from 12.6% in the March quarter.

Infosys’ shares closed marginally higher at the NSE on July 23 at ₹1,052.9 apiece.

title: What Actually Matters.
content:
GitHub is restructuring its bug bounty programme to enhance the quality of submissions amid a rise in low-quality, AI-generated reports.

A new VIP tier will reward top researchers with higher payouts and faster responses, emphasising quality over quantity in submissions.

GitHub has announced a major overhaul of its bug bounty programme, introducing an invite-only VIP tier for top security researchers while lowering payouts in its public programme to focus on higher-quality vulnerability reports.

The changes will take effect from July 27, 2026.

The Microsoft-owned platform said the update comes after months of reviewing its bug bounty programme, which has seen a growing number of submissions, including an increase in low-quality and AI-generated reports.

As part of the restructuring, GitHub is launching a permanent private VIP programme for researchers who consistently report high-impact security vulnerabilities. They will receive higher rewards, faster response times, and closer collaboration with GitHub’s security engineering team.

Under the new VIP payout structure, researchers can earn $1,000 for low-severity bugs, $7,500 for medium-severity issues, $20,000 for high-severity vulnerabilities, and over $30,000 for critical findings.

To qualify, they must demonstrate a strong track record by reporting one critical bug, two high-severity bugs, four medium-severity bugs, or seven low-severity bugs.

“The core shift here is in what we’re incentivising: you don’t earn more by submitting more. You earn more by submitting better,” GitHub said in the blog post.

The company has also revised payouts for its public bug bounty programme. Instead of offering payout ranges, it will now use fixed rewards to make compensation more predictable.

Under the updated public programme, researchers will receive $250 for low-severity reports, $2,000 for medium, $5,000 for high, and $10,000 for critical vulnerabilities.

GitHub said the public programme will continue to serve as an entry point for researchers who may eventually qualify for the VIP tier.

To reduce spam and AI-generated submissions, the company is also introducing a HackerOne signal requirement. New researchers who do not yet meet the platform’s trust threshold will initially be limited to four submissions while building their reputation.

The company added that the measure is intended to improve report quality rather than discourage newcomers.

The reports submitted before July 27 will continue to be evaluated under the existing payout structure. Looking ahead, the company will continue investing in faster response times, clearer communication, stronger engagement with the security research community, and improved collaboration through industry events such as DEF CON.

title: Advertise with Us
content:
AMD and Cerebras also announced a partnership to deliver a disaggregated AI inference system combining AMD's Helios rack-scale infrastructure with Cerebras' Wafer-Scale Engine.

By separating inference processing across the two compute platforms, the companies say the architecture can deliver up to five times higher tokens per second per watt than a Cerebras Wafer-Scale Engine-only configuration.

The claim is based on July 2026 modelling by AMD Performance Labs and Cerebras using the Kimi 2.6 1T model at a comparable interactivity point.

Lisa Su, AMD CEO, said, “Together with Cerebras, we are extending that leadership into the most latency-sensitive applications and creating a powerful new platform for real-time agentic AI.”

“The demand for ultra-fast inference is growing at an unprecedented pace. Cerebras delivers the world’s fastest, ultra-low-latency inference,” said Cerebras CEO Andrew Feldman.

Cerebras plans to deploy AMD Helios systems in its data centres, with the joint solution expected to become available initially through Cerebras Cloud in the second half of this year.

Cerebras is an AI chipmaker best known for its Wafer-Scale Engine (WSE), a processor built from an entire silicon wafer rather than individual chips.

It develops AI hardware and systems for training and inference, positioning its wafer-scale architecture as a faster and more efficient alternative to large GPU clusters.

The company went public on the NASDAQ on May 14, after raising more than $2 billion in private funding over roughly 10 years since its founding in 2015.

Its final private funding round was a $1 billion Series H completed in February, valuing the company at approximately $23 billion.

Cerebras has also secured partnerships with two of the biggest names in AI infrastructure.

In January, OpenAI signed a multi-year agreement to deploy 750 MW of Cerebras wafer-scale AI systems to power low-latency inference for ChatGPT and other services, with the rollout planned through 2028.

Two months later, Amazon Web Services (AWS) announced that it would deploy Cerebras systems in its data centres and make them available through Amazon Bedrock.

The collaboration combines AWS Trainium chips for the prefill stage of inference with Cerebras’ Wafer-Scale Engine for decoding, with the companies claiming the architecture can deliver up to 5× higher token throughput in the same hardware footprint.

title: Advertise with Us
content:
AMD and Moonshot AI have jointly developed a new inference stack for Kimi K2.6 that they say significantly improves the performance of AI coding agents running on AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs.

Instead of optimising existing chatbot infrastructure, the companies redesigned the serving software around AI agents that write code, call tools and maintain long-running conversations.

In benchmark tests, the new stack reduced worst-case response latency by 3.2× and increased total token throughput by 7.7%.

The companies argue that AI agents place different demands on infrastructure than chatbots because they maintain much longer conversations, repeatedly access earlier context and spend much of their time waiting for tools such as web search or code execution.

As AMD puts it, “Agentic coding is cache-dominated and bursty,” making efficient memory management more important than simply adding more compute.

To address this, AMD built a new software layer called Unified Memory & Bandwidth Pool (UMBP) that allows AI models to retrieve previously processed context from GPU memory, system memory or storage instead of recalculating it.

According to the company, this turns cache management into something the scheduler can actively optimise rather than treating it as passive storage. AMD said the architecture lets the system decide not just “who has the prefix” but “who can serve it fastest.”

The companies evaluated the software using a custom benchmark derived from ProgramBench, which runs real Kimi coding sessions rather than synthetic inference requests.

In one configuration with 128 concurrent coding sessions, enabling the new cache architecture reduced p99 time-to-first-token from 17.3 seconds to 5.4 seconds while increasing throughput by 7.7%.

A second experiment, which simulated requests moving between inference workers, produced a 4.9% throughput improvement and a 1.6× reduction in tail latency by allowing cached context to remain accessible after migration.

Beyond the cache architecture, AMD introduced additional optimisations including incremental transfer of model state between inference stages, a tokeniser that processes only newly added conversation turns instead of re-tokenising entire sessions, and scheduling techniques that overlap tool execution with model inference to reduce idle GPU time.

AMD said it also verified that the infrastructure changes did not reduce model quality using Moonshot AI’s Kimi Vendor Verifier.

The company reported that enabling constrained tool decoding achieved 100% JSON schema accuracy while maintaining tool-calling performance comparable with Moonshot’s reference implementation. AMD said the “performance wins come with no accuracy tax.”

The companies said future work will focus on optimising the stack for the upcoming Kimi K3 model and extending the software to additional inference engines including AMD’s ATOM platform as well as the open-source SGLang and vLLM frameworks.

The announcement follows Moonshot AI’s release of Kimi K3 last week, a 2.8-trillion-parameter open-weight model designed for reasoning, coding and agentic workloads.

The model quickly rose to the top of several coding benchmarks and supports a 1 million-token context window, intensifying competition with frontier models from Anthropic and OpenAI.

Recently, AMD has broadened adoption of its AI hardware across the industry. The company has unveiled partnerships with OpenAI, Meta, Oracle, and Microsoft around its next-generation AI infrastructure, while its latest agreement with Anthropic includes deploying up to 2 GW of AMD Instinct MI450 GPUs and a multi-year engineering collaboration.

title: What Actually Matters.
content:
AI4Bharat developed FOCUS, a benchmark to assess the accuracy of vision-language models in evaluating AI outputs.

Evaluator VLMs, often used as 'AI judges', showed a significant failure rate in identifying mistakes, missing issues over half the time.

Researchers from AI4Bharat at IIT Madras and BITS Pilani Hyderabad have developed a new benchmark called FOCUS to test how reliably vision-language models (VLMs) evaluate the outputs of other AI models.

The research paper, titled “Seeing Isn’t Believing: Uncovering Blind Spots in Evaluator Vision-Language Models,” has been accepted at the Conference on Language Modeling (COLM) 2026.

Vision-language models are increasingly being used as “AI judges” to evaluate tasks such as image captioning, visual question answering, and text-to-image generation. However, the researchers questioned whether these evaluator models are accurate enough to be trusted on their own.

To investigate this, the team created FOCUS, a benchmark designed to measure how well evaluator VLMs detect mistakes across both image-to-text (I2T) and text-to-image (T2I) tasks.

The benchmark contains more than 4,000 carefully designed test cases covering 40 different types of perturbations, or intentional changes that reduce output quality. These examples were created through a human-in-the-loop process and validated by expert annotators.

Using FOCUS, the researchers evaluated several frontier vision-language models across three commonly used evaluation methods while testing different prompting strategies.

The study found that current evaluator VLMs often fail to identify degraded outputs. In some cases, the models missed quality issues in more than 50% of the test samples. Their performance was particularly weaker when evaluating text-to-image generation compared to image-to-text tasks.

According to the researchers, these findings suggest that AI models should not yet be relied upon as standalone evaluators for benchmarking or training other AI systems.

Instead, they recommend using human oversight alongside AI evaluation and treating automated evaluation scores with caution until more reliable systems are developed.

Along with the paper, the researchers have also open-sourced the FOCUS dataset and codebase to help the broader AI community study and improve evaluator vision-language models.

The work was led by Mohammed Safi Ur Rahman Khan, Sanjay Suryanarayanan, Tushar Anand, and Mitesh Khapra, with affiliations to AI4Bharat at IIT Madras and BITS Pilani Hyderabad.

title: JAN AI & VTU Bring Human-Centred AI Training to Women Engineering Students
content:
The company is training women engineers to use AI to address local challenges instead of focusing solely on automation.

What Actually Matters.

JAN AI collaborates with VTU to train women engineers in rural Karnataka to use AI for local challenges.

The 'She Innovates' initiative prioritises community understanding over traditional technology-focused training.

AI startup JAN AI has partnered with Visvesvaraya Technological University (VTU) and other organisations to train women engineering students to use AI to solve real-world challenges in rural Karnataka.

The initiative called ‘She Innovates’ recently concluded its second six-day residential bootcamp, bringing together 55 women engineering students from seven districts across the state.

The programme was organised by JAN AI in partnership with the Visvesvaraya Research & Innovation Foundation (VRIF), VTU, UN Women, Wipro, the Karnataka Digital Economy Mission (KDEM), and supported by TiE Bangalore and TiE Hubli.

Unlike conventional AI training programmes that begin with technology, She Innovates first exposed students to communities through village visits, empathy interviews and market research. Participants from Bengaluru, Belagavi, Chikkodi, Haveri, Vijayanagara, Mangaluru and Uttar Kannada worked to identify local problems before using generative AI, design thinking and rapid prototyping to develop startup-ready solutions.

According to JAN AI, the programme aims to encourage students to build AI applications that address grassroots challenges instead of focusing only on automation.

“Artificial intelligence is not about replacing human potential; it is about expanding it,” said Madan Padaki, Founder of JAN AI.

“At JAN AI, we believe the most impactful AI solutions don’t begin with technology; they begin with understanding the real challenges people face. When we empower young women to see problems in their communities as opportunities to innovate, AI becomes accessible, relevant and capable of creating lasting social and economic impact,” he added.

Students said the programme changed how they viewed entrepreneurship by teaching them to understand people’s needs before building technology.

“Coming into the bootcamp, I thought innovation was about building technology. I leave with the understanding that it begins with understanding people,” said participant Swati Patil.

During the six-day programme, participants conducted field visits, validated ideas with local communities and learnt to apply AI only after identifying genuine problems. The organisers said the initiative was designed to help students develop entrepreneurial thinking while using AI as a tool to create practical social and economic impact.

Speaking at the valedictory session, Prof Vidyashankar S, Chairman of VRIF and Vice-Chancellor of VTU, said programmes like She Innovates are important for developing innovators who can combine research, technology and entrepreneurship to solve societal challenges.

The company noted that the initiative is part of its broader vision of making AI more accessible and inclusive while encouraging young women to build AI solutions that are developed in India and designed to solve India’s real-world problems.

Indian cloud provider Utho Cloud plans to deploy 10,000 GPUs over the next two years as it looks to expand AI computing infrastructure in India.

The company said the deployment will take place over the next seven to eight quarters and will include NVIDIA H200, H100, A100, RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell, and L4 GPUs. The infrastructure will be hosted in India and support AI inference as well as large-scale model training.

Utho said the expansion is intended to address growing demand for AI compute while offering GPU capacity without long wait times. It added that customers will be billed in Indian rupees and that pricing will be up to 60% lower than rates charged by traditional hyperscale cloud providers.

“With this expansion, we will offer guaranteed GPU availability without extended wait times, sovereign AI compute with data and model training hosted within customer jurisdictions, transparent and predictable pricing, and the flexibility to support workloads ranging from AI inference to large-scale model training,” Manoj Dhanda, Founder and CEO of Utho Cloud, said in a statement.

“By combining 100% data residency, compliance with the Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, and cost-efficient AI infrastructure, we aim to remove the barriers that have long limited access to high-performance AI computing and accelerate India's journey towards becoming a global AI powerhouse,” he added.

The company said the infrastructure will allow customers to keep data and model training within India while retaining ownership of their intellectual property. It will also provide round-the-clock technical support for production AI workloads.

The announcement comes as enterprises globally face shortages of AI chips, higher infrastructure costs, and longer procurement timelines. Utho said its platform is intended to reduce dependence on overseas infrastructure by providing locally hosted AI compute with predictable pricing.

The Noida-based company, which offers cloud infrastructure with data residency in India, has more than 51,000 users and serves businesses across B2B, B2E, and B2G segments, including FIITJEE, Jindal Steel & Power, and APL Apollo.

content:
The White House has accused Chinese AI startup Moonshot AI of using Anthropic’s Claude Fable model to develop its newly launched Kimi K3, alleging the company carried out large-scale model distillation and used infrastructure designed to avoid detection.

In a post on X, White House Office of Science and Technology Policy Director Michael Kratsios said the US had information indicating that Moonshot AI “distilled Anthropic’s Fable for the development of its K3 model.”

“To do this they developed a sophisticated internal platform to conduct large scale distillation against US models, allowing them to quickly switch between multiple methods of access to avoid detection,” Kratsios wrote.

The accusation comes days after Moonshot unveiled Kimi K3, an open-weight model that drew attention for approaching the performance of leading US frontier models.

He also alleged that Moonshot AI had acquired servers equipped with NVIDIA GB300 GPUs and had accessed GB300 systems in Thailand “likely to train its AI models.”

Kratsios distinguished between legitimate model distillation and what he described as industrial-scale theft of proprietary technology.

“The United States strongly supports the free and fair development of AI,” he said. “Legitimate AI distillation used to create smaller, more efficient models plays a vital role in this open innovation ecosystem. However, large-scale, covert industrial distillation aimed at stealing proprietary US technology and undermining American research is unacceptable.”

The US government has not released technical evidence supporting the allegations, and Moonshot AI had not publicly responded at the time of publication.

The accusations come less than a week after Moonshot AI launched Kimi K3, a 2.8 trillion-parameter open-weight mixture-of-experts model with a one million-token context window.

The company said K3 was built for reasoning, coding and agentic workloads, and positioned it against Anthropic’s Fable 5 and OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 series.

The allegations also revive concerns over AI model distillation, a technique in which a smaller model learns from the outputs of a larger one. The approach is widely used across the industry for efficiency and cost reduction.

However, AI companies have increasingly argued that using proprietary frontier models without permission to create competing systems crosses legal and commercial boundaries.

Anthropic’s Fable 5 has itself been at the centre of recent US policy actions. The model was temporarily restricted last month after the US government imposed export controls citing national security concerns before restoring global access on July 1 after those controls were lifted.

ST Telemedia Global Data Centres, India (STT GDC India) has launched STT Jaipur 1, Rajasthan’s first high-performance data centre, marking the company’s entry into the state as it expands its AI and cloud infrastructure footprint beyond India’s tier-1 cities.

The new facility is designed to support high-performance computing (HPC), cloud workloads, enterprise applications and AI-driven use cases, catering to growing demand for compute-intensive infrastructure from enterprises, government organisations, cloud providers and digital-native businesses.

With the launch, STT GDC India has expanded its national network to 34 data centres across 10 cities, with a cumulative 613 MW IT load capacity, reinforcing its strategy to build digital infrastructure in emerging technology hubs.

STT Jaipur 1 is being developed with an IT design capacity of 6 MW, a total power load of 10 MVA, and is housed in a three-storey facility spread across 5,971 square metres. According to the company, the data centre has been designed with a focus on energy efficiency, operational resilience and environmental, social and governance (ESG) principles to support customers’ sustainability goals.

Commenting on the launch, Bimal Khandelwal, Chief Executive Officer of STT GDC India, said, “India’s digital growth is being driven by increasing demand for data-intensive applications, cloud adoption and high-performance computing capabilities. Infrastructure will be critical in enabling this next phase of growth. The launch of STT Jaipur 1 represents a strategic investment in Rajasthan’s digital future and reflects our conviction that the next wave of digital infrastructure growth will extend well beyond India’s tier-1 cities.”

He added that Rajasthan is emerging as a key destination for technology investments.

“With STT Jaipur 1, we are bringing high-performance data centre capabilities to the region, enabling enterprises, cloud providers, and public sector organisations to scale securely and efficiently. As the state’s first enterprise-grade data centre, this facility will play a pivotal role in supporting Rajasthan’s digital economy and strengthening India's broader AI infrastructure ecosystem,” he mentioned.

The company said the launch comes amid rising demand for AI, cloud computing and data-intensive applications, which are driving the need for scalable and resilient digital infrastructure across India. The Jaipur facility is expected to support enterprises looking to deploy advanced computing workloads while strengthening the state's digital infrastructure ecosystem.

The announcement is part of STT GDC India’s broader expansion strategy to extend enterprise-grade digital infrastructure beyond established metro markets and support India’s growing AI and digital economy.

content:
Microsoft and French AI startup Mistral have expanded their partnership with a multibillion-dollar agreement to increase AI compute capacity in Europe, while making Mistral’s latest models available across Microsoft’s AI platform for enterprise customers, particularly those in regulated industries.

The partnership includes Microsoft’s commitment to use part of Mistral’s Europe-based GPU infrastructure, which will be built using thousands of NVIDIA Vera Rubin GPUs. Microsoft said the additional capacity will support AI development and help meet growing demand for its cloud and AI services.

The companies are bringing Mistral's Medium 3.5 and OCR 4 models to Microsoft Foundry, while Medium 3.5 is now also available in Microsoft Copilot Studio. Customers will be able to build AI applications using the same models and tools across Azure, Azure Local and fully disconnected environments.

Azure and Azure Local will support three deployment options: cloud-hosted deployments, cloud-connected customer-controlled environments, and fully disconnected deployments for organisations with strict operational or regulatory requirements.

The announcement comes as governments and enterprises in Europe seek greater control over where AI models run and how sensitive data is handled. Microsoft said the partnership extends its sovereign cloud strategy by combining Mistral's models with Azure’s security, compliance and deployment capabilities.

“Europe should have access to the world’s most capable AI without compromising control over their data, operations or digital future,” said Brad Smith, Vice Chair and President at Microsoft. “By bringing Mistral's frontier European models into our sovereign cloud portfolio and enabling them across public cloud, cloud-connected and fully disconnected environments, we are honouring the European Digital Commitments we made and giving customers a trusted foundation for AI they can operate on their own terms.”

Arthur Mensch, Co-founder and CEO of Mistral, said the partnership will help the company reach more enterprise and public-sector customers.

“Our mission has always been to put frontier AI in the hands of every organisation while keeping them in control of their technology,” Mensch said. “With Microsoft as our partner, our models reach enterprises and public institutions at global scale, delivered through a platform trusted for the most demanding, regulated workloads and available everywhere our customers operate.”

Microsoft and Mistral also said they will jointly pursue enterprise customers in Europe and other markets by funding proof-of-concept projects, providing Azure credits and conducting customer workshops to accelerate AI adoption.

Google has launched three new AI models under the Gemini lineup: Gemini 3.6 Flash, Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite, and Gemini 3.5 Flash Cyber.

Gemini 3.6 Flash and Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite are available immediately through the Gemini API in Google AI Studio and Android Studio, Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, and the Gemini app. Google said it will also begin rolling out Flash-Lite in Google Search.

The company said Gemini 3.6 Flash replaces Gemini 3.5 Flash as its primary workhorse model, offering lower token usage, lower inference costs, and improved performance across coding, knowledge work and multimodal tasks.

“Our newest Gemini models deliver the efficiency, latency, and reliability to build AI agents at scale,” Tulsee Doshi, Senior Director of Product Management at Google, wrote in a blog post.

Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite targets high-throughput workloads with lower latency, while Gemini 3.5 Flash Cyber is a specialised model for cybersecurity applications. Modelled as a rival to Anthropic’s Claude Mythos, it will initially be available only to governments and selected partners through Google’s CodeMender AI code security agent that can scan and fix software vulnerabilities.

“AI models have become capable of finding security vulnerabilities faster than current systems can fix them,” Google said. “Tackling this growing threat requires an approach to securing software that is highly capable and efficient.”

Google also disclosed that Gemini 4 has entered pre-training, calling it its “most ambitious pre-training run yet”, while Gemini 3.5 Pro remains in testing with partners ahead of a broader release.

Gemini 3.6 Flash is priced at $1.50 per million input tokens and $7.50 per million output tokens, lower than Gemini 3.5 Flash. Google said the model uses 17% fewer output tokens than its predecessor on the Artificial Analysis Index, which offers a holistic measure of AI capabilities, and requires fewer reasoning steps and tool calls for multi-step workflows.

According to the company, Gemini 3.6 Flash improved its score on software engineering benchmark DeepSWE to 49% from 37%, OpenAI’s MLE Bench to 63.9% from 49.7%, edge applications-focused OSWorld-Verified to 83.0% from 78.4%, and GDPval-AA v2 to 1,421 from 1,349 on real-world evaluations.

Google added that customers including Harvey and Hebbia have used the model for document parsing, chart analysis, and report drafting.

Google said the model also includes updated safeguards against chemical, biological, radiological, nuclear, and cyber-offensive misuse while reducing refusals for legitimate use cases.

For cost-sensitive workloads, Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite costs $0.30 per million input tokens and $2.50 per million output tokens. The company said the model generates 350 output tokens per second, according to Artificial Analysis, and is intended for applications such as document processing, agentic search and large-scale automation.

Google said Flash-Lite outperformed Gemini 3 Flash on several benchmarks, including SWE-Bench Pro (54.2% versus 49.6%) and OSWorld-Verified (74.0% versus 65.1%), while also improving over Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite on coding, long-context reasoning, and real-world task execution.

AMD and Anthropic have announced a strategic partnership under which Anthropic will deploy up to 2 gigawatts of AMD’s Instinct MI450 Series GPUs in AMD’s Helios rack-scale systems, while AMD has committed to make an equity investment of up to $5 billion in the AI company.

The first gigawatt of deployments is scheduled to begin in the first half of 2027. The announcement expands Anthropic’s use of AMD hardware, building on its existing deployment of AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs.

Anthropic said it will deploy AMD Helios systems powered by Instinct MI455X GPUs, EPYC Venice CPUs, Pensando networking and ROCm software to support training and inference for its Claude family of models.

The companies will also launch a multi-year engineering collaboration focused on software optimisation.

Anthropic will use Claude to optimise workloads for AMD Instinct GPUs and accelerate development of AMD’s ROCm software stack. AMD, in turn, will adopt Claude across its engineering and product development teams.

“The collaboration brings together Anthropic’s leadership in frontier AI with the full strength of AMD high-performance computing,” said Lisa Su, chair and CEO of AMD. “Together, we will accelerate AI adoption at scale and establish Helios as a major platform for the next generation of AI infrastructure.”

Tom Brown, Co-founder and Chief Compute Officer at Anthropic, said compute capacity remains central to the company's ability to train and serve Claude.

“By partnering with AMD across the stack, we are securing the capacity we need and optimising it for training and serving Claude,” Brown said. “Running across a diversified range of hardware lets us map the right workloads to the right hardware.”

The announcement comes as Anthropic continues to secure dedicated computing capacity through long-term infrastructure partnerships.

The company already relies on Amazon Web Services as its primary cloud provider and has infrastructure agreements with Google Cloud. In recent months, it has also signed deals for additional compute capacity with SpaceX, Broadcom and other partners as demand for Claude has increased.

Anthropic, founded in 2021, has become one of the world’s most valuable AI startups. In February, it raised $30 billion in a Series G funding round at a $380 billion post-money valuation.

For AMD, the partnership represents one of its largest AI infrastructure deployments to date and strengthens its position in the market for AI accelerators, where it competes with NVIDIA and other chipmakers.

title: When Every Employee Can Talk to Data, Governance Becomes the Deciding Factor
content:
The evaluation ran models, including GPT-5.6 Sol and a more capable, unreleased model.

OpenAI said one of its internal cybersecurity evaluations found that AI models compromised parts of Hugging Face’s production infrastructure by exploiting vulnerabilities in OpenAI’s research environment.

The incident occurred last week during an internal benchmark designed to measure advanced cyber capabilities.

According to OpenAI, the evaluation intentionally ran models, including GPT-5.6 Sol and a more capable, unreleased model, with reduced cyber-safety refusals to assess their ability to complete complex exploitation tasks.

“We consider this incident to be an unprecedented cyber incident, involving state-of-the-art cyber capabilities, and are responding accordingly,” OpenAI said in its blog post.

OpenAI said the models first identified and exploited a previously unknown vulnerability in an internally hosted package registry cache proxy to obtain internet access from a sandboxed research environment.

“While operating in our sandboxed testing environment, our models spent a substantial amount of inference compute finding a way to obtain open Internet access, in pursuit of solving the evaluation problem,” it said.

After moving through OpenAI’s internal systems, the models searched for resources related to the ExploitGym benchmark and ultimately found a path into Hugging Face’s production infrastructure.

“In one example, the model chained together multiple attack vectors, including using stolen credentials and zero-day vulnerabilities to find a remote code execution path on the Hugging Face servers,” OpenAI said.

The company said the models were attempting to obtain benchmark solutions directly rather than pursuing broader objectives.

OpenAI added that its security team detected the activity internally, while Hugging Face independently identified and contained the intrusion on its own infrastructure before the two companies began a joint investigation.

OpenAI said it has since disclosed the zero-day vulnerability to the affected software vendor and is implementing stricter infrastructure controls, expanding monitoring during model evaluations, and strengthening safeguards around future cyber capability testing. Hugging Face has also joined OpenAI's trusted access programme to use the company's models for defensive security work.

The incident comes as AI companies increasingly test whether advanced models can autonomously discover, chain and exploit vulnerabilities across multiple systems.

OpenAI said recent evaluations by the UK AI Security Institute indicate models such as GPT-5.6 Sol can sustain complex cyber operations over extended periods, and the latest incident suggests those capabilities can translate to real-world environments.

“We’re grateful for the collaboration with OpenAI on this and other topics. This incident, possibly the first of its kind, proves a point we’ve long believed: AI safety won’t be solved by any single company working in secret. It will be solved in the open, collaboratively, with broad access to AI for every defender, everywhere,” said Clem Delangue, co-founder and CEO of Hugging Face.

OpenAI said it will publish additional findings after completing its joint forensic investigation with Hugging Face, including details on the vulnerabilities, attack path and lessons for securing future model evaluations.

As Indian banks and NBFCs swap static dashboards for conversational AI, data governance has become the industry’s central concern. Experts explain how regulated enterprises can adopt natural-language analytics without compromising compliance or data control.

What Actually Matters.

Indian banks and NBFCs are shifting from static dashboards to conversational AI for enhanced customer interaction.

Data governance has emerged as a critical concern amid increased accessibility of information within organisations.

As India’s banking, insurance and non-banking finance sectors embrace enterprise AI, one critical shift demands attention. Organisations are moving away from dashboards towards conversational AI. While this enables customers' queries and issues to be resolved almost instantly, it also comes with a cost: information flows within the organisation become far more accessible.

For institutions operating under RBI, SEBI and IRDAI oversight, that shift raises a question sharper than most technology transitions: who gets to see what, and can the organisation prove it?

This is becoming a pressing issue for firms in the sector because the Guidance on Regulatory Principles for Model Risk Management, 2026, by the RBI mandates board-level oversight, model classification, ‘kill switch’ mechanisms, and mandatory human oversight of automated decisions. The framework applies across commercial banks, small finance banks, payments banks, cooperative banks, NBFCs and credit information companies.

Supratik Shankar, Co-Founder of enterprise data platform Dview, argues that this is the real inflection point in enterprise AI adoption—and one the industry has been slow to grapple with. “A dashboard is pre-scoped by a data team, but a natural language interface is unbounded, so governance can no longer live inside report design.”

Dview has built its data and analytics stack, comprising a data ingestion layer, a query engine, and a conversational analytics layer, for banks, NBFCs and fintechs that cannot afford to treat data exposure as merely a security lapse. In these sectors, Shankar notes, a governance failure is a regulatory event.

Access Control Before the Model Sees a Query

The company’s core design decision, according to Shankar, is to resolve permissions before a question ever reaches the language model. “The system resolves user identity, role and permissioned data scope at the moment of query, not at the moment of responses.”

In practice, this means a chief risk officer and a branch collections officer asking an identical question receive answers drawn from different, role-appropriate slices of the same dataset.

This becomes particularly relevant given the newer risks that conversational interfaces introduce, such as adversarial phrasing designed to extract data outside a user’s authority. Shankar says the platform treats this as an engineering problem rather than a policy one. “No prompt engineering can circumvent a data access boundary that is enforced below the model.”

Shams Tabrej, CEO of Ezeepay, tells AIM that the cost of compliance will be high in the early years. “Given the governance, documentation, monitoring, audit trails and expertise that need to be built, NBFCs and fintechs will likely need heavier investment in technology, people and oversight than large banks with mature governance already.”

Srividhya Sridhar of Vivriti Next offers a counterpoint, noting that automated decision-making is already more prevalent at new-age NBFCs and fintechs than at legacy banks. As a result, the governance gap may not necessarily track institutional size in the way many assume.

Avoiding a Rebuild of Legacy Infrastructure

A recurring obstacle for large financial institutions is that their data sits across legacy on-premise systems and multiple cloud providers, often without consistent metadata. This is precisely the condition that migration-heavy vendors have historically used to justify multi-year rebuilds.

Dview argues that this is unnecessary. Its data ingestion layer connects to more than 100 source systems, from core banking applications to spreadsheets, without requiring organisations to replace existing infrastructure.

Sitting above that ingestion layer is the Unified Knowledge Layer, which encodes what a given data field means to different business functions. “This context precision eliminates the ambiguity that is the source of most enterprise AI hallucinations,” Shankar says, describing the layer as central to both accuracy and speed of deployment.

Measuring Return Before Committing Capital

Enterprise AI projects are frequently criticised for stalling at the proof-of-concept stage because financial outcomes remain unclear. Ezeepay’s approach, Tabrej says, is to anchor every deployment to a cost or loss already visible on the client’s books before any platform code is written.

He cites a public sector bank example where the company projected a reduction in annual fraud losses against a comparatively modest platform investment.

The company also runs a 15-day proof of concept inside a client’s own production cloud environment, rather than a vendor-hosted demonstration. “Multi-year contracts are signed after evidence, not before it,” Tabrej says, describing this as central to how the company avoids the stalled-pilot problem common across the sector.

What Happens to Existing Data Teams

As natural-language querying absorbs routine data retrieval work, there is a broader industry question about what happens to analysts and engineers whose jobs have historically involved exactly that task. Shankar was clear that the company does not view this as a displacement story.

“The shift is structural, not subtractive,” he says, arguing that time freed from ad-hoc reporting is redirected towards data product development, model fine-tuning and governance architecture—roles he described as increasingly scarce across regulated industries.

On-Premise Deployment & the Compliance Requirement

For sectors where regulation prohibits sensitive operational data leaving a regulated entity’s own infrastructure, Dview deploys its full stack inside a client’s Virtual Private Cloud, including fine-tuned language models that run without external inference calls. Shankar was careful not to overstate the guarantees this provides around accuracy across all possible queries.

“No probabilistic system can offer a mathematical guarantee of 100% precision across all possible queries at all times,” he says, adding that the aim instead is to make deviations from precision detectable and traceable before they become compliance events.

A Broader Industry Pattern

Dview’s account of its own architecture reflects a wider pattern visible across enterprise AI vendors serving regulated sectors: the technical difficulty of conversational analytics has increasingly moved away from language model capability itself and towards the infrastructure surrounding it—identity resolution, metadata, audit logging and deployment location.

For banks, insurers and NBFCs weighing whether to adopt these tools, that shift suggests the more useful due-diligence questions are less about model performance and more about where data sits, who can query it, and what evidence exists if a regulator asks.

Z.ai, the Chinese AI lab behind the GLM family of models, has completed construction of a one-gigawatt AI data centre built entirely with Chinese-made chips, according to a report from Bloomberg.

This marks one of China’s largest known AI computing deployments and a significant step in the country’s push to reduce reliance on NVIDIA hardware.

According to the report, the company is partially operating the facility, which will be used to train its frontier GLM foundation models.

A person familiar with the project said the company has also built or operates multiple AI computing clusters containing more than 10,000 chips each.

The project comes as Chinese AI developers race to replace NVIDIA accelerators with domestic alternatives following successive rounds of US export restrictions.

Huawei has emerged as the country’s largest AI chip supplier with nearly 50% market share, while Alibaba, through its T-Head unit, and Baidu are developing proprietary AI processors for their own cloud platforms.

A new generation of independent chip companies, including Biren Technology, Iluvatar CoreX, Moore Threads, and MetaX, has also expanded aggressively through IPOs and fresh fundraising, targeting AI training and inference workloads.

According to reports, DeepSeek and Z.ai have explored developing custom AI chips as well.

NVIDIA has progressively lost access to China’s AI market. Currently, NVIDIA’s H20 is the only advanced AI GPU that can be legally exported to China, and even then, shipments require US export licenses.

The H20 was specifically designed to comply with US export controls, but last April, it was made subject to an indefinite licensing requirement before the US later agreed to approve licenses for eligible exports.

More powerful AI GPUs, including the H100, H200, B200, GB200, and other Blackwell products, remain under current US export control rules.

Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) has acquired two large land parcels in Visakhapatnam and Pune that are expected to house OpenAI’s first data centre facilities in India, according to a report by The Economic Times.

The Andhra Pradesh government has allotted 200 acres to TCS in Anakapalli district near Visakhapatnam, a region that is rapidly emerging as a hub for AI infrastructure. The site is located close to Google’s under-construction 1 GW hyperscale data centre, positioning the area as a key destination for large-scale AI and cloud investments.

Separately, TCS has purchased an 88-acre land parcel in Bopkhel, Pune, from Hemisphere Properties for ₹640.5 crore. The public sector enterprise is responsible for monetising assets formerly owned by Videsh Sanchar Nigam Limited (VSNL), now Tata Communications.

According to the report, the two sites are expected to support OpenAI’s infrastructure expansion in India as the company scales its computing capacity to serve growing demand for AI services.

The Visakhapatnam site adds to Andhra Pradesh’s efforts to attract hyperscale data centre investments, while the Pune acquisition strengthens TCS’ infrastructure footprint in one of India’s largest technology hubs. The report said both locations are being considered for OpenAI’s first data centre facilities in the country.

The development follows a broader trend of global AI companies expanding data centre capacity in India to meet rising demand for model training and inference workloads.

The country has also been positioning itself as a destination for AI infrastructure through state-backed compute initiatives and growing private sector investments.

The land acquisitions build on the strategic partnership announced by The Tata Group and OpenAI in February. Under the agreement, OpenAI became the first customer of TCS’ HyperVault data centre business, with an initial commitment of 100 MW of AI-ready capacity that could scale to 1 GW over time. The partnership is part of OpenAI’s global Stargate initiative to build AI infrastructure outside the US while supporting data residency, security and low-latency AI services in India.

Samsung has established a robotics division that reports directly to the CEO to enhance its robotics strategy and commercialisation efforts.

The new RX division will focus on developing humanoid robots for manufacturing, home, and retail applications.

Samsung Electronics has created a dedicated robotics division that will report directly to its CEO as the South Korean company steps up efforts to develop and commercialise robotics technologies, Reuters reported. It said the robots will first be deployed at manufacturing sites before expanding into home and retail applications.

The new RX, or Robotics eXperience, division will lead the company’s long-term robotics strategy, technology development and business execution as Samsung looks to make robotics a future growth engine. The company became the largest shareholder in Rainbow Robotics in late 2024 to accelerate humanoid robot development and has since increased its focus on physical AI and industrial automation.

It also appointed Executive Vice President Lee Dongkun to lead its Robotics Strategy Team. Lee previously led robotics strategy at Hyundai Motor Group, including overseeing the direction of Boston Dynamics. Samsung said it will also establish robotics research hubs in the United States, China and Japan to strengthen its capabilities by drawing on local expertise and innovation ecosystems.

According to a company statement cited by reports, the RX division will oversee Samsung’s mid- to long-term robotics strategy while expanding research capabilities in South Korea and overseas.

The planned research hubs will support technology development in regions where robotics innovation is advancing rapidly. Samsung said the move will help improve its competitiveness through collaboration with local ecosystems.

The announcement builds on Samsung’s broader push into robotics over the past year. During its January earnings conference call, the company said it expected to achieve “tangible” results in its humanoid robotics business this year.

Samsung’s announcement also comes as companies increase investments in humanoid robots for industrial use. Last week, Hyundai Motor Group said it would acquire SoftBank’s remaining stake in Boston Dynamics, giving it full ownership of the robotics company.

In April, Samsung said it was open to investments and acquisitions to accelerate robotics development and commercialisation. It also said it would work with local companies on technology development where required.

Samsung said advances in technologies such as physical AI are making robotics businesses increasingly viable. The company plans to develop humanoid robots to improve productivity and user experience.

The announcement reflects the growing convergence of AI and robotics, with companies increasingly combining foundation models and physical AI to develop humanoid robots. Samsung has said advances in physical AI are making robotics commercially viable.

Indian clinicians exhibit higher trust in AI tools than their global counterparts, despite lower adoption rates.

Only 42% of Indian clinicians currently use AI, below the global average of 49%.

Indian clinicians trust artificial intelligence (AI) more than their global counterparts, but its adoption in clinical practice remains below the global average, according to Elsevier’s Clinician of the Future 2026 report.

The report found that 42% of clinicians in India currently use AI for work compared to the global average of 49%. Despite the lower adoption, 43% of Indian clinicians said they trust AI tools, higher than the global average of 37%.

Based on responses from 2,757 clinicians, including 2,065 doctors and 692 nurses across 118 countries, the report also found that Indian healthcare professionals reported better workplace conditions and greater institutional preparedness for AI than their global peers.

Around 53% of Indian respondents said their institutions have good AI governance, compared to 40% globally. Similarly, 50% rated their access to digital tools positively, while 44% said they receive adequate AI training, both higher than the global averages of 41% and 32%, respectively.

Indian clinicians also reported lower workplace pressure. Nearly 79% said they have sufficient time to provide quality patient care, compared to 65% globally. Only 12% said they were considering leaving their jobs, significantly lower than the global average of 24%.

Elsevier also found that AI is becoming increasingly common in healthcare worldwide. Nearly half of clinicians now use AI at work, with 56% of AI users regularly relying on general-purpose tools such as ChatGPT and Microsoft Copilot. Meanwhile, 34% frequently use clinical-specific AI tools for tasks such as clinical decision-making, second opinions and patient care support.

The report noted that clinicians expect AI to become more deeply integrated into healthcare over the next decade. Around 80% believe AI will become a critical assistant in clinical decision-making within the next five to 10 years, while 58% said clinicians using AI are likely to deliver better-quality care than those who do not.

Despite growing confidence in AI, Elsevier highlighted the need for greater transparency around how AI models are trained and how they generate outputs. The report said clinicians need to trust these systems as they increasingly rely on them to support life-critical medical decisions.

Among the countries surveyed, Japan recorded the highest trust in AI at 54%, followed by China (49%), while the United States (19%) and the United Kingdom (21%) reported the lowest levels of trust.

Google is developing a new AI server chip, internally called Frozen v2, that is designed to run its Gemini models more efficiently by embedding parts of the models directly into the chip’s hardware, according to a report by The Information.

The chip is expected to process six to 10 times more AI tokens for the same amount of electricity than Google’s latest tensor processing units (TPUs), if internal targets are met.

Unlike Google’s general-purpose TPUs, Frozen v2 is being built specifically for inference, the stage where trained AI models generate responses. By hardwiring portions of Gemini’s neural network architecture into silicon, Google expects to reduce the amount of computation required to serve AI models while lowering power consumption. The chip is not intended to replace TPUs but to complement them for large-scale inference workloads.

The project comes as Google faces growing demand for AI compute across its own products and Google Cloud.

According to the report, shortages in AI computing capacity have forced the company to prioritise internal workloads and turn away some external cloud customers. Improving inference efficiency could allow Google to serve more AI requests without expanding data centre capacity at the same pace.

The report said Frozen v2 could enter production as early as 2028. The chip is expected to be used primarily for Google’s Gemini models, rather than supporting a broad range of AI workloads like existing TPUs.

Google has expanded its custom silicon efforts over the past decade to reduce reliance on third-party AI hardware. Its TPU lineup powers AI training and inference across Google services and Google Cloud, where the company also offers TPU access to external developers and enterprises.

IT services firm Cognizant has secured a multi-year technology services contract from US health insurer Centene Corp, in a deal valued at more than $500 million and potentially approaching $1 billion, according to a Moneycontrol report citing people familiar with the matter.

The report said the exact value of the engagement could vary depending on its final structure.

As Centene is an existing Cognizant customer, the contract is expected to comprise both renewal of existing work and new business.

According to the report, Cognizant is expected to deploy its TriZetto healthcare software platform alongside its recently launched agentic AI offerings, including Flowsource and Agent Foundry, to support functions such as medical claims processing, billing automation, and customer service operations.

AIM has reached out to Cognizant regarding the development but did not receive a response at the time of publishing.

Cognizant and Centene had entered into a $2.7 billion master services agreement in 2014 through Health Net, but the arrangement was restructured after Centene acquired Health Net in 2016. Centene is a Fortune 500 company that primarily acts as an intermediary for government sponsored health programmes, focusing on uninsured and low-income groups.

The reported deal comes as large IT services providers increasingly pitch AI-led transformation rather than traditional labour-arbitrage outsourcing, with enterprises restructuring long-term contracts into shorter, outcome-based engagements. In the January-March 2026 quarter, Cognizant reported a 21% year-over-year increase in bookings.

Cognizant is scheduled to report its second-quarter results on July 29, 2026. Its shares closed 0.29% lower on Nasdaq on July 20.

Accenture has appointed former McKinsey & Company partner Pradeep Prabhala as the lead of its India Market Unit, effective September 1, as the global consulting and technology services company doubles down on artificial intelligence-led transformation and India’s expanding GCC market.

Prabhala will lead Accenture’s India business, working with domestic clients on data and AI-led transformation initiatives while also supporting multinational companies setting up and expanding GCCs in the country, the company said in a statement on July 21.

The appointment comes as global consulting and IT services firms are increasingly repositioning their India operations beyond traditional outsourcing, focusing instead on AI deployment, digital transformation and GCC advisory services as enterprises ramp up technology investments.

Prabhala joins Accenture from McKinsey & Company, where he was a partner leading the firm’s consumer sector practice in India and agriculture practice across Asia.

Before that, he spent nearly a decade at Monitor Deloitte, advising companies on growth strategy, market expansion, mergers and acquisitions, and digital transformation.

In his new role, Prabhala will also help global clients build and scale GCCs, which have emerged as one of the fastest-growing segments of India’s technology and business services ecosystem, with multinational companies increasingly using them for engineering, AI, product development and innovation.

“India is a strategic market for Accenture, and we are focused on accelerating growth here. As clients deepen their focus on technology-led reinvention and unlocking new value from data and AI, we see tremendous opportunity to help them lead,” Arundhati Chakraborty, Global Lead, Finance and GCC and Executive Sponsor, India Market Unit, Accenture said in the statement.

Beyond his consulting career, Prabhala is an early-stage investor in AI, enterprise software and deep technology startups across India and the US.

The Telangana government has partnered with Microsoft, the 1M1B Foundation (One Million for One Billion), and MeitY Startup Hub to establish India’s first Green Skills and Applied AI Centre of Excellence (CoE) dedicated to Green Pharma, as the state looks to build a future-ready workforce for AI-driven sustainable manufacturing.

The centre, expected to become operational by August, will train young people in artificial intelligence, sustainable manufacturing, and emerging technologies, supporting the state’s ambition to become a global hub for sustainable pharmaceutical manufacturing under its Next-Gen Life Sciences Policy 2026–30.

The roadmap for the centre was presented to state IT and Industries Minister Duddilla Sridhar Babu. The CoE will include dedicated learning zones focused on Applied AI, Green Pharma, solar energy, electric vehicles, and wind energy. Participants will gain hands-on experience through industry-led projects, innovation cohorts, internships, mentorship, incubation support, and career-readiness programmes.

The Hyderabad facility is one of five Green Skills and Applied AI Centres of Excellence being established across India by Microsoft and the 1M1B Foundation in collaboration with MeitY Startup Hub. Nationally, the initiative aims to engage one lakh youth in Applied AI and Green Skills by 2030 while creating pathways to 50,000 jobs, internships, apprenticeships, and entrepreneurship opportunities.

Speaking on the initiative, Babu said, “Telangana’s next phase of growth would depend on a future-ready workforce capable of leading AI-driven transformation and sustainable innovation in life sciences and advanced manufacturing.”

Highlighting AI’s growing role in sustainable industries, Rajiv Kumar, President and Managing Director, Microsoft India Development Centre, said, “By combining Applied AI with Green Skills, we are preparing a new generation of innovators who can create solutions for both economic growth and climate resilience."

Manav Subodh, Founder and CEO of 1M1B Foundation, said the initiative would prepare young people for the next phase of industrial transformation. “The future of Green Pharma would be built at the intersection of AI, sustainability and human talent.”

Salesforce has launched SMB Growth Kit in India, a bundled offering for small and medium businesses that combines Agentforce Sales, Slack and Tableau into a single platform.

Salesforce said the offering brings customer data, team communication and business analytics together on a single platform, replacing multiple disconnected applications.

The company said businesses adopting the package can go live within four to six weeks through structured onboarding and implementation support.

The package is available immediately and includes onboarding, implementation and post-deployment support. Salesforce said it will deliver the offering through selected reseller partners across India.

According to the company, Agentforce Sales is intended to give SMBs a single view of leads, opportunities and sales pipelines while reducing reliance on spreadsheets and manual recordkeeping.

It includes automated lead assignment, workflow automation, mobile access and AI features such as opportunity scoring, forecasting and recommendations.

Slack serves as the collaboration layer, allowing teams across sales, customer support, HR, IT and operations to work from a single interface. Tableau provides dashboards for tracking pipeline health, revenue trends and business performance using data connected with Salesforce.

“India’s SMBs are moving quickly toward AI, but ambition alone is not enough. Many businesses are investing in AI, but far fewer have implemented it because their customer data, team conversations and business insights are still scattered,” said Mankiran Chowhan, Managing Director, Salesforce India.

“SMB Growth Kit gives growing businesses one connected system where sales activity, team conversations and live insights work together, helping teams act with more confidence, fewer blind spots and less guesswork,” she added.

Swaroop Kaja, RVP, Sales, Salesforce India, said the company built the offering to simplify sales operations and collaboration.

“We launched SMB Growth Kit to give growing businesses one connected way to run sales, collaborate on deals and understand business performance in real time. With Agentforce Sales, Slack and Tableau working together, teams can spend less time chasing updates and more time moving customers forward,” Kaja said.

He added that the combined platform also creates a data foundation for businesses adopting AI as they scale.

The Karnataka government has approved the establishment of a Centre of Excellence in Artificial Intelligence (CoE-AI) at the Indian Institute of Information Technology (IIIT), Raichur, under the IT-BT Department’s Local Economy Accelerator Programme (LEAP). The project has been approved with a total outlay of ₹12 crore.

The centre aims to expand AI-driven research, skilling, innovation and entrepreneurship beyond Bengaluru, with a particular focus on tier-2 and tier-3 cities. It is expected to serve as a regional AI hub for North Karnataka while supporting the state’s broader strategy to decentralise technology-led growth.

Announcing the decision, Karnataka IT-BT Minister Priyank Kharge wrote in a LinkedIn post, “The government of Karnataka has approved the establishment of a Centre of Excellence for Artificial Intelligence at the Indian Institute of Information Technology (IIIT), Raichur, under the IT-BT Department, Karnataka’s LEAP. With a total outlay of ₹12 crore, this marks another important milestone in our mission to strengthen Karnataka’s AI ecosystem #BeyondBengaluru.”

According to the minister, the CoE will focus on developing practical AI applications across sectors including agriculture, healthcare, education, MSMEs and governance. The initiative is also expected to create opportunities for startups, industry, entrepreneurs and students in North Karnataka.

“The CoE will expand access to AI-driven research, skilling, innovation and entrepreneurship across tier-2 and tier-3 regions while serving as a regional AI hub for North Karnataka,” he stated.

Kharge added that the centre would help strengthen Karnataka’s AI leadership while ensuring that innovation extends beyond the state’s capital.

“More importantly, it will develop practical AI solutions for sectors such as agriculture, healthcare, education, MSMEs and governance while creating new opportunities for industries, entrepreneurs and young innovators. Foundational initiatives like these will strengthen our leadership in AI while ensuring that the next chapter of innovation is written across every region of the State,” Kharge mentioned.

Karnataka’s #BeyondBengaluru initiative seeks to expand the state’s technology ecosystem into emerging innovation hubs by strengthening digital infrastructure, research capabilities and talent development across regions.

HCLTech has expanded its India footprint with the launch of a new Global Technology Center in Gujarat International Finance Tec-City (GIFT City), strengthening its focus on AI-led innovation for the financial services sector while deepening industry-academia collaboration in the state.

The facility, inaugurated by Gujarat Deputy Chief Minister Harsh Sanghavi, will deliver AI-powered solutions for HCLTech’s global financial services clients. It will also function as a hub for developing next-generation technology solutions and nurturing skilled talent

Alongside the launch, HCLTech signed memoranda of understanding (MoUs) with the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Gandhinagar and Gujarat Technological University (GTU) to promote research, innovation, and workforce development in artificial intelligence.

The partnerships will focus on AI research for financial services, software development, and industry-aligned skill-building. Students and faculty from both institutions will gain hands-on exposure to real-world technology projects and digital transformation initiatives.

“We are delighted to welcome HCLTech to GIFT City. HCLTech’s commitment to creating local jobs and nurturing local talent aligns strongly with our vision of enabling Gujarat’s youth to access global career opportunities closer to home. The launch of the Global Technology Centre and the AI Lab marks an important step in strengthening GIFT City’s innovation ecosystem and advancing its position as a leading global TechFin hub,” Sanghavi added.

Sanghavi added that HCLTech’s experience in building technology capabilities across locations would contribute significantly to Gujarat’s innovation ecosystem as GIFT City evolves into a global destination for business and technology.

Highlighting the company’s expansion strategy, C Vijayakumar, CEO and Managing Director, HCLTech, said, “We are pleased to establish our presence in the state to engineer the future of financial services clients with innovative AI solutions. At HCLTech, we look forward to contributing to the local technology ecosystem in the state and boosting industry-academia collaboration to create a pool of future-ready talent.”

The announcement reinforces GIFT City’s growing position as a technology and financial services hub, with AI emerging as a key focus area for enterprises expanding operations in the region.

Uttar Pradesh is doubling down on its ambitions to become India’s next deep-tech powerhouse, with Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath directing officials to prepare a comprehensive roadmap for robotics, artificial intelligence (AI), quantum computing, semiconductors, and other emerging technologies. Central to this vision is the development of Park for Robotics, Artificial Intelligence, GPU Clusters and Advanced Technical Innovation (PRAGATI), a 75-acre integrated robotics and advanced manufacturing cluster in Noida, alongside two deep-tech innovation hubs in Noida and Lucknow.

During a review meeting of the Information Technology and Electronics Department, Adityanath said, “The ‘PRAGATI’ project to be developed in Noida will provide the state with a world-class foundation for robotics and advanced manufacturing, while the U Hubs being established in Lucknow and Noida will emerge as major centres of deep tech innovation by bringing research, innovation, startups, industry, investors and educational institutions onto a common platform.”

“Work should be carried out with the objective of making Uttar Pradesh not merely a consumer of new technologies, but a global centre for research, innovation and high-technology-based manufacturing,” he added.

The proposed PRAGATI park, to be developed over approximately 75 acres in Noida, is envisioned as India’s first integrated robotics and advanced manufacturing cluster.

The facility will house a robotics testing and certification centre, rapid prototyping and manufacturing facilities, AI compute infrastructure, GPU clusters, a motion capture lab, a physical AI data centre, startup incubation facilities, and co-working spaces. The project will also bring together global manufacturers, component suppliers, R&D centres, and specialised service providers within a single ecosystem.

According to the government, Noida was selected due to its strong electronics manufacturing base, proximity to Noida International Airport, Jewar, the Dedicated Freight Corridor, the Defence Industrial Corridor, and a well-established industrial and academic ecosystem. The state expects the project to generate over one lakh direct and indirect jobs while contributing more than ₹2,000 crore in gross value addition over the next five years.

Highlighting the broader vision, the Chief Minister said, “Artificial Intelligence and robotics are the principal foundations of the coming industrial revolution. Therefore, while world-class manufacturing infrastructure should be developed on one hand, a strong deep tech ecosystem promoting research, innovation and entrepreneurship should also be created on the other.”

He further stressed the need for collaboration across stakeholders, stating, “An effective coordination mechanism should be established among industry, educational and research institutions, startups, investors and technology experts so that new technologies can rapidly move from laboratories to industry, enabling Uttar Pradesh to emerge as a major hub for global technology investment.”

Complementing the manufacturing cluster, Uttar Pradesh will establish two U Hubs—one each in Noida and Lucknow—with an allocation of ₹100 crore in the 2026–27 state budget. The hubs are intended to function as centres of excellence that connect research institutions, startups, industry, investors, and academia.

The Noida U Hub will focus on quantum computing, semiconductor design, physical AI, robotics, defence technology, and advanced biotechnology, while the Lucknow U-Hub will specialise in applied AI, GovTech, healthcare AI, biosciences, and agri-biotechnology. Their operational framework has been designed by an expert committee chaired by the Director of IIT Kanpur after studying leading global deep-tech ecosystems.

The CM directed that the U Hubs should go beyond being startup workspaces. “A robust platform should be created where technologies developed in research laboratories are commercialised, innovation receives investment, and young people get opportunities to progress from research to entrepreneurship,” he said, adding that the centres should operate “entirely professional, result-oriented and aligned with global best standards.”

Recognising the need for skilled talent, Adityanath also called for large-scale training programmes in AI, machine learning, cybersecurity, cloud computing, semiconductors, and data science.

“Providing the youth of Uttar Pradesh with skills aligned to future technologies is the greatest need of the time,” he said, directing officials to develop world-class training and certification programmes aligned with industry needs through collaboration between educational institutions and industry.

The state also plans to revise its Information Technology Policy to make it more investor-friendly and employment-oriented, while expanding the IT ecosystem beyond Noida and Ghaziabad into tier-2 and tier-3 cities.

“The Information Technology Policy should be made more practical, investor-friendly and employment-oriented in accordance with changing global requirements,” the CM said. “The expansion of the IT industry should not remain confined to Gautam Buddh Nagar and Ghaziabad but should extend to tier-2 and tier-3 cities.”

He added that the policy’s primary objective should be employment generation. “The fundamental objective of the policy should be to create the maximum possible quality employment opportunities for the youth of the state. Local youth should be encouraged in skill development, internships, research, innovation and patents. At the same time, processes related to land, infrastructure and other approvals should be made simple, transparent and time-bound for investors."

The announcements build on Uttar Pradesh’s recent push into AI, semiconductors, and data centres, positioning the state as a destination for high-tech manufacturing and digital infrastructure investments.

Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) has expanded its artificial intelligence partnership with Google Cloud by launching a Gemini Experience Center in Kolkata focused on consumer businesses, as India’s largest IT services company steps up investments in industry-specific AI adoption.

The Kolkata facility, TCS’ eighth such centre globally and third in India, is designed to showcase AI-led innovations tailored for consumer business needs and built with Google Cloud and Google’s Gemini models.

According to a statement, the centre will play a critical role in helping enterprises transform their business using TCS’ Human+AI Autonomy model, which will enable organisations to co-create solutions built with Gemini, addressing evolving needs across retail, consumer packaged goods (CPG), and travel, tourism and hospitality (TTH) sectors.

The launch comes as large IT services firms increasingly invest in dedicated AI innovation hubs with hyperscaler partners to move enterprise clients from AI pilots to production deployments.

TCS said it plans to expand the network to 10 Gemini Experience Centers globally by the end of 2026, including four in India.

TCS added that it has built more than 3,000 industry- and context-specific AI agents using Gemini Enterprise, covering industries including consumer goods, retail, travel, transportation and hospitality.

The Kolkata centre adds to TCS’ existing Gemini Experience Centers for retail in Chennai and banking and financial services in Bengaluru, as part of the company’s focus on vertical-specific AI solutions rather than generic deployments.
