title: India Joins Australia, Canada to Advance AI Infra, Workforce Skilling
content:
The MoU operationalises the ACITI partnership, with a focus on AI, hardware supply chains, critical minerals, and commercialising emerging technologies.

What Actually Matters.

India, Australia, and Canada have signed an MoU to enhance cooperation on critical and emerging technologies through the ACITI Partnership.

The agreement focuses on AI, clean energy technologies, critical minerals, and resilient supply chains to accelerate innovation and commercialisation.

India, Australia, and Canada have signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) to deepen cooperation under the Australia-Canada-India Technology and Innovation (ACITI) Partnership, a trilateral initiative agreed in November 2025 to strengthen collaboration on critical and emerging technologies. The agreement provides the framework to implement the partnership announced by the three countries last year.

The MoU aims to expand collaboration across AI, critical minerals, clean energy technologies, and resilient technology supply chains. It also seeks to strengthen ties between governments, research institutions and industry to accelerate innovation and commercialisation of emerging technologies.

It promotes collaboration in AI adoption, workforce skills, and the AI startup ecosystem, while addressing policy, regulation, and risk management. It also covers related fields such as semiconductors, data centres, cloud computing, digital public infrastructure, IoT, robotics, high-performance computing, and cybersecurity, fostering innovation and security in the digital landscape.

According to Australia's Department of Industry, Science and Resources, the partnership will support joint research, talent mobility, business engagement and policy cooperation. It establishes annual ministerial meetings, senior officials' dialogues and thematic working groups to identify and oversee collaborative projects, while promoting responsible development and deployment of AI and other emerging technologies.

The three countries will also work to build more resilient supply chains for hardware components and critical minerals that underpin AI infrastructure and advanced manufacturing. The collaboration is expected to support secure access to semiconductor inputs, computing hardware and other strategic technologies while reducing supply chain vulnerabilities.

It also opens avenues for broader cooperation in areas including trade, defence. and space technologies.

title: Govt to Study AI’s Impact on GCC Growth as India Bets on Higher-Value Roles
content:
TCS secured a net profit of ₹13,349 crore, a decline of 2.7% sequentially, and its operating margin also declined to 24% from 25.3% a quarter ago.

What Actually Matters.

TCS achieved an annualised AI revenue run rate of $2.6 billion, marking a 13.6% sequential increase.

The company's consolidated revenue rose by 13.9% year-on-year, reaching ₹72,275 crore.

Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) said its annualised AI revenue run rate reached $2.6 billion during the June quarter, up 13.6% sequentially, as India's largest IT services exporter reported a 13.9% year-on-year increase in consolidated revenue to ₹72,275 crore.

The Mumbai-headquartered firm’s net profit rose to ₹13,349 crore, up 4.6% from ₹12,760 crore recorded in the corresponding quarter of the last fiscal year, while operating margin stood at 24%. However, profit slid approximately 2.7% sequentially.

On a constant currency basis in dollar terms, the sequential growth remained flat.

The company also secured $9.5 billion in total contract value (TCV), led by several AI-focused mega deals across manufacturing, utilities, healthcare, and enterprise software, including an $800 million deal with Swedish industrial manufacturer SKF to redesign the company's enterprise operations around an AI-first digital core.

It also signed multi-million-dollar AI engagements with ServiceNow and a Europe-based Fortune Global 50 company, and won contracts involving AI-driven utility transformation, autonomous IT operations, and AI-powered software engineering.

The company also expanded its AI ecosystem through strategic partnerships with Anthropic and Mistral, while deepening collaborations with Google Cloud, Oracle, and ServiceNow. TCS said it will equip 50,000 employees with Anthropic's Claude models as it looks to accelerate enterprise AI adoption and build industry-specific AI offerings.

While the number of $100+ million and $50+ million deals remained the same, TCS added more $1+ million, $5+ million, and $10+ million deals to its pipeline.

North America continued to dominate the deal pipeline, with 48.3% of the share. In terms of verticals, the banking, financial services, and insurance sector took the largest share of the pie, while consumer business shrank from 15.6% in Q1 FY26 to 15% a year later.

The quarterly performance indicates a broader trend sweeping India's $300-billion IT services industry, where AI has rapidly become the primary driver of large technology spending even as traditional discretionary projects remain subdued.

Over the past year, companies including TCS, Infosys, HCLTech, Wipro and Tech Mahindra have increasingly reported that clients are redirecting budgets from conventional application development and maintenance towards AI-enabled modernisation, agentic AI, cloud transformation and automation initiatives.

“Q1 FY27 reflects continued growth momentum and the strength of our strategic positioning, despite geopolitical and macro-economic headwinds. We delivered a strong order book of $9.5 billion, including a marquee AI-led transformation deal with SKF, while continuing to add clients across key revenue bands and scaling our AI business to a $2.6 billion annualised revenue run rate,” K Krithivasan, Chief Executive Officer and Managing Director, said in a statement.

“As customers accelerate investments in AI, modernisation, cybersecurity, sovereign cloud and platform simplification, our strong deal conversion, improving client mining and expanding ecosystem partnerships position TCS well to translate opportunity into sustained growth,” he added.

Since the emergence of generative AI, India's IT majors have announced billions of dollars worth of AI-related deal wins, but monetisation has remained subdued as enterprises moved cautiously from experimentation to production deployments.

“We won multiple AI-led transformation deals with our dual commitment to AI-led optimisation as well as innovation-led outcomes. These wins validate our approach to AI-led efficient ITOps, accelerated Software Engineering and Modernisation, AI-first process redesign and implementation of SaaS solutions and Autonomous GBS,” Chief Operating Officer Aarthi Subramanian said.

TCS ended the quarter with 593,798 employees, up nearly 9,000 from the previous quarter but down nearly 19,000 year-on-year, while annualised IT services attrition stood at 13.6%.

The board declared an interim dividend of ₹12 per share.

Shares of TCS closed at ₹2,047.70 on July 9 on the BSE, down 0.5% from the previous close of ₹2,058.50.

title: Mistral Bets on Physical AI With 8 Bn Parameter Autonomous Robot Navigation Model
content:
SpaceXAI has priced Grok 4.5 at $2 per million input tokens and $6 per million output tokens.

SpaceXAI has launched Grok 4.5, its latest AI model, positioning it for coding, agentic tasks, and knowledge work.

The model is available in Grok Build, Cursor, and the SpaceXAI API. However, it is not yet available in the European Union and is expected to be available there in mid-July.

“Grok 4.5 is SpaceXAI’s smartest model built to excel at coding, agentic tasks, and knowledge work,” the company said. “It’s our strongest model ever and was trained alongside Cursor.”

Grok 4.5 runs at 80 tokens per second. It can handle software engineering tasks ranging from Rust and C/C++ programming to building complete applications from a single prompt.

Grok 4.5 is a mixture-of-experts (MoE) model. Cursor said the training included trillions of tokens from Cursor, covering developer interactions with codebases and software tools. Grok 4.5 was trained on datasets covering coding, science, engineering, and mathematics, with reinforcement learning focused on software engineering and other technical tasks.

According to SpaceXAI, the model was trained across tens of thousands of NVIDIA GB300 GPUs using data filtering, deduplication, quality scoring, and domain-specific selection.

On software engineering benchmarks, SpaceXAI said Grok 4.5 achieved a 62.0% pass@1 score on DeepSWE 1.0, behind Fable Max at 66.1% and GPT 5.5 xhigh at 64.31%.

On SWE Marathon, however, it led with a 29.0% resolution rate, ahead of Opus 4.8 Max at 26.0% and Fable Max at 24.0%. On Terminal Bench 2.1, it scored 83.3%, close to Fable Max’s 84.3% and GPT 5.5 xhigh’s 83.4%.

SpaceXAI also said the model generates fewer output tokens than competing models. On SWE Bench Pro, Grok 4.5 used an average of 15,954 output tokens per task, compared with 67,020 for Opus 4.8 Max, which the company said translates to about 4.2 times fewer tokens.

The company said the model delivers “roughly 2x the token efficiency of comparable leading models,” reducing the number of steps required to complete tasks.

It is also the default model in Grok Build, where it can create Excel models involving web research, multi-sheet formulas, and notes, as well as PowerPoint presentations and Word documents.

title: Semiconductor Fabs to Benefit as Govt Scraps Import Duty on Critical Electronic Components
content:
French AI startup Mistral expands into robotics with Robostral Navigate, an 8B navigation model that enables autonomous movement using a single camera.

What Actually Matters.

Mistral has launched Robostral Navigate, an 8-billion-parameter model for autonomous robot navigation using a single RGB camera.

The model facilitates navigation through complex environments using natural language instructions, enhancing user interaction.

French AI startup Mistral has expanded beyond large language models into robotics with the launch of Robostral Navigate, its first embodied AI model designed for robots to navigate complex environments using only a single RGB camera and natural language instructions.

The 8-billion-parameter model allows wheeled, legged, and aerial robots to interpret verbal instructions such as "go to the kitchen" or "move to the loading dock" while autonomously planning their route through unfamiliar environments.

Unlike conventional robotic navigation systems that rely on LiDAR, depth sensors, or multiple cameras, Robostral Navigate operates using a single standard RGB camera, significantly reducing hardware complexity and deployment costs.

According to Mistral, the model achieves a 76.6% success rate on the unseen R2R-CE benchmark and 79.4% on seen environments, outperforming the best existing monocular navigation approach by 9.7 percentage points and surpassing systems that use depth sensors or multiple cameras by 4.5 percentage points. The company said the model was trained entirely in simulation before being transferred to real-world robotic platforms.

The company said Robostral Navigate is hardware-agnostic, enabling it to work across different robot manufacturers and form factors without requiring specialised sensor configurations. Mistral positions the model as a foundation for logistics, warehouse automation, industrial inspection, and other enterprise robotics applications where cost-effective navigation is critical.

The launch follows Mistral's acquisition of Austrian robotics startup Emmi AI in May, signalling the company's broader ambitions in physical AI.

title: OpenAI Launches GPT-Live with Real-Time Voice Conversations Powered by GPT-5.5
content:
The model allows users to interrupt the model, pause without being cut off, and have faster back-and-forth conversations.

OpenAI has launched GPT-Live, a new voice model that allows users to have more natural conversations with ChatGPT by allowing AI to listen and speak simultaneously.

The company said the model is rolling out globally starting today on iOS, Android, and ChatGPT.com, with GPT-Live-1 becoming the default voice model for Go, Plus, and Pro users, while GPT-Live-1 mini will power the Free tier.

Unlike previous versions of ChatGPT Voice that processed conversations in turns, GPT-Live is built on a full-duplex architecture that continuously processes audio as it generates speech. This allows users to interrupt the model, pause without being cut off, and have faster back-and-forth conversations.

For queries that require web search or deeper reasoning, GPT-Live hands the task to OpenAI’s latest frontier model while continuing the conversation. At launch, GPT-5.5 powers these background tasks, and OpenAI said future frontier models will automatically replace it as they become available.

“We’re launching GPT-Live, a new generation of voice models that make talking with AI feel much more like having a real conversation,” OpenAI said.

The company said more than 150 million people use ChatGPT’s voice and dictation features every week. GPT-Live adds support for visual response cards for topics such as weather, stocks, and sports during voice conversations, while continuing to support search, memory, images, and file uploads. Users can also choose different reasoning levels, including Instant, Medium, and High, depending on the complexity of the task.

OpenAI said GPT-Live separates conversation handling from reasoning tasks. While GPT-Live manages the interaction, GPT-5.5 performs search and reasoning in the background, allowing the conversation to continue without waiting for those tasks to finish.

According to OpenAI’s internal evaluations, GPT-Live-1 and GPT-Live-1 mini were preferred over Advanced Voice Mode in conversations measuring conversational flow, interruptions, and overall interaction quality. The company also reported improvements on benchmarks including GPQA for scientific reasoning, BrowseComp for web search, and τ³-Voice Telecom for multi-turn customer support tasks.

OpenAI said it expanded safety testing for GPT-Live with audio-native evaluations covering areas such as self-harm, emotional reliance, violence, and sexual content.

The company added safeguards that can intervene during live conversations by steering responses, surfacing safety resources, or ending conversations in higher-risk situations. It also introduced protections for teen users through parental controls and age-appropriate behaviour.

“GPT-Live was designed to be safe by default,” the company said.

At launch, GPT-Live does not support voice conversations with video or screen sharing, though OpenAI said those capabilities are planned for a future release. Users who need those features can continue using the legacy versions of ChatGPT Voice, including Standard Voice Mode and Advanced Voice Mode.

GPT-Live is OpenAI’s latest effort to make voice interaction a primary interface for AI systems by combining continuous conversation with its latest reasoning models in the background.

Aurigo founder Balaji Sreenivasan on building an AI-native company for the full construction lifecycle spanning capital planning, project delivery, and asset management for some of the largest infrastructure programs in North America.

When Balaji Sreenivasan founded Aurigo in 2003, he wasn't trying to build one of North America's leading infrastructure software companies. He wanted to solve a problem.

Capital owners were still managing complex capital programs with disconnected systems and paper-driven processes. He believed software could bring clarity to the decisions that shape ports, highways, roads, and other critical infrastructure.

More than two decades later, Aurigo has become one of North America's leading providers of software for capital planning, project delivery, and asset management. Its AI-native platform supports more than $450 billion in capital programs across North America, helping more than 300 organisations plan, build, and maintain over 40,000 infrastructure projects. The company has evolved significantly, but the thinking that shaped it began long before Aurigo itself.

The philosophy that has guided Aurigo's growth can be traced back much further than the company's founding.

"I think the thought that stayed in my head was that you could write code and solve a problem that you previously couldn't."

After being introduced to a Spectrum computer in the early 1980s, he taught himself BASIC and began writing simple programs. One of them catalogued his comic book collection, but what stayed with him wasn't the program itself. It was the realisation that technology could make previously impossible tasks possible. That idea eventually became the foundation for Aurigo.

The company began by helping field inspectors replace paper-based processes with digital workflows. As customers adopted the software, Aurigo expanded into project management, contractor payments, capital planning, and right-of-way. Over time, those capabilities evolved into an integrated platform supporting the full capital program lifecycle.

Large capital programs often run over budget and behind schedule. Managing these investments, many of them funded by taxpayers, requires visibility into how funding is allocated, how projects progress, and how assets are maintained long after construction is complete. Aurigo's approach has always been to bring greater transparency, accountability, and confidence to those decisions through software.

Long-term partnerships have given Aurigo a front-row seat to how infrastructure management continues to evolve. Rather than simply keeping pace, the company has helped shape that evolution, investing early in cloud technologies and later in artificial intelligence so customers are equipped for the challenges ahead, not just those of today. As customers entrusted Aurigo with increasingly critical infrastructure programs, the company continued to strengthen its commitment to security and compliance, reflected most recently by Aurigo Masterworks achieving FedRAMP Class C certification in 2025.

Yet when Balaji talks about the future, the conversation rarely starts with the software. It starts with people.

Many companies are racing to add intelligent capabilities to existing products, but the real advantage comes from context. Years of solving real customer challenges, combined with structured project and construction data accumulated across the infrastructure lifecycle, became the foundation for Lumina, the company's AI foundation engine.

"We had a large data model. So we took that data model and built our AI foundation engine called Lumina."

For Balaji, sustainable AI platforms are built on years of domain expertise rather than being layered onto existing software. The real value of AI comes from the context behind it, not the model alone. That's why Aurigo's engineers focus on building intelligent capabilities grounded in decades of project data and infrastructure expertise, helping capital owners make better decisions across capital programs worth billions of dollars. Their work shapes programs that affect everyday life, from the roads people travel and the utilities they depend on to the facilities where they work and innovate.

The biggest shift in software development isn't just how products are built. It's how engineers spend their time. At Aurigo, AI accounts for more than 80% of code generation, giving teams more time to focus on complex challenges. Engineering output has increased significantly over the past year, and rather than reducing headcount, Aurigo has reinvested that capacity into new products and new markets.

"The question isn't how much code someone writes. It's whether they're solving the right problem."

The industry has spent too long measuring engineering by the code it produces. As more deterministic work becomes automated, success is increasingly measured by judgment, systems thinking, and the ability to design intelligent solutions rather than simply implement them. Aurigo's internal framework reflects this, evaluating engineers not only on their use of AI tools but on their ability to orchestrate workflows and build autonomous systems.

That shift in how engineering is measured points to a larger change in how customers may come to think about software itself. Balaji believes organisations are beginning to ask a more fundamental question: whether they should pay for software licenses at all, or simply pay for outcomes. If that shift accelerates, it could reshape how software companies package, price, and deliver their products.

The engineers who have the greatest impact think across systems, work across disciplines, and understand how people, workflows, and AI come together to make that possible. They influence product direction, shape what gets built next, and work closely with customers. That culture extends to how Aurigo has built its global organisation. The company's Bengaluru office began as a straightforward business decision.

"We initially came for the cost, but we stayed for the talent."

Today, it has grown into one of Aurigo's strongest engineering centres, with teams contributing to product strategy, platform innovation, and AI initiatives alongside colleagues in Austin, Toronto, and Cape Town.

The qualities Aurigo looks for in its engineers are also what drew the company to the AIM Chess League. For Balaji, chess embodies discipline, strategic thinking, and the ability to make sound decisions under uncertainty. The engineers who thrive are comfortable with ambiguity, recognise patterns, weigh trade-offs carefully, and never stop learning. Chess demands exactly that.

"The reason we're associated with the chess initiative is that we want innovative thinkers. Where does that thinking happen outside of tech? It happens in chess, and it happens in sports. You're thinking on your feet. You're thinking about your next move."

The AIM Chess League brings together technology professionals through competition, learning, and a shared intellectual pursuit, the kind of environment where ideas are challenged, perspectives are broadened, and better innovators emerge. As AI takes over more routine work, the ability to think several moves ahead only becomes more valuable.

What endures is the ability to ask better questions, exercise sound judgment, and make thoughtful decisions when the path forward isn't obvious. Those are the qualities that have shaped Aurigo for more than two decades, and they continue to define the people the company wants to build with.

title: Microsoft’s New TypeScript 7 Promises 8–12x Faster Builds With Native Go Compiler
content:
Microsoft says the new language server cuts the number of failed commands by over 80% and server crashes by more than 60% compared with TypeScript 6.

Microsoft has released TypeScript 7, a major overhaul of the programming language that replaces its long-standing JavaScript implementation with a native compiler written in Go.

The company says the new release typically delivers 8–12x faster full builds, with benchmarked projects seeing speedups of up to 11.9x and reduced memory consumption across large codebases.

The new compiler is now available through the standard ‘typescript’ npm package, replacing the earlier preview builds distributed as @typescript/native-preview.

Microsoft said the native implementation was designed to preserve compatibility with previous TypeScript behaviour while introducing native execution, shared-memory multithreading, and new compiler optimisations.

Microsoft published benchmark results of compile times and memory usage across several large open-source projects.

The performance gains extend beyond compilation. Microsoft said opening a file containing an error in the VS Code codebase previously took around 17.5 seconds before diagnostics appeared, compared with under 1.3 seconds in TypeScript 7.

The company added that the new language server has reduced the number of failing language-server commands by more than 80% and server crashes by over 60% compared with TypeScript 6.

A significant part of the speedup comes from native multithreading. TypeScript 7 parallelises parsing, type checking, and code generation, while introducing new ‘--checkers’ and ‘--builders’ options that allow developers to tune parallel execution based on the number of available CPU cores and memory.

Microsoft said increasing the number of type-checking workers from four to eight pushed some projects beyond 16x faster build times, although this increases memory usage.

Microsoft spent more than a year validating the compiler across large production codebases with internal teams, including Office, Teams, Xbox, and Power BI, as well as companies such as Bloomberg, Canva, Figma, Google, Linear, Notion, Slack, Vercel, and Vanta.

According to the company, Slack reduced CI type-checking time from about 7.5 minutes to 1.25 minutes, while Microsoft’s News Services team reported saving around 400 hours per month previously spent waiting for CI builds.

The release also introduces a rebuilt ‘--watch’ mode based on a Go port of Parcel's file-watching system, new Language Server Protocol support for editors, and configuration changes inherited from TypeScript 6.

Some workflows, including Vue, Astro, Svelte, MDX, and Angular template tooling, will continue using TypeScript 6 until the new compiler exposes a stable programmatic API, which Microsoft expects to arrive in a future TypeScript 7.1 release.

The release marks the completion of Microsoft’s Go-based rewrite of TypeScript, first announced in March last year and previously available through the ‘@typescript/native-preview’ package.

China is preparing to allow some of its largest artificial intelligence companies to purchase a limited number of NVIDIA H200 AI chips, reversing months of resistance to approving imports of the US-made processors, according to a report by The Information.

The report said Chinese officials have informed companies including Alibaba, ByteDance and DeepSeek in recent weeks that they are likely to receive approval to buy H200 chips. However, the number of processors they will be allowed to import is expected to be capped at fewer than 2,00,000 units in total, less than half of what the companies had initially requested.

The move marks a shift in Beijing’s stance. While the US government had already granted export approvals to roughly 10 Chinese companies to purchase H200 chips, Chinese authorities had so far withheld domestic approval as they sought to reduce reliance on foreign semiconductors and encourage adoption of locally developed alternatives.

According to The Information, the approved H200 chips will be restricted to training AI models using public data and cannot be used to handle sensitive customer information. The policy is intended to ease a shortage of advanced AI computing capacity while maintaining safeguards around data security.

China’s leading AI developers have faced growing pressure to secure computing resources as demand for model training continues to rise. The shortage has been compounded by US export controls on advanced AI chips and Beijing’s push to support domestic chipmakers.

NVIDIA shares rose about 1% following the report.

The development comes days after reports emerged that DeepSeek and Z.ai are developing their own AI inference chips to reduce dependence on NVIDIA and Huawei.

NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang said in May that the company’s market share in China had fallen to zero as US export controls blocked sales of advanced AI chips to the country.

Kerala Chief Minister V D Satheesan is scheduled to inaugurate the Naviq Technology campus in Kochi on July 23.

"Naviq reflects a clear structural shift in how travel technology services are delivered, pairing deep industry expertise with an AI-first model built for speed and commercial impact," said Jason Wright, Partner at Apax Partners, an investor in the venture.

title: Cognizant to Train 15,000 Forward Deployed Engineers Under Frontier Workforce Model
content:
Cognizant plans to build a workforce of 5,000 Frontier Certified Engineers and 10,000 Frontier Business Operators by the end of 2026.

Cognizant said it will expand its AI-focused workforce by creating 15,000 specialised professionals, essentially forward-deployed engineers, under its newly announced Frontier programme, as IT services companies increasingly shift investments from AI experimentation to large-scale enterprise deployment.

The Nasdaq-listed technology services company said it aims to build a workforce of 5,000 Frontier Certified Engineers and 10,000 Frontier Business Operators, with its first deployment-ready batch expected by the fourth quarter of 2026.

Cognizant also plans to augment its own frontier talent pipeline through annual direct hires of Frontier-native talent from American and global universities.

The initiative comes as global IT services firms race to build AI capabilities amid rising enterprise demand for agentic AI, automation, and industry-specific AI deployments.

Rather than focusing only on AI model implementation, Cognizant said the programme is designed to combine technical expertise with operational and domain knowledge to help clients translate AI investments into measurable business outcomes.

"Closing the AI outcome gap demands talent who not only understand a client's industry deeply but can also reimagine the way work is structured and take end-to-end responsibility for delivering results in collaboration with clients, on any model or cloud the client selects," Cognizant CEO Ravi Kumar S said in a statement.

The company said its frontier workforce will be model- and cloud-agnostic, allowing teams to work across AI platforms from providers including OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Microsoft, Amazon Web Services, NVIDAI, Salesforce, and ServiceNow.

It plans to strengthen its AI talent pipeline through expanded training infrastructure, certification programmes, and responsible AI education across its workforce.

The programme will be organised around two roles.

Frontier Certified Engineers are AI specialists who will design, deploy and manage enterprise-grade agentic AI systems, combining deep industry expertise with full-stack AI engineering. They will build the retrieval and context layers that keep AI systems grounded in business-specific knowledge, orchestrate multiple AI agents into production, and remain responsible for monitoring, tuning, and improving these systems after deployment.

Meanwhile, Frontier Business Operators will oversee day-to-day business outcomes in workplaces where human employees and AI agents work together, using their operational expertise to manage AI-driven workflows, handle exceptions, and continuously refine agent performance to improve reliability and align with client requirements.

Many enterprises are now looking at forward-deployed engineering as a new revenue stream as AI cannibalises revenue. Within days of one another, both Amazon Web Services and Microsoft announced major investments in dedicated engineering organisations that will work directly with enterprise customers to deploy AI.

GCCs currently contribute nearly 2% to India's GDP, with the IT sector being the largest export area.

The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) will assess whether AI is affecting the pace of global capability centre (GCC) expansion even after a series of labour and tax reforms targeted at boosting the sector.

The review comes as the government evaluates whether policy changes have translated into stronger GCC growth and what role AI may be playing in altering investment decisions.

Speaking at the CII GCC Business Summit in New Delhi, MeitY Secretary S Krishnan said the government wants to measure the outcomes of recent reforms, including changes to labour regulations and safe harbour tax provisions. If GCC momentum has not accelerated as expected, the government will examine whether AI is a contributing factor.

Krishnan noted that GCCs now contribute nearly 2% of India’s GDP, while IT and IT-enabled services remain the country’s largest export sector at about $250 billion. He said AI should be deployed across GCCs to leverage India’s talent base and cost advantages. He also argued that slower enterprise adoption of AI globally presents an opportunity for India’s GCC ecosystem.

The government’s assessment comes alongside comments from Chief Economic Adviser V Anantha Nageswaran, who said AI is likely to displace routine and rule-based work but will also create demand for higher-value skills and capabilities.

Addressing the same summit, Nageswaran urged GCCs to invest in skilling, capability development, and innovation. He said India’s long-term advantage would depend on moving beyond low-cost execution and building expertise around emerging technologies.

“AI does not build, deploy, or govern itself. Someone has to design these systems, train them, test them, correct them, and hold them to account,” Nageswaran said. “Someone has to decide where they should be used and where they must not be used.”

He argued that AI would not hollow out GCCs. Instead, centres that adapt could increase the value their workforce generates.

The Centre has introduced several measures to strengthen the GCC ecosystem. Nageswaran highlighted the expansion of the transfer pricing safe harbour regime, which aims to improve tax certainty by raising thresholds and expediting approvals. The government has also launched a framework to encourage GCC expansion into tier-2 and tier-3 cities.

Additionally, in the Budget 2026, the union government revised the transfer pricing safe harbour framework for GCCs, allowing eligible centres to qualify for a five-year safe harbour at a 15.5% operating margin. The measure sought to reduce transfer pricing disputes, improve tax certainty and make India a more attractive destination for multinational firms looking to establish GCCs.

At the same time, both officials also stressed that policy support alone would not determine India’s future position in the global GCC market. Krishnan said AI deployment could unlock higher-order technology jobs in India, even as lower-level roles become redundant. Nageswaran warned that India’s competitive edge could erode if skill development and innovation fail to keep pace with global competition.

title: Federal Official Mentions Cognizant as US Intensifies H-1B Fraud Probe
content:
“We have whistleblowers talking about some of the biggest companies like Cognizant who have been in chatter of issues with PERM and H-1B Visas.”

The United States government has escalated its crackdown on alleged fraud involving H-1B visa and PERM abuse, labour trafficking, with companies like Cognizant being mentioned by a senior federal official.

“For far too long, fraudsters believed they could game the US employment-based visa system and get away with it. They were wrong. This isn’t just paperwork fraud; it’s the exploitation of vulnerable workers, forced labor, the displacement of American workers, and abusive human trafficking,” Anthony D’Esposito, Labour Department Inspector General, said in a statement.

In an interview with Fox News on July 8, D’Esposito said the investigators had already issued dozens of subpoenas, as part of what he called as the Trump administration’s most aggressive action against foreign labour fraud.

“We have whistleblowers talking about some of the biggest companies like Cognizant who have been in chatter of issues with PERM and H-1B Visas,” he told Fox News.

The H-1B visa is a non-immigrant US work visa that allows American companies to temporarily employ foreign professionals in specialised occupations. The visa is initially granted for a period of up to three years and can be extended for another three years, capped at a maximum of six years.

The PERM programme, meanwhile, is the labour certification as a mandatory step towards an employment-based Green Card, where an employer proves to the Department of Labour that they could not find a qualified, willing US worker for the role.

This crackdown followed a June legal setback for the administration, when a federal judge struck down Trump administration’s controversial immigration measures requiring employers to pay a controversial $100,000 fee for new H-1B visas. US President Donald Trump introduced the ruling last year through a presidential proclamation.

The probe is expected to be closely watched in India, as Indian nationals consistently account for over 70% of all H-1B approvals. Large technology firms such as Cognizant frequently rely on this skilled-worker pipeline to bring Indian professionals to the United States.

title: OpenAI Launches GPT-Live with Real-Time Voice Conversations Powered by GPT-5.5
content:
Following the acquisition, Verloop.io’s team and operations will be integrated into Nurix AI.

Enterprise AI startup Nurix AI has acquired conversational AI company Verloop.io, as it looks to build a broader platform for deploying AI agents across voice- and chat-based customer interactions.

The Bengaluru-based company said the acquisition combines its voice AI platform, NuPlay, with Verloop.io’s chat automation capabilities and enterprise customer base across India and the Middle East.

Nurix AI, founded by Mukesh Bansal, builds AI agents for enterprise workflows, focusing on customer engagement and operational automation. The company is backed by Accel, General Catalyst, and Prosus.

Verloop.io, founded by Gaurav Singh, has built conversational AI products for sectors including banking, fintech, retail, and telecommunications. The company says it currently powers more than 20 million customer interactions each month.

The deal comes as enterprises move beyond experimenting with generative AI tools and begin deploying agents in production environments. While voice agents are increasingly being used for customer support, sales and collections, chat-based interfaces remain central to digital customer journeys, particularly in messaging-first markets such as India and the Middle East.

“AI is becoming a core operating layer for enterprises, but its value will be measured by real business outcomes, not pilots,” Mukesh Bansal, Founder and CEO of Nurix AI, said in a statement. “Acquiring Verloop.io strengthens our ability to help enterprises move from experimentation to measurable ROI. Their expertise in chat automation, combined with Nurix’s work in voice AI, gives us a stronger platform to automate workflows across key customer touchpoints.”

Through the acquisition, Nurix plans to support enterprises with AI agents that can handle both synchronous voice interactions and asynchronous chat-led workflows. The company said this could be particularly relevant for high-volume use cases in financial services and retail, where businesses need to manage customer conversations across multiple channels.

Verloop.io’s team and operations will become part of Nurix AI. Singh will join Nurix’s leadership team and help shape product strategy, enterprise go-to-market efforts, and develop the company’s next-generation AI agents.

“Over the last decade, we’ve learned that enterprises don’t struggle to understand the possibilities of AI, but they struggle to deploy it reliably at scale,” said Singh. “Together with Nurix AI, we have exactly the kind of agentic platform we believe the market needs, and together we can dramatically accelerate how quickly enterprises adopt autonomous AI across the customer lifecycle.”

The acquisition also gives Nurix a stronger foothold in chat-led customer engagement, an area where Verloop.io has built experience in regulated industries.

title: Semiconductor Fabs to Benefit as Govt Scraps Import Duty on Critical Electronic Components
content:
The waiver of basic customs duty covers essential inputs such as capital goods and equipment for producing lithium-ion cells, including machinery to enhance domestic production.

What Actually Matters.

The government has waived customs duty on essential machinery for lithium-ion battery and electronics manufacturing until March 2029.

The removal of basic customs duty aims to enhance domestic production capabilities in the electronics sector.

The Centre has expanded customs duty concessions for specified machinery, equipment, and components used in electronics and lithium-ion battery manufacturing by extending the validity of existing exemptions until March 31, 2029.

The Finance Ministry has issued notifications waiving the basic customs duty (BCD) on goods used in the manufacture of key electronic components, extending the duty relief on essential inputs and capital goods for domestic production.

The government has removed BCD on capital goods and equipment used to produce lithium-ion cells for electric vehicles and consumer electronics, including machinery at various stages of cell manufacturing, to support domestic production.

It also includes machinery for powder preparation, slurry mixing, coating, and other production processes. It also covers auxiliary systems, such as solvent recovery units and effluent treatment plants, that support battery manufacturing.

Additionally, the notification extends duty exemptions to certain inputs for manufacturing electronic goods, including PCBAs, camera modules, connectors, USB cables, and other specified components.

The changes amend the customs exemption schedule by inserting and revising entries covering electronic components and lithium-ion battery manufacturing equipment. The notification specifies that imports must satisfy the conditions set out in the relevant exemption entries to qualify for the concessional treatment.

The duty waiver is intended to reduce the cost of importing critical manufacturing inputs while supporting India's electronics manufacturing ecosystem. Industry is expected to benefit from lower input costs for products such as smartphones, consumer electronics, and battery cells, although the notification itself does not specify any production or investment targets.

The latest customs notification forms part of the government's broader programme of tariff rationalisation for the electronics sector. In recent years, India has used a combination of changes to customs duties, production-linked incentive (PLI) schemes, and semiconductor initiatives to expand domestic manufacturing capacity and increase local value addition in electronics and advanced battery technologies.

The notification does not alter customs duties on finished electronic products; instead, it focuses on components, machinery, and equipment used in domestic manufacturing.

title: Indian IT Braces for Soft Start to FY27 as AI Margins Remain a Mirage
content:
Entire says its distributed Git network sustained 570,000 repository clones per hour and 2.1 million Git pushes per hour in early testing, targeting AI coding agents that generate heavy concurrent Git traffic.

Entire, the developer startup founded by former GitHub CEO Thomas Dohmke, has launched a preview of its distributed Git hosting network, claiming it can sustain around 570,000 Git clones per hour from a single repository, 586 pushes per second (about 2.1 million per hour), and roughly 470 combined clone-and-push operations per second in agent-style workloads.

The company said early testing put the platform up to 25 times ahead of competing Git hosting performance claims, compared with Cursor Origin's claimed 81,000 pushes per hour.

The service lets developers mirror existing GitHub repositories onto Entire's regional infrastructure, allowing AI coding agents to clone and fetch code from nearby mirrors instead of repeatedly hitting GitHub, reducing read bottlenecks and rate-limit issues during high-concurrency workloads.

“We believe that Git hosting must return to its original promise: a truly distributed network, not a system where the world's software lives in a single location,” says Dohmke.

He added that the company plans to ‘decentralise and open source our Git network’ over the coming months.

“By doing so, we enable any developer or agent to host their code in-region, pushing, pulling, and cloning close to where they operate, fast and without bottlenecks, while still part of a global, collaborative network.”

The service is available today to existing Entire users across the US, Europe, and Australia, while new users will join via a waitlist as the company gradually expands capacity.

Entire launched in February with a semantic memory layer that records every AI coding session, prompt, tool call and checkpoint alongside source code.

The platform integrates with coding agents including Anthropic's Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, Cursor, Factory AI and GitHub Copilot, and has since added features such as Entire Blame, which links code to the AI session and prompt that produced it, Entire Review for multi-agent code reviews, and semantic search across both code and the reasoning behind code changes.

Entire emerged from stealth in February with a $60 million seed round at a $300 million valuation, led by Felicis with participation from Madrona, M12 and Basis Set.

Analysts expect a muted start to FY27 as Indian IT’s enterprise spending remains cautious, while AI is yet to generate meaningful high-margin revenues.

India's IT sector seems to be at the mercy of an ominous prophecy. As was the case in the last quarter of FY26, brokerages and analysts expect a subdued start to FY27, with macro uncertainty, cautious enterprise spending, and AI-led disruption continuing to weigh on growth.

Brokerage firm Motilal Oswal Financial Services expects demand across the sector to stay soft in the first quarter, with macro uncertainty, AI-driven disruption, and geopolitical overhangs continuing to weigh on discretionary spending and client decision-making.

“Against this backdrop, we build in tepid QoQ growth across our coverage universe for 1QFY27, with the soft start likely extending into 2QFY27 as well,” it said.

The mood was sombre even before Indian IT rolled out of Q1.

Accenture, often considered the bellwether for India's IT services sector, received a muted response from investors after the Irish tech giant trimmed its full-year revenue growth guidance to 3–4% in local currency from the 3–5% range it had projected in March. New bookings, seen as an indicator of future revenue as they reflect work expected to be billed over the next 12–18 months, fell 2% in dollar terms and 3% in local currency to $19.3 billion, weighing on Indian IT stocks.

Meanwhile, the broader IT sector continues to navigate multiple headwinds, including the volatile situation in the Middle East, frontier AI models and forward-deployed engineers threatening to cannibalise its revenue, and the collapse of the traditional per-hour billing model.

“We expect Indian IT to begin FY27 with another quarter of modest growth, with tier-1 companies likely to report around 0.5–1.5% constant currency growth. The underlying demand environment remains cautious, as enterprises continue to prioritise efficiency-led technology investments over large discretionary transformation programmes,” Gaurav Vasu, Founder and CEO of business intelligence firm UnearthInsight, tells AIM.

Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), the country's largest IT services company, will announce its Q1 FY27 results on July 9, kicking off the IT earnings season.

According to Motilal Oswal, TCS is expected to report flat sequential revenue growth in constant currency, as steady execution in banking and consumer verticals is likely to be offset by continued softness in communications and cautious discretionary spending across manufacturing and North America.

Infosys is expected to lead large-cap growth at around 2% quarter-on-quarter in constant currency, aided by a two-month contribution from its recent Optimum and Stratus acquisitions for a total of $560 million, while Tech Mahindra is expected to grow around 1% on the back of large telecom deal ramp-ups.

However, the brokerage firm noted that HCLTech and Wipro are expected to decline, hurt by client-specific issues, delayed ramp-ups, and seasonal weakness.

Tier-2 firms, once again, are expected to outperform their larger peers, with Hexaware Technologies leading the pack with an expected 4.8% sequential growth on a constant currency basis, followed by Persistent Systems and Mphasis, among others.

Vasu notes that while artificial intelligence is now embedded across most engagements, it is still driving productivity rather than creating a separate high-margin revenue stream for these companies. Hence, margins are likely to remain range-bound, with wage hikes and continued AI investments offsetting the benefits of rupee depreciation.

Equirus Securities also expects the top six Indian IT services companies to report a modest constant-currency US-dollar revenue performance, ranging from -1.7% to +1.1% quarter-on-quarter.

“Enterprise technology spending is expected to remain measured during the June quarter as global macroeconomic uncertainty, geopolitical developments and a continued focus on AI-led productivity gains keep discretionary IT investments under pressure,” per Equirus.

UnearthInsight forecasts Indian IT’s full-year FY27 growth to remain subdued at 3–4%

As AIM analysed earlier, the Nifty IT index closed the first half of the year down nearly 29%, making it the worst-performing sectoral index on the exchange and one of the roughest first halves for the Indian IT sector since the dot-com crash of 2001.

With large-cap growth expected to be flat to negative and a guidance-trimming cycle likely underway, the sector heads into results season with low expectations, leaving room for either an expected prolonged slowdown or a modestly positive surprise if deal pipelines prove more resilient than feared.

title: US Insurance Giant Nationwide Opens 1st International GCC in Hyderabad
content:
The company wants engineers who can take AI systems from design to production while working directly with enterprise customers.

Indian AI Startup Sarvam AI is hiring forward-deployed engineers (FDEs) as the company expands deployments of its AI platform across enterprises and public institutions in India.

Sarvam is building what it describes as a sovereign AI platform for India, spanning research, foundation models, infrastructure, and applications. The company works with enterprises and public institutions, with customers including Tata Capital, SBI Life, CRED, IDFC, and LIC.

Sarvam’s hiring also comes as forward-deployed engineering becomes a priority across the AI industry. Last week, AWS announced a $1 billion forward-deployed engineering organisation that will embed engineers with enterprise customers to build production AI systems. Microsoft followed with the Microsoft Frontier Company, backed by a $2.5 billion investment and a team of around 6,000 engineers and AI specialists focused on helping customers deploy AI at scale.

According to the job posting, the role will involve working directly with enterprise customers to integrate Sarvam’s AI platform into business workflows. Engineers will be responsible for taking AI systems from design to production while working closely with customer engineering teams.

“We’re looking for an FDE to work directly with enterprise clients integrating our platform into their business workflows,” the company said in the job listing. “You will be embedded with clients—understanding their operational processes, configuring the platform for their needs, debugging issues end-to-end, and ensuring they achieve high-quality outcomes across their use cases.”

The company said the role combines software engineering with customer-facing responsibilities. Engineers will write integration scripts, configure platforms, fix bugs, and serve as the primary technical contact for enterprise accounts.

Sarvam said FDEs will “own the technical arc of customer engagements, from scoping the solution through to the system running in production.” The role also includes designing AI systems that meet reliability, latency, accuracy, and cost requirements, as well as deploying them in customer environments.

The company expects engineers to work across a range of AI applications, including voice and conversational systems, developer tools built around Sarvam's APIs, translation and dubbing pipelines, and agentic AI workflows.

“FDSEs are hands-on engineers, not technical project managers,” the job description states.

Engineers will be expected to build evaluation pipelines, measure system performance, and iterate based on production data while sharing feedback with Sarvam’s product and research teams.

Sarvam is looking for candidates with strong AI fundamentals, including experience with large language models, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), context engineering, memory systems, structured outputs, and agentic frameworks such as LangGraph, LlamaIndex, or Google ADK. The company also expects candidates to have experience across backend development, cloud infrastructure, and distributed systems.

The company said it values engineers who have shipped AI products, contributed to open-source projects, or built production systems. Experience deploying AI in regulated sectors such as banking, financial services, insurance, or the public sector will be an advantage.

Sarvam AI recently closed its Series B funding, raising $234 million toward a planned $300 million round at a $1.5 billion valuation. The round was led by HCLTech and Bessemer Venture Partners, with participation from existing investors including Khosla Ventures and Peak XV Partners.

The expansion comes as the company enters its 100th year of operations.

US-based insurance and financial services company Nationwide has established its first international global capability centre (GCC) in Hyderabad, marking the company’s expansion beyond its three US campuses and strengthening Telangana’s position as a global hub for banking and insurance technology.

The new entity, Nationwide Global Services Centre Private Limited (Nationwide India), will become the company’s first international campus and operate as part of Nationwide’s global 24/7 operating model aimed at improving agility, accelerating innovation and supporting business growth.

The Hyderabad centre will be led by Vikas Jaswal, who has been appointed Senior Vice President and Managing Director, Nationwide Global Services India.

The company said the India centre will build critical capabilities, support business operations and enhance productivity across the organisation.

“Today, nine of the world’s top 10 BFSI giants are driving innovation, advanced product engineering from Hyderabad. I am delighted to welcome Nationwide, another leading American insurance company, to Telangana’s growing line-up of strong global value centres (GVCs),” said Duddilla Sridhar Babu, Telangana Minister for Information Technology, Electronics, Communications, Industries and Commerce, and Legislative Affairs.

Nationwide said Hyderabad was selected because of its mature GCC ecosystem, deep technology talent pool and ability to support engineering, digital and business capabilities. Jaswal stated that the India campus is central to Nationwide’s long-term growth strategy.

“The Hyderabad campus enables Nationwide to meet increased business demand, growth goals, and expands our global operational capabilities,” he said.

He added that India's skilled workforce and Hyderabad’s established capability centre ecosystem made the city a natural choice for the company’s international expansion.

Jaswal, who brings more than 25 years of experience in building and scaling global capability centres in India, will oversee operations, talent, innovation and capability development while working closely with Nationwide’s global leadership teams.

Beyond business operations, Nationwide said the Hyderabad campus will offer flexible work models, a people-first culture and community engagement initiatives as it builds its India workforce.

The expansion comes as Nationwide enters its 100th year of operations. The company said it recorded its fifth consecutive year of record growth in 2025, reaching its strongest financial position to date, driven by robust performance across both its financial services and property and casualty businesses.

What Actually Matters.

Ford has opened a new 800-seat facility in Coimbatore to enhance its global business continuity operations.

The centre will support finance and business functions, serving Ford's global markets from India.

Ford Business Solutions (FBS) India, the global capability centre (GCC) of Ford Motor Company, has opened a new office in Coimbatore, Tamil Nadu, to strengthen the resilience of its global operations.

The facility, inaugurated at SVB Tech Park, is FBS’ third location in India after Chennai and Bengaluru. It will support accounting, Ford Credit, and business operations teams serving Ford’s global markets.

The new centre will act as a dedicated business continuity hub, helping Ford maintain critical operations without disruption. Spread across three floors and covering more than 82,000 sq ft, the facility can accommodate around 800 employees and is part of the company’s strategy to support global operations from India.

Gopinath Chidambaram, Technical Director for Gen AI, Cloud and Analytics at Ford Motor Company, told AIM that this GCC is focused on a specific vertical and will not look at AI operations.

Gangapriya Chakraverti, India Site Head and Managing Director of FBS, said the company selected Coimbatore because of its talent base and growing business ecosystem.

“We’ve had team members from this city working for us for some time now and seen firsthand the strength of the talent pool here. Coimbatore has also grown into a vibrant, thriving business hub, and we wanted to build a presence in a city that has so much to offer,” she added.

The centre includes more than 230 workstations on each floor, along with meeting rooms, boardrooms, focus rooms, and collaborative spaces designed for hybrid work.

The company said the opening comes as India’s GCC sector takes on greater strategic responsibilities for multinational firms. Ford said its India teams now support technology and business transformation efforts across the company’s global operations.

Keerthana Sampath, Tamil Nadu’s Minister for Industries, Investment Promotion and Commerce, said the new facility reflects the state’s position as a destination for global capability centres and knowledge-based industries.

Ford Business Solutions India employs more than 12,000 people across its operations and supports every division of Ford Motor Company worldwide. The Coimbatore centre joins the company’s Global Technology and Business Centre in Chennai and its Technology Incubation Centre in Bengaluru.

As AI pilots struggle to reach production across enterprise environments, one supply chain technology company is betting on combining neural AI with older, structured forms of reasoning.

What Actually Matters.

95% of enterprise AI pilots fail to progress beyond initial demonstrations due to various challenges.

Organisational change management is a critical issue intertwined with data quality and architecture in AI implementation.

A 2025 MIT study noted that 95% of enterprise AI pilots fail to move beyond an initial demonstration. The reasons are familiar: messy data, resistant organisations, or technology oversold ahead of its capability.

However, Ashwin Rao, Chief Technology Officer at o9 Solutions, a supply chain planning company, argues that these explanations miss a more basic problem with architecture itself.

"I don't think those are separate problems. In my experience, the hardest problem in enterprise AI is organisational change management. Data quality matters as well. But both of those issues are closely connected to architecture,” Rao tells AIM.

Most enterprise AI products built since 2022 lean heavily on large language models, using them to interpret queries, generate analyses, and produce recommendations.

"A standard LLM-based agent can often generate a plausible answer to each question individually," he says. "The challenge is that it does not inherently understand how those decisions connect across the business."

He points to a recurring failure pattern: "A system might recommend a replenishment quantity that violates a contractual minimum order, or identify a relationship in the data and mistake correlation for causation."

This is the gap o9 says its hybrid model is designed to close. The company calls the approach neurosymbolic AI, combining neural AI, which learns patterns from data, with symbolic AI, which operates from defined rules and structured relationships. Neural AI resembles learning through repetition and experience. Symbolic AI resembles coaching and technique.

The company has built this into a framework it describes as ‘10-80-10’.

The first 10% of the process involves the language model interpreting intent: which products, locations, and planning periods are in question. The middle 80% is enterprise reasoning, where the system traces plans, forecasts, inventory positions, and decisions across the business to identify the actual cause. The final 10% returns to the language model, which communicates the findings in business terms.

"In many cases, the inventory issue that appears in a report is not the actual cause," Rao says. "Excess inventory may be linked to a forecasting assumption, a production policy, a procurement decision, or a combination of factors."

The architecture predates the current generative AI boom by years. o9 had been developing the Enterprise Knowledge Graph and its underlying planning models for 15 years before large language models became widely available.

"What changed in 2022 was not the need for the Enterprise Knowledge Graph," he notes. "What changed was who could use it. The capability existed already, but required specialist users. Language models opened access to it and also made it possible to work with unstructured sources such as emails and supplier communications at scale”

This puts o9 at odds with prevailing market sentiment, where boards and executives have made substantial commitments to generative AI and, in some cases, expect to see more of it rather than less. Rao says this produces friction in early conversations, though it tends to resolve quickly.

"What we typically find, however, is that the conversation quickly shifts from language capability to decision-making," he explains. "The question becomes less about how much of the system is powered by an LLM and more about whether the system can be trusted when decisions have real operational and financial consequences."

That question of trust extends to how enterprises handle disagreement between functions. Finance, supply chain, and commercial teams frequently work from different assumptions and different numbers. Rao does not present the Enterprise Knowledge Graph as a tool for forcing consensus.

"When teams disagree, the system helps make the disagreement explicit," he says. "Is it a different demand assumption? A supply constraint? A financial target? A policy decision?" The aim, he notes, is a shared context for decision-making rather than agreement on outcomes.

On sudden disruptions, such as port strikes or geopolitical shocks, Rao is measured about what the system can offer. "No system can reliably predict every black swan event," he adds. "What matters is how quickly the organisation can understand what changed and decide what to do next."

In these situations, neural AI interprets incoming signals while the symbolic layer connects them to inventory, capacity, and financial outcomes that already exist within the business.

Asked whether o9's investment in India reflects faster adoption of complex AI architectures among Indian enterprises compared to Western markets, Rao declines to frame it in geographic terms. "What tends to separate successful enterprise AI initiatives from unsuccessful ones is not geography. It is whether the organisation has connected its data, decisions, and processes in a way that allows AI to operate within the realities of the business," he shares.

The broader argument is that the industry's pilot failures are not primarily a language problem. They are a structural one, rooted in whether systems can connect to the actual mechanics of how a business runs, and whether their conclusions can be traced and trusted when the financial stakes are real.

title: India’s Retail GCCs Surpass 5 Global Peer Markets Combined as AI Talent Shortage Looms, Finds Report
content:
AI professionals currently represent fewer than one in 20 employees across India's retail GCC ecosystem.

India’s retail and FMCG global capability centre (GCC) ecosystem has emerged as the world’s largest and most AI-mature destination, surpassing the combined scale of five competing global markets.

However, a severe shortage of senior AI talent threatens to slow the sector’s next phase of growth, according to a new report by TeamLease Digital.

The report, ‘The Retail Pivot: Consumer GCCs Find Their India Edge’, found that India is home to 180 retail GCCs employing around 2,72,300 professionals, making its retail GCC workforce 34% larger than Poland, the Philippines, Mexico, Germany and Egypt. India also leads peer markets in AI adoption, with AI professionals accounting for 5–7% of the retail GCC workforce, ahead of destinations such as Germany.

Despite this lead, AI expertise remains scarce. AI professionals currently represent fewer than one in 20 employees across India’s retail GCC ecosystem, while only 320 professionals have more than eight years of AI experience, averaging fewer than two senior AI specialists per centre.

“The report highlights both India's scale and the challenges accompanying its rapid evolution,” said Neeti Sharma, CEO, TeamLease Digital.

“With just 320 senior AI professionals across 180 GCCs and more than half of all AI talent concentrated in one city, we are looking at a capability concentration risk that most GCC leadership teams haven't formally priced in,” Sharma added.

The report notes that hiring demand across retail GCCs doubled between 2024 and 2025, marking the strongest growth period in three years. More than 52,000 job opportunities were generated in 2025 alone.

Technology, customer success and supply chain functions currently account for around 60% of the workforce, but are expected to drive more than 80% of hiring demand by 2028.

Technology and engineering roles are projected to increase from 25,140 positions in 2025 to over 41,000 by 2028, while data and analytics is expected to become the fastest-growing capability after rebounding sharply in 2025 as GenAI adoption accelerated and demand shifted toward AI infrastructure.

The report identifies skills such as LLM engineering, GenAIOps, MLOps and vector databases as growing at over 100% year-on-year, while traditional process-oriented skills—including spreadsheet-based planning, manual QA testing and rule-based analytics—are witnessing steep declines. Finance and shared services roles face a projected 42% displacement rate.

Bengaluru continues to dominate India’s retail GCC ecosystem with nearly 84,000 professionals, followed by Delhi-NCR (over 66,000) and Hyderabad (around 45,000).

The city also accounts for 54% of India’s retail GCC AI talent, making it the primary destination for advanced global AI mandates. Hyderabad is emerging as the leading secondary AI hub, while Pune is positioning itself as an engineering-focused alternative.

AI workforce penetration has grown from 2.1% in 2022 to 4.8% in 2025, and is expected to reach 7.2% in 2026.

One of the report’s more striking findings is that retail GCCs are sourcing most of their AI talent from outside the retail sector.

Of the 28,500 professionals hired over the past year, 90.2% came from other industries, including IT services (17.5%), product companies (14%), and consulting firms (10.5%).

Attrition also remains a challenge, particularly among early-career professionals. Employees with one to two years of experience recorded the highest attrition rate at 25%, while finance functions reported churn of 22%.

The growing shortage of AI talent is also reshaping compensation.

According to the report, AI and machine learning specialists command the highest salary premiums across the retail workforce in the GCC.

Professionals with three to six years of AI experience earn a median compensation of ₹46 lakh, roughly twice the market median for comparable experience levels.

Those with six to 10 years of experience earn a median of ₹68 lakh, representing a 1.7x premium over the broader market.

At senior leadership levels, professionals combining deep domain expertise with AI capabilities now command compensation exceeding ₹1.2 crore annually, placing many roles near or above the $100,000 salary benchmark in India.

Currently, only 22 of the top 50 retail GCCs have active GenAI teams, indicating significant room for expansion as India’s retail capability centres increasingly evolve from operational support hubs into global AI and product innovation centres.

SambaNova has secured a $1 billion Series F first close at an $11 billion valuation to expand its AI inference platform and global enterprise deployments.

What Actually Matters.

SambaNova has raised $1 billion in Series F funding, achieving an $11 billion valuation to enhance its AI inference platform.

The funding will support global enterprise deployments as demand for AI inference infrastructure continues to rise.

US-based AI chip startup SambaNova has raised $1 billion in a Series F funding round at an $11 billion valuation, as the company looks to capitalise on growing enterprise demand for AI inference infrastructure.

The company will use the capital to expand its AI infrastructure platform and accelerate enterprise AI deployments globally as demand for inference computing continues to grow.

The round, led by General Atlantic, saw significant participation from Seligman Ventures, T Rowe Price Associates and Capital Group. Existing and new investors also include funds and accounts managed by BlackRock, Intel Capital, Qatar Investment Authority (QIA), Battery Ventures, Atlantic Bridge, Walden International, Redline Capital, Temasek, GIC, GV, MSD Capital, WRVI Capital, SK Telecom, and Vista Equity Partners.

Founded in 2017 by Rodrigo Liang, Kunle Olukotun, and Christopher Ré, SambaNova develops proprietary Reconfigurable Dataflow Units (RDUs) alongside a full-stack AI platform designed specifically for inference, the process of running trained AI models in production. The company says its architecture delivers higher performance and energy efficiency than conventional GPU-based systems for enterprise AI workloads.

It counts Intel and Saudi Aramco among its clients that have deployed SambaNova’s RDUs for computing solutions.

"This financing marks a pivotal moment for SambaNova and validates our vision that inference is the defining workload of the AI era," said Rodrigo Liang, Co-founder and CEO of SambaNova, in a statement.

"As enterprises race to operationalise AI, they need infrastructure purpose-built for inference at scale. With General Atlantic's partnership and the continued support of our investors, we are well positioned to accelerate innovation and help customers deploy AI faster, more efficiently and at lower cost," Liang added.

Earlier this year, SambaNova introduced its SN50 chip and disclosed a funding round of over $350 million in conjunction with a strategic partnership with Intel.

Martín Escobari, Co-President and Head of Global Growth Equity at General Atlantic, said the investment reflects the firm's confidence in the company's technology and market opportunity.

"SambaNova's differentiated platform is purpose-built for the rapidly growing inference market," he added.

Alongside the funding announcement, SambaNova revealed that JPMorganChase has selected its RDUs for fast, on-premises AI inference. Meanwhile, SoftBank was the first deployment partner for its SN50 AI chip.

The partnership will integrate Claude into UST’s engineering, industry, and enterprise platforms for clients.

What Actually Matters.

UST partners with Anthropic to integrate Claude AI models into engineering and enterprise platforms.

The collaboration aims to enhance AI deployment from pilot projects to enterprise-scale applications.

IT services company UST has collaborated with Anthropic to integrate the Claude family of AI models into its engineering platforms, enterprise solutions, and internal operations, while training and certifying 20,000 employees globally.

The partnership aims to help enterprises move from AI pilots to enterprise-scale deployments by combining Claude’s capabilities with UST’s engineering and domain expertise.

“Our alliance with Anthropic reflects UST's unwavering commitment to helping clients navigate the AI landscape with confidence and achieve meaningful business outcomes,” Krishna Sudheendra, CEO at UST, said in a statement.

Under the agreement, UST will expand the use of Claude across consulting, data, automation, cloud, infrastructure, and security services, as well as industry-specific platforms for sectors including healthcare, telecom, and banking.

UST said it is integrating Claude into engineering platforms used by semiconductor, automotive, manufacturing, telecom, embedded systems and IoT companies. The company expects the integration to support design verification, semiconductor validation, factory operations, and field services.

One of the first implementations will be through UST-iDEC, the company’s hardware and silicon validation platform. The company claims the platform reduces validation cycle times by 50–70% and shortens standard four-day turnaround times to 48 hours.

Claude will serve as the reasoning layer within the platform, helping engineers automate testing and identify faults earlier in the development process.

The company will also integrate Claude into healthcare, telecom, and banking platforms. These include UST CarePath for healthcare workflows, UST IntelliOps for network operations, and UST FinX for banking modernisation and compliance processes.

Beyond customer-facing platforms, UST plans to expand the use of Claude across its own legal, talent, marketing, infrastructure, and finance functions. The company said it is developing Claude-based workflows with human oversight built into key decision points.

Paul Smith, Chief Commercial Officer at Anthropic, said UST is “proving Claude inside their own engineering first, training 20,000 of their own people on it, before bringing it into the systems they build and run for clients”.

UST said it will create specialised teams to deploy Claude, with support from Anthropic’s training, certification, and technical guidance.

title: Enterprise AI-Focused TELUS Digital Taps IISc for Research, Talent Development
content:
With the agreement, TELUS and IISc aim to support joint projects, talent development, and exchange of researchers.

What Actually Matters.

TELUS Digital and IISc have formed a partnership for joint research and talent development in AI.

The collaboration aims to enhance the exchange of researchers between the two organisations.

TELUS Digital, a global tech and customer service company that helps enterprises build digital products, manage customer care, and train AI models, has signed an agreement with the Indian Institute of Science (IISc). The agreement covers research collaboration, talent development, and exchange between the two organisations.

TELUS Digital provides digital customer experience services and works on transformation projects for its clients. The company operates with teams that support client products and services, and works on business challenges, risk management and innovation projects for clients globally.

It operates technology and customer service centres in multiple locations in India, including Bengaluru.

Amith Nair, General Manager of AI Services Delivery at TELUS Digital, said that while IISc has researchers, TELUS Digital brings AI and engineering problems at a scale not found in a classroom.

Amar Naik, Vice President, Engineering at TELUS Digital, added that IISc researchers will work with the company's teams on research and development projects and take part in internships and assistantships.

"IISc researchers will work alongside our teams on live R&D projects, move through internships and assistantships with us, and graduate having already solved the kind of problems we hire for,” Naik noted in a statement.

"This partnership will facilitate converting scientific research into practical solutions that can be deployed,” Prof Ambedkar Dukkipati, Chair of the Centre for Scientific and Industrial Consultancy at IISc, shared.

The partnership sets out four areas of work: joint research and development projects; workshops, training and internships for students; exchange of researchers, students and publications between the organisations; and academic events and interactions between experts.

TELUS Digital said the agreement extends its activities in India, describing the partnership as a long-term arrangement related to research and technology development in the country.
