Google has selected 20 AI-first Indian startups spanning agentic AI, climate tech, healthcare, and developer infrastructure.

What Actually Matters.

Google has chosen 20 AI-first startups from nearly 2,500 applications for its 2026 Accelerator in India.

The selected startups focus on diverse fields including healthcare, climate tech, and developer infrastructure.

Google has unveiled the 2026 cohort of its Google for Startups Accelerator: India, selecting 20 AI-first startups from nearly 2,500 applications as the programme marks its 10th anniversary in the country. The three-month accelerator will provide founders with access to Google's AI stack, technical mentorship, and go-to-market support to help them scale their products.

"India's startup ecosystem is moving into a new frontier of agentic workflows and physical AI systems engineered to solve high-stakes, real-world challenges," Preeti Lobana, Vice President and Country Manager, Google India, said in a statement.

The latest cohort focuses on agentic AI, multimodal systems and physical AI, with startups spanning legal technology, healthcare, climate, developer tools, manufacturing, finance, cybersecurity, and voice AI.

"By equipping these pioneering founders with Google's full AI stack and deep technical mentorship, we are not only accelerating their path to global enterprise scale but also cementing the sovereign capabilities required to advance the India AI Mission and build a resilient, inclusive digital economy," she added.

Among the companies selected are Adalat AI, which is building an end-to-end justice technology stack to automate clerical processes in Indian courts; Aurassure, which combines AI with modular sensors to deliver hyperlocal climate intelligence; Aikenist, whose QuickSuite platform uses AI to optimise radiology workflows; and Jidoka, which develops AI-powered computer vision systems for automated inspection in manufacturing.

The cohort strongly highlights developer infrastructure represented through startups including CraftifAI, H2Loop AI, CreateOS by NodeOps, Pipeshift, PotpieAI, and TartanHQ, while fintech entrants include Binocs, Dodo Payments, and OnFinanceAI. Other selected startups are Ayna, FlexifyMe, Fitsol, Proxgy, Soundverse AI, SuperBryn, and Zeron.

The programme began with an in-person bootcamp at its Bengaluru campus and will focus over the coming months on product refinement, architecture optimisation, and preparing startups for large-scale deployment

The cohort strongly highlights developer infrastructure represented through startups including CraftifAI, H2Loop AI, CreateOS by NodeOps, Pipeshift, PotpieAI, and TartanHQ, while fintech entrants include Binocs, Dodo Payments, and OnFinanceAI. Other selected startups are Ayna, FlexifyMe, Fitsol, Proxgy, Soundverse AI, SuperBryn, and Zeron.

The programme began with an in-person bootcamp at its Bengaluru campus and will focus over the coming months on product refinement, architecture optimisation, and preparing startups for large-scale deployment

title: After DeepSeek, Z.ai Explores Building AI Chip as GLM Demand Surges: Report
content:
Z.ai is seeing rapid adoption of its GLM models as the Chinese AI company looks for reliable computing infrastructure.

Chinese AI startup Z.ai (formerly Zhipu AI) is considering developing its own AI chip as soaring demand for its GLM family of large language models is adding pressure on computing capacity, according to a report by The Information.

The company is reportedly looking beyond off-the-shelf processors to secure long-term access to computing power amid growing demand for AI training and inference.

According to The Information, Z.ai has begun weighing the feasibility of designing a proprietary chip, although the discussions remain at an early stage and no final decision has been made.

AIM could not independently verify the report.

The report said interest in the project has been fueled by the rapid adoption of Z.ai’s GLM models. The increase in usage has intensified the need for reliable computing infrastructure as competition among Chinese AI developers accelerates.

Any custom chip initiative would represent a significant strategic expansion for the Beijing-based company. Developing AI processors typically requires years of engineering work, substantial capital investment, and manufacturing partnerships, with only a handful of AI companies globally tasting success.

The reported deliberations also come as Chinese AI companies continue to face restrictions on access to the most advanced US-made AI chips, prompting many firms to diversify their hardware strategies through domestic suppliers and custom silicon.

Currently, NVIDIA’s H20 is the only advanced AI GPU that can be legally exported to China, and even then, shipments require US export licenses.

The H20 was specifically designed to comply with US export controls, but last April, it was subjected to an indefinite licensing requirement before the US later agreed to approve licenses for eligible exports.

Z.ai’s rival, DeepSeek, is also developing its first custom AI chip for inference, according to a recent Reuters report. The project began about a year ago and remains in its early stages. DeepSeek has been holding discussions with chip design firms, foundries, and memory suppliers while privately expanding its chip engineering team.

Z.ai has become one of China’s leading AI startups, with its GLM models gaining traction among developers and enterprises. The company has continued releasing increasingly capable open-source models while competing with domestic rivals and international AI labs.

Its latest model, GLM 5.2, performs competitively against closed models such as Claude Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5 on coding benchmarks, including Terminal-Bench, SWE-Bench, and agentic evaluations. It often narrows the performance gap while operating at a fraction of the cost.

content:
The Reliance Jio-backed firm has introduced an AI tool aimed at solopreneurs, home businesses, and small enterprises across the country

What Actually Matters.

Jio Haptik has launched SOLO, an AI platform for solopreneurs and small businesses in India.

The platform aims to support marketing, sales, and customer engagement for micro, small, and medium enterprises.

Conversational AI platform Jio Haptik has launched SOLO, a platform designed to give solopreneurs and small businesses access to tools for marketing, sales, and customer support. The company has set a target of reaching 2 million entrepreneurs across India within three years.

SOLO is targeting micro, small and medium enterprises and intends to handle content creation, customer engagement, lead generation, sales, and support for them.

Ahshad Jussawala, CEO of Jio Haptik, said larger businesses have historically had dedicated teams for marketing, sales, and customer support, while smaller businesses have had to manage with fewer resources. "We believe accessible AI and AI teams can change that equation at scale," he said in a statement.

The platform operates through two components: Tara, which handles marketing tasks, and Ved, which manages sales and support. According to the company, the system works independently rather than only in response to individual prompts, while giving business owners a review and approval step before content or messages are sent to customers.

Jio Haptik developed SOLO using inputs from several solopreneurs together with data from Interakt, a customer engagement company whose user base includes more than 100,000 small and medium businesses. The company said more than 10,000 businesses have signed up during an early access period.

Saumil Shah, Chief Technology Officer at Jio Haptik, said the company aims to build systems capable of taking on tasks rather than only functioning as agents responding to instructions. "We've combined autonomous planning, execution, and continuous learning into an AI business team designed specifically for entrepreneurs," he noted.

Shah said Tara and Ved are built to interpret business context, coordinate across departments, and work towards defined outcomes, adding that he expects this approach to change how businesses operate over the next decade.

To use the platform, business owners have to connect a website or Instagram account or upload an image of a product. The system then generates marketing plans, content, images and video, places advertising, and responds to customer messages on WhatsApp, following up with leads.

SOLO is available on Android and iOS. The platform offers a free tier, with paid plans starting at ₹2,000 per month.

title: Accenture Wins NATO's Multi-Million-Euro Digital Infrastructure Contract
content:
Accenture will work with Italian firm Leonardo to build a secure, cloud-enabled business network for NATO over seven years.

Accenture has secured a multi-million euro contract from the NATO Communications and Information Agency (NCIA) to help modernise the alliance's digital infrastructure, marking one of the consulting firm's significant public sector technology engagements in the defence sector.

The contract is part of NATO's Protected Business Network (PBN) programme, an initiative aimed at replacing legacy information technology systems with a more secure, cloud-enabled digital enterprise.

Under the agreement, Accenture will work alongside Italian aerospace and defence company Leonardo to deliver the project over the next seven years.

"Under the Protected Business Network, NATO is taking a key step to modernise its digital infrastructure and enable a more connected, data-driven enterprise, ensuring we deliver digital capabilities at speed and scale", NCIA General Manager Dylan Browne said in a statement.

The programme is intended to improve the alliance's digital resilience by providing a standardised and secure technology environment for NATO personnel across domains.

Financial terms of the contract were not disclosed, although NATO described it as a multi-million euro award.

The engagement comes as governments and defence organisations globally ramp up investments in secure cloud infrastructure, cybersecurity, and artificial intelligence amid rising geopolitical tensions and increasing cyber threats.

For Accenture, the deal expands its footprint in government and defence technology projects, an area where global consulting firms are seeing growing demand for digital transformation and secure enterprise platforms.

For the third quarter of fiscal year 2026, Accenture reported revenue of $18.7 billion, up 6% in dollar terms and 3% in local currency. However, its new bookings fell 2% in dollar terms and 3% in local currency, to $19.3 billion.

The NCIA oversees NATO's technology and cyber infrastructure, supporting command and control systems, communications networks, and digital services across operations.

title: IT Firm UST to Embed Claude Across Enterprise Platforms, Train 20,000 Employees
content:
The partnership will integrate Claude into UST’s engineering, industry, and enterprise platforms for clients.

What Actually Matters.

UST partners with Anthropic to integrate Claude AI models into engineering and enterprise platforms.

The collaboration aims to enhance AI deployment from pilot projects to enterprise-scale applications.

IT services company UST has collaborated with Anthropic to integrate the Claude family of AI models into its engineering platforms, enterprise solutions, and internal operations, while training and certifying 20,000 employees globally.

The partnership aims to help enterprises move from AI pilots to enterprise-scale deployments by combining Claude’s capabilities with UST’s engineering and domain expertise.

“Our alliance with Anthropic reflects UST's unwavering commitment to helping clients navigate the AI landscape with confidence and achieve meaningful business outcomes,” Krishna Sudheendra, CEO at UST, said in a statement.

Under the agreement, UST will expand the use of Claude across consulting, data, automation, cloud, infrastructure, and security services, as well as industry-specific platforms for sectors including healthcare, telecom, and banking.

UST said it is integrating Claude into engineering platforms used by semiconductor, automotive, manufacturing, telecom, embedded systems and IoT companies. The company expects the integration to support design verification, semiconductor validation, factory operations, and field services.

One of the first implementations will be through UST-iDEC, the company’s hardware and silicon validation platform. The company claims the platform reduces validation cycle times by 50–70% and shortens standard four-day turnaround times to 48 hours.

Claude will serve as the reasoning layer within the platform, helping engineers automate testing and identify faults earlier in the development process.

The company will also integrate Claude into healthcare, telecom, and banking platforms. These include UST CarePath for healthcare workflows, UST IntelliOps for network operations, and UST FinX for banking modernisation and compliance processes.

Beyond customer-facing platforms, UST plans to expand the use of Claude across its own legal, talent, marketing, infrastructure, and finance functions. The company said it is developing Claude-based workflows with human oversight built into key decision points.

Paul Smith, Chief Commercial Officer at Anthropic, said UST is “proving Claude inside their own engineering first, training 20,000 of their own people on it, before bringing it into the systems they build and run for clients”.

UST said it will create specialised teams to deploy Claude, with support from Anthropic’s training, certification, and technical guidance.

With the agreement, TELUS and IISc aim to support joint projects, talent development, and exchange of researchers.

What Actually Matters.

TELUS Digital and IISc have formed a partnership for joint research and talent development in AI.

The collaboration aims to enhance the exchange of researchers between the two organisations.

TELUS Digital, a global tech and customer service company that helps enterprises build digital products, manage customer care, and train AI models, has signed an agreement with the Indian Institute of Science (IISc). The agreement covers research collaboration, talent development, and exchange between the two organisations.

TELUS Digital provides digital customer experience services and works on transformation projects for its clients. The company operates with teams that support client products and services, and works on business challenges, risk management and innovation projects for clients globally.

It operates technology and customer service centres in multiple locations in India, including Bengaluru.

Amith Nair, General Manager of AI Services Delivery at TELUS Digital, said that while IISc has researchers, TELUS Digital brings AI and engineering problems at a scale not found in a classroom.

Amar Naik, Vice President, Engineering at TELUS Digital, added that IISc researchers will work with the company's teams on research and development projects and take part in internships and assistantships.

"IISc researchers will work alongside our teams on live R&D projects, move through internships and assistantships with us, and graduate having already solved the kind of problems we hire for,” Naik noted in a statement.

"This partnership will facilitate converting scientific research into practical solutions that can be deployed,” Prof Ambedkar Dukkipati, Chair of the Centre for Scientific and Industrial Consultancy at IISc, shared.

The partnership sets out four areas of work: joint research and development projects; workshops, training and internships for students; exchange of researchers, students and publications between the organisations; and academic events and interactions between experts.

TELUS Digital said the agreement extends its activities in India, describing the partnership as a long-term arrangement related to research and technology development in the country.

title: Perplexity is Building a Claude Code, Cursor Competitor: Report
content:
Perplexity has reportedly been using the AI tool internally since May.

Perplexity is developing an AI coding tool, marking the startup’s latest move into the increasingly competitive market for AI software engineering assistants currently led by Cursor, Anthropic, and OpenAI, according to a Business Insider report.

Codenamed ‘Teammate’, the company’s engineers have been using the tool since May, according to the report.

The platform is built to handle long-horizon software engineering tasks, and internal engineers have been using it to find bugs in the company’s systems; it is also said to provide access to multiple AI models.

AIM reached out to Perplexity for a comment but did not receive a response at the time of publishing.

Founded as an AI-powered search startup, Perplexity has steadily expanded into a broader AI platform with products including its Comet AI browser, enterprise search offerings, shopping features, finance research tools, and APIs. The company was last valued at $20 billion in a funding round completed last year.

In recent months, the company has introduced Perplexity Computer, an AI agent for executing multi-step workflows, and Brain, a persistent memory system that learns from previous tasks.

Brain builds a continuously updated context graph, improving answer correctness by 25% and recall by 16%, while reducing costs on history-dependent tasks by 13%. It initially launched in Research Preview for Max and Enterprise Max subscribers.

In another recent development, Reuters reported that Perplexity will soon adopt NVIDIA's new Vera CPUs for AI agent workloads.

Nate Kupp, VP for Computer Enterprise and Infrastructure at Perplexity, said the processor was around 1.5 times faster than conventional server CPUs for AI agent coding tasks, making it a good fit for workloads where agents continuously execute and coordinate software tasks.

In April, the company revealed that its revenue had shot up fivefold, from $100 million to $500 million, as it expanded its team by 34%. It expects to double its revenue again in 2026 while maintaining a relatively small team.

Perplexity’s annual recurring revenue rose from $16 million to $305 million over the past two years, according to a recent Financial Times report, which also noted that the figure had exceeded $450 million as of March.

title: [Exclusive] Bengaluru Startup QpiAI Open-Sources Quantum SDK for Developers, Researchers
content:
The quantum startup aims to expand access to quantum software and connect users to its quantum computers through QCloud.

What Actually Matters.

QpiAI has open-sourced its Quantum Software Development Kit, enhancing access for developers and researchers globally.

The SDK enables users to build quantum algorithms and connect to QpiAI's 8-qubit and 25-qubit quantum computers via QCloud.

QpiAI has open-sourced its Quantum Software Development Kit (SDK), opening up the platform to developers, researchers, startups, and universities worldwide. The Bengaluru-based quantum computing startup said the SDK allows users to build and run quantum algorithms and connect directly to its 8-qubit and 25-qubit quantum computers through QpiAI-QCloud.

With the release, the company aims to expand access to quantum software development and support applications across finance, logistics, materials science, chemistry, security, AI, optimisation, and scientific computing. The SDK is available on GitHub and can be integrated into existing development workflows.

“India is entering a defining decade for quantum technologies, and open-source software will be critical to building the talent, research, and innovation base that national leadership requires,” Nagendra Nagaraja, Founder and CEO of QpiAI, said in a statement.

Nagaraja told AIM that the startup wants to lower the barrier to entry for students and developers for quantum adoption. “We want developers, universities, and startups to build on Indian and global quantum infrastructure and contribute to a competitive quantum ecosystem,” he added.

The Python-based SDK includes tools for circuit creation, simulation, algorithm development, and workflow execution. It also supports AI-assisted and agentic development workflows, while local simulators allow developers to test algorithms before running them on quantum hardware.

QpiAI said the platform also supports AI-assisted and agentic development workflows.

The SDK can support coursework, research projects, hackathons, and developer training programmes. Early institutional adopters will also be eligible to join the QpiAI Academic & Innovation Network, which offers preferential commercial terms on QpiAI QCloud packages.

Lakshya Priyadarshi, VP of Quantum Platforms and Solutions at QpiAI, said that wider adoption depends on providing developers with easier access to experimentation and deployment.

“The QpiAI Quantum SDK is a practical bridge between quantum theory, simulation, real hardware, and industry applications,” he said. “By putting a strong software foundation in the hands of engineers and developers, we want to help build a diverse global quantum application ecosystem.”

The release also aligns with the objectives of India’s National Quantum Mission, according to the company.

QpiAI develops quantum processors, software platforms, and quantum-AI applications and operates a quantum foundry in Jakkur, Bengaluru, that supports superconducting, semiconductor, and photonic qubit technologies.

title: Meta Launches Muse Image AI Model With Web Search Feature, Previews Muse Video
content:
Meta has also released Content Seal, an invisible watermark designed to help identify AI-generated images.

Meta has launched Muse Image, its latest AI image generation model, and previewed Muse Video, a video generation model developed by Meta Superintelligence Labs.

Muse Image is available on the Meta AI app, Meta AI website, Instagram Stories in the US, and WhatsApp in select countries, while Muse Video will be rolled out to creators and Meta AI at a later date.

Unlike conventional image generation models that map prompts directly to outputs, Meta said Muse Image operates as an AI agent capable of invoking tools such as web search and code execution before producing an image.

According to the company, the model can refine its own outputs during inference and improve image quality by increasing test-time compute. It uses web search to retrieve factual and real-time information for prompts involving current events or knowledge-intensive topics.

“We’re excited to launch Muse Image and preview Muse Video, the first media-generation models developed by Meta Superintelligence Labs,” the company said in a statement. “Instead of directly mapping prompts to images, Muse Image operates as an agent: it invokes search and coding tools to improve accuracy, self-refines its own generations, and improves through scaling test-time compute.”

Muse Image can generate QR codes, plots, GIFs, websites with embedded images, and interactive visual experiences by writing and executing code during inference.

The company said Muse Image integrates with its multimodel AI Muse Spark, allowing both models to share tools and jointly plan media generation tasks. Meta added that the image model supports iterative editing, multi-reference image composition, and precise modifications while maintaining consistency across multiple edits.

Meta also introduced Content Seal, an invisible watermarking system that embeds provenance information into AI-generated images. According to the company, the watermark survives cropping, compression, resizing, and screenshots. Meta said it plans to extend the technology to AI-generated videos and is previewing a detection tool that allows users to verify whether an image contains a Content Seal watermark.

On benchmarks, Meta said Muse Image ranks second on Arena’s human preference Elo leaderboard behind OpenAI’s GPT-Image 2 for text-to-image generation, single-image editing, and multi-image editing.

Muse Video ranks third on the text-to-video leaderboard, behind Gemini Ombi Flash and Seedance 2.0.

Alongside Muse Image, Meta previewed Muse Video, which is built on the same pretraining foundation and supports native audio generation. The model focuses on prompt adherence, visual fidelity, and temporal consistency, as the Big Tech company continues to improve its audio-video synchronisation and fast-motion accuracy.

“Muse Image connects deeply with the Meta ecosystem,” the company said. “Our ongoing investments in image and video generation will further enable creators and businesses to generate dynamic content across Meta products.”

title: OpenAI Set to Release GPT-5.6 After US Govt Finally Lifts Restrictions
content:
The approval follows review of national security and cybersecurity risks associated with the frontier AI model.

The US government has lifted restrictions on the public release of OpenAI’s GPT-5.6, clearing the way for the company to make its latest AI model broadly available after weeks of limited access under a government review process.

“GPT-5.6 Sol, along with Terra and Luna, will launch publicly this Thursday. We’re expanding preview access globally now,” the company announced in a post on X.

According to a report by Axios, the decision comes after additional testing and consultations between OpenAI and US officials over national security concerns.

The GPT-5.6 family consists of three models—the flagship GPT-5.6 Sol model, GPT-5.6 Terra as the mid-tier offering, and GPT-5.6 Luna as the lower-cost option.

The US government had initially ordered OpenAI to restrict GPT-5.6 only to a small group of government-approved partners while federal agencies evaluated the model’s capabilities and potential cybersecurity risks. The review was part of a broader effort to assess whether increasingly capable AI systems could be misused by foreign adversaries or exploited for offensive cyber operations before they reached the public.

“We don’t believe this kind of government access process should become the long-term default,” OpenAI had said in a statement when it was asked to halt GPT-5.6’s release in late June.

The AI giant is also reportedly considering giving a 5% stake in the company to the US government. According to the Financial Times, OpenAI chief Sam Altman believes such a move would help improve the industry’s relations with the Donald Trump administration

The Trump administration’s restrictions on frontier AI models come in light of unprecedented government oversight.

Anthropic’s Mythos 5 and Fable 5 models also faced temporary restrictions before some of those limits were eased. The company has also extended access to Claude Fable 5 for users on all paid plans until July 12.

The US government has been working with leading AI developers on a framework to evaluate frontier AI systems before their public release, balancing national security concerns with the need to maintain the competitiveness of US AI companies.

title: Axis Max Life Partners with GreyLabs AI to Improve Sales Conversions
content:
Axis Max Life has analysed over 6 lakh customer calls using voice AI software to identify high-intent customers and reshape its sales strategy.

What Actually Matters.

Axis Max Life has implemented GreyLabs AI's Voice AI Suite to enhance its sales strategy and improve customer call analysis.

The company has shifted focus from customer demographics to the content of customer conversations for predicting sales conversions.

Axis Max Life Insurance has deployed GreyLabs AI's Voice AI Suite, a system built for BFSI firms, to review customer calls and support its sales teams. The company says it has now moved from selective call reviews to full AI-based assessment of calls, and has contributed to a nearly 15% rise in sales conversions.

Among the findings from the deployment, Axis Max Life says the first 90–120 seconds of a sales call predict whether a customer will convert, more so than demographic information about the customer. The company says this has changed its approach, from focusing on who a customer is to focusing on what the customer says during the call.

Axis Max Life has expanded its digital insurance business over the past five years. The company says its online business has grown 10x in this period, with digital channels now making up around 15% of its annualised premium equivalent. One in three new customers is acquired online.

As the digital business grew, the number and range of telesales conversations increased beyond what existing review processes could cover. Axis Max Life said this led it to partner with GreyLabs AI to build a system for analysing customer conversations at scale.

Under the partnership, Axis Max Life reviews calls from more than 700 agents, covering over 6 lakh calls and 1.4 crore minutes of customer interaction. It noted that follow-up messages built around what customers said during calls, rather than where they stopped responding, have led to higher click-through rates.

Aman Goel, Founder and CEO of GreyLabs AI, said in a statement, "What this deployment demonstrates is that when AI is implemented with the right guardrails, the right intent, and a genuine focus on business outcomes rather than technology for its own sake, the results are transformative."

Vaibhav Kumar, Head of Product Management and E-Commerce at Axis Max Life Insurance, added, "GreyLabs AI's Voice AI Suite has given us an ability to listen to our customers at scale, not just what they say, but what they mean. The intelligence we've gained has helped us serve customers better, design more relevant products."

Axis Max Life and GreyLabs AI say they are looking at further uses of AI across the sales process, including a Voice AI Calling Agent to contact prospects and guide them through the purchase process. Both companies describe this as part of a wider move across India's BFSI sector toward AI use under compliance and regulatory oversight.

Microsoft’s Xbox division will eliminate around 3,200 roles during FY27, as 1,600 jobs were cut immediately.

Microsoft is eliminating around 4,800 jobs, or about 2.1% of its global workforce, as it restructures parts of its gaming business.

The layoffs primarily affect Xbox and commercial sales verticals, according to an internal memo sent to employees by Amy Coleman, Executive Vice President and Chief People Officer.

In the memo, Coleman said the decision was driven by changes in customer needs, business models, and the way technology is being built and deployed, rather than by AI replacing employees.

“I also want to be direct that the roles eliminated today are not being replaced by AI,” Coleman wrote. “At the same time, what is true is that AI is changing how work gets done. Some of the tasks we do every day can now be automated, and that means we all need to keep learning, keep building new skills, and keep adapting as the work evolves.”

Coleman said Microsoft had tried to reduce the need for layoffs by moving employees into other roles. Over the past year, the company redeployed more than 4,000 employees internally, including another 500 this month. She also said more than 30% of eligible employees opted into the company's recent voluntary retirement programme.

“We will also transition four of our gaming studios to operate under new management, with the goal of preserving both their intellectual property and ongoing projects,” Coleman wrote.

Explaining the restructuring, Coleman said Microsoft’s business had to change as the technology industry evolves.

“The way technology is built, deployed, and used is transforming faster than at any point in my time here,” she said. “Our customers’ needs are shifting, the business models that serve them are shifting, and that means the work itself—what we do, where we focus, and how we’re organised—has to transform too.”

She added that the latest changes in Microsoft's commercial business build on the company’s recently announced Frontier Company strategy, which involves embedding engineering teams more closely with customers to help accelerate technology deployments.

The Xbox division is also being restructured to align with the company’s long-term business priorities, while engineering teams across Microsoft will adjust their structure and focus.

Microsoft’s Xbox division will eliminate around 3,200 roles during FY27, Xbox CEO Asha Sharma shared in a post on X.

Xbox’s restructuring includes about 1,600 job cuts effective immediately, while four game studios will move out of Xbox under new ownership or management.

Sharma said Xbox’s business “today is not healthy,” adding that the company operates “at margins that are 3–10x lower than comparable platform and publishing businesses.”

Compulsion Games and Double Fine Productions will become independent studios with their intellectual property and game catalogues. Ninja Theory and Undead Labs will move to new ownership with funding to continue development of the Senua and State of Decay franchises.

Sharma added that the company is also reducing roles across Activision, Bethesda/ZeniMax, Blizzard, King, Mojang, and Xbox Game Studios, while shifting investments toward higher-priority projects.

The platform business will also change. Sharma said some parts of Xbox currently have as many as 14 layers of management, while platform teams have grown 40% since the beginning of the current console generation despite declines in player base and playtime.

“We will reduce management layers to no more than 5, and where possible, 3,” Sharma wrote on X. “We will deliver success through a flatter organisation that is built around makers, player-coaches, and directly responsible individuals.”

Meanwhile, Coleman said Microsoft would continue investing in employee training, including AI skills, while providing financial support and career resources to affected employees.

Nxtra and Deloitte believe that investments in sovereign digital infrastructure will be central to India's AI economy.

Traditional data centres were never designed for AI workloads. They were built for variable CPU loads, lower rack density, and air cooling. But AI workloads need dense GPU clusters, near-continuous utilisation, faster networking, stronger cooling, and tighter data controls.

The demand is compounded by companies increasingly sanctioning AI tools for their employees. According to a Deloitte survey shared with AIM, AI workloads could reach over 50% of total Indian data centre capacity by 2033.

Talking to AIM, Ashish Arora, CEO of the data centre company Nxtra by Airtel, believes that AI's next phase of growth will depend not only on compute power but also on resilient, secure, and sustainable infrastructure capable of supporting mission-critical workloads across industries.

"Our goal is to make AI deployments predictable, telecom-grade, secure, and cost-effective at scale while remaining sustainable by design, so enterprises can focus on creating value rather than operating infrastructure," he says.

According to Cushman & Wakefield’s report, India’s operational data centre capacity stands at ~1,600 MW; however, AI-specific capacity is estimated at only around 20–25%. This figure is expected to grow exponentially as India’s AI market balloons to $131 billion by 2032, registering a compound annual growth rate of 39%, per Avendus Capital.

“The challenge for enterprises now is whether enough AI-ready capacity will be commissioned in their preferred geography and on their preferred timeline,” Kumar adds.

Retrofitting older sites is expensive and slow. Operators must either invest in enhanced power, cooling, MEP, and structural systems or risk owning sites that cannot support future AI demand.

Anjani Kumar, Partner, Deloitte India, observes that traditional enterprise racks typically run at 5–15 kW, while AI training and large-scale inference are moving toward 30 kW+ per rack. Advanced AI clusters are already reaching 80–100 kW, with some next-generation liquid-cooled deployments moving beyond 100 kW per rack.

Cooling often accounts for about 40% of data centre power consumption, and AI-led demand could need 40–45 TWh of additional power, per the Deloitte survey. Operators need advanced cooling architectures such as direct-to-chip liquid cooling and immersion cooling; however, this increases upfront costs and requires facility redesign.

Liquid cooling is expected to become dominant in India as it is typically closed-loop and uses very little water. However, it can exacerbate local water stress. “More data centres mean more freshwater diversion for cooling, often coinciding with India’s recurrent water shortages and summer heat stress,” the Council on Energy, Environment, and Water (CEEW) noted in its blog.

Moreover, established data centre hubs such as Mumbai, Chennai, Delhi-NCR, and Bengaluru are already under pressure. They account for most of India’s operational capacity, but local transmission capacity, substation readiness, and grid redundancy remain key constraints. Future AI-led capacity is also expected to cluster in specific zones outside metropolitan areas, where large campuses of 100–200 MW+ will require stronger power planning upfront.

“Locating renewable energy plants farther away would entail substantial investments in transmission infrastructure, adding pressure on the already strained finances of distribution companies,” CEEW noted.

However, India’s AI data-centre growth essentially depends on imported GPUs, with the country only being able to secure a little over 38,000 GPUs through the IndiaAI Mission. Currently, most India-bound AI accelerators are NVIDIA-led today, while AMD and custom-chip adoption remain limited, according to Kumar.

“API-based cloud AI is faster and cheaper at low usage. However, as usage grows, token costs become a recurring operating cost and can make dedicated digital infrastructure more economical,” he mentions.

Need for Sovereign Data Centres

India generates nearly 20% of the world’s data but hosts only about 3% of global data centre capacity. This creates a sovereignty gap because the demand for Indian data and AI workloads is growing faster than domestic infrastructure. Sovereign AI data centres are needed to process, store, and govern more of this value within India.

“Sovereign AI data centres are critical for India. They are foundational infrastructure for how India trains, hosts, governs, and scales AI. Without them, India's data, models, public services, and regulated industries remain dependent on infrastructure controlled outside its borders,” Kumar adds.

Indian enterprises are increasingly concerned about foreign-controlled AI stacks. According to Deloitte, around 82% of Indian firms report that 21–60% of their AI stack is foreign-owned or foreign-controlled, and 77% are at least moderately concerned.

India’s DPDP framework, RBI localisation rules, and sector-specific compliance requirements make auditable infrastructure important for sensitive workloads in sectors including banking, insurance, healthcare, telecom, and the public sector.

Kumar highlights that India is backing local foundational and large language models from teams such as Sarvam AI, BharatGen, Gnani.ai, and Socket. These models need Indian datasets, local evaluation, retraining capacity and inference hosting. Meanwhile, platforms such as AIKosh and Bhashini are strategic assets because they support AI in Indian languages and local contexts.

Nxtra also believes that investments in sovereign digital infrastructure will be central to India's AI economy as they would help enterprises move beyond isolated pilots toward enterprise-scale AI deployment.

The company operates a network of 15 hyperscale data centres and over 120 edge data centres in India. Its portfolio spans startups, GCCs, hyperscalers, and enterprises modernising mission-critical workloads.

In March, it secured $1 billion in investments to expand its network, targeting a 25% market share. Nxtra, along with Google and AdaniConneX, recently broke ground in Visakhapatnam to build a gigawatt-scale AI data centre.

We provide secure and compliant facilities protected by multiple layers of physical security and advanced cybersecurity controls, ensuring the safety of critical workloads and sensitive data,” Arora shares.

At the same time, the company prioritises energy-efficient operations. The company’s core data centres now run on 49% renewable energy, contracting 483 GW of renewable energy so far.

Arora notes that standardised infrastructure enables organisations to shift investments away from infrastructure management towards building AI-driven products and business innovation. "Scale converts infrastructure from a barrier into an enabler. Our approach is to capture these efficiencies so organisations can adopt AI more ethically, affordably, faster and with confidence," he states.

Looking ahead, Nxtra expects three major trends to shape India's AI infrastructure landscape: the emergence of sovereign AI ecosystems for governments and regulated industries, data centres evolving into integrated innovation platforms combining compute, storage, networking, and security, and wider enterprise AI adoption driven by reliable, low-latency infrastructure supporting intelligent automation, edge computing, and real-time decision-making.

Large-scale data centre networks in India are primed to significantly reduce the cost of enterprise AI adoption by standardising infrastructure, improving operational efficiencies, shortening deployment timelines, and lowering security and compliance costs.

title: Zeta Co-Founder Bhavin Turakhia Launches Neo With $30 Mn Personal Bet on Enterprise AI
content:
Neo will roll out Tasket for AI-led task delegation, Friday for AI assistants and agents, Studio for knowledge management, and Drive for human-agent file collaboration.

What Actually Matters.

Neo aims to unify disconnected workplace tools and knowledge for enterprises adopting AI.

The platform integrates task management, knowledge management, and file collaboration into a single solution.

Neo AI, a Bengaluru-based enterprise artificial intelligence startup founded by serial entrepreneur Bhavin Turakhia, is building a unified work platform to help companies overcome fragmented knowledge and disconnected workplace tools as they accelerate the adoption of large language models and AI copilots.

The company brings task management, knowledge management, file collaboration and AI agents onto a single platform, seeking to address a key challenge facing enterprises: information required by AI systems is often scattered across software-as-a-service applications, documents, project-management tools and employees’ institutional knowledge.

“Most organisations fail to capture the value of AI because context is fragmented, knowledge is scattered across teams and tools remain disconnected,” Turakhia said in a post on X. “Neo changes that by centralising context and making AI a first-class participant in every workflow, not a tab beside it.”

Friday, the company’s agent layer, is connected to more than 1,000 external applications, according to reports. The platform is also designed to be model-agnostic, allowing enterprises to choose or switch the underlying AI models used across their workflows rather than being locked into a single provider.

Neo has already been deployed internally across Turakhia’s companies, including Zeta and Titan, since April. The startup is expected to begin an external rollout with select customers in India and the US in August, before a broader release planned around January. It will initially target knowledge workers at technology, consulting and professional-services firms.

Neo currently has around 45–50 employees, including about 18 engineers, and plans to grow to roughly 100 people by the end of the year. Turakhia said the initial platform was built in under three months by a team of fewer than 20 engineers, with AI used extensively during development.

He claimed the team achieved in three months what would otherwise have taken years under a conventional software-development approach. Neo is expected to follow a pricing model combining a per-seat fee with charges based on token consumption.

The launch is Turakhia’s fifth major entrepreneurial venture after Directi, Radix, Titan and Zeta.

Neo enters an increasingly crowded enterprise AI market. It will compete with productivity incumbents such as Microsoft Copilot and Google Gemini for Workspace, as well as with AI-enabled collaboration and work-management platforms, including Notion AI, ClickUp, Asana, and Atlassian.

The DRHP filing follows reports that Eternal-backed Cult.fit was targeting an IPO fundraise of ₹3,500 crore to ₹4,000 crore at an estimated valuation of around $2 billion.

What Actually Matters.

Cult.fit has filed its DRHP for an IPO, aiming to raise ₹950 crore alongside an offer for sale of nearly 17.86 crore shares.

The company is valued at around $2 billion, with plans for a total fundraise of ₹3,500 crore to ₹4,000 crore pending finalisation.

Fitness unicorn Cult.fit has filed its DRHP for an IPO comprising a fresh issue of up to ₹950 crore in shares and an offer for sale (OFS) of up to 17.86 crore shares.

The filing sets the stage for a public-market debut by one of India’s largest organised fitness platforms, which spans offline gyms, digital fitness classes, sports facilities, activewear and fitness equipment.

Several of Cult.fit’s early and institutional backers are set to pare their holdings through the OFS. The list includes Temasek Holdings, through MacRitchie Investments, Schroders Capital, German fitness operator LifeFit Group, Accel, Tata Digital and Co-Founder Mukesh Bansal.

The DRHP comes shortly after reports that the Eternal-backed company was exploring an IPO-sized fundraise of ₹3,500 crore to ₹4,000 crore at a valuation of around $2 billion. The final issue size and valuation will be determined closer to the launch of the public offering.

Cult.fit has built its business around a hybrid model, combining subscription-led fitness centres with digital offerings and a growing consumer products business. As of March 31, it operated 708 fitness centres across India and had more than 9.87 lakh paid members.

Its revenue streams extend beyond gym memberships and online classes. The company sells fitness equipment, recovery products such as massagers, fitness accessories, apparel and footwear under its active lifestyle portfolio.

The company is now led by CEO Naresh Krishnaswamy, while Co-Founders Bansal and Ankit Nagori no longer hold executive positions. Bansal, however, remains among the shareholders participating in the OFS.

Cult.fit reported operating revenue of ₹1,720.6 crore in FY26, while its net loss stood at ₹251 crore. The numbers underline the scale the company has built in India’s organised fitness market, even as profitability remains a work in progress.

Despite the strong earnings guidance, Samsung’s stock dropped as much as 7.9% in early trading.

Samsung Electronics on July 7 issued its earnings guidance for the second quarter of 2026, projecting another record quarter as strong demand for AI memory chips continued to drive its semiconductor business.

The South Korean technology giant expects consolidated revenue of approximately 171 trillion won and an operating profit of around 89.4 trillion won ($58.4 billion) for the April–June quarter. The projected operating profit compares with 4.7 trillion won in the year-ago quarter and 57.2 trillion won in the previous quarter.

The projected operating profit represents a 19-fold increase from the same period last year, while revenue is expected to more than double year over year.

Samsung’s projected operating profit of 89.4 trillion won (about $58.4 billion) is roughly in line with and slightly above NVIDIA’s most recently reported quarterly operating income of about $53.5 billion. However, a direct comparison of net profit is not yet possible, as Samsung has yet to disclose its net profit for the quarter. NVIDIA reported quarterly net income of $58.3 billion.

The preliminary figures exceeded analyst expectations, reflecting continued strength in the memory chip market as cloud providers and technology companies expanded AI infrastructure. Higher prices for DRAM and NAND flash memory, particularly high-bandwidth memory (HBM) used in AI accelerators, continued to support Samsung’s earnings growth.

Tight supply of conventional memory chips, as manufacturers shifted production capacity towards HBM, also contributed to higher prices during the quarter.

Despite the strong earnings guidance, Samsung’s stock dropped as much as 7.9% in early trading. Shares of SK Hynix also fell up to 7.3%, contributing to a nearly 6% decline in the KOSPI index.

Analysts pointed to concerns over whether hyperscale cloud companies would sustain their pace of AI infrastructure investments and whether future returns would justify the industry’s aggressive capital spending plans.

According to Reuters, some analysts also said Samsung’s operating profit could have crossed KRW 100 trillion had the company not set aside substantial provisions for employee bonuses in its semiconductor division.

Samsung is expected to release its full second-quarter financial results later this month, when it will disclose net profit and provide additional details on the quarter's performance.

The broader AI memory sector remains in focus, with rival SK Hynix set to begin trading on the Nasdaq on July 10 through a roughly $28 billion American depositary share (ADS) listing—one of the largest foreign listings in US history.

title: Magnum Opens New R&D Centre in Bengaluru to Accelerate Ice Cream Product Innovation for India
content:
The centre will support innovation across brands, including Kwality Wall's, Cornetto, Magnum, Carte D'Or, Feast, and Twister

The Magnum Ice Cream Company (TMICC), the world's largest ice cream business with 21% of global market share, has inaugurated a new 13,000 sq ft Research, Design & Innovation (RD&I) Centre in Bengaluru to strengthen its product innovation capabilities and accelerate the development of ice cream products tailored to Indian consumers.

Located in Whitefield, the facility houses a state-of-the-art laboratory and a digitally enabled pilot plant that bring together ice cream science, culinary expertise, packaging development, and consumer technical insights under one roof.

The centre will support innovation across brands including Kwality Wall's, Cornetto, Magnum, Carte D'Or, Feast, and Twister, focusing on product development, packaging, regulatory assessment, and consumer-led innovation.

The Bengaluru facility features advanced capabilities such as ice cream manufacturing, sensory testing, packaging assessment, cold-chain validation, climate testing, transport simulations, and 3D packaging prototyping. It is designed to speed up experimentation across multiple product formats, including cups, cones, sticks, kulfi and premium ice cream cakes, while ensuring products are developed for Indian market conditions.

"Kwality Wall's has been part of the Indian ice cream scene for more than seven decades, consistently delighting consumers with new flavours and familiar icons. As part of The Magnum Ice Cream Company, we now have access to world-class R&D capabilities, deeper product expertise and a sharper innovation ecosystem. The new Bengaluru ice cream centre will help us respond faster to evolving consumer preferences, create products that are relevant to Indian tastes and occasions, and continue building a future-ready ice cream business in India," said Chitrank Goel, Deputy Managing Director, Kwality Wall's (India) Limited, in a statement.

The Magnum Ice Cream Company owns a 61.9% stake in the Indian business of Kwality Wall's.

The company said the Bengaluru centre will collaborate closely with TMICC's Global Design Centre in Colworth, UK, and its regional innovation hub in Istanbul, Turkey, combining global R&D expertise with local consumer insights to strengthen its innovation pipeline, improve product quality, and accelerate speed-to-market for India-specific offerings.

"The new Bengaluru RD&I Centre brings together our global science, technology and culinary expertise with deep local consumer insight, helping us to move faster from idea to market-ready innovation. From product and packaging development to sensory assessment and cold-chain validation, this new centre will play an important role in creating products that are more relevant, more distinctive and more exciting for consumers in India," said Zbigniew Lewicki, Chief Research, Development & Innovation Officer, The Magnum Ice Cream Company.

According to the company, the new RD&I Centre is part of its broader strategy to strengthen innovation, premiumisation, and local execution in India as demand for premium ice cream products continues to grow.

content:
DXC Technology signed a multi-year Anthropic partnership and opened a Bengaluru facility for AI development and customer collaboration.

What Actually Matters.

DXC Technology has entered a multi-year partnership with Anthropic to enhance AI development.

The new Bengaluru facility serves as a major hub for customer collaboration and AI initiatives.

IT services and consulting company DXC Technology recently signed a multi-year global partnership with Anthropic and opened a new customer experience centre in Bengaluru.

Through the Anthropic collaboration, DXC has become one of a small number of global premier partners in the Claude Partner Network. The companies plan to train tens of thousands of forward-deployed, Claude-certified engineers and builders. The aim is to bring Claude models into production within systems DXC operates for banks, airlines, insurers, manufacturers, and government agencies.

DXC’s Bengaluru site spans 200,000 sq ft and is among DXC's largest global delivery hubs. The building houses customer experience zones, fluid collaboration hubs, ideation studios, co-creation labs, and partner experience zones, alongside an AI Hub, a cyber range, forensics labs, a security operations centre, and a network operations centre.

DXC stated the facility supports work from solution design through deployment and monitoring, and will feature its work across AI, consulting, engineering, cloud, cybersecurity, and network transformation.

Ramnath Venkataraman, President, Consulting & Engineering Services at DXC Technology, said the centre brings engineering staff together in a space built for collaboration with customers and partners.

“We can co-create, engineer, and scale AI-powered solutions that address complex business challenges," he said. He added that working alongside customers throughout the process is intended to help them move from ideas to business outcomes.

Rob Le Busque, President of Asia Pacific & Japan at DXC Technology, said the centre combines consulting, engineering, and operations work in one location. Le Busque said the site is meant to help "create connected enterprises where people work alongside AI agents to engineer and run the systems of record for our customers."

title: 95% of NVIDIA’s Grace Blackwell GPUs Yet to Be Deployed: Report
content:
Air Street Capital estimates that only 100,128 of the world’s 1.66 million announced NVIDIA Grace Blackwell GPUs had been deployed as of July.

More than 95% of the world’s announced NVIDIA Grace Blackwell GPU capacity has yet to be deployed, according to Air Street Capital’s latest State of AI Report Compute Index, which tracks major AI compute deployments worldwide.

The index estimates that 100,128 Grace Blackwell GPUs (GB200/GB300) had been deployed as of July 1, compared with an announced pipeline of around 1.66 million GPUs, meaning less than 5% of the announced capacity is operational. Another 308,640 GPUs are in the installation phase

The accompanying deployment data shows that the largest announced projects remain largely unbuilt. Saudi Arabia’s HUMAIN project accounts for roughly 600,000 announced Grace Blackwell GPUs, while Stargate Abilene, the OpenAI, Oracle, and Crusoe-backed project, accounts for about 450,000.

South Korea’s national AI programme has announced around 260,000 GPUs, while Nscale’s Microsoft deployment totals roughly 200,000 announced accelerators.

In contrast, deployed Grace Blackwell systems remain comparatively small, with the first GB300 clusters only recently entering production.

The report also tracks previous NVIDIA GPU generations. Hopper-based clusters remain the largest deployed AI systems globally, led by xAI’s Colossus 1 with around 200,000 H100/H200/GH200 GPUs, followed by Tesla Cortex with roughly 66,000 GPUs and Meta's GenAI clusters with about 49,000 GPUs.

Earlier A100 deployments remain concentrated in research compute, with Meta Research SuperCluster leading at around 16,000 A100 GPUs.

The State of AI Report Compute Index is an ongoing dataset maintained by Air Street Capital that tracks publicly disclosed AI compute infrastructure across GPU generations, including A100, Hopper, Blackwell and Grace Blackwell systems.

According to the project’s methodology, the index compiles information from company announcements, public procurement documents, regulatory filings, hyperscaler disclosures, government announcements, satellite imagery, vendor data and industry sources.

Each installation is classified as announced, installed, or deployed based on publicly verifiable evidence, with the database updated continuously as projects progress.

The deployment figures come as NVIDIA prepares its next AI platform transition.

At GTC 2026 in March, the company revealed that the Vera Rubin platform has entered production, scheduled to succeed Grace Blackwell in the second half of 2026, with Rubin Ultra planned for 2027 as part of its annual data centre roadmap.

At the event and subsequent earnings discussions, NVIDIA said it has visibility into at least $1 trillion in revenue from its Blackwell and Rubin platforms through 2027.

title: Broadcom, Apple Extend Custom Chip Partnership Through 2031
content:
New multi-year agreements cover the development and supply of custom ASIC silicon for multiple future generations of Apple products.

Broadcom has extended and expanded its long-running technology partnership with Apple through 2031, signing new multi-year agreements to develop and supply a range of custom application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) silicon products for multiple generations of Apple devices.

The announcement was disclosed in a Form 8-K filed with the US Securities and Exchange Commission on July 6. Broadcom said the agreements expand the companies’ existing collaboration but did not disclose financial terms, product categories or expected shipment volumes.

Broadcom has been one of Apple’s key semiconductor suppliers for more than a decade, providing wireless connectivity chips, radio-frequency components and other custom silicon used across iPhones and other Apple devices.

In 2023, the companies announced a separate multi-billion-dollar agreement to develop 5G radio frequency components manufactured in the United States.

While Apple has since introduced more in-house silicon, including proprietary networking chips in some products, Broadcom has remained a strategic supplier for specialised custom semiconductor designs.

Analysts cited in a Reuters report said that Apple accounts for 20% of Broadcom’s revenue.

The Apple agreement also reinforces Broadcom’s strategy of securing long-term custom silicon partnerships with some of the world's largest technology companies.

In recent months, the company has expanded similar multi-year chip development agreements with Google, Meta and OpenAI as demand for bespoke AI processors accelerates.

Last month, OpenAI unveiled its first custom AI inference chip, Jalapeño, developed with Broadcom and manufactured by TSMC.

Broadcom reported another record quarter in June, with revenue rising 20% year over year to $15 billion, driven by continued demand for AI infrastructure.

Revenue from the company’s AI semiconductor business climbed 46% to $4.4 billion, while Broadcom projected AI revenue of about $5.1 billion for the current quarter.

Broadcom’s AI chip business is also anchored by its long-standing partnership with Google, which has collaborated with the company on every generation of its custom Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) since 2014.

In April, the companies extended that relationship through 2031 under a long-term agreement in which Broadcom will develop and supply future generations of Google’s custom AI chips, while also providing networking and other components for Google’s next-generation AI racks.

The TPUs power Google’s internal AI workloads as well as Google Cloud services, positioning Broadcom at the centre of one of the industry’s largest custom AI silicon programmes.

title: GalaxEye’s Mission Drishti Satellite Hit by Solar Storm After System Validation
content:
GalaxEye says the maiden OptoSAR mission validated key systems and plans to launch two new OptoSAR satellites within the next 24 months.

What Actually Matters.

GalaxEye lost communication with its Mission Drishti satellite due to a solar storm anomaly after initial system validation.

The satellite, the world's first OptoSAR, successfully completed critical operational tests before communication issues arose.

Bengaluru-based space tech startup GalaxEye has lost communication with its Mission Drishti satellite following an anomaly linked to a geomagnetic solar storm.

The satellite, launched aboard a SpaceX mission on May 3, had successfully completed a major portion of its Launch and Early Orbit Phase (LEOP) and validated several critical spacecraft systems before communication became intermittent and was eventually lost.

The company said the initial root cause analysis suggests radiation effects associated with the solar storm likely impacted a critical onboard system. Recovery efforts remain underway, although GalaxEye said the likelihood of restoring contact appears low.

Mission Drishti was developed as the world’s first OptoSAR satellite, combining optical and synthetic aperture radar imaging capabilities. According to the company, the mission successfully established communication after launch, executed deployment and attitude control activities, operated onboard computing and communications systems, and demonstrated in-house mission operations from its Bengaluru Mission Control Centre.

Despite the anomaly, GalaxEye said the satellite validated critical technologies, operational processes and infrastructure required to design, build, launch, and operate advanced space systems.

“Mission Drishti marks the culmination of years of innovation, engineering, and execution by our team,” Suyash Singh, Co-founder and CEO of GalaxEye, said in a statement. He said the mission had generated engineering insights that would help improve future spacecraft and accelerate the company’s plans to bring more manufacturing, supply chain, and satellite development activities in-house.

The company now plans to launch two new OptoSAR satellites within the next 24 months and expand its in-house capabilities.

Founded in 2021 by five IIT Madras alumni, GalaxEye develops Earth observation systems based on its proprietary OptoSAR technology. The startup has raised around $20 million from investors, including Speciale Invest, Mela Ventures, Infosys, Ideaforge, and Rainmatter (by Zerodha).

title: Only 25% of Indian Organisations Feel Workforce Ready for AI, Kyndryl Report Finds
content:
Kyndryl survey finds Indian firms are adopting AI quickly, but few yet say their workforce is ready for the change.

What Actually Matters.

Only 25% of Indian organisations feel their workforce is ready for AI, a decline from previous years.

There is a significant gap between AI ambitions and the current skills of the workforce.

Kyndryl has published its second annual People Readiness Report, based on a global study of 1,100 senior business and technology leaders across eight countries, including India.

The report points to a decline in workforce readiness for AI and a gap between what organisations expect from AI and what they have put in place to support it.

The report states that AI success does not depend only on strategy, use cases, or technology, but on whether organisations redesign work and manage the changes that follow across their workforce. It also states that trust in AI can be built through changes to operating models and governance.

In India, 25% of organisations say their workforce is prepared to use AI, down 12 percentage points from 2025. Kyndryl says this points to a widening gap between AI ambitions and workforce readiness, as organisations work to give employees the skills needed for AI-based work.

At the same time, 69% of organisations in India have redesigned roles within or across functions to support AI adoption, and 33% have set formal budgets and upskilling plans. Kyndryl says the pace of this change is outpacing the development of governance, trust, and oversight structures.

Lingraju Sawkar, President - Kyndryl APxJ, said, “While organisations continue to invest in AI technologies and expand use cases, scaling impact will require businesses to rethink how work gets done, redesign roles, build new capabilities and establish governance frameworks that foster trust and responsible adoption.”

Among other findings in India, the report states that 56% of organisations say AI is deployed broadly or built into core business processes, up from 36% in 2025. It states that 81% of Indian leaders are concerned that AI advancement will move faster than their workforce capabilities, governance frameworks, and operating models. On AI agents, 84% of organisations expect autonomous AI systems to make material decisions within 12 months, while 28% say they trust such systems to operate without human oversight.

The report notes that worldwide spending on AI is forecast to reach $2.52 trillion in 2026, a 44% rise from the previous year, according to Gartner, Inc.

Kim Basile, CIO, Kyndryl, said, “The data shows that the organisations investing in people—whether it’s rethinking roles and workflows, dedicating resources for upskilling and retraining, or guiding employees through change—are experiencing positive outcomes at a much higher rate.”

Mark Paulek, Chief Human Resources Officer, Kyndryl, said, “AI’s ability to reshape work is challenging organisations to reshape their workforce more rapidly than ever before. The leaders pulling ahead are aligning skills, roles and decision-making with how work is actually changing.”

The report identifies a group it calls Pacesetters, comprising 9% of organisations worldwide that have redesigned roles around AI, put change management in place so staff understand the new operating model, and built workforce readiness. Kyndryl says these organisations are roughly twice as likely to have governance measures fully in place across every area measured in the study.

According to the global findings, Pacesetters are 1.5 times more likely to report AI-related revenue growth and 1.6 times more likely to report improved innovation in products and services.

Globally, 23% of organisations say their workforce is fully ready for AI, a fall of six percentage points from the previous year, and 79% say AI will move faster than their workforce, governance, and operating models. On AI agents, 81% of organisations globally expect them to make impactful decisions within a year, while 25% say they trust such systems without human oversight.

The report also outlines steps organisations are taking to prepare their workforce. Globally, 61% say they have already redesigned roles, and 24% are creating new roles focused on managing AI.

On skills, 52% of leaders say it has become harder to find employees with the skills needed for their AI strategy, and a third have training programmes in place to help staff work alongside AI tools. On governance, 33% of organisations say they have clear policies on which decisions AI can and cannot make, and 27% use a registry to monitor their AI systems.

The project began about a year ago, and DeepSeek has been holding discussions with multiple companies in the semiconductor industry supply chain.

Chinese AI startup DeepSeek is developing its first in-house AI chip designed for inference, reported Reuters, citing three people familiar with the matter.

According to Reuters, the project began about a year ago and remains in its early stages. DeepSeek has been holding discussions with chip design firms, foundries, and memory suppliers while privately expanding its chip engineering team.

AIM could not independently verify the report.

The AI company is looking to reduce its dependence on NVIDIA and Huawei processors, which DeepSeek has relied on to train and deploy its AI models.

DeepSeek has used both NVIDIA and Huawei hardware across different model generations. The company previously said its R1 reasoning model was trained using NVIDIA’s H800 GPUs before those chips were restricted for China.

More recently, it has shifted further towards Huawei’s ecosystem, releasing its V4 model adapted for Huawei’s Ascend chips, with Huawei stating that its processors were used for part of the training of the lighter V4-Flash model.

Currently, NVIDIA’s H20 is the only advanced AI GPU that can be legally exported to China, and even then, shipments require US export licenses.

The H20 was specifically designed to comply with US export controls, but last April, it was made subject to an indefinite licensing requirement before the US later agreed to approve licenses for eligible exports.

More powerful AI GPUs, including the H100, H200, B200, GB200, and other Blackwell products, remain under current US export control rules.

The development comes as the Chinese AI company seeks its first external capital. DeepSeek recently closed a $7 billion funding round, valuing the company at over $50 billion and marking a departure from its long-standing policy of rejecting outside investment.

DeepSeek’s hardware ambitions also reflect China’s broader push to develop domestic AI infrastructure as US export controls continue to restrict access to NVIDIA’s most advanced processors.

Huawei has emerged as the country’s largest AI chip supplier with nearly 50% market share, while Alibaba, through its T-Head unit, and Baidu are developing proprietary AI processors for their own cloud platforms.

A new generation of independent chip companies, including Biren Technology, Iluvatar CoreX, Moore Threads, and MetaX, has also expanded aggressively through IPOs and fresh fundraising, targeting AI training and inference workloads as US export controls accelerate demand for domestic alternatives.

content:
Despite the strong earnings guidance, Samsung’s stock dropped as much as 7.9% in early trading.

Samsung Electronics on July 7 issued its earnings guidance for the second quarter of 2026, projecting another record quarter as strong demand for AI memory chips continued to drive its semiconductor business.

The South Korean technology giant expects consolidated revenue of approximately 171 trillion won and an operating profit of around 89.4 trillion won ($58.4 billion) for the April–June quarter. The projected operating profit compares with 4.7 trillion won in the year-ago quarter and 57.2 trillion won in the previous quarter.

The projected operating profit represents a 19-fold increase from the same period last year, while revenue is expected to more than double year over year.

Samsung’s projected operating profit of 89.4 trillion won (about $58.4 billion) is roughly in line with and slightly above NVIDIA’s most recently reported quarterly operating income of about $53.5 billion. However, a direct comparison of net profit is not yet possible, as Samsung has yet to disclose its net profit for the quarter. NVIDIA reported quarterly net income of $58.3 billion.

The preliminary figures exceeded analyst expectations, reflecting continued strength in the memory chip market as cloud providers and technology companies expanded AI infrastructure. Higher prices for DRAM and NAND flash memory, particularly high-bandwidth memory (HBM) used in AI accelerators, continued to support Samsung’s earnings growth.

Tight supply of conventional memory chips, as manufacturers shifted production capacity towards HBM, also contributed to higher prices during the quarter.

Despite the strong earnings guidance, Samsung’s stock dropped as much as 7.9% in early trading. Shares of SK Hynix also fell up to 7.3%, contributing to a nearly 6% decline in the KOSPI index.

Analysts pointed to concerns over whether hyperscale cloud companies would sustain their pace of AI infrastructure investments and whether future returns would justify the industry’s aggressive capital spending plans.

According to Reuters, some analysts also said Samsung’s operating profit could have crossed KRW 100 trillion had the company not set aside substantial provisions for employee bonuses in its semiconductor division.

Samsung is expected to release its full second-quarter financial results later this month, when it will disclose net profit and provide additional details on the quarter's performance.

The broader AI memory sector remains in focus, with rival SK Hynix set to begin trading on the Nasdaq on July 10 through a roughly $28 billion American depositary share (ADS) listing—one of the largest foreign listings in US history.

title: Telangana Govt Strengthens Life Sciences Ecosystem With ₹800 Cr Oncology Pharma Facility
content:
The project is expected to generate around 500 direct employment opportunities.

Telangana has inaugurated a new integrated oncology manufacturing facility of Ciro Pharma at Biotech Park Phase III in Karakapatla, Siddipet, to strengthen its life sciences and pharmaceutical manufacturing ecosystem.

Established with an investment of ₹800 crore ($84 million), the facility will manufacture advanced oncology medicines, including oral formulations, sterile injectables, lyophilised powder injections, and soft gel capsules. The project is expected to generate around 500 direct employment opportunities while enhancing Telangana's manufacturing capabilities in high-value pharmaceutical products.

The inauguration aligns with Telangana's broader strategy to position itself as a leading destination for pharmaceutical manufacturing, biotechnology research, AI-enabled healthcare innovation, and sustainable pharmaceutical production. The government has been actively promoting investments across the life sciences sector to drive economic growth while creating skilled employment opportunities.

The new facility is expected to bolster the state's position as a global hub for life sciences, particularly in the manufacturing of specialised cancer therapies that cater to both domestic and international markets.

Speaking at the inauguration, Sridhar Babu Duddilla, Minister of Information Technology, Electronics, Communications, Industries & Legislative Affairs in the Telangana government, reiterated the state government’s commitment to building a globally competitive life sciences ecosystem by attracting high-value investments and expanding advanced manufacturing capabilities.

"Our government is committed to making Telangana a global life sciences innovation hub by promoting world-class manufacturing, research, AI-driven healthcare, sustainable green pharma, and high-value investments that generate quality employment and drive inclusive economic growth," he mentioned on X.

title: Hyderabad Startup Cosmoserve to Test Robotic Satellite Capture Aboard Skyroot Rocket
content:
Cosmoserve plans an in-orbit demonstration of debris-removal technology during Vikram-1’s maiden launch. It is separately collaborating with Pixxel for a larger satellite platform.

What Actually Matters.

Cosmoserve's Mission Embrace aims to demonstrate the world's first soft-robotic capture of an object in orbit.

The mission will be part of Skyroot Aerospace's Vikram-1 maiden launch, scheduled between July 12 and August 4, 2026.

Hyderabad-based space tech startup Cosmoserve Space has announced Mission Embrace, an orbital technology demonstration that will attempt what the company claims is the world’s first soft-robotic capture of an object in orbit.

The mission will fly aboard Skyroot Aerospace’s Vikram-1 maiden orbital launch, Mission Aagaman, during the approved launch window between July 12 and August 4, 2026. The startup said the mission will validate a robotic capture system designed to support future space debris removal operations.

“Mission Embrace forms part of India’s first private orbital launch carrying satellite payloads while also attempting the world’s first demonstration of soft robotic capture in orbit,” Chiranjeevi Phanindra, Founder and CEO of Cosmoserve Space, said in statement.

The soft robotic capture technology intends to latch onto inactive and non-cooperative satellites, which form a growing share of orbital debris around Earth.

However, the technology differs from Cosmoserve’s partnership with space tech startup Pixxel to develop a technology demonstration mission for space debris removal. Phanindra confirmed to AIM that Mission Embrace is a separate effort focused solely on validating the company’s soft robotic capture technology in orbit.

“The primary technologies we are developing are the soft robotic capture system and navigation system. All these systems will eventually go into a larger satellite platform [being developed with Pixxel] where we will demonstrate chasing an object in space, capturing it and pulling it down,” he said.

Space debris has emerged as a major challenge for satellite operators as the number of spacecraft in orbit continues to rise. Cosmoserve is developing Active Debris Removal (ADR) technologies to address the issue.

Its long-term plan includes developing a dual-spacecraft system in which a robotic servicer spacecraft captures and removes defunct satellites from orbit. The company said its approach could deliver debris-removal services at a fraction of the cost of comparable solutions.

Cosmoserve said the technology is suited for debris-removal missions because inactive satellites often lack standard docking interfaces. The company views the demonstration as a key step towards commercial debris-removal operations.

“We developed this technology from concept to flight-ready hardware in just four months within a company that is less than a year old, without compromising engineering rigour. Through this mission with Skyroot, we are demonstrating how rapidly India’s private space ecosystem can innovate through collaboration,” Phanindra added.

The company, which was incorporated less than a year ago, said the programme underwent a review process overseen by an independent committee comprising former ISRO scientists and industry experts. The technology cleared system concept, preliminary design, critical design, and flight readiness reviews before receiving approval for flight.

Additionally, in June last year, ISRO launched the SpaDeX (Space Docking Experiment) mission, on board which it had the ‘Debris Capture Robotic Manipulator’. Developed by ISRO’s Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre, the experiment focused on demonstrating the capability to capture tethered debris in space using visual servoing and object motion prediction.
