Six months of AI anxiety, record foreign selling, aggressive M&A, and a shrinking Nifty footprint have left India's $315-billion technology machine looking for its next big opportunity.

What Actually Matters.

The Indian IT sector faced a challenging first half of 2026, with the Nifty IT index dropping nearly 29%.

AI-induced pricing pressures are forcing IT companies to reassess their revenue models as tech budgets shrink.

At the end of June, while Wall Street's biggest tech names partied through another record-setting session, the mood at Dalal Street was far more sombre.

The Nifty IT index closed the first half of the year down close to 29%, making it the worst-performing sectoral index on the exchange and one of the roughest first halves for the Indian IT sector since the dot-com crash of 2001.

At first glance, the answer seems to be AI pricing pressure. Global companies are cutting their tech budgets as AI tools can now handle coding and maintenance work, forcing IT companies to review their pricing model. The market is mirroring a long-term structural threat.

“The IT industry has survived bigger issues like COVID-19 and the dot-com crash. This is also one of those,” Srinivas Padmanabhuni, an AI expert and technologist who previously worked as Principal Research Scientist and Associate Vice President at Infosys Labs, tells AIM.

But the story seems far more contradictory. IT companies are shopping for mega deals, diversifying their revenue streams, and churning profits, even if at a slower growth rate.

“One thing for sure is that non-linear models have to evolve. The linear FTE-driven (full-time equivalent) models are definitely under pressure because AI is all about efficiency,” he adds.

AI Disruption Finally Priced In

For most of 2024 and 2025, brokerages treated "AI will eat services revenue and jobs" as a distant tail risk worth a footnote rather than a valuation call. That changed decisively through 2026.

Industry analysts tracking enterprise technology spending suggest that the regular 2–3% annual deflation figure spanning both Indian and global IT players could be dwarfed by the cumulative revenue compression from AI-driven productivity gains over the next three to five years.

In an earlier interaction with AIM, Gaurav Vasu, Founder and CEO of UnearthInsight, said, “AI is clearly shrinking the need for a lot of traditional tech and tech services. We have actually been saying for a long time that over the next three to five years, overall deflation could be in the 10–15% range.”

On June 19, the global consulting giant—Indian IT's most-watched read-through stock, given how closely its business mirrors TCS and Infosys—trimmed its annual revenue growth forecast by just one percentage point, from a 3–5% range down to 3–4%. But what followed was a bloodbath.

Accenture's stock cratered nearly 18% in a single session, dragging down other Indian IT stocks, including TCS and Infosys. Accenture's order book had fallen nearly 15% year-on-year, a direct signal that large enterprise clients are simply committing less money to the kind of big, people-heavy, multi-year contracts that built the Indian IT industry over two decades.

An even more pointed episode was in May, when OpenAI and Anthropic unveiled their "deployment" venture built around embedding forward-deployed engineers directly inside large organisations to redesign workflows around AI, bypassing the traditional systems-integrator layer entirely.

“In May, both OpenAI and Anthropic launched their private equity-backed services companies, and they committed huge investments. That was a defining point in the IT services ecosystem and gave clarity to people that IT services were far from being dead,” says Praveen Bhadada, CEO and Managing Director of consulting firm Neovay Global.

“For companies to take advantage of AI, they just don't need the tools. They also need people who can make these tools a utility in the truest sense. That reaffirmation of the relevance of IT services happened from there,” he explains.

Macro Headwinds

Meanwhile, geopolitics added pressure to the topline.

The US-Iran war rattled both the markets as well as the rupee. Between January 1 and April 1, 2026, the rupee depreciated by roughly 3%, falling from around ₹90.01 to ₹92.74 against the US dollar. That translated into modest margin gains as the IT sector stabilised short-term finances.

However, sustained growth depends less on currency movements and more on a recovery in client spending and execution in new technology areas. US clients are wary about spending since a fragile US-Iran ceasefire, and SaaSpocalypse fears as foundational models drive market narratives, brokerages kept a "risk-off" mood alive for large stretches of the year.

With around 60% of Indian IT's revenue still coming from the US, every wobble in American corporate confidence about discretionary technology spending shows up in Indian order books within a quarter or two.

Moreover, the Donald Trump administration's H-1B visa restrictions are not making it any easier for IT companies to serve their US clients. They have also upended the careers of many Indian engineers, leaving them grappling with an uncertain future and limited employment opportunities back home.

“Some individuals are coming to GCCs through their internal transfer. But that is a very small number compared to the number of people who are back and are struggling. Many of them are searching for other opportunities,” says Aditya Narayan Mishra, Managing Director and CEO of talent solutions and recruitment firm CIEL HR.

Deals and Acquisitions

Every major Indian IT company spent the first half of 2026 racing to reposition itself as an AI-first services and platform business, and the deal numbers underneath that repositioning are genuinely large.

TCS struck a marquee tie-up with French AI lab Mistral in May, becoming the first global systems integrator to build custom enterprise AI models on Mistral's "Forge" platform.

Infosys also leaned hard into the "enterprise AI" pitch through its Topaz platform. It has kept a steady acquisition drumbeat through the year too, with two deals—Optimum Healthcare IT and Australian cybersecurity specialist The Missing Link—awaiting regulatory sign-off, part of a deliberate push into healthcare.

HCLTech is now putting hard numbers on its AI business rather than folding it into broader "digital" revenue, with annualised "Advanced AI" revenue crossing $620 million in Q4 FY26 alone.

Even as AI anxiety dominated boardroom conversations and headlines, the industry is also reshaping itself with aggressive consolidation, buying up smaller, AI-native, or domain-specialist firms. Also, enterprise clients are consolidating their vendor rosters down to fewer, larger partners.

Persistent Systems’ voluntary public takeover offer of German digital engineering firm Nagarro at €81 per share ($1.4 billion deal) on June 27 was the latest example.

In addition, Wipro's deal to acquire Mindsprint, the IT and digital services arm of Singapore's Olam Group, bundled an outright acquisition into a broader transformation contract, giving it instant supply-chain and agribusiness domain IP it would have taken years to build organically.

Among other mid-tier IT firms, Coforge’s acquisition of Silicon Valley-based digital engineering firm Encora for an enterprise value of $2.5 billion strengthened its position in the AI-led engineering, data, and cloud services markets.

The pattern across the sector is consistent: rather than building AI-native, domain-specific or cybersecurity capabilities from scratch, India's IT majors are focusing on consolidation to stay ahead and on par with AI giants.

Hiring Shift

The job story is more nuanced than the mass hysteria of AI-driven layoffs. However, while AI hiring may be on the rise, the broader headcount has taken a hit.

According to job portal Naukri’s monthly JobSpeak report, AI hiring in the Indian IT sector rose 16% year-over-year in June, while overall IT jobs declined 3%. Last month, TCS said it expected hiring to slow down and that it was moving towards having an equal number of employees and AI agents in the workforce.

This is only a continuation of recent trends. TCS, the largest employer in Indian IT services, shed nearly 23,500 employees in FY26 to end the year at 584,519, following a formal restructuring programme.

“This isn't a temporary correction; it's a structural re-architecture of the talent pyramid. AI is compressing the middle layer that once absorbed years of execution work, while senior roles remain largely status quo. Fresher hiring itself has slowed, with a sharper focus on AI-native talent over volume,” says Saravanan (Saran) Balasundaram, Founder and CEO of talent solutions firm Han Digital Solution.

“The gap left behind isn't being filled by permanent headcount; it's being absorbed by a growing temporary workforce, cushioning the shock of layoffs and emerging AI skills,” he adds.

Companies are also expecting entry-level engineers to show significantly higher readiness, including familiarity with AI-assisted development, problem-solving skills, and the ability to build production-grade applications much earlier than before, as AIM reported earlier.

Six months into its toughest year in over a decade, Indian IT is no longer debating whether AI will reshape the industry. The real question heading into the Q1 FY27 earnings season is whether the sector can reinvent itself quickly enough to turn efficiency-driven disruption into its next growth engine.

title: Ecolab Acquires CoolIT for $4.75bn to Strengthen AI Data Centre Cooling Business
content:
With AI REX at the centre of its AI-first strategy, Naukri aims to build a more intelligent hiring ecosystem that reduces manual recruitment work while improving candidate discovery.

What Actually Matters.

Naukri has launched AI REX, an AI-driven recruitment platform to enhance hiring efficiency and reduce manual tasks for recruiters.

AI REX automates key recruitment stages, analysing job descriptions and candidate qualifications to recommend suitable matches.

India’s largest job portal, Naukri, has launched a new AI-powered recruitment platform to make hiring faster and more efficient for both recruiters and job seekers.

The company unveiled a suite of AI-driven hiring products, led by AI REX, an autonomous talent-sourcing platform that automates key stages of recruitment, from understanding job requirements to identifying suitable candidates.

Unlike traditional recruitment tools that rely mainly on keyword searches, AI REX analyses job descriptions, candidate skills, and professional experience to recommend matches. The platform is designed to reduce manual work for recruiters by automatically sourcing, screening, and shortlisting candidates.

According to Naukri, organisations using AI REX can reduce talent sourcing timelines, allowing hiring teams to focus more on evaluating candidates rather than manually filtering resumes.

Beyond talent sourcing, the company has also introduced AI-assisted search, intelligent candidate recommendations, and automated shortlisting features. These tools are designed to simplify recruitment workflows while improving hiring accuracy.

The new platform also aims to improve the experience for job seekers. AI-powered recommendations can suggest roles that better match a candidate’s skills, experience and career goals, helping users discover more relevant opportunities rather than relying solely on manual searches.

The launch comes at a time when demand for AI talent continues to grow across India.

According to the company’s latest JobSpeak Report, hiring for AI roles in the IT sector grew 16% year-on-year in June, even though overall IT hiring declined by 3% during the same period. Across industries, demand for professionals with AI and machine learning skills increased by 25%, reflecting the broader adoption of AI across business functions.

As companies increasingly use AI to streamline operations, recruitment is also emerging as a major area for automation.

With CoolIT’s expertise in liquid cooling, Ecolab aims to provide comprehensive solutions across the AI value chain, targeting $4 billion in annual revenue from its Global High Tech business by 2030.

Ecolab has completed its acquisition of Canada’s advanced liquid-cooling company, CoolIT Systems, for approximately $4.75 billion, deepening its presence in the rapidly expanding AI infrastructure market and positioning itself to capitalise on growing demand for advanced data centre cooling technologies.

The US-based water, hygiene and infection prevention solutions provider said the transaction closed earlier than expected and expands its capabilities across the AI value chain, from water used in semiconductor manufacturing to cooling systems designed for high-density AI data centres.

“At the heart of AI is water. We need water to produce chips, power chips, and cool chips,” Christophe Beck, Chairman and CEO of Ecolab, said in a statement. “Ecolab is now uniquely positioned to offer end-to-end solutions across the full AI value chain, from ultra-pure water to produce the most advanced chips, to high-performing water systems for optimised power generation, to direct liquid cooling for the most powerful AI data centres.”

The acquisition comes as AI workloads drive a fundamental shift in data centre design. Traditional air-cooling systems are increasingly struggling to handle the heat generated by advanced AI processors, prompting operators to adopt liquid cooling technologies to improve efficiency and reduce power consumption.

CoolIT is a key supplier of direct liquid cooling systems used in high-performance computing environments. The company works with leading chipmakers, including NVIDIA and AMD, whose latest AI accelerators are significantly increasing power densities inside servers. As hyperscalers and cloud providers race to deploy AI infrastructure, liquid cooling has emerged as a critical technology for supporting next-generation GPU clusters.

“NVIDIA has collaborated with Ecolab and CoolIT across a broad range of liquid‑cooling initiatives, including coolant qualification, coolant health monitoring, cooling infrastructure development, and next‑generation AI factory technologies,” said Ali Heydari, Technical Director and Engineer at NVIDIA, and Saket Karajgikar, Senior Engineering Manager and ASME Fellow at NVIDIA.

The company’s year-to-date sales have grown by more than 100%, reflecting surging demand for AI-related cooling solutions.

“The world’s demand for AI is accelerating, driving exponential growth in semiconductors, data centres, energy and water demand. Ecolab’s acquisition of CoolIT positions us to help deliver the growth needed while advancing resource efficiency and sustainability,” Beck added.

Following the acquisition, Ecolab said its Global High Tech business has reached approximately $1.5 billion in annualised 2026 sales, up from around $150 million in 2021. The company is targeting $4 billion in annual revenue from the segment by 2030.

title: LTM Launches BlueVerse RightLogic as Enterprises Grapple with Rising Security Threats
content:
BlueVerse RightLogic combines AI and cybersecurity assessments to help enterprises identify vulnerabilities, prioritise remediation, and strengthen governance as AI adoption accelerates.

LTM, formerly known as LTIMindtree, has launched BlueVerse RightLogic, a cybersecurity assessment and risk assurance framework to help enterprises identify, assess, and remediate cyber risks as organisations increasingly deploy artificial intelligence across their operations.

The offering comes as enterprises face a growing threat landscape, with AI capable of autonomously identifying and exploiting vulnerabilities, while expanding digital infrastructure, applications, and software supply chains have increased the attack surface.

The company said this has elevated cybersecurity from an IT concern to a board-level priority.

According to LTM, BlueVerse RightLogic provides a unified view of enterprise cyber exposure by combining AI and cybersecurity assessments with a structured remediation framework. The platform evaluates software supply chain risks, legacy systems, network exposure, identity and access controls, AI-specific risks, and governance readiness, while integrating both external threat exposure and internal security preparedness.

“AI-driven threats are autonomous, scalable and continuous, and they demand a fundamentally different approach to cybersecurity. With BlueVerse RightLogic, we enable organisations to quantify exposure, prioritise action and build a defensible security posture that supports safe and scalable AI adoption," Krishnan Iyer, Chief Growth Officer, LTM, said in a statement.

The company said the framework is delivered through a four-to six-week engagement that includes cyber diagnostics, domain-specific assessments, a board-level risk summary and a prioritised remediation roadmap.

It also extends into implementation through partner-led execution covering infrastructure, applications, and open source dependencies.

title: Bihar Partners With Google, Microsoft, CoRover, Sarvam AI for AI-Driven Governance
content:
The Bihar government is in the final stages of drafting its own Artificial Intelligence Policy.

The Bihar government has signed memorandums of understanding (MoUs) with Google, Microsoft, CoRover (BharatGPT), and Sarvam AI to accelerate its AI roadmap, marking a significant step towards building an AI-driven governance ecosystem.

The non-financial partnerships will focus on technical expertise, capacity building, innovation support, and knowledge sharing to strengthen AI adoption across governance, education, and workforce development.

Under the collaborations, Bihar plans to roll out AI-based skilling programmes for government officials, teachers, and youth, while promoting AI awareness among school students to create a future-ready talent pipeline. The initiative aims to equip citizens with practical AI skills while supporting the state's broader digital transformation agenda.

As part of the collaboration, CoRover will provide technical guidance, training support, and innovation expertise to strengthen Bihar's AI ecosystem.

The state's skilling programme seeks to build AI capabilities among government employees, educators, and young professionals while encouraging AI literacy from the school level onwards.

Alongside the industry partnerships, the Bihar government is in the final stages of drafting its own Artificial Intelligence Policy, which will provide a structured roadmap for AI adoption across governance, education, and industry. The policy has been prepared following consultations with technology companies, industry leaders, and academic experts to establish a framework for responsible AI deployment.

To strengthen research and innovation capabilities, Bihar is also collaborating with the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Patna to establish an advanced IT and AI research centre along with a state-of-the-art research laboratory. The initiative is expected to promote deeptech research, support startups, and build a robust AI innovation ecosystem within the state.

The government also plans to leverage its existing data centre as the backbone for AI-enabled government applications, while future AI-powered services will increasingly utilise cloud-based technologies to improve efficiency and scalability. Officials believe the AI initiatives will enhance public service delivery, improve the implementation of welfare schemes, attract technology investments, create employment opportunities, and position Bihar as an emerging destination for AI and digital innovation in India.

title: NIIT Brings StackRoute, RPS Consulting Under New Enterprise Tech Business
content:
The move aims to address changing enterprise talent needs by helping organisations build future-ready technology talent and manage large-scale workforce transformation.

What Actually Matters.

NIIT has launched its Enterprise Tech business, integrating StackRoute and RPS Consulting to meet evolving enterprise talent requirements.

The initiative aims to assist organisations in developing future-ready technology talent and managing workforce transformation.

NIIT Limited, a skills and talent development company, has unveiled its Enterprise Tech business, combining the capabilities of technology training companies StackRoute and RPS Consulting into a single technology-focused offering.

The move aims to address changing enterprise talent needs by helping organisations build future-ready technology talent and manage large-scale workforce transformation. The announcement was made at the World Digital Architect Conclave 2026.

Also, NIIT has named Vishnupriya Raghavan to head the Enterprise Tech business, with responsibility for helping enterprises build digital fluency, strengthen workforce capabilities, and support digital transformation efforts.

The Enterprise Tech platform covers role readiness, technology skilling, leadership development, OEM-led capability programmes and enterprise-scale capability transformation. It is designed to help organisations and their partner networks build technology capabilities across roles, teams and business ecosystems.

Its focus areas include AI-first engineering, AI-led site reliability engineering, cloud transformation, cybersecurity, data engineering, enterprise architecture, engineering intelligence, and technology leadership.

Delivered through structured learning pathways and hands-on, real-world practice, the offering is intended to help enterprises build automation-ready, AI-native teams.

The integration combines RPS Consulting's OEM partnerships with StackRoute's engineering expertise, forming a broader Enterprise Tech offering to build workforce capabilities at scale.

Commenting on the integration, Pankaj Jathar, Chief Executive Officer, NIIT Limited, said, "The future of enterprise growth will be shaped by how effectively organisations build and evolve workforce capabilities in an era being transformed by AI."

He added that bringing StackRoute and RPS Consulting together reflects the company's aim to help organisations build future-ready talent through combined technology expertise, leadership development, and learning-led transformation.

Vishnupriya Raghavan, Senior Vice President & Business Head – Enterprise Tech, NIIT Ltd., said, "Enterprise Tech brings together StackRoute and RPS Consulting to provide a unified technology skilling and capability-building offering across engineering, architecture, cloud, cybersecurity, data and AI."

She said the combination of StackRoute's engineering and learning strength with RPS Consulting's OEM ecosystem is intended to give clients broader capability and scale for continuous workforce transformation, with structured learning pathways aimed at helping organisations build future-ready teams.

title: HCLTech Bags $1.14 Bn Mega AI Deal from Fortune Global 50 European Firm
content:
HCLTech’s six-year contract, which runs until December 2031, includes the transformation and management of the client's global digital workplace and enterprise networks.

HCLTech has signed a strategic agreement worth an estimated $1.14 billion with a Europe-headquartered Fortune Global 50 company to build an AI-led operating model for its global digital workplace and enterprise network operations, the IT services company said in a stock exchange filing on Friday.

The contract, with an initial term of about six years that begins in July 2026 and runs through December 2031, can be extended by another five years.

HCLTech, in a statement, said the engagement is entirely a net new business for the company.

As part of the deal, HCLTech will transform and manage the client's global digital workplace and enterprise networks using an AI-driven operating model.

The company, however, did not disclose the customer's identity, citing confidentiality.

The announcement marks one of the largest contract wins disclosed by the Noida- headquartered IT services firm and indicates the growing demand for AI-powered infrastructure and workplace transformation projects among large global enterprises.

The deal also adds to a string of AI-focused engagements announced by HCLTech in recent months.

Last month, HCLTech acquired a 10.5% stake in AI startup Sarvam AI for ₹1,427 crore ($150 million).

For Indian IT services companies as well, large deal wins have become an important driver of revenue visibility at a time when discretionary technology spending remains uneven.

Companies including HCLTech, Infosys, TCS, Wipro and Tech Mahindra have been signing large deals even as clients remain selective on new technology investments outside AI and cost optimisation initiatives.

NVIDIA says the initiative will help AI companies access large-scale computing without waiting for new infrastructure to be built.

NVIDIA has introduced a new business model with AI cloud providers that combines revenue sharing and credit support to expand access to large-scale AI infrastructure for startups, model developers, enterprises, research organisations, and regional AI players.

The company said it addresses the growing shift in AI demand from model training to production inference, where AI factories operate continuously to generate tokens at scale.

Under the arrangement, AI cloud providers will procure NVIDIA infrastructure and offer NVIDIA-powered cloud services to customers. NVIDIA will receive revenue from hardware sales as well as a share of cloud revenue generated from the supported capacity.

“This new model enables AI clouds to procure NVIDIA infrastructure for AI-native, enterprise and ISV customers through economic alignment with a revenue-sharing and credit-support model,” NVIDIA said in a blog post.

According to the company, the structure aims to help AI companies gain faster access to computing capacity without waiting for data centre site selection, power procurement, construction, and hardware deployment.

The initiative is already underway, with AI cloud providers building NVIDIA DSX AI factories across multiple regions. Sharon AI and Firmus are among the first companies to adopt the model.

Sharon AI plans to deploy up to 40,000 NVIDIA Grace Blackwell GB300 GPUs.

Meanwhile, Firmus is building a DSX AI factory campus in Batam, Indonesia, which the company expects to scale to 360 MW and support up to 170,000 NVIDIA GPUs.

NVIDIA said the model supports AI-native companies, including model builders, inference providers, agent platforms, and enterprises that require large-scale computing for model training, post-training, fine-tuning, and agentic inference. The company added that customers increasingly need both reliable compute capacity and commercial flexibility as AI applications move from pilot projects to production.

title: Microsoft Invests $2.5 Bn to Launch Frontier Company to Help Businesses Deploy AI
content:
Microsoft also named Rodrigo Kede Lima as President of the Frontier Company.

Microsoft has announced Microsoft Frontier Company, a new business unit to help enterprises deploy AI systems at scale. The initiative is backed by a $2.5 billion investment and a team of 6,000 industry and engineering experts who will be embedded with customers.

Microsoft also named Rodrigo Kede Lima as President of Microsoft Frontier Company. Lima previously led Microsoft’s enterprise business across the Americas and Asia and will oversee the new organisation.

The company said the new organisation will combine AI engineering, industry expertise, change management and continuous improvement to help customers design, deploy and refine AI systems tied to measurable business outcomes.

“Today we are introducing Microsoft Frontier Company, a new operating business focused on delivering Frontier Transformation through AI for our customers around the world,” the company wrote in a blog post.

Microsoft said enterprises are moving beyond AI experimentation and are now seeking measurable returns while ensuring their proprietary knowledge remains protected.

The company said organisations need an intelligence platform where their proprietary data, expertise, workflows and decision-making processes can improve over time while allowing customers to choose the AI models that best fit their needs. It also said enterprises require trusted platforms that provide governance, security and cost management across AI deployments.

Microsoft said the new business will focus on connecting these capabilities through AI engineering to create a continuous improvement cycle for agentic business processes.

The company cited projects with the London Stock Exchange Group, Land O'Lakes, Unilever and Novo Nordisk as early examples of customer deployments delivering business outcomes.

Microsoft also said it will work with systems integrators, including Accenture, Capgemini, EY, KPMG and PwC to expand the offering globally.

A key part of the initiative is Microsoft's commitment that customer data and intellectual property will not be used to train AI models.

“Central to this approach is a principle that is non-negotiable: a customer’s IQ is protected. Their data, their IP, their competitive advantage — none of it is used to train models in ways that commoditise what differentiates them in their industry,” Microsoft said.

The company added that it will continue supporting a model-agnostic approach rather than locking customers into a single AI provider.

“Customers shouldn't be locked into a single model any more than they should be locked into a single technology vendor,” it said. “Microsoft's platform gives organisations the flexibility to run the right model for each scenario — whether it comes from OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft AI, open source or a specialised model tuned for a specific industry — without ceding control to any one of them.”

Amazon Web Services (AWS) also recently announced a $1 billion investment to launch a new Forward Deployed Engineering (FDE) organisation that will place AI engineers inside customer teams to co-develop and deploy agentic AI systems.

The new unit targets enterprises that have moved beyond AI pilots and want to integrate AI into business operations. AWS said the teams will work directly with customers’ engineering, business, and security teams to build production AI systems using their own data and governance frameworks.

title: Skyroot Sets Date for Vikram-1 Orbital Test Flight from Sriharikota
content:
Skyroot Aerospace’s Mission Aagaman will test India’s first privately developed orbital rocket and gather flight data for future launches.

What Actually Matters.

Skyroot Aerospace is preparing for the maiden test flight of Vikram-1, India’s first privately developed orbital-class rocket.

The launch window for Mission Aagaman is set from 12 July to 4 August, pending clearances and weather conditions.

Hyderabad-based space tech startup Skyroot Aerospace has opened the launch window for the maiden test flight of Vikram-1, India’s first privately developed orbital-class rocket. The startup is India’s first and only space tech unicorn, reaching a $1.1 billion valuation after raising nearly $60 million in its last funding round.

With liftoff targeted no earlier than July 12 from SDSC-SHAR in Sriharikota, the launch window for this upcoming test flight extends until August 4 and remains subject to the completion of assembly and testing operations, as well as weather, safety, and range clearances.

The company announced the launch window as part of Mission Aagaman, named after the Sanskrit word for ‘arrival’. The mission aims to establish India’s private orbital launch capability and collect in-flight performance data across the rocket’s systems to support the development of a commercial launch programme.

Mission Aagaman marks Skyroot’s second mission after the successful launch of Vikram-S in November 2022, which became the first privately built rocket to reach space from Indian soil.

The upcoming flight will be partially commercial, carrying a mix of domestic and international customer payloads. The company plans to begin full commercial operations after one or two successful orbital demonstration missions.

“We want to understand how the vehicle performs from lift-off through every phase of ascent. This data cannot be fully replicated through ground testing. It will help us validate our designs and inform subsequent vehicle development as we build a reliable, high-cadence commercial launch programme,” said Pawan Kumar Chandana, Co-founder and CEO of Skyroot Aerospace, in a statement.

Skyroot said all stages of Vikram-1 have been integrated and stacked at the launch pad. The mission will gather data on propulsion, stage separation, guidance, navigation, control, and overall vehicle performance.

Vikram-1 is a multi-stage launch vehicle built with an all-carbon composite structure and powered by propulsion systems developed in-house, including 3D-printed engines and solid-fuel boosters. The rocket can carry satellites weighing up to 350 kg to low Earth orbit. Its maiden mission will target a 450 km orbit with a 60-degree inclination.

The flight-ready vehicle was unveiled by Prime Minister Narendra Modi in November 2025 during the inauguration of Skyroot’s Infinity campus.

Naga Bharath Daka, Co-founder and COO of Skyroot Aerospace, added, “With Vikram-1, we take our biggest step yet toward a reliable, high-cadence launch programme built in India, for India and the world. This mission is designed as both a technology demonstration and a learning mission.”

Skyroot said frequent access to orbit remains a challenge for satellite operators that often wait months or years for launch opportunities. The company’s ‘Cab to Space’ model aims to provide dedicated access to orbit using infrastructure and support enabled through India’s space sector reforms.

Skyroot said increased launch capacity could support sectors including communications, navigation, agriculture, fisheries, disaster management, and national security.

Enterprises are grappling with the ever increasing token costs. So, how to put an end to this?

Access to advanced AI has become a challenge for enterprises and organisations.

As powerful models become accessible with just a few clicks and are heavily promoted in software engineering, companies are increasingly debating how much AI access to allow their employees.

Some have taken a strict approach. After exceeding its annual AI budget in just one month, Uber introduced a $1,500 monthly per-employee limit to contain token costs. Amazon and Meta, too, have reportedly begun steering employees towards cheaper AI models and imposing tighter controls on usage.

This creates a paradox. Enterprise adoption is expected to become the primary revenue driver for model providers, yet enterprises are simultaneously restricting AI usage.

Founder and CEO of Palo Alto Networks, Nikesh Arora, argued on X that if consumer AI largely involves giving away free AI while burning capital, enterprise customers will ultimately fund frontier AI.

He suggested that labs need to ‘forward price’ tokens by reducing costs to encourage experimentation and workflow reimagination. “CIOs are busy restricting AI use and working on making the use more efficient,” he wrote.

Today, much of the enterprise AI ecosystem is focused on reducing AI costs by redesigning workflows. Enterprises are increasingly adopting powerful open source models, aided by Chinese AI companies that offer frontier-level performance at a fraction of the cost, or building routing architectures that send tasks to the most appropriate model.

However, the comparison between open source and proprietary models based solely on token prices is misplaced.

“Comparing proprietary APIs with open source models purely on token prices misses the real economic tradeoff,” says Leslie Joseph, Principal Analyst at Forrester Research, in an interaction with AIM.

The total cost of ownership includes infrastructure, engineering, governance, operations and ongoing model management.

“Open source becomes attractive at sufficient scale or where data sovereignty is critical. For many organisations, managed proprietary models remain the lower-cost option once operational complexity is considered,” adds Joseph.

Even companies that have successfully migrated to open source models acknowledge this trade-off.

Cloudflare recently highlighted why this operational complexity matters. While announcing support for Moonshot AI’s Kimi K2.5 model, it said that serving frontier open-source models at scale requires substantial engineering beyond downloading model weights, including extensive optimisation of the inference stack.

Although the effort reduced inference costs for some internal workloads by 77%, Cloudflare noted that these optimisations require specialist infrastructure expertise, which platforms such as Workers AI package into a managed service.

Recently, Florent Crivello, CEO and co-founder of Lindy, an AI platform for building customisable no-code agents, wrote on X that the company had shifted all of its traffic to DeepSeek V4, replacing Anthropic’s models.

According to Crivello, the migration is saving the company millions of dollars while improving performance, although it required significant engineering effort. “I think these things are stickier than they sound—it’s not easy to switch models,” he tells AIM.

He highlighted the trust US frontier AI models have earned and the brand impact shown in the saying, “no one ever got fired for picking Anthropic.”

Crivello added that for many companies, the cost of switching to Chinese AI models is not worth the effort.

The New Playbook for Enterprise AI

Another approach enterprises are adopting is improving AI discipline across the organisation through model routing and usage optimisation.

Recently, Brian Armstrong, CEO of Coinbase, revealed on X that the company made open-weight models such as GLM 5.2 and Kimi 2.7 the default via its internal LLM gateway, while still allowing engineers to choose any model they deemed appropriate.

Armstrong said the company had “cut our AI spend nearly in half, while our token usage continues to grow.”

This was also possible because 91% of employees never reached their AI usage limits, allowing Coinbase to replace tighter restrictions with cheaper default models.

The company also implemented automated model routing. Its internal AI preprocesses prompts and directs requests to the most cost-effective model based on the task, pricing and cache availability.

Employees are also encouraged to keep context windows lean by starting new sessions for different tasks, limiting file context, disconnecting unused tools and avoiding unnecessary token consumption.

Similarly, in an interview with VentureBeat, Farhan Thawar, head of engineering at Shopify, revealed that the company has built an internal LLM proxy that sits between employees and AI providers.

The system purchases tokens in bulk, automatically routes traffic across providers and monitors token consumption, using circuit breakers rather than hard usage limits.

In an interaction with AIM, Nikhil Gandhi, senior vice president of engineering at Yahoo, said the company created a central AI council early in its adoption journey after realising that allowing every team to build independently would lead to fragmentation.

The council evaluates models, develops reusable AI agents and shares best practices across engineering teams.

“None of the models are designed to work out of the box. You have to give them the right context,” he says.

He added that the centralised approach has delivered “a lot more bang for the buck” by preventing teams from duplicating work.

Even so, many enterprises are unlikely to have the time, budget or engineering resources to build their own routing systems and AI infrastructure. For many, managed AI APIs remain the more practical option.

Gandhi adds that for enterprises deeply integrated with a particular AI stack, the engineering overhead of switching can outweigh the potential savings, making it an ROI decision rather than a purely technical one.

Not Using LLMs for Everything

“The cost of the underlying infrastructure has risen sharply in a short span of time,” Sujatha Iyer, head of AI security at Zoho, tells AIM.

“As storing enormous volumes of data, processing it, training models and running inference at scale all carry a significant cost, eventually someone has to pay for it.”

She adds that consumer AI apps often pay for this with user data, whereas enterprise AI bears the cost through token spending and rising AI budgets.

She also argues that the larger question is whether every AI requirement needs an LLM, whether open or closed.

“Enterprises can also work with purpose-built machine learning models wherever they can,” she says. Iyer believes that adopting machine learning models and right-sized models where appropriate can often be more effective in enterprise settings.

She also notes that context is the real differentiator in enterprise workflows. “Even a simple query may draw from multiple systems, permission layers and business rules before it gives a meaningful answer.”

According to Iyer, ease of access to context layers must therefore begin early in the software development lifecycle.

“The data access and permission layer has to be designed from day one.”

FDEs Will Train ‘Enterprise Waymos of the World’

The trend also explains the growing focus on Forward Deployed Engineers, or FDEs, across leading AI labs.

These are engineers who work closely with enterprise companies on behalf of AI model makers to help integrate LLMs efficiently into their processes.

Arora says these engineers will train the “enterprise Waymos of the world” by teaching generic AI models how each business operates, gradually turning them into autonomous enterprise systems capable of running complex workflows.

OpenAI has built a dedicated Forward Deployed Engineering organisation and has recently expanded the effort through its Deployment Company, while Anthropic has been scaling its Applied AI team and deploying engineers directly to strategic enterprise customers.

However, not everyone believes this FDE-heavy model is permanent.

Joseph argues that “Today's reliance on Forward Deployed Engineers reflects the immaturity of enterprise AI platforms more than a fundamental limitation of LLMs.”

He believes today’s enterprise AI tooling, including orchestration frameworks, governance systems, and evaluation platforms, still cannot automate much of the integration work required to deploy AI within businesses. As those platforms mature, much of that engineering will become built into the software itself.

FDEs will still be needed, he says, but their role will increasingly shift from integrating and deploying AI systems to adapting them to each organisation’s business processes.

Iyer shares a similar view. While acknowledging the value of FDEs, she also says, “Over time, more reliability should move into the platform itself, but enterprises will still need people who can translate business context into the right AI solution.”

Besides, Joseph also says, “High token prices are creating budget pressure, but they are not the main reason enterprise AI adoption is slowing. The market is moving from experimentation to economic discipline.”

He argues that CIOs are no longer funding AI because of its novelty, but because it can deliver measurable business outcomes.

“Token costs matter, but they are only one part of the equation alongside governance, orchestration, data access, reliability, and integration.”

Joseph believes that enterprises focusing only on reducing inference costs, or indulging in ‘tokenmaxxing’, are often optimising the wrong variable. “The bigger challenge is designing AI systems that consistently generate business value.”

title: Cognizant Launches Governance Platform to Manage Agentic AI Risks in Enterprises
content:
Cognizant has launched Neuro AI Trust, a governance platform that provides real-time monitoring and policy enforcement across AI models and agents.

Cognizant has launched Neuro AI Trust, an AI governance platform to help enterprises monitor, govern, and manage risks across AI models, agents, and applications as organisations increasingly deploy agentic AI systems.

The platform provides enterprises with continuous governance and real-time visibility into AI environments, allowing organisations to monitor AI behaviour, enforce policies, and identify operational or compliance risks as AI systems become more autonomous and interconnected.

The launch comes as enterprises move beyond deploying individual AI models to managing multiple large language models, AI agents, and autonomous workflows, making governance and oversight more complex.

According to Cognizant, Neuro AI Trust introduces a centralised control layer that continuously monitors AI systems using "Guardian Agents", while an intelligence layer evaluates interactions in real time and applies governance policies, guardrails, and automated controls aligned with business and regulatory requirements. The platform also offers a dashboard to track AI system health, security, and risk.

"As agentic AI moves into enterprise operations, the constraint is no longer capability but trust. Technology leaders expect governance, accountability and transparency to be addressed by AI platforms," Jennifer Hamel, Research Vice President, Enterprise Data and AI Services at IDC, said in a statement.

Cognizant has already deployed the platform internally across its AI-enabled intranet, which serves its workforce of around 350,000 employees.

Neuro AI Trust supports governance frameworks such as the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, the EU AI Act, OECD AI Principles and ISO/IEC 42001, while allowing enterprises to update governance policies without modifying application code.

It is also designed to detect model drift, monitor multi-agent interactions, predict potential policy violations, escalate high-risk decisions for human review, and maintain audit-ready records of AI interactions.

The platform integrates with Cognizant's broader AI portfolio, including its Neuro AI Multi-Agent Accelerator, as the company expands its enterprise AI offerings amid growing demand for governance and compliance capabilities.

As Indian enterprises move AI out of sandboxes and into core operations, the case for locally governed infrastructure, built on cost, compliance, and real-time performance, is no longer theoretical.

What Actually Matters.

Enterprise AI in India is transitioning from experimental to production-level integration in various operational areas.

Financial challenges, particularly rising costs of infrastructure, are hindering the scaling of AI in enterprises.

Enterprise AI in India has reached an inflection point. What began as a wave of proof-of-concept deployments has given way to something far more consequential: production-scale AI that touches billing systems, customer interactions, operational workflows, and regulated data.

The infrastructure underpinning this shift, however, is under severe stress, and the companies navigating it most successfully are turning to sovereign cloud providers based inside the country.

The Infrastructure Reckoning

The primary challenge enterprises encounter when scaling AI isn’t technical but financial. Companies transitioning from experimentation to full deployment often find that their token usage and GPU requirements quickly surpass expectations, rapidly depleting their budgets.

Memory prices have surged by six to ten times, pushing the cost of a single AI-grade server from approximately ₹15–20 lakh to ₹60–70 lakh, a reality that is forcing many enterprises to reconsider in-house procurement and look to cloud providers capable of pooling and optimising these scarce resources.

"The correct estimation of the infrastructure required comes with experience and optimisations, because sometimes AI is there and it's giving results, but then you realise the number of tokens used is so high that it has emptied all your budget,” Vinay Chhabra, Co-founder and Managing Director at AceCloud, tells AIM.

Infrastructure challenges arise from understanding the infrastructure, how much it can deliver, and at what cost.

For companies lacking the capital, cloud providers offer an advantage: by continuously running GPU infrastructure across various workloads—inferencing during business hours, overnight batch processing, and parallel encoding—they achieve higher utilization rates than standalone enterprises. This efficiency reduces per-unit costs.

The Regulatory Catalyst

India's evolving regulatory environment is proving to be as powerful a driver of sovereign cloud adoption as economics. The Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act and the Reserve Bank of India's strict data localisation mandates make data residency a legal and operational requirement, not just an option.

For enterprises in BFSI and healthcare, where regulatory exposure is highest, this has accelerated migrations to India-based infrastructure with an urgency that earlier compliance frameworks never produced.

The challenge for enterprises, however, lies not merely in complying with existing mandates but in keeping pace with evolving frameworks. Both the DPDP Act's implementation rules and RBI's technology governance frameworks are subject to revision.

Organisations managing complex multi-cloud environments find it increasingly difficult to maintain continuous compliance across this shifting landscape, prompting a growing cohort to consolidate regulated workloads within dedicated sovereign infrastructure.

To address this, AceCloud is building an AI-driven platform to monitor regulatory changes and flag compliance implications in near real-time.

Data residency is now super critical to a country's sovereignty because data leakage is a real possibility and happens all the time.

“When there is data sovereignty, you have to keep your data in the sovereign cloud, and to that extent, it accelerates the adoption of Indian cloud providers,” says Chhabra. “It is definitely harder than before, but it is desirable and required for the safety and security of the country.”

Latency and the Real-Time AI Imperative

Beyond compliance, performance is key. AI tools needing real-time responses—voice bots, workflows, medical systems—are sensitive to latency. Overseas data centres add 250 milliseconds of round-trip delay before processing.

For a three-stage voice bot pipeline comprising speech-to-text, LLM inference, and text-to-speech, this compounds delays to 600 milliseconds or more, producing an unnatural conversational experience that customers immediately notice.

Chhabra explains that local AI infrastructure is crucial. In agentic AI, agents frequently communicate with LLMs. Hosting an LLM remotely results in accumulating latencies that significantly degrade the real-life experience. Conversely, localizing the LLM improves latency management, enabling real-time actions.

The Hybrid Inflection Point

India's enterprise cloud market is witnessing a structural correction. Cloud repatriation is accelerating, driven by the financial reality that cloud spend, for IT-intensive businesses, can represent 10% or more of total operating costs.

CFOs are pressing CIOs to justify those expenditures, and non-critical workloads are being assessed for repatriation. This is creating a structural opening for sovereign cloud providers offering a middle path: the operational simplicity of managed cloud, without the cost structure or data-residency limitations of global hyperscalers.

"AceCloud fills a very sweet spot in this game. Even if you want to bring infrastructure in-house, you still have to maintain it, employ IT people, and manage uptime and security. AceCloud helps enterprises control their costs while removing the headache of managing in-house IT infrastructure,” says Chhabra.

Securing the Agentic Frontier

One of the most significant upcoming changes is the shift to agentic AI—autonomous systems that can perform multi-step workflows, update databases, initiate operational tasks, and communicate with core enterprise systems.

As these capabilities mature, the attack surface for data exposure expands considerably, and the case for keeping agentic workflows within a sovereign, isolated environment becomes compelling.

The industry is developing layered controls, including versioned storage that prevents permanent deletion, the Model Context Protocol (MCP) defining permissible API commands, hallucination monitoring with automated halts, and context integrity checks to prevent agents from drifting from their goals.

Autonomous agentic AI is given considerable power. The companies need to have controls on what they can and cannot access, and an assessment of the damage they can cause.

“With MCP coming into play, you can regulate which commands the agent can give through APIs even while giving them autonomy. They know their limits and cannot exceed those limits," adds Chhabra.

The Road Ahead

Over the next three to five years, India's AI infrastructure will be shaped by three forces: expansion of the DPDP framework, a shift to liquid data centre cooling increasing GPU density, and a looming power constraint that may limit the country's AI ambitions.

Nuclear power, already under consideration by data centre operators in the United States, is a scenario Chhabra believes will become relevant in India as well.

For AceCloud, the strategic roadmap is to build out the value stack above the GPU layer, offering inference-as-a-service, optimised voice-bot hosting, video-processing pipelines, and other managed AI capabilities.

As Chhabra puts it, the GPU is rapidly becoming a commodity. What will differentiate the providers leading India's sovereign AI era is what they build on top of it.

title: Cognizant Launches Governance Platform to Manage Agentic AI Risks in Enterprises
content:
WhatsApp said the feature is not yet live and includes safeguards against impersonation, but the government wants further consultations before any launch.

The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) on July 1 directed Meta-owned WhatsApp to halt the rollout of its upcoming username feature in India, citing concerns that it could increase cyber fraud, phishing, impersonation, and identity spoofing.

The ministry has asked the company to submit a detailed explanation of the feature, supported by relevant documents, within three days.

In a notice sent to WhatsApp’s Chief Compliance Officer for India, the ministry instructed the company not to launch the feature until consultations with the government are completed “to the satisfaction of the Government.”

Earlier this week, WhatsApp announced that it had begun a phased global rollout of usernames, including in India. The feature allows users to communicate without sharing their phone numbers by reserving unique usernames.

MeitY said the feature could have unintended security consequences.

“It is felt that the feature may materially increase the incidence of online fraud, phishing, digital arrest scams and impersonation attacks, by enabling bad actors to solicit and message victims,” the notice said.

The ministry further warned that the feature could lead to identity spoofing.

“Furthermore, this feature may facilitate impersonation and identity spoofing, including impersonation of individuals, public authorities, financial institutions, and Government agencies, by permitting the adoption of usernames closely resembling those of genuine persons or institutions,” the notice added.

The government also reminded WhatsApp that, as a significant social media intermediary under India’s IT Rules, it is required to meet due diligence obligations under Section 79 of the Information Technology Act and the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021.

It warned that the directive was issued “without prejudice to any other action” that may be taken by the government or law enforcement agencies under existing laws.

Responding to the notice, a WhatsApp spokesperson said the username feature is not yet live and will be introduced gradually later this year.

“We’ve announced the option for people to reserve their preferred username on WhatsApp,” the spokesperson said in a statement. “The ability to use a username is not yet live and will roll out slowly later this year.”

The company said users will still need a phone number to register for WhatsApp and argued that it has built several safeguards into the feature to reduce abuse.

“To protect against impersonation, we’ve held the highest-profile names—think public figures, government entities, celebrities, verified Meta accounts—so they can only ever be claimed by their legitimate owners and lookalike derivatives of known names are held as well,” the spokesperson said.

WhatsApp added that users will need to know another person’s exact username before initiating a conversation. It also said it will limit how many new people an account can contact, block repeated attempts to guess usernames, and use automated systems to detect impersonation and abuse.

The company said that before users respond to a first-time message, WhatsApp will indicate whether the sender is a new account, an existing contact, shares mutual groups, or is located in another country.

Cognizant has launched Neuro AI Trust, a governance platform that provides real-time monitoring and policy enforcement across AI models and agents.

Cognizant has launched Neuro AI Trust, an AI governance platform to help enterprises monitor, govern, and manage risks across AI models, agents, and applications as organisations increasingly deploy agentic AI systems.

The platform provides enterprises with continuous governance and real-time visibility into AI environments, allowing organisations to monitor AI behaviour, enforce policies, and identify operational or compliance risks as AI systems become more autonomous and interconnected.

The launch comes as enterprises move beyond deploying individual AI models to managing multiple large language models, AI agents, and autonomous workflows, making governance and oversight more complex.

According to Cognizant, Neuro AI Trust introduces a centralised control layer that continuously monitors AI systems using "Guardian Agents", while an intelligence layer evaluates interactions in real time and applies governance policies, guardrails, and automated controls aligned with business and regulatory requirements. The platform also offers a dashboard to track AI system health, security, and risk.

"As agentic AI moves into enterprise operations, the constraint is no longer capability but trust. Technology leaders expect governance, accountability and transparency to be addressed by AI platforms," Jennifer Hamel, Research Vice President, Enterprise Data and AI Services at IDC, said in a statement.

Cognizant has already deployed the platform internally across its AI-enabled intranet, which serves its workforce of around 350,000 employees.

Neuro AI Trust supports governance frameworks such as the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, the EU AI Act, OECD AI Principles and ISO/IEC 42001, while allowing enterprises to update governance policies without modifying application code.

It is also designed to detect model drift, monitor multi-agent interactions, predict potential policy violations, escalate high-risk decisions for human review, and maintain audit-ready records of AI interactions.

The platform integrates with Cognizant's broader AI portfolio, including its Neuro AI Multi-Agent Accelerator, as the company expands its enterprise AI offerings amid growing demand for governance and compliance capabilities.

title: Meta Plans AI Cloud Business to Challenge AWS, Azure, Google Cloud: Report
content:
Meta is weighing both hosted AI model APIs and raw compute services for developers and enterprises.

Meta is planning to launch a cloud infrastructure business to sell AI computing power and host AI models for external customers, according to a report by Bloomberg.

The proposed business would put Meta in direct competition with cloud providers such as Amazon Web Services (AWS), Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud. The report added that the company is exploring ways to monetise excess AI infrastructure as it continues investing heavily in data centres and AI chips.

One proposal under consideration would allow developers to access AI models hosted on Meta’s infrastructure through an API, similar to AWS’s Bedrock service. Meta would operate the underlying data centres and hardware while charging customers to use models, including its own Muse Spark models.

The company is also evaluating the possibility of renting out raw AI computing capacity, similar to cloud infrastructure providers such as CoreWeave. The effort is part of an internal initiative called Meta Compute, which oversees the company’s AI infrastructure strategy, Bloomberg reported.

AIM has reached out to Meta for a comment.

In April, Meta raised its capital expenditure forecast to $125–145 billion for 2026, up from its previous guidance of $115–135 billion, citing additional investments in AI data centres, infrastructure hardware, and future capacity requirements.

Meta is building multiple AI data centre campuses, including Prometheus in Ohio and Hyperion in Louisiana, US, which is expected to scale to 5 GW of computing capacity.

Moreover, Meta has supplemented its in-house infrastructure with external AI computing capacity through multi-billion-dollar agreements with CoreWeave and Google.

A cloud business could provide one avenue for recovering part of that spending. Established cloud providers generate billions of dollars in quarterly revenue by renting computing resources, storage, and software to enterprises. Demand for AI infrastructure has also increased as companies build and deploy large AI models.

Meta’s strategy mirrors a recent move by SpaceX, which has begun monetising excess AI computing capacity through its Memphis-based data centre. Earlier this year, SpaceX signed a deal to provide Anthropic with access to the full capacity of its Colossus 1 AI cluster and later entered a multi-year agreement with Google, under which Google will pay $920 million per month from October 2026 through June 2029 for AI compute.

Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg had earlier indicated that he was open to commercialising surplus AI infrastructure. Speaking during the company’s call with shareholders in May, he said customers had approached Meta about purchasing compute capacity or accessing AI models through an API service.

He added that the company had not pursued those opportunities because it still expected to use the infrastructure internally, but said selling excess capacity remained a possibility if Meta eventually built more compute than it required.

Karthik Rameshkumar’s appointment places India at the core of Entire's product strategy.

Entire, the developer platform founded by former GitHub chief executive Thomas Dohmke, has appointed Karthik Rameshkumar as its field chief technology officer, marking the company’s first formal leadership appointment focused on India.

Rameshkumar will be responsible for carrying developer and enterprise feedback from the region back into Entire’s product and engineering teams.

Entire came out of stealth in February with a $60 million seed round led by Felicis, with participation from Madrona, Basis Set and M12, Microsoft’s venture arm. The company described it as the largest seed raise for a developer tools startup, valuing it at $300 million.

Dohmke left GitHub in August 2025, after four years as chief executive and a decade at Microsoft, to build Entire.

The company’s aim is to build a developer platform designed for an era in which AI agents, rather than only humans, produce numerous codes.

Its architecture rests on three layers—a Git-compatible database meant to unify code, intent, and reasoning; a semantic reasoning layer intended to enable multiple agents to coordinate; and a user interface built around agent-to-human collaboration.

Its first released product, an open-source command-line tool called Checkpoints, records the prompts and reasoning behind AI-generated commits alongside the code itself. It currently supports third-party coding tools.

Being remote-first, the company has nearly tripled its headcount to 40 since their launch.

Rameshkumar joins Entire after leading GitHub’s field engineering effort in Asia Pacific, where he served as Field CTO, APAC, directing solutions engineers and cloud solutions architects across the region.

Before GitHub, he built Twilio’s global support delivery centre for cloud-based communications in Bengaluru. He also worked at DigitalOcean and led customer experience at Hevo Data.

His role at Entire, Rameshkumar says, is to bridge developers, enterprise customers and the company’s engineering teams, feeding product feedback directly into the company’s roadmap.

India Is More Than a GTM Market

The early-India bet hinges on the size and growth of the country’s developer base and its weight in open source, rather than a later-stage GTM decision that many startups make.

“India has always been a very exciting developer market,” he tells AIM. Rameshkumar says Entire is on a spree to find the best developers in the world, and the company believes India is the ideal destination. “We [India] have an amazing talent pool that’s second to none.”

According to GitHub, India is now the second-largest developer market, only behind the United States. The country has 27 million developers on the platform and is projected to become GitHub's largest developer community by 2030.

Entire’s India push also places it among a growing cohort of AI startups, including OpenAI, Anthropic, ElevenLabs and Wispr, that have recently expanded their leadership, hiring or go-to-market presence in the country, reflecting India’s growing importance as both a developer ecosystem and enterprise AI market

Building for the AI Agent Era

Entire’s strategy also explains why Rameshkumar and several others left an established platform like GitHub to build something new. They believe the next generation of developer infrastructure cannot simply be layered onto tools built for human-first software development.

Unlike a synchronous assistant that only responds to prompts, an agent can work asynchronously on tasks assigned by a user. That, he argued, makes agents a fundamentally different category, not just a more advanced assistant.

Rameshkumar also argues that version control, issue trackers and pull requests were built around how humans record and hand off work to one another. This breaks down once AI agents start doing large parts of that work themselves.

“With agents being treated as equal citizens in the software teams, infrastructure has to be built with agents at the center of the experience,” he says.

For example, Checkpoints is designed to preserve provenance in an AI-first development workflow, allowing teams to trace how code was created.

On the future roadmap, he says, Entire will provide a unified way to access all the features required throughout their development lifecycle rather than reaching for a new tool at every stage.

Lessons From GitHub

Working with developers at Github, Dohmke and Rameshkumar have seen AI-assisted coding evolve from an emerging technology into daily workflows, giving them an edge over many newer AI coding startups.

Several members of the Entire team, including Rameshkumar, continue to contribute to open-source projects. The company runs an active Discord where the team responds directly to developer feedback instead of through support.

The proximity to developers also underpins how Entire treats the line between consumer tooling and enterprise software, which Rameshkumar sees as largely artificial.

“The developer who turns up to a community meetup on a Saturday evening is the same person who shows up to an enterprise event the following Tuesday, carrying the same feedback into both rooms,” says Rameshkumar.

Rather than separating consumer and enterprise efforts, Entire builds for developers once, then adds governance, analytics, and controls so organisations can scale deployments without sacrificing developer appeal.

The company joins a new class of AI-native software engineering startups, such as Poolside, Factory, and Magic, that are rebuilding the software development stack around AI agents rather than traditional developer workflows.

It will now need to win over developers who have built their preferred toolset and habits to integrate Entire’s products into their stack, a challenging task.

Developers, Rameshkumar says, are creatures of habit, a pattern observed throughout his career across cloud infrastructure, CPaaS, and AI-assisted coding. Moving them from a trusted workflow is harder than building new technology.

Developers now more readily embrace tools that expand their capabilities and act quickly through feedback, issues, or pull requests.

He points to Entire’s own CLI tool as evidence, noting that it has drawn over 4,600 stars on GitHub and an active base of outside contributors within five months. He read that as a sign that developers will cross the habit barrier once a tool visibly solves a problem they already have, rather than being asked to adopt something on faith.

title: Agnikul, Finland’s ICEYE Partner for India’s SAR Satellite and Launch Capability
content:
The partnership aims to combine satellite manufacturing and launch services to support sovereign Earth observation programmes.

What Actually Matters.

Agnikul Cosmos and ICEYE are collaborating to develop SAR satellite capabilities in India.

The partnership aims to create a self-sufficient Earth observation ecosystem without reliance on foreign technology.

Chennai’s space startup, Agnikul Cosmos, and Finland’s ICEYE have signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) to explore building, launching, and operating Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) Earth observation (EO) systems from India.

The agreement seeks to combine ICEYE’s satellite expertise and manufacturing plans in India with Agnikul’s launch capabilities to create an end-to-end sovereign earth observation ecosystem.

The two companies said the collaboration would explore manufacturing SAR satellites in India and launch them on indigenous rockets without relying on foreign launch schedules. They also plan to develop a repeatable satellite-to-launch model that can support long-term deployment programmes and serve international markets.

This announcement comes just after ICEYE partnered with Hyderabad-based Dhruva Space for satellite manufacturing and EO systems.

“Previously, building and launching a satellite system privately in India mostly meant piecing together foreign technology and waiting on timelines that we as a nation did not control,” said Srinath Ravichandran, Co-founder and CEO at Agnikul Cosmos. “This partnership aims to change that equation.”

He further added in a statement that applications such as disaster response, sensitive area monitoring and security are national priorities, and India deserves sovereign capabilities to support them.

The partnership with Agnikul will combine the Indian startup’s responsive launch infrastructure with ICEYE’s SAR technology, which is already deployed across sovereign programmes in Europe. The companies said the model could support applications such as disaster response, security and monitoring of sensitive areas.

The collaboration extends beyond a single satellite mission and seeks to bring manufacturing, launch, and operational capabilities under a single framework.

Moin SPM, Co-founder and COO at Agnikul, said that the partnership extends beyond a single mission. “By combining manufacturing, launch and operational capabilities under one ecosystem, we can create a repeatable model that can support long-term deployment programmes for customers in India and around the world.”

ICEYE said India is becoming an important market as demand for sovereign intelligence capabilities grows worldwide.

“Partnerships built around speed, reliability and long-term execution are becoming increasingly important in these times, and this is what we seek to build with Agnikul," said Rafał Modrzewski, CEO at ICEYE.

For Agnikul, the agreement adds to its portfolio of international commercial partnerships across India, the Middle East and Australia. The company said the partnership aligns with its ambition to expand its role in the global space transportation market.

ICEYE said India could serve as a manufacturing hub for satellites intended for both domestic and international programmes. The company operates a SAR satellite constellation with more than 70 satellites and has delivered sovereign satellite constellations to seven European governments, including Poland, Sweden and Germany.

title: IIT (ISM) Dhanbad, AGI Partner to Build AI Models for Critical Mineral Exploration
content:
The partnership aims to accelerate critical mineral exploration by combining AI with geological, geophysical and GIS data analysis.

What Actually Matters.

IIT (ISM) Dhanbad and AGI are collaborating to develop AI models for critical mineral exploration in India.

The partnership aims to analyse geological and geophysical data to identify high-potential mineral deposits.

IIT (ISM) Dhanbad’s Technology Innovation and Translation Research Park (TTRP), which operates under the aegis of the TEXMiN – Innovation Hub, has signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) with Airborne Geoscience International (AGI) to develop AI and machine learning-based systems for critical mineral exploration in India.

The collaboration aims to build proprietary AI models that can combine and analyse geological, geophysical, geochemical and GIS data to identify and rank high-potential mineral deposits. According to the partners, the technology will help reduce uncertainty in early-stage exploration and speed up the discovery of critical and deep-seated minerals.

The initiative comes as India seeks to strengthen domestic supplies of minerals such as lithium, cobalt, nickel, and rare earth elements, which are essential for batteries, electric vehicles, solar panels and wind turbines. India currently depends heavily on imports for many of these minerals.

The partnership also aligns with the government’s National Critical Mineral Mission (NCMM), launched in 2025 with an outlay of ₹16,300 crore to boost domestic exploration and build self-reliance across the mineral value chain.

Prof Dheeraj Kumar, Deputy Director of IIT (ISM) Dhanbad and Project Director of TEXMiN, said, “The collaboration combines AGI’s advanced airborne geoscience technologies with TEXMiN’s expertise in AI and mineral prospectivity modelling to develop practical tools that can support faster and more informed exploration.”

“India’s geoscience data holds significant untapped value and the partnership will help transform raw survey data into actionable exploration intelligence. AI-driven analysis can play an important role in accelerating discoveries and strengthening India’s resource security,” added Sudipto Mukerji, Managing Director of AGI.

The organisations also plan to create what they describe as India’s first world-class mineral prospectivity database by integrating airborne and ground geophysical surveys with AI-based analysis.

TEXMiN, set up by the Department of Science and Technology at IIT (ISM) Dhanbad, focuses on developing mining technologies using AI, drones, robotics and other digital tools. AGI is India’s first technology aggregator for airborne geoscience exploration and operates across India, Australia, the UK and Canada.

The partners believe the collaboration will help improve exploration efficiency, attract investment in India’s mining sector and contribute to the country’s Aatmanirbhar Bharat, Viksit Bharat and net-zero ambitions.

VOC Port has launched PortGPT, an AI application built on BharatGPT, becoming the first major Indian port with enterprise generative AI.

What Actually Matters.

VOC Port in Tamil Nadu has launched PortGPT, an enterprise AI application built on BharatGPT.

This makes VOC Port the first major Indian port to implement generative AI for internal operations.

The V.O. Chidambaranar (VOC) Port Authority in Thoothukudi, Tamil Nadu, has launched PortGPT, a mobile application that uses generative AI for internal operations. Union Minister for Ports, Shipping and Waterways Sarbananda Sonowal launched the application in New Delhi.

The port authority states that this makes VOC Port the first major port in India to deploy an enterprise generative AI platform through a mobile application.

PortGPT was developed by Sahana Systems Limited, using CoRover's platform, and runs on BharatGPT, a large language model developed in India. The application is intended to give port officials access to information, support internal workflows, and assist decision-making through a mobile interface.

The port authority has linked the launch to the government's Maritime Amrit Kaal Vision 2047, a policy framework for port infrastructure development.

At the same event, the port authority presented data from its first sustainability report. According to the report, renewable energy now offsets close to 94% of the port's energy consumption, and net carbon emissions have fallen by around 45%.

The company also states that carbon intensity per tonne of cargo has dropped by close to 50% over the past four years.

The Minister also released a case study titled The Hydrogen Pivot: Orchestrating the Green Transition at VOC Port, prepared by the Indian Institute of Management Calcutta, which documents the port's shift toward renewable energy use.

Separately, the VOC Port Authority signed a memorandum of understanding with Gati Shakti Vishwavidyalaya. The agreement covers research, logistics education, skill development, and the creation of a Centre of Excellence in Maritime Logistics and Port Management
