The question worth asking is whether Apple just delivered on what it had already promised or built something genuinely new. The two are not the same.

What Actually Matters.

Apple's latest Siri update has been met with early praise but raises questions about its originality.

Users have expressed frustration over Siri's stagnation, leading to legal action against Apple.

On the homepage of Apple Intelligence, Apple calls it “AI for the rest of us”.

Instead, the ‘us’ inadvertently gestures towards a user base that spent years frustrated by a stagnant assistant—and the ones who even sued Apple for the delay, a lawsuit the company eventually settled.

But at this year’s developer conference, Apple finally unveiled a completely overhauled Siri, earning early praise in iOS betas.

While the next iPhone will cost significantly more due to ongoing memory issues, the question is whether that price will at least come with something worth paying for.

With Apple Intelligence and the new Siri, rebranded as Siri AI, Apple is promising a meaningful change in how one billion iPhone users experience the ecosystem.

Today, Siri AI operates at the operating system level, allowing it to access your Messages, Mail, Photos, and on-screen content in real time without switching apps.

It can now execute tasks contextually. Pointing the camera at a plate of food yields a nutritional breakdown, while a single prompt can split a bill via Apple Cash

In the Passwords app, Apple Intelligence can automatically go to individual websites to change and fix insecure passwords on your behalf.

Powering all of this is a dual-model architecture: Apple’s own Foundation Models (AFM), running on-device, paired with Google’s Gemini for more demanding tasks, with the AFM Cloud Pro model, built in collaboration with Google, running on NVIDIA GPUs in Google’s cloud for the heaviest workloads.

But the question worth asking is whether Apple just delivered on what it had already promised or built something genuinely new. The two are not the same.

Siri AI Was Exciting 2 Years Ago, But Not Today

Jesai Tarun, an iOS developer and Founder of Sentient, tells AIM, “I think Siri is exactly what Apple promised. Nothing more, nothing less.”

“What they promised was impressive two years ago. It’s no longer impressive today,” he adds.

He notes that while Siri AI is limited to basic, app-specific tool calls, a truly exciting shift would be agentic AI, like Gemini on Pixel devices, which can autonomously navigate the entire Android OS by interacting directly with the screen.

For such agentic capabilities, Apple doesn’t have such powerful models yet. Apple Photos, for instance, illustrates the shallow limits of the tool-call approach, serving as a prime example of how AI is restricted to only a fraction of an app’s features.

System prompts from the ‘Apple Intelligence Report’ reveal that the voice-editing demo shown at WWDC—such as adjusting brightness and rotation—accounts for virtually all of Siri’s capabilities.

Because a model faces a hard ceiling on how many tool calls it can process at once, developers can only expose a handful of basic commands, leaving the vast majority of deeper app functions completely out of reach.

This same constraint shapes Siri’s on-device architecture. While the local model handles simple tasks like summaries or basic actions, any query requiring meaningful reasoning is offloaded to Apple’s Private Cloud Compute (PCC) servers.

If that server-side model needs personal context, such as a text message about a shopping list, it requests the data from the iPhone.

The local device then runs a retrieval search, extracts the text snippet, and sends it back to the cloud. Ultimately, the on-device model isn’t doing the reasoning but functions purely as a retrieval engine.

While Apple Intelligence uses on-device models for basic writing tools, advanced local processing is restricted to high-tier hardware.

On 12GB RAM devices like the iPhone 17 Pro, Apple deploys a multimodal LLM specifically to improve dictation and speech-to-text, allowing it to process audio directly and infer meaning from unclear speech. Beyond this, however, its local capabilities remain thin.

Nowhere Close to Gemini on the Pixel Series

The deeper bottleneck is Apple’s dependency on Google for foundational model capabilities.

Lacking a web crawler like Google’s or an automated synthetic data loop like Anthropic’s, Apple pays Google an estimated $1 billion annually to use Gemini as a ‘teacher’ model.

Apple distils Gemini’s outputs to train its own leaner, proprietary models, which run securely within Apple’s Private Cloud Compute infrastructure.

Yet, because the ceiling of Apple’s AI is bound to the specific Gemini version it last distilled, Apple remains trapped in a cycle of retraining whenever Google upgrades its models.

Since March, Gemini on the Pixel 10 has been able to autonomously navigate app interfaces to complete multi-step tasks like ordering food or booking a ride.

It operates on two layers: AppFunctions, which lets developers explicitly expose app actions, and a UI automation fallback, allowing Gemini to read accessibility trees and click through apps that have zero formal integration work.

This raises an obvious question: since both Apple and Google rely on Gemini-derived models, why can Android do this while Siri cannot?

The bottleneck isn’t the model but the operating system.

Apple’s App Intents framework requires developers to explicitly pre-declare every single action Siri is permitted to take. Without an intent, Siri has no fallback.

Furthermore, iOS’s strict sandboxing architecture prevents apps from accessing data or processes outside their own container, making Android-style screen automation structurally impossible unless Apple opens up the OS layer.

Google, on the other hand, allows Gemini on the Pixel 10 to actively parse accessibility trees and overlay controls directly over third-party apps.

Apple is likely to avoid doing this because granting an AI agent systemic permission to ‘read’ and control everything on a user’s screen creates massive security risks, like data scraping or accidental authorisation, that fundamentally clash with iOS’s core privacy ethos,

Siri can only trigger pre-defined functions. It cannot read a screen and start tapping, and no amount of model training closes that architectural gap.

It is also worth noting that while both ecosystems point to Gemini, they are not utilising it in the same way.

Google has direct, native access to the most high-end, unconstrained versions of its frontier models. Apple, by contrast, does not run Gemini out of the box. Instead, it uses a process called model distillation—essentially using the massive reasoning outputs of Google’s raw models as a ‘teacher’ to train Apple’s own smaller, highly specialised Apple Foundation Models (AFM).

While this allows Apple’s models to run natively and privately on Apple Silicon, a distilled student model structurally lacks the deep, raw emergent reasoning capabilities of the massive frontier model it was cloned from.

Enterprise Agents to Follow Siri AI’s Architecture?

Having said that, experts across the ecosystem have continued to praise Apple’s orchestration process, despite the limitations of features.

Max Weinbach, an analyst from Creative Strategies, shared in a post on X, “I can near guarantee you enterprise agents will follow Apple’s Siri architecture. It’s the perfect mix of on-device and cloud.”

Based on official documentation, Apple Intelligence prioritises privacy by defaulting to on-device processing. When a user makes a request, the local hardware handles the initial processing to determine whether the task can be completed locally, keeping personal context entirely on the device.

For complex reasoning tasks that exceed local capabilities, the device routes a structured request to Apple’s PCC.

To protect this data in transit, your device scrambles the payload so it can only be unlocked by a certified Apple server.

Since the cloud model must temporarily read the data to fulfil your request, true end-to-end encryption is not possible. Instead, Apple relies on a highly restricted server design that forces the system to handle the data securely without ever saving it.

PCC is designed for stateless computation: the personal data contained in the request is used exclusively to fulfil that specific prompt and is completely erased after the response is returned, preventing any data retention, logging, or unauthorised access.

Why Siri AI Won’t Change Your Life

While Apple has provided a framework called App Intents to bridge the gap between Siri and third-party apps, the system places an immense burden entirely on the developer.

In practice, Apple possesses no native ability to integrate with external applications on its own. Instead, developers are forced to do an exhaustive amount of manual heavy lifting to integrate with the Siri AI index.

According to Tarun, making App Intents function properly requires an overwhelming amount of backend work.

If an app contains dozens of features, a developer cannot simply let the AI figure them out; they must sit down and explicitly expose and map every single function for Siri to use.

“I have to re-architect my back end, spend so much time thinking about what feature I should expose to Siri, and every time I make some changes to the app, I have to then make sure to do that again,” he says.

“It is basically a crazy amount of work.”

Besides, is it in app developers’ best interests to integrate their features to work with Siri AI?

For one, we have the big tech apps. The return on investment for someone like Meta in integrating WhatsApp with Siri is basically about improving Siri. Would the company want to make Siri a better assistant so that users would prefer using it over Meta’s AI in WhatsApp?

“Apple is not gonna be able to integrate Siri AI heavily with Gmail and Google. It’s in Google’s best interest not to make Siri AI fancy, because they have Gemini inside Gmail,” says Tarun.

This dynamic was already proven with Apple’s Vision Pro, which lacked native Netflix or YouTube apps at launch because competitors had no incentive to enrich Apple’s ecosystem while building competing hardware platforms of their own.

Besides, even if app developers without competing AI products may still prefer users to spend time inside their apps rather than automate actions using Siri, since automation reduces engagement. “It’s in everyone’s best interest to just get you into their app to see advertisements,” says Tarun.

However, this defensive stance from developers may ultimately be forced to shift as market dynamics evolve.

Avi Greengart, Founder and Lead Analyst at Techsponential, tells AIM that while many apps rely on advertising, that business model is already under pressure from Apple’s privacy initiatives, which allow users to prevent apps from tracking their usage data.

Developers will inevitably have to find other ways to generate income, including charging directly for their apps and services.

Greengart notes that ecosystem stakeholders still have a brief window to adapt because Siri’s current agentic capabilities are restricted, and the broader consumer market has yet to fully upgrade its hardware.

“They have some time; Siri AI has limited agentic capabilities today, and most of the iOS base doesn’t support Apple’s best on-device models today,” he explains.

While he expects several holdouts to resist, clinging to the old app-centric paradigm, he argues that economic reality will eventually force their hand.

Put simply, if a user asks Siri to book a ride or order groceries, Siri will naturally route that business to the apps it can actually communicate with, leaving non-integrated competitors effectively invisible.

“Once Siri pushes more business to an app or service that supports the Intents API over alternatives that it can’t access, that will force competitors to support agentic APIs as well or lose out on both direct and indirect engagement,” Greengart warns.

“In my tests of the Apple Intelligence beta, Siri will soon do most of what today’s mainstream consumers actually want to do with AI,” says Greengart.

Will Siri Pose a Threat to ChatGPT?

Does this mean Siri will pose a threat to the nearly 68 million daily active users on ChatGPT who are on the iOS platform?

For one, Greengart says that users who are already paying for an AI service on Google, OpenAI or Anthropic may not replace it with Siri for any task. Besides, the broader ecosystem comes into effect.

“Even if you have an iPhone, if you’re a heavy Gmail, Workspace, and Maps user, it may still make sense to stick with Google directly for AI interactions.”

Tarun believes Apple’s window to position Siri as a legitimate threat to OpenAI closed the moment it failed to launch immediately after ChatGPT’s debut. By now, consumer habits have ossified, and ‘ChatGPT’ has become completely synonymous with AI queries. Breaking that ingrained behaviour and persuading users to proactively choose Siri is a massive uphill battle.

Google faced the exact same headwind. Despite a rapid rollout, standalone Gemini adoption lagged behind OpenAI.

Its true scale today relies on ‘invisible’ distribution, embedded silently inside Gmail, Docs, and Search Overviews.

“On average, everyone will just continue using ChatGPT,” says Tarun.

title: Samsung, SK Hynix Anchor South Korea’s $576 Bn AI and Chip Strategy to Assert Dominance
content:
Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, along with suppliers, will invest $518.3 billion to build two new semiconductor fabrication plants.

What Actually Matters.

South Korea plans to invest over $576 billion in its semiconductor and AI strategy to enhance its global competitiveness.

Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix will spearhead the initiative with $518.3 billion allocated for new fabrication plants.

South Korea has announced a semiconductor and AI strategy backed by more than $576 billion in planned investments, as President Lee Jae Myung sought to strengthen the country’s position in the global chip race and promote industrial growth beyond the Seoul metropolitan region.

The initiative will be led by Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, which together with suppliers will invest 800 trillion won ($518.3 billion) to establish two new semiconductor fabrication plants each in the country’s southwest, Industry Minister Kim Jung-kwan said.

The government also expects another 81 trillion won ($52 billion) to be invested in a semiconductor packaging cluster in the Chungcheong region.

Speaking alongside the heads of Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, Lee described the strategy as a ‘great leap forward’ built around what he called the ‘triple axis’ of semiconductors, physical AI and data centres.

“We must secure the core elements of AI faster than any other country,” the president said in a televised address.

Lee said the southwest was chosen because of its untapped electricity capacity, while existing semiconductor hubs have little room for further expansion.

“To meet the rapidly increasing demand for semiconductors, we need to quickly complete the production hubs that are currently under construction,” Lee said.

Industry Minister Kim also said South Korea plans to double its DRAM production within five years by accelerating the construction of fabrication plants in the Seoul metropolitan area, targeting completion by the mid-2030s.

The investment comes as demand for high-bandwidth memory (HBM) chips continues to rise, driven by AI infrastructure. Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix together produce about two-thirds of the world's memory chips, while SK Hynix is NVIDIA's largest HBM supplier.

Counterpoint Research estimates SK Hynix held a 58% share of the global HBM market in the first quarter of 2026, with Samsung accounting for another 21%, giving South Korean companies nearly 80% of the market.

NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang recently visited South Korea, where he signed an AI partnership with SK Hynix to further expand HBM production, saying global demand continues to outpace supply.

With the $576 billion package, South Korea is positioning itself as a stable chips superpower, buoying Samsung and SK Hynix up the semiconductor supply chain.

title: Micromax, Phison JV to Invest ₹1,000 Cr in India Memory Chip Manufacturing: Report
content:
Maruti Suzuki onboarded the five startups from its incubation programme to improve battery recycling, customer engagement and AI-driven operations.

What Actually Matters.

Maruti Suzuki has partnered with five startups to enhance operational efficiency and sustainability in its business.

The selected startups focus on lithium-ion battery recycling, AI-driven customer engagement, and procurement automation.

Maruti Suzuki India has partnered with five startups to co-create technology solutions aimed at improving operational efficiency, customer experience and sustainability across its business operations.

The startups MiniMines, Easework AI, Sarvam AI, Siftly, and CodeMate AI were selected from the fifth cohort of the Maruti Suzuki Incubation Program (MSIP), conducted in partnership with IIM Bangalore’s startup incubator, NSRCEL.

The collaborations span a range of use cases, from lithium-ion battery recycling and procurement automation to generative AI-powered customer engagement and software development. According to the company, the startups will work closely with Maruti Suzuki teams to address specific business challenges and deploy practical solutions.

MiniMines will focus on environmentally friendly recycling of end-of-life lithium-ion batteries and extraction of valuable materials. Easework AI will deploy agentic AI to automate procurement workflows related to indirect consumables, while Sarvam AI will build multilingual generative AI agents to improve customer interactions across touchpoints.

Siftly will enhance brand visibility through generative AI, and CodeMate AI will accelerate software application development for business processes.

Commenting on the partnerships, Hisashi Takeuchi, Managing Director and CEO of Maruti Suzuki India, said in a statement, “At Maruti Suzuki, we have been actively working with startups to co-create innovative and practical solutions to address real business challenges. We are delighted to collaborate with five more startups.”

The automaker has launched several innovative programmes to advance the automobile and mobility sectors. The Accelerator programme, launched in January 2019, collaborates with growth-stage startups to advance cutting-edge technological development. The Incubation Program, launched in August 2020 with NSRCEL, supports early-stage mobility startups by providing mentorship and access to IIM Bangalore.

The Mobility Challenge, launched in June 2021, helps mature startups showcase their innovations. The Nurture programme, introduced in 2023 with IIM Calcutta Innovation Park, focuses on pre-incubation for idea-stage startups. Lastly, the FundRays initiative, launched in September 2025, aims to enhance investment readiness for alumni startups from these programs in partnership with ISB Hyderabad.

Since 2019, the company screened around 7,400 startups, engaged with more than 250, and onboarded 38 as business partners.

content:
Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong said the objective is “not to suppress usage” but to build infrastructure capable of supporting exponential growth in AI workloads while keeping costs under control.

What Actually Matters.

Coinbase has significantly reduced AI spending by nearly half through optimised access to large language models.

The company has shifted to cheaper default models and automated routing to manage costs effectively.

Coinbase has reduced its internal AI spending by nearly half after overhauling how employees access and use large language models, replacing usage limits with cheaper default models, automated routing, and aggressive caching.

CEO Brian Armstrong, in a post on X, said the company is experimenting with making open-weight models such as GLM 5.2 and Kimi 2.7 the default through its internal LLM gateway, while still allowing engineers to choose any model they consider appropriate for a task.

Armstrong said the company has “cut our AI spend nearly in half, while our token usage continues to grow.” He added that the objective is “not to suppress usage” but to build infrastructure capable of supporting exponential growth in AI workloads while keeping costs under control.

The company found that 91% of employees never reached their AI usage caps, leading it to abandon tighter limits in favour of cheaper default models.

Engineers remain free to select frontier models when needed, while code reviews deliberately use multiple models to cross-check one another’s outputs.

A second change is automated model routing. Coinbase’s internal AI harnesses preprocessed prompts and direct requests to the most cost-effective model based on the task, pricing, and cache availability.

Armstrong said that planning workloads may justify a frontier model, whereas execution tasks often do not. “Ultimately, humans shouldn’t be choosing models—AI can automate this task,” he wrote.

Mark Landgrebe, a senior software engineer at the company, said on X that the company routes AI requests through an internally developed gateway that provides a single endpoint for dozens of models while applying cross-provider failover, prompt redaction, logging and cost controls before requests reach external AI providers.

He added that the routing system also factors in cache state, keeping conversations on the same model while cached context remains valid and only reconsidering model selection after the cache's time-to-live expires.

The company also significantly increased cache utilisation. “For example, our cache hit rate went from 5% to 60% in LibreChat once properly implemented,” said Armstrong, based on a result enabling repeated requests to reuse cached responses rather than generating fresh tokens.

Landgrebe said cache hits require identical prompt prefixes, prompting Coinbase to maintain long, stable prefixes across conversations so only newly generated tokens are processed at full inference cost.

Coinbase has also instructed employees to keep context windows lean by starting new sessions for different tasks, limiting file context, disconnecting unused tools and avoiding unnecessary token consumption.

Landgrebe also revealed that third-party AI coding tools are routed through Coinbase’s internal AI gateway.

He said default models for those tools are set through a lightweight client-side launcher, while the company is working to extend gateway-based automatic model routing into more customisable coding harnesses.

Instead of enforcing hard spending limits, Coinbase now emphasises visibility into AI usage. Employees can use any model and consume as many tokens as required, but spending is transparent, and higher AI usage is expected to correspond with greater business impact.

This follows Coinbase’s broader push to become an AI-native company. In May, the company cut about 700 jobs, or roughly 14% of its workforce, as Armstrong said advances in AI were enabling smaller, more productive teams and a flatter organisational structure.

Enterprises are now increasingly scrutinising AI inference costs amid a broader backlash against “tokenmaxxing”, the practice of maximising AI token usage without clear productivity gains.

Recently, Uber reportedly introduced monthly spending caps of $1,500 per AI coding tool after exhausting its annual AI coding budget within four months. The company said the limits apply to agentic coding tools such as Cursor and Claude Code, while executives have questioned whether higher token consumption translates into proportionally better products.

Reports also suggest that other companies, including Amazon, Meta, and Walmart, have also begun steering employees toward cheaper AI models or introducing tighter governance around AI usage as inference costs climb.

title: Dating Apps are Hardcoded to Match Looks. Wavelength's AI Wants to Fix That
content:
As the AI race intensifies, Musk says Grok 4.5 is now in private beta, bringing a more powerful foundation model and an ambitious release roadmap for xAI.

What Actually Matters.

Elon Musk announced Grok 4.5 has entered private beta testing at SpaceX and Tesla, showing promising early performance.

The model is built on a new 1.5-trillion-parameter V9 foundation, enhanced with training data from the AI coding platform Cursor.

Elon Musk has announced that Grok 4.5, the next version of xAI’s chatbot, has entered private beta testing at SpaceX and Tesla. According to Musk, early internal evaluations suggest the model performs close to, and in some cases exceeds, Anthropic’s Claude Opus, although these claims have not been independently verified.

In a series of posts on X, Musk said Grok 4.5 is built on xAI’s new 1.5-trillion-parameter V9 foundation model and has received additional training using data from the AI coding platform Cursor. He added that reinforcement learning continues to improve the model and praised the teams involved in its development.

Grok 4.5, based on our 1.5T V9 foundation model, with Cursor data added in supplemental training, is now in private beta at SpaceX & Tesla. Early evals show performance close to, perhaps exceeding Opus.

RL is continuing to significantly improve the model, and the Grok Build…

— Elon Musk (@elonmusk) June 28, 2026

Musk also outlined an ambitious roadmap, saying, “The new AI models trained from scratch will be released every month for the rest of the year, reflecting a much faster development cycle than previous versions.”

Clarifying his earlier comments, Musk said he was not suggesting that the V9 foundation model would dramatically outperform every competing AI system. Instead, he described it as “a solid workhorse in the same league as Opus”, with future improvements expected through continuous model training and optimisation.

He also said Grok 4.5 would represent a significant upgrade over Grok 4.3, which was based on the older 500-billion-parameter V8 model trained in December. According to Musk, the V8 model has several fundamental limitations that the new version aims to address.

Beyond the model itself, Musk said xAI is accelerating development by improving its software infrastructure. He revealed that engineers from SpaceX’s Starlink and Starship programmes have shifted much of their focus to the company’s AI efforts, helping speed up model development.

The latest announcement comes as competition in artificial intelligence continues to intensify, with companies including OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and xAI racing to build more capable large language models. If xAI delivers on its plan to release new models every month, the company could significantly increase the pace of competition in the AI industry over the coming months.

Rejecting traditional swipe-based algorithms, Wavelength uses conversational AI to match people based on personality and behavioural insights.

What Actually Matters.

Wavelength's AI matches users based on personality and behavioural insights, moving away from traditional swipe-based methods.

Many GenZ users experience fatigue from existing dating apps, with a significant percentage feeling overwhelmed by the process.

The burnout on dating apps is real. Many users, especially GenZs, are fatigued by endless swapping that takes a considerable emotional toll. The fatigue is as high as among 79% of GenZ users, according to a Forbes Health survey.

Many dating apps are now using artificial intelligence to compress swiping. Tinder is using AI to personalise curation on the basis of user interests and behaviour. Hinge offers a conversation assistant, while Bumble’s AI learns users values and relationship goals to make their case to others.

However, Jayanth Emmadi, Co-founder and CTO of dating app Wavelength, believes those modeld reward attractiveness more than compatibility. “Most platforms match people based on how many likes they receive,” he tells AIM.

Wavelength is also trying to rethink online dating and moving away from swipe-based matchmaking, but not with a square focus on looks. Co-founded by CEO Ishaan Gupta, COO Vinit Sarode, and Emmadi, the platform offers an AI companion called Wave that gets to know users through conversations before suggesting potential matches. The idea is to spend time understanding a user's personality, relationship goals, and preferences through natural interactions.

"We wanted people to feel like they were talking to someone who genuinely understands them, not just another chatbot," says Emmadi.

Unlike traditional dating platforms, where users immediately begin browsing profiles, Wavelength asks users to interact with Wave first.

However, early on, the founders realised that simply creating another chatbot would not solve the problem.

“Building a companion that truly understands you and remembers you was one of our biggest challenges. If a person tells Wave about someone they went on a date with and the next day it completely forgets that conversation, the person will feel irritated because it’s supposed to understand them.” Emmadi notes.

To overcome this, the team designed Wave with long-term conversational memory, enabling it to retain prior interactions and continuously improve its understanding of each user.

But the challenge extended beyond conversations. Most dating platforms rely on variations of the Elo rating system, originally designed to rank chess players. Users who receive more likes are generally shown to similarly popular profiles.

Changing that meant developing an entirely new matchmaking algorithm that combines conversational insights with behavioural patterns rather than popularity scores.

“We understand you first and recommend matches based on that understanding- not just whether people are liking you,” he adds.

Before launching publicly, Bengaluru-based Wavelength, founded in September last year, spent months in beta.

The founders built two WhatsApp communities, one for men and the other for women, with a total of nearly 6,000 members. Users regularly shared feedback, while the founders also conducted one-on-one calls to better understand their experiences.

Since launching publicly in September last year, Wavelength has grown to around 12,000 users in India. Its app has a 4.0 rating on Google Play Store. The founders say that nearly 95–96% of its user acquisition has come organically through social media content and word-of-mouth referrals.

Those conversations revealed something unexpected.

“The first thing we realised was that people start trusting Wave when they feel understood. Sometimes Wave gives users an insight about themselves that they already knew deep down but had never consciously recognised. That’s when trust begins,” says Jayanth.

“Instead of overwhelming users with hundreds of profiles, Wave attempts to simplify decision-making by understanding individuals first,” he explains.

One of the team’s biggest surprises came from analysing more than 800 successful matches during beta testing. Contrary to the common perception that dating apps favour conventionally attractive users, many successful matches involved people with compelling personalities or unique life experiences.

“These were regular people who had some crazy spark in their lives. Maybe they had travelled to 26 countries, built something meaningful professionally, or were simply emotionally available,” Jayanth notes.

Rather than highlighting appearance, Wave introduces users through stories.

“Someone who climbed Mount Everest alone may hesitate to write that achievement on a dating profile for fear of appearing boastful. But Wave can naturally explain what that accomplishment says about the person’s resilience and character,” he affirms.

For the founders, helping personalities become visible beyond photographs is one of the platform’s biggest advantages.

Interestingly, many users continued interacting with Wave even after finding partners.

One feature, called Debrief, allows users to discuss dates, seek advice after difficult conversations, or simply reflect on their experiences. According to Jayanth, some beta users even replaced general-purpose AI assistants with Wave for relationship-related conversations.

“Some of our friends who found partners through Wavelength still use Wave, not because they want more matches but because it has become like a mutual friend who understands both people,” he explains.

According to findings published by researchers from the Federal University of ABC, Brazil, AI-powered systems have the potential to move dating platforms beyond quantity-driven interactions and towards more meaningful compatibility.

For the founders, that suggests AI could eventually play a larger role than simply introducing people.

Like any young product, Wavelength has encountered several design challenges.

One early feature automatically expired matches after 24 hours—a decision intended to encourage quicker responses. However, Jayanth acknowledges that many users felt frustrated after missing potential connections simply because they had not opened the app.

“Following user feedback, the company extended the window to 48 hours and is now exploring more flexible systems where timers begin only after users view recommendations,” he adds.

While the company is currently focused on product development and user growth, its long-term business model will centre on premium subscriptions, with paid features planned as the platform matures.

The startup currently operates with a team of seven people. In December last year, it raised $500,000 in pre-seed funding from Antler after participating in the accelerator’s cohort. It is currently refine the product before it looks for growth capital.

Another challenge lies in understanding rejection.

“People usually say there was ‘no spark’. They don’t want to sound rude, so it’s difficult to collect meaningful feedback. But without that feedback, it’s also difficult to improve recommendations”, he explains.

The team is also working on improving how Wave introduces potential matches. “Instead of simply informing users that someone is ‘99% compatible,’ the AI attempts to explain why that individual might genuinely be worth getting to know,” he notes.

While Wavelength began as a matchmaking platform, its founders now envision something much broader. Jayanth believes AI could eventually help people maintain all kinds of relationships, not only romantic ones.

“There will be an AI for your professional life. I think there will also be one for your social life,” he confirms.

He imagines Wave helping users reconnect with old friends, strengthen family relationships, suggest activities for couples, or even mediate conflicts when needed.

As artificial intelligence increasingly moves beyond productivity tools into everyday human experiences, startups like Wavelength are asking a new question, not whether AI can recommend better matches but whether it can help people feel understood before helping them fall in love.

Emergent and Delhigence AI power custom software for Madhya Pradesh Premier League, bringing AI-driven efficiency to cricket administration.

The Madhya Pradesh Premier League has partnered with Emergent and Delhigence AI to modernise cricket administration through custom software.

The new platform aims to streamline finance, operations, and league management, enhancing visibility and efficiency.

The Madhya Pradesh Premier League (MPL) has partnered with AI software creation platform Emergent and technology firm Delhigence AI to modernise cricket administration, deploying a custom-built platform to streamline finance, operations, and league management processes.

Built by Delhigence AI on Emergent’s platform, the software is already being used by MPL’s finance and administration teams to manage key workflows with greater visibility, structure and speed. The project is being led by Mahanaaryaman Scindia, President of the Madhya Pradesh Cricket Association (MPCA), as part of a broader effort to strengthen the administrative backbone of cricket in the state. What began as a finance and operations platform for the league is expected to evolve into a wider technology stack supporting governance, monitoring, and administrative workflows across cricketing activities managed by the MPCA.

Speaking about the initiative, Scindia said in a statement, “AI gives us an opportunity to rethink how sports administration works, not in theory, but in the everyday systems that help a league run better.”

Mukund Jha, Co-founder and CEO of Emergent, added, “Earlier, building software for those workflows required long timelines, large teams, and heavy development cycles. With Emergent, teams can translate real operational problems into working software much faster. What MPL and Delhigence AI are doing is a glimpse of how AI can modernise not just companies, but institutions.”

The deployment reflects a wider trend of sporting organisations exploring AI beyond performance analytics and fan engagement, with increasing focus on governance, operations, and administration.

title: Why Agentic AI Could Become Healthcare’s Intelligent Operating Layer
content:
DSpark is a new speculative decoding framework that accelerates DeepSeek V4 Flash and Pro by improving draft token acceptance and dynamically adjusting verification during inference.

What Actually Matters.

DeepSeek V4 introduces a speculative decoding framework that significantly accelerates language model inference.

The new system enhances text generation speed by up to 85% while maintaining throughput.

DeepSeek has introduced a new speculative decoding framework designed to accelerate large language model inference by combining semi-autoregressive token generation with confidence-based verification scheduling.

According to the company, the system increases per-user text-generation speed by 60–85% compared with its previous production baseline while maintaining the same aggregate throughput.

The researchers said the method also “enables performance tiers that were previously unattainable” under strict interactivity constraints.

Speculative decoding speeds up inference by using a lightweight draft model that proposes multiple tokens before a larger target model verifies them.

Existing parallel draft models can generate long token blocks quickly, but often suffer declining acceptance rates because each token is predicted independently. To address this, DeepSeek said the new framework “unifies high-throughput parallel generation with adaptive, load-aware verification.”

It is achieved by pairing a parallel backbone with a lightweight sequential module and dynamically adjusting the number of draft tokens verified based on predicted acceptance probabilities and system load.

On offline benchmarks covering mathematical reasoning, code generation, and chat workloads, DeepSeek said the framework consistently outperformed both autoregressive and parallel speculative decoding methods.

Across Qwen3 4B, 8B and 14B models, it increased the average accepted draft length by 26.7% to 30.9% over Eagle3 and by 16.3% to 18.4% over DFlash, allowing more tokens to be accepted in each verification round.

DeepSeek also reported production deployment results from its DeepSeek-V4 serving system under live user traffic.

Compared with the earlier MTP-1 production baseline, the new approach increased per-user generation speeds by 60–85% on DeepSeek-V4-Flash and 57–78% on DeepSeek-V4-Pro at matched throughput levels.

The company said it “mitigates verification overhead to maintain robust throughput” under high-concurrency workloads, allowing the serving system to sustain performance at stricter latency targets.

DeepSeek is open-sourcing checkpoints for the new decoding framework for DeepSeek-V4-Flash (preview) and DeepSeek-V4-Pro (preview), alongside DeepSpec, a training repository that supports Eagle3, DFlash, and the new method for speculative decoding research.

DeepSeek has also open-sourced the DSpark implementation through its DeepSpec GitHub repository and released DSpark-enabled DeepSeek-V4 Flash and Pro checkpoints on Hugging Face, allowing developers to reproduce the framework and deploy the speculative decoding module with the preview models.

The release comes days after DeepSeek completed its first external fundraising round, raising more than 50 billion yuan ($7.4 billion) at a valuation exceeding $50 billion, according to multiple reports.

Founder Liang Wenfeng reportedly contributed about $3 billion to the round, with investors including Tencent, battery maker CATL and China's National Artificial Intelligence Industry Investment Fund.

The AI giant will use the new capital to fund AI infrastructure, product development, and conduct a major hiring push, with DeepSeek planning to at least double the size of every department as it expands beyond its research-focused roots.

title: NeevCloud Launches Agentic Studio to Run AI Agents in Secure Sandbox Environments
content:
Agentic Studio is built to help enterprises deploy AI agents securely while retaining control over where their data and workloads are executed.

What Actually Matters.

NeevCloud has launched Agentic Studio, enabling secure deployment of AI agents in isolated environments.

The platform allows enterprises to test and scale AI workflows without risking exposure to production systems.

Bengaluru-based cloud provider NeevCloud has launched Agentic Studio, a managed sandbox environment for running AI agents and code execution workloads in isolated compute environments, as enterprises look to deploy agentic AI while keeping data and workloads within India’s borders.

The company said the platform allows organisations to deploy, test and scale AI-driven workflows without exposing production systems.

Agentic Studio provisions isolated compute environments on demand, enabling enterprises to run AI agents, scripts and multi-step workflows without managing the underlying infrastructure.

“The industry has spent two years making agents smarter. The unsolved problem is giving them somewhere safe to act. Agentic Studio is designed to bridge that gap,” said Vijayakumar Nadar, Chief AI Officer of NeevCloud.

According to the company, enterprises can create a new sandbox in seconds, choose a compute template, configure resources and execute AI workloads in isolated environments. The platform also supports filesystem snapshots, pause, restore and fork capabilities, allowing teams to reproduce and manage stateful workflows.

NeevCloud said the platform addresses growing demand for sovereign AI infrastructure as governments and regulated industries pay closer attention to where AI workloads are executed and under which jurisdiction they operate.

“Sovereign AI is not just about where data is stored, it is about where intelligence acts,” said Narendra Sen, Founder and CEO of NeevCloud. “Agentic Studio ensures that when an AI agent retrieves a document, executes a financial reconciliation, or automates a customer support workflow, every action happens within a controlled, auditable environment on Indian soil. That is what enterprise-grade sovereign AI looks like in practice.”

The platform supports multi-agent orchestration by assigning separate compute environments to planning, execution, validation and reporting agents. It also includes browser and VNC templates for web automation, along with on-demand compute resources.

NeevCloud said Agentic Studio can be used across customer support, software development, financial operations, document processing, research, education, DevOps and IT automation.

It also supports coding workflows such as running tests, inspecting repositories, automating bug triage and validating code changes in isolated environments.

The company said the platform is intended for organisations in sectors including banking, financial services, healthcare and government that require greater control over where AI workloads execute and how data is handled.

NeevCloud currently operates two data centres, one in Raipur and another in Indore. Earlier this year, the company partnered with space startup AgniKul Cosmos to develop what it described as India's first orbital AI data centre platform. The proof-of-concept mission is expected before the end of 2026, with commercial operations targeted for 2027.

content:
Tech Mahindra will roll out Perplexity Enterprise Pro across its sales and customer-facing teams.

What Actually Matters.

Tech Mahindra is partnering with Perplexity to enhance sales operations through the deployment of the Enterprise Pro platform.

The initiative aims to improve productivity and customer engagement for sales and customer-facing teams.

Tech Mahindra has partnered with AI startup Perplexity to deploy its Enterprise Pro platform across the IT services firm's sales organisation to improve productivity and customer engagement.

The deployment will cover sales and customer-facing teams, including customer partners and senior sales leaders, enabling them to access real-time business, industry and technology insights.

The platform is expected to help employees research customer priorities, identify emerging business opportunities, and tailor customer interactions.

The move is part of Tech Mahindra's broader strategy to embed artificial intelligence across enterprise functions as IT services firms look to use AI internally to improve sales effectiveness and operational efficiency, alongside delivering AI-led transformation projects for clients.

“AI is transforming how enterprises engage with customers, make decisions, and create value. By integrating Perplexity Enterprise Pro into our sales processes, we are empowering our teams with trusted, real-time intelligence that helps them better understand customer priorities, engage with greater context, and deliver more impactful solutions,” Mohit Joshi, CEO and Managing Director, Tech Mahindra, said in a statement.

According to the company, Perplexity Enterprise Pro’s AI-powered search and answer capabilities will enable teams to quickly access information, reduce research time, improve productivity, and enhance the quality of customer conversations throughout the sales lifecycle.

“Tech Mahindra brings deep enterprise expertise and a strong delivery presence across the world. Putting Perplexity Enterprise Pro in their sales teams' hands gives them fast, source-backed answers when it matters most to clients," Aravind Srinivas, CEO and Co-founder, Perplexity, said.

The platform allows organisations to train, deploy and improve open models while retaining control over their data, intellectual property and AI systems.

What Actually Matters.

Palantir and NVIDIA have launched a joint initiative to deploy AI models in sovereign environments for US government agencies.

The platform allows organisations to train and enhance open models while maintaining control over their data and intellectual property.

Palantir Technologies has announced an initiative with NVIDIA to develop an AI engine that enables the deployment of NVIDIA’s Nemotron open models in sovereign environments, targeting US government agencies and operators of critical infrastructure.

The joint offering combines NVIDIA’s AI platform, including its compute infrastructure, AI ecosystem and Nemotron open models, with Palantir’s Artificial Intelligence Platform (AIP), Foundry, Ontology and Apollo.

The companies said the platform allows organisations to train, deploy and improve open models while retaining control over their data, intellectual property and AI systems.

The platform includes capabilities such as explicit data authorisation, customer-specific isolation, secure perimeter enforcement, data portability, right to erasure and audit logs.

Customers will also be able to own and improve models tailored to their operational requirements by using telemetry, trace data and post-training feedback generated within their environments.

The companies said the offering enables US government agencies to deploy base and customised Nemotron models in classified, air-gapped and other sensitive environments. It also supports context engineering to optimise prompts and workflows, model engineering to modify model weights using proprietary data, and enterprise deployment through NVIDIA AI Enterprise software and NVIDIA NIM microservices.

“Combining Palantir infrastructure with NVIDIA’s AI and Nemotron models will allow the U.S. government to unleash the full power of LLMs while removing the underlying security risks and rational concerns around proprietary insights migrating into the weights of closed models,” said Alex Karp, Co-founder and CEO of Palantir. “Moreover, many of our US clients are already using these models, including multiple supporting critical US infrastructure — both private and public — and this will facilitate their radical expansion.”

NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang said open-source AI is becoming increasingly important for national security and public safety.

“Open source AI is foundational to national security, public safety and U.S. technology leadership,” Huang said. “Palantir's Nemotron-powered intelligent engine shows how open models can strengthen America’s leadership in AI — giving U.S. government agencies a secure, customisable and fully controlled foundation to build mission-critical AI systems in support of national security.”

The announcement builds on the companies’ previously announced Sovereign AI Operating System Reference Architecture, which is intended to help governments deploy and manage AI systems within their own infrastructure.

title: Micromax, Phison JV to Invest ₹1,000 Cr in India Memory Chip Manufacturing: Report
content:
MiPhi will use the investment to expand its existing manufacturing facility in Greater Noida, Uttar Pradesh

What Actually Matters.

Micromax and Phison's joint venture, MiPhi, plans to invest ₹1,000 crore to expand manufacturing in India.

The investment aims to increase production of memory products for AI infrastructure and data centres.

Micromax and Taiwan-based Phison’s memory semiconductor joint venture, MiPhi, plans to invest around ₹1,000 crore to expand its manufacturing operations in India, according to a report by Moneycontrol.

The company is ramping up production to meet rising demand for memory products used in AI infrastructure, data centres, enterprises, and automobiles.

It expects to cross ₹ 1,000 crore in revenue this fiscal year and sees rapid growth over the next two to three years, backed by a growing order pipeline from domestic and international customers.

“We are looking at around Rs 1,000 crore of capital expenditure to significantly expand our manufacturing footprint in India,” MiPhi co-founder Rahul Sharma told the media outlet.

MiPhi will use the investment to expand its existing manufacturing facility in Greater Noida, Uttar Pradesh. Sharma said MiPhi began operations in January 2025, but commercial growth accelerated only after customer validation cycles were completed.

“Growth has accelerated now because product validation takes time. We are moving into triple-digit growth this year alone,” he said.

The expansion comes as India steps up efforts to build a domestic semiconductor ecosystem while global demand for memory chips continues to rise alongside AI deployments and data centre investments.

MiPhi manufactures enterprise solid-state drives (SSDs) and embedded memory products. Its enterprise SSDs are supplied to cloud service providers, data centres, system integrators, and OEMs manufacturing in India, while its embedded memory products are used in automobiles, smartphones, televisions, routers and other connected devices.

The company also expects exports to become a major growth driver. According to Sharma, it has started receiving commercial orders from both India and overseas.

“If execution continues as planned and the order pipeline converts, we believe the company has the potential to become a unicorn in the next two to three years,” he told Moneycontrol.

Beyond manufacturing, MiPhi plans to strengthen semiconductor design capabilities in India. Under the partnership, Phison will transfer controller technologies, research expertise, and intellectual property to Indian engineering teams to help build local capabilities in firmware, controller design, and enterprise storage technologies.

“We provide the most cutting-edge products, technical support and intellectual property. You build the technology locally. This creates a much stronger business because you own the technology and the customer channels. It’s not just about distribution,” Borris Chang, Executive Director at MiPhi and Chief of Staff at Phison, told the outlet.

The company is also expanding into AI software through its AI Adaptive Memory software layer, which is designed to improve memory utilisation for AI workloads, reducing dependence on high-end GPUs and lowering infrastructure costs.

MiPhi has begun deploying the technology with select educational institutions and is in discussions with additional universities as it looks to broaden access to AI computing infrastructure.

The company is betting on continued demand for memory solutions across AI infrastructure, enterprise storage, automotive electronics, and data centres as it expands its presence in both domestic and international markets.

Capgemini is driving Bentley Motors' digital transformation to enhance luxury vehicle production and operational efficiency.

The collaboration focuses on leveraging AI and data capabilities to improve accountability and decision-making processes.

Capgemini is collaborating with Bentley Motors to accelerate the luxury carmaker's digital transformation, leveraging data and AI to support Bentley's Beyond100+ strategy and modernise operations across its manufacturing and enterprise ecosystem.

As Bentley's digital transformation lead, Capgemini will provide the digital infrastructure and systems integration needed to modernise manufacturing technology systems and streamline back-office operations at Bentley's Dream Factory in Crewe.

"Bentley Motors represents the pinnacle of British quality and manufacturing prowess, and we're delighted to be supporting them to transform its digital operations. The brand's legacy and ambitious vision offer exciting opportunities to drive innovation through data and AI, enabled by Capgemini's deep expertise in integrating and modernising complex enterprise and manufacturing systems at scale," Rob Pears, UK Head of Manufacturing, Automotive and Life Sciences at Capgemini, said in a statement.

Bentley views the partnership as a critical step in advancing its long-term digital ambitions as the company continues its transformation toward a more connected and intelligent manufacturing ecosystem.

title: ₹40,000-Crore PCB Imports to Be Replaced by Domestic Manufacturing as Jewar Emerges as Electronics Hub: Ashwini Vaishnaw
content:
Jewar is poised to emerge as one of India's leading hubs for electronics and semiconductor manufacturing in the coming years

What Actually Matters.

Jewar is set to become a key hub for electronics and semiconductor manufacturing in India.

Recent investments in electronics projects will boost domestic production of advanced Printed Circuit Boards.

Union Minister for Electronics and Information Technology Ashwini Vaishnaw and UP Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath recently laid the foundation stones for two major electronics manufacturing projects worth ₹6,750 crore at the Yamuna Expressway Industrial Development Authority in Jewar. This marks a significant step towards strengthening India’s electronics manufacturing ecosystem and reducing dependence on imports.

The projects, led by Amber Enterprises India and Ascent Circuits, are expected to accelerate domestic production of advanced Printed Circuit Boards (PCBs), strengthen India’s electronics value chain, and further the Centre’s Make in India, Aatmanirbhar Bharat, and Viksit Bharat initiatives.

Addressing the gathering, Vaishnaw said Jewar is emerging as one of India’s most important electronics manufacturing destinations.

“Jewar is poised to emerge as one of India’s leading hubs for electronics and semiconductor manufacturing in the coming years,” he said.

Explaining the significance of the projects, the minister noted that the new facilities will manufacture advanced multi-layer PCBs—critical components used in modern electronic devices.

“PCBs worth nearly ₹40,000 crore, which were earlier imported into the country, will now be manufactured domestically, with Jewar emerging as a major production centre,” Vaishnaw said.

He added that after establishing a semiconductor ecosystem, Uttar Pradesh is now well-positioned to become a major electronics manufacturing hub.

“Several new electronics manufacturing projects would be established in Uttar Pradesh, enabling the State to emerge as one of the country's leading electronics and semiconductor manufacturing hubs,” he said, adding that the investments would strengthen India’s technological self-reliance and expand domestic manufacturing across the electronics value chain.

Highlighting the role of infrastructure, Vaishnaw said the proposed Delhi–Lucknow–Varanasi–Patna–Siliguri Bullet Train corridor would significantly improve connectivity and industrial development.

“The proposed Delhi–Lucknow–Varanasi–Patna–Siliguri Bullet Train corridor will redefine connectivity across Uttar Pradesh and act as a catalyst for industrial and economic growth,” he said.

According to the minister, world-class transport infrastructure combined with a robust electronics manufacturing ecosystem will further enhance Uttar Pradesh’s attractiveness as an investment destination.

During the event, CM Adityanath also laid the foundation stone for the first industrial unit within the Electronics Manufacturing Cluster (EMC) being developed in YEIDA’s Sector-10.

The cluster is being developed across 206 acres at an estimated investment of ₹417 crore, including ₹144 crore in central government assistance. The facility is expected to attract additional investments in high-value electronics manufacturing while strengthening Uttar Pradesh's position as one of India’s leading electronics production hubs.

The projects complement the Centre’s broader semiconductor strategy under the India Semiconductor Mission.

As of June, the government has approved 12 semiconductor manufacturing projects with a cumulative investment pipeline of approximately ₹1.64 lakh crore, including one semiconductor fabrication unit, two compound semiconductor fabrication units, and nine semiconductor packaging facilities.

The government is also expanding India’s chip design ecosystem through the Design Linked Incentive (DLI) Scheme. So far, 24 design projects are being supported, 105 companies have received access to advanced Electronic Design Automation (EDA) tools, and 23 chip tape-outs have been completed across multiple technology nodes.

Announced in the Union Budget 2026–27, India Semiconductor Mission 2.0 aims to further strengthen the domestic ecosystem by promoting semiconductor equipment, materials, indigenous intellectual property, resilient supply chains, and advanced manufacturing capabilities, reinforcing India’s ambition to become a trusted global semiconductor and electronics manufacturing hub.

title: OpenAI Launches GPT-5.6 as US Government Clears Anthropic’s Mythos 5 Return
content:
Both companies are phasing access to their latest AI models while working with Washington on a framework for deploying increasingly capable systems.

What Actually Matters.

OpenAI has launched GPT-5.6, featuring three models: Sol, Terra, and Luna, with varying capabilities and pricing.

The initial rollout of GPT-5.6 will be limited to a select group of trusted partners, following discussions with the US government.

OpenAI has launched GPT-5.6, a new family of AI models comprising Sol, Terra, and Luna, and said it will begin with a limited preview for a select group of trusted partners before a broader rollout in the coming weeks.

The company said GPT-5.6 Sol is its flagship model, Terra is a lower-cost model with performance comparable to GPT-5.5, and Luna is its fastest and most affordable offering.

“Terra has competitive performance to GPT‑5.5 while being 2x cheaper and Luna brings strong capability at our lowest cost,” the company said in a statement.

The models will initially be available via the API and Codex, with access to ChatGPT planned later.

During the preview, pricing starts at $5 per million input tokens and $30 per million output tokens for Sol, $2.50 and $15 for Terra, and $1 and $6 for Luna. The company also said GPT-5.6 Sol will launch on Cerebras in July with speeds of up to 750 tokens per second for select customers.

OpenAI said the limited rollout follows discussions with the US government. “As part of our ongoing engagement with the US government, we previewed our plans and the models’ capabilities ahead of today’s launch,” the company said. “At their request, we are starting with a limited preview for a small group of trusted partners whose participation has been shared with the government, before releasing more broadly.”

The company added that it does not want such a process to become standard. “We don’t believe this kind of government access process should become the long-term default. It keeps the best tools from users, developers, enterprises, cyber defenders, and global partners who need them,” it said.

“We are taking this short-term step because we believe it is the strongest path to broader availability in the coming weeks, while we work with the Administration to develop the cyber Executive Order framework and a repeatable process for future model releases,” OpenAI added.

Anthropic Gets Green Light

Following OpenAI’s announcement, Anthropic on June 27 said it has started restoring access to its Claude Mythos 5 cybersecurity model for a limited group of US organisations after working with the US government.

“The government notified us that Mythos 5, our strongest cybersecurity model, can be redeployed to a set of US organisations that operate and defend critical infrastructure,” the company wrote on X.

The company added that it is continuing to work with the government to expand access to Mythos 5 and make Fable 5 available for general use again.

The announcement follows restrictions imposed earlier this month that limited access to the two models. Anthropic did not disclose which organisations would regain access or provide a timeline for when broader access to Mythos 5 or public availability of Fable 5 could resume.

What GPT-5.6 Can Do

OpenAI said GPT-5.6 introduces a new ‘max reasoning effort’ mode and an ‘ultra mode’ that uses subagents to tackle complex tasks.

According to the company, GPT-5.6 Sol achieves state-of-the-art performance on TerminalBench 2.1 for coding workflows, with GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra scoring 91.9% to outperform Mythos 5 and Fable 5. OpenAI also said GPT-5.6 improved results on biology and cybersecurity benchmarks compared with GPT-5.5.

Moreover, OpenAI said that GPT-5.6 Sol delivered performance comparable to that of Mythos Preview on ExploitBench, using roughly one-third of the output tokens.

The company also highlighted changes to its safety measures, saying GPT-5.6 ships with its ‘most robust safeguards to date.’ OpenAI said it strengthened protections against higher-risk cyber activity through layered safeguards, automated red-teaming, account-level monitoring and real-time misuse detection.

“GPT-5.6 Sol is better at helping people find and fix vulnerabilities than reliably carrying out end-to-end attacks,” OpenAI said.

It added that the model remains below the Cyber Critical risk threshold defined in its Preparedness Framework, but introduced additional safeguards because of its improved capabilities.

To improve the system’s resilience, OpenAI said it devoted more than 700,000 A100-equivalent GPU hours to automated red-teaming to identify jailbreaks and other weaknesses before release.

title: OpenAI Appoints Uber Veteran Prabhjeet Singh as India Managing Director
content:
He will oversee consumer growth, enterprise partnerships, regulatory engagement, and operations across the country.

What Actually Matters.

Prabhjeet Singh has been appointed as OpenAI's Managing Director for India, starting in September.

Singh will focus on consumer growth, enterprise partnerships, and regulatory engagement in India.

OpenAI has appointed former Uber India and South Asia President Prabhjeet Singh as its Managing Director for India.

Singh will join the company in September and report to Kiran Mani, the former JioStar executive who was appointed Managing Director for Asia Pacific earlier this year.

The company said Singh will be OpenAI’s most senior leader in India, responsible for consumer growth, enterprise adoption, strategic partnerships, regulatory engagement and operations.

“India is one of OpenAI’s top priority markets, and Prabhjeet’s appointment reflects our continued investment in the country,” the company said. “His focus will include building partnerships and supporting India’s wider AI ecosystem, while helping more consumers, businesses, institutions and government bodies benefit from AI.”

India is OpenAI’s second-largest market by ChatGPT users after the United States, with around 100 million weekly active users, according to CEO Sam Altman.

Before joining OpenAI, Singh led Uber’s mobility business across India, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh. He spent 11 years at the company and played a key role in expanding its operations across the region before announcing his resignation on June 26.

An alumnus of IIT Kharagpur and IIM Ahmedabad, Singh brings experience in scaling consumer technology businesses in India at a time when OpenAI is increasing its focus on enterprise adoption and ecosystem partnerships in the country.

SpaceX went public with an incredibly thin public float, with only a tiny fraction of its total shares available to trade. When the buyers rushed in, the floor fell out.

What Actually Matters.

SpaceX's IPO featured a very limited public float, leading to significant volatility in share prices.

A swift sell-off followed a peak valuation, resulting in a rapid loss of nearly $1 trillion in market capitalisation.

Elon Musk’s blockbuster SpaceX IPO debuted at $135 per share, and within two trading sessions, demand drove the price above $200.

At its peak valuation, the company—whose empire now spans reusable rockets, AI coding tools, and the controversial social media platform X—was hit by a brutal sell-off that wiped nearly $1 trillion off its market capitalisation in just a few days. This decline represents one of the fastest capital contractions in market history.

However, investors are still debating what triggered the sell-off. Some blame SpaceX's announcement of its first-ever investment-grade bond sale, which aims to raise $25 billion to refinance an earlier bridge loan. Instead of creating new shares, which would shrink the value of what current investors own, SpaceX is essentially taking out a massive, lower-interest corporate loan to pay off its older debts.

Campbell Harvey, a Canadian economist and a professor of finance at Duke University, isn’t surprised that the company is going to the bond market. “It is well documented that after an IPO, on average, the ratings for borrowing improve,” he tells AIM.

How IPO Improved SpaceX’s Rating

SpaceX’s balance sheets will soon be public, with its second-quarter earnings right around the corner. This has prompted the major credit agencies to open the door to institutional investors. Moody’s assigned SpaceX a first-time investment-grade Baa1 rating, while Fitch issued a BBB+ and S&P Global stepped in with a BBB.

“This means that post IPO, the interest rate that they would pay on corporate borrowing decreases,” adds Harvey.

Numerous academic studies have demonstrated that an IPO establishes what economists call ‘value certainty’. By subjecting its balance sheet to rigorous public disclosure, a newly public firm slashes information asymmetry for lenders, allowing it to migrate away from expensive private debt and unlock highly favourable institutional credit terms.

Beyond restructuring older debt, Harvey also observes that looking at other companies across the broader economy makes it clear that a major capital expenditure push is underway.

SpaceX is among many firms turning to the bond market to raise the immense capital required to build out massive computing capacity. AI infrastructure companies, including hyperscalers, data centre operators, and semiconductor firms, raised roughly $159 billion in debt this year already.

Across multiple bond offerings since late 2025, Amazon has raised roughly $57 billion from debt markets, while Alphabet raised over $52 billion to fund its physical infrastructure footprint, even taking the rare step of issuing a highly secure 100-year ‘century bond’ to fund its multi-decade AI computing timeline.

Meta too tapped the debt market with a massive $30 billion investment-grade bond initiative, choosing to lock in institutional debt to power its immense GPU clusters rather than relying strictly on operational cash flow or stock issuance.

Following its consolidation of xAI and its recent blockbuster acquisition of the AI coding platform Cursor, SpaceX's financial footprint has fundamentally shifted from a traditional aerospace operation to an AI infrastructure behemoth.

SpaceX’s AI capex hit a staggering $7.7 billion in just the first quarter of 2026 alone, positioning its annualised AI spending at over $30 billion.

To feed this insatiable appetite for AI clusters like its massive Colossus megadata centre, SpaceX is tapping the public bond market alongside other tech titans.

Moreover, the $25 billion bond deal isn’t actually piling new debt onto SpaceX's back.

“The bond is a refinance of the bridge loan, which removes an uncertainty about when that might happen and won’t add to the debt burden as the bridge is being paid off,” notes Nicolas Owens, equity analyst at financial services firm Morningstar.

Instead, the bond is a direct swap. SpaceX is using this multi-part bond sale to permanently wipe out the temporary $20 billion ‘bridge’ loan it took out earlier to clean up high-interest debt from its xAI and X mergers.

By trading a short-term, ticking-clock loan for long-term corporate bonds, the company completely eliminates the risk of a sudden cash crunch when the old loan comes due in 2027, all while keeping its total debt balance unchanged.

However, other experts suggest that borrowing such a massive sum right after hitting peak valuation signals deep underlying pressure on cash flow. They point out that for a venture as capital-intensive as SpaceX, the spectacular post-IPO momentum has quickly evaporated, and the brutal costs of running its empire are now hitting hard.

The Double-Edged Sword Called Thin Float

Besides, SpaceX went public with an incredibly thin public float, meaning only a tiny fraction of its total shares were actually available to trade on the open market.

When a generation-defining company with a massive cult following hits the public market, the sheer volume of buy orders creates an extreme demand squeeze.

“I think the thin float, especially for such a high-profile company, has a big effect on the share price volatility, probably both on the upside and the downside,” says Owens.

The lack of available shares was a massive double-edged sword, supercharging the initial rally when buyers flooded in, but completely removing the floor during the sell-off. Analysts consistently cite this exact mechanic when evaluating historic, low-float IPOs that experienced massive boom-and-bust cycles.

A few years ago, Rivian and Arm Holdings both experienced sharp post-listing rallies as limited public floats amplified buying pressure, prompting analysts to argue that scarcity, rather than fundamentals alone, was driving valuations. As additional shares became available and investor enthusiasm cooled, those stocks experienced significantly greater volatility than companies with larger public floats.

In the case of SpaceX, its valuation has become untethered from traditional financial metrics, trading at a price-to-sales ratio near 104x—a figure nearly double that of the most expensive stocks in the S&P 500.

While the market has priced the company at over $2 trillion, analysts at Morningstar have placed its fair value significantly lower, at approximately $780 billion.

Cursor Deal is Pocket Change

Having said that, there is also a debate about whether the recent all-stock acquisition of Cursor may have triggered the downfall.

Days after its IPO, SpaceX announced that it would acquire AI coding startup Cursor for $60 billion, based on a previous agreement that stated SpaceX held the right to either purchase the company outright for that price or pay $10 billion for a joint partnership to integrate compute and AI-training resources.

However, analysts doubt whether this deterred the selloff. “The $60 billion acquisition is not surprising, it was expected. Furthermore, for a company that is worth over $2 trillion, $60 billion is a rounding error,” says Harvey.

“I don’t think that SpaceX’s recent stock declines are a reaction to the Cursor acquisition; more so, they seem related to overall market sentiment,” Owens concurs.

Besides, there are concerns that the acquisition, or the capital-heavy investments into compute infrastructure, will mark the major cash flow that Starlink provides to cross-subsidise the other initiatives.

Starlink, currently the company’s only profitable segment, hit 10.3 million subscribers by the end of Q1 2026. While the service remains a financial powerhouse, generating $1.19 billion in operating income for that quarter alone, its profitability is facing pressure as the business expands into price-sensitive global markets.

As of Q1 2026, Starlink’s average revenue per user (ARPU) has declined to $66, down from $86 a year earlier, signalling that the company is trading higher margins for aggressive subscriber volume to feed its broader AI ambitions.

In the long run, however, Harvey believes that it is wise for the company to protect this cash flow, despite its other ventures. “I don't think that SpaceX will do anything to compromise the viability of Starlink.”

Sinking Together

In recent days, the overall market sentiment has been shaped by a broad reassessment of the AI trade and heightened macroeconomic uncertainty. Investors have increasingly questioned whether the hundreds of billions of dollars being poured into AI infrastructure can ultimately generate returns that justify current valuations, even as soaring DRAM and HBM memory prices make AI deployments more expensive.

At the same time, lingering uncertainty following the Iran conflict and disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz has stoked fears that higher energy prices could feed into inflation, raising concerns that the US Federal Reserve may have to keep interest rates higher for longer or even tighten policy further. Although oil prices have since eased following signs of a truce and the gradual resumption of tanker traffic through the strait, the geopolitical uncertainty has kept investors on tenterhooks.

Investors are now busy locking in gains and rebalancing portfolios ahead of quarter-end, triggering a broad sell-off across AI and semiconductor stocks.

Alphabet suffered its worst single-day decline in more than a year following high-profile AI talent departures, NVIDIA slid more than 4%, while Micron Technology fell 13% in its worst trading session in over a year.

The rout spread globally, with Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix each dropping more than 12%, dragging South Korea's KOSPI sharply lower as investors rotated out of some of the market's biggest AI winners.

For SpaceX, a rebound may be on the anvil as Starlink’s revenue pipeline remains intact. However, it may not escape volatility just yet.
