title: Anthropic Selects Indian IT Firm Hexaware as Authorised Reseller for Claude AI Models on Amazon Bedrock
content:
The new facility will house an executive briefing centre to host customer engagements, product demonstrations, and strategic partner collaborations.

What Actually Matters.

Pegasystems has opened a new office in Bengaluru with an investment exceeding ₹60 crore.

The facility includes an Executive Briefing Centre for customer engagements and product demonstrations.

Pegasystems, an AI-powered platform for enterprise transformation and commonly known as Pega, has inaugurated a new office at EcoWorld Tech Park in Bengaluru with an investment of more than ₹60 crore, expanding its presence in India and establishing a new Executive Briefing Centre (EBC) for client engagement, product demonstrations, and executive collaboration.

The facility, which is 1.5x larger than Pega’s previous Bengaluru office, will serve as a hub for engineering, client engagement, and business development across the Asia-Pacific region.

The inauguration was attended by Karnataka’s Minister for Home, Information Technology & Biotechnology and e-Governance, Priyank M Kharge, along with Pega Founder and CEO Alan Trefler and senior company executives.

At the centre of the new office is the Bengaluru EBC, which will host executive meetings, partner collaborations, product demonstrations, solution showcases, roadmap discussions, advisory sessions, and customer events. Pega said the investment is intended to strengthen engagement with enterprise customers and partners in the region.

The office has more than 350 seats and over 35 meeting and conference rooms across connected floors. It also includes collaboration areas, technology-enabled meeting rooms, wellness spaces, and employee amenities. The facility is certified under LEED, WELL, and IGBC Platinum standards.

“Karnataka warmly welcomes Pegasystems’expanded presence in Bengaluru,” said Kharge during the opening. “This investment is a strong endorsement of the state’s position as a global technology hub and reflects the confidence that leading enterprises place in Karnataka’s talent and ecosystem.”

Dr Manjula N, IAS, Secretary to Government, Department of Electronics, Information Technology, Biotechnology, and Science & Technology, and Chairperson of the BWSSB, Government of Karnataka, said Pega’s investment would strengthen Bengaluru's position as a centre for engineering and enterprise innovation.

“Karnataka's growth as a global technology hub is being shaped by a strong talent base, forward-looking policy, and institutions that help innovation move from idea to implementation,” she said. “Pegasystems’ investment in Bengaluru adds to this momentum by strengthening the city's role as a centre for advanced engineering, enterprise innovation, and strategic collaboration.”

“India is central to Pega’s global growth strategy, and this expansion reflects the confidence we have in the talent and capabilities here,” Trefler said. “The new Bengaluru Executive Briefing Centre is a significant addition, designed to offer our clients a premier destination to experience Pega’s innovation first-hand and deepen the partnerships that are critical to our shared success.”

Deepak Visweswaraiah, Senior Vice President and Managing Director, Pega India, said the new office would support client demonstrations and executive discussions while providing capacity for the company’s next phase of growth.

title: Gnani.ai Launches New Speech-to-Text Model, Claims to Outperform Global Rivals
content:
Gnani.ai said Prisma v2.5 delivers lower word error rates for rural Hindi and noisy Dravidian speech than competing models.

What Actually Matters.

Gnani.ai has launched Prisma v2.5, a speech-to-text model touted for its high accuracy in Indian languages.

The model reportedly outperforms global rivals in accuracy for rural Hindi and noisy Dravidian speech environments.

Indian voice AI startup Gnani.ai has launched Prisma v2.5, a speech-to-text model that the company claims delivers the highest speech recognition accuracy for Indian languages across multiple independent benchmarks.

The release confirms AIM’s earlier exclusive report that Gnani.ai was developing a new speech-to-text model for enterprise use, among five new AI models.

The company said Prisma v2.5 is available through its API and is targeting enterprise deployments across sectors, including banking, financial services, insurance, healthcare, retail, and telecom.

The Bengaluru-based startup said the model ranked first in 27 of 48 evaluations and led in eight of nine Indian languages tested on datasets including Kathbath, Kathbath Noisy, Gramvaani, CommonVoice, FLEURS, IndicTTS, MUCS 2021, and the IITM Evaluation Set.

According to the company, Prisma v2.5 achieved 15% lower word error rates (WER) for rural Hindi dialects and 18% lower WER in noisy Dravidian language environments compared with competing global and Indic speech recognition models.

It achieved the lowest WER on the Gramvaani benchmark, which captures conversational speech from semi-urban and rural Hindi speakers, recording a 22% WER compared to 27.5% for ElevenLabs, 26.4% for Microsoft, 23.4% for Sarvam, and 34% for Deepgram, per the company.

The model was trained on 14 million hours of proprietary speech data spanning 12 Indian languages, which Gnani.ai claimed is 14 times more than any competing model has publicly disclosed.

The company said the model supports word-level code-switching between language pairs such as Hindi-English and Tamil-English without requiring language tagging. It also includes native support for GSM and VoIP audio codecs, enabling transcription of low-quality telephony audio commonly used in tier-2 and tier-3 cities.

Gnani.ai added that post-training optimisations doubled inference throughput compared with the previous version without reducing accuracy.

“Most ASR models are built for ideal studio conditions. Indian calls happen over compressed network lines, in at least two languages inside a single sentence, in accents no studio corpus has ever captured. Gnani Prisma v2.5 is built for that reality,” said Ganesh Gopalan, CEO and Co-founder of Gnani.ai, in a statement.

The company said the model addresses transcription errors involving numerals, alphanumeric strings, named entities, and short utterances, which are common in enterprise call centre applications.

Neysa CEO Sharad Sanghi says inference—not model training—is emerging as the defining challenge for organisations looking to scale AI.

What Actually Matters.

Inference is becoming the key challenge for organisations aiming to scale AI, according to Neysa CEO Sharad Sanghi.

Neysa is poised to leverage India's growing data centre capacity, planning to deploy 20,000 GPUs for AI workloads.

Access to GPUs has emerged as a critical factor for companies building and deploying AI systems. According to the Indian government, the country's data centre capacity increased from about 375 MW in 2020 to around 1.5 GW in 2025, and is projected to reach roughly 8 GW by 2030.

Indian neo cloud provider Neysa is looking to capitalise on this growth. Its Velocis platform offers GPU-as-a-service, allowing businesses to train, fine-tune, and deploy AI workloads. Following its $1.2 billion funding round earlier this year and its entry into the unicorn club, the company is heavily investing in AI infrastructure across India, with a planned deployment of 20,000 GPUs.

“We’re aggressively scaling our silicon inventory across leading GPU platforms, and ensuring that we cater equally to the enterprise segment that deserves a world-class AI-PaaS offering,” CEO Sharad Sanghi tells AIM in an exclusive interview.

Sanghi co-founded Neysa in 2023 with Anindya Das. Before launching the company, he founded data centre services provider Netmagic Solutions, which was acquired by NTT Communications in 2012.

The company expects NVIDIA’s latest Blackwell GPUs, including the B300s, to lead the AI infrastructure push.

“Our Blackwells are already on the way. The IndiaAI Mission is a source of utilisation for us as well. We need those GPUs as quickly as possible to meet a lot of those requirements,” Karan Kirpalani, Chief Product Officer at Neysa, tells AIM.

Kirpalani also reveals that an IIT campus has placed an order for more than 200 servers. He adds that several AI-native startups, including Shodh AI, Navana.ai, Smallest.ai, GreyLabs AI, Protecto, and Kogo AI, are building and deploying their models on Neysa’s Velocis Cloud.

Neysa’s expansion comes amid a renewed interest in accelerating India's AI infrastructure. Companies including Yotta, Adani, RMZ, and AirTrunk are committing billions of dollars to AI-ready data centres, while the IndiaAI Mission is making domestic GPU capacity available to startups, researchers, and public institutions.

Recently, Amazon increased its AI infrastructure commitments in India and will now invest an additional $13 billion over the next four years to expand its cloud services. Meanwhile, Google is establishing a large-scale AI hub in Vishakhapatnam in collaboration with AdaniConneX and Nxtra by Airtel, and Microsoft has pledged $17.5 billion through 2029 to expand its AI and cloud footprint.

Frontier Models or Applications?

The debate over whether India should invest in building frontier foundation models or focus on applications has intensified in recent months. Sanghi rejects the idea that the two approaches are mutually exclusive.

“I believe that framing India’s strategy as a choice between building frontier foundation models or building applications is an analytical error,” he says.

In Sanghi’s view, strong technology ecosystems require progress at both layers.

“Frontier models matter because they expand what becomes possible. Applications matter because they turn that capability into economic value and real-world utility. The ecosystem needs both,” he explains.

Sanghi affirms Neysa’s execution layer looks to serve all kinds of AI deployments, whether it’s a team is training a massive, localised multilingual model like BharatGen’s Param 2, or deploying specialised agentic workflows.

Inference is Key

Sanghi says inference—not model training—is emerging as the defining challenge for organisations looking to scale AI.

“Training a model is a finite capital expense, but inference is a continuous operational expenditure that dictates the ultimate viability of an enterprise AI product,” he says. “As applications graduate from isolated pilots to core business workflows, inference becomes a recurring dependency layer.”

He adds that enterprises are no longer evaluating infrastructure solely on compute power. Instead, factors such as token economics, latency, data residency, and operational reliability are becoming critical.

Neysa’s Velocis AI platform, launched in 2024, addresses these challenges by combining orchestration, model serving, and observability into a unified AI platform. Sanghi says the company has already deployed optimised inference environments for workloads exceeding 140 billion tokens per month, helping enterprises lower infrastructure costs while maintaining production performance.

The platform is built for latency-sensitive workloads including voice AI, enterprise copilots, search, workflow automation, speech-to-text, text-to-speech, and OCR. It also aims to allay concerns around overseas data routing and data sovereignty by keeping inference and enterprise data within India.

Neysa has also recently partnered with AI inference startup Pipeshift to launch a production-grade, real-time inference platform deployed entirely within India. The offering combines Pipeshift’s managed inference platform with Velocis AI cloud, allowing enterprises to deploy open-source models such as Llama, DeepSeek, Mistral, Gemma, Qwen, and GPT-OSS in dedicated single-tenant environments through OpenAI-compatible APIs.

Challenging Hyperscalers

Despite the rise of Indian AI startups, most firms continue to rely on cloud providers such as AWS, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud. Sanghi believes AI workloads require a different infrastructure approach from the traditional cloud model.

“Traditional hyperscalers built highly successful platforms optimised for the CPU-driven web and application hosting era,” he says. “Production-scale AI introduces high-density architectural demands that legacy, virtualised environments were simply not designed to handle.”

To compete with global cloud providers, Sanghi argues that AI-focused infrastructure companies must offer both performance and operational advantages. In one case, Neysa delivered nearly 90% cost savings compared with proprietary models running on hyperscale clouds, Kirpalani says.

Through its Velocis Cloud platform, Neysa also provides dedicated bare-metal environments. “We provide dedicated, single-tenant bare-metal environments that eliminate the shared rate limits, noisy-neighbour bottlenecks, and cross-region routing overheads common in legacy clouds,” Sanghi says.

Sanghi also highlights the need to simplify AI operations for developers and data science teams. “By offering a seamless, single pane of glass experience that allows them to spin up GPUs as bare metal, virtual machines, or containers and publish models into inference with granular visibility and control, we’re expanding the frontier of choice.”

He believes the winner in the AI infrastructure race will be the platform that can deliver predictable economics and operational reliability.

title: After Anthropic Restrictions, US Govt Asks OpenAI to Delay GPT-5.6 Rollout: Report
content:
OpenAI is also considering postponing its initial public offering (IPO) until 2027.

What Actually Matters.

The US government has requested OpenAI to delay the release of GPT-5.6 due to national security concerns.

OpenAI plans to release GPT-5.6 in phases, with limited access granted on a case-by-case basis.

The US government has asked OpenAI to delay the broad release of its upcoming AI model, GPT-5.6, citing national security concerns, according to The Information. According to the proposed plan, the model would be released in phases, with the US government approving early users on a case-by-case basis.

The report said OpenAI CEO Sam Altman informed employees that GPT-5.6 would first be made available to a limited group of partners rather than launching widely. During this preview period, access will be granted on a customer-by-customer basis with government approval.

According to The Information, the request came from the White House’s Office of the National Cyber Director and the Office of Science and Technology Policy, as the US government increases its scrutiny of frontier AI models and their potential security implications.

AIM reached out to OpenAI for a comment, but hasn’t received a response at the time of publication.

The arrangement gives the US government an unprecedented role in determining early access to a frontier AI model before its wider launch. While the Donald Trump administration has largely promoted rapid AI development, it has also introduced measures to review the capabilities of the most advanced systems before they become widely available.

The report added that OpenAI believes the limited preview is the quickest path toward an eventual broader launch. By working with the government during the initial deployment, the company hopes to address security concerns before expanding access.

The development follows heightened scrutiny over the risks posed by increasingly capable AI systems, including concerns about cybersecurity, misuse by hostile actors, and the possibility that advanced models could expose sensitive capabilities if released without adequate safeguards.

Recently, the Trump administration took a tougher stance toward Anthropic’s frontier models. It recently issued an export-control directive banning all foreign nationals worldwide from accessing Dario Amodei-led company's most advanced AI models, Fable 5 and Mythos 5, citing national security concerns.

OpenAI is also considering postponing its initial public offering (IPO) until 2027 as executives debate whether current market conditions justify going public before achieving a higher valuation, according to a report by The New York Times.

The ChatGPT maker confidentially filed paperwork for a US IPO earlier this month and initially targeted a public listing later this year. However, advisers have reportedly urged the company to wait as technology stocks remain volatile and investor appetite for large offerings has weakened.

OpenAI is seeking a valuation of as much as $1 trillion, and CEO Sam Altman has resisted suggestions to lower that target in exchange for a faster public debut. The company is now reportedly weighing whether to wait until market conditions improve rather than accept a lower valuation.

According to OutSystems, the future of enterprise AI lies in agentic systems engineering, where applications, AI agents, enterprise data and security controls operate within a unified framework.

What Actually Matters.

AI is transforming software development, enabling tasks to be completed much faster than before.

A governance challenge is emerging as organisations adopt numerous AI-generated applications and agents.

Artificial intelligence is rapidly changing how software is built inside enterprises. Tasks that once took teams of developers weeks to complete can now be generated in hours with AI-assisted coding tools. However, as companies race to adopt these technologies, a new challenge is emerging revolving around how organisations govern the growing number of AI-generated applications and how agents are being deployed across their systems.

According to Gartner, nearly 90% of enterprise software engineers are expected to use AI-assisted coding tools within the next 12 to 18 months. More than 40% of code today is already generated with the help of AI, while close to 60% of developers actively use AI tools in their workflows.

For Vivek Ganesh, Country Head and Regional Vice President, India at OutSystems, the question is no longer whether enterprises will use AI for software development. The bigger concern is what happens when hundreds of developers begin building AI-powered applications and agents simultaneously.

“The problem that CIOs are trying to solve today is no longer application development. It is agent sprawl,” said Ganesh during the MachineCon GCC Summit 2026.

From Application Sprawl to Agent Sprawl

Over the past two decades, enterprises have gone through several waves of software development from traditional coding to rapid application development, low-code platforms and no-code tools.

AI-assisted development represents the latest evolution.

However, while AI is making software creation easier, it is also creating a governance challenge. Ganesh warned that if hundreds of developers across a GCC begin creating AI agents every day, organisations could quickly lose visibility and control over what is being deployed.

“Imagine if 500 or 600 developers start building agents every single day and deploying them across the enterprise. The amount of agent sprawl that would happen is unimaginable,” he added.

The concern is particularly relevant for large enterprises operating across multiple geographies, where security, compliance and data governance requirements remain critical.

Why Most AI Projects Never Reach Production

Despite growing enthusiasm around generative AI and agentic systems, many organisations continue to struggle with moving AI initiatives beyond pilot stages.

Ganesh pointed to a commonly cited industry statistic suggesting that nearly 90% to 95% of AI projects fail to reach production environments.

According to him, the issue is often not the AI model itself but the lack of enterprise-grade governance frameworks.

“The reason many AI projects get stuck at the proof-of-concept stage is that the tools being used cannot easily go into deployment. Security guardrails and compliance requirements are often missing,” he explained.

As a result, CIOs are increasingly looking for ways to establish common orchestration layers that can manage application development, AI agents, security controls and enterprise data from a single platform.

AI is Reshaping Business Processes

Beyond software development, enterprises are also using AI to transform operational workflows.

Ganesh shared the example of a banking organisation that sought to reduce customer onboarding timelines. What previously took three to four weeks was first reduced to one week, then to just four hours. The bank is now aiming to bring that process down to 40 minutes.

Such improvements are being driven through a combination of AI-powered automation, business workflow optimisation and human oversight.

Rather than replacing employees entirely, organisations are increasingly adopting a ‘human-in-the-loop’ approach where AI agents handle repetitive tasks while humans remain responsible for validation and decision-making.

“If 30% to 40% of a business process can be automated through agents while maintaining human oversight, that is the ideal situation,” he noted.

The Rise of Agentic Systems Engineering

As enterprises expand their AI initiatives, a new concept known as agentic systems engineering is gaining attention.

The idea centres on creating environments in which applications, AI agents, security controls and enterprise data can work together within a unified framework.

This approach becomes particularly important for legacy modernisation efforts. Many organisations continue to rely on decades-old ERP systems, core banking platforms and customer relationship management software. Replacing these systems entirely is often impractical.

Instead, companies are exploring ways to modernise surrounding applications while keeping core infrastructure intact.

“Your core ERP is not going to change. Your core banking platform is not going to change. But the application architecture around it needs to be modernised,” Ganesh said.

Agentic systems can help bridge that gap by connecting modern AI-powered services with existing enterprise infrastructure.

The Next Phase of Enterprise AI

For enterprise leaders, the focus is gradually shifting away from experimenting with AI and toward scaling it responsibly.

The conversation is no longer centred on whether developers should use AI coding assistants or whether enterprises should deploy AI agents. Those shifts are already underway.

Instead, CIOs are increasingly being asked to define governance frameworks, establish security guardrails and ensure that AI systems align with business objectives.

As AI-generated code becomes commonplace and autonomous agents become embedded within business workflows, enterprises may find that managing AI is ultimately more challenging than building it.

“The biggest question organisations need to ask is not what AI can do. It is what business problem needs to be solved first,” Ganesh opined.

title: Reserve Bank of India Proposes Risk Management Framework For AI Models
content:
The Reserve Bank of India proposes a risk management framework for AI models within institutions of finance and banking.

What Actually Matters.

The Reserve Bank of India has proposed a risk management framework specifically for AI models in financial institutions.

Inadequate management of model risks can result in poor decisions, financial losses, and compliance issues.

The Reserve Bank of India has introduced a draft for the management of AI models. The Economic Times noted that regulated entities are increasingly relying on models for business processes, customer services, risk management and cyber defence. The authority warns that inadequate management of model risks could lead to flawed decisions, financial losses, operational disruptions and compliance failures.

The draft ‘Guidance on Regulatory Principles for Model Risk Management, 2026’ applies to commercial banks, small finance banks, payments banks, cooperative banks, NBFCs, all-India financial institutions, asset reconstruction companies and credit information companies. The framework mandates models “must be covered under a board-approved Model Risk Management Framework”, according to reports.

The models must be independently validated before and after deployment, following modifications and at periodic intervals. Models require approval from the risk committee.

The draft proposes safeguards for AI systems. The draft requires entities to define explainability thresholds for AI models and apply higher standards where model outputs influence material decisions or have significant customer impact. When systems lack explainability, the text states entities must implement enhanced validation, monitoring, output verification and usage restrictions.

The framework introduces rules for AI systems that face customers. The draft states entities must inform users that they are interacting with an AI-based system and provide an option to switch to human assistance on request. The authority expects institutions to establish robust human oversight mechanisms for AI models and to include arrangements to override, suspend or deactivate models, including kill-switch arrangements.

The new chip could deliver up to 50% higher performance or 70% greater energy efficiency than its 2nm technology, depending on operating conditions.

What Actually Matters.

IBM has introduced the world’s first sub-1 nanometre chip technology with a new three-dimensional transistor architecture called nanostack.

The experimental 0.7nm chip features nearly 100 billion transistors, doubling the density of its previous 2nm chip.

IBM has unveiled what it says is the world’s first sub-1 nanometre (nm) chip technology, introducing an experimental 0.7nm semiconductor built around a new three-dimensional transistor architecture called nanostack.

The company said the research chip packs nearly 100 billion transistors onto a chip roughly the size of a fingernail, almost twice the transistor density of its 2nm chip announced in 2021, and demonstrates a path to extending Moore’s Law beyond current manufacturing limits.

According to IBM, the new chip could deliver up to 50% higher performance or 70% greater energy efficiency than its 2nm technology, depending on operating conditions.

The company said the technology is intended for future AI infrastructure, cloud computing systems and next-generation electronic devices, though commercial deployment is not expected for at least five years.

The breakthrough centres on IBM’s new nanostack architecture, which vertically stacks and staggers nanosheet transistors instead of arranging them solely in a two-dimensional layout.

The design uses sequential 3D integration to increase transistor density while allowing different semiconductor materials in each stacked layer, enabling engineers to optimise performance and power characteristics independently.

“This industry-first innovation continues IBM’s legacy of leading in next-generation technologies and sets the foundation for the next era of computing,” says Jay Gambetta, Director of IBM Research and IBM Fellow.

IBM said researchers experimentally validated the architecture through ultra-thin dielectric bonding, dual-channel engineering and functional CMOS inverter operation, demonstrating that the stacked design can perform logic operations.

Separately, research presented at the VLSI 2026 conference showed the nanostack approach achieving 40% SRAM scaling, which IBM said could help improve memory density and bandwidth for AI workloads.

The company said the technology represents the first logic platform to extend below the 1nm process node into the angstrom era.

While process node names no longer correspond directly to physical transistor dimensions, IBM said the 0.7nm node demonstrates that further scaling remains feasible despite the industry's increasing physical constraints.

IBM continues to develop the technology through its semiconductor research centre in Albany, New York, alongside partners including ASML, Lam Research, Tokyo Electron and SCREEN Semiconductor Solutions.

The facility is expected to house a High Numerical Aperture Extreme Ultraviolet (High NA EUV) lithography system, which IBM said will support future generations of advanced chip manufacturing.

The announcement builds on IBM’s long-running semiconductor research programme, which produced the industry’s first 2nm chip prototype in 2021.

The company conducts much of its semiconductor R&D at its Albany, New York, research facility, where it is working with partners including Lam Research, Tokyo Electron and SCREEN Semiconductor Solutions to develop High Numerical Aperture Extreme Ultraviolet (High-NA EUV) lithography processes and tools for future logic scaling.

The site is also set to house an ASML High-NA EUV lithography system, designed to print increasingly smaller and denser circuits.

Earlier this year, IBM and Lam Research expanded their partnership through a five-year agreement to develop materials, fabrication processes and High-NA EUV technologies for sub-1nm logic, building on more than a decade of collaboration spanning 7nm, nanosheet and 2nm semiconductor research.

Although IBM exited commercial chip manufacturing after selling its fabrication business to GlobalFoundries in 2015, it continues to develop next-generation semiconductor technologies through research partnerships that can later be adopted by foundries.

title: Anthropic Selects Indian IT Firm Hexaware as Authorised Reseller for Claude AI Models on Amazon Bedrock
content:
Hexaware can now sell, integrate, and support Anthropic's Claude models for enterprise customers globally.

What Actually Matters.

Hexaware Technologies has been appointed as an authorised reseller of Anthropic's Claude AI models on Amazon Bedrock.

The partnership allows Hexaware to sell, integrate, and support large language models for enterprise customers globally.

IT services company Hexaware Technologies has become an authorised reseller of Anthropic's Claude artificial intelligence models on Amazon Bedrock, allowing it to sell, integrate, and support the large language models for enterprise customers globally.

Amazon Bedrock is a fully managed AWS service that lets developers build AI-powered applications with access to top-tier foundational models.

The move expands Hexaware's AI portfolio as IT services providers increasingly deepen partnerships with leading AI model developers to offer enterprise generative AI solutions.

Hexaware said the partnership will enable customers to access Claude models through a single commercial framework covering procurement, deployment, support, and managed services.

The offering includes customised deployments using retrieval augmented generation (RAG), prompt engineering and domain-specific tuning, alongside governance features to enable secure adoption in regulated industries.

The company plans to combine the models with its consulting, systems integration, and industry-specific solutions for clients across sectors, including financial services, healthcare, manufacturing, transportation, and retail.

“This authorisation reflects the foundational AI capability that we’ve built and the trust our clients have placed in us. Claude’s safety-first design is what highly regulated industries need—and Hexaware has the domain knowledge, engineering excellence, and delivery scale to take it from a model to a working solution,” Siddharth Dhar, President and Global Head – Digital IT Operations and AI, Hexaware, said in a statement.

The company intends to deploy Claude-powered applications for use cases such as intelligent document processing, compliance automation, customer service, clinical data summarisation, supply chain intelligence, and AI-assisted software engineering. It is also expanding AI-led offerings across software development, cybersecurity, and private equity transformation, supported by a dedicated AI centre of excellence.

Gnani.ai said Prisma v2.5 delivers lower word error rates for rural Hindi and noisy Dravidian speech than competing models.

What Actually Matters.

Gnani.ai has launched Prisma v2.5, a speech-to-text model touted for its high accuracy in Indian languages.

The model reportedly outperforms global rivals in accuracy for rural Hindi and noisy Dravidian speech environments.

Indian voice AI startup Gnani.ai has launched Prisma v2.5, a speech-to-text model that the company claims delivers the highest speech recognition accuracy for Indian languages across multiple independent benchmarks.

The release confirms AIM’s earlier exclusive report that Gnani.ai was developing a new speech-to-text model for enterprise use, among five new AI models.

The company said Prisma v2.5 is available through its API and is targeting enterprise deployments across sectors, including banking, financial services, insurance, healthcare, retail, and telecom.

The Bengaluru-based startup said the model ranked first in 27 of 48 evaluations and led in eight of nine Indian languages tested on datasets including Kathbath, Kathbath Noisy, Gramvaani, CommonVoice, FLEURS, IndicTTS, MUCS 2021, and the IITM Evaluation Set.

According to the company, Prisma v2.5 achieved 15% lower word error rates (WER) for rural Hindi dialects and 18% lower WER in noisy Dravidian language environments compared with competing global and Indic speech recognition models.

It achieved the lowest WER on the Gramvaani benchmark, which captures conversational speech from semi-urban and rural Hindi speakers, recording a 22% WER compared to 27.5% for ElevenLabs, 26.4% for Microsoft, 23.4% for Sarvam, and 34% for Deepgram, per the company.

The model was trained on 14 million hours of proprietary speech data spanning 12 Indian languages, which Gnani.ai claimed is 14 times more than any competing model has publicly disclosed.

The company said the model supports word-level code-switching between language pairs such as Hindi-English and Tamil-English without requiring language tagging. It also includes native support for GSM and VoIP audio codecs, enabling transcription of low-quality telephony audio commonly used in tier-2 and tier-3 cities.

Gnani.ai added that post-training optimisations doubled inference throughput compared with the previous version without reducing accuracy.

“Most ASR models are built for ideal studio conditions. Indian calls happen over compressed network lines, in at least two languages inside a single sentence, in accents no studio corpus has ever captured. Gnani Prisma v2.5 is built for that reality,” said Ganesh Gopalan, CEO and Co-founder of Gnani.ai, in a statement.

The company said the model addresses transcription errors involving numerals, alphanumeric strings, named entities, and short utterances, which are common in enterprise call centre applications.

In March, the company said its ecosystem had grown to 13 million users, hosting more than 2 million public AI models and 500,000 public datasets

What Actually Matters.

Hugging Face has surpassed a $100 million annual revenue run rate, reflecting its growth in the open-source AI sector.

The company prioritises an open AI ecosystem, keeping services free for 97% of users while hosting extensive models and datasets.

Hugging Face has surpassed a $100 million annual revenue run rate, according to co-founder and CEO Clement Delangue, marking a new financial milestone for one of the largest open-source AI platforms.

Announcing the milestone in a post on X, Delangue said the company has prioritised building an open AI ecosystem over maximising short-term revenue.

He said Hugging Face continues to ‘store and serve hundreds of petabytes of models and datasets’ while keeping the platform ‘free and open-source for 97% of our users.’

The company has built its business around hosting open AI models, datasets, evaluation tools, developer libraries and collaborative machine learning workflows.

Delangue said that approach has helped Hugging Face establish ‘one of the most loved platforms in tech,’ with network effects, a defensible position and what he described as a sustainable AI business.

The CEO also pointed to growing enterprise interest in open and locally deployed AI systems, writing that he was excited ‘as more companies start to see the value of open and local AI.’

The financial milestone comes as Hugging Face continues to cement its position as the largest platform for open-source AI.

In its State of Open Source report published in March, the company said its ecosystem had grown to 13 million users, hosting more than 2 million public AI models and 500,000 public datasets, with users increasingly contributing fine-tuned models, benchmarks and AI applications rather than simply consuming pretrained systems.

The report also found that more than 30% of Fortune 500 companies now maintain verified accounts on the platform, reflecting growing enterprise adoption alongside its open-source community.

The platform has also broadened its focus beyond software, expanding into open-source robotics following its acquisition of Pollen Robotics and the launch of new developer-focused hardware.

Over the years, Delangue has repeatedly stated that the company is profitable. As per Crunchbase, it has raised nearly $400 million in eight funding rounds, backed by Sequoia Capital, Google, and NVIDIA, among others.

As of its last funding round in August 2023, Hugging Face is currently valued at $4.5 billion.

The company earns revenue through a freemium business model, offering paid subscriptions, enterprise software and AI infrastructure while keeping most of its platform free.

Its main revenue streams include Hugging Face Pro subscriptions for individual developers, Team and Enterprise Hub plans that provide organisations with security, governance and collaboration features, as well as usage-based charges for AI inference, compute and dedicated deployment infrastructure.

The company also generates revenue through cloud infrastructure partnerships and enterprise AI services, with management saying its business is primarily driven by enterprise customers rather than its free community.

Hugging Face has surpassed a $100 million annual revenue run rate, according to co-founder and CEO Clement Delangue, marking a new financial milestone for one of the largest open-source AI platforms.

Announcing the milestone in a post on X, Delangue said the company has prioritised building an open AI ecosystem over maximising short-term revenue.

He said Hugging Face continues to ‘store and serve hundreds of petabytes of models and datasets’ while keeping the platform ‘free and open-source for 97% of our users.’

The company has built its business around hosting open AI models, datasets, evaluation tools, developer libraries and collaborative machine learning workflows.

Delangue said that approach has helped Hugging Face establish ‘one of the most loved platforms in tech,’ with network effects, a defensible position and what he described as a sustainable AI business.

The CEO also pointed to growing enterprise interest in open and locally deployed AI systems, writing that he was excited ‘as more companies start to see the value of open and local AI.’

The financial milestone comes as Hugging Face continues to cement its position as the largest platform for open-source AI.

In its State of Open Source report published in March, the company said its ecosystem had grown to 13 million users, hosting more than 2 million public AI models and 500,000 public datasets, with users increasingly contributing fine-tuned models, benchmarks and AI applications rather than simply consuming pretrained systems.

The report also found that more than 30% of Fortune 500 companies now maintain verified accounts on the platform, reflecting growing enterprise adoption alongside its open-source community.

The platform has also broadened its focus beyond software, expanding into open-source robotics following its acquisition of Pollen Robotics and the launch of new developer-focused hardware.

Over the years, Delangue has repeatedly stated that the company is profitable. As per Crunchbase, it has raised nearly $400 million in eight funding rounds, backed by Sequoia Capital, Google, and NVIDIA, among others.

As of its last funding round in August 2023, Hugging Face is currently valued at $4.5 billion.

The company earns revenue through a freemium business model, offering paid subscriptions, enterprise software and AI infrastructure while keeping most of its platform free.

Its main revenue streams include Hugging Face Pro subscriptions for individual developers, Team and Enterprise Hub plans that provide organisations with security, governance and collaboration features, as well as usage-based charges for AI inference, compute and dedicated deployment infrastructure.

The company also generates revenue through cloud infrastructure partnerships and enterprise AI services, with management saying its business is primarily driven by enterprise customers rather than its free community.

title: AI Coding Tool Costs to Exceed Developer Salaries by 2028: Gartner Report
content:
Gartner forecasts that expenditure on AI coding tools will exceed software developer salaries by 2028 due to rising token consumption.

What Actually Matters.

Gartner predicts that spending on AI coding tools will surpass software developer salaries by 2028.

The increase is driven by rising token consumption and a shift to consumption-based pricing models.

Expenditure on artificial intelligence coding tools will exceed the salary of a software developer by 2028, according to a report by Gartner. Its forecast is based on an increase in token consumption by language models and a transition to consumption-based licensing models by technology vendors.

Under consumption-based pricing, token consumption directly determines the price of coding tools. The report notes that technology vendors provide limited transparency regarding how token consumption is calculated and billed, which prevents enterprises from forecasting and controlling budgets.

Nitish Tyagi, Senior Principal Analyst at Gartner, said in a statement, “Token discipline will not emerge through developer choice alone, as developers tend to optimise for speed and convenience over cost efficiency. Without a governed engineering operating model, costs can escalate faster than the productivity gains these tools are designed to deliver.”

Tyagi further noted, “Most organisations still lack the maturity and frameworks to effectively measure cost versus business impact. Software engineering leaders are increasingly concerned as token-driven AI spend becomes harder to justify, with budgets often being depleted earlier than expected.”

The research identifies usage patterns and governance gaps as drivers of expenditure. Issues include autonomy in workflows without oversight, unedited context windows, and an absence of feedback mechanisms. Additionally, coding agents currently lack cost optimisation capabilities.

“AI coding costs will continue to rise as infrastructure investment and profitability challenges push model pricing higher,” said Tyagi. “At the same time, as more developers adopt AI tools, light users are expected to rapidly become mainstream users as familiarity and reliance increase, driving further growth in token consumption and overall spend.”

To manage budgets, Gartner recommended that engineering leaders implement operating models for tool usage. This involves establishing decision frameworks that classify tasks and aligning model selection with task complexity. The firm has advised directing routine tasks to smaller models while reserving frontier models for complex work.

It has also adivsed organisations to train developers in context engineering to lower token consumption by limiting input to relevant information. Finally, the report suggested introducing governance controls, such as token thresholds, and reviewing token usage during development cycles to locate inefficiencies.

content:
Airbound aims to build a 10,000-flight-a-day drone delivery network across Andhra Pradesh.

What Actually Matters.

Airbound is developing a large-scale drone delivery network in Andhra Pradesh, aiming for 10,000 daily flights.

The network will initially connect Amaravati, Vijayawada, and Guntur, starting operations in Guntur.

Aerospace startup Airbound has signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) with Andhra Pradesh Drone Corporation (APDC) to develop a large-scale drone delivery network across the Amaravati Capital Region, aiming to accelerate the development of drone-led logistics infrastructure in India.

The partnership targets enabling 10,000 daily drone flights across Andhra Pradesh over the next year. The network will initially focus on connecting Amaravati, Vijayawada, and Guntur, with operations expected to begin in Guntur first.

Under the collaboration, Airbound will work with stakeholders across healthcare, logistics, and e-commerce to establish drone-based delivery services. The initiative is expected to improve mid-mile connectivity, enable faster movement of healthcare supplies and commercial goods, and support the development of Andhra Pradesh's emerging drone economy.

Airbound said the network will be powered by its proprietary blended-wing-body tailsitter aircraft, designed for large-scale aerial logistics. The Bengaluru-based startup claims the platform can reduce delivery costs significantly compared with conventional transportation methods.

"By partnering with a home-grown company to build one of the world's largest drone delivery networks, Andhra Pradesh is demonstrating that cutting-edge technology can be designed, built and scaled in India," Civil Aviation Minister Ram Mohan Naidu said during the announcement.

Airbound Founder and CEO Naman Pushp said the partnership aims to transform drone delivery into shared public infrastructure rather than a niche service. "When we make that work in Amaravati, Vijayawada, and Guntur, it becomes a template for how cities and states across India can treat drone delivery as shared infrastructure," he said.

The rollout will include pilot operations, route mapping, regulatory coordination, and the gradual development of interconnected drone corridors across the Amaravati region. Airbound has completed more than 10,000 flights in India, including healthcare logistics operations with Narayana Health.

The acquisition will bring iMerit’s expertise in AI model training, reinforcement learning and multimodal evaluation to EXL, helping clients build more reliable and industry-specific AI systems.

What Actually Matters.

EXL is acquiring iMerit for up to $310 million to enhance its enterprise AI capabilities.

The deal includes an upfront payment of $170 million and performance-based incentives.

Data and AI company EXL has announced plans to acquire AI training and model evaluation firm iMerit in a deal valued at up to $310 million, as it looks to strengthen its position in the rapidly growing enterprise AI market.

The acquisition, expected to close in the third quarter of 2026, includes an upfront payment of $170 million and up to $140 million in incentives and earnouts tied to performance milestones over the next two years.

The deal will expand EXL’s capabilities in AI model training, evaluation and reinforcement learning, helping enterprises move AI projects from experimentation to large-scale deployment.

iMerit works with leading AI companies to train and improve large language models and multimodal AI systems. Its clients use the company’s expertise to enhance the accuracy and reliability of AI models across text, image, video, voice and LiDAR data.

According to EXL, the acquisition will give it closer access to foundation model developers and provide insights into how advanced AI models are trained, fine-tuned and optimised. The company said this will help its clients build industry-specific AI systems tailored to their business needs.

A key part of the acquisition is iMerit’s proprietary Ango platform, which supports AI model evaluation, chain-of-thought reasoning, red teaming and multimodal testing. EXL also gains access to iMerit’s ‘Scholars’ network, a global pool of experts, including physicians, scientists, engineers and linguists who provide human feedback for AI training and reinforcement learning.

EXL plans to integrate Ango with its existing AI platforms, including EXLerate.ai, EXLdata.ai and EXL.decision.ai, creating an end-to-end enterprise AI ecosystem.

“Success with AI requires industry-specific data, rigorous evaluation and reinforcement learning,” said Rohit Kapoor, Chairman and CEO of EXL. He added that the acquisition would strengthen the company’s ability to deliver trusted and accountable AI solutions for enterprises.

The deal is expected to further expand EXL’s presence in sectors such as healthcare, insurance, banking and capital markets while also opening opportunities in emerging AI fields, including autonomous mobility, robotics and physical AI.

title: Infosys Partners With Sentara to Expand Enterprise AI Adoption Across US Healthcare Operations
content:
The IT services major will help US-based healthcare provider Sentara build an enterprise AI framework spanning IT systems, hospital operations and clinical support.

What Actually Matters.

Infosys is partnering with Sentara to implement artificial intelligence across its healthcare operations.

The collaboration aims to transition AI initiatives from pilot projects to production-scale deployments.

Infosys has partnered with US-based healthcare provider Sentara to deploy artificial intelligence across its enterprise operations, marking another AI-focused transformation engagement for the country’s second-largest IT services company.

Under the collaboration, Infosys will help Sentara, which operates as a not-for-profit organisation, build an enterprise AI foundation spanning IT systems, hospital operations and clinical support using its AI platform, Infosys Topaz Fabric.

The engagement aims to move AI initiatives from pilot projects to production-scale deployments across the healthcare organisation.

The partnership will focus on identifying AI use cases across care management, employee productivity and digital patient-facing services, while putting in place governance and operational frameworks required for responsible AI deployment in regulated healthcare environments.

“As we continue to advance our digital strategy, working with Infosys enables us to take a thoughtful and scalable approach to AI adoption across the enterprise. This collaboration helps ensure AI is deployed in ways that genuinely improve how our hospital teams work, supporting efficiency, care delivery and the communities we serve while remaining secure, compliant and patient-centred,” Jamisson Fowler, SVP and Chief Digital Officer, Sentara said in a statement.

The deal comes as Indian IT services companies increasingly position themselves as partners for enterprise AI adoption rather than providers of standalone AI tools.

Large vendors, including Infosys, TCS, Wipro and HCLTech, have been signing AI transformation engagements across industries as enterprises shift from experimentation to deploying AI at scale.

“Healthcare organisations are at a pivotal moment where AI can meaningfully enhance clinical and operational outcomes when it is adopted responsibly and at scale,” Venky Ananth, EVP and Global Head, Healthcare, Infosys, said.

Sentara operates 12 hospitals across Virginia and Northeastern North Carolina, employs around 34,000 people and serves more than one million health plan members across Virginia and Florida.

The companies did not disclose the financial terms of the engagement.

title: HCLTech Expands Gemini Enterprise Push with Google Cloud & ServiceNow Partnership
content:
The collaboration introduces AI-powered solutions for field services, customer experience and manufacturing, aiming to improve operational efficiency while maintaining oversight and security.

What Actually Matters.

HCLTech has partnered with Google Cloud and ServiceNow to enhance AI deployment using the Gemini Enterprise platform.

The collaboration aims to automate business processes, improving operational efficiency in field services and customer experience.

HCLTech has expanded its partnership with Google Cloud and ServiceNow to help enterprises deploy and scale artificial intelligence (AI) agents using the Gemini Enterprise platform.

The announcement was made ahead of the Google Cloud Summit Sydney 2026. The collaboration builds on HCLTech’s recently launched Gemini Enterprise business unit and combines Google Cloud’s Gemini AI capabilities, ServiceNow’s workflow platform and HCLTech’s implementation expertise to support enterprise adoption of agentic AI.

As part of the partnership, HCLTech will introduce AI-powered solutions designed to automate business processes and improve operational efficiency. These solutions will be based on ServiceNow’s Blueprint for Agentic Business, a framework that helps organisations adopt AI in a structured, outcome-focused manner.

One of the key offerings is a next-generation Factory Shop Floor Assistant that provides real-time operational insights in manufacturing environments, helping businesses improve decision-making and productivity.

The initial solutions will focus on two areas, which are field services and customer experience. In field services, Gemini Live will be integrated with ServiceNow Field Service Management to provide technicians with real-time audio and visual intelligence, enabling faster issue resolution. For customer experience, the solution aims to ensure customer intent is maintained across different communication channels.

The companies are also introducing tools to improve governance and monitoring of AI systems. HCLTech will use ServiceNow’s AI Control Tower to enhance visibility over AI agents operating within Gemini Enterprise. Moreover, an ITOps ServiceNow Agent, available through the Google Cloud Marketplace, will support incident management and remediation in enterprise IT environments.

Satish Thomas, Vice President of Applied AI and Platform Ecosystem at Google Cloud, said, “The partnership would help organisations safely scale AI across their operations.”

“The collaboration would help businesses build a foundation for an ‘agentic enterprise’ by connecting AI agents across workflows, systems and teams,” noted Michael Park, Senior Vice President of Global Partnerships and Channels at ServiceNow.

HCLTech executives said the partnership is designed to help enterprises move beyond AI pilot projects and deploy AI solutions at scale while maintaining governance, security and operational oversight.

title: Amazon Ramps Up India AI Infra Investment, Commits Additional $13 Bn
content:
The investment is part of Amazon’s broader $48 billion commitment to expand AI, cloud, e-commerce, and logistics operations in India between 2026 and 2030.

What Actually Matters.

Amazon is investing an additional $13 billion to enhance AI and cloud infrastructure in India.

This investment is part of a larger $48 billion commitment aimed at expanding various operations in the country by 2030.

Amazon will invest an additional $13 billion to expand AI and cloud infrastructure in India, CEO Andy Jassy announced during a meeting with Prime Minister Narendra Modi in New Delhi.

This new commitment brings Amazon’s planned AI and cloud infrastructure investment to more than $21 billion through 2030—and increases its overall India investment plans to $48 billion, which also includes expanding its e-commerce and logistics footprint.

According to the company, the fresh investments will expand AWS data centre capacity in Mumbai and Hyderabad, increasing access to custom AI chips, managed AI services, cloud infrastructure, and developer tools for startups, enterprises, and government organisations.

Amazon said the expanded infrastructure will support production-scale AI workloads using services including Amazon Bedrock, AWS's managed generative AI platform, alongside the company’s Trainium AI chips.

The company also highlighted developer tools, including Amazon Kiro and Quick, which it said are enabling developers and information workers in India to build AI agents and other AI-powered applications.

Jassy said that the investment aims to meet the “strong demand across our business in India”. He added that Amazon's priorities remain aligned with India’s goals of “democratising access to AI, digitising small businesses, creating jobs, and enabling exports.”

The company said hundreds of thousands of Indian organisations, including the National Health Authority, Government e-Marketplace, Apollo Tyres, Delhivery, Physics Wallah, Axis Bank, and HDFC Bank, already use AWS for AI and cloud workloads.

Amazon added that the investment will allow customers to continue storing data within India while accessing its AI infrastructure and services.

The latest commitment comes less than six months after Amazon announced $35 billion in new investments in India. With the new plans, Amazon said its cumulative investments in the country between 2010 and 2030 will exceed $88 billion.

Amazon also outlined broader India expansion plans, including opening more than 20 fulfilment centres and over 100 last-mile delivery stations this year.

The company recently launched Sammaan, a welfare programme for delivery associates, and said it aims to support 3.8 million jobs by 2030, enable $80 billion in ecommerce exports, bring AI to 15 million small businesses, and provide AI education to 4 million government school students.

In a post on X, Prime Minister Modi shared that this signals a ‘growing interest across the world to invest in India.’

Amazon’s latest commitment adds to a wave of multibillion-dollar AI infrastructure investments by global technology companies in India.

Last year, Microsoft announced a $3 billion investment over two years to expand cloud and AI infrastructure, establish new data centres and train 10 million people in AI skills. A few months later, the company increased its commitment, announcing a further $17.5 billion investment through 2029 to expand hyperscale AI infrastructure and operations in the country.

Similarly, Google announced a $15 billion investment over 2026–2030 to establish its first AI hub in Visakhapatnam in partnership with AdaniConneX and Airtel. The company broke ground on the project in April 2026, with the hub set to include a gigawatt-scale AI data centre, subsea cable gateway, fibre infrastructure, and clean energy systems.

title: Eros Launches AI-Powered Music Platform With Virtual Artists & Mohammed Rafi Legacy Project
content:
The first album under the partnership is scheduled for release on July 31, marking the singer’s birth anniversary.

What Actually Matters.

Eros Music Worlds is launched as the world's first AI-powered Large Cultural Music Platform.

The platform integrates various music genres and artist legacy projects while maintaining human creative control.

Eros Innovation has launched Eros Music Worlds, an AI-powered music platform that the company describes as the world’s first ‘Large Cultural Music Platform’.

The new platform aims to build a music ecosystem that goes beyond traditional record labels by combining character-led music franchises, non-film music, devotional content, folk and sufi genres, artist legacy projects and live entertainment experiences.

Powered by Eros’ Large Cultural Models (LCMs), the platform uses AI trained on licensed and rights-cleared material. According to the company, the technology is designed to interpret human-created compositions in light of cultural and emotional contexts while maintaining human creative control.

The platform launches with seven AI-native artists inspired by characters from Eros films and storytelling worlds. The first artists, Jordan and Tanu, have already released their debut singles and music videos across major streaming platforms, including Spotify, Apple Music, Amazon Music, YouTube Music and JioSaavn. Other AI-native artists, like Munna, Langda Tyagi and Mudit, will be introduced in phases.

A key highlight of the announcement is Eros’ partnership with the Mohammed Rafi family under a new initiative called Eros Legacy Voices. The collaboration will focus on three areas, which are new recordings, a flagship live concert experience and the Mohammed Rafi Academy. The first album under the partnership is scheduled for release on July 31, marking the singer’s birth anniversary.

Ridhima Lulla, Co-Founder and Co-President of Eros Innovation, said, “The platform combines human creativity with AI technology while ensuring cultural authenticity.” She added that the partnership with the Mohammed Rafi family aims to introduce the singer’s legacy to a new generation through ethically developed AI tools.

Shahid Rafi welcomed the initiative, saying the collaboration respects the singer’s legacy and has been built on proper consent and family involvement.

The launch comes at a time when the global music industry is debating the use of AI-generated content and copyrighted material. Eros said its models are trained exclusively on owned or licensed content, positioning the platform as a rights-cleared alternative to many AI music initiatives currently facing legal scrutiny.

title: For Manufacturers Like Tata AutoComp, AI is About Rewiring Entire Assembly Line
content:
Figma is repositioning its design canvas as a collaborative workspace for humans, code, and AI agents.

What Actually Matters.

Figma is transforming its design canvas into an intelligent workspace that integrates humans, code, and AI agents.

New AI agents and code-native design tools aim to streamline workflows and enhance creativity by automating repetitive tasks.

Figma has announced a suite of AI-focused product updates at its annual Config 2026 conference in San Francisco, as the company looks to turn its design platform into what it calls an “intelligent canvas” for full-stack digital creation. The announcements include new AI agents, code-native design tools, generative plugin creation, and workflow automation capabilities.

The company said the new features aim to help users automate repetitive tasks, generate new ideas, and build digital products from a single environment.

“Too often, the tools we have for building force us into false choices between design and code, humans and agents, prompting and direct manipulation,” said Dylan Field, Co-founder and CEO of Figma. “This ends up constraining creativity instead of pushing it further.”

The centrepiece of the announcement is a set of new agent-driven capabilities. Figma introduced agent skills, which allow teams to convert repetitive workflows into reusable actions that can be shared across organisations. The company also expanded the context available to its AI agent through third-party connectors, web search, and file attachments.

Figma also launched generative plugins, enabling users to create custom plugins using natural language prompts.

The platform is also adding Figma Weave workflows, which integrate more than 20 AI tools into the design canvas. Figma said the feature simplifies complex AI workflows and marks the first step towards deeper integration between Figma and Figma Weave later this year.

Alongside the product announcements, Figma released its third annual AI and Design Report. The study found that AI’s impact is increasingly extending beyond individual productivity into team collaboration. Respondents were six times more likely to say AI had ‘significantly impacted’ how they collaborate with others compared with two years ago.

The report also found that 57% of respondents believe design has become more important as AI adoption grows. Among developers, that figure rose from 44% in 2025 to 65% in 2026. Companies with the highest levels of AI adoption were 25% more likely to say design had increased in importance.

Among the new tools, Figma introduced code layers, which allow teams to work directly with code on the design canvas. Users can clone repositories, generate design directions using AI, convert flows into editable design layers, and sync changes back to code.

The company also announced Motion, a tool for creating animations and transitions. Users can generate animations through prompts or edit them manually on a timeline. Another addition, Shaders, enables users to create visual effects through prompts using WebGPU-powered rendering.

Separately, Figma announced its first Config India event, to be held in Bengaluru on October 15, 2026. Last year, it also opened its office in Bengaluru.

Tata AutoComp Systems is deploying AI across its 61 manufacturing plants to automate quality inspection, predict equipment failures, and retrain its workforce.

What Actually Matters.

Tata AutoComp is integrating AI across its 61 global manufacturing plants to enhance production efficiency.

The company’s Digital Factory programme focuses on automating quality inspection and improving equipment maintenance.

On automotive factory floors around the world, intelligence is entering the assembly line in various ways. Predictive maintenance flags unreliable equipment, digital twins bypass supply chain bottlenecks, and computer vision systems inspect painted surfaces.

Indian automakers are also following suit.

Among them is Tata AutoComp Systems, which operates 61 manufacturing facilities across India, North America, Latin America, Europe, and China, and employs over 20,000 people. It supplies components to original equipment manufacturers across passenger vehicles, commercial vehicles, two- and three-wheelers, and tractors. The company generated nearly ₹13,100 crore in revenue in FY25.

The Pune-headquartered company, founded in 1995, has been building what it calls a Digital Factory programme, an effort to layer artificial intelligence and connected systems across its production operations. The scope is broad: quality inspection, equipment maintenance, workforce training, and supply chain management.

The starting point was the inspection line.

"Quality control was the natural starting point. Traditional human inspection could statistically sample less than 5% of parts; AI-driven computer vision now scans 100% of parts in real time on a moving line. The implications for zero-defect manufacturing are profound," Arvind Goel, Vice Chairman at Tata AutoComp Systems Ltd tells AIM.

Manufacturers have been moving towards full-coverage inspection, standardising data models across facilities so that inspection results can be centralised and cross-plant patterns identified. A defect spotted at one plant can be compared against similar processes elsewhere to detect systemic equipment or supplier issues.

At Tata AutoComp, that data feeds into dashboards that surface quality deviations within a shift, rather than after it.

"Previously, operators manually checked parts for surface defects—a tiring, sampling-based process prone to misses. Today, AI-powered digital inspection systems evaluate every part on a moving line in real time, making instant OK/Not OK decisions before defective components advance downstream," Goel said.

Maintenance, Supply Chain, and Training

The second area of focus is equipment maintenance, where the company has moved away from calendar-based servicing towards a model driven by sensor data. Industrial IoT devices now feed machine readings into AI models that attempt to forecast failures before they occur.

"On machine maintenance, the shift is equally dramatic—from calendar-based servicing regardless of actual machine condition to AI-driven prediction of failure days in advance, enabling maintenance during planned windows rather than emergency shutdowns," Goel said.

The business case for this approach is well-established across manufacturing. According to Deloitte, predictive maintenance can reduce maintenance costs by 25–30% and eliminate 70% of unplanned breakdowns. For an automotive parts plant, where a line stoppage cascades into scrapped batches and schedule disruptions across a supply chain, the stakes are considerable.

Tata AutoComp frames the objective in direct terms: reducing severe equipment failures and associated maintenance costs, with maintenance windows shifted from emergency to planned slots.

Beyond the production floor, the company has been applying AI to supply chain management. It is deploying AI-powered control towers—systems that bring real-time visibility to demand forecasting and inventory management to reduce both overproduction and stockouts.

On workforce training, the company has introduced virtual reality-based learning programmes for shopfloor operators, citing a reduction in training time of up to 30% without disrupting live production. The approach is part of a broader attempt to build a digital skills base across a workforce that has historically worked in manual assembly roles.

The Technology Foundation

Tata AutoComp says its AI strategy is built on a centralised data platform rather than standalone tools. The company has built a unified data and AI layer that stores AI-ready data, constructs data products, and operationalises use cases across functions. Alongside this, it has been deploying Manufacturing Execution Systems for part traceability, Energy Management Systems, and AI-guided video analytics for plant safety.

The company is also building an "AI Playground"—a facility that gives internal business teams direct exposure to AI tools applied to automotive use cases—and employee digital assistants to give staff a single interface for accessing information.

"Integration across enterprise systems, shop-floor OT layers, and cloud-based AI platforms is a deliberate architectural priority, not an afterthought," Goel said.

Barriers

The company identifies three obstacles that have consistently slowed AI deployment.

The first is legacy infrastructure. Many machines on older plant floors were not built with connectivity in mind, making it necessary to retrofit sensors and data ports before any AI model can operate on them. The second is what the company calls the "digital quotient" deficit—the gap between what AI systems require of frontline workers and what those workers currently know.

"Frontline operators are being asked to work in fundamentally new ways. Strong digital training programmes and structured change management plans are non-negotiable—ultimately, these operators must become advocates, not resistors, of the AI transformation," Goel said.

The third barrier is capital. Computer vision hardware, data infrastructure, and robotics require substantial upfront investment, and in a thin-margin industry, securing that approval requires a tightly defined business case.

A study by Tata Consultancy Services and Amazon Web Services, which surveyed 216 senior manufacturing leaders across North America and Europe, found that while 75% of respondents expected AI to become one of the top three contributors to their operating margins by 2026, only 21% reported full AI readiness. The gap between intent and infrastructure is a recurring theme across the sector.

What Happens to Workers

The question of how AI changes the composition of a factory workforce is one that Tata AutoComp addresses directly, describing the outcome as role redesign rather than headcount reduction.

The company points to the emergence of new internal designations—business technology leads and digital technology leads—that sit within business units and bridge the gap between production teams and digital systems. On the floor itself, the company cites the example of a machine operator transitioning into a robot operator, responsible for programming, supervising, and troubleshooting AI-guided machinery.

"The manual task changes; the operator's value deepens. We are making deliberate investments in reskilling and cross-skilling programmes to transition traditional assembly roles into technology-centric functions—robotics maintenance, data analytics, connected systems management," Goel said.

Tata AutoComp also points to adjacent opportunities created by the broader transition in the automotive sector, noting that cross-skilling opens pathways into EV battery supply chains and localised logistics.

Across India, 54% of manufacturing companies have now implemented AI and analytics technologies, per a PwC India report, and the pressure to do so is growing. India's smart factory market is valued at $7.7 billion in 2025 and is projected to reach $17 billion by 2032, growing at 12% annually, according to P&S Intelligence.

For large-scale suppliers such as Tata AutoComp, the question is less whether to invest than how quickly the operational and cultural infrastructure can be built to support it.

"AI amplifies human capability," Goel said. "The workforce of a Digital Factory is more empowered, not diminished."

title: GLM-5.2 Gets Fastest API Yet, Exceeding 280 Tokens Per Second
content:
Developed by Baseten, the API serves Z.ai’s GLM-5.2 at over 280 tokens per second, targeting high-volume coding and agentic AI workloads.

What Actually Matters.

Baseten has developed the fastest API for Z.ai's GLM-5.2, achieving over 280 tokens per second.

The API's high performance is attributed to various inference optimisations, including model quantisation and cache management.

Baseten, a San Francisco-based AI infrastructure startup, said it has built what it describes as the fastest API implementation of Z.ai’s open-source frontier model, GLM-5.2, delivering more than 280 tokens per second, according to measurements published by Artificial Analysis.

The company said the performance comes from a series of inference optimisations spanning model quantisation, cache management, routing, speculative decoding and infrastructure design.

The announcement was detailed in a technical post on X by Philip Kiely, Baseten’s Head of AI Education.

GLM-5.2 is Z.ai’s 744-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model with 40 billion active parameters, support for up to a one-million-token context window, and an MIT licence.

The China-based model has drawn attention for benchmark results that place it alongside leading proprietary systems while offering significantly lower inference costs.

According to Baseten, the model is currently served through its model APIs and dedicated deployments, with customers including Notion.

The company said GLM-5.2 can deliver performance comparable to leading frontier models while costing 70–80% less per token.

A key part of the deployment is an in-house quantisation process that converts the model’s original FP8 weights into NVIDIA’s NVFP4 format for execution on Blackwell GPUs.

Baseten said testing showed the quantised model maintained comparable performance on agent-focused evaluations such as the Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard (BFCL) while improving both throughput and latency.

The company also implemented cache-aware routing using NVIDIA’s Dynamo toolkit. Requests are directed to inference replicas that already contain relevant key-value cache data, reducing repeated prefill computation and lowering time-to-first-token latency.

Baseten reported an average time-to-first-token performance of roughly 800 milliseconds for GLM-5.2 workloads, as measured by Artificial Analysis.

Another major optimisation involves separating the prefill and decode stages of inference. Rather than processing both workloads on the same GPU node, Baseten runs them on dedicated infrastructure pools.

The company said this “prefill-decode disaggregation” doubled tokens-per-second performance compared with conventional aggregated deployments in internal benchmarks.

Baseten further boosted throughput by supporting GLM-5.2’s Multi-Token Prediction layers, a speculative decoding technique that generates multiple draft tokens in a single forward pass before verification.

The company said the approach provides a lossless speed improvement and that additional optimisation opportunities remain.

GLM-5.2 has generated significant attention across the AI industry since its launch earlier this month, with developers and startup founders highlighting its performance on coding and agentic software engineering tasks.

According to Z.ai, the open-weight model matches or exceeds leading proprietary systems on several long-horizon coding benchmarks, edging out OpenAI’s GPT-5.5 on FrontierSWE while trailing Anthropic’s Claude Opus 4.8 by roughly one percentage point.

“In practice, GLM-5.2 meets or exceeds the capabilities suggested by its benchmarks. It's a genuinely great model for writing code, operating agents, and other frontier language model tasks,” wrote Keily.

In a global legal first, AI Law Firm Garfield AI secured a £7,000 court victory for a freelancer, pairing AI preparation with human courtroom advocacy.

What Actually Matters.

Garfield AI achieved a historic court victory, marking the first successful use of an AI lawyer in a trial.

The case involved a freelancer recovering £7,000 for unpaid work, highlighting the accessibility of legal support via AI.

A British AI law firm, Garfield AI, has won in an English court, marking what is considered the first instance of a trial won with the assistance of an AI lawyer.

Tamires Camal Taquidir, a freelance HR consultant, paid Garfield AI around £400 to draft a legal letter and initiate court proceedings concerning an unpaid debt of £7,000.

“I was owed money for work I had done, but it felt like the process of recovering it could be too stressful, expensive and time-consuming. Garfield made it possible for me to pursue the claim and keep going. When the counterclaim was brought, it was intended to intimidate me, but I knew I had accessible, cost-effective, and competent support. I'm delighted by the result,” Taquidir told The Financial Times.

Philip Young, CEO and Co-founder of Garfield, described it as a "historic moment" for access to justice and noted that many small businesses have had to forgo debts due to the high cost of litigation relative to the potential recovery. “Here, a freelancer who had done the work and not been paid was able to take her case all the way to trial, resist a counterclaim, and win,” he said.

Garfield can handle claims ranging from £30 to £10,000 and prepares the case, subsequently enlisting a human barrister to represent the client in court.

“AI did not replace the judge, the barrister or the legal system. What it did was make the process more accessible, more efficient, and more affordable, so that a meritorious claimant could get to the point where her case could be heard, and justice could be done,” Young added.

While the AI lawyer automated the document-heavy preparation stages, the firm integrated human expertise for oral presentation. Shortly before the trial, Garfield AI instructed Dominic Li, a junior barrister from One Essex Court, to represent Taquidir in front of the judge.

It produced four witness statements and compiled a set of documents for the three-hour trial held at Wandsworth County Court on May 14. The court ruled in favour of Taquidir and awarded her the outstanding amount.

Li, barrister for the claimant, told FT, “This was a hard-fought small claim that turned on the existence and terms of an oral agreement. Garfield AI's preparation helped ensure the case was presented clearly and efficiently, while the advocacy at trial remained essential and a fundamentally human exercise.”
