While hardware remains important, industry leaders argue that the real competitive advantage lies in the software that drives these systems.

What Actually Matters.

India's drone industry is shifting focus from manufacturing to software-driven capabilities.

Government initiatives have fostered a growing ecosystem of drone startups and technology firms.

For much of the past decade, India’s drone ambitions have been framed around manufacturing. Government incentives, import restrictions and procurement programmes have focused on building domestic production capabilities and reducing dependence on foreign suppliers. Those efforts have helped create a rapidly expanding ecosystem of drone startups, defence contractors and technology companies serving both civilian and military markets.

Indian drone companies raised $178 million in equity funding in 2025, a 45% jump over the same period in 2024, according to data from Tracxn, suggesting investor conviction is moving in step with the technology argument.

Yet, conversations with founders, investors and industry experts suggest that the next phase of growth may be defined by a different set of capabilities altogether.

While hardware remains essential, companies increasingly view navigation systems, autonomous decision-making, secure communications, encryption technologies and computing architectures as the technologies that will ultimately determine competitive advantage. The focus is gradually shifting from building drones to building the software that allows autonomous systems to navigate, communicate, coordinate and survive in contested environments.

Sai Pattabiram, Founder of Zuppa Geo Navigation Technologies, believes the industry is already undergoing that transition.

“The drone is essentially a flying computer,” he says. Once the human pilot is replaced by electronics and onboard intelligence, the aircraft becomes a computing platform whose effectiveness depends on the software controlling it. In his view, the autopilot and the underlying computing architecture are more strategically important than the airframe itself.

That perspective is increasingly finding support beyond startup founders.

Sadhika Agarwal, who leads investments at Equirus InnovateX Fund, says recent conflicts have demonstrated that “low-cost, software-defined drone systems could be decisive battlefield assets”. The growing importance of autonomy and software, she argues, has also exposed the risks associated with dependence on concentrated supplier bases and created opportunities for countries capable of building alternative technology stacks.

The Value is Moving Up the Stack

The first wave of India’s drone ecosystem was built around manufacturing capability. Companies focused on airframes, sensors, batteries and communications equipment while policymakers prioritised domestic production and localisation.

Today, many founders argue that the industry’s centre of gravity is moving higher up the technology stack. Yet, the component data tells a more sobering story: as of 2024, roughly 85% of drone components, autopilots, sensors and GPS units are still imported, and domestic suppliers primarily provide mechanical parts rather than electronics, according to industry data compiled by Nexdigm. The gap between where value currently sits and where the ecosystem aspires to be remains wide.

Bengaluru-based Zulu Defence offers one example of that shift. Founder Nagendran Kandasamy says the company differentiates itself through software architecture rather than hardware design. Instead of treating each drone as an independent product, the company develops systems that allow multiple assets to work together, share capabilities and function as a coordinated network.

One of its systems separates intelligence gathering from expendable platforms. Rather than placing expensive sensors and cameras on a drone intended for a one-time mission, those capabilities are mounted on a reusable platform that guides another asset towards its target. According to Kandasamy, the value lies in the software that enables different systems to communicate and coordinate effectively.

Warfare is Becoming a Software Problem

Recent conflicts have accelerated this shift. From Ukraine to West Asia, military planners have witnessed how autonomous systems, electronic warfare capabilities and software-driven operations can alter battlefield dynamics. In many cases, relatively inexpensive unmanned systems have challenged far costlier conventional assets.

Pattabiram argues that these developments have fundamentally changed where military advantage resides.

“If you take the West Asia war, for example, the whole game has changed to the radio spectrum, the electronic spectrum, the wireless spectrum,” he says. “It has changed to algorithm, software, and AI.”

His assessment suggests that military capability is increasingly shaped by factors that are often invisible to the public. Communications resilience, autonomous navigation, sensor fusion, artificial intelligence and radio-frequency dominance are becoming as important as aircraft, tanks or artillery.

The lesson has since been reinforced closer to home. Defence Secretary Rajesh Singh described Operation Sindoor as a “reality check” for the armed forces, saying the four-day conflict exposed specific capability gaps in electronic warfare, counter-UAV systems, and military-grade drones capable of operating in GPS-denied environments.

Speaking on the sidelines of the Defence Tech Seminar STRIDE, organised by the Indian Army’s Southern Command in Pune on 12 September 2025, he said, “certain capability gaps were noticed [during Operation Sindoor]. These include electronic warfare, counter-unmanned systems, a stronger manufacturing base for military-grade drones that can survive in GPS-denied and contested environments, and various types of low-level radars.”

The admission is significant. It is the clearest government acknowledgement yet that the gap lies not in airframes but in the software and electronics stack that determines how those platforms perform under adversarial conditions.

The scale of that gap became visible during the conflict itself. Industry sources told Swarajya Magazine that the government’s overnight demand for drones during Sindoor was nearly ten times what the domestic industry could supply, a shortfall that a deeper local supply chain would have allowed to be addressed in days rather than requiring a scramble for foreign alternatives.

Cyber Security Emerges as the Next Battleground

As autonomous systems become more sophisticated, cybersecurity is becoming inseparable from operational performance.

Much of India’s public discussion around drones has focused on localisation, procurement and manufacturing. Founders building military systems, however, increasingly point to software security as an area that requires equal attention.

Pattabiram argues that vulnerabilities often emerge through software and communications systems rather than through the aircraft itself. Referring to incidents involving compromised drones, he says the industry needs to focus more on secure autopilots, trusted computing architectures and resilient communications frameworks.

“There needs to be movement beyond that,” he says while discussing the challenges posed by electronic warfare and cyber threats.

Zulu Defence has responded to similar concerns by embedding encryption and anti-jamming technologies into its products. Kandasamy says the company is using high levels of encryption and multiple layers of protection to prevent unauthorised access and reduce the risk of hostile interference.

The significance of these capabilities extends beyond individual drones. As autonomous systems become increasingly networked, a successful cyber intrusion can affect entire operational chains rather than a single platform. Protecting software, communications and control systems is therefore becoming as important as improving range, payload or endurance.

Building Sovereign Defence Technologies

The growing emphasis on software is also reshaping discussions around technological sovereignty.

In India’s artificial intelligence ecosystem, much of the public debate centres on building domestic alternatives to large language models. Pattabiram argues that greater strategic value may lie in specialised technologies, in which India can establish differentiated capabilities.

“I think we need to identify specific areas where we can truly deliver value,” he says, pointing to defence autonomy, navigation technologies and secure operating architectures as examples of areas where domestic innovation could create long-term strategic advantages.

The challenge, however, extends beyond technology development.

Shivanghi Sukumar, an AI expert and competition lawyer, notes that the structure of defence procurement will play a significant role in determining which innovations ultimately succeed.

“The Indian government is effectively a monopsony in the defence drone market,” she says, arguing that procurement decisions can heavily influence which companies survive and scale. While operational requirements must remain stringent, she says procurement frameworks should also ensure that capable new entrants have a pathway to adoption.

Her observation highlights a broader reality facing the sector. Developing advanced software and autonomous capabilities is only one part of the challenge. Creating pathways for those technologies to be tested, deployed and scaled remains equally important.

India’s drone industry was built on manufacturing ambitions, and those ambitions remain important. Yet, the conversations emerging from across the ecosystem suggest that the next stage of development will be defined less by airframes and assembly lines and more by software, autonomy, cyber resilience and secure computing systems.

The companies that shape the future of defence technology may not necessarily be those producing the most drones. They may instead be the organisations building the operating systems, navigation architectures and intelligence layers that determine how autonomous systems function once they enter the battlefield.

title: Cyient Foundation Partners with Telangana Universities, Govt to Build Future Skills Ecosystem
content:
Cyient Foundation has proposed an investment of approximately ₹7.5 crore over three years.

What Actually Matters.

Cyient Foundation has initiated a collaborative programme with Telangana universities and government to enhance future skills and employability.

An investment of approximately ₹7.5 crore is planned over three years to support this initiative.

Cyient Foundation, the CSR arm of global technology company Cyient, has launched a major multi-stakeholder initiative with Telangana’s higher education institutions and government bodies to strengthen innovation, entrepreneurship, employability, and future-ready skills across the state.

The initiative, formalised through a series of memorandums of understanding (MoUs), brings together five state universities—Osmania University, Kakatiya University, Jawaharlal Nehru Technological University Hyderabad, Palamuru University, and Dr BR Ambedkar Open University—along with the Telangana government’s Commissionerate of Collegiate Education (CCE) and Commissionerate of Technical Education (CTE).

As part of the programme, Cyient Foundation has proposed an investment of approximately ₹7.5 crore over three years, subject to approvals and implementation milestones.

The initiative aims to create a scalable model for industry-academia-government collaboration focused on entrepreneurship, faculty development, innovation ecosystems, mentorship, and employability.

The programme will reach 152 government degree colleges and 59 government polytechnics through partnerships with the CCE and CTE, providing students across urban and rural Telangana with access to industry exposure, skill development, and entrepreneurship opportunities.

Speaking on the initiative, Dr BVR Mohan Reddy, Founder Chairman, Cyient, said, "This initiative reflects our belief that meaningful collaboration between government, academia, and industry can transform aspirations into opportunities. By empowering students, faculty, and communities across Telangana, we are not just creating skilled professionals—we are enabling future innovators, job creators, and nation-builders."

A major focus of the initiative will be preparing students for emerging technologies and future industry demands.

Training programmes will cover areas such as generative AI, data analytics, robotics and automation, Internet of Things (IoT), drone technology, GIS and geospatial technologies, Industry 4.0, cloud technologies, and certification-led learning pathways.

The Foundation will also establish three Rural Skill Development Centres at Palamuru University and Dr BR Ambedkar Open University in Narayanpet, Mahabubnagar, and Warangal. The centres are expected to train around 600 youth annually, with a focus on healthcare, electronics manufacturing, and digital commerce. The programme aims to ensure more than 50% participation from women while improving employment outcomes.

In parallel, the Entrepreneurship Development Programme (EDP) is expected to reach over 4,000 students every year, with around 400 participants receiving structured entrepreneurship training. The initiative is projected to generate nearly 200 business ideas and 40 startup teams annually.

To strengthen Telangana’s innovation ecosystem, the programme will also support 20–25 startups each year through incubation and mentorship, with an estimated 5–10 startups progressing toward commercialisation annually. Additionally, more than 200 faculty members will be trained, while over 50 industry experts will be engaged as mentors.

The initiative is expected to create a strong pipeline of skilled professionals, entrepreneurs, innovators, and job creators while positioning Telangana’s higher education institutions as key drivers of innovation-led and inclusive economic growth.

BharatGen will immediately begin co-leading workstreams on distributed model training as part of Project Tapestry. The initiative seeks to bring together data, compute resources, talent, and funding from multiple countries and organisations to develop frontier AI systems while preserving national ownership and control.

“India has long believed that science advances fastest when it is open and shared. Project Tapestry, which lets nations build frontier AI together while retaining sovereignty over their data and models, reflects the collaborative, self-reliant innovation India is advancing,” said Professor Ajay Sood, Principal Scientific Adviser to the Government of India.

The project is built around a distributed development architecture in which a base model is developed centrally and then adapted by participating organisations using local data. Participants can contribute improvements back to the shared model while retaining ownership of their data and any derivative models they create.

“As India builds frontier AI rooted in its own languages and knowledge, IIT Bombay and BharatGen, supported by the India AI mission, are proud to support and participate as a founding contributor in Project Tapestry, an open, global consortium for nations to advance frontier AI together,” said Shireesh Kedare, Director of IIT Bombay and Chairman of BharatGen.

Project Tapestry was launched last month during a technical workshop in Paris attended by around 30 AI leaders from countries including the United States, France, India, Vietnam, Japan, Switzerland, and the United Arab Emirates. Participants included organisations such as Pleias, PRAIRE, AMI Labs, Software Heritage, and Current AI.

According to the AI Alliance, the initiative is designed to enable countries and institutions to collaborate on AI development without transferring sensitive datasets to a centralised provider.

“AI is becoming essential infrastructure. No single company or country should determine who can build on it, adapt it, or benefit from it. Project Tapestry is a test of whether frontier AI can be built as open infrastructure: collaborative, capable, and sovereign by design,” said Dr Yann LeCun, Chief Science Advisor of the AI Alliance and Executive Chairman of AMI Labs.

Vietnam has also emerged as an early participant in the project. The National Innovation Center and FPT Corporation are working with Project Tapestry to develop AI systems aligned with Vietnamese language, culture, and industry requirements while maintaining local ownership and governance.

“With the National Innovation Center and FPT Corporation engaged, Project Tapestry gives Vietnam a path to help build frontier AI that reflects its language, culture, industries, and institutions while retaining control over its own data, models, and deployment,” said Dr Christopher Nguyen, Chief Architect of Project Tapestry and CEO of Aitomatic.

The AI Alliance said future AI capabilities will increasingly depend on access to scientific, technical, industrial, and national datasets that are often unavailable on the open web. Project Tapestry aims to create a framework for using such data in AI development without requiring organisations to surrender control over it.

“Project Tapestry aims to build the most capable frontier AI possible in a way that ensures the value and control of that AI is retained by those developing and deploying it—whether they are in industry, government, a non-profit or an individual,” said Dr Anthony Annunziata, Chairman of the AI Alliance and Director of AI Open Innovation at IBM.

title: Nobel-Winning AlphaFold Scientist John Jumper Leaves Google DeepMind for Anthropic
content:
For his work on AlphaFold, Jumper shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry with Demis Hassabis and scientist David Baker.

What Actually Matters.

John Jumper, a Nobel Prize-winning scientist, is leaving Google DeepMind to join AI startup Anthropic.

He expressed gratitude for his time at Google DeepMind and credited Demis Hassabis for his leadership opportunity.

John Jumper, the Nobel Prize-winning scientist behind AlphaFold, has announced that he is leaving Google DeepMind after nearly nine years to join AI startup Anthropic.

In a post on X, Jumper wrote, “After nearly 9 years, I have decided to leave Google DeepMind and join Anthropic (after taking some time to recharge).”

He added that he was ‘incredibly grateful’ for his time at the company and credited Google DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis for giving him the opportunity to lead the AlphaFold team shortly after completing his PhD.

“Demis Hassabis took a real chance letting me lead the AlphaFold team just six months after finishing my PhD, and the entire GDM team taught me so much about how to do great science,” he wrote.

Jumper’s departure comes amid an intensifying competition among leading AI companies, including Anthropic, OpenAI, Google DeepMind and Meta to recruit top research talent. His move follows the recent exit of Gemini co-lead Noam Shazeer from Google to OpenAI.

Best known as the co-creator of AlphaFold, Jumper helped build the AI system that transformed structural biology by accurately predicting protein structures from amino acid sequences. AlphaFold has predicted more than 200 million protein structures, creating a publicly accessible database that researchers use to accelerate biological research and drug discovery.

For his work on AlphaFold, Jumper shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry with Hassabis and scientist David Baker.

Responding to Jumper’s announcement, Hassabis praised his longtime colleague’s contributions. “What we achieved with AlphaFold changed the world, and showed the field what was possible with AI for science and medicine,” he wrote on X.

Neither Jumper nor Anthropic disclosed the role he will assume at Anthropic. The hire is expected to strengthen the company’s scientific research ambitions. Anthropic is scheduled to host a science-focused event later this month.

In his farewell message, Jumper described Google DeepMind as ‘a special place’ and said he would continue to follow the lab’s future discoveries with enthusiasm.

title: Keralam Bets Big on AI, GenZ Startups, Geospatial Intelligence in Revised Budget 2026
content:
One of the headline announcements is a ₹50 crore programme designed to nurture young entrepreneurs and innovators in Keralam.

What Actually Matters.

Keralam's revised 2026-27 Budget includes a ₹50 crore initiative to support GenZ entrepreneurs and innovators.

The state aims to modernise governance through a pioneering geospatial intelligence programme.

Keralam has unveiled an ambitious technology-driven growth strategy in its revised 2026-27 Budget, announcing a dedicated ₹50 crore fund for GenZ entrepreneurs, a pioneering Malayalam AI initiative, and a state-wide geospatial intelligence programme aimed at modernising governance.

Presenting his maiden Budget in the Legislative Assembly, Chief Minister VD Satheesan, who also holds the finance portfolio, acknowledged the state's fiscal challenges but outlined a long-term roadmap focused on innovation, entrepreneurship, digital transformation, and infrastructure development to build a “New Age Kerala.”

One of the headline announcements is a ₹50 crore programme designed to nurture young entrepreneurs and innovators. The initiative will connect GenZ talent with startups, research institutions, and innovation centres, while encouraging participation in emerging fields such as artificial intelligence, robotics, data science, the Internet of Things (IoT), and virtual reality.

The Budget also places significant emphasis on ensuring Malayalam remains relevant in the AI era. To ensure the language is not left behind as artificial intelligence systems evolve, the government has allocated ₹10 crore to create an open Malayalam language dataset and the development of indigenous AI models tailored to the language.

In a first-of-its-kind move, Keralam has established a dedicated Artificial Intelligence portfolio that will bring together AI policy formulation, startup promotion, research, innovation, and ethical oversight under a single framework. The minister in charge of the portfolio is PK Kunhalikutty.

Another major initiative announced in the Budget is Mission Geo Keralam, which seeks to integrate geospatial intelligence into governance and public administration. Under the programme, the Kerala State Remote Sensing and Environment Centre will be transformed into the state's nodal geospatial agency and will lead the development of an integrated Kerala Geospatial Intelligence System.

The proposed platform will leverage AI, spatial data, and real-time analytics to improve decision-making across government departments, making geospatial intelligence a core component of governance and public service delivery.

The announcements reflect Keralam's broader strategy of using technology, innovation, and entrepreneurship as key drivers of economic growth while simultaneously strengthening public service delivery and creating new opportunities for the state's youth.

title: Researchers Have Found a New Way to Enhance AI Performance Across Image Editing, Drug Discovery
content:
Beyond creative applications, the technology has potential uses in molecular design, drug discovery, and scientific simulations where precise modelling is critical.

What Actually Matters.

Researchers at Clarkson University developed a new mathematical framework called Rex to enhance AI performance.

Rex improves accuracy and control in applications like image editing and drug discovery by refining diffusion and flow-matching models.

Researchers at Clarkson University, US, have developed a new mathematical framework that could make artificial intelligence systems more accurate and controllable across applications ranging from image editing to drug discovery and scientific simulations.

The framework, called Rex, was created by Zander Blasingame, a postdoctoral researcher, and Chen Liu, Professor of Electrical and Computer Engineering at Clarkson University. Their research paper, “Rex: A Family of Reversible Exponential (Stochastic) Runge-Kutta Solvers,” has been selected for presentation at the International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML) 2026, one of the world’s leading AI conferences.

The new framework focuses on improving diffusion and flow-matching models, which form the foundation of many modern generative AI systems, including image generators, molecular design tools, and scientific simulators. These models typically work by transforming random noise into useful outputs such as images or molecular structures.

While this process is effective for generating new content, many applications require AI systems to reverse it and recover the original information. Existing methods often introduce errors during this step, limiting accuracy and control.

According to the researchers, Rex addresses this challenge by aligning the forward and reverse processes more closely, enabling AI systems to retrace their steps with significantly greater precision.

“One important application of exact inversion solvers is round-trip image editing. While all reversible methods accumulate some numerical error, Rex achieves orders-of-magnitude lower inversion error than competing approaches,” Blasingame said in a statement.

The researchers said the framework could lead to more precise image-editing tools by allowing users to modify AI-generated images while preserving important details. Beyond creative applications, the technology could also improve molecular simulations used in chemistry and drug discovery, where accurately modelling complex processes is critical.

A key advantage of the framework is that it can be integrated into existing diffusion and flow-matching models without requiring developers to redesign entire AI systems. This could make adoption easier for researchers and companies already working with generative AI technologies.

title: If AI Can't Accelerate Accenture’s Growth, Does it Leave Hope for Anyone Else?
content:
SingleStore claimed it has been running unified operational and analytical workloads in production since 2019.

What Actually Matters.

SingleStore claims it has been providing unified operational and analytical workloads since 2019.

Raj Verma criticises Databricks for suggesting it was the first to unify databases.

SingleStore CEO Raj Verma has pushed back against Databricks’ claim that it is among the first to unify transactional and analytical databases, arguing that SingleStore has been delivering that capability to enterprise customers for years.

“We agree with Ali Ghodsi at Databricks that unifying transactional and analytical databases is the way to go,” Verma wrote in a LinkedIn post. “But it’s a stretch to say they are the first ones to solve it.”

Verma also criticised what he described as Databricks’ approach to openness, saying the company was promoting a ‘lock-in’ architecture disguised as open source.

He added that the market would ultimately decide the winner based on execution and performance. “Performance is what matters,” Verma wrote. “Let the best solution win.”

The comments came a day after Databricks unveiled Lakebase, its serverless PostgreSQL database, and Lakehouse//RT, a real-time analytics engine, at its Data + AI Summit 2026.

Databricks CEO Ali Ghodsi argued during his keynote that enterprises continue to maintain separate systems for transactional and analytical workloads and called for a unified architecture.

In a blog post titled ‘Welcome to the Party, Databricks’, SingleStore said Databricks’ vision validates a category it has been building since 2019.

“When Ghodsi says customers want one data copy, fewer pipelines, lower latency, and analytics on fresh operational data, he is describing exactly why SingleStore exists,” the company wrote.

SingleStore argued that Databricks’ Lakehouse Transactional and Analytical Processing (LTAP) architecture relies on two separate engines—a transactional layer powered by Lakebase and an analytical layer powered by the Lakehouse platform—sharing a common storage layer.

“Sharing a storage layer is not the same as a unified query engine,” the company said. “SingleStore runs transactions, analytics, ingestion, search, and application-serving workloads in one distributed SQL engine.”

The database vendor also questioned Databricks’ reliance on PostgreSQL compatibility for transactional workloads, arguing that modern AI applications and agents require systems designed for horizontal scalability.

“Handling 10,000 concurrent agent sessions while simultaneously running analytical joins on live operational data was not on the original design brief,” SingleStore wrote. “Agents need broad operational context at low latency, under high concurrency, from a system that scales horizontally when load spikes.”

SingleStore further challenged the benchmarks presented for Lakehouse//RT, arguing that the headline latency figures were based on TPC-H Q6, a benchmark involving a single-table scan and aggregation rather than complex joins.

‘The millisecond headline is Q6. The joint performance claim is relative and unverifiable," the company said. “Neither, together, proves that Lakehouse//RT handles concurrent writes, operational reads, analytical joins, and agent/application load in one engine.”

The company maintained that enterprises are looking for a platform capable of handling transactions, analytics, search and application serving on a single data foundation.

“Databricks validated the problem. SingleStore built the database that solves it,” the company said.

AI bookings are surging at Accenture, yet it has cut growth guidance as demand remains uneven.

What Actually Matters.

Accenture lowered its full-year revenue growth guidance despite strong AI bookings, indicating uneven demand.

New bookings for Accenture declined by 2% in dollar terms, reaching their lowest in six quarters.

Accenture's latest earnings delivered an uncomfortable message for investors betting on an AI-driven boom in technology services.

The Irish tech giant reported third-quarter fiscal 2026 revenue of $18.7 billion on June 18, up 6% in dollar terms and 3% in local currency.

Diluted earnings per share rose 9% to $3.80, operating margin expanded 20 basis points to 17%, and the company returned $2.2 billion to shareholders during the quarter. On those metrics alone, the results read as upbeat.

However, new bookings, the order book that determines what Accenture will actually bill in the next 12-18 months, fell 2% in dollar terms and 3% in local currency, to $19.3 billion. This was the lowest booking level in six quarters. Also, in the most telling move, Accenture trimmed its full-year revenue growth guidance to 3–4% in local currency, down from the 3–5% range it had set in March.

That slowdown in enterprise IT spending on account of AI projects greatly troubled investors. Accenture’s stock plunged to its lowest level since 2017, down 17.97% on the New York Stock Exchange at the close trading day on June 18.

The lower guidance troubled Indian IT stocks too.

By Friday morning, Dalal Street saw a week's worth of gains in IT stocks wiped out. India's Nifty IT index fell more than 5% within the first hour of trade on June 19, with TCS, Infosys, HCLTech, and Wipro all down, dragging the broader Nifty 50 and Sensex out of a five-session winning streak.

What Actually Went Wrong

Accenture's leadership was candid about two specific drags on the quarter.

First, CEO Julie Sweet told analysts that the Middle East conflict shaved roughly $100 million off revenue, entirely from consulting work. The impact was split between a direct hit to Accenture's regional business and a knock-on effect on discretionary spending elsewhere, particularly in the Products and Resources industry groups, as clients pulled back during the final weeks of the quarter. Separately, the company's sales pipeline in the Gulf and wider EMEA region took a $400 million hit as clients delayed decision-making.

Second, a handful of large managed-services contracts—deals in the $300 million to $500 million range—slipped out of this fiscal year and into FY27, for what Sweet described as company-specific reasons rather than a broader deterioration in demand.

Citi's Bryan Keane estimated the slippage at more than $2 billion. Sweet responded that the timing shift would not meaningfully boost fourth-quarter results because the deals had moved further out rather than merely later into the fiscal year.

AI Bookings are Rising But Not Revenue Growth

Accenture said it added approximately 100 new clients running advanced AI projects during the quarter and that bookings tied to its key AI and data partners—a group that includes Anthropic, OpenAI, Google's Gemini, NVIDIA, Databricks, Palantir, Snowflake, and Mistral—are on track to more than double compared with fiscal year 2025.

The company also said it now has 104 clients with bookings of $100 million or more so far this fiscal year, up 13% from the same period last year. “This is one of the best indicators of the depth of our client relationships and the scale of the reinvention programmes we are helping deliver,” Sweet said.

Gaurav Vasu, Founder of the Bengaluru-based technology services and consulting firm UnearthInsight, tells AIM that the results reinforce the view that discretionary technology spending remains constrained despite the industry's increasingly aggressive AI narrative.

Accenture continues to gain market share in BFSI and the consumer segment, he notes, but its own guidance suggests demand remains uneven, with clients spending selectively rather than broadly.

“AI has yet to materially alter the industry's underlying economics. If Accenture—the largest technology services company globally, with the deepest consulting capabilities, strong hyperscaler partnerships, and an advanced AI positioning—is still delivering organic growth in the low-single-digit range, it raises questions about how much AI is currently translating into incremental industry revenue,” he ponders.

What it Means for Indian IT

For Indian IT, the read-through from Accenture's results remains worrying. Accenture's continued market share gains indicate that available spending is being concentrated among a smaller set of stronger vendors rather than expanding across the industry.

It has already spent $9 billion in acquisitions in the current fiscal year, spurring debate over organic versus inorganic growth.

If Accenture's organic growth remains subdued despite its consulting advantage and AI positioning, Vasu believes that means the AI-led recovery in technology services demand that the market has been anticipating is still some distance away.

According to him, Indian IT services growth is likely to remain in the 3–4% range, with acquisitions and other inorganic initiatives contributing a meaningful share of that growth while a recovery in discretionary spending stays gradual.

That assessment is broadly consistent with commentary from Indian IT companies themselves, most of which have entered the fiscal year with muted growth expectations and limited visibility on a broader demand recovery.

Enterprises in India face up to 11,000 compliance instances annually from over 3.2 million regulatory websites. TeamLease RegTech is deploying AI to shift compliance from reactive record-keeping to predictive, intelligence-driven risk management for businesses nationwide.

What Actually Matters.

Indian enterprises face a daunting compliance burden, with up to 11,000 instances annually from over 3.2 million regulatory websites.

TeamLease RegTech is leveraging AI to transform compliance from a reactive process to a proactive, intelligence-driven risk management approach.

In the past year alone, TeamLease RegTech tracked approximately 13,000 regulatory changes across India's sprawling web of government websites, a figure that offers a glimpse into the staggering compliance burden facing Indian enterprises today.

That number comes from monitoring over 3,756 odd websites publishing regulatory updates from union, state, and local bodies, spanning departments covering labour, finance, environment, electricity, food regulation, legal metrology, and dozens of other domains. For most businesses, keeping pace with this torrent of mandates, amendments, and new obligations is not merely difficult—it is, without the right systems, nearly impossible.

The Scale of the Problem

To understand just how complex regulatory compliance has become for Indian enterprises, consider a mid-sized food-processing company which is neither a conglomerate nor a start-up, with two plants, two offices, and a handful of warehouses. According to a recent TeamLease RegTech report, such a company faces roughly 3,200 unique compliance obligations in a year.

When frequency is factored in—daily, weekly, monthly, quarterly, and annual filings—the total swells to approximately 11,000 compliance instances annually.

With around 250 working days in a year, that translates to 13 unique obligations and nearly 50 total compliance tasks every single day, for just one entity.

Rishi Agrawal, Chief Executive Officer of TeamLease RegTech, says the sheer fragmentation of India’s regulatory architecture is what makes this so hard to manage. “Obligations are multi-locational, multi-entity, multi-state. They involve different forms, formats, calculations, duty structures, and penalties. The volume and fragmentation together make it very difficult and very risky for large enterprises to cope, especially when they are relying on manual or spreadsheet-based workflows.”

The information asymmetry compounds the problem. Regulatory updates are frequently buried multiple levels deep within departmental websites, and technical issues like documents that fail to load, pages that time out, which make even basic access a challenge. Large enterprises can deploy sizeable teams to monitor these changes; smaller businesses and MSMEs typically cannot.

When Spreadsheets Stop Working

For years, many Indian enterprises have managed compliance through a combination of spreadsheets, email chains, and in-house legal teams. At a certain scale, that approach begins to fracture.

TeamLease RegTech’s platform currently serves around 3,200 entities and processed 25 million compliance instances last year. Those instances generated approximately five million pieces of compliance evidence—licences, consents, registrations, returns, challans, registers, no-objection certificates, exemptions, and more.

Agrawal is direct about where manual systems fail. “For organisations dealing with thousands of unique obligations, tens of thousands of annual instances, and continuous regulatory change, manual or spreadsheet tracking cannot reliably capture all requirements, track all deadlines and changes, or maintain evidences and versions. At that scale, the risk of missed obligations and penalties becomes systemic, not incidental.”

Until recently, compliance technology has largely served as a system of record—logging who did what, where, and when, and answering reactive questions such as what is pending, with whom, and for how long. That is now beginning to change.

Building Intelligence Into Compliance

TeamLease RegTech is positioning itself at the intersection of compliance and artificial intelligence, moving its platform from a passive repository of records towards what Agrawal describes as a system of intelligence.

The premise is straightforward: the platform already holds vast amounts of structured compliance data. Applied correctly, AI can turn that data into foresight rather than hindsight.

“We are using the data already in the system to find patterns, highlight risk hotspots, and identify weak links in people, processes, and documents,” Agrawal explains. “The goal is to move from simply recording what has happened to predicting what is likely to go wrong—and preventing it before it does.”

In practical terms, this means the platform can now identify which licences or registrations are at risk of lapsing before renewal applications have been filed, flag documents that do not match current statutory formats, and catch mismatches such as a GST return filed for the wrong month or a discrepancy between a company name and its GST number.

The AI layer also performs pre-submission validation—checking, for instance, whether all mandatory fields in a form have been completed, or whether the correct version of a statutory document has been used. Agrawal describes this as being “compliant at the root”, addressing errors before they reach the regulator rather than after.

Benchmarking and Behavioural Analytics

Beyond flagging individual errors, the platform is beginning to offer enterprise-level behavioural analytics. Companies can be benchmarked against peers—anonymously and without exposing any other customer’s data—on overall compliance performance.

“We can tell a retailer, for example, that they are in the bottom quartile of compliance behaviour among 18 similar companies on our platform,” Agrawal says. “That kind of context changes how leadership thinks about the issue. It is no longer just an administrative function—it becomes a question of competitive risk.”

The system can also identify patterns within an organisation: which individuals are most likely to cause compliance failures in the coming months, which acts or regulations are most vulnerable for a particular enterprise, and which locations or entities show problematic behaviour over time.

For boards and senior management, these are not abstract concerns. Non-compliance in India can result in licence cancellations, factory closures, and, in certain cases, personal liability for directors.

Uneven Adoption, Clear Direction

Despite the technology’s potential, Agrawal acknowledges that AI adoption within enterprise compliance remains patchy. Most organisations today use artificial intelligence in a superficial manner—querying generic tools for quick answers rather than embedding AI into core compliance workflows.

“A lot of companies are still at the stage of going to a general-purpose AI tool, asking a question, and getting a response. That is the extent of it. What we are building is domain-specific, deeply embedded, and connected to real enterprise data,” he says.

The distinction matters. Generic AI tools have no visibility into a company’s specific obligations, deadlines, or historical compliance behaviour. Domain-specific platforms, by contrast, can combine regulatory knowledge with enterprise data to generate insights that are immediately actionable.

TeamLease RegTech’s direction—from system of record to system of intelligence—reflects a broader shift in how compliance is being reconceived. Rather than a reactive, documentation-heavy exercise, it is increasingly being treated as a live risk management function, one that demands continuous monitoring, predictive analytics, and pre-emptive action.

With 13,000 regulatory changes tracked in a single year—and that number unlikely to shrink—the appetite for such intelligence, among enterprises of all sizes, is only set to grow.

title: Reliance Approves Jio IPO, Paving the Way for One of India’s Largest Public Listings
content:
The planned IPO comes as Reliance accelerates investments in artificial intelligence, data centres and AI-generated media content through its various businesses.

What Actually Matters.

Jio Platforms has announced plans for an IPO, potentially one of India's largest public listings.

The IPO demonstrates India's capability to build technology companies of global scale and value.

Jio Platforms, the telecom and digital services arm of Reliance Industries, has announced plans for an initial public offering (IPO) that could be among the largest share sales in India’s history.

Speaking at Reliance Industries’ annual general meeting, Chairman Mukesh Ambani said the company’s board had approved the draft prospectus for Jio’s public listing. While the company has not yet disclosed the offer size or valuation, media reports estimate that the IPO could raise around $4 billion.

“The proposed listing of Jio will demonstrate to the world that India can build technology companies of global scale, global capability, and global value,” Ambani said during the meeting.

Launched in 2016, Jio disrupted India’s telecom sector with low-cost mobile data plans and quickly grew into the country’s largest telecom operator. The company now serves more than 500 million subscribers and has expanded into cloud computing, enterprise solutions, artificial intelligence and digital infrastructure.

The IPO announcement comes after months of anticipation. Ambani had previously indicated that Jio would go public in the first half of 2026.

The development follows another significant move in India’s capital markets. The National Stock Exchange (NSE) recently filed draft papers for its own long-awaited IPO, which is expected to raise more than $3 billion. Together, the Jio and NSE listings could rank among the country’s largest public offerings in recent years.

Jio’s public market debut also comes as Reliance accelerates its ambitions beyond telecommunications into artificial intelligence and digital infrastructure. Earlier this month, Meta announced plans to lease capacity at an AI-enabled data centre being built by Reliance in Gujarat. The facility is expected to have a capacity of 168 megawatts and builds on Meta’s $5.7 billion investment in Jio in 2020.

Reliance’s AI ambitions are also extending into media and entertainment. Recently, JioStar, the media joint venture between Reliance Industries and Disney, announced plans to expand its AI-generated content efforts following the success of its AI-produced series Mahabharat: Ek Dharmayudh, which reportedly attracted 6.5 million views on its first day. The company is now developing several AI-led productions, including Makaraj, a new television series, Hanuman, a feature film based on the Ramayana, and multiple short-form dramas. JioStar is also looking to hire around 80 AI specialists and engineers to support its growing AI content strategy.

Ambani asserted that Jio's listing will demonstrate to the world that India can build technology companies of global scale, capability, and value. “India should not be a mere consumer of AI created elsewhere, it must become a creator, adopter, & global leader in AI,” he added.

According to investment bank Jefferies, Jio was valued at around $180 billion last year, potentially making it one of the world’s most valuable telecom companies. The proposed listing would also mark Reliance Group’s first major public offering since Reliance Petroleum’s listing in 2006.

Hexaware plans to create nearly 1,000 high-skilled jobs over the next three years.

What Actually Matters.

GIFT City is an offshore financial hub that bypasses Indian regulatory controls and operates in foreign currencies.

It allows international financial institutions and corporations to move capital in and out of India seamlessly.

Beyond Mumbai, GIFT City (Gujarat International Finance Tec-City) is emerging as a thriving hub for financial services by addressing the critical friction points that limit traditional financial hubs.

It overcomes strict regulatory capital controls imposed by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) by operating as a legally distinct, offshore jurisdiction. It acts as an International Financial Services Centre (IFSC) that trades and settles transactions almost exclusively in foreign currencies. There are over 1,034 institutions operating within IFSC alone.

“This setup creates a seamless gateway that allows international banks, alternative investment funds (AIFs), and multinational corporations to bypass standard local exchange regulations and move capital into and out of India without currency translation delays,” observes Alouk Kumar, CEO, Inductus Group, in a conversation with AIM.

Among them is IT consulting firm Hexaware Technologies, which has inaugurated a new delivery centre at GIFT City as a global hub for banking, financial services and insurance (BFSI) innovation. The centre is expected to play a key role in delivering digital transformation, artificial intelligence (AI), cloud modernisation, data engineering, and next-generation software services to Hexaware’s global clientele.

The company plans to create nearly 1,000 high-skilled jobs over the next three years, spanning software engineering, AI, cloud computing, digital transformation, data analytics, business operations, and customer experience services.

Moreover, the move adds to GIFT City’s appeal as a competitive destination, not just for digital and financial services, but now also for IT innovation.

Speaking about the rationale behind the investment, Vikash Kumar Jain, Chief Financial Officer of Hexaware Technologies, tells AIM that GIFT City provides an ecosystem specifically designed for international financial services operations.

“GIFT City suits the kind of work our global BFSI clients are asking us to take on. As India’s first and only operational IFSC, it gives us a setting built specifically for financial services, with a regulatory environment geared to cross-border activity,” Jain says.

Jain further highlights that the centre is set up to serve global clients. “Demand from these clients keeps growing as banks and insurers modernise their systems, and GIFT City gives us a base to meet that demand and add to our global delivery network,” he notes.

“The physical, fiscal, and regulatory ecosystem of this offshore zone gives it a sharp operational advantage over other Indian financial centres. By replacing the multi-layered, bureaucratic web with a single, consolidated authority, the International Financial Services Centres Authority (IFSCA), GIFT City has drastically accelerated corporate onboarding and product approvals,” Kumar adds.

The IFSCA is responsible for developing and regulating financial products, services, and institutions within IFSCs.

GIFT City’s financial scale reflects this regulatory ease: banking assets within the IFSC have grown 7x in five years, rising to over $106 billion, alongside total commitments raised by fund management entities surpassing $32 billion. It operates as a highly specialised, cost-effective portal explicitly optimised for international derivative trading, global treasury management, and offshore financing, handling high monthly exchange turnovers that clear $100 billion in May.

By offshoring a slice of the regulatory landscape while remaining geographically tied to one of the world's fastest-growing economies, GIFT City significantly recaptures the massive volume of India-centric business that historically went straight to competing global zones like Dubai or Singapore.

To secure global competitiveness, the hub offers an aggressive tax neutrality framework that includes a tax holiday for 10 consecutive years within a 15-year window, complete exemption from localised levies like the Goods and Services Tax (GST) and stamp duties, and an estimated 20% reduction in operating costs, per the Gujarat government.

Gujarat Emerging as a Strategic Talent Hub

Beyond infrastructure and policy advantages, Hexaware sees Gujarat as a long-term strategic destination for technology talent.

“GIFT City presents a compelling proposition for a company of Hexaware’s focus and scale. The financial services landscape, the quality of talent, and the policy framework the state government has put in place made this a clear decision for us,” Jain says.

The company expects a significant portion of its future workforce to be sourced locally, helping create opportunities for professionals outside traditional technology hubs such as Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Pune, and Chennai.

“We plan to hire around 1,000 professionals over the next three years. A good share of that will be sourced locally as we build capability closer to emerging talent pools. The emphasis is less on headcount than on the high-value skills that support our delivery for clients,” Jain explains.

The launch also reflects a broader shift taking place across the global capability centre (GCC) and IT services landscape. As enterprises increasingly seek business outcomes rather than operational support, delivery centres are evolving into strategic innovation hubs.

“Whether it is a GCC or a service provider, clients now expect teams to drive AI adoption and modernisation and to solve hard business problems, rather than simply add capacity,” he observes.

Jain describes Hexaware’s investment as being closely aligned with the broader objectives behind GIFT City.

“GIFT City is a government-backed initiative, and an investment like ours is part of what gives it momentum. Our presence brings skilled jobs and international business activity into the state, which is precisely the outcome the project was designed to create,” he says. “As more firms commit to the location, we expect GIFT City to weigh more heavily in India’s financial and digital economy over time.”

To systematically feed this sophisticated corporate demand, GIFT City has integrated an institutional pipeline that blends advanced academic research with live market operations.

The GIFT International Fintech Institute (GIFT IFI), an Asian Development Bank-backed initiative driven by a premier academic consortium including IIT Gandhinagar, Ahmedabad University, and the University of California, San Diego, trains specialists in blockchain rails, regtech, and automated risk engines.

Hexaware’s new delivery centre arrives at a time when financial institutions worldwide are rapidly investing in AI, automation, and cloud technologies to improve efficiency, customer experience, and operational resilience. According to the World Economic Forum, AI investments across banking, insurance, capital markets, and payments businesses are expected to reach $97 billion by 2027.

R Srikrishna, CEO and Executive Director of Hexaware, says the company’s expansion aligns closely with its broader strategy of staying closer to customers while leveraging India’s technology talent. “GIFT City represents a unique convergence of financial services, technology, and innovation,” he notes

title: China Will Have a Mythos-Class AI Model by Year-End, Says Z.ai Founder
content:
The release of GLM-5.2 has reignited discussion about how soon Chinese AI companies could rival the world's most advanced models.

What Actually Matters.

China is progressing rapidly towards advanced AI capabilities, potentially surpassing expectations.

The recent release of GLM-5.2 has intensified the conversation around Chinese AI models' competitiveness.

China may be much closer to achieving frontier AI capabilities than many industry observers expect, according to Jie Tang, Founder of Chinese AI startup Z.ai.

SpaceX CEO Elon Musk has forecasted that top Chinese large language models could reach the performance level of Anthropic’s newly released Claude Fable 5 by the first quarter of 2027. To which, Zhipu AI Co-Founder Tang Jie immediately pushed back, stating that Chinese models will get there sooner.

The exchange took place on X after a user asked about the timeline for Chinese AI models to achieve ‘Fable-class’ capabilities, citing the recent release of Z.ai's GLM-5.2.

The user argued that GLM-5.2 had already narrowed the gap with leading Western models, placing it roughly at the level of Claude Opus 4.7–4.8 with an estimated seven-month lag. Based on that assessment, the user suggested that China could reach ‘Fable’ status by late 2026.

“Possibly in the first quarter of 2027,” Musk responded.

Tang pushed back on that timeline, replying, “It won’t take that long.”

Anthropic recently unveiled Claude Fable 5 and the more powerful Claude Mythos 5, setting new standards in coding, reasoning, science, and agentic tasks. Days later, US export restrictions forced the company to withdraw the models from international markets.

In response to this, Z.ai launched GLM-5.2, its latest flagship model built for long-horizon coding, software engineering, and autonomous agent workflows.

The company claims the model delivers major improvements in agentic reasoning and complex engineering tasks, while supporting a context window of up to one million tokens.

According to Z.ai, GLM-5.2 is designed specifically for long-horizon tasks where AI systems must plan, reason, and execute over extended periods rather than generate isolated responses. The model introduces multiple reasoning modes and builds on the GLM-5 family launched earlier this year.

The release has intensified discussion around China’s progress in frontier AI.

According to benchmark results shared by Z.ai, GLM-5.2 outperforms OpenAI's GPT-5.5 on several coding and engineering evaluations, suggesting that Chinese AI labs are narrowing the gap with their US rivals.

Founded by computer scientist Jie Tang and originally known as Zhipu AI, Z.ai is widely regarded as one of China’s leading AI Tigers—a group of startups competing with firms such as DeepSeek, MiniMax, Moonshot AI, and Western leaders including OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google.

The company rebranded globally as Z.ai in 2025 and has increasingly focused on open-source releases and AI agents.

The company’s recent model releases have arrived at a rapid pace. GLM-5 debuted in February with a focus on agentic engineering and coding tasks, followed by GLM-5.1 in April, which expanded autonomous software engineering capabilities.

title: Midjourney Enters Healthcare With 60-Second Full-Body Scanner and Spa Concept
content:
Midjourney aims to deploy more than 50,000 scanners globally by 2031, with a capacity of up to 1 billion scans per month.

What Actually Matters.

Midjourney Medical introduces a full-body scanner using ultrasound technology to provide rapid health imaging in about 60 seconds.

The scanner can generate extensive health data, aiming to enhance access to personal health information through AI analysis.

Midjourney, the AI startup known for its image generation platform, has announced a new healthcare initiative called Midjourney Medical, unveiling plans to develop a full-body scanning system that uses ultrasound waves to create detailed images of the human body in about 60 seconds.

The company said the system, called the Midjourney Scanner, will provide users with more frequent access to health data by combining large-scale imaging with AI-based analysis. Alongside the scanner, Midjourney plans to launch a spa business where the scans will be integrated into regular wellness visits.

“We're building a bold new kind of machine to reimagine the foundations of healthcare and our relationships to our bodies,” the company said in its announcement.

According to Midjourney, the scanner works by lowering a person into a water-filled chamber through a ring containing approximately 500,000 ultrasonic transducers. These components act as both transmitters and receivers, sending sound waves through the body and collecting the resulting signals.

The company said the system generates terabytes of data every second, which are processed by a cluster of computers to reconstruct three-dimensional images of internal structures. Midjourney claims the resulting scans could offer MRI-like imaging at significantly higher speeds.

“The goal is for this process to take no more than 60 seconds. You go into the water, you come out of the water, and you're done,” the company said.

Midjourney said it has already produced reconstructed scan images showing various parts of the body, including the abdomen and thighs, alongside AI-generated segmentations that identify anatomical structures.

The company plans to open its first Midjourney Spa in San Francisco in 2027. The facility will include hot tubs, saunas, cold plunges, and scanning rooms, allowing visitors to undergo scans as part of routine spa visits.

“It should be a place you love going, whether it’s by yourself, or with friends,” Midjourney said. “The scans are a side-effect. You barely think of them when going to the spa. But suddenly, you have a huge library of data about your health.”

Over the next year, Midjourney plans to refine its hardware and imaging algorithms, conduct research trials, and build its first research facility. The company said a second-generation scanner is already in development, with a third-generation system planned for 2028 featuring custom silicon.

The company expects regulatory approvals to be a key milestone. Initially, the scanners will provide body composition maps, while additional diagnostic capabilities will require approval from the US Food and Drug Administration.

“We think it's completely possible that with enough early imaging in the future, the world could avoid 30% of all deaths and 50% of all healthcare costs,” the company said.

The announcement marks a significant expansion beyond Midjourney’s image-generation business. The company described itself as a “community-backed research lab” funded by users rather than investors and said it is exploring multiple long-term projects beyond healthcare.

Midjourney, founded in 2021 by David Holz, has built one of the most popular AI image-generation platforms without raising external funding. The company reportedly crossed $500 million in annual recurring revenue in 2025 while remaining fully self-funded.

title: Pramaana Labs Raises $27 Million in Seed Round Led by Khosla Ventures
content:
Indian agricultural robotics firm Niqo Robotics has been selected to represent India at the government’s flagship deep-tech conclave in France.

What Actually Matters.

Niqo Robotics is representing India at Bharat Innovates 2026 in France, selected from over 2,000 applicants.

The company focuses on AI-powered agricultural solutions, with products already in use in the US and India.

Bengaluru-based agricultural robotics company Niqo Robotics has been chosen to participate in Bharat Innovates 2026, the Indian government’s deep-tech conclave held in Nice, France, from June 14–16. The company is the only precision-AI farm robotics firm among the 120 participants selected from more than 2,000 applicants.

The event was inaugurated by Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and French President Emmanuel Macron. Bharat Innovates is designed to provide Indian deep-tech companies with access to global markets, investors, and industry partners.

Niqo Robotics develops AI-powered weeding, thinning and precision spraying systems for agricultural use. Its products are currently deployed commercially in the United States and India. The company is now looking to expand into Europe and Australia.

At the heart of its product range is Niqo Sense, a proprietary AI camera platform that can be integrated with multiple machine types and retrofitted onto existing farm equipment. The system processes plant-level decisions in real time without cloud connectivity, and the company claims more than 99% accuracy in field conditions. It operates on a one-time purchase model with no subscription fees, and includes 24/7 service support and locally stocked spare parts.

Speaking about the selection, Founder and Chief Executive Jaisimha Rao said the participation is an opportunity to demonstrate that India can build Physical AI products that are “technically advanced, commercially ready and relevant for farmers anywhere in the world”. He added that the company is seeking strategic investors and partners to help scale into European, Australian and other international agricultural markets.

Niqo describes its core AI-enabled weeding business as approaching self-sustainability, which the company attributes to repeat commercial demand and a focus on unit economics over scale.

France was chosen as the entry point into Europe partly because of its established agricultural sector and its position within Europe's agritech ecosystem. The company cited rising labour costs, tightening restrictions on chemical herbicides, and growing demand for precision automation as factors making European markets relevant for its technology.

title: Nearly a Quarter of AI Learners are Not Software Engineers, Says Scaler Report
content:
The report found that AI upskilling has led to an average salary increase of 147%, with early-career professionals recording the highest gains.

What Actually Matters.

AI skills are increasingly sought after by professionals from non-technical backgrounds, with nearly a quarter of learners coming from diverse fields.

The integration of AI into various sectors is creating career opportunities beyond traditional engineering roles, including consulting and finance.

Artificial intelligence is no longer a skill reserved for software engineers. A new report by AI-native technology company Scaler suggests that professionals from diverse educational and professional backgrounds are increasingly turning to AI to accelerate their careers and improve earning potential.

According to the India AI Workforce Report 2026, based on insights from 11,444 professionals, nearly 25% of AI learners now come from non-technical backgrounds. The report also found that more than half of AI-enabled career outcomes are emerging outside traditional engineering roles, including consulting, marketing, finance, human resources, academia, and leadership positions.

The findings highlight a broader shift in how AI is being adopted across India’s workforce. As organisations integrate AI into everyday operations, professionals are using AI skills to improve productivity and access new career opportunities.

Women are also playing a larger role in this transformation. The report found that women who transitioned into AI-enabled careers reported an average salary increase of 145%, while female quality assurance engineers recorded the highest gains at 574%.

The growth of AI learning is also spreading beyond metropolitan cities. Nearly one in five AI learners now comes from tier-2 cities such as Lucknow, Jaipur, Patna, Indore, Coimbatore, and Nagpur, signalling a wider distribution of AI talent across the country.

Bengaluru continues to lead India’s AI talent landscape accounting for 19% of learners, followed by Pune, Hyderabad, Mumbai, and Chennai.

The report further noted that AI upskilling has delivered significant career benefits with professionals reporting an average salary increase of 147%. Early-career professionals recorded the highest growth, with salaries increasing by an average of 155% after acquiring AI skills.

Commenting on the report, Abhimanyu Saxena, Co-founder at InterviewBit and Scaler, said that India’s AI talent story is becoming more inclusive and distributed. He added that while discussions around AI often focus on job displacement, the findings suggest that AI is creating new opportunities for professionals willing to adapt and learn new skills.

JPMorgan’s decision was linked to the wording of Anthropic’s licensing agreement and usage terms.

What Actually Matters.

JPMorgan has restricted access to Anthropic's Claude models for its Hong Kong employees due to licensing agreement concerns.

This decision aligns with similar restrictions implemented by Goldman Sachs in Hong Kong regarding Anthropic's terms of service.

JPMorgan Chase has blocked employees in Hong Kong from accessing Anthropic’s Claude models, according to a Financial Times report, making it the latest Wall Street bank to tighten controls on the use of advanced AI models in the Asian financial hub.

The move affects Claude models available through the bank’s internal platform, where employees can select from a list of approved large language models (LLMs). The report added that JPMorgan’s decision was linked to the wording of Anthropic’s licensing agreement and usage terms.

title: Anthropic Becomes First AI Startup to Join Frontier's Carbon Removal Initiative
content:
Anthropic joined Frontier, a carbon-removal coalition backed by major technology companies, as the group announced an additional $915 million in funding commitments.

What Actually Matters.

Anthropic is the first AI startup to join the Frontier carbon-removal coalition.

Frontier secured an additional $915 million in funding commitments, totalling nearly $1.8 billion.

Anthropic has become the first artificial intelligence startup to join Frontier, a coalition formed to accelerate carbon-removal technologies, as the group announced an additional $915 million in purchase commitments to scale the emerging industry.

The new funding brings Frontier's total commitments to nearly $1.8 billion, building on the $1 billion Advanced Market Commitment (AMC) launched in 2022 by companies including Google, Stripe, Shopify, and Meta. The coalition uses long-term purchasing commitments to support companies developing technologies that remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere.

Frontier said the new Growth AMC is designed to help promising carbon-removal companies scale beyond the pilot stage and reach commercial deployment. The coalition plans to focus on technologies capable of delivering carbon removal at a gigaton scale and expects future projects to demonstrate a pathway to government support or subsidy.

"The question today in carbon removal is whether demand will keep pace with that technology development," said Hannah Bebbington Valori, Head of Frontier, in a statement. She added that the new commitment was intended to ensure "the best companies can keep building at pace."

Anthropic's participation marks the first climate-focused initiative publicly announced by the AI company, whose rapid growth has, in part, led to increased scrutiny of AI's energy and environmental impact.

The coalition said it will concentrate investments on technologies it believes can scale most rapidly, including direct air capture, enhanced rock weathering, ocean alkalinity enhancement, and carbon-removal systems integrated into wastewater treatment facilities.

According to Frontier, more than 50 carbon-removal projects have already received support through the programme. The organisation has contracted nearly $700 million across projects designed to remove approximately 1.8 million tonnes of carbon dioxide.

The announcement also comes as AI companies face mounting pressure to address the environmental footprint of increasingly power-hungry data centres and large-scale AI models.

Frontier said the latest funding round reflects growing confidence that carbon-removal technologies will play a critical role in helping companies meet long-term climate goals, particularly for emissions that remain difficult to eliminate through conventional decarbonisation efforts.

title: Reliance Taps Databricks to Build Intelligence as Ambani Commits to Democratising AI
content:
Reliance Industries is working with Databricks to unify enterprise data across its businesses in India.

What Actually Matters.

Reliance Industries aims to democratise AI for all Indians, enhancing accessibility and opportunities.

The collaboration with Databricks focuses on unifying enterprise data for broader economic benefits.

Reliance Industries Chairman and Managing Director Mukesh Ambani has outlined the conglomerate's vision to make AI accessible to every Indian, as the company advances a large-scale data and AI transformation in partnership with Databricks.

Speaking at the Data + AI Summit 2026 hosted by Databricks, Ambani said Reliance's ambitions extend beyond deploying AI within its own businesses to democratising intelligence across the country.

"Our mission is to democratise intelligence for 1.5 billion Indians," Ambani said. "Our motto is simple. AI everywhere for everyone."

The billionaire industrialist said Reliance sees AI as a tool to create broader economic opportunities and improve access to essential services. "We want AI to create a more equal India, bring prosperity to every farmer, entrepreneur, and neighbourhood shopkeeper, transforming education, healthcare, and public services for every Indian," he said.

Ambani argued that India offers a unique environment for developing and testing AI applications."India is perhaps the most demanding test bed for AI because of our scale of aspirations, diversity, language needs, affordability constraints, and speed of adoption," he said. "Solutions that work for India [can] serve other [developing economies]."

Reliance is also deepening its focus on digital infrastructure and AI across its telecom, retail, energy, media and materials businesses. At the centre of that effort is a partnership with Databricks, the US-based data and AI platform provider. Ambani said the collaboration was driven by a broader strategic vision rather than a simple technology upgrade.

"Our ambition was not simply to modernise infrastructure. It was to build the foundation for innovation, productivity, customer value, and societal value," he said.

In a LinkedIn post during the summit, Nick Eayrs, Vice President of Field Engineering for Asia Pacific and Japan at Databricks, described Reliance's programme as "one of the world's largest data and AI transformations."

Reliance has migrated vast amounts of data from its telecom, retail, energy, media, and materials businesses onto a unified Databricks platform. Ambani also mentioned that leaders are already using Databricks Genie “to ask questions in natural language and receive useful intelligence in real time.”

He added that the platform is intended to provide a common data foundation across Reliance's businesses and support AI-powered analytics and natural-language access to enterprise data.

“Together with Databricks, we hope to create a blueprint for how enterprises can harness data and AI. Responsibly, openly and at scale,” he added.

The Reliance chairman also framed AI as an opportunity for emerging economies, arguing that technologies developed for India's scale and complexity could have applications across other developing markets.

"The Global South represents four-fifths of humanity," Ambani said, arguing that solutions built for India could ultimately serve countries facing similar challenges.

Reliance has been expanding its AI partnerships ever since it committed to invest ₹10 lakh crore ($110 billion) over seven years to build AI infrastructure. It is building an AI-ready data centre in Jamnagar, Gujarat and recently announced that it will lease the facility to Meta. The facility will operate fully on renewable energy and use desalinated seawater for cooling.

What Actually Matters.

US retail giant Target has leased over 8.3 lakh sq ft of office space in Bengaluru.

The 10-year agreement for their Global Capability Centre is valued at an estimated ₹1,250 crore.

US retail giant Target leased more than 8.3 lakh sq ft of office space at Embassy Manyata Business Park in north Bengaluru (owned by Embassy Office Parks REIT) last year under a 10-year agreement valued at an estimated ₹1,250 crore, expanding the footprint of its India-based global capability centre (GCC).

Property registration documents reviewed by AIM show that Target Corporation India has signed a fresh lease for 8,31,126 sq ft across the ground floor and 10 upper floors of a newly developed building, Gulmohar L4, at Manyata Embassy Business Park in Nagavara, Bengaluru.

The lease commenced on September 1, 2025, but the deed was registered in April 2026.

The office space has been leased from Manyata Promoters at a rental rate of ₹105 per sq ft per month, translating into a monthly rental outgo of about ₹8.73 crore. The agreement includes a security deposit of ₹52.36 crore and a 15% rent escalation every three years. Based on these terms, the total rental commitment over the lease tenure is estimated at around ₹1,250 crore.

Raja Seetharaman, Co-founder at Propstack, a real estate data analytics platform, said in a statement, “This underscores a growing trend among top-tier GCCs to scale up operations within familiar tech ecosystems.” He added that the multi-year commitment shows the enduring premium that dominant tech hubs like Bengaluru command for quality institutional real estate.

The transaction ranks among the largest office leasing deals signed by a multinational GCC in Bengaluru in recent months and underscores continued demand for large-format office campuses from global enterprises expanding their India operations.

Confirming the move, a Target in India spokesperson told AIM that this expansion is part of the company’s long-term real estate strategy to provide the right infrastructure and environmental support in the country.

“The new office space will be designed to provide a team member experience consistent with our existing facilities. It will offer the space and flexibility we need to meet the collaborative manner in which we work, and will be ready for occupation in late 2026,” the spokesperson added.

The new office is located adjacent to Target’s existing Bengaluru operations at Manyata Tech Park and is expected to support the Minneapolis-headquartered retailer’s growing technology, analytics, digital, and business services functions that serve its global business.

For Embassy REIT, the transaction adds to a series of large leasing deals that have helped maintain strong occupancy and leasing momentum across its portfolio. The REIT leased 6.4 million sq ft during FY26 and has reported continued demand from global occupiers, particularly GCCs.

The deal also highlights sustained demand for premium office space from multinational companies expanding their India-based capability centres. Bengaluru remains the country’s largest GCC market, attracting global corporations seeking technology talent and operational scale. According to a recent report by real estate consultancy Vestian, GCCs leased 31.8 million sq ft of office space across India’s top seven cities in 2024, accounting for 37% of total office absorption during the year.
