title: AI Already Performs 37% of Entry-Level Tasks in India, Cognizant-Pearson Study Finds
content:
In India, 63% of organisations have allocated time for AI training, compared with 49% in the United States.

What Actually Matters.

Artificial intelligence currently performs 37% of entry-level tasks in India, exceeding the global average.

Entry-level roles are evolving towards supervising AI systems rather than just executing tasks.

Artificial intelligence is already performing 37% of entry-level tasks in India, higher than the global average of 33%, according to a joint study released by Cognizant and Pearson on June 18.

The report, titled The AI Workforce Pulse: The Adaptability Imperative, surveyed 750 HR leaders across India, the United States and the United Kingdom. It found that 18% of HR leaders in India said AI now handles half or more of entry-level work.

The study suggests that entry-level roles are shifting from task execution to supervising and working alongside AI systems. Nearly all respondents (96%) expect entry-level jobs to evolve into roles that involve managing AI systems within the next five years, while 94% believe AI will create new entry-level positions that do not exist today.

The report also found that 98% of HR professionals are increasing their focus on AI skills, including for non-technical roles. Employees are increasingly expected to validate AI outputs, interpret results and apply human judgment.

“India is at the forefront of how AI is transforming entry-level work, with organisations already embedding AI into day-to-day operations at scale,” said Rajesh Varrier, Managing Director, Cognizant India. “We are seeing a fundamental redesign of roles, where early-career talent is expected to work alongside AI and focus on higher-value outcomes.”

The findings also point to a growing emphasis on human and interdisciplinary skills. Nearly all respondents (97%) said soft skills have become more important as AI automates routine work. About 69% of HR leaders globally and 65% in India said broad, interdisciplinary backgrounds are now more valuable for early-career talent than highly specialised degrees.

In addition, two-thirds of respondents said they value liberal arts degrees more than they did before the rise of AI.

While demand for AI skills is increasing, organisations continue to face challenges in workforce preparation. The study found that 91% of HR professionals reported increased employee demand for AI training over the past year, while 60% said their learning and development programs are unable to keep pace with the rate of change.

In India, 63% of organisations have allocated time for AI training, compared with 49% in the United States. However, 61% reported difficulties finding talent with the required skills.

The report also highlighted the role of middle managers in AI adoption. About 95% of HR leaders said middle managers are critical to helping employees use AI effectively, while 92% said they play a key role in redefining jobs as AI reshapes workplace responsibilities.

“AI is reshaping the talent landscape and exposing the limits of traditional talent and learning models,” said Kathy Diaz, Chief People Officer, Cognizant. “With the fundamental shift in entry-level tasks and skill requirements changing rapidly, organisations must rethink how they hire and develop talent at pace.”

The survey was conducted by Wakefield Research between March 23 and April 3, 2026, among HR professionals at the director level and above from companies employing at least 1,000 people across India, the US and the UK.

title: Pramaana Labs Raises $27 Million in Seed Round Led by Khosla Ventures
content:
Pramaana Labs has raised $27 million in a seed round led by Khosla Ventures to build AI verification systems for regulated industries.

What Actually Matters.

Pramaana Labs has secured $27 million in seed funding led by Khosla Ventures to enhance AI verification systems.

The funds will support training models, hiring AI researchers, and expanding expertise in regulated industries.

Pramaana Labs, an AI verification and accountability platform, has closed a $27 million seed funding round led by Khosla Ventures. Accel, BoldCap, Nexus Venture Partners, Premji Invest, and Unbound also participated in the round.

The company’s early backers include Pushmeet Kohli, Vice President at Google DeepMind, and Sriram Rajamani, Corporate Vice President at Microsoft CoreAI.

Pramaana Labs said it will use the funds to train its formalisation and prover models, hire AI researchers, and expand its network of domain experts across regulated verticals, including tax, healthcare, cybersecurity, and financial compliance.

The company was founded in 2025 by Ranjan Rajagopalan, Krishnan Raghavan, and Sanjay Ganapathy Subramaniam. It builds AI systems designed to convert complex human knowledge into machine-verifiable outputs, where each claim is grounded and traceable. The company says it is the first to apply formal verification to commercial, high-stakes domains such as tax, healthcare, financial compliance, and government policy.

Its system works by encoding the rules of a given domain—such as the US tax code, clinical protocols, or financial regulations—into a formal language that machines can process with mathematical precision.

The company’s research division includes academics from IIT Delhi, IIT Madras, and UC Berkeley, and it also collaborates with Stanford's Centaur Lab on related research.

Pramaana Labs competes with other companies in this space, including Harmonic, Axiom Math, and Logical Intelligence.

title: Hexaware to Invest £25 Million in the UK, Create 1,200 Jobs in AI & Quantum Computing
content:
Hexaware will set up research centres in Manchester and Leeds while expanding its Birmingham delivery centre to tap into the growing demand for AI-led transformation in the UK.

What Actually Matters.

Hexaware is set to invest £25 million in the UK, creating around 1,200 jobs in AI and quantum computing.

New research centres will be established in Manchester and Leeds, alongside an expanded delivery centre in Birmingham.

IT services company Hexaware Technologies will invest £25 million in the United Kingdom over the next three to five years, a move that is expected to create around 1,200 jobs across artificial intelligence (AI), digital services and quantum computing, as the company deepens its presence in one of its fastest-growing markets.

The investment, announced by the UK government during the G7 Summit on June 16 as part of a broader package of international commitments linked to the country’s AI and clean energy agenda, will see Hexaware establish new research and development centres in Manchester and Leeds and expand its delivery centre in Birmingham.

The company said the investment will focus on AI research, digital innovation for citizen services and talent development, while supporting public-sector modernisation initiatives in the UK.

“The UK is one of our fastest-growing markets,” said Parameshwaran Iyer, executive vice president and head of UK and Europe at Hexaware. “Our UK clients are moving fast on AI, and having research and delivery talent on the ground here means we can build with them rather than for them.”

The announcement comes as global IT services firms increasingly expand local delivery and research capabilities in key overseas markets to meet growing demand for AI-led transformation projects and comply with localisation requirements from government and regulated-sector clients.

Hexaware Chief Executive R Srikrishna said the company plans to work with local institutions and government bodies while investing in young talent and emerging technologies.

The company has operated in the UK for more than three decades and opened its UK headquarters in Canary Wharf, London, in 2025.

The UK is Hexaware’s second-largest market globally and its fastest-growing geography, according to the company.

“Hexaware has worked alongside businesses in the UK for more than three decades. We have very high ambitions for our growth, creating impact in the UK and proudly supporting the Government’s inclusive vision for AI,” Srikrishna said.

He added that the investments are focused on developing young talent, working with unique, publicly available datasets, and collaborating with the government at all levels across the country.

What Actually Matters.

OpenAI has hired Noam Shazeer, a leading figure in AI research and co-creator of the Transformer architecture.

Shazeer previously served as vice president of engineering at Google and co-lead of its Gemini AI models.

OpenAI has hired Noam Shazeer, Google’s Gemini co-lead and one of the researchers behind the Transformer architecture that powers today’s leading large language models.

Shazeer confirmed the move in a post on X. “I’m excited to share that I’ll be joining OpenAI and look forward to working with the exceptional team there,” he wrote.

Calling the decision difficult, he added, “I’m incredibly proud of the amazing team at Google and everything we’ve built together. It has been an honour and a pleasure to work with all of you.”

The departure is a significant blow to Google’s AI efforts. Shazeer currently serves as a vice president of engineering and co-lead of Gemini, Google’s flagship family of AI models.

He returned to Google DeepMind in 2024 after co-founding Character.AI, the chatbot startup that quickly became one of the most prominent AI companies outside the major tech giants.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman publicly welcomed the hire, writing on X that Shazeer was “one of the people I have most wanted to work with since the very beginning of OpenAI,” adding that the company had waited a decade to make it happen.

Shazeer was a co-author of the landmark 2017 ‘Attention Is All You Need’ paper that introduced the Transformer architecture, the foundation of today’s LLMs. He also helped pioneer Mixture-of-Experts architectures, contributed to Google’s LaMDA conversational AI system, and played important roles in developing major language models such as PaLM and Gemini.

The move comes less than two years after Google spent billions to bring him back.

Shazeer joined Google in 2000 and spent more than two decades at the company before leaving in 2021 after Google declined to release a chatbot he had developed with Daniel De Freitas. The pair went on to found Character.AI, which quickly gained millions of users and attracted significant investor interest.

In 2024, Google struck a deal worth roughly $2.7 billion to license Character.AI’s technology and rehire Shazeer and several key employees. Following the transaction, Shazeer became a technical lead for Gemini, working alongside senior Google AI leaders, including Jeff Dean and Oriol Vinyals.

His jump to OpenAI is the latest example of the escalating AI talent war among OpenAI, Google, Meta, and Anthropic. Leading AI researchers and engineers have become some of the most sought-after employees in the technology industry, with companies increasingly relying on aggressive recruiting, acqui-hire deals and multimillion-dollar compensation packages to gain an edge in the race to build more powerful models.

The timing is particularly notable as OpenAI continues to expand its research organisation and prepare for a potential future public offering.

title: AIM — India's Leading AI & Data Science Media Platform
content:
The India-France relationship is evolving beyond defence to include deep-tech collaboration.

Indian startups are leveraging France as a strategic base for global market entry and partnerships.

For years, the India-France relationship has been defined by Rafale fighter jets, nuclear cooperation and joint space missions. At Bharat Innovates 2026, that narrative shifted.

The three-day event, which concluded on 16 June, saw participation by nearly 120 startups, who not only pitched to investors but also engaged in supply chain negotiations, signed commercial MoUs, and secured market access. The Indian deep-tech ventures increasingly needed this to scale globally.

Startups spanning sectors such as AI, space, agritech, healthcare, climate technology and defence, offered a glimpse into India's rapidly expanding deep-tech ecosystem.

"India is moving beyond being a technology adopter to becoming a global technology provider," Namrata Ashok of IIT Bombay, who attended the event, wrote in a LinkedIn post.

France, with about 18,000 startups, is one of Europe's top innovation hubs. In the first nine months of 2025, French startups raised €5.8 billion, mainly in AI, deep tech, greentech, and health tech. Indian founders see France as a place for innovation and a gateway to the EU.

For instance, Niqo Robotics, which develops AI-powered precision spraying technology for agriculture, sees Europe as the next best market for expansion.

Jaisimha Rao, Founder of Niqo Robotics, said that farmers are under increasing pressure to reduce chemical use while maintaining productivity. As a result, precision agriculture has become a growing priority across the continent and offers them an opportunity to serve the market.

Rao’s ambition reflected across segments. Some of the companies were building for the long haul and finding the right partners to collaborate.

"We're working with a French launch aggregator for our upcoming launches,” Ronak Kumar Samantray, Founder of TakeMe2Space, said. The startup is also in talks with the country’s sensor manufacturer to collaborate.

Another space tech startup, EON Space Labs, which develops imaging tech for satellites, drones, and defence, is exploring collaborations with European partners in optics, earth observation, and dual-use defence tech. "While discussions are at an early stage, the quality of interactions has been extremely encouraging," Founder Punit Badeka said.

The significance of such partnerships extends beyond individual companies. About 13 French universities signed partnership agreements with 11 Indian Institutes of Technology (IITs) and the Indian Institute of Science (IISc) to enhance cooperation in student exchanges, joint research, innovation support, academic collaboration, and talent development.

Deep-tech companies often require years of product development, specialised manufacturing partners and international customers to scale. If the conversations at Bharat Innovates lead to tangible commercial partnerships, they could lay the foundation for a lasting India-France innovation corridor.

title: Mistral AI Wants to Help India Build Sovereign AI, Says CEO After Meeting PM Modi
content:
Mensch said Mistral AI is working to develop sovereign AI capabilities across different regions and sees an opportunity to support India’s ambitions in the space.

What Actually Matters.

Mistral AI aims to support India's ambitions in developing sovereign AI capabilities.

PM Modi and Mistral CEO discussed the importance of human-centric and inclusive AI.

During his visit to France following the G7 Summit, Prime Minister Narendra Modi met Mistral AI CEO Arthur Mensch to discuss sovereign AI and full-stack AI infrastructure.

“Exchanged views on trusted AI, innovation and the need to ensure that AI remains human-centric and inclusive,” PM Modi wrote in a post on X.

“Talked about prospects for partnerships in India in diverse aspects relating to AI,” he added.

Mensch said Mistral AI is working to develop sovereign AI capabilities across different regions and sees an opportunity to support India's ambitions in the space.

“We’re a company building sovereign AI capabilities across the world, and the discussion revolved around how to build a full-stack solution that is resilient and that is escaping foreign control,” Mensch said.

He added that the conversation also covered making AI accessible to citizens and government employees while ensuring that India develops the skills needed to build and deploy the technology.

“It also revolved a lot around how to make AI available to everyone, both to the citizens, to the civil servants,” he said. “We want to make sure that the people of India are trained on that technology, become better at building it through startups, for instance, that we would love to be partnering with.”

The comments come as India seeks to strengthen its AI ecosystem through investments in compute infrastructure, foundation models, and talent development under the IndiaAI Mission.

Mensch’s remarks also align with Mistral’s broader positioning around AI sovereignty. Earlier this week, he announced that the company would launch a new family of AI models this summer and open an early-access programme in July for selected partners across research, government, and industry.

“This model and upcoming ones will be open-weight,” Mensch wrote on X. “We believe this is critical for our customer confidence and for the research and developer communities.”

He argued that organisations should be able to inspect, audit, and improve AI systems rather than relying solely on models accessed through third-party interfaces.

Mistral is also expanding its infrastructure offerings through Studio, its deployment platform, and its training platform Forge. According to Mensch, the company can run AI systems in a customer’s virtual private cloud, data centre, or on infrastructure operated independently of US service providers.

“We’re working with companies and governments around the world to make sure their AI systems are up and running outside of external control,” he wrote.

The Paris-based startup has increasingly positioned itself as an alternative to US AI providers, focusing on open-weight models and sovereign AI deployments for governments and enterprises. The company was co-founded in 2023 by Mensch, Chief Science Officer Guillaume Lample, and Chief Technology Officer Timothée Lacroix.

During his stay in Paris, PM Modi is expected to hold a series of bilateral meetings and participate in the VivaTech Summit 2026, Europe’s largest technology and startup event.

title: Dhruva Space, Finland’s ICEYE Partner for Satellite Manufacturing and Earth Observation
content:
HCLTech will help Volkswagen Group's e.solutions develop and scale next-generation infotainment and connectivity software.

What Actually Matters.

HCLTech has secured a multi-year contract to assist Volkswagen Group's e.solutions in developing automotive infotainment software.

The collaboration focuses on creating human-machine interface software for various vehicle programmes built on Android Automotive.

IT services firm HCLTech has secured a multi-year engineering services contract from Volkswagen Group's e.solutions to support the development of next-generation automotive infotainment and connectivity platforms.

Under the agreement, HCLTech will work with Germany-based e.solutions on the development, integration, and validation of human-machine interface (HMI) software for multiple vehicle programmes.

The platforms will be built on Android Automotive and will support connected in-car experiences across different vehicle models and markets.

The engagement comes as global automakers increasingly invest in software-defined vehicles, with software capabilities, connectivity features, and digital cockpit experiences becoming key differentiators.

Volkswagen Group-owned e.solutions develops infotainment and communication software for automotive manufacturers and suppliers. The company said the partnership intends to help scale software development across multiple vehicle programmes while maintaining consistency in user experience and software quality.

“Our partnership with HCLTech enables us to scale HMI software development across diverse vehicle programs while maintaining the highest standards of quality, consistency, and user experience. Together, we are building the foundation for the next generation of software-defined mobility,” Uwe Reder, CEO, e.solutions, said in a statement.

For HCLTech, the deal strengthens its presence in automotive engineering and mobility services, an area where IT service providers are seeing growing demand from automakers seeking external engineering talent to accelerate software development cycles.

“By combining AI-driven engineering and a deep understanding of the automotive sector, we will empower e.solutions to accelerate and develop world-class infotainment platforms,” said Pankaj Tagra, Chief Growth Officer and Global Head, Mobility at HCLTech.

HCLTech, which employs more than 227,000 people globally, reported revenue of $14.7 billion for the 12 months ended March 2026.

title: CtrlS Secures ₹7,000 Crore Investment Commitment from CPP Investments to Accelerate India Data Centre Expansion
content:
The partnership will examine joint production, data services, and ground infrastructure opportunities from India for global markets.

What Actually Matters.

Dhruva Space and ICEYE have partnered to explore satellite manufacturing and Earth observation services.

The collaboration aims to leverage Dhruva's engineering and manufacturing with ICEYE's satellite expertise.

Hyderabad-based spacetech startup Dhruva Space and Finland’s ICEYE, which works on satellite imagery, have signed an MoU to explore collaboration across satellite manufacturing, space systems production, Earth observation (EO) services, disaster management solutions, and ground segment infrastructure.

Announced at Bharat Innovates 2026, the partnership will combine Dhruva’s spacecraft engineering, manufacturing, launch integration, and ground station capabilities with ICEYE’s synthetic aperture radar (SAR) satellite constellation and EO expertise.

The companies said they will assess opportunities in India and overseas markets on a project-by-project basis.

Sanjay Nekkanti, Co-founder and CEO of Dhruva Space, said the partnership combines the strengths of both companies across manufacturing, space systems, data delivery and applications.

“Partnerships such as these will be instrumental in scaling sovereign capabilities, strengthening supply chains, and delivering space-enabled solutions to customers around the world,” he noted in a statement.

Under the agreement, the companies will evaluate large-scale production of space components and subsystems from India, leveraging Dhruva Space’s manufacturing capabilities and its upcoming 280,000 sq ft assembly, integration and testing (AIT) facility.

Once operational, the facility is expected to support scalable production of space hardware and serve ICEYE’s global manufacturing requirements from India.

They will also explore the joint development and manufacturing of satellite buses and other space systems for domestic and international programmes. They plan to expand access to EO data and analytics in India. Through Dhruva Space’s AstraView platform, customers will gain access to ICEYE’s SAR constellation, enabling all-weather imaging services for government and commercial users.

The partnership will further examine applications in disaster management, agriculture, maritime monitoring and climate monitoring. The companies will also assess the use of Dhruva Space’s ground station network to improve data accessibility, speed up downlink capabilities and develop ground-station-as-a-service offerings.

Rafal Modrzewski, Co-founder and CEO of ICEYE, said India is an important market for EO and sovereign space capabilities.

“Through this collaboration with Dhruva Space, we look forward to exploring opportunities that combine local manufacturing, rapid data access, and innovative applications for customers across sectors,” Modrzewski said.

The companies said the collaboration aims to support India’s space ecosystem while serving global markets through manufacturing, infrastructure, data, and application-focused opportunities.

title: Bengaluru-Karnataka Emerges as Asia’s No. 2 AI Innovation Hub, Enters Global Top 10 for Startup Performance & R&D
content:
The partnership includes a ₹4,000 crore investment by CPP Investments for an 8.2% stake in CtrlS at a pre-money valuation of ₹44,914 crore (C$6.6 billion)

What Actually Matters.

CtrlS Datacenters has secured a ₹7,000 crore investment commitment from CPP Investments to enhance India's data centre infrastructure.

CPP Investments will acquire an 8.2% stake in CtrlS through a ₹4,000 crore investment at a significant pre-money valuation.

In one of the largest investments in India’s digital infrastructure sector, CtrlS Datacenters has secured a commitment of up to ₹7,000 crore from Canada Pension Plan Investment Board (CPP Investments) to expand hyperscale and AI-ready data centre infrastructure across the country.

The partnership includes a ₹4,000 crore investment by CPP Investments for an 8.2% stake in CtrlS at a pre-money valuation of ₹44,914 crore (C$6.6 billion). Additionally, the two companies will establish a joint venture focused on developing hyperscale data center campuses across India, with CPP Investments committing up to ₹3,000 crore and holding a 48% stake, while CtrlS will retain 52%.

The investment comes at a time when demand for digital infrastructure is surging, driven by cloud adoption, hyperscaler expansion, artificial intelligence workloads, and India's rapidly growing digital economy. The partnership is expected to accelerate the development of next-generation data center capacity to support these emerging requirements.

Commenting on the development, Sridhar Pinnapureddy, Founder and CEO of CtrlS Datacentres, said that “India's AI moment is not on the horizon, it is already here. The demand signals from hyperscalers, cloud service providers, and enterprises are clear and unmistakable.”

He added that this investment reflects the confidence global investors have in CtrlS’ leadership position, execution capabilities, and the significant opportunity ahead.

Highlighting India's strategic importance, Max Biagosch, senior managing director and global head of real assets at CPP Investments, said, “As one of the world’s fastest growing digital markets, India represents an important pillar of our global datacenter strategy. Demand for datacentre infrastructure in India continues to accelerate, driven by hyperscale expansion, strong domestic cloud growth and emerging AI-led demand.”

CPP Investments has been actively expanding its global data centre portfolio across key international markets. In India, the institution has maintained a strong presence since making its first investment in 2009 and opening its Mumbai office in 2015. As of March 31, 2026, CPP Investments held more than ₹1.85 lakh crore (C$27 billion) in net assets in India, making it one of the country’s largest international institutional investors.

The deal also underscores growing global investor confidence in India's emergence as a major hub for AI, cloud, and digital infrastructure, as the country prepares for the next phase of technology-led growth.

Between 2021 and 2025, Bengaluru-Karnataka generated $46 billion in startup exits, attracted $39 billion in venture capital funding, and recorded 190% ecosystem value growth.

What Actually Matters.

Bengaluru-Karnataka ranks as Asia’s second-largest AI-native startup hub, reflecting its growing prominence in the tech landscape.

The region is now among the global top 10 for startup performance and research and development, according to the GSER 2026.

Bengaluru-Karnataka has emerged as Asia’s second-ranked AI-native startup hub while securing a place in the global top 10 for startup performance and research and development, according to the Global Startup Ecosystem Report (GSER) 2026 released by Startup Genome at VivaTech Paris.

The report places Bengaluru-Karnataka at 15th globally among startup ecosystems, highlighting the region’s rapid rise as a global centre for AI, deep-tech innovation, venture capital, and research commercialisation.

The findings, announced jointly by the Karnataka government and the Karnataka Digital Economy Mission (KDEM), show that the ecosystem has outpaced both regional and global growth trends over the past four years.

Between 2021 and 2025, Bengaluru-Karnataka generated $46 billion in startup exits, attracted $39 billion in venture capital funding, and recorded 190% ecosystem value growth, compared to the global average of 149% and Asia’s average of 66%.

The report estimates Bengaluru-Karnataka’s total startup ecosystem value at $152.8 billion, reinforcing its status as India’s largest startup hub and one of the world’s most valuable innovation ecosystems.

A major highlight of the report is Bengaluru-Karnataka’s growing influence in artificial intelligence. Ranked No. 2 in Asia for AI-native startup activity, the ecosystem has emerged as the country’s primary AI innovation centre, accounting for approximately 58% of India’s AI startup funding.

The report also notes stronger-than-average growth in early-stage AI investments, signalling sustained momentum in AI entrepreneurship.

Beyond AI, Bengaluru-Karnataka recorded significant gains in innovation output. The ecosystem improved its ranking in the R&D Engine category from the global top 30 in 2025 to the global top 10 in 2026, reflecting increased patent generation, research activity, and commercialisation of emerging technologies.

The report attributes this progress to the presence of leading institutions such as IISc, ISRO, DRDO, C-DAC, and NAL, alongside growing investments in quantum technologies, aerospace, and deep-tech sectors.

The ecosystem also demonstrated strong capital efficiency. Bengaluru ranked among the global top 10 ecosystems for performance and third in Asia, supported by 304 startup exits, 30 active unicorns, and an average exit timeline of 8.2 years—significantly faster than the global average of 11.1 years.

Startup Genome further ranked Bengaluru-Karnataka among the top 15 ecosystems globally for funding momentum and fourth in Asia, reflecting continued investor confidence and a growing pipeline of high-growth startups.

Commenting on the report, Priyank Kharge, Minister for IT & BT, Karnataka government, said, “Bengaluru-Karnataka is no longer just India’s startup capital; it is increasingly a global deep tech and AI innovation hub.”

The report also recognised Bengaluru-Karnataka’s strength in talent development, ranking it among the top 30 ecosystems globally for talent strength, and placing it among Asia’s leading destinations for affordable technology talent.

Overall, the GSER 2026 findings position Bengaluru-Karnataka as one of the fastest-growing and most capital-efficient startup ecosystems globally, with strong fundamentals across AI innovation, research output, venture funding, talent development, and startup value creation.

The alliance also aligns with Adani Group's broader vision of building 5 GW of green energy-powered AI-ready data centre capacity by 2035.

What Actually Matters.

Adani Group and Jabil have partnered to manufacture AI and data centre equipment in India.

The collaboration aims to produce advanced AI-ready infrastructure, including high-density AI racks and cooling systems.

As the global race to build AI infrastructure intensifies, Adani Group and US-based manufacturing giant Jabil have partnered to produce vertically integrated AI and data centre infrastructure equipment in India.

Union Minister of Electronics and Information Technology Ashwini Vaishnaw, as well as Maharashtra Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis, inaugurated Jabil’s new manufacturing facility in Pune.

“AI data centres have become a huge growth engine worldwide. Manufacturing all the major electronic components of AI data centres in India is crucial," Vaishnaw said.

Jabil is also set to open a manufacturing facility in Sanand, Gujarat, to produce silicon photonics.

Adani’s collaboration with Jabil aims to harness the latter’s large-scale manufacturing capacity for AI-ready data centre equipment, including building multi-gigawatt manufacturing capacity for high-density AI racks in India.

The platform is expected to produce advanced liquid-cooled AI racks, servers, storage systems, and networking equipment while also manufacturing supporting infrastructure such as power distribution units (PDUs), coolant distribution units (CDUs), transformers, switchgears, and thermal management systems.

The partnership combines Adani Group's infrastructure, renewable energy, and logistics capabilities with Jabil's six decades of engineering and advanced manufacturing expertise. Infosys has won a long-term IT transformation mandate from Finland’s Valmet, underscoring growing enterprise demand for AI-led modernisation.

What Actually Matters.

Infosys has secured a long-term IT transformation mandate from Valmet, reflecting growing enterprise interest in AI-led modernisation.

The partnership will enhance Valmet's operational efficiency by modernising core IT services and aligning IT with business priorities.

Infosys has secured a long-term IT transformation mandate from Finnish industrial technology company Valmet, as enterprises increasingly turn to artificial intelligence to modernise technology operations and improve efficiency.

Under the partnership announced on June 16, the IT services major will modernise Valmet’s core IT services and deliver end-to-end IT transformation to enhance operational efficiency and enable closer alignment between IT operations and business priorities.

Financial details of the deal were not disclosed.

The engagement will see Infosys deploy its AI platform, Topaz, and cloud suite, Cobalt, to automate and optimise IT operations, improve issue resolution and strengthen operational resilience across Valmet’s technology landscape.

The deal highlights how large technology services firms are repositioning traditional infrastructure management contracts around AI-led transformation, pitching automation and predictive operations as a way for clients to lower costs and improve business agility.

Valmet, which provides technology, automation and services to process industries, said the initiative aims to create a more resilient and scalable digital foundation to support its long-term growth strategy. The company reported net sales of about €5.2 billion in 2025 and employs around 18,500 people globally.

Infosys said the programme would leverage a human-in-the-loop approach to AI deployment, enabling governance and oversight while embedding intelligence across IT operations.

“In today’s rapidly evolving business landscape, enterprises must embrace AI-first, business-aligned, and future-ready ecosystems to unlock value at scale. Our collaboration with Valmet exemplifies Infosys’ commitment to driving transformative outcomes by leveraging the power of Infosys Topaz and Infosys Cobalt,” Jasmeet Singh, Executive Vice President and Global Head of Manufacturing, Infosys, said in a statement.

The agreement adds to a series of AI-focused transformation engagements being pursued by Indian IT services companies as clients shift spending from discretionary digital projects towards productivity and efficiency initiatives powered by generative AI and automation.

title: Unilever Partners with Accenture to Scale Digital Twins Across Global Manufacturing Network
content:
Over the next 18 months, Unilever plans to develop 40 new digital twins to enhance operational insights and automate processes.

What Actually Matters.

Unilever is collaborating with Accenture to implement AI-enabled digital twins across its manufacturing network.

The initiative aims to enhance operational insights, improve efficiency, and increase responsiveness to consumer demands.

Unilever is partnering with Accenture to scale the use of AI-enabled digital twins across its global manufacturing network. It aims to use the technology to help factories improve quality, boost efficiency, and respond more quickly to consumer demand.

Digital twins are virtual models of factory equipment and production lines. They use live data from physical systems on the shop floor to monitor and predict how machines and processes perform.

By integrating digital twins with AI-enabled insights and agentic capabilities, Unilever is equipping manufacturing teams with advanced tools to identify issues earlier, simulate scenarios more quickly, and make smarter decisions throughout the production cycle.

Building on digital twins already in use, Unilever plans to expand adoption over the next 18 months by creating more than 40 new digital twins.

“Unilever has long been recognised for its supply chain excellence, and expanding the use of manufacturing digital twins reflects the company’s continued focus on both technology and people,” Nicole van Det, CEO of Accenture Netherlands and Nordics and Global Account Lead for Unilever, said in a statement.

Accenture is supporting Unilever in deploying industrial AI capabilities that use advanced analytics and AI agents to predict maintenance needs, improve performance, and help teams act faster.

“Having invested early in AI, the company is setting the standard for pairing advanced tools with smart process design and disciplined execution on the shop floor. Together, we’re setting the benchmark for how industrial AI creates long-lasting value in the consumer goods sector,” van Det added.

Digital twins at Unilever are significantly enhancing production efficiency and product quality across various global sites. In Haldia, India, an energy twin has optimised thermal energy use in powder detergent production, contributing to climate goals. In Gandhidham, India, it has cut quality defects in Dove soap by 30%, the company claims.

Unilever’s partnership with Accenture in manufacturing AI builds on previously announced efforts to scale next-generation technology across business operations. This includes identifying and testing new AI solutions through the AI Horizon3 Lab located in Toronto, Canada.

title: DeepSeek Raises $7.4 Bnn, Surpasses $50 Bn Valuation in Major AI Funding Round
content:
Adobe and LinkedIn have launched a joint global initiative offering free, role-specific AI training for marketing professionals across digital marketing, content, social, and analytics.

What Actually Matters.

Adobe and LinkedIn have launched a free AI training initiative specifically for marketing professionals.

The programme includes four role-based courses available in 47 languages, covering various marketing aspects.

Adobe and LinkedIn have launched AI Essentials for Marketers, a joint global initiative designed to help marketing professionals build AI skills for an increasingly agentic workplace.

The initiative offers four role-based courses available in 47 languages, covering digital marketing, content and creative, social and communications, and data and analytics. Courses are available free of charge on LinkedIn Learning, with expanded content on Adobe Experience League. The curriculum was developed by BrandWorks, LinkedIn's in-house strategy and creative team, in short-form, social-first formats.

The programme comes as demand for AI-literate marketers accelerates sharply. According to data from the LinkedIn Economic Graph, which spans 1.3 billion members, over 71 million companies, and 42,000 skills, AI skills are the number one area of focus for marketing professionals today. The share of marketing job postings requiring AI literacy has more than doubled year-on-year, up 113%, the data shows.

Rachel Thornton, Chief Marketing Officer, Enterprise at Adobe, positioned the initiative as a broader reimagining of marketing practice. "AI Essentials for Marketers is about more than mastering new tools; it's about reimagining what creativity, marketing strategy, and customer relationships look like in an AI-powered era," she said in a statement.

"Marketers are navigating the shift to AI, and it is both daunting and exciting," LinkedIn CMO Jessica Jensen added. "Together with Adobe, we're helping make AI skills accessible to every marketer, not just technical specialists, through scalable, practical learning designed for the realities of modern work."

Participants who complete courses earn certificates that can be displayed directly on their LinkedIn profiles. Adobe and LinkedIn said they will add content regularly to keep pace with evolving AI capabilities.

The company has continued to expand its portfolio with DeepSeek-V4-Pro, a 1.6 trillion-parameter model designed to improve efficiency and lower AI deployment costs.

What Actually Matters.

DeepSeek raised over $7.4 billion, surpassing a $50 billion valuation, becoming one of China's leading AI companies.

The company's founder contributed approximately $3 billion, with significant interest from investors including Tencent.

Chinese artificial intelligence startup DeepSeek has reportedly raised more than $7.4 billion (over 50 billion yuan) in a new funding round, pushing its valuation above $50 billion and making it one of China’s most valuable AI companies.

According to reports from The Information and The Wall Street Journal, DeepSeek Founder and CEO Liang Wenfeng contributed around $3 billion to the funding round. Several investors also participated through a limited partnership managed by Wenfeng. Earlier reports had suggested that Chinese technology giant Tencent was considering an investment of nearly $1.5 billion in the company.

DeepSeek, based in Hangzhou, gained global attention in early 2025 after releasing its open-source reasoning model, DeepSeek-R1. The model drew comparisons with OpenAI’s advanced reasoning systems while requiring significantly less computing power. The launch sparked concerns across the technology industry and briefly triggered a major sell-off in AI chip stocks including shares of NVIDIA.

The company has since continued expanding its AI capabilities. In April, DeepSeek launched DeepSeek-V4-Pro, a large language model with 1.6 trillion parameters. The model uses a mixture-of-experts architecture activating only a portion of its parameters when responding to queries helping reduce computing costs while maintaining performance.

The company has also focused on improving efficiency. It claims its latest model can process much larger prompts while using significantly less memory than previous versions, lowering the cost of running AI applications.

DeepSeek’s growing influence has attracted attention from global technology companies. Reports suggest that Microsoft is exploring the use of a customised version of DeepSeek’s AI models for its enterprise AI offerings.

The company is reportedly evaluating a fine-tuned DeepSeek model as a lower-cost alternative to some of the AI systems currently provided by OpenAI and Anthropic.

The funding comes at a time when competition in the global AI industry is intensifying, with Chinese firms increasingly challenging the dominance of American AI companies. DeepSeek’s latest funding round is expected to support further research, model development, and expansion of its AI ecosystem as it looks to strengthen its position in the rapidly evolving AI market.

title: Oracle Introduces AI-Powered Assistant for Hotels Through OPERA Cloud Platform
content:
The new OPERA Cloud Assistant allows hotel employees to ask operational questions in natural language and receive instant guidance without consulting manuals or supervisors.

What Actually Matters.

Oracle's new OPERA Cloud Assistant enables hotel staff to ask operational questions in natural language for instant guidance.

The AI features help automate routine tasks and improve decision-making by providing quick access to operational information.

Oracle has developed a new suite of artificial intelligence (AI) features for its hospitality platform, OPERA Cloud, to help hotels streamline operations, improve efficiency, and deliver better guest experiences.

Called Oracle OPERA Cloud Assistant, the new AI-powered tools are built directly into the OPERA Cloud platform and are available to customers worldwide at no additional cost.

During the announcement, Oracle stated that the new capabilities will help hotel staff automate routine tasks, access operational information more quickly, and make better decisions in real time.

One of the key features is an AI assistant that allows hotel employees to ask questions in natural language and receive instant guidance. Instead of searching through manuals or consulting managers, staff can ask questions such as “How do I run a report?” or “How do I resolve this guest issue?” and receive immediate answers.

The platform also includes AI-powered language translation enabling staff to access information and communicate more effectively across Oracle Hospitality’s network which spans more than 230 countries and territories.

According to Oracle, the new features can also assist hotels with room assignments. The AI analyses reservation details, guest preferences, previous stay history, and operational requirements to recommend the most suitable room for each guest. The company says this could help improve guest satisfaction while reducing workload for front desk teams.

Another addition is AI-generated rate code descriptions. These descriptions are automatically created using existing hotel data, helping properties maintain consistent pricing information across multiple booking channels and improve revenue management practices.

The platform also supports multilingual operations by automatically translating configuration descriptions and operational content allowing hotel brands to maintain consistency across global locations.

“AI has the potential to transform hotel operations when it is seamlessly integrated into associates’ daily work,” said Laura Calin, Senior Vice President, Oracle Consumer Industries, in a statement. She added that the new features help reduce operational friction and allow hotel staff to focus more on guest service.

Scott Strickland, Chief Commercial Officer at Wyndham Hotels & Resorts, noted that AI is helping hotels make better decisions, reduce complexity, and respond more effectively to changing guest needs. Wyndham currently operates more than 2,100 properties using OPERA Cloud.

The new capabilities are designed to improve Oracle’s productivity, increase profitability and help hospitality businesses deliver more personalised guest experiences while maintaining operational efficiency.

Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) has signed a multi-year deal with English Premier League club Tottenham Hotspur to support the football team's digital transformation efforts, as the IT major continues to deepen its presence in the sports and entertainment technology segment.

Under the agreement, TCS will become Tottenham Hotspur's digital transformation partner, helping the club modernise its digital infrastructure, strengthen cybersecurity capabilities, deploy analytics tools, and enhance fan engagement across its digital platforms.

The partnership adds to TCS' growing portfolio of sports-related technology engagements globally. The Mumbai-headquartered company has increasingly used high-profile sporting associations to showcase its digital, data, and customer experience capabilities, while also expanding relationships with enterprises in adjacent sectors.

For Tottenham, the partnership comes as football clubs invest more heavily in technology to monetise fan relationships, personalise digital experiences, and derive insights from growing volumes of customer data.

“By combining data, technology, and design, we aim to help the (Tottenham Hotspur) Club deepen engagement with fans, create more connected and intuitive digital experiences across touchpoints”, Girish Ramachandran, President of Growth Markets at TCS, said in a statement.

The North London club, which won the UEFA Europa League in the 2024-25 season, has also been investing in expanding its digital ecosystem beyond matchday experiences.

"Our ongoing digital transformation at Spurs underpins our wider aims to deepen fan engagement and enhance user experiences across our growing range of digital touchpoints. In a LinkedIn post, Madhya Pradesh Chief Minister Mohan Yadav mentioned that the meeting focused on leveraging AI-powered technologies, including voice AI, multilingual citizen service platforms, digital document management systems, and sector-specific solutions for agriculture, healthcare, and rural development.

The discussions focused on how emerging technologies can help improve accessibility, efficiency, and responsiveness in public service delivery.

"Had a productive discussion with Ananth Nagaraj, Founder of Gnani.ai, at Vallabh Bhavan on leveraging artificial intelligence to enhance governance and citizen service delivery in Madhya Pradesh," the chief minister posted.

Speaking about the engagement, state officials emphasised the government's commitment to adopting innovative technologies that can make governance more citizen-centric while improving administrative efficiency.

The deliberations also examined the potential of multilingual AI solutions to bridge language barriers and expand access to government services, particularly for citizens in rural and underserved regions.

They identified voice-based interfaces and AI-enabled document management systems as key areas that could streamline interactions between citizens and government departments.

The initiative aligns with the broader national push towards digital governance and the adoption of indigenous technology solutions. Madhya Pradesh officials reiterated the state's focus on integrating innovation into governance frameworks to improve service delivery outcomes.

The discussions come at a time when several state governments are increasingly evaluating AI-driven tools to modernise public administration, improve operational efficiency, and deliver services at scale.

In May, CM Yadav held discussions with senior officials from Google Cloud India on strengthening administrative efficiency through AI-driven technologies.

Enterprise AI’s real frontier isn’t more workflows, it’s execution. With 78% of organisations stuck in pilot mode and only 14% reaching production scale, the gap between AI ambition and operational reality is 2026’s defining leadership challenge.

What Actually Matters.

Most organisations have AI initiatives, yet few can demonstrate tangible changes from these efforts.

A significant gap exists between AI pilot projects and achieving measurable, production-level outcomes.

Most organisations have AI running somewhere. Very few can point to what it has actually changed.

That single observation captures the defining tension of enterprise technology in 2026. Boards are approving budgets, vendors are announcing breakthroughs, and pilot dashboards are lighting up. Yet, across industries and geographies, including India, one of the world’s most ambitious AI markets, the gap between a promising proof of concept and measurable, production-grade outcomes has never felt wider.

The problem, increasingly, is not access to AI. It is the operating infrastructure required to turn AI into results.

From Experimentation to the Execution Crisis

For the better part of three years, enterprise AI conversations revolved around possibility. Which use cases could be automated? Which models should be procured? Which teams should pilot what? That era, by most accounts, is over. What has replaced it is a harder, less glamorous question: why aren’t the pilots translating?

A March 2026 survey, by Wharton Human AI Research centre, of 650 enterprise technology leaders found that 78% of organisations have at least one AI agent pilot underway, yet only 14% have successfully scaled one to organisation-wide operational use. The scaling gap is not primarily a technology problem—the models are capable, and the tooling has improved dramatically. The gap is organisational and operational: most enterprises lack the evaluation infrastructure, monitoring tooling, and dedicated ownership structures needed to move a promising pilot into reliable production.

Forrester's root-cause analysis of failed deployments is particularly instructive. Unclear success criteria account for 41% of failures; insufficient data or tool access for 33%; and evaluation drift for 26%. Not one of those is a model-quality problem. All three are operating model problems.

Meanwhile, Gartner projects that 40% of agentic AI projects will be cancelled by 2027 if governance, observability, and clear success criteria are not established first. With the agentic AI market valued at $11 billion and growing at nearly 46% annually, the financial stakes of continued pilot purgatory are substantial.

The India Story: High Ambition, Uneven Execution

India presents a particularly instructive case study.

On paper, the momentum is extraordinary. About 99% of Indian enterprises plan to increase AI investments over the next 12 months, with year-on-year budget growth averaging 19%, the highest in the Asia Pacific region. A joint IBM–IndiaAI study projects a $500 billion AI opportunity for India by 2030, and 67% of Indian enterprises aim to appoint a Chief AI Officer within two years.

Yet, the execution picture is considerably less uniform. Nearly 72% of organisations surveyed said they remain behind global peers in AI adoption, highlighting the challenge of moving from pilot projects to scaled, enterprise-wide deployments. Only 15% are currently scaling AI through significant cross-functional investments, while the remainder continue operating pilot-stage initiatives.

According to Deloitte's 2026 State of AI in the Enterprise report, Indian enterprises are moving beyond experimentation and leading global peers in at-scale AI adoption across functions, including product development (62%), strategy and operations (56%), and marketing and sales (55%). However, 40% of Indian respondents report significant or full usage of AI, compared with a global average of approximately 28%, indicating that while some are operationalising AI effectively, many others are still catching up.

Mukesh Gandhi, Founder and CEO of Creative Synergies Group, sounds optimistic as he tells AIM that AI adoption will continue to accelerate in 2026, yet meaningful transformation requires more than just investment in next-generation infrastructure.

“It demands a relentless focus on the fundamentals. To convert ambition into dependable value, leaders must resist the temptation of big-bang projects and instead prioritise targeted, operational wins. The winners will be those who exercise the patience to fix structural deficits, pairing disciplined execution with a modernised culture to bridge the divide between strategy and readiness," he adds.

More Workflows is Not the Answer

There is a persistent instinct in enterprise technology to solve execution problems by adding more process layers, more dashboards, more use cases, and more automation workflows. The evidence suggests this instinct is misguided.

A 2026 Voice of the Market report from Momentum, drawing on more than 2,000 active B2B sales opportunities across 150 industries, found that 88% of teams claim AI adoption, but only 24% have embedded it into revenue workflows.

The report identified a growing mismatch between the AI narrative and the realities organisations face day to day—the enterprise technology market operating in two parallel realities: the aspirational narrative of AI-powered transformation promoted by vendors, and the operational reality of organisations drowning in manual processes, integration failures, and tool proliferation.

Rohit Kapoor, Chairman and CEO of EXL tells AIM, "AI's true potential is unlocked when it becomes part of how work gets done every day, not a bolt-on or a point solution. The real impact comes from selecting the workflows that matter most, reimagining them for the AI era, and embedding intelligence at scale. AI in Action is about moving from ambition to execution."

The ServiceNow AI Maturity Index, drawing on Indian enterprise data, echoed this view. India has a generational opportunity to lead globally by developing AI-ready talent, redesigning workflows, and reorienting business models around continuous innovation, points out the report.

“The era of scattered pilots is behind us. Competing globally now requires bold execution, integrated strategy, and genuine human-AI collaboration based on trust, transparency, and skill,” the report said.

Governance as Architecture, Not Afterthought

One consistent finding across multiple 2026 research programmes is that the organisations making visible progress on AI are not necessarily those with the largest budgets. They are the ones that treated governance as architecture, embedded into workflows from the outset, rather than as a compliance checkbox applied after deployment.

An IBM Institute for Business Value study found that 83% of Indian executives say effective governance is key to successful AI infrastructure, yet only 4% have embedded frameworks to manage AI-related risks. This gap between intent and infrastructure is where many transformation programmes quietly stall.

As AI experimentation gives way to enterprise execution, many organisations are now designing hub-and-spoke operating models to federate AI delivery across the enterprise while maintaining a consistent foundation of platforms, standards, and governance. In this model, a central AI centre of excellence serves as the hub for strategy, enablement, and governance rather than as a gatekeeper, providing infrastructure, reusable assets, training, and guardrails, while business units take ownership of delivery, funding, and outcomes.

Deloitte's research is clear on what separates leading organisations: they streamline workflows that AI can execute end to end, while humans focus on judgement, exception handling, and strategic oversight. The goal is not replacing humans or merely assisting them, but creating complementary working partnerships where the combined output exceeds what either could achieve alone.

What Enterprise Leaders Must Do Now

The pilot phase is over. The question now is not whether to deploy AI but whether the operating structure around it, ownership, governance, delivery frameworks, and talent, can support production-grade outcomes.

Three priorities are emerging for enterprise leaders navigating this transition. First, define success criteria before deployment, not after. Forrester’s analysis is unambiguous: the majority of AI project failures trace back to unclear KPIs established at the outset.

Second, treat AI as an operating model rather than a technology initiative. The distinction matters because it determines where accountability sits and how resources are allocated.

Third, invest in governance architecture proportionate to the complexity of what is being deployed. Agentic AI, systems capable of taking multi-step actions across live enterprise data, demands a fundamentally different oversight model than a static chatbot.

Zinnov’s India AI Adoption report identified roughly 26% of surveyed enterprises as ‘Enforcers’, organisations issuing top-down AI directives without the execution muscle to deliver on them. They represent the most expensive failure mode in the data.

The ambition to lead on AI is well-established across Indian and global enterprises alike. What remains to be built is the execution infrastructure to honour it.

title: Microsoft Enhances Copilot Cowork with Flexible Pay-As-You-Go Pricing
content:
Microsoft is also exploring a budget-friendly option with a refined version of the DeepSeek V4 AI model, which would be hosted on Azure to ensure data security.

What Actually Matters.

Microsoft is introducing a pay-as-you-go pricing model for its Copilot Cowork platform to enhance accessibility and affordability.

A budget-friendly version of the DeepSeek V4 AI model is being considered, aiming to reduce costs while ensuring data security on Azure.

Microsoft is changing the payment structure for its AI-driven Copilot Cowork platform by implementing usage-based pricing as it broadens access to the enterprise productivity tool and pushes for more affordable AI models to cut costs.

Moreover, in an effort to cut expenses, Microsoft is considering a refined version of DeepSeek V4 or another open-source AI model as a more budget-friendly alternative to the Anthropic and OpenAI models that currently support Copilot Cowork. The company anticipates revealing its final decision in the upcoming weeks, as reported by Axios.

Should Microsoft proceed with DeepSeek, the model would be optional for clients and entirely hosted on Azure, ensuring that customer data remains within Microsoft’s cloud and is protected by Azure’s enterprise security, compliance, and data-residency measures.

Charles Lamanna, Microsoft's EVP for Copilot, told Axios that testing revealed Copilot Cowork cannot be offered for unlimited use. “We have users who do hundreds of tasks a week, which is great—they’re way productive—but the consequence is the costs can go very high,” Lamanna said.

Under the new structure announced yesterday, the tool still necessitates a paid Microsoft 365 Copilot subscription. Now, each task executed is charged separately based on the amount of computing power it uses.

“Copilot Cowork requires the Microsoft 365 Copilot User Subscription License (USL). Users are then billed for Cowork on a usage-based basis, with charges determined by the tasks they run,” the company said in a statement.

Light tasks use few sources and require limited reasoning to produce one output. While medium tasks use multiple sources and structured reasoning for two or more outputs, heavy tasks aggregate broadly and generate many outputs. Microsoft has identified four user personas based on these task types.

According to Microsoft, grouping users by persona and their light, medium, and heavy tasks, and applying a cost per prompt, creates a flexible cost model. This model estimates costs by multiplying the number of users in each segment by their expected prompt volume for each task type, then summing the results.

“Before usage ramps, admins can set spending limits and allocate budgets using the cost management controls described above. Tenants that had at least one user in the Frontier programme (March 30 to June 16) who used Cowork during that period get a grace period on Cowork usage and will not be billed until July 1 to support the transition,” it said.

At general availability, Copilot Cowork uses Anthropic models, Opus 4.8 and Sonnet 4.6. In the Frontier environment, customers can access GPT 5.5, with Cowork version 1 arriving soon.

Cowork 1 will offer cost-effectiveness, high quality, and enterprise-grade performance while eliminating model bias for everyday Copilot tasks and cost-sensitive workloads.

title: At One Point, Cursor Accounted for Up to 50% of Anthropic Revenue: Report
content:
The relationship later came under pressure as Anthropic expanded into AI coding tools, prompting Cursor to accelerate development of its own models.

What Actually Matters.

Cursor once contributed up to 50% of Anthropic's revenue during its early growth phase.

The partnership was mutually beneficial, as Cursor relied on Anthropic's Claude models for its products.

AI coding startup Cursor once generated roughly 40–50% of Anthropic's revenue during its early growth phase, according to a Business Insider report citing a person familiar with the figures.

Cursor relied heavily on Anthropic's Claude models to power its coding products, while Anthropic benefited from the startup’s rapid adoption among developers and enterprises.

One employee cited by the report described the dynamic as both companies realising “they needed each other”, while also acknowledging that Anthropic was simultaneously developing a competing coding product.

Tensions increased after Anthropic launched Claude Code, which quickly gained traction among software developers.

According to the report, Anthropic executives had previously characterised the product internally to Cursor leaders as more of a research effort than a major commercial initiative.

Claude Code subsequently expanded into one of Anthropic's fastest-growing businesses, reaching a reported $2.5 billion annualised revenue run rate by February 2026, surpassing Cursor’s run rate at the time.

The relationship had already become a strategic concern for Cursor before Claude Code's launch. According to the report, executives were alarmed after Anthropic cut off rival coding startup Windsurf’s access to Claude Code during its acquisition talks with OpenAI, highlighting the risks of relying on a single AI provider.

The competitive threat reportedly triggered an internal response at Cursor. The report stated that CEO Michael Truell held an ‘emergency’ all-hands meeting in January and pushed the company to accelerate development of its own AI models to reduce reliance on external providers.

Cursor has since launched Composer, a family of coding-focused models that the company says it is increasingly developing in-house.

The report also noted that Cursor’s revenue later grew beyond $1 billion and reportedly doubled again in recent months, while the company now serves 60% of Fortune 500 firms and employs roughly 700 people.

Founded in 2022 by MIT graduates Michael Truell, Sualeh Asif, Aman Sanger, and Arvid Lunnemark, Cursor began as a standalone fork of Microsoft's VS Code editor before emerging as one of the fastest-growing AI software companies.

The startup crossed $1 billion in annualised revenue in 2025 and later launched its own Composer model family. The latest Composer 2.5 release has improved the model's standing on software engineering benchmarks, helping Cursor narrow the performance gap with frontier coding models from Anthropic and OpenAI.

Cursor’s growth has accelerated dramatically in 2026. According to Forbes, the company surpassed a $4 billion annualised revenue run rate in early June, up from roughly $2 billion in February, with about 75% of revenue now coming from enterprise customers.

Cursor has raised more than $2.8 billion to date. Its latest disclosed funding round was a $2.3 billion Series D in November 2025, which valued the company at $29.3 billion and was led by investors including Thrive Capital, Andreessen Horowitz and Accel.

Cursor had reportedly been in discussions to raise approximately $2 billion at a valuation of around $50 billion in April. Those fundraising plans were effectively superseded by a partnership with SpaceX.

In April, Cursor partnered with xAI and SpaceX, gaining access to the Colossus AI supercomputer. The agreement includes a potential $60 billion acquisition option and billions of dollars in committed compute resources, according to public disclosures.

title: OpenAI Spent $34 Billion in 2025: Report
content:
OpenAI generated $13.07 billion in revenue but incurred a $20.9 billion operating loss.

What Actually Matters.

OpenAI generated over $13 billion in revenue but faced a significant operating loss of nearly $21 billion.

The majority of expenses were attributed to research and development, amounting to over $19 billion.

OpenAI brought in $13.07 billion in revenue last year but spent $34 billion to get there, according to audited financial statements first reported by independent journalist Ed Zitron and verified by the Financial Times.

The biggest bill was research and development at $19.18 billion, which covers model training and computing infrastructure. Cost of revenue totalled $7.5 billion, sales and marketing totalled $5.73 billion, and general and administrative expenses totalled $1.57 billion.

That resulted in an operating loss of $20.92 billion in 2025.

A large chunk of that spending went to Microsoft. According to Zitron's analysis, OpenAI paid Microsoft $17.2 billion during 2025, $10.59 billion of which was classified as research and development, most likely for model training costs. The rest was split across cost of revenue, sales and marketing, and administrative charges.

On the revenue side, SoftBank paid OpenAI $867 million during the year, and Microsoft paid an additional $303 million.

However, Zitron revealed that OpenAI also recorded a $41.55 billion accounting charge triggered by the company’s conversion from a non-profit to a for-profit entity, totalling the loss to $60.35 billion.

OpenAI brought that figure down to $38.53 billion by removing two line items from its accounts: $17.87 billion described in the filings as “net loss attributable to noncontrolling members’ capital,” and a further $3.95 billion described as “net loss attributable to redeemable noncontrolling interests.”

Before that restructuring, investors held convertible interests instead of regular equity. As OpenAI's valuation rose, those instruments had to be revalued upward under accounting rules, creating a large non-cash loss on paper.

The disclosures come as OpenAI prepares for a public listing. The company confirmed a few days ago that it had confidentially filed a draft S-1 registration statement with the SEC, though it has not announced an IPO timeline.

title: Women-Led AI Hackathon WitchHunt 2026 Crowns Winners Across Health, Education, Climate & Smart Cities Segments
content:
WitchHunt 2026 concluded in Bengaluru with 6,151 participants from 23 states, producing 373 working AI prototypes that tackle challenges across four impact sectors.

What Actually Matters.

WitchHunt 2026, a women-first AI hackathon, concluded in Bengaluru with over 6,151 participants and 373 AI prototypes developed.

Winning teams addressed challenges in climate action, health, education, and smart cities, showcasing innovative solutions like AI-powered farming and maternal health companions.

Young innovators from across India took centre stage at the grand finale of WitchHunt 2026, a women-first AI hackathon that saw participants develop 373 functional prototypes, aimed at solving real-world challenges across healthcare, education, climate action and smart cities segments.

Organised by HopeWorks Foundation in partnership with AI4India and the Karnataka Digital Economy Mission (KDEM), the four-month programme concluded at Jyoti Nivas College Autonomous in Bengaluru. The event brought together 6,151 participants from 23 states, making it one of India’s largest women-focused AI innovation initiatives.

Teams from Nellore, Udupi and Delhi emerged as winners across different categories. Bytebusters from Nellore won the Climate Action track with an AI-powered farming solution, while aipaglus from Delhi secured the Health and Wellbeing category for developing an AI maternal health companion called MaaSakhi. Karnataka-based team We4 won the Education track with CallSakhi, while an offline voice-first mentor designed for rural girls and female coders from Delhi topped the Smart Cities category with a localised urban infrastructure monitoring platform.

The event was inaugurated by Karnataka IT and BT Minister Priyank Kharge, who encouraged students to focus on solving meaningful problems rather than replicating existing business models.

“Move up the value chain. Replicating another e-commerce platform is great, but India needs real innovation. My request to youngsters is to upskill fast and start creating and building for the world rather than just servicing it,” Kharge said.

He also highlighted Karnataka’s efforts to support startups through initiatives such as the ₹300 crore Nipuna Karnataka reskilling programme and the state’s upcoming government-first policy, which aims to enable startups to test solutions in government-backed sandbox environments.

A recurring theme throughout the event was India’s need to become a creator of AI technologies rather than merely a consumer. Debjani Ghosh, Distinguished Fellow at NITI Aayog, stressed the importance of building indigenous AI capabilities.

“India is one of the largest users of AI today, but it must also become one of the largest builders of AI. Women must play a larger role in shaping the future of artificial intelligence,” she added.

Gokul V Subramaniam, President of Intel India, echoed the sentiment, urging students to focus on frugal innovation tailored to real-world challenges such as limited connectivity and affordability.

The hackathon recorded a nearly 50% idea-to-prototype conversion rate with participants developing 373 working solutions from 779 submitted ideas. More than 300 industry mentors and 70 AI experts supported the programme.

A total prize pool of ₹19 lakh was awarded to winning teams, while organisers announced plans for the next edition of WitchHunt, aiming to further strengthen women’s participation in India’s growing AI ecosystem.

title: BHASHINI, GeM Join Hands to Make Public Procurement Accessible in 22 Indian Languages
content:
Under the agreement, GeM and BHASHINI will jointly debelop multilingual digital resources through initiatives such as BHASHINI Udyat, Mitra, Appmitra, Sahyogi, and Pravakta.

What Actually Matters.

The MoU between BHASHINI and GeM aims to enhance multilingual capabilities in India's public procurement system.

The initiative will utilise AI-powered language technologies to assist users in accessing services in 22 Indian languages.

In a move to break language barriers in government procurement, the Digital India BHASHINI Division (DIBD) and the Government e-Marketplace (GeM) have signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) to strengthen multilingual digital capabilities across India's public procurement ecosystem.

The collaboration, launched under the ‘BHASHINI for Seva/Sanchalan—A BHASHINI Sahayogi Program’, seeks to integrate AI-powered language technologies into GeM’s platform, enabling buyers, sellers, MSMEs, startups, and entrepreneurs to access procurement services in their preferred languages.

The partnership will leverage BHASHINI, India’s National Language Digital Public Infrastructure, to support seamless interaction across 22 officially recognised Indian languages and other regional languages through voice-first technologies and generative AI solutions.

Under the agreement, GeM and BHASHINI will jointly work on multilingual digital resources through initiatives such as BHASHINI Udyat, Mitra, Appmitra, Sahyogi, and Pravakta. The collaboration will focus on translation API integration, domain-specific language models, multilingual glossaries, voice-enabled services, voice bots, and linguistic dataset development tailored for public procurement and government service delivery.

The initiative is expected to make procurement services more inclusive by reducing language barriers across seller onboarding, platform navigation, communication, and stakeholder engagement, thereby expanding access to government business opportunities.

Officials noted that multilingual technologies are increasingly critical for improving Ease of Doing Business (EoDB), particularly for MSMEs, startups, and businesses operating across diverse linguistic regions. The collaboration aims to ensure that language does not limit participation in government procurement or access to economic opportunities.

As part of the partnership, both organisations will also promote language data contributions through BhashaDaan, conduct awareness and capacity-building programmes, and encourage wider adoption of multilingual AI tools across institutions within the GeM ecosystem.

Highlighting the significance of the initiative, Ajit B Chavan, Additional CEO and Chief Seller Officer, GeM, said, “The collaboration aims to leverage BHASHINI’s AI-powered language technologies to break linguistic barriers in public procurement and make GeM more accessible to buyers and sellers across the country.”

Echoing the vision, Amitabh Nag, CEO, Digital India BHASHINI Division, said, “BHASHINI is committed to making digital public infrastructure truly inclusive by enabling citizens and enterprises to interact in their preferred Indian languages. Our collaboration with GeM will help democratise access to public procurement through multilingual and voice-enabled technologies, ensuring that language is no longer a barrier to participation.”

The partnership reinforces BHASHINI's role as India’s population-scale language infrastructure while supporting GeM’s vision of creating a transparent, efficient, and inclusive public procurement ecosystem with wider participation from buyers and sellers across the country.
