Chinese AI models have priced their APIs 5–10x lower than those of Anthropic and OpenAI. But is that sustainable?

What Actually Matters.

Chinese AI models are significantly underpricing their APIs compared to US counterparts, creating a competitive advantage.

The trend of switching to lower-cost Chinese models is gaining traction among developers, leading to substantial cost savings.

The tokenmaxxing phenomenon has rattled both AI lab CEOs and customers. The former have acknowledged that token pricing is a major issue, while the latter increasingly face pressure to control inference costs.

But Chinese AI models seem to be at an advantage. Their APIs are often priced 5–10x lower than comparable US offerings while delivering similar performance.

Several founders and developers have reported significant savings after switching from Western models to DeepSeek.

Recently, Florent Crivello, CEO and Co-founder of Lindy, an AI platform building customisable, no-code agents, wrote on X that the company shifted 100% of its traffic to DeepSeek V4, moving away from Anthropic’s models. According to Crivello, the transition is saving the company millions of dollars while improving performance across several core use cases. He added that Chinese models are likely to exert margin pressure on AI APIs for the foreseeable future.

The trend is beginning to show up in spending data as well. Ramp, the American fintech giant, reported that DeepSeek was among the fastest-growing software vendors on its spend management platform in June 2026. Its workloads are using DeepSeek’s first-party API rather than self-hosted deployments.

The cost differential is stark. While DeepSeek has priced its V4 Pro at $0.435 per 1 million input tokens and $0.87 per 1 million output tokens, Claude models are priced much higher. Sonnet 4.6, the most widely used Claude model, is priced at $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens. Meanwhile, the now suspended Fable 5 is priced at $10 and $50, respectively.

The growing adoption of lower-cost Chinese models is also increasing competitive pressure on US providers. According to a WSJ report, OpenAI is considering significant token-price reductions to compete more aggressively, while Google has consistently expanded its portfolio of lower-cost Gemini offerings.

I Went From $3,000/Month on Claude to $5/Week on DeepSeek

And honestly? 80% of my work is identical.

For the past two months, I was burning $3-5K monthly on Claude Code. Every idea from design to development to testing - full end-to-end automation, even simulating users to test…

— Xiaoyin Qu (@quxiaoyin) May 27, 2026

But how are Chinese AI models offering such low prices when many US AI companies continue to struggle with the economics of large-scale AI deployment?

“The low cost of Chinese AI APIs reflects a combination of genuine technical efficiency and strategic ecosystem economics,” observes Marc Einstein, Research Director at Counterpoint Research.

“Advances in model architecture and infrastructure optimisation have reduced underlying costs, while major platforms are willing to operate at thinner margins because AI services help drive broader cloud and enterprise adoption,” he tells AIM.

The Economics of ‘Cheap API’

Chinese models succeed in three areas: software optimisation, lower operating costs, and hardware strategies.

Technical efficiency has become a defining characteristic of the Chinese AI ecosystem, driven in part by export-control-related compute constraints. Models from DeepSeek, Qwen, Zhipu, and Kimi increasingly rely on techniques that reduce both training and inference costs.

For example, DeepSeek’s R1 family introduced Group Relative Policy Optimisation (GRPO), which removes the need for a separate critic model during reinforcement learning. The approach reduces memory requirements by up to 50% and lowers training costs substantially compared with traditional PPO-based methods.

More recently, Fuli Luo, head of Xiaomi’s MiMo family of models, explained in a post on X the rationale behind the company’s latest API price cuts. According to Luo, infrastructure and software optimisations increased cacheable token capacity fivefold and reduced caching costs by roughly 80%, allowing the company to operate near break-even despite the aggressive pricing.

The notion that low-cost APIs are loss-making is also challenged in disclosures from Chinese AI firms.

According to its IPO prospectus, MiniMax’s Open Platform business generated a 69.4% gross margin during the first nine months of 2025. Zhipu also reported an 18.9% gross profit margin in its Open Platform and API business, which provides cloud-based services built around its general-purpose models.

The Base Cost of Compute

Beyond software, Chinese AI labs benefit from structurally lower operating costs.

“Chinese AI labs spend far less on virtually every aspect of the model development and deployment pipeline: compute infrastructure, R&D, training, and inference,” notes Kyle Chan, fellow at the John L Thornton China Center at Brookings Institution.

Meanwhile, NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang has estimated that while a 1 GW data centre costs roughly $40–60 billion to build in the West, comparable Chinese facilities may cost closer to $26 billion.

Engineering talent is also significantly cheaper than in Silicon Valley, while industrial-scale electricity and permitting costs remain lower.

These factors allow Chinese firms to stretch capital much further than many of their Western counterparts.

However, Chan notes that China’s cheap inputs are partially “offset by more energy-efficient chips and hardware systems in the US.”

The US ecosystem relies on unthrottled GPUs to maximise performance per watt and token throughput, thereby improving deployment economics despite higher operating costs. Yet American AI companies continue to shoulder far larger infrastructure and frontier-model investment programmes, suggesting that lower operating costs may still give Chinese providers an advantage in inference and model deployment.

Giants like Alibaba are further lowering costs by reducing their dependence on third-party hardware vendors like NVIDIA.

In its Q4 FY25 earnings, Alibaba revealed that it is actively leveraging its proprietary T-Head silicon to bypass the severe 60–80% margin premiums typically charged by global merchant chip vendors. It disclosed that T-Head chips have achieved scaled mass production, with cumulative shipments surpassing 470,000 units, and now power more than 60% of Alibaba Cloud’s external AI workloads.

While acknowledging that domestic silicon may still lag behind frontier US GPUs in raw peak performance, CEO Eddie Wu emphasised during an earnings call that this closed-loop strategy guarantees superior value for money.

Chinese AI models are currently running on a mix of infrastructure, including NVIDIA GPUs available within China, Huawei's Ascend chips, and, in some cases, overseas compute resources.

One notable example came in early 2025, when DeepSeek made its first confirmed international deployment at the Aramco Digital Data Center in Dammam, Saudi Arabia, as part of the kingdom's $14.9 billion push into AI and digital infrastructure. By hosting its models on Saudi infrastructure, which could provide access to more advanced hardware and alternative architectures, such as Groq accelerators, DeepSeek may gain access to compute resources that are difficult or impossible to deploy domestically.

Why a Large-Scale Shift is Unlikely

Given the revenue US AI labs earn from APIs, Chinese models do pose a genuine threat.

“OpenAI derives an estimated 73% of its revenue from consumer subscriptions and 27% from APIs, while Anthropic remains more heavily dependent on API and enterprise customers, with an estimated 85% of revenue coming from APIs,” Einstein notes.

However, can Chinese models eat into OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s API revenue on a large scale?

“While lower-cost Chinese models may attract price-sensitive developers, the more likely outcome is a segmented market, where lower-cost providers capture experimentation and cost-sensitive workloads, while frontier labs compete on performance, trust, security, and enterprise value,” Einstein adds.

Several developers across Reddit, Hacker News, and Chinese forums increasingly describe model selection as a routing problem rather than a winner-takes-all contest, reserving frontier models for complex coding and agentic workflows while directing bulk inference workloads toward lower-cost providers.

One contributor on the Chinese internet forum Zhihu suggested using DeepSeek, particularly for workloads involving large outputs, repeated inputs that benefit from caching, and applications with lower multimodal and latency requirements.

“DeepSeek’s price cut is not about stealing GPT-5.5 workloads. A rational user almost never moves GPT-5.5-level tasks to DeepSeek,” added the contributor. “If that happens, either the task was overestimated before, or the quality requirement was never that high.”

Even Crivello observes that Lindy’s migration required significant engineering work. “I think these things are stickier than they sound—it's not easy to switch models,” he tells AIM.

He also points to the trust that US-based frontier AI models have earned and the brand effects conveyed by the popular phrase that does the rounds among developers: ‘no one ever got fired for picking Anthropic.’ “And for a lot of companies, this spend [to switch to Chinese AI models] isn't worth optimising,” adds Crivello.

Pricing advantages aside, data sovereignty remains a structural barrier that enterprise adoption cannot route around. Sending sensitive workloads to API servers outside the United States creates real compliance exposure for US government contractors, financial institutions, and healthcare companies operating under sector-specific data regulations.

Can the Economics Hold?

For companies such as Alibaba, low API prices are part of a broader strategy to drive consumption, expand market share, and strengthen adjacent cloud businesses. Its broader presence across China’s technology ecosystem helps absorb these losses and supports the strategy economically.

But for pure-play Chinese AI labs, can this model support the enormous costs of AI development over the long term?

“You can see in some of their financial statements that many are struggling to recoup the costs of computing and training,” Chan says.

Despite healthy API economics, overall profitability remains elusive. Zhipu reported a net loss of RMB 4.72 billion ($657 million) in 2025, driven largely by R&D spending and rising compute costs.

MiniMax likewise posted a loss of $1.87 billion for the year, with R&D expenditure of $252.8 million far outpacing its $79 million in revenue.

DeepSeek operated for nearly two years without external funding and was financed by its parent company, the hedge fund High-Flyer Capital. “However, even DeepSeek is feeling pressure to raise capital to expand compute infrastructure,” says Chan, pointing to the company's first external fundraising effort to raise about RMB 50 billion ($7.4 billion) at a valuation of RMB 350–400 billion ($52–59 billion).

Aggressive pricing may be winning Chinese AI labs market share today, but whether they emerge as a durable force in the industry will ultimately depend on how effectively they balance low-cost offerings with the immense investment required to remain competitive at the frontier.

title: Deeptech Startup SiMa.ai Unveils Agentic Software, SoM to Reduce Reliance on NVIDIA GPUs
content:
The company says its new platform cuts the time to deploy physical AI from months to days.

What Actually Matters.

SiMa.ai has launched Palette Neat, an agentic software environment to streamline physical AI deployment.

The new platform aims to reduce deployment time for robotics and autonomous systems from months to days.

Edge AI startup SiMa.ai has launched Palette Neat, an agentic software environment for physical AI, alongside a production-ready version of its Modalix system-on-module (SoM), as the startup seeks to reduce developers’ reliance on NVIDIA’s GPU ecosystem.

The company said the platform aims to shorten deployment timelines for robotics, drones, industrial systems, and autonomous machines.

Palette Neat aims to help developers move physical AI workloads to its hardware with minimal software rewriting. SiMa.ai also introduced a pin-compatible Modalix SoM that works with NVIDIA Orin carrier boards, allowing customers to switch hardware without redesigning systems. The company plans to make Palette Neat generally available after testing it with more than 20 customers globally.

“So we did an alpha and a beta, and then we engaged with 20-plus customers globally,” Krishna Rangasayee, Founder and CEO of SiMa.ai, told AIM. “What we’re announcing now is general access.”

SiMa.ai believes the challenge in physical AI lies less in hardware and more in software migration. Developers often spend weeks or months adapting applications built around NVIDIA’s CUDA ecosystem when shifting to new hardware.

Palette Neat uses an agentic workflow that allows developers to describe applications using natural language. The company says the software then maps workloads to its silicon, reducing manual integration work.

“Our secret sauce is not that you can instruct in English, but that you can take English and make it build a complex system,” Rangasayee said.

He said developers can define systems using prompts instead of writing large amounts of code. “You can just describe ‘build me a robot, it has 16 cameras, radar, LiDAR. Here’s my data set. Here’s my accuracy criteria. Here’s my performance, here’s my power. Build it on SiMa,’” Rangasayee explained in the interview.

The launch also includes SiMa.ai’s Modalix SoM, which the company designed as a pin-compatible replacement for the NVIDIA Orin module. Krishna said the hardware removes a major barrier for developers who want to change platforms without redesigning carrier boards.

The launch comes as chipmakers and startups push alternatives for AI inference, particularly at the edge. While NVIDIA remains dominant in model training, companies increasingly focus on systems that process AI workloads inside robots, vehicles, and industrial machines.

Krishna argued that physical AI workloads require specialised architectures that balance power consumption, latency, and sensor processing.

“They will rule the training world for a long time. I have no doubts,” he said, referring to NVIDIA. “But inference is a very different ballgame.”

SiMa.ai’s software-first approach aims to reduce the effort required to move applications away from GPU-based systems. “Everybody will have to pick a specialised architecture.”

title: SpaceX to Acquire Cursor in $60 Billion All-Stock Deal
content:
The acquisition formalises a relationship that began earlier this year between the two companies.

What Actually Matters.

SpaceX's acquisition of Cursor is valued at $60 billion and formalises a relationship initiated earlier this year.

The deal involves merging SpaceX subsidiary X67 Inc with Anysphere, which will remain a wholly owned subsidiary post-merger.

SpaceX has agreed to acquire Anysphere, the company behind AI coding platform Cursor, in an all-stock transaction that values the startup at an implied equity value of $60 billion, according to a Form 8-K filed with the US Securities and Exchange Commission on June 16.

The deal will see X67 Inc, a wholly owned SpaceX subsidiary, merge with Anysphere, with Anysphere surviving as a wholly owned subsidiary of SpaceX.

The transaction remains subject to customary closing conditions, including regulatory approvals. SpaceX said it expects the merger to close during the third quarter of 2026.

The acquisition formalises a relationship that began earlier this year when SpaceX secured an option to acquire Anysphere for $60 billion.

That agreement also included an alternative structure under which SpaceX would have paid $10 billion if the acquisition did not proceed.

Founded in 2022 by MIT graduates Michael Truell, Sualeh Asif, Aman Sanger, and Arvid Lunnemark, Cursor began as a standalone fork of Microsoft’s VS Code editor before emerging as one of the fastest-growing AI software companies.

Cursor has raised more than $2.8 billion to date. Its latest disclosed funding round was a $2.3 billion Series D in November 2025, which valued the company at $29.3 billion and was led by investors including Thrive Capital, Andreessen Horowitz and Accel.

The Cursor acquisition follows a series of major corporate moves by SpaceX in 2026.

In February, the company completed an all-stock acquisition of xAI, folding Elon Musk’s AI company into the SpaceX group as a wholly owned subsidiary in a transaction that valued xAI at roughly $250 billion and the combined business at about $1.25 trillion.

SpaceX completed its long-awaited Nasdaq debut a few days ago, raising $75 billion before underwriters exercised an additional allotment option, increasing total proceeds to approximately $85.7 billion, making it the largest IPO on record.

title: Wipro to Certify 10,000 Employees on Anthropic's Claude Models as it Launches Dedicated AI Centre
content:
Wipro is deepening its enterprise AI push with a dedicated centre for Anthropic's Claude models and plans to certify 10,000 employees over the next 18 months.

What Actually Matters.

Wipro is launching a dedicated centre for Anthropic's Claude models to enhance its enterprise AI capabilities.

The company plans to certify 10,000 employees on Claude models over the next 18 months as part of a major talent development initiative.

Wipro plans to certify 10,000 frontline delivery professionals on Anthropic's Claude AI models over the next 18 months as it pushes to deepen enterprise AI capabilities.

The company has launched an Applied AI Centre of Excellence (CoE) for Claude models at its Bengaluru innovation hub, according to a statement.

The facility, housed within Wipro's newly formed AI-Native Business and Platforms Unit, will support the development and deployment of AI applications for enterprise clients.

The centre will focus on developing AI-led solutions for sectors including mortgage services, healthcare, airlines, manufacturing, and consumer businesses. Claude models will be integrated across Wipro's platform offerings and used internally across functions such as finance, HR, and sales.

The certification programme is among the largest talent-development initiatives announced by the company around a specific AI model ecosystem and is designed to create a broad base of practitioners capable of designing, deploying, and operating AI-enabled systems in enterprise environments.

Wipro is also building a global pool of forward deployed engineers trained on Claude models who will work inside client environments to integrate AI into business workflows and accelerate adoption.

The announcement comes as IT services companies expand partnerships with leading AI model providers, including Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google, while investing heavily in workforce training to capture a larger share of enterprise AI spending.

“Wipro is strengthening its enterprise AI leadership with the Applied AI Center of Excellence for Claude models, powered by Anthropic. This marks a fundamental shift in how we deliver, and advances our strategy of being consulting-led and AI-powered,” Srini Pallia, Chief Executive Officer and Managing Director, Wipro, said in a statement.

“Embedding Forward Deployed Engineers within client environments, alongside integrating AI across our own operations, enables us to accelerate enterprise-scale adoption with a clear focus on business value,” he added.

title: Women-Led AI Hackathon WitchHunt 2026 Crowns Winners Across Health, Education, Climate & Smart Cities Segments
content:
The new deposition and etch systems want to push manufacturing limits in advanced AI chip production.

What Actually Matters.

Applied Materials has launched two new systems aimed at enhancing semiconductor manufacturing for advanced AI chips.

The Centris Spectral SiN ALD and Producer Selectra Mo Etch systems support the creation of deep, narrow 3D structures in chips.

Applied Materials has launched two semiconductor manufacturing systems to help chipmakers process materials for deep, narrow 3D structures used in advanced logic and memory chips.

The company introduced the Centris Spectral SiN ALD and Producer Selectra Mo Etch systems to support scaling in logic and memory chips. The systems aim to improve processing precision in high-aspect-ratio 3D structures. Applied Materials said leading logic and memory chipmakers are already using the systems for advanced node manufacturing.

The launch comes as demand for AI computing drives chipmakers towards advanced 3D device architectures. These include gate-all-around transistors and high-layer-count 3D NAND memory. Existing deposition and etch methods often struggle to distribute materials evenly in deep structures. This can reduce electrical performance and manufacturing yield.

“As the industry pushes the limits of AI computing, the biggest opportunities are increasingly found in materials engineering,” said Prabu Raja, President of the Semiconductor Products Group at Applied Materials.

The new systems improve control over dielectric film deposition and metal removal. The company said this could help chipmakers improve device performance, energy efficiency and manufacturing yield for next-generation AI chips.

“From transistor structures to memory stacks, chipmakers need new ways to precisely deposit and selectively remove materials in extremely complex 3D architectures,” Raja added.

The Centris Spectral SiN ALD system focuses on depositing silicon nitride in challenging 3D chip structures by using microwave plasma technology at low temperatures. This process supports uniform film deposition in tall and narrow structures.

The company said the system could support scaling in both DRAM and logic devices. In gate-all-around transistors, it can form liners for transistor contacts to reduce resistance and capacitance.

Applied Materials added that leading chipmakers have started adopting the system. It forms part of the company’s Spectral ALD platform.

The Producer Selectra Mo Etch system, on the other hand, aims to support higher layer counts in 3D NAND memory chips. The system selectively removes molybdenum used in wordline metallisation. This process helps isolate wordlines and reduce electrical shorts.

Applied Materials said the system improves etching precision across deep structures. It also reduces variability in 3D NAND stacks, thereby improving data retention. The company said manufacturers have already validated the system for high-volume production.

title: Ahead of NEET Re-Exam, Centre Temporarily Blocks Telegram to Prevent Paper Leak
content:
The National Testing Agency had highlighted a major concern of fraudsters attempting to deceive students.

What Actually Matters.

The Centre has temporarily restricted access to Telegram to prevent cheating ahead of the NEET re-examination.

The National Testing Agency highlighted concerns over Telegram being used by fraudsters to sell fake exam paper leaks.

In an unprecedented move aimed at safeguarding the integrity of the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination, the Centre has ordered a temporary restriction on access to Telegram in India until June 22 and directed the platform to disable its message-editing feature through June 30, citing its misuse by organised cheating rackets and cyber fraud networks.

The action follows recommendations from the National Testing Agency (NTA), which said Telegram had become a key channel for fraudsters attempting to deceive students with fake claims of leaked examination papers ahead of the NEET re-examination scheduled for June 21.

According to an NTA statement, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) invoked provisions under the Information Technology Act to impose a time-bound restriction on Telegram access during the examination period. Simultaneously, the platform has been directed to disable its message-editing feature in India, a tool authorities say has been exploited to fabricate false "paper leak" evidence after examinations are conducted.

"The measures are calibrated and bounded in time," the NTA said, adding that the restrictions are intended to protect candidates and maintain public order in the run-up to one of the country's largest entrance examinations.

The agency revealed that several Telegram channels openly operating under names such as "PAPER LEAKED NEET," "Re-NEET 2026," "Private Mafia," and "REE NEET MAFIAA" were allegedly demanding payments ranging from a few thousand rupees to several lakh rupees in exchange for purported access to examination papers.

"NTA reiterates that no such paper is available outside the secured examination chain. The promise of any such material is, in every instance, a fraud," the agency said.

Authorities argued that while individual channels and groups had been removed over the past several weeks, platform-wide intervention became necessary because channel-by-channel enforcement was insufficient to curb the scale of the activity.

Why Message Editing Feature Was Targeted

A major concern highlighted by the NTA was Telegram's message-editing capability, which allows administrators to alter previously posted messages while retaining the original timestamp.

According to the agency, the feature has been misused in multiple examinations to create misleading evidence of paper leaks. In such cases, administrators allegedly edited older messages after the exam to insert actual question papers, making it appear that the content had been shared before the examination.

"The resulting chat is then circulated as purported evidence that the paper was in circulation before the examination," the NTA noted.

By suspending the editing feature until June 30, authorities hope to eliminate this avenue of misinformation during the post-examination period.

Multi-Agency Operation

The crackdown involved coordinated action by several government agencies. The Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), under the Ministry of Home Affairs, has been monitoring Telegram channels and coordinating takedowns based on inputs from NTA and state police agencies.

The NTA credited I4C and MeitY for facilitating the removal of numerous fraudulent channels, groups, and bots that were promoting fake paper leaks and scams targeting students.

State law enforcement agencies have also intensified investigations. The Bihar Police Economic Offences Unit issued a public advisory warning students against paper-leak scams, while the Ahmedabad City Cyber Crime Branch recently arrested members of an interstate cyber fraud syndicate allegedly operating eight Telegram channels linked to the racket.

Investigators found transactions worth approximately ₹1.5 crore routed through fraudulent accounts, with nearly 1,000 mobile numbers contacted within a month.

While acknowledging that the temporary restriction will affect millions of legitimate Telegram users, the NTA described the move as a "measure of last resort" taken after less restrictive remedies failed to adequately address the threat.

The agency emphasised that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination will proceed as scheduled on June 21 and that the security of the examination remains uncompromised.

"Every candidate and parent is reassured of NTA's commitment to conducting a fair, secure and credible examination," the statement said.

Students have been advised to rely only on official NTA communications and avoid unverified claims circulating on social media platforms. The agency also urged candidates to report suspicious solicitations through the National Cyber Crime Helpline (1930) or the Cyber Crime Reporting Portal.

The original NEET (UG) 2026 examination, conducted on May 3, was officially cancelled after allegations of large-scale paper leak and irregularities.

title: Reliance Is Sabotaging Telegram Access Outside India, Claims Pavel Durov
content:
Telegram CEO accuses Reliance of disrupting Telegram access beyond India through alleged BGP route hijacking.

What Actually Matters.

Telegram CEO Pavel Durov accuses Reliance Industries of intentionally disrupting Telegram access outside India.

Durov claims Reliance is using BGP hijacking to misroute Telegram traffic, affecting users in multiple countries.

Telegram CEO Pavel Durov has accused Indian telecom operator Reliance Industries of disrupting access to Telegram for millions of users outside India through what he described as a ‘rogue’ form of BGP hijacking.

In a post on X, Durov alleged that Reliance's network was announcing unauthorised internet routes, causing Telegram traffic from countries including the UAE to be incorrectly routed and resulting in connectivity issues for users. He said the problem appeared intentional because Reliance had allegedly ignored multiple reports about the issue.

“The sabotage seems intentional, as Reliance has ignored multiple reports,” Durov wrote. He further claimed the incident could be linked to competitive pressures, noting that Reliance is partially owned by Meta, the parent company of WhatsApp, Telegram's largest messaging rival.

Durov also urged network operators worldwide to reject unauthorised BGP announcements originating from Reliance’s AS18101 autonomous system, arguing that doing so would help prevent route hijacks and maintain stable internet access for users.

— Pavel Durov (@durov) June 16, 2026

“Such abuse of global Internet routing is alarming,” Durov wrote, adding that he would not be surprised if Reliance or WhatsApp were involved in lobbying efforts aimed at restricting Telegram's operations in India.

BGP, or Border Gateway Protocol, is the routing system that directs internet traffic between networks worldwide. Incorrect or unauthorised route announcements can redirect traffic away from its intended destination, potentially causing outages, degraded performance, or traffic interception.

If other telecom operators adopted and propagated those announcements, traffic intended for Telegram could be redirected to other networks rather than Telegram’s servers. This can potentially disrupt access to the service for users across multiple networks and countries.

Several researchers on X pointed to public routing records showing Telegram IP prefixes being announced through the Reliance network and propagated beyond India.

While some characterised the incident as a BGP hijack affecting international traffic, others wrote it could have resulted from an accidental routing error rather than a deliberate action.

AIM reached out to Reliance for a comment on Durov’s allegations but had not received a response at the time of publication.

The allegations come at a time when India has temporarily blocked Telegram over claims that the platform was used by organised groups involved in the NEET medical entrance exam paper leak case.

The restriction was imposed until June 22, with authorities arguing that Telegram had become a channel for distributing leaked exam materials and coordinating fraud.

Durov criticised the move, saying it had ‘punished’ more than 150 million ordinary users in Telegram's largest market while failing to stop the leaks.

“The ban has not stopped anything, and the leaks simply moved to other apps,” he wrote on X, arguing that enforcement efforts should focus on those responsible for the leaks rather than the platform itself.

title: MeitY Urges IT Industry to Embrace AI Transformation, Focus on Reskilling Workforce
content:
The consultation highlighted how client expectations are evolving from traditional process outsourcing to end-to-end digital transformation services powered by AI.

What Actually Matters.

The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology urges the IT industry to embrace an AI-driven services ecosystem.

There is a significant shift in client expectations towards end-to-end digital transformation services powered by AI.

As AI reshapes the global technology landscape, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) has called on India's IT services industry to accelerate its transition to an AI-driven services ecosystem, focusing on reskilling and talent development rather than fears of job displacement.

The message came during an industry consultation on “Supporting AI Transformation of IT Services Industry”, convened by MeitY in Kochi and chaired by S Krishnan, Secretary, MeitY.

The consultation brought together senior government officials, industry leaders, and technology stakeholders to discuss the future of India's $246 billion IT exports sector amid rapid advances in Generative AI, automation, and cloud technologies.

Addressing participants, Krishnan emphasised the growing demand for AI-skilled professionals and India's opportunity to emerge as a global talent hub.

“The development and deployment of AI applications will require a large number of trained human resources. That is what India has to offer to the world. The focus must shift from concerns about job loss to investing in reskilling, upskilling, talent development, and technological upgradation,” he said.

The consultation highlighted how client expectations are evolving from traditional process outsourcing to end-to-end digital transformation services powered by AI. As a result, IT and Business Process Management (BPM) firms are increasingly investing in generative AI, agentic AI, analytics, automation, and cloud-based platforms while developing AI-powered products, co-pilots, and enterprise solutions.

Officials noted that the transformation is creating demand for new-age skills and domain-specific expertise across sectors such as banking and financial services (BFSI), healthcare, manufacturing, and retail.

Focus on Workforce Transformation

A key theme of the discussion was the need for large-scale reskilling and upskilling of India's nearly six million-strong IT and BPM workforce to maintain the country's global competitiveness.

Participants examined how the industry is adapting to AI-led changes in service delivery and discussed government interventions to support talent development, technology adoption, and innovation.

The meeting also explored strategies to expand IT and BPM operations into emerging technology hubs beyond traditional metropolitan centres, creating new employment opportunities, and promoting balanced regional growth.

The consultation is part of the government's broader efforts under the IndiaAI Mission, approved by the Union Cabinet in March 2024, which seeks to strengthen India's AI ecosystem through investments in computing infrastructure, AI applications, startup support, and future-ready skills.

Hoovu’s Sarvam-powered HR assistant offers a glimpse into how Indian startups are deploying AI for real-world use cases.

Siddharth Jindal·JUNE 16, 2026, 11:44 AM·Updated OCTOBER 4, 2026, 11:51 AM

What Actually Matters.

Hoovu's Sarvam-powered HR assistant demonstrates real-world AI applications in Indian startups.

Rhea Karuturi pivoted from Silicon Valley to India, wanting to contribute to local AI development.

A recent trip to San Francisco left entrepreneur Rhea Karuturi with a simple observation. While Silicon Valley was abuzz with discussions around AI, many Indian companies were still figuring out how to use the technology.

Karuturi, who co-founded floral brand Hoovu with her sister Yeshoda, tells AIM that a series of talks by Sarvam AI co-founder and CEO Pratyush Kumar convinced her that India needed more builders experimenting with AI locally. At that time, she was exploring the idea of starting an AI venture in Silicon Valley.

“But after attending those talks, I felt that if I was going to build something, it should be in India,” she recalls.

Founded in 2019, Bengaluru-based Hoovu sells fresh puja flowers and devotional products through online and quick commerce channels. The startup gained national attention after appearing on Season 2 of Shark Tank India, where it secured ₹1 crore for 2% equity from Aman Gupta and Peyush Bansal at a ₹50 crore valuation. The company is profitable today.

After listening to Kumar, she started experimenting with Sarvam’s models and APIs. A Stanford-trained computer scientist, Karuturi turned a late-night prototype into a production-ready HR assistant for Hoovu’s warehouse workforce.

The result was Vanaja, an AI HR assistant that interacts with warehouse packing staff in regional languages and helps employees access information related to attendance and monthly pay. Powered by Sarvam’s Saarika v2.5 automatic speech recognition model and Bulbul v2 text-to-speech model, the assistant can converse with workers in their preferred language.

The assistant is named after one of Hoovu’s earliest employees, who passed away unexpectedly from a heart attack last year. “When I was building it at around 3 am, I thought it would be nice to name it after her,” Karuturi says.

Building AI for the Factory Floor

Hoovu employs around 150 women across warehouse operations in multiple cities. Unlike many enterprise AI tools built for office workers, Vanaja was created with frontline employees in mind.

“I think usually when people think of AI, they think of people like you and me, sitting at a desk with a laptop and a degree using it,” she says. “But seeing the people in my warehouse interact with it and be so excited was really cool.”

The AI assistant helps employees access salary information, ask HR-related questions, seek guidance on benefits and workplace issues, and share feedback. Human HR teams remain in the loop, stepping in whenever concerns or complaints need to be escalated.

According to Karuturi, the goal is not to replace HR staff but to extend their reach.

“With 150 ladies, they might have certain questions that they may not feel comfortable asking HR, or maybe they don’t have access to HR all the time because we’re in nine cities,” she explains.

The HR assistant is only one of several AI projects underway at Hoovu. The company has been using AI for warehouse planning, generating daily operational schedules, and helping teams respond to unexpected disruptions.

Why India Needs Its Own AI Ecosystem

The project received an unexpected push from the Sarvam team. After Karuturi shared an early version of the prototype online, Sarvam developer Sneha Prabhu reached out with suggestions to reduce latency and improve the experience.

“She gave me a few tips, and because of her encouragement, I worked on it a little bit more,” she recalls.

While Karuturi used Anthropic’s Claude to help build the application, she believes Indian AI companies such as Sarvam play an important role in the country’s technological future.

Her comments come at a time when geopolitics is increasingly shaping access to AI models. Anthropic recently withdrew Fable 5, a Mythos-class model for general use, following a US export-control directive issued on national security grounds. The company disabled access to Fable 5 and Mythos 5 for all customers, including foreign nationals inside and outside the United States, as well as foreign-national employees.

The development reinforced Karuturi’s belief that India must continue building its own AI capabilities while also adopting the best global technologies.

“India as a country should not be bargaining with an American company to be able to protect its most important companies,” she says, referring to the Indian government’s reported efforts to gain access to Anthropic Mythos. “That might be the reality of the present, but it should not be the future.”

She argues that India’s challenge is not just about building frontier models but ensuring AI reaches more people and businesses. While companies should use the best models available globally, the country must also invest in developing its own capabilities.

“And all my excitement about Claude and getting people to play with it—gone today! Why should we use a technology trying to lock us out? It’s like collecting pennies on the railroad tracks,” she posted on X.

title: Adani Group, Jabil Partner to Build AI Data Centre Hardware Platform in India
content:
The companies intend to build multi-gigawatt AI rack manufacturing capacity in India to serve hyperscalers, colocation operators and enterprise data centre customers.

What Actually Matters.

Adani Group and Jabil are partnering to create AI data centre hardware manufacturing in India.

The focus will be on high-density AI racks and essential infrastructure components.

Adani Group and US-based manufacturing services company Jabil have announced plans to form an alliance to establish an AI and data centre infrastructure manufacturing platform in India, targeting both domestic and global demand for AI-ready hardware.

The proposed platform will focus on manufacturing high-density AI racks, servers, storage systems, networking equipment, power distribution units (PDUs), coolant distribution units (CDUs), transformers, switchgears, bus bars and thermal management systems.

The companies said they intend to build multi-gigawatt AI rack manufacturing capacity in India to serve hyperscalers, colocation operators and enterprise data centre customers.

The announcement comes as demand for AI infrastructure continues to rise globally and India seeks to expand domestic manufacturing capabilities for data centre hardware.

“The world is entering an Intelligence Revolution more profound than any previous Industrial Revolution. Nations that master the symmetry between energy and compute will shape the next decade,” said Gautam Adani, Chairman of Adani Group.

“Our alliance with Jabil represents a decisive step in building India's complete AI infrastructure stack — from green power generation to world-class hardware manufacturing,” he added.

The companies said they are currently working on operational frameworks and formal agreements for the alliance. They estimate the initiative addresses a global market opportunity exceeding $3 trillion over the next seven years, driven by investments in AI computing infrastructure.

The platform will combine Jabil's manufacturing and engineering capabilities with Adani Group’s infrastructure, energy, logistics and data centre operations.

According to the companies, the alliance is expected to manufacture both “white space” computing equipment and “grey space” infrastructure components used in data centres, offering an end-to-end hardware ecosystem for infrastructure developers.

India’s data centre market is projected to reach between 5 GW and 8 GW of capacity by 2030, supported by growth in AI workloads, cloud adoption and data localisation requirements, the companies said. They also cited more than $50 billion in planned investments by hyperscalers across India's data centre, cloud and AI ecosystem.

The alliance aligns with Adani Group’s previously announced plan to invest $100 billion toward building 5 GW of green-energy-powered, AI-ready data centre capacity by 2035.

Jabil, which reported revenue of $29.8 billion in fiscal 2025, has expanded its data centre infrastructure capabilities through acquisitions, including Hanley Energy Group and Mikros Technologies.

“This strategic collaboration with Adani Group is another step forward in our efforts to create long-term value for customers throughout the AI ecosystem by offering scalable solutions across the product lifecycle,” said Mike Dastoor, Chief Executive Officer of Jabil.

“By combining Jabil’s more than sixty years of engineering expertise and advanced manufacturing capabilities with Adani's infrastructure and energy platform, we can expect to execute down to the rack level for hyperscalers and enterprises here in India and across the globe,” he added.

The companies said the initiative is expected to support domestic manufacturing, create engineering jobs and position India as an export hub for AI and data centre hardware.

Equal AI raised $30 million in Series B funding to expand its AI assistant platform.

The funding round was co-led by Prosus Ventures and Tomales Bay Capital, attracting various notable investors.

Hyderabad-based consumer AI startup Equal AI has raised $30 Mn in a Series B funding round co-led by Prosus Ventures and Tomales Bay Capital, as investors continue to back AI-native consumer applications in India.

The round also saw participation from Valiant Fund, Think Investments, PhonePe founder Sameer Nigam, Airtel family office member Zubin Bharti Mittal, Skyflow co-founder Anshu Sharma, Meta India and Southeast Asia Vice President Sandhya Devanathan, and CtrlS Datacenters Chairman Sridhar Pinnapureddy.

The latest investment follows Equal AI's $10 million Series A funding round in November 2024, which was also led by Prosus Ventures and Tomales Bay Capital.

Founded in 2022 by Keshav Reddy, Equal initially focused on consent-based data-sharing and identity infrastructure for enterprises across banking, lending, insurance, telecom, and digital services. The Hyderabad-based startup entered the consumer AI segment in October 2025 with the launch of its AI-powered call assistant.

According to the company, the platform has surpassed 1 million monthly active users and 350,000 daily active users within eight months of launch. Its AI assistant helps users identify callers, block spam calls, understand caller intent, and perform actions on their behalf.

Equal AI said the fresh capital will be used to expand its consumer offerings and strengthen its AI assistant capabilities across communications, financial services, shopping, lifestyle, and concierge services.

Alongside its consumer business, the company continues to operate its enterprise infrastructure platform, which it claims serves more than 350 customers and processes over 1 billion transactions annually.

Researchers argue progress beyond human-level AI could come through scaling, self-improvement, paradigm shifts, or multi-agent systems.

What Actually Matters.

Researchers outline four pathways for advancing from artificial general intelligence to artificial superintelligence.

Key mechanisms include scaling, recursive self-improvement, algorithmic breakthroughs, and multi-agent systems.

Google DeepMind researchers, including Co-Founder Shane Legg, have published a paper outlining four potential pathways from artificial general intelligence (AGI) to artificial superintelligence (ASI).

The researchers argue that AI progress could continue well beyond human-level capabilities through scaling, recursive self-improvement, algorithmic breakthroughs and multi-agent systems.

The paper, From AGI to ASI, defines AGI as a system capable of achieving at least median human performance across a broad range of cognitive tasks, while ASI is described as a system capable of outperforming organisations comprising thousands of human experts working over periods measured in years.

Rather than forecasting specific dates, the authors focus on the mechanisms that could continue advancing AI after AGI is reached and the factors that could constrain further progress.

The paper identifies four possible routes from AGI to ASI: continued scaling of compute, models and data; algorithmic paradigm shifts that improve efficiency or unlock new capabilities; recursive self-improvement through automated AI research; and large-scale collectives of AI agents whose combined capabilities exceed those of individual systems.

One of the report’s central arguments is that forecasting compute growth is relatively tractable because it can be decomposed into three measurable factors: hardware improvements, infrastructure investment and algorithmic efficiency gains.

The paper cites estimates suggesting that hardware capabilities are improving by roughly 1.5x per year, AI infrastructure investment by around 2.5x per year, and algorithmic efficiency by as much as 6x annually.

Combined, those trends imply effective compute growth of roughly 10x per year, according to estimates cited in the report.

The authors note that this figure is at the lower end of public estimates and could be higher. However, they emphasise that predicting how additional compute translates into new capabilities remains substantially harder than forecasting compute growth itself.

“The four pathways are not mutually exclusive and progress may happen on all of them simultaneously, which could lead to compounding (not just additive) increases in artificial intelligence,” the researchers write.

While scaling remains the most visible route today, the report argues that superintelligence may not require dramatically smarter individual models.

Even if progress in individual systems slows near AGI-level performance, coordinating millions of AGI agents could still produce superhuman collective intelligence. In this scenario, quantitative scaling of agent populations, rather than qualitative leaps in individual reasoning, could be sufficient to surpass the capabilities of large human organisations.

The researchers also discuss what they call an “abstraction barrier”, a potential limitation on individual AI systems. The hypothesis suggests that models trained primarily on human-generated knowledge may inherit the conceptual frameworks embedded in that data and struggle to discover entirely new abstractions.

“While this barrier could potentially cap the intelligence of any single AI instance at AGI-level, collective ASI might still be achievable through multi-agent scaling.”

The paper also revisits the concept of an intelligence explosion. While continued scaling implies exponential growth, the authors argue that recursive AI-driven research could create feedback loops that accelerate growth rates themselves, producing hyperbolic dynamics often associated with singularity scenarios.

“While today the pathway of scaling (models & data) seems most promising to deliver progress, it is unclear how long exponential growth rates can be sustained economically and in terms of hardware production and natural resources,” the authors write.

The paper points to several potential constraints on future AI progress, including hardware supply, energy availability, the exhaustion of internet-scale data sources, economic limits and unresolved questions around AI alignment.

The authors do not provide formal timelines for AGI or ASI. “The long-standing goal of creating AGI may come into reach for our generation, perhaps within the next decade or less,” the researchers write.

title: LTM Launches AI-Native Managed Services Platform as it Looks Beyond Manpower-led Delivery
content:
As AI reshapes IT services, LTM's new agentic AI platform aims to automate technology operations and reduce dependence on traditional manpower-led support.

What Actually Matters.

LTM has introduced BlueVerse for iRun, an AI-native managed services platform aimed at automating technology operations.

The platform seeks to reduce reliance on traditional manpower-led support models in the IT services sector.

LTM, formerly LTIMindtree, has launched BlueVerse for iRun, an AI-native managed services platform that uses agentic AI to automate technology operations, marking the latest push by IT services firms to reduce reliance on traditional manpower-led support models.

The offering is designed to help enterprises manage increasingly complex technology environments spanning cloud infrastructure, software applications, and cybersecurity systems through a combination of AI agents and human oversight.

The launch comes at a time when IT services companies are under pressure to demonstrate how artificial intelligence can improve productivity in large managed services contracts, a business that has historically depended on adding engineers to support growing workloads.

LTM said its BlueVerse AI ecosystem creates a unified intelligence layer that brings together enterprise data, telemetry, workflows, and operational information. The company said the platform can identify root causes of issues, recommend actions, and execute tasks within predefined governance controls.

According to the company, the platform aims to automate 60–70% of issue resolution processes, reduce incident closure times by 40–60%, and prevent up to half of potential disruptions before they occur.

“Enterprises today expect managed services to deliver more than efficiency—they expect intelligence, adaptability, and measurable outcomes,” Krishnan Iyer, Chief Growth Officer, LTM, said in a statement. “BlueVerse for iRun brings together agentic AI, operational intelligence, and governed automation to help clients move beyond effort-led models to resilient, outcome-driven operations that scale with confidence.”

The launch reflects a broader shift underway in the IT services industry, where vendors are increasingly embedding AI agents into application management, infrastructure operations, and cybersecurity services. The goal is to move away from contracts tied primarily to headcount and effort, and toward models focused on automation and business outcomes.

For providers such as LTM, such platforms could also help improve margins by automating repetitive operational tasks, while enabling engineers to focus on higher-value transformation projects.

BlueVerse for iRun will be offered across application management, infrastructure services and cybersecurity operations, the company said.

title: India’s AI Boom Could Double Data Centre Water Consumption by 2030: Report
content:
A CEEW report highlighted the environmental cost of AI growth, estimating that a single 100 MW hyperscale data centre can consume nearly 20 lakh litres of water every day.

What Actually Matters.

India's ambition to be an AI hub could significantly strain water resources due to increased data centre consumption.

Data centres are projected to consume about 358 billion litres of water annually by 2030, up from 150 billion litres in 2024-25.

India’s ambition to become a global artificial intelligence (AI) hub could significantly increase pressure on the country’s water resources, according to recent studies tracking the environmental impact of AI infrastructure.

A report by the Council on Energy, Environment and Water (CEEW) estimated that India’s data centres consumed around 150 billion litres of water in 2024-25. As AI adoption accelerates and digital infrastructure expands, that figure is expected to rise to nearly 358 billion litres annually by 2030.

The growing demand is largely driven by data centres, which power AI applications ranging from chatbots and image generators to enterprise AI systems. These facilities house thousands of servers that generate substantial heat and require continuous cooling to function efficiently.

Many data centres use water-based cooling systems, where water absorbs heat from servers and is partially lost through evaporation. According to CEEW, a typical 100-megawatt hyperscale data centre can consume nearly 20 lakh litres of water per day, although usage varies with cooling technologies and local conditions.

The concern comes as India rapidly expands its AI and cloud infrastructure. Government data shows the country’s data-centre capacity increased from around 375 MW in 2020 to 1,500 MW in 2025. Industry estimates suggest this could grow to between 8,000 MW and 10,000 MW by the end of the decade.

Global technology companies, including Google, Microsoft and Amazon alongside domestic players such as Reliance Industries, are investing heavily in AI infrastructure across the country.

However, more than 65% of India’s data-centre capacity is concentrated in cities such as Mumbai, Chennai, Hyderabad, Bengaluru, and Noida, according to CEEW. Several of these cities already face water stress. Bengaluru experienced a major water crisis in 2024, while Chennai and Hyderabad have repeatedly dealt with water shortages in recent years.

Daswin De Silva, Professor of Analytics and AI at La Trobe University, noted in the report that larger AI-focused facilities will continue to increase demand for both water and energy. He suggested that future cooling systems should rely more on reclaimed water, seawater, closed-loop liquid cooling, and hybrid dry-cooling technologies.

Guillaume Dourdin, CEO of Veolia India, also highlighted the need for sustainable water management as India’s data-centre footprint expands, particularly in regions already facing water scarcity.

title: ‘Human Capital Does Not Become Less Valuable as Token Capital Grows,’ Says Satya Nadella
content:
The Microsoft chief warned against a future in which a handful of AI models capture most of the economic value created by AI.

What Actually Matters.

Satya Nadella emphasises the importance of developing AI capabilities alongside human expertise in organisations.

He warns against a future where a few AI models monopolise economic value, stressing the need for a cognitive loop between humans and AI.

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said companies must build and retain their own AI capabilities alongside human expertise, arguing that organisational knowledge should not be ceded to a small number of AI models.

In a post on X on Monday, Nadella said the transition to an AI-driven economy differs from previous technology shifts because businesses can now create “a real cognitive loop between people and digital systems.”

“What is at stake is not some digital tool or system and its use, but how organisations continue to learn, build IP, differentiate, and thrive in a world where AI models can continuously absorb the expertise of humans and organisations and commoditise it,” he wrote.

Nadella said every company would need to develop both ‘human capital’ and ‘token capital’. He described human capital as the knowledge, judgement, relationships and ingenuity of employees, while token capital represents the AI capabilities a company builds and owns.

“Human capital does not become less valuable as token capital grows. It only becomes more valuable,” Nadella said, adding that human agency remains essential for setting goals, building relationships and identifying patterns. “Without human direction, you have compute running in circles.”

According to Nadella, the opportunity for businesses lies not in selecting the most capable AI model but in creating systems that allow human and AI capabilities to learn from one another over time.

“This means the real opportunity is not in picking the best model but instead in building a learning loop on top of models where human capital and token capital compound,” he said.

Nadella argued that companies should be able to replace underlying AI models without losing institutional knowledge accumulated through their own systems. He said businesses need architectures that allow agentic systems to improve while maintaining control over intellectual property.

“Companies need to turn their workflows, domain knowledge, and accumulated judgment into AI systems that improve with each use,” he wrote.

The Microsoft chief warned against a future in which a handful of AI models capture most of the economic value created by AI. Such an outcome, he said, could lead to industries losing control of their expertise and knowledge.

“The last thing any of us wants is a world where every company across every sector is ceding value to a few models that eat everything they see,” Nadella said. “If all the value is accrued by only a few models, the political economy will simply not tolerate it.”

Drawing a parallel with globalisation, Nadella said policymakers and businesses should avoid creating an AI economy in which gains are concentrated among a small number of companies while industries see their knowledge commoditised.

He called for the development of a broader AI ecosystem in which organisations own the learning systems built on top of foundation models.

“In my view, our priority has to be building a frontier ecosystem, not just a frontier model, so value flows broadly across every company, every industry, and every country,” Nadella said.

title: Sarvam AI Raises $234 Mn in HCLTech-Led Series B Round at $1.5 Bn Valuation
content:
HCLTech also acquired a 10.46% stake in the company through an all-cash minority investment.

What Actually Matters.

Sarvam AI has secured $234 million in its Series B funding round, reaching a valuation of $1.5 billion.

HCLTech led the investment with a commitment of $150 million and acquired a 10.46% stake in Sarvam.

Indian AI startup Sarvam AI has raised $234 million in the first close of its planned $300 million Series B round at a post-money valuation of $1.5 billion.

The round was led by HCLTech, which committed $150 million as a strategic investor. Existing investors Bessemer Venture Partners, Khosla Ventures, and Peak XV Partners also participated in the funding.

Sarvam said the capital will be used to fund research on its next frontier model focused on agentic AI, coding and cybersecurity applications, while also expanding access to large-scale compute infrastructure and supporting deployments across enterprises and government projects.

“We are clear that research-led innovation to create AI that works at India’s scale is a very large opportunity,” said Pratyush Kumar, Co-founder of Sarvam. “That means models that understand our voices, read our documents, and serve intelligence at a cost every enterprise and government can afford.”

The company develops AI models, infrastructure and enterprise software products.

According to Sarvam, its recently released Sarvam 105B reasoning model matches or outperforms larger models on knowledge, reasoning and agentic benchmarks, while its Sarvam 30B model is designed to run on consumer hardware. The company also offers vision and speech models trained in India.

Sarvam said its conversational AI platform now handles more than 2 million interactions a day, while its inference platform processes over 10 million API calls daily. Usage on the inference platform has tripled in the past three months, the company said.

The startup added that its vision models are being used to digitise more than 35 million pages of documents, while its speech models transcribe over 500,000 hours of audio every month.

HCLTech said the partnership would combine Sarvam’s AI research with its enterprise customer base and engineering capabilities.

“Our investment in Sarvam marks a significant step toward building India's trusted and globally competitive AI ecosystem,” said C Vijayakumar, CEO and Managing Director of HCLTech. “By bringing together Sarvam's research in AI models with HCLTech’s global presence, we are creating a full-stack AI platform for enterprises and governments.”

Sarvam said its products are being deployed across banking, insurance, government and defence sectors. “Sarvam’s conversational platform now handles over 2 million interactions a day, with usage doubling in the last two months,” the company said in a statement.

It added that its multilingual voice platform collected data from 17 million farmers for the Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare and supported policy renewal campaigns covering 45 million policyholders for a large insurance company.

“Our ambition is to diffuse this technology widely in India, creating significant value across sectors for citizens, small businesses, enterprises, and state and central governments,” said Vivek Raghavan, Co-founder of Sarvam. “The partnership with HCLTech provides a unique example of an Indian corporate helping build foundational strength in AI.”

Pankaj Mitra, partner at Bessemer Venture Partners, said Sarvam has built capabilities across voice, agentic AI and foundation models, positioning it to serve both enterprise and government customers.

Founded in August 2023 by AI4Bharat veterans Raghavan and Kumar, Sarvam raised a $41 million Series A round led by Lightspeed within months of its launch. The Bengaluru-based company has worked with organisations including SBI Life, Tata Capital and government agencies, and serves customers across financial services, insurance and the public sector.

The funding comes days after Anthropic restricted access to its Fable 5 and Mythos 5 AI models following a US government directive, renewing focus on the need for sovereign AI capabilities for enterprise and public-sector use cases.

content:
Fin’s AI agents can handle customer queries across chat, email, phone, WhatsApp, SMS and Slack.

What Actually Matters.

Salesforce plans to acquire customer service AI firm Fin for approximately $3.6 billion.

Fin's AI agents can manage customer queries across multiple channels, enhancing Salesforce's AI capabilities.

Salesforce has announced plans to acquire customer service AI company Fin, formerly known as Intercom, for approximately $3.6 billion.

The acquisition is expected to strengthen Salesforce’s AI agent offerings by bringing Fin’s customer support platform and proprietary AI model, Apex, into the Salesforce ecosystem.

The transaction is subject to regulatory approvals and customary closing conditions and is expected to close in the fourth quarter of Salesforce’s fiscal year 2027.

“Fin brings proven agent technology, a deep commitment to customer success, and an incredible AI team that will complement Agentforce with powerful service agent capabilities,” Salesforce Chair and CEO Marc Benioff said in a statement. “Together, we'll help companies of every size seize this opportunity — accelerating time to value with trusted agents that deliver measurable outcomes at scale.”

Fin’s AI Agent handles customer support queries across channels, including live chat, email, WhatsApp, SMS, phone and Slack. The company said its AI system can resolve customer issues end-to-end and is powered by Apex, a model developed specifically for customer support.

The deal comes as Salesforce continues to expand its AI business. The company said Agentforce, its AI agent platform, reached $1.2 billion in annual recurring revenue in the first quarter of fiscal 2027, up 205% year-on-year.

According to Salesforce, Fin’s packaged AI offerings will complement Agentforce by providing faster deployment options for small and medium-sized businesses as well as commercial customers seeking quicker implementation of AI-powered customer service tools.

“Our technology has defined this category and set the new standards for what great customer service looks like today,” said Eoghan McCabe, Chief Executive Officer and Co-Founder of Fin. “By joining forces with Salesforce, we can deploy it far and wide at a rate far faster than we could have ever achieved on our own."

Salesforce said Fin’s technology has delivered autonomous resolution rates averaging 76% of customer support volume in some deployments. The acquisition will also add Fin's AI engineering team and customer base of more than 30,000 companies.

The company said the acquisition will not affect its fiscal year 2027 financial guidance or its capital return program.

title: Indian IT Once Feared GCCs. Now, it is Racing to Monetise GCC-as-a-Service
content:
The expansion reflects EXL’s broader AI strategy with nearly 60% of the company’s revenue now generated from data and AI services, according to company executives.

What Actually Matters.

EXL has expanded its Chennai hub, increasing capacity to approximately 550 employees to support its AI and analytics initiatives.

The centre will enhance EXL's healthcare and payment integrity services, focusing on improving operational efficiency and fraud detection.

Global data and AI company EXL has expanded its operations in Chennai, adding capacity for 265 employees and increasing the facility’s total capacity to around 550 employees. The move reflects the company’s continued investment in artificial intelligence, analytics and healthcare-focused solutions as enterprises increasingly adopt AI-driven technologies.

The expanded Chennai centre will support EXL’s growing healthcare and payment integrity businesses, bringing together professionals specialising in AI, advanced analytics, data science and healthcare operations.

The company said the facility will play a key role in developing solutions that help healthcare organisations improve payment accuracy, detect fraud, reduce wastage and improve operational efficiency.

“Chennai has emerged as an important destination for technology, analytics and business services talent, making it a natural choice for our continued expansion,” said Vikas Bhalla, President and Head of AI Services and Operations at EXL.

The expansion comes as EXL deepens its focus on enterprise AI. Earlier this week, the company announced it had achieved Gold Tier Status in the Databricks Partner Program, strengthening its collaboration with Databricks to help enterprises build trusted, secure data foundations for AI adoption.

Through its EXLdata.ai platform, the company aims to help organisations improve data governance, transparency, compliance, and security areas that have become increasingly important as businesses move AI projects from pilot stages to large-scale deployment.

The Chennai expansion is expected to create new opportunities across AI engineering, product development, data analytics and healthcare consulting. It also reinforces Chennai’s position as a growing technology and innovation hub.

Headquartered in New York, EXL employs more than 67,000 people globally and serves clients across industries including healthcare, insurance, banking, retail, media and energy. The company recently raised its 2026 revenue guidance after reporting strong first-quarter growth reflecting rising demand for AI-powered business solutions.

GCCs are evolving into a major growth strategy as IT firms seek new revenue pools in building and running AI-native captive centres.

What Actually Matters.

GCCs are becoming integral to India's IT firms, focusing on AI-native transformation.

TCS has established a dedicated unit to assist clients in building and running GCCs.

When Tata Consultancy Services launched a dedicated business its Global Value & Innovation Centres (GVIC) Business Unit this month to help clients build and run global capability centres (GCCs), it wasn't entering a new market so much as formalising a shift already reshaping India's IT industry.

The new unit, which will be headed by Soumen Roy, formerly Country Head for TCS Canada and reporting directly to CEO K Krithivasan, promises to help enterprises establish AI-native GCCs and transform existing centres into "value- and innovation-led operating models."

The announcement lands at a moment when India's GCC story is gathering pace. The country currently hosts over 2,000 GCCs employing more than two million professionals. By 2030, the value of the GCC market in India is expected to reach $105–110 billion, according to a joint report by FICCI and Anarock.

For India's IT services majors, that scale represents both an opportunity and an existential question. They are racing to build the very captive centres that once threatened their business model.

Every Major IT Firm Has Made Its Move

TCS's announcement arrives as its peers are already building serious GCC practices.

Infosys moved most comprehensively. In November 2025, it unveiled its AI-First GCC Model built on its Agentic Foundry, EdgeVerve AI Next platform, and Infosys Topaz. The model combines end-to-end GCC setup, AI-powered process transformation, talent development via Infosys Springboard, and flexible operating models, including build-operate-transfer (BOT) and joint venture arrangements.

The company cited a track record of over 100 GCC engagements across industries. Its clients include Lufthansa Systems, with which it struck a $300 million IT transformation deal in February last year to establish a new GCC in Bengaluru. It also reportedly secured a $500 million deal from US-based Truist Financial to set up and run a technology and operations hub in Hyderabad.

Meanwhile, Cognizant approached the opportunity through a platform-led model. The company appointed Sailaja Josyula as Global Head of its GCC Service Line to define and execute its global GCC strategy, and positioned GCC-as-a-service as an end-to-end, outcome-driven offering with emphasis on digital engineering, data, and AI-led transformation.

In April 2025, it partnered with Citizens Financial Group to launch a GCC on its own Hyderabad campus, which has scaled to 1,000 IT and data analytics professionals.

Also, Wipro formalised its GCC play in mid-2025, appointing Sandeep Dhar, a veteran of the GCC and consulting ecosystem, as Global Head of its GCC Practice. Wipro also launched a dedicated AI-Native Business and Platforms Unit in April 2026, which intersects directly with its GCC ambitions.

HCLTech also signalled its commitment in May 2025 by appointing Kiran Cherukuri as its Global GCC Practice Leader.

Late Entry?

Given the pace of developments over the last year and a half, has TCS' arrived a little late? Gaurav Vasu, Co-Founder and CEO of business research platform UnearthInsights, acknowledges the momentum but tempers the TCS narrative.

"TCS's announcement of a dedicated GVIC business unit is more of a formalisation of an existing market trend than a transformative strategic shift," he tells AIM. "Most leading IT services firms, including Infosys, Wipro, Persistent, and others, have already established dedicated GCC leadership teams and practices. In that context, TCS was relatively late in formally announcing a standalone GCC-focused unit."

Shalini Pillay, India Leader for Global Capability Centres at KPMG, says the GCC model has more than proven its benefits to global enterprises. "Over the past 18 months, one has witnessed every significant IT services firm establish a GCC or GVIC vertical, as they have begun to focus very aggressively on the GCC opportunity," she says.

The central dynamic driving this move is as much about structural threat as it is about opportunity. As global enterprises have grown more confident in the GCC model, they are taking delivery functions in-house that they previously outsourced. That insourcing impulse, if left unaddressed, erodes the revenue base of traditional outsourcing.

"In an attempt to preempt some of this loss of revenue, while also taking advantage of building on the existing offshore delivery centre model that IT services players had established for many of their global clients, they have all begun to pivot the offshore development centre into a GCC setup through the build-operate-transfer route," Pillay explains.

For enterprises that want the benefits of a captive centre but are wary of doing it alone, the BOT model presents a viable opportunity.

“As the work becomes more strategic, the last thing an enterprise wants is difficult, tactical hand-offs or partners whose value proposition is essentially office infrastructure and talent supplied at a premium,” observes Praveen Bhadada, CEO and Managing Director of consulting firm Neovay Global.

"Working with an integrated player lets them combine economies of scale with a genuinely integrated experience across strategy, build, talent, and run, under one accountable relationship. It is the better outcome for the talent pool on both sides: people can see continuity, scale, and impact in one place," he adds.

New Profit Pool or Margin-Dilutive Hedge?

The question of whether the GCC services push generates genuine new profit or merely cannibalises existing revenue remains contested.

"It is a combination of a defensive response to some extent, but more importantly, it is a real opportunity to leverage scale, capacity, and tech capabilities, and to gear up for the GCC opportunity," Pillay acknowledges.

Vasu is more sceptical. "GCC services are not necessarily a new profit pool for the industry. Enterprises are increasingly choosing to build their own GCCs rather than relying entirely on traditional outsourcing models. As a result, IT services firms are helping clients set up capabilities that they might otherwise have delivered themselves through offshore outsourcing engagements. In that sense, GCC enablement is partly cannibalising the traditional outsourcing opportunity. It is also typically a lower-margin business than large-scale outsourcing contracts."

As the GCC enablement market expands, so does the diversity of players. While specialist firms such as ANSR and Zinnov pioneered the space. Big Four consultancies, strategy firms, real estate platforms, and now every major IT services provider is hoping to grab a share of the growing pie.
