From Mistral tie-ups to proprietary agentic platforms, India's technology services majors are racing to reinvent themselves for the AI era.

What Actually Matters.

Indian IT firms are shifting focus from traditional outsourcing to enterprise AI solutions amid slowing growth.

Major companies are forming alliances with AI pioneers and developing proprietary platforms to enhance their offerings.

Faced with slowing growth in their core outsourcing businesses and the prospect of AI automating much of the work they traditionally sold, India's top IT services companies are racing to reinvent themselves.

From building proprietary AI platforms to signing alliances with OpenAI, Mistral, Anthropic, Microsoft, and Google, firms including TCS, Infosys, HCLTech, and Wipro are aggressively repositioning themselves as enterprise AI partners rather than providers of labour-intensive technology services.

IT firms have been busy rolling out AI products and finding new partners in global AI pioneers.

India’s IT bellwether TCS recently partnered with French AI startup Mistral to develop and deploy custom AI systems for enterprises. Wipro has expanded its alliance with ServiceNow to help clients roll out agentic AI workflows. HCLTech unveiled an autonomous finance platform built on Google Cloud's Gemini stack. Mphasis launched Tria, an enterprise AI platform designed to move companies beyond AI pilots and into automated decision-making at scale.

Taken together, these moves reveal that India's $300 billion technology services industry is in the middle of a structural reinvention, as the old model of selling labour-intensive IT services priced per headcount or per hour is under existential pressure.

The question animating boardrooms, investor calls, and analyst reports is whether the pivot to enterprise AI can happen fast enough, and at sufficient scale, to compensate for the slowdown in the businesses that have historically paid the bills.

“Historically, Indian IT firms have been built around a technology services model. The AI era may require them to evolve towards delivering enterprise AI applications and outcome-oriented solutions, which involves changes not only in technology capabilities but also in operating models, talent structures, commercial frameworks, and go-to-market approaches,” Gaurav Vasu, Founder and CEO of business research platform UnearthInsights, tells AIM.

AI-led offerings currently contribute only a small proportion of overall IT revenues. While partnerships with players such as Mistral, OpenAI, Anthropic, and cloud providers are accelerating, they have not yet reached a scale sufficient to materially offset broader pressures on traditional services revenues.

The Platform Race

At the heart of the sector's response is a race to build and own enterprise AI platforms—composable stacks of models, agents, data infrastructure, and workflows that can sit within a client's technology environment and orchestrate intelligent automation.

Infosys launched its Topaz Fabric platform in November 2025, describing it as a composable stack of AI agents, services, and models designed to unify IT service delivery across the enterprise. The company followed this up in January 2026 with a collaboration with Cognition, maker of the AI software engineer Devin.

Wipro, which pledged $1 billion over three years to advance AI through its ai360 initiative, launched its Wipro Intelligence platform suite in late 2025. Tech Mahindra launched TechM Orion in July 2025, and LTM also took a similar path with its BlueVerse platform, an AI-native ecosystem built around intelligent agents and modular architecture.

These proprietary platforms are complemented by a flurry of agreements with the major AI providers and hyperscalers.

The objective is to become the layer that helps enterprises deploy, manage, and govern AI systems. Whoever owns that layer stands to capture a larger share of AI spending than firms that simply provide implementation services.

The Logic of the Bet

There are twin reasons behind the enterprise AI push.

On the defensive side, the traditional IT services model—build and run large application estates, staff augmentation, business process outsourcing—is being hollowed out by the same AI tools that Indian IT firms are now trying to sell. If Indian IT firms do not own a share of that automation stack, they risk being disintermediated by the AI platforms themselves.

On the opportunity side, enterprises globally are spending heavily on AI transformation, and they need implementation partners who understand their industries, regulatory environments, and technology estates. Indian IT firms, with decades of experience running complex enterprise systems for global clients, are well-positioned to play that role, but only if they can credibly demonstrate AI capability alongside domain expertise.

"Every corporate is going to talk about it, and services organisations absolutely need to infuse that in everything they do. Whatever offerings they have will need to be powered by AI, and that will happen to different degrees. If you don't have the capability, you will join hands with a frontier AI organisation and do it jointly, or you will invest in creating your own assets, accelerators, and platforms," says Siddhartha Tipnis, Partner and Technology Sector Leader at Deloitte India.

The strategic logic of the enterprise AI push is hard to argue with. The harder question is one of maturity and scale.

"Partnerships with AI providers, hyperscalers, and model developers are strategically important for Indian IT services companies, but they are still at a relatively early stage of maturity," cautions Vasu.

The Partner-Competitor Problem

The AI partnerships are further complicated when the platforms themselves simultaneously develop their own enterprise implementation capabilities.

In May, OpenAI launched what it called the OpenAI Deployment Company—a $4 billion venture backed by TPG, Brookfield, and Bain Capital, designed to embed ‘forward deployed engineers’ directly inside corporations. Also,Anthropic launched its Enterprise AI Services initiative, launched in partnership with institutions including Blackstone, Hellman & Friedman, and Goldman Sachs. Under this model, Anthropic's Applied AI engineers work directly with enterprise customers to identify use cases, build solutions, and deploy Claude-based applications.

This work sits squarely in the domain traditionally occupied by systems integrators and IT services firms.

However, this doesn’t mean that the current wave of AI investment is misguided. On the contrary, for Indian IT firms, building credible enterprise AI capabilities is essential to remain relevant to large clients.

What investors and clients are both watching is execution—whether the platforms, partnerships, and proprietary offerings announced over the past eighteen months can be converted into repeatable, scalable revenue streams. The sector has shown it can build compelling AI narratives. The harder test is whether it can convert those narratives into durable growth.

TCS has set up a dedicated Claude-focused business unit as it deepens its enterprise AI push amid rising demand for governance-led deployments.

What Actually Matters.

TCS has partnered with Anthropic to enhance its AI capabilities for regulated sectors.

A dedicated business unit for Anthropic's Claude models will be established within TCS.

Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) has now partnered with Anthropic, which recently released Claude Fable 5 for hard knowledge work and coding problems, as the Indian IT services giant looks to expand its enterprise AI offerings and accelerate adoption among clients in heavily regulated sectors.

As part of the partnership, TCS will establish a dedicated business unit focused on Anthropic's Claude family of AI models and will provide access to the technology to 50,000 employees across functions, including engineering, finance, legal, marketing, and sales.

The company said the move would allow it to gain first-hand experience deploying AI internally while helping clients move AI initiatives beyond pilot projects into production environments.

Under the agreement, TCS and Anthropic will jointly develop and market AI solutions for industries including financial services, public services, healthcare, life sciences, aviation, telecomm and medical technology. They will collaborate on domain-specific workflows, application modernisation initiatives, and customer experience projects.

“We built Claude to be safe, trusted, and helpful, particularly in contexts where accuracy matters most. This partnership deepens our commitment to India, our second-largest market, with TCS bringing Claude to enterprises and professionals across the region and globally, including 50,000 of its employees,” Dario Amodei, Co-founder and CEO, Anthropic, said in a statement.

TCS will also integrate Claude into some of its existing businesses and platforms. Diligenta, TCS' UK-based life and pensions administration business, plans to use Claude for customer service and process automation initiatives. Meanwhile, teams working on banking and financial services products will use Claude Code to improve software engineering and IT operations productivity.

The collaboration extends to workforce development as well. TCS iON, the company's assessment and learning platform that conducts more than 75 million assessments annually across India, will offer training and certification programmes focused on Claude models. The initiative aims to build a larger pool of AI-skilled professionals as enterprises ramp up investments in generative AI technologies.

“Enterprise AI value comes from understanding business context, orchestrating complex systems, and applying deep AI engineering talent,” K Krithivasan, CEO and MD, TCS, said in a statement. “By combining Claude with our industry expertise, engineering rigour, and large-scale transformation capabilities, we will help customers move faster to production, especially in industries where trust, resilience, and regulatory discipline are critical.”

The partnership comes as global IT services firms increasingly align with leading foundation model providers to strengthen their AI portfolios and respond to growing enterprise demand for generative AI deployments.

Unlike experimental use cases, organisations in sectors such as banking, healthcare, life sciences, and public services face stricter requirements around governance, auditability, and accuracy, creating opportunities for services companies that can bridge the gap between AI models and enterprise-scale implementation.

title: Can India’s AI Curriculum Overhaul Deliver Industry-Ready Talent?
content:
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman recently acknowledged that the cost of using AI has become a major concern for customers.

What Actually Matters.

OpenAI is considering significant price cuts for its AI services amid intensifying competition with Anthropic.

The rising cost of AI usage has become a pressing concern for customers, prompting OpenAI to seek ways to provide more value.

IPO-bound OpenAI is considering significant price cuts for its AI services as it prepares for a potential pricing war with rival Anthropic, according to a report by The Wall Street Journal.

The company is weighing reducing the price of tokens, which are the units used to measure and bill AI usage, as executives anticipate that Anthropic could make similar moves. The discussions are ongoing, and no final decision has been made, the report added.

The deliberations come as businesses increasingly scrutinise their spending on AI tools. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman recently acknowledged that the cost of using AI has become a major concern for customers and said the company is looking for ways to deliver more value while lowering expenses for users.

Any broad-based price cuts could put additional pressure on the finances of both OpenAI and Anthropic. Despite rapid revenue growth, the companies continue to spend heavily on computing infrastructure and chips needed to train and run advanced AI models, resulting in substantial losses.

According to OpenAI President Greg Brockman, the ChatGPT maker is projected to spend $50 billion on computing in 2026.

The reported move reflects intensifying competition between the two AI firms in the enterprise market. Anthropic has gained momentum in recent months following the popularity of its coding product, Claude Code, among software developers.

OpenAI was last valued at $852 billion and is generating roughly $24 billion in annualised revenue, while Anthropic recently reached a $965 billion valuation and is estimated to be running at nearly $47 billion in annualised revenue

OpenAI’s coding agent Codex has grown rapidly, surpassing 5 million weekly active users, according to the company, as its use extends beyond software development to broader workplace tasks.

At the same time, some companies are beginning to question whether their growing AI bills are generating sufficient returns. The debate has fuelled discussion in Silicon Valley around tokenmaxxing—the practice of consuming large amounts of AI computing resources in pursuit of productivity gains that may not always translate into financial benefits.

A potential price war could test whether AI companies can sustain their current business models.

The competition is also unfolding as both companies prepare for eventual public listings.

OpenAI confidentially filed for an initial public offering earlier this week, following Anthropic’s own confidential IPO filing. Altman has reportedly told employees that OpenAI aims to go public within the next year, although the company said there are still initiatives it would prefer to pursue while remaining private.

title: Microsoft Restricts Internal Use of Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5 Over Data Retention Concerns
content:
The company is reviewing Anthropic’s 30-day data retention policy and the extended storage of flagged content before approving broader employee access.

What Actually Matters.

Microsoft has restricted internal access to Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5 due to concerns over its data retention practices.

The restriction follows the launch of Claude Fable 5, which retains user data for 30 days and flagged content for up to two years.

Microsoft has restricted employees from using Anthropic’s newly launched Claude Fable 5 AI model internally, citing concerns over the startup’s data retention practices, according to a report by The Verge.

The move comes a day after Anthropic introduced Claude Fable 5, the public-facing version of its Mythos-class model.

While Microsoft has already made the model available to customers through GitHub Copilot and Microsoft Foundry, employees inside the company are currently unable to access it as legal and compliance teams review the implications of Anthropic’s policies.

The restriction reportedly stems from a key difference between Claude Fable 5 and Anthropic’s earlier models. Most Claude models available to Microsoft employees comply with Zero Data Retention (ZDR) requirements, meaning user prompts and outputs are not stored.

Claude Fable 5, however, retains user data for 30 days to support Anthropic’s new safety monitoring systems. Content flagged by those systems can be stored for as long as two years, creating concerns around the handling of sensitive customer and corporate information.

Microsoft’s legal teams are evaluating whether the model can meet the company’s internal standards for protecting confidential data before broader employee access is approved, according to the report.

Claude Fable 5 is Anthropic’s most capable publicly available model to date. The company has described it as particularly strong in software engineering, research and complex knowledge work, while also incorporating safeguards for sensitive areas such as cybersecurity, biology and chemistry.

Anthropic introduced those safeguards because the underlying Mythos model demonstrated advanced capabilities that the company previously considered too risky for broad release. The public-facing Fable 5 version includes restrictions that route certain high-risk requests to less capable models, while Claude Mythos 5 remains available only to a limited group of vetted organisations through Anthropic’s Project Glasswing programme.

The development also follows Microsoft’s recent efforts to reduce its internal reliance on certain Anthropic tools. Last month, the company began cancelling many internal Claude Code licenses and directing engineers toward GitHub Copilot CLI, Microsoft’s own AI-powered coding assistant.

For now, Microsoft employees can continue using other Claude models that comply with the company’s data-handling requirements, while Claude Fable 5 remains under review.

title: TCS Partners With Anthropic to Build AI Solutions for Regulated Sectors, Train 50,000 Employees
content:
The collaboration combines LTTS’ engineering expertise with Databricks’ data and AI platform to unlock value from decades of industrial and operational data.

What Actually Matters.

LTTS and Databricks have partnered to develop Industrial AI solutions for asset-intensive industries.

The collaboration aims to enhance asset reliability, operational efficiency, and sustainability using operational data.

L&T Technology Services (LTTS) has announced a strategic partnership with Databricks to develop and deliver Industrial AI solutions for asset-intensive industries such as energy, petrochemicals and manufacturing.

The collaboration aims to help industrial companies use operational and engineering data more effectively to improve asset reliability, operational efficiency and sustainability performance.

Under the partnership, LTTS will combine its engineering and industry expertise with Databricks’ data and AI platform to create solutions that can transform large volumes of plant and operational data into actionable insights.

The companies said the partnership will focus on advancing what they call ‘Engineering Intelligence’, enabling enterprises to make faster and more informed decisions across the asset lifecycle.

The joint solutions will cover areas such as predictive asset reliability, energy and emissions optimisation, production intelligence, quality management and sustainability analytics.

According to the companies, the solutions will use real-time operational data, artificial intelligence, machine learning, and natural-language-based insights to help engineers and plant operators analyse and act on critical information more efficiently.

Julien Debard, Director for Energy and Utilities at Databricks, said many industrial organisations already have access to vast amounts of operational data, but often lack the engineering context needed to generate meaningful insights.

He added that the partnership combines LTTS’ expertise in sectors such as power generation, refining and industrial infrastructure with Databricks’ AI and analytics capabilities to help organisations improve decision-making across operations.

“Industrial enterprises are sitting on decades of operational and engineering data that can improve performance, sustainability and competitiveness,” noted Alind Saxena, Executive Director and President- Strategic Initiatives and Growth Markets at LTTS.

He added that the partnership aims to help organisations convert this data into practical business outcomes by combining AI-driven analytics with engineering expertise.

LTTS said the collaboration will primarily support clients in the energy, petrochemicals and industrial sectors globally.

The company currently serves several large industrial customers and has worked on more than 600 major plants worldwide.

title: Adobe Widens Access to AI-Powered CX Enterprise Coworker
content:
Adobe’s solution brings together customer data, content, insights, and AI agents to coordinate marketing and customer experience operations.

What Actually Matters.

Adobe introduces CX Enterprise Coworker, an AI-powered solution aimed at enhancing customer experiences and automating marketing workflows.

The platform integrates data, content, insights, and AI agents to streamline operations across various marketing functions.

Adobe has announced the general availability of CX Enterprise Coworker, a new AI-powered solution designed to help businesses improve customer experiences and automate marketing workflows.

The offering was officially launched in April this year at the Adobe Summit.

The new offering is part of Adobe’s Customer Experience (CX) Enterprise platform and aims to help organisations move beyond AI experimentation and achieve measurable business outcomes.

According to Adobe, CX Enterprise Coworker acts as a central intelligence layer that brings together data, content, customer insights, and AI agents from both Adobe and third-party applications. The platform can coordinate workflows across analytics, content creation, customer journey management, and marketing operations.

Anjul Bhambhri, Senior Vice President of Engineering, Customer Experience Orchestration at Adobe, said in a statement, “Many organisations are struggling to translate AI adoption into measurable business results. CX Enterprise Coworker was built to help teams deliver better outcomes, reshaping workflows with agentic AI that is grounded in brand, customer and channel intelligence.”

The solution is designed to support businesses across three key areas—marketing campaigns, customer engagement, and marketing operations.

For marketing teams, the platform can help simplify campaign creation by identifying target audiences, generating on-brand content, and building customer journeys based on business goals such as engagement or conversions. Teams can review and approve recommendations before campaigns are launched.

In customer engagement, the AI system continuously monitors performance signals and customer interactions across multiple channels. It can identify opportunities to improve conversions, deliver personalised offers, and help retain customers who may be at risk of disengaging.

The company added that the solution is built on open standards such as Model Context Protocol (MCP) and Agent2Agent (A2A), enabling it to work across Adobe applications as well as third-party AI platforms from companies including Amazon Web Services, Anthropic, Google Cloud, Microsoft, and OpenAI.

The solution is designed for both large enterprises and smaller marketing teams looking to automate customer experience workflows using AI.

content:
The facility brings together AI, emerging technologies, industry expertise and human-centred design, allowing business leaders to test ideas and evaluate transformation opportunities.

What Actually Matters.

EY GDS has launched the ey.ai Center for Reimagination in Bengaluru to help businesses implement AI at scale.

The centre combines AI, emerging technologies, and human-centred design to facilitate real business transformations.

EY Global Delivery Services (GDS) has launched the ey.ai Center for Reimagination, a new AI-focused innovation hub in Bengaluru aimed at helping businesses explore and implement AI at scale.

The centre is designed to help organisations move beyond AI experimentation and translate emerging technologies into real business outcomes.

The launch comes as EY continues to expand its AI capabilities following the global organisation’s announced $1.4 billion investment in AI.

The ey.ai Center for Reimagination brings together AI, emerging technologies, industry expertise and human-centred design under one roof. The facility allows business leaders to test ideas, simulate business scenarios and explore how technologies such as agentic AI, robotics, digital twins and conversational AI can transform their operations.

Janet Truncale, Global Chair and CEO of EY, said, “AI is fundamentally changing how organisations make decisions and create value.”

“The ey.ai Center for Reimagination is where strategy meets execution. It provides a space for leaders to test ideas responsibly, define a path to scale and reimagine their organisations with confidence,” she added.

Ajay Anand, Global Vice Chair of EY Global Delivery Services, said many organisations understand the potential of AI but struggle to implement it effectively.

“AI is no longer a future ambition; it’s a present-day business imperative. The centre is designed to help leaders move from intent to execution and translate AI ambition into real business impact,” he noted.

While the centre’s initial focus is on industries including life sciences, industrial products, consumer products, retail, banking, capital markets and energy, the company said many of the technologies and use cases showcased at the facility can be applied across sectors.

Apart from helping enterprises adopt AI, it is also expected to create new high-skilled jobs in areas such as AI engineering, immersive experience design, digital twins, simulation technologies and sector transformation.

The facility will serve as a collaborative environment where organisations can explore future business models, test emerging technologies and develop strategies to navigate AI-led disruption while accelerating innovation and growth.

title: Infosys Bags Multi-Country ERP Transformation Mandate from IHH Healthcare
content:
The project will begin in Hong Kong, Malaysia and Singapore as the healthcare provider looks to unify operations and deploy AI across core business functions.

What Actually Matters.

Infosys has secured a multi-year ERP transformation mandate from IHH Healthcare to enhance operations across multiple countries.

The project will start in Hong Kong, Malaysia, and Singapore, focusing on standardising and streamlining business processes.

Infosys has secured a multi-year enterprise resource planning (ERP) transformation mandate from healthcare provider IHH Healthcare, as the IT services major deepens its focus on large-scale AI-led transformation programmes in the healthcare sector.

Under the engagement, Infosys will help IHH Healthcare standardise and streamline business processes across its markets, beginning with Hong Kong, Malaysia and Singapore.

The programme aims to consolidate the healthcare group's legacy ERP systems and integrate functions across finance, procurement, supply chain, human resources and enterprise performance management.

The project will be powered by Infosys Topaz, Infosys’ generative and agentic AI platform, which the company said will embed AI capabilities into IHH's business workflows and improve decision-making through greater real-time visibility into operational data.

“As we continue to optimise and future-proof our operations across markets, this ERP collaboration with Infosys will drive greater cost efficiency while empowering our teams to focus on what matters most—caring for patients,” Dilip Kadambi, Group Chief Financial Officer, IHH Healthcare, said in a statement.

The deal comes as global enterprises increasingly move beyond pilot projects to modernise core business systems with AI capabilities.

According to the companies, the transformation will create a centralised digital foundation for IHH Healthcare, enabling the healthcare group to improve operational efficiency, reduce costs and strengthen regulatory compliance across markets. The initiative is also expected to support faster, data-driven decision-making across the organisation.

“This collaboration with IHH Healthcare reflects our ability to operationalise AI-led transformation at scale. By leveraging Infosys Topaz, we are consolidating fragmented systems into a unified, cloud-based platform that enables real-time decision-making, simplifies cross-market operations, and accelerates enterprise-wide adoption,” Venky Ananth, Executive Vice President and Global Head of Healthcare, said.

IHH Healthcare operates 89 hospitals and around 190 healthcare facilities across 10 countries, including India, Malaysia, Singapore, Turkey and Greater China.

title: Eros Brings Cultural AI Ecosystem to UK with $355 Mn Investment
content:
The initiative will strengthen collaboration between India and the UK in artificial intelligence, storytelling, and creative industries.

What Actually Matters.

Eros Innovation launched a Cultural AI Platform designed to understand and preserve culture across multiple languages.

The platform features Eros LCVM and Eros Persona AI, enhancing multilingual voice generation and cultural context understanding.

Eros Innovation has announced a £265 million ($355 million) investment commitment in the United Kingdom over the next five years and licensed its cultural AI dataset to its UK operations, marking a major expansion of its artificial intelligence and content production initiatives.

The announcement was made at London Tech Week where the company also unveiled new film and entertainment projects under its Eros Brahmand, Eros Universe, and Eros Remastered programmes.

Eros said the investment will support film production, AI research, animation, microdrama content, music studios, and cultural AI development in the UK. The company will also establish what it described as a sovereign-grade cultural AI capability in Britain using its rights-cleared cultural dataset.

According to Eros, the dataset has been independently valued at $1.7 billion by OxValue.AI, a University of Oxford spin-out. The dataset is built from more than 11,000 films and over 100,000 characters forming the foundation of the company’s cultural AI models.

As part of the initiative, the company will develop AI training and research activities in the UK and explore academic partnerships with British institutions.

The company also confirmed that two upcoming productions, Nandi: War of Kailasa and Tanu Weds Manu – The Next Chapter, will be filmed in the UK in 2026. Both projects are part of a broader slate of 15 productions announced during the event.

Kanishka Narayan, Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State at the UK’s Department for Science, Innovation and Technology, said the investment reflected growing collaboration between India and the United Kingdom in artificial intelligence, technology, and creative industries.

Swaneet Singh, Co-President of Eros Innovation, said “The company was bringing not only investment but also a cultural AI ecosystem to Britain.”

“What we are bringing to Britain is a sovereign-grade cultural artificial intelligence capability, one of the world’s largest rights-cleared cultural datasets, the AI Studio that will operate on it, and a long-term partnership with British talent and institutions,” he added.

Ridhima Lulla, Co-founder and Co-President of Eros Innovation noted that the company aims to combine storytelling, culture, and artificial intelligence to create new forms of entertainment.

title: Bengaluru-Based HyperNorm AI Raises $2.2 Mn to Bring Explainable AI to Wealth Management
content:
The startup plans to use the funding to enhance product development, grow its engineering and AI research teams, and expand in the US and other international markets.

What Actually Matters.

HyperNorm AI has raised $2.2 million in seed funding to enhance its AI tools for wealth management.

The funding will support product development and the expansion of the engineering and AI research teams.

HyperNorm AI, a startup building artificial intelligence-powered tools for wealth advisors, has raised $2.2 million in a seed funding round co-led by Capital 2B and SenseAI Ventures.

The round also saw participation from Boundless Ventures, iOPEX Technologies, and angel investors, including Dr Amit Sheth and Bhavin Manek.

The Bengaluru-based company will use the fresh funding to accelerate product development, expand its presence in the United States and other international markets, and strengthen its engineering and AI research teams.

Founded in 2024 by Keyur Faldu and Peeyush Jain, HyperNorm AI’s decision intelligence platform helps wealth advisors manage complex investment portfolios, including equities, fixed income, structured products, alternatives, and foreign exchange. The platform is designed to identify which portfolios need attention, explain why action may be required, and suggest recommendations based on a client’s investment goals.

HyperNorm AI uses causal reasoning and explainable AI to analyse market events, assess their impact on portfolios and generate recommendations that align with a client’s investment mandate.

“Modern wealth management does not suffer from a lack of information. It suffers from a lack of clarity on what matters now and what action should be taken,” said Keyur Faldu, Co-founder and CEO of HyperNorm AI, in a statement.

According to the company, its platform is already being used by paying clients across the US, Singapore, and India.

Amit Behl, Partner at Capital 2B, said HyperNorm AI is building an AI-native platform that can transform complex portfolio data into clear and explainable investment decisions.

“The platform helps advisors understand complex financial instruments and navigate increasingly sophisticated markets”, added Rahul Agarwalla, Managing Partner, SenseAI Ventures.

HyperNorm AI aims to create a new category at the intersection of artificial intelligence and wealth management by helping advisors make faster, more informed and transparent investment decisions.

title: Haleon to Invest ₹2,000 Crore in First India Manufacturing Facility in Madhya Pradesh
content:
The site is expected to generate up to 500 direct jobs, along with indirect employment opportunities.

What Actually Matters.

Haleon is investing ₹2,000 crore to establish its first manufacturing facility in India.

The new facility in Madhya Pradesh is expected to create around 500 direct jobs and additional indirect employment.

Haleon has announced an investment of approximately ₹2,000 crore to establish its first manufacturing facility in India, marking a significant expansion of its presence in the country’s fast-growing consumer health market.

The greenfield facility will be set up at Pithampur in Madhya Pradesh and is expected to strengthen the company’s supply chain, boost exports, and support its long-term growth strategy in India and Asia.

Spread across more than 40 acres in the Smart Industrial Park, the facility is aligned with the government’s ‘Make in India’ vision and is designed to enhance domestic manufacturing capacity while improving export competitiveness across wider Asia.

The site is expected to generate up to 500 direct jobs, along with indirect employment opportunities, and will focus on local talent development and supplier ecosystem integration.

Brian McNamara, CEO at Haleon, said, “India is a key strategic market for Haleon and an important driver of our long-term growth. This investment strengthens our local manufacturing footprint and expands our reach in one of the world’s fastest-growing consumer health markets. By increasing access to our trusted brands and building our capabilities on the ground, we are well positioned to capture the significant opportunities ahead. We aim to expand access to better everyday health for more than 300 million additional consumers in India. This will be key to achieving our broader ambition to reach one billion more consumers globally by 2030.”

The company said the facility will feature future-ready automated manufacturing systems based on Haleon’s global advanced blueprint and is expected to become operational by 2029–30.

It will primarily support the production of oral health products, including established brands such as Sensodyne, which has been part of India’s oral care landscape for over a decade.

Once operational, the plant will support both domestic consumption and exports, reinforcing India’s position as a key hub in Haleon’s global manufacturing and supply network.

Kedar Lele, CEO India and President, Haleon ISC, added, “India is central to Haleon’s growth ambitions, both in South Asia and globally. Our investment in this new site will bring us closer to consumers, strengthen access to our brands, and support sustainable long-term growth. As demand for trusted everyday health solutions continues to grow, this facility will enhance our ability to serve consumers across India and global markets, particularly in Oral Health, while reinforcing our commitment to making everyday health more accessible to millions.”

title: OpenAI Researcher Says AI Benchmarks Fail to Measure Frontier Model Capabilities
content:
The platform supports 61 languages and is designed to handle accented speech, background noise and industry-specific terminology in real time.

What Actually Matters.

Krisp launched a real-time voice translation API, enhancing multilingual communication across various industries.

The platform supports 61 languages and effectively manages background noise, accented speech, and specific terminology.

Voice AI company Krisp has launched Voice Translation v3, a new version of its real-time translation platform, along with a self-service Voice Translation API that allows developers to integrate the technology into their own applications.

The company said the platform is designed to improve multilingual communication in industries such as healthcare, financial services, customer support and business process outsourcing (BPO).

According to Krisp, the translation engine supports 61 languages and can translate conversations in real time while handling challenges such as background noise, accented speech and industry-specific terminology.

The latest version introduces several features aimed at enterprise customers. These include automated quality assessment of translated calls, live bilingual transcripts, language auto-selection, custom vocabulary controls and call auditing tools that allow administrators to review conversations from both the agent and customer perspectives.

Davit Baghdasaryan, CEO and Co-Founder of Krisp, said the company developed the technology for environments where translation accuracy is critical.

“Real-time voice translation is growing rapidly, but many systems have not been tested in situations where accuracy is essential. We built our engine for sectors such as healthcare, insurance and financial services, where mistakes can have serious consequences,” he added.

Alongside the enterprise offering, Krisp has also opened access to developers through its new Voice Translation API. The API allows developers to send speech input and receive translated speech and text output through a single connection. JavaScript and Python software development kits (SDKs) are available at launch with additional support planned.

Robert Schoenfield, Executive Vice President of Licensing and Partnerships at Krisp, said that developers building applications in areas such as telehealth, customer support and fintech require translation tools that perform reliably in real-world conditions.

The company noted that the technology has already been used in live deployments. In one healthcare implementation, the company reported that the system handled 90% of multilingual calls without requiring a human interpreter and achieved 96% translation accuracy across more than eight languages.

Noam Brown argues benchmark scores increasingly depend on inference compute, obscuring the true capabilities of frontier models.

What Actually Matters.

Current AI benchmarks often understate the capabilities of frontier models due to reliance on inference compute.

Benchmark results are influenced by the resources spent on tasks, making single-number scores less reliable.

OpenAI researcher Noam Brown has argued that current AI benchmarks increasingly understate the capabilities of frontier models because performance is becoming heavily dependent on the amount of inference compute used at test time, rather than solely on the underlying model itself.

In a post on X, Brown said benchmark results are increasingly shaped by the amount of tokens, money, or wall-clock time spent on a task. As a result, single-number benchmark scores may no longer accurately capture the ceiling of modern AI systems' capabilities.

Brown pointed to the release of GPT-5.5 as an example. Initial reactions to the model were muted because its benchmark improvements over GPT-5.4 appeared relatively small.

However, he said users quickly discovered that the model represented a significant jump in capability in practice. According to Brown, the discrepancy stemmed from benchmark evaluations that did not control for test-time compute.

“GPT-5.5 wasn't being evaluated at the same token budget (or dollar budget) as 5.4,” Brown wrote. “Once we control for test-time compute, 5.5 looks substantially stronger than 5.4.”

Left: On one cyber evaluation, 5.5 shows only modest gains over 5.4 when both are measured at their maximum test-time compute. Right: On a different cyber evaluation, 5.5 is clearly far more capable than 5.4 when performance is normalised for tokens, cost, or latency. (Source: Noam Brown, X)

The issue becomes more pronounced as models become more capable, he said. Historically, evaluators could increase inference spending until model performance plateaued. But recent evidence suggests those plateaus may be moving farther out, or may not appear at practical evaluation budgets at all.

Brown cited experiments by former OpenAI researcher Andrej Karpathy and cyber evaluations conducted by the UK AI Security Institute showing performance continuing to improve after hundreds of experiments or more than 100 million tokens of inference. He argued that stronger models appear increasingly capable of operating over longer horizons, allowing them to benefit more from additional compute.

The AI Security Institute cyber evaluation, where both Mythos and GPT-5.5 continue to improve rapidly even beyond 100 million tokens of inference. (Source: Noam Brown, X)

Rather than reporting a single benchmark score, Brown proposed that AI labs publish performance curves showing results relative to inference budgets measured in tokens, cost, or time. He noted that some benchmarks, including ARC-AGI, already measure performance as a function of cost.

The argument extends beyond model evaluation into AI safety and release decisions. Frontier Labs routinely conducts cyber, biosecurity, and other risk assessments before deploying new models. Brown questioned how such evaluations should be performed if capabilities depend heavily on inference spending.

He cited the release of Gemini 3 Deep Think, which drew criticism from parts of the AI safety community because it achieved substantially higher benchmark scores than previous models, without a dedicated system card to evaluate its risks.

“The real outrage should have been that when Gemini 3 and other models were released, their system cards did not measure benchmark performance as a function of test-time compute,” he wrote.

“Preparedness frameworks and responsible scaling policies should explicitly account for inference compute when determining whether a model crosses a safety threshold,” Brown adds.

The discussion drew responses from both researchers and practitioners.

Elie Bakouch, a researcher from Prime Intellect, questioned Brown’s suggestion that evaluating an AI agent over a one-year horizon may require running it for a full year. He argued that AI and human time are not directly comparable and that large-scale parallelisation could potentially accelerate such evaluations.

Bakouch also noted that token counts may understate compute usage in systems such as autonomous research agents, where substantial resources can be spent on tool calls and external training runs.

Since the launch of OpenAI's o1 reasoning model in 2024, researchers have increasingly observed that performance can continue to improve as models consume more compute during inference. Brown argued that the latest generation of reasoning systems is pushing those limits even further, making inference budget a critical variable in both capability measurement and AI safety policy.

“If this trend continues, which I fully expect, benchmark scores that don't account for inference compute usage will become less informative each model release cycle,” he wrote.

title: ClickHouse Hires Databricks Veteran Ed Lenta to Lead APAC Expansion
content:
The company also named Takeshi Kaneko as Country Manager for Japan. Kaneko previously led Nutanix Japan and held senior roles at Red Hat and Microsoft in the country.

What Actually Matters.

ClickHouse appointed Ed Lenta as Vice President for Asia Pacific to drive market expansion and adoption of its products.

The company aims to strengthen its global revenue organisation with several strategic leadership hires across various sectors.

ClickHouse has appointed Ed Lenta as Vice President for Asia Pacific and Japan, part of a broader expansion of its global go-to-market leadership as the company scales to meet rising demand for real-time data infrastructure.

Lenta, based in Singapore, will lead sales and market expansion across APJ, focusing on adoption of ClickHouse Cloud and its open-source database among enterprises and public sector organisations.

He joins from Databricks, where he served as General Manager for APJ, overseeing operations across more than twenty countries. Earlier, he held roles at Amazon Web Services and VMware during their early growth phases in the region.

The APJ expansion is part of a wider buildout of ClickHouse’s global revenue organisation. The company has hired Billy Schoeffel as Vice President for Financial Services, Kenneth Melero for Public Sector, Maged Shehata for Global Solutions Architecture, and Andrew Straus for Revenue Strategy and Operations.

The expansion builds on earlier leadership additions, including the appointment of Kevin Egan as Chief Revenue Officer. The company said the hires are aimed at strengthening coverage across enterprise sales, public sector, and solution engineering as customers modernise data infrastructure for AI workloads.

ClickHouse is positioning itself as a core data layer for AI-driven applications, particularly as enterprises adopt agentic systems that require high-speed, cost-efficient analytics. Lenta said organisations in APJ are rethinking architectures around performance and efficiency, where ClickHouse claims an advantage over traditional data warehouses.

The leadership push comes as the company reports strong growth. ClickHouse said it has crossed $250 million in annual run-rate revenue, more than tripling year-on-year, and surpassed 4,000 customers, including adding over 1,000 net new customers in a single quarter.

Enterprise adoption is also widening. Customers highlighted at its Open House 2026 conference include Visa, Cisco, Intuit, Shopify, DoorDash, Mercado Libre, Zoox, and Jump Trading.

The company said the latest hires are intended to support that scale, adding regional leadership and operational capacity as demand for real-time analytics and AI infrastructure accelerates.

title: Bengaluru-Based HyperNorm AI Raises $2.2 Mn to Bring Explainable AI to Wealth Management
content:
The platform will support compute capacity powered by Broadcom’s XPUs and networking systems for frontier AI labs, including Anthropic and OpenAI.

What Actually Matters.

Broadcom, Apollo, and Blackstone have launched a $35 billion initiative to accelerate global AI compute deployments exceeding 20 gigawatts by 2028.

The initiative will support frontier AI labs, including Anthropic and OpenAI, with Broadcom’s XPUs and networking systems.

Broadcom has partnered with Apollo and Blackstone to launch the AI XPV Platform, a financing and infrastructure initiative designed to accelerate more than 20 gigawatts of global AI compute deployments by 2028.

The companies said the platform will support compute capacity powered by Broadcom’s XPUs and networking systems for frontier AI labs, including Anthropic and OpenAI.

It is being launched with an initial $35 billion transaction led by Apollo in partnership with Blackstone. The funding will support Anthropic’s previously announced expansion of more than 1 GW of compute infrastructure.

Deployment is expected to begin at Fluidstack-based sites from mid-2026. The initiative also aims to lower per-token delivery costs while enabling large-scale AI model training and inference.

Hock Tan, President and CEO of Broadcom, said in a statement that the platform aligns capital with Broadcom’s technology roadmap to help customers “realise their most ambitious AI visions with speed and certainty.”

It creates a framework for future deployments of XPU-based compute systems and networking infrastructure. The company expects the model to help frontier AI companies expand capacity with faster access to financing and technology.

Apollo said the scale of AI demand requires collaboration between infrastructure and financial players. “Our investment in this platform reflects our conviction in Broadcom’s technology leadership and Anthropic’s frontier roadmap,” said Jim Zelter, President of Apollo. He added that the firm aims to provide the capital needed for efficient expansion.

Blackstone also said growing compute demand has opened opportunities across the AI infrastructure ecosystem. Jon Gray, President of Blackstone, said the company would support financing through its credit and insurance business.

title: Haleon to Invest ₹2,000 Crore in First India Manufacturing Facility in Madhya Pradesh
content:
The platform combines speech recognition, natural language understanding, and generative AI to enable human-like conversations in regional languages and dialects.

What Actually Matters.

Shunya Labs has launched a multilingual Voice AI platform supporting over 216 Indian languages and dialects to enhance digital accessibility.

The platform is designed for India's diverse linguistic landscape, allowing users to communicate in their preferred languages.

AI company Shunya Labs has launched a new multilingual Voice AI platform that supports more than 216 languages and dialects to improve digital accessibility and communication across India.

The company said the platform has been designed specifically for India’s diverse linguistic landscape and can help enterprises, government agencies, and businesses interact with users in their preferred languages rather than relying on English-only systems.

According to Shunya Labs, the platform combines speech recognition, natural language understanding, and generative AI capabilities to deliver human-like conversations across multiple regional languages and dialects. The technology can be used for customer support, citizen services, healthcare assistance, financial inclusion programmes, education services, and enterprise communications.

Speaking on the launch, Founder and CEO Ritu Mehrotra said, “India’s digital future will be shaped not just by technology, but by accessibility. We want every Indian to interact with technology naturally in their preferred language.”

One of the key features of the platform is its CPU-first architecture, which allows organisations to deploy voice AI systems without depending heavily on expensive GPU infrastructure. According to the company, this enables enterprises to run voice AI applications on standard servers either on-premise or in the cloud.

The approach is particularly focused on sectors such as banking, financial services, healthcare, customer support, and government services, where cost, latency, and data privacy are critical considerations.

The company added that its proprietary speech recognition, translation, and voice generation models have been trained on Indic and Asian language datasets to improve accuracy across multiple languages.

title: Zoho Launches India-Designed Server Nathu La, Claims 30% Lower Ownership Cost
content:
The social media giant will lease 168 MW of capacity at a Jamnagar facility while backing nearly 1 GW of renewable energy projects across India.

What Actually Matters.

Meta has partnered with Reliance Industries to establish its first AI-enabled data centre in India, located in Jamnagar, Gujarat.

The data centre will initially have a capacity of 168 megawatts, with potential for future expansion.

Meta has entered an agreement with Reliance Industries to lease capacity at a new AI-enabled data centre in Jamnagar, Gujarat, marking its first such facility in India as the company expands infrastructure to support its AI ambitions.

Under the agreement announced on June 9, Reliance will build a data centre with an initial capacity of 168 megawatts (MW), which Meta will lease with options to scale further.

The facility will be powered by renewable energy and cooled using desalinated seawater, with Meta covering the costs of the energy and water required to operate the site.

“We’re proud to be working with Reliance to build our first AI-enabled data centre in India. This world-class facility in Jamnagar will help us scale our AI infrastructure globally while deepening our long-term investment in India's economy,” said Mark Zuckerberg, founder and CEO of Meta.

The investment comes as Meta continues to expand its global infrastructure footprint to support AI technologies and services. The company said India was a key market due to its growing digital economy, large user base, and existing partnership with Reliance.

Meta said the Jamnagar facility will form part of its broader infrastructure strategy in the region alongside network investments, including Project Waterworth, a subsea cable system designed to improve connectivity.

The announcement also extends a relationship between Meta and Reliance that began with Meta’s $5.7 billion investment in Jio Platforms in 2020. The companies have since collaborated on connectivity, commerce, and AI initiatives in India.

“This partnership with Meta marks a transformative moment for India’s digital infrastructure. Building India’s first built-to-suit AI data centre for a global technology leader of Meta’s scale demonstrates India's readiness to be at the forefront of the global AI revolution,” said Reliance Industries Chairman Mukesh D Ambani.

Separately, Meta announced agreements for nearly 1 gigawatt of renewable energy capacity in India. The company contracted 837 MW of new solar and wind projects with CleanMax across Rajasthan and Karnataka, bringing its total announced capacity with the provider to more than 900 MW.

It also signed agreements for 88 MW of solar and wind projects with Fourth Partner Energy across Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Maharashtra, and Uttar Pradesh.

Meta said the renewable energy agreements, together with Reliance’s plans to support the Jamnagar facility with renewable power, are intended to help meet its goal of matching all operations with 100% clean and renewable energy while reducing value chain emissions in the region.

title: Anthropic Releases Claude Fable 5, Its First Mythos-Class Model for General Users
content:
Nathu La is based on Intel Xeon 6 processors and was built in collaboration with Intel’s engineering teams.

What Actually Matters.

Zoho has launched Nathu La, an indigenously designed server aimed at reducing technology import reliance.

The server boasts lower power consumption and total ownership costs, benefiting AI inference applications.

Zoho Corporation has announced the launch of Nathu La, an indigenously designed server, as it moves deeper into owning its full technology stack from hardware to applications.

The company said the server delivers equivalent performance with 12-18% lower power consumption and 20-30% lower total cost of ownership, a shift it believes will directly reduce AI inference costs.

The server has been developed at Zoho’s Nagpur facility over more than five years, marking one of the few instances of an Indian software company building a homegrown server platform with domestic intellectual property.

The launch comes at a time when India’s digital infrastructure is expanding rapidly but continues to rely heavily on imported server technology, often involving licensing costs and external dependencies. Zoho’s move positions it as an outlier attempting to localise the foundational layer of computing infrastructure.

“We are proud to build a server system that is truly designed in India and taking a step towards creating sovereign technology,” said Shailesh Davey, CEO of Zoho Corp. He added that the initiative reflects the company’s long-term focus on building complex systems using talent from smaller towns, backed by sustained R&D investments.

Nathu La is designed for workloads including virtualisation, high performance computing, AI inference and storage. The company said the system includes customised power delivery subsystems, an in-house data centre secure control module, and modular chassis options that allow deployment flexibility across environments.

Several components, including the DC-SCM and network interface cards, have been designed internally and assembled through Indian electronics manufacturing partners.

Zoho has filed over five patents related to thermal management and cost-optimised server architecture as part of the project.

The hardware push is tied closely to Zoho’s broader strategy of controlling its entire stack. The company plans to run its own applications on Nathu La servers across its data centres, allowing tighter integration between software and infrastructure. This, Zoho argues, will improve performance, reduce operational costs and strengthen data governance for global customers.

“With AI advancements, inference costs are rising rapidly,” Davey said. “With our strategy of using contextual, right-sized models, running on our own platform, on our own servers, in our own data centres, we are compounding the benefits accrued from owning and operating our entire technology stack.”

Zoho’s design philosophy for Nathu La draws from the Open Compute Project, focusing on modularity, thermal efficiency and easier maintenance. The company claims these choices will help bring down both energy consumption and long-term infrastructure costs across its data centre footprint.

The effort also reflects a policy and market shift. In 2023, the Indian government introduced import restrictions on compute devices including servers, underscoring the need for domestic capability in core infrastructure technologies. Zoho had begun work on the project earlier, setting up a small R&D team in Nagpur in 2020.

Alongside the hardware development, Zoho has been investing in building engineering talent outside traditional tech hubs. Its SETU programme in Nagpur, aimed at training students in electronics system design and manufacturing, has trained over 300 students so far. Some of them have worked directly on the Nathu La project.

The company said the initiative is designed to counter the erosion of foundational engineering skills in an era of AI-assisted development, with a focus on hands-on problem solving and first-principles thinking.

What Actually Matters.

Anthropic launched Claude Fable 5, its first Mythos-class model available for general use, showcasing advanced capabilities.

Claude Mythos 5, a variant with fewer safeguards, is aimed at select cybersecurity and life sciences researchers.

Anthropic on June 9 launched Claude Fable 5, its first Mythos-class model for general use, while also introducing Claude Mythos 5, a version with some safeguards removed for a limited group of cybersecurity and life sciences researchers.

“Fable 5’s capabilities exceed those of any model we’ve ever made generally available,” Anthropic said in a blog post. The company said the model delivers state-of-the-art performance across software engineering, knowledge work, vision, scientific research, and other benchmarks.

To address potential misuse, Anthropic said Fable 5 includes safeguards that redirect some cybersecurity, biology, chemistry, and model-distillation-related requests to Claude Opus 4.8 instead.

“Without safeguards, Fable 5’s capabilities in areas like cybersecurity could be misused to cause serious damage,” the company said in a statement.

Anthropic said Mythos 5 is the same underlying model as Fable 5, but with some safeguards removed. The company said Claude Mythos 5 will initially be rolled out through Project Glasswing, its initiative with the US government, replacing Claude Mythos Preview for participating organisations. Access will initially be limited to a small group of cyber defenders and infrastructure providers.

The company said Mythos 5 has “the strongest cybersecurity capabilities of any model in the world” and plans to expand access through a broader trusted access program.

On coding benchmarks, Claude Mythos 5/Fable 5 scored 80.3% on SWE-Bench Pro, 29.3% on FrontierCode (Diamond), and 88.0% on Terminal-Bench 2.1, outperforming Claude Opus 4.8, GPT 5.5, and Gemini 3.1 Pro across all three evaluations.

Anthropic priced both Fable 5 and Mythos 5 at $10 per million input tokens and $50 per million output tokens, less than half the cost of Claude Mythos Preview.

The company said Claude Fable 5 is immediately available through the Claude API and consumption-based Enterprise plans. The company is also making the model available at no additional cost to Pro, Max, Team, and seat-based Enterprise subscribers until June 22.

Starting June 23, access on those plans will require usage credits, although Anthropic said it may extend the free access period if capacity permits. The company added that it plans to eventually restore Fable 5 as a standard feature across subscription plans once sufficient computing capacity becomes available.

“We expect demand for Fable 5 to be very high, and difficult to predict,” Anthropic said.

The company highlighted several benchmark results and customer tests.

Stripe reported that Fable 5 completed a codebase-wide migration in a 50-million-line Ruby codebase in a day, a task that Anthropic said “would otherwise have taken a whole team over two months by hand.”

In knowledge work, Anthropic said Fable 5 achieved the highest score on Hebbia’s Finance Benchmark for senior-level reasoning. The company also said the model can perform vision-based tasks such as extracting data from scientific figures and rebuilding web applications from screenshots.

Anthropic reported advances in scientific research using Mythos 5. Internal protein design teams found the model accelerated parts of the drug design process by around ten times. The company said Mythos 5 independently completed tasks, including selecting binding sites, running protein-design tools, and recovering from failures.

The company also said Mythos 5 generated molecular biology hypotheses that its scientists preferred over those produced by earlier Opus-class models about 80% of the time. Some of these hypotheses have moved to experimental evaluation.

To support monitoring and abuse prevention, Anthropic announced a new policy requiring 30-day retention of business customer data for Mythos-class models and future models of similar capability. The company said the data would not be used to train future Claude models and would be deleted after 30 days in most cases.

title: Cambridge Scientists Test World’s First AI-Designed Universal Vaccine in Human
content:
Researchers at Cambridge University say the technology could help prepare for future pandemics by enabling vaccines to target entire virus families before new outbreaks emerge.

What Actually Matters.

Cambridge researchers tested the world’s first AI-designed universal vaccine in humans, marking a milestone in vaccine innovation.

The experimental vaccine aims to protect against entire virus families, potentially addressing future outbreaks of rapidly evolving viruses.

Researchers at the University of Cambridge have tested the world’s first artificial intelligence-designed universal vaccine in humans, marking a significant step in vaccine development and pandemic preparedness.

The experimental vaccine has been designed to protect against an entire family of viruses rather than a single strain. Scientists at Cambridge University say it could eventually help tackle future outbreaks caused by rapidly evolving viruses, including those related to SARS, MERS, and COVID-19.

Unlike conventional vaccines which are updated to target new variants, the AI-designed vaccine uses a specially created “super antigen” that trains the immune system to recognise common features shared across multiple viruses.

Researchers at Cambridge University used a machine-learning algorithm trained on genetic data from sarbecoviruses, a group that includes the viruses responsible for SARS and COVID-19. The AI then designed the vaccine antigen, the component that triggers an immune response in the body.

Professor Jonathan Heeney, a researcher at the University of Cambridge and co-author of the study, said the technology could change the way vaccines are developed.

“We’ve converted vaccine development from being reactive to being future-proof. The approach could help scientists prepare for future pandemic threats before they emerge,” he noted in a statement.

The vaccine was tested in an early-stage Phase 1 trial involving nearly 40 participants between 2021 and 2023. The trial primarily aimed to assess safety and determine whether the vaccine could stimulate an immune response.

According to the study published in the Journal of Infection, the vaccine did not cause any serious side effects. However, researchers found that its effect on triggering immune responses was limited, describing the results as "modest." Additional studies are required to better assess the vaccine's overall effectiveness.

Despite the limited results, scientists have welcomed the breakthrough. Professor Saul Faust of the University of Southampton said the technology shows promise for designing vaccines against rapidly changing viruses. Professor Andy Pollard, Director of the Oxford Vaccine Group, described the findings as “fascinating” and said artificial intelligence could become a “game changer” in vaccine research.

Researchers at Cambridge University are now planning a larger phase 2 trial to better understand how well the vaccine can protect against a broad range of viruses and whether it can help prevent future pandemics.

title: LTM Unveils Outcome-Based Pricing Model as AI Agents Reshape IT Services Contracts
content:
The BlueVerse Currency framework will link pricing to business outcomes rather than effort spent, reflecting a broader shift in how IT services firms are monetising AI-led transformation initiatives.

What Actually Matters.

LTM has launched an outcome-based pricing model, BlueVerse Currency, linking costs to business results rather than effort.

This new framework reflects a shift in IT services towards monetising AI-led transformations and productivity gains.

LTM, formerly LTIMindtree, has introduced an outcome-based pricing framework for AI engagements, as technology services providers look to move away from traditional effort-linked billing models in the agentic AI era.

The company launched BlueVerse Currency, a commercial model that ties pricing to measurable business outcomes instead of the amount of work or resources consumed.

The offering is designed for enterprises deploying AI agents across core business processes and comes as IT services firms increasingly experiment with new contracting structures to capture productivity gains generated by artificial intelligence.

According to the company, the model combines multiple elements of its BlueVerse AI stack, including human expertise, reusable technology assets, AI agents, orchestration platforms and computing resources, into a single commercial framework.

LTM said the model introduces outcome-linked pricing tied to business results and allows clients and service providers to share productivity gains generated through AI deployments.

It also supports the reallocation of resources during the course of a contract and enables savings from AI-driven efficiencies to be redirected towards new projects and innovation initiatives.

The pricing framework is built on a hybrid structure comprising fixed and variable components and can be applied across areas such as application development and maintenance, business transformation programmes and AI engineering engagements.

“Enterprises are increasingly looking to align technology investments more closely with measurable business outcomes,” Venu Lambu, CEO and Managing Director, LTM, said in a statement. “BlueVerse Currency brings together talent, plaƞorms, and intelligent agents into a unified commercial model—enabling clients to move from input-based constructs to outcome-led value creation.”

With enterprises seeking clearer returns on AI investments, outcome-based commercial models are expected to gain traction, particularly in engagements where automation and AI-led productivity improvements can be measured and linked to business metrics.

LTM employs more than 87,000 people across 40 countries and has positioned its BlueVerse platform as a gateway for enterprises looking to deploy agentic AI at scale.

title: AIM — India's Leading AI & Data Science Media Platform
content:
Current AI benchmarks often understate the capabilities of frontier models due to reliance on inference compute.

Benchmark results are influenced by the resources spent on tasks, making single-number scores less reliable.

OpenAI researcher Noam Brown has argued that current AI benchmarks increasingly understate the capabilities of frontier models because performance is becoming heavily dependent on the amount of inference compute used at test time, rather than solely on the underlying model itself.

In a post on X, Brown said benchmark results are increasingly shaped by the amount of tokens, money, or wall-clock time spent on a task. As a result, single-number benchmark scores may no longer accurately capture the ceiling of modern AI systems' capabilities.

Brown pointed to the release of GPT-5.5 as an example. Initial reactions to the model were muted because its benchmark improvements over GPT-5.4 appeared relatively small.

However, he said users quickly discovered that the model represented a significant jump in capability in practice. According to Brown, the discrepancy stemmed from benchmark evaluations that did not control for test-time compute.

“GPT-5.5 wasn't being evaluated at the same token budget (or dollar budget) as 5.4,” Brown wrote. “Once we control for test-time compute, 5.5 looks substantially stronger than 5.4.”

Left: On one cyber evaluation, 5.5 shows only modest gains over 5.4 when both are measured at their maximum test-time compute. Right: On a different cyber evaluation, 5.5 is clearly far more capable than 5.4 when performance is normalised for tokens, cost, or latency. (Source: Noam Brown, X)

The issue becomes more pronounced as models become more capable, he said. Historically, evaluators could increase inference spending until model performance plateaued. But recent evidence suggests those plateaus may be moving farther out, or may not appear at practical evaluation budgets at all.

Brown cited experiments by former OpenAI researcher Andrej Karpathy and cyber evaluations conducted by the UK AI Security Institute showing performance continuing to improve after hundreds of experiments or more than 100 million tokens of inference. He argued that stronger models appear increasingly capable of operating over longer horizons, allowing them to benefit more from additional compute.

The AI Security Institute cyber evaluation, where both Mythos and GPT-5.5 continue to improve rapidly even beyond 100 million tokens of inference. (Source: Noam Brown, X)

Rather than reporting a single benchmark score, Brown proposed that AI labs publish performance curves showing results relative to inference budgets measured in tokens, cost, or time. He noted that some benchmarks, including ARC-AGI, already measure performance as a function of cost.

The argument extends beyond model evaluation into AI safety and release decisions. Frontier Labs routinely conducts cyber, biosecurity, and other risk assessments before deploying new models. Brown questioned how such evaluations should be performed if capabilities depend heavily on inference spending.

He cited the release of Gemini 3 Deep Think, which drew criticism from parts of the AI safety community because it achieved substantially higher benchmark scores than previous models, without a dedicated system card to evaluate its risks.

“The real outrage should have been that when Gemini 3 and other models were released, their system cards did not measure benchmark performance as a function of test-time compute,” he wrote.

“Preparedness frameworks and responsible scaling policies should explicitly account for inference compute when determining whether a model crosses a safety threshold,” Brown adds.

The discussion drew responses from both researchers and practitioners.

Elie Bakouch, a researcher from Prime Intellect, questioned Brown’s suggestion that evaluating an AI agent over a one-year horizon may require running it for a full year. He argued that AI and human time are not directly comparable and that large-scale parallelisation could potentially accelerate such evaluations.

Bakouch also noted that token counts may understate compute usage in systems such as autonomous research agents, where substantial resources can be spent on tool calls and external training runs.

Since the launch of OpenAI's o1 reasoning model in 2024, researchers have increasingly observed that performance can continue to improve as models consume more compute during inference. Brown argued that the latest generation of reasoning systems is pushing those limits even further, making inference budget a critical variable in both capability measurement and AI safety policy.

“If this trend continues, which I fully expect, benchmark scores that don't account for inference compute usage will become less informative each model release cycle,” he wrote.

title: Bengaluru’s AGNIT Semiconductors Opens GaN Testing Lab at IISc With ₹3 Cr Investment
content:
The new facility aims to speed up validation and commercialisation of indigenous semiconductor technologies.

What Actually Matters.

AGNIT Semiconductors has launched a GaN testing lab at IISc with a ₹3 crore investment to enhance semiconductor validation.

The facility aims to support high-power RF applications in telecom and defence by reducing reliance on external testing.

Bengaluru-based semiconductor startup AGNIT Semiconductors has invested ₹3 crore ($300,000) to launch a gallium nitride (GaN) testing and qualification laboratory at the Indian Institute of Science (IISc) in Bengaluru.

The company unveiled the 350 sq ft facility to support in-house validation and reliability testing for high-power radio-frequency (RF) applications in telecom and defence. This comes just after the company raised $2.6 million in a seed extension equity round in March this year.

“India’s semiconductor ambitions require not only chip design and fabrication capabilities but also robust indigenous validation and reliability ecosystems,” said Hareesh Chandrasekar, Co-founder and CEO of AGNIT Semiconductors, in a statement.

The company aims to manufacture 100,000 chips over the next 24 months.

It said the facility will help reduce dependence on external testing infrastructure and speed up the commercialisation of indigenous GaN technologies. The laboratory will support applications across telecom, satellite communications, next-generation wireless systems, and defence.

The lab also houses equipment for testing and pre-qualification of GaN semiconductor components. These include an environmental chamber that operates between -60°C and 125°C, RF test and measurement benches, a connectorised load-pull testing station, and automated PCB assembly systems.

AGNIT said the infrastructure will allow it to conduct PCB assembly, power amplifier board characterisation, reliability data generation, and in-house qualification testing.

The company expects the facility to help move products more quickly from development to deployment and to support changing telecom and defence requirements.

Until now, AGNIT has relied on shared infrastructure at IISc for testing and validation. The new laboratory will allow closer integration with its design and fabrication teams. A dedicated team of five to eight engineers and researchers will run the facility.

AGNIT also plans to expand the laboratory to conduct accelerated lifetime testing and qualification for military-grade components. The company said the move could strengthen reliability testing for semiconductor products developed in India.

Founded as a GaN semiconductor company focused on radio-frequency applications, AGNIT has raised a total of ₹60 crore ($6.2 million) from investors, including 3one4 Capital and Zephyr Peacock, with participation from Lakshmi Narayanan, former Cognizant CEO and angel investor.
