title: Mphasis Q4 Net Profit Rises 14% YoY as AI-Led Deals Gain Traction
content:
The company reported a consolidated net profit of ₹509.6 crore for Q4FY26, up from ₹446.5 crore a year ago.

What Actually Matters.

Mphasis reported a 14% year-on-year rise in net profit for the March quarter.

Artificial intelligence-led deals significantly contributed to new contract wins for the company.

IT services firm Mphasis reported a 14% year-on-year (YoY) rise in March-quarter net profit, with artificial intelligence-led deals accounting for a majority of its new contract wins.

The company reported a consolidated net profit of ₹509.6 crore for Q4FY26, up from ₹446.5 crore a year ago, while revenue rose 14.4% YoY and 6% sequentially to ₹4,242.7 crore. In constant currency, the company’s revenue grew 2.5% sequentially and 7.1% YoY.

Earnings per share for the quarter increased 13.7% YoY to ₹26.7.

For the full year, revenue grew 11.6% to ₹15,879.6 crore, while net profit rose to ₹1,862.6 crore from ₹1,702.1 crore in FY25. Mphasis reported constant currency revenue growth of 6.7% YoY for FY26.

The company has witnessed a growing role of AI in its deal pipeline. Mphasis reported total contract value wins of $2.1 billion in FY26, up 68% YoY, with nearly 60% of these deals being AI-led. In the March quarter alone, the company signed deals worth $407 million, of which 64% were driven by AI.

“The value of true AI lies not in isolated use cases, but in systematically embedding intelligence at scale across applications, processes, and decision flows. This shift is enabling enterprises to re-architect themselves around what we describe as agentic AI, systems that are not only predictive, but capable of driving decisions and actions in a governed, autonomous manner,” Chief Executive Officer and Managing Director Nitin Rakesh said during the quarterly earnings call.

He added that the company is also seeing a decisive shift among enterprises from experimentation to scale deployment of AI initiatives.

The company’s operating margin for the quarter stood at 15.4%, expanding 20 basis points sequentially and 10 basis points YoY. However, for the full year, operating margin remained flat at 15.3%.

The banking and financial services segment continued to anchor growth, contributing ₹2303.3 crore in quarterly revenue, followed by technology, media and telecom at ₹689.4 crore and insurance at ₹679.1 crore. The company said it recorded a one-time impact related to the implementation of India’s new labour codes during the year.

Mphasis also continued to invest in building out its AI capabilities through acquisitions. The recent buyout of Canada-based Theory and Practice (TAP), which brings a decision intelligence platform combining AI with behavioural economics, is expected to add a new layer to its AI stack and strengthen its Neo platform strategy.

“Our recent acquisition of TAP creates a combination that allows us to move beyond task automation, towards systems that can reason over business objectives, constraints, and domain context, using AI at scale,” Rakesh said.

This comes as a broader shift is underway in the IT services industry, where firms are moving from traditional headcount-led growth models to AI-enabled, non-linear revenue streams and are balancing AI-driven growth opportunities with pricing pressures in legacy services.

Moreover, the board recommended a final dividend of ₹62 per share for FY26, subject to shareholder approval, and approved the reappointment of CEO Nitin Rakesh for another five-year term starting October 2026.

Shares of Mphasis opened at ₹2,314.5 per share on NSE, up nearly 3% from the previous close.

The company has deliberately chosen Bengaluru for its deep engineering ecosystem and expertise in system design, architecture, and platform engineering.

What Actually Matters.

Raksul has established a Global Capability Centre in Bengaluru, focusing on AI-led platform engineering.

The company chose Bengaluru for its strong engineering ecosystem and expertise in system design.

Japanese multi-service platform company Raksul has launched a new GCC in Bengaluru, as a strategic hub for AI-led platform engineering and global technology decision-making.

The move comes amid Raksul’s rapid business expansion across multiple domains—including e-commerce, fintech, and marketing services—which has significantly increased system complexity and driven the need for high-quality engineering talent.

“Raksul is showing very rapid growth momentum, and this has increased our system complexity… To support this, we are seeking very good engineering talent,” Toshiharu Takeuchi, CTO, Raksul, tells AIM.

Starting with a handful of employees, the company doesn’t want to extend beyond 100 in headcount.

Unlike traditional GCCs that scale through large hiring volumes, Raksul is adopting a “nano GCC” approach—starting with a small, high-density team focused on solving high-impact problems using AI.

“It’s not about building capacity anymore. It’s about building capabilities,” Sujit Kulkarni, Site Leader, Raksul India, highlighting a broader shift in GCC strategy.

The Bengaluru centre will focus on core platform systems such as authentication, identity platforms, and shared infrastructure—critical components that cut across Raksul’s multi-service ecosystem.

“India will focus on deep expertise in platform engineering, shared infrastructure, and identity systems… these systems interact with multiple Raksul businesses,” Takeuchi noted.

AI is embedded across Raksul’s entire software development lifecycle—from coding to testing and reviews—fundamentally reshaping how teams operate.

As a result, the company is prioritising senior-level hiring to ensure architectural rigour and effective AI implementation.

Raksul’s model reflects a broader shift in how engineering teams are structured in the AI era, moving away from traditional pyramid models.

“Traditional pyramid-like structures are going away. We are focusing on highly qualified engineers who can work with AI agents as colleagues,” Kulkarni mentioned.

The company is also actively minimising repetitive and operational tasks, which are increasingly being handled by AI systems.

“Any task which is repetitive in nature should be reduced… this is not what we expect from humans,” he said.

Raksul’s GCC strategy follows a three-location model spanning Tokyo, Vietnam, and Bengaluru, with each hub playing a clearly defined and complementary role. Tokyo anchors product strategy and customer understanding, leveraging its proximity to the core market.

Vietnam focuses on execution and development, driving delivery efficiency. Bengaluru, meanwhile, is positioned as the centre for platform engineering and architectural leadership, shaping the company’s core technology capabilities and decision-making.

“The technical guidance and leadership will come from Bengaluru,” Takeuchi mentioned, underscoring India’s growing strategic importance.

Raksul made it clear that its India strategy is not driven by cost savings, but by capability building and innovation.

Instead, the focus is on enabling decision-making and ownership within the India team.

“I want the India team to be involved in decision-making… not just filling resource gaps,” he added.

The company’s broader vision is to build a unified, AI-powered platform to support small and mid-sized businesses (SMBs), particularly in Japan, where demographic challenges are reshaping the economy.

“We want to provide a one-stop solution for SMBs… integrating HR, finance, procurement, and operations,” Takeuchi mentioned.

This ambition is expected to create complex engineering challenges—further reinforcing the need for advanced platform capabilities in India.

Raksul’s approach reflects a growing trend among global companies—especially from Japan—towards smaller, high-impact GCCs that prioritise innovation over scale.

“Instead of large teams, companies are now looking at high-density teams with strong capabilities,” Kulkarni observed.

title: Meta Reports 33% Revenue Growth, Testing Early Versions of Business AI
content:
The company also confirms employee headcount reduction starting in May.

What Actually Matters.

Meta Platforms reported significant revenue and net income growth in the first quarter.

The company is actively testing early versions of business AI for customer interactions and advertising.

Meta Platforms reported a 33% year-over-year increase in first-quarter revenue to $56.3 billion on April 29, reflecting sustained advertising demand and the strategic deployment of automated enterprise software.

The parent company of Facebook and Instagram recorded a net income of $26.8 billion and a 41% operating margin for the quarter ending in March. Daily active users across its suite of social media applications reached 3.56 billion.

The firm is actively trialling conversational AI tools to manage customer interactions and execute advertising campaigns for corporate clients.

CEO Mark Zuckerberg confirmed the initiative, stating the company is “already testing an early version of business AIs.” The volume of these automated communications has accelerated rapidly over the last three months.

CFO Susan Li noted the messaging platform currently handles “more than 10 million conversations each week being facilitated through business AIs, up from 1 million at the start of the year.”

To support these enterprise tools, Meta released Muse Spark, the first foundational language model from its internal research division, Meta Superintelligence Labs.

Li stated they are seeing “double-digit per cent increases in Meta AI sessions per user” following the broad rollout of the new Muse Spark model.

Zuckerberg also highlighted the ‘Meta Compute initiative,’ noting they are rolling out more than 1 gigawatt (GW) of their own custom silicon developed in partnership with Broadcom. They are also deploying 6 GW of AMD hardware, as per the deal announced in February.

Scaling the computing hardware required for these agentic systems prompted the company to raise its 2026 capital expenditure forecast by $10 billion.

The new budget range, set between $125 billion and $145 billion, will finance server components and physical data centre expansion. This reallocation underscores a broader shift in the technology sector towards resource-intensive machine learning infrastructure.

To mitigate the rising hardware costs, Meta will implement structural workforce adjustments.

Following a 5% headcount reduction in 2025, recent reports have suggested the company is preparing for redundancies affecting approximately 10% of its current workforce, or around 8,000 employees, beginning in May 2026.

Li also confirmed on the earnings call, saying that “We recently shared internally that we plan to reduce the size of our employee base in May.”

Addressing the financial rationale for the upcoming cuts, she stated, “We believe a leaner operating model will allow us to move more quickly while also helping to offset the substantial investments we're making.”

Beyond consumer and advertiser tools, Meta is heavily leveraging agentic workflows internally. Zuckerberg noted a dramatic shift in developer velocity, stating that ‘one or two people are building something in a week that would have previously taken dozens of people months.’

Moving into the second quarter, Meta plans to launch its business AI services in additional international markets. The firm will simultaneously deploy automated creative tools across its advertising network while preparing for scheduled legal trials regarding youth safety regulations in the United States.

Children are moving from playing games to creating immersive experiences, thanks to the ease of Luau scripting offered by platforms like Roblox.

Smruthi NadigTechnology Journalist

What Actually Matters.

Children are increasingly transitioning from playing video games to creating their own immersive experiences.

Platforms like Roblox and the Luau scripting language enable young developers to build complex games with ease.

On a weekday afternoon, 10-year-old Vishwas, who wishes to go by his first name, leans over his laptop that seems to nearly envelop his adolescent head. His fingers hover over the trackpad, measured, methodical, as if strategically placing crosshairs over a virtual target.

But all this posture and precision is not about aiming in a game. It’s about designing one.

Vishwas wants to build a game that travels far and wide. He is strategically placing microtransactions in a tycoon game where players compete to earn money, climb leaderboards, and steal collectable digital creatures called “brainrots”—the hook of his game.

He is designing the game so that when players buy special passes, he will earn Robux, the primary virtual currency on the Roblox platform, which hosts user-generated 3D games. He can then spend Robux on other games. It is a closed loop of value creation and reinvestment, described with startling clarity by a child who has not yet learned basic algebra.

He discovered Roblox the way many children now discover digital worlds—through YouTube Shorts. Strategy videos led him to Blox Fruits—another popular action-adventure game hosted on Roblox, which now has over 150 million daily active users, and around 56% of them are under 17, according to TAR.

He initially tried using AI to build the game, but gave up quickly when he found an alternative that allowed him to build it himself—Luau.

Reinventing the Gaming Architecture

Roblox runs on Luau, a scripting language derived from Lua and designed to be lightweight and embeddable within larger systems. It features simple commands, a forgiving syntax, and rich tooling that automatically flags common errors as you code, making it easier for beginners to learn within an integrated environment.

Dhruvanandan V, a medical software writer, explains why that matters. In medical software, customers need flexibility to customise validation logic without touching the core infrastructure. Roblox applies the same principle to millions of creators.

“It is lightweight and embeddable, used to configure functionality for other languages. Roblox has created a tiny sandbox for Lua code to run inside the main software,” he tells AIM. “Lua can be embedded. This is very important.”

The sandbox is the quiet enabler. Children can write scripts, design worlds, and experiment with logic without breaking the system itself. They operate inside guardrails, but within those guardrails, they have astonishing freedom.

Twenty years ago, building a game required downloading engines, navigating forums, and editing files that could crash your computer if handled incorrectly. Creation was a niche hobby layered on top of consumption. Now, the architecture has changed.

Building As You Go

Ridhav Surya V, eight years old, discovered Roblox through a friend. For him, the platform has a more social value. “I play with [my] friends. It is a little addictive,” he says, adding that it is fun because “we can kill non-player characters (NPCs) by stealing brainrots while communicating through in-game chats.”

He imagines a feature he calls the ‘Red Carpet’, a game where players compete to grab limited brainrots. The idea is not about narrative or art, but competition. He understands that making such a system work is difficult. “Coding is hard,” he laments.

And yet he wants to learn. That’s because Roblox makes it easier with Luau, playing a considerable role in lowering the median age at which children encounter coding logic, from middle school to primary grades. Around 73% of Roblox’s users are under 18, and they are learning scripting, multiplayer system design, and user engagement loops.

And then there’s monetisation.

Roblox operates a virtual economy built on Robux, where players spend real money on in-game items, upgrades, and access. Developers earn Robux from these transactions and convert it into cash through the DevEx (Developer Exchange) system, where 1 Robux is approximately $0.0038 as of 2025, according to the Roblox DevForum.

While creators may receive a significant share of in-game spending in Robux terms, effective real-world earnings are lower, often estimated at around 20–30% of total user spend, the forum data shows. Roblox does not disclose a fixed, universal revenue split.

The scale of payouts, however, is substantial. Roblox paid $923 million to creators in 2024 and has crossed $1 billion in annual payouts, according to its economic impact report. At the same time, earnings are highly uneven. The top 1,000 creators earn over $1 million annually on average, while the median creator earns roughly $1,000–1,500 per year.

The New Arcade

The shift is dramatic. From competitive and social multiplayer games like Fortnite and PUBG that defined Gen Z gaming, Gen Alpha prefers more interactive, immersive gaming that blends user-generated content with communities.

Just a generation older, Vinodh MC played games that were far more contained. Finite.

“The conversations about gaming I had with my friends concerned how good we were at sniping enemies or how smoothly we could handle platforming in games,” the 26-year-old data scientist recalls.

Now, he observes, the focus is on trading and collecting objects with other players online. “Skill has very little to do with the gaming of today.” It is not that modern games lack complexity. However, ownership, scarcity and timing often matter more than dexterity.

The rise of creator-led ecosystems like Roblox has also marked a sharp departure from traditional game development, where building games required formal training, expensive tools, and studio backing. The new platforms collapse these barriers, offering built-in engines, Lua scripting, and instant global distribution.

Unlike conventional pipelines, where developers build for players, these ecosystems let players become developers. Kids are drawn to this model not just for creativity, but for ownership, visibility, and the ability to monetise their ideas early, making game design feel participatory rather than professionalised.

India’s interest in Roblox picked up in Q1 2024, when the platform saw a 58% year-over-year jump in the country. But this was long coming. The COVID-19 lockdown saw a surge in online gaming, with India becoming the world’s fastest-growing mobile gaming market in 2020, per KPMG. Now, the country is estimated to have more than 500 million gamers, with Grand View Research projecting the market to sustain a double-digit growth till 2030, reaching $35 billion.

More Indian studios are building original intellectual property, experimenting with scalable formats and aiming for global audiences. That reflects in the massive popularity of Indian IP games like FAU-G, Ludo King, and Indus Battle Royale.

YouTube also plays a powerful role in shaping how children approach gaming, with the massive popularity of gaming channels like PewDiePie, IShowSpeed, Kai Cenat, and Techno Gamerz. These creators play popular titles with a mix of high-energy commentary, humour, and creative gameplay.

“The kids are introduced to gaming via YouTube, and they learn how to play based on what they see,” Vinodh comments.

Anuj Sahani, Head of KIGI and Director of Publishing at KRAFTON India, says India has transitioned from a largely consumption-driven gaming market to an emerging development ecosystem.

“A significant change in the ecosystem is that young users are increasingly learning logic, design thinking, and programming fundamentals by building interactive experiences, not just consuming them.”

“This expands the entry point into game development beyond traditional engineering pathways,” he highlights.

The rise of game engines, creator platforms, and embedded scripting tools has dramatically lowered technical barriers. But scale is only part of the story.

Imitation, Aesthetics, and the Loop

From an industry perspective, an eight-year-old experimenting with Luau is not just playing. They are accumulating systems-thinking experience.

Vinodh sees both the opportunity and the risk.

“Game design is a very interesting problem, and I like that so many kids are into building their own games,” he says. But he worries about imitation.

“Like anyone who starts a new hobby, kids start with imitating games that they see, but some games have concepts of gambling in them and some monetary system that will be traded,” he warns. “This makes gaming mostly about how lucky you are, which increases the time you spend in it.”

He is particularly struck by his younger cousin’s [Vishwas] motivation. “The only reason he wants to build a game in Roblox is to earn Robux by selling his game and then spending that in other games to collect various brainrots.”

Modern gaming platforms have developed extraordinarily sophisticated behavioural systems. They now use reinforcement learning to design a game, teaching an AI agent to learn to play through trial-and-error and using those strategies to create challenging NPCs and game levels. They optimise incentives, timing, and reward schedules at scale. They blur the line between entertainment and economics.

Creation then becomes a means to design monetisation and accumulate currency through predatory game mechanics.

“Roblox's slot-machining model doesn't have a lot to do with player skill or honing it,” Vinodh highlights.

There is also an aesthetic difference that troubles him.

“When it came to graphics and the look of the game, optimisation was an important conversation we had with friends growing up,” he says. Hardware limitations made optimisation a point of pride.

Today, even mid-range laptops come with 8GB of RAM, and the games children gravitate toward are often deliberately low-poly to support massive multiplayer environments. “There’s no aesthetic pleasure to be had in this low-effort game created over a weekend,” he argues.

Vinodh sees modern online games as perpetually unfinished, endlessly updated to sustain engagement. His sharpest critique lingers. “Roblox games have come to represent everything wrong with the internet: gambling, engagement farming, micro transactions, and collectables being paywalled for real money.”

An Editable Childhood

But there are some safeguards.

Roblox uses a tiered age-verification system that combines facial age estimation and optional ID checks to unlock features such as chat and voice, according to the platform’s safety guidelines. Users are grouped into age bands that control communication and content access, with stricter limits for under-13s. Guardrails include chat filtering, parental controls, content ratings, and moderation systems.

However, since basic access doesn’t require verification, risks remain on this large user-generated platform. The UK research and innovation agency Revealing Reality found “deeply disturbing risks” in an investigation last year, identifying that children could still encounter inappropriate content and interact with adults despite safety controls.

“More concerning still, these environments offer plenty of open but secluded corners of virtual maps where users can pull someone aside for what amounts to a private voice conversation, away from other players,” it noted.

Despite these concerns, what makes this moment historically significant is not simply that children are spending time online. It is that they are building within those spaces.

Back at the laptop, Vishwas is still designing his tycoon game. He talks about leaderboards and brainrots with equal seriousness. Meanwhile, Surya admits that coding is hard, but is determined to try.

They do not see the game, any game, as a finished world. They see it as editable.

“Raksul is showing very rapid growth momentum, and this has increased our system complexity… To support this, we are seeking very good engineering talent,” Toshiharu Takeuchi, CTO, Raksul, tells AIM.

Starting with a handful of employees, the company doesn’t want to extend beyond 100 in headcount.

Unlike traditional GCCs that scale through large hiring volumes, Raksul is adopting a “nano GCC” approach—starting with a small, high-density team focused on solving high-impact problems using AI.

“It’s not about building capacity anymore. It’s about building capabilities,” Sujit Kulkarni, Site Leader, Raksul India, highlighting a broader shift in GCC strategy.

The Bengaluru centre will focus on core platform systems such as authentication, identity platforms, and shared infrastructure—critical components that cut across Raksul’s multi-service ecosystem.

“India will focus on deep expertise in platform engineering, shared infrastructure, and identity systems… these systems interact with multiple Raksul businesses,” Takeuchi noted.

AI is embedded across Raksul’s entire software development lifecycle—from coding to testing and reviews—fundamentally reshaping how teams operate.

As a result, the company is prioritising senior-level hiring to ensure architectural rigour and effective AI implementation.

Raksul’s model reflects a broader shift in how engineering teams are structured in the AI era, moving away from traditional pyramid models.

“Traditional pyramid-like structures are going away. We are focusing on highly qualified engineers who can work with AI agents as colleagues,” Kulkarni mentioned.

The company is also actively minimising repetitive and operational tasks, which are increasingly being handled by AI systems.

“Any task which is repetitive in nature should be reduced… this is not what we expect from humans,” he said.

Raksul’s GCC strategy follows a three-location model spanning Tokyo, Vietnam, and Bengaluru, with each hub playing a clearly defined and complementary role. Tokyo anchors product strategy and customer understanding, leveraging its proximity to the core market.

Vietnam focuses on execution and development, driving delivery efficiency. Bengaluru, meanwhile, is positioned as the centre for platform engineering and architectural leadership, shaping the company’s core technology capabilities and decision-making.

“The technical guidance and leadership will come from Bengaluru,” Takeuchi mentioned, underscoring India’s growing strategic importance.

Raksul made it clear that its India strategy is not driven by cost savings, but by capability building and innovation.

Instead, the focus is on enabling decision-making and ownership within the India team.

“I want the India team to be involved in decision-making… not just filling resource gaps,” he added.

The company’s broader vision is to build a unified, AI-powered platform to support small and mid-sized businesses (SMBs), particularly in Japan, where demographic challenges are reshaping the economy.

“We want to provide a one-stop solution for SMBs… integrating HR, finance, procurement, and operations,” Takeuchi mentioned.

This ambition is expected to create complex engineering challenges—further reinforcing the need for advanced platform capabilities in India.

Raksul’s approach reflects a growing trend among global companies—especially from Japan—towards smaller, high-impact GCCs that prioritise innovation over scale.

“Instead of large teams, companies are now looking at high-density teams with strong capabilities,” Kulkarni observed.

title: Maharashtra Approves AI Policy 2026 With ₹10,000 Crore Investment, Targets 1.5 Lakh Jobs
content:
Around two lakh youth will be trained in AI technologies to create a workforce aligned with emerging industry demand.

What Actually Matters.

Maharashtra approved an AI Policy for 2026 with a significant investment.

The policy aims to create numerous jobs and train many young people in AI.

The Maharashtra Cabinet on April 29 approved the state’s Artificial Intelligence Policy 2026, outlining an ambitious roadmap to attract ₹10,000 crore in investments and generate 1.5 lakh employment opportunities in the sector, as per reports.

The policy focuses on building a robust AI ecosystem through infrastructure, innovation, and skill development. As part of this, the government plans to establish six AI Centres of Excellence and five AI Innovation Cities across the state.

State Electronics, Information Technology and AI Minister Ashish Shelar said the primary objective of the policy is large-scale job creation, supported by targeted skilling initiatives. Around two lakh youth will be trained in AI technologies to create a workforce aligned with emerging industry demands.

To drive adoption, the policy aims to develop 50 AI tools and use cases across sectors, while supporting businesses in integrating AI into their operations. The state will provide 2,000 GPUs to strengthen the computing infrastructure critical for AI deployment. Moreover, 5,000 MSMEs will receive financial assistance to adopt AI technologies.

In a bid to boost innovation, the government will set up a ₹500 crore venture capital fund to support AI startups and potential unicorns, with the state contributing ₹250 crore. Subsidies for machinery purchases will also be extended to AI-driven industries.

The policy also includes plans to develop AI-based agents to simplify citizen-government interactions, as well as financial support for building datasets in Marathi and other regional languages.

Notably, Maharashtra aims to become the first state in India to introduce a dedicated framework for ethical AI.

title: Musk Accuses OpenAI Executives of Turning Charity Into Business
content:
Musk is expected to continue his testimony on April 29. A verdict could arrive as early as mid-May.

What Actually Matters.

Elon Musk is suing OpenAI, alleging it abandoned its original charitable mission.

Musk claims OpenAI transitioned into a profit-driven enterprise, contrary to its founding ethos.

Billionaire Elon Musk took the stand on April 28 in a closely watched trial that could influence the future of OpenAI, portraying his lawsuit as a defence of charitable principles rather than a business dispute.

Musk is suing OpenAI, along with Co-Founder and CEO Sam Altman and President Greg Brockman, alleging they abandoned the organisation’s original mission of developing AI for the benefit of humanity. He claims the company instead evolved into a profit-driven enterprise, contrary to its founding ethos.

“If we make it OK to loot a charity, the entire foundation of charitable giving in America will be destroyed,” Musk told the court. “That’s my concern.”

He further asserted that OpenAI was fundamentally his creation. “I came up with the idea, the name, recruited the key people, taught them everything I know, provided all of the initial funding,” Musk said, adding that it was “specifically meant to be for a charity that does not benefit any individual person.”

Attorneys for OpenAI pushed back strongly. Attorney William Savitt, representing the company and Altman, argued that Musk himself had previously supported transitioning OpenAI towards a for-profit model and sought greater control over the organisation.

According to Savitt, Musk wanted “the keys to the kingdom” and only turned against OpenAI after failing to secure a leadership role. “We are here because Mr Musk didn’t get his way,” he told jurors.

The defence also emphasised that OpenAI’s creation of a for-profit arm in 2019 was essential to securing the massive computing resources and talent needed to compete with rivals such as Google DeepMind. Investments from partners, including Microsoft, were framed as necessary for scaling advanced AI systems.

Musk is seeking $150 billion in damages from OpenAI and Microsoft, with any proceeds directed to OpenAI’s nonprofit arm. He is also asking the court to restore OpenAI to a nonprofit structure and remove Altman and Brockman from leadership roles.

The case includes allegations of breach of charitable trust and unjust enrichment, raising broader questions about how nonprofit-founded tech organisations evolve into commercial entities.

The trial has also revived long-standing disagreements over AI safety. Musk testified that concerns about AI risks were central to OpenAI’s founding.

The outcome of the trial could have far-reaching consequences. It may influence OpenAI’s potential IPO, which analysts suggest could value the company near $1 trillion, and shape public perception of AI governance.

It also highlights growing tensions in the AI industry, where organisations increasingly balance public-interest narratives with the capital-intensive realities of building advanced systems.

Musk, who later founded AI startup xAI, which is now integrated into SpaceX, is expected to continue his testimony on April 29. A verdict could arrive as early as mid-May.

title: AWS Launches Desktop AI Assistant That Connects Apps and Data
content:
Amazon Quick connects with tools such as Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, Salesforce, Zoom, Slack, and Jira.

What Actually Matters.

Amazon Web Services launched Amazon Quick, a new desktop AI assistant.

This AI assistant integrates with various enterprise applications and local files.

Amazon Web Services has launched a desktop application for its AI assistant, Amazon Quick, that can work across enterprise applications, local files, and workflows.

The assistant connects with tools such as Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, Salesforce, Zoom, Slack, and Jira, allowing users to access and act on information without switching between applications.

It runs locally on a user’s device, remains active in the background, and builds context over time using data from emails, calendars, documents, and other systems.

“Quick is built to break you free from those walled gardens,” Jigar Thakkar, Vice President of Agentic AI for Business at Amazon Quick, said in a statement. “Whether you use Slack or Teams, Outlook or Gmail, Salesforce or ServiceNow, Quick works across all of them seamlessly.”

The company said the assistant indexes documents and interactions to create a “personal knowledge graph,” enabling it to generate responses grounded in an organisation’s data. It also learns from user behaviour across sessions, improving personalisation and task execution over time.

Amazon Quick can automate workflows that span multiple tools. For example, users can request it to extract data from a browser-based system, process it using a local script, and insert results into a document in a single command.

AWS said the assistant moves AI usage from reactive prompts to proactive assistance. Running continuously in the background, it can surface relevant documents, flag scheduling conflicts, and prepare context for meetings without user input.

“Combining what Quick knows about you with its proactive, always-on approach helps shift you from reacting to the day as it happens to actually getting ahead of your to-do list,” Thakkar said.

The company also introduced new capabilities alongside the desktop app. Users can generate presentations, dashboards, documents, and images directly within the interface. A preview feature allows users to build custom applications and dashboards using natural language, with outputs connected to live business data.

AWS said integrations are expanding, including new Microsoft 365 extensions that embed Quick into Outlook, Word, Excel, and PowerPoint. Additional connectors include Google Workspace, Airtable, Dropbox, and Microsoft Teams.

The company stated that user data processed by Quick remains private and is not used to train external AI models.

The launch comes as enterprises seek AI systems that can operate across fragmented software environments while maintaining compliance and data control.
